Hi, nice to meet you too. Well, honestly, my job sent me. I do general maintenance, and lately I just keep forgetting... well, everything. Scheduled callbacks, work orders, even just basic follow-ups I promised people. It’s piled up so much. 

Like last Tuesday, I was supposed to fix this leaky P-trap in unit 3B, and the tenant has this little dog—a Pomeranian, I think? Cutest thing, but it barks at absolutely everything. My sister had a Pomeranian back in the 90s named Buster, and he used to chew straight through the drywall, if you can believe that. We had to patch the hallway baseboards like four times because he'd just go right through the plaster... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. The work orders. Yeah, I completely forgot to go back and finish the sink, and that kind of thing keeps happening. So work basically sent me here to get it sorted out before I lose my shot at moving up to a lead position. I really need that promotion, but my desk is just a mountain of forgotten slips right now.

Yeah, honestly... I remember being exactly this way way back in grade school, long before I had all this pressure from work. Like, I think about my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable. She had this massive terrarium in the back of the classroom with a bearded dragon in it. Spiky little guy, but really docile. I used to get to feed it crickets sometimes. Crickets are so loud, though, aren't they? We actually had a huge cricket infestation in the boiler room of one of our apartment buildings just last month. The tenants on the first floor were going absolutely crazy because they chirp right at that frequency that just drills into your skull when you're trying to sleep. I had to call pest control, but the guy they sent out was like two hours late, and he parked his van right blocking the dumpster, which is a huge violation for the trash pickup... 

Wait, sorry. You asked about when I was a kid. Right. 

But yeah, Mrs. Gable and the rest of my teachers, they always told my parents I was really bright. But I was just constantly misplacing my papers. Like, every single day. I'd miss parts of the directions they gave, and they always had to come by my desk and give me extra reminders just to get me to finish my classwork. So it's definitely been happening since I was little.

Not really, no. Sitting still isn't really a problem for me. I can actually sit in my work van for hours if I need to. Speaking of the van, I had to take it into the shop on Friday because the AC just completely gave out. It was blowing this hot, musty air, and in this heat, it's just miserable. The mechanic said it was a Freon leak, which is funny because it reminded me of this ancient refrigerator we had to haul out of unit 4A last month. 

The tenant moved out and just unplugged it, but they left a whole bag of tilapia in the freezer. Oh my gosh, the smell when we opened that door. We had to use industrial bleach on the floorboards, and the lady across the hall, Mrs. Higgins, came out into the hallway complaining about the odor. She was wearing this bright pink bathrobe with little flamingos all over it. I mean, who even buys a flamingo bathrobe? It was so bright it practically hurt my eyes, and she had these matching fuzzy slippers... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right, being restless. Yeah, no, I don't feel like I have to be moving around or anything like that. I'm fine sitting still.

Alcohol? Oh, hardly ever. I mean, maybe a beer at a barbecue once in a blue moon, but that's really it. I actually went to this huge neighborhood cookout over the Fourth of July weekend. My buddy Dave was hosting it, and he has this massive, custom-built smoker in his backyard. I swear, the thing looks like a small locomotive. He spent, like, fourteen hours smoking this brisket, and he kept talking about the specific type of hickory wood he used. He ordered it special from some farm out in Tennessee, I think. 

He was so proud of it, but honestly, his wife makes this potato salad that completely steals the show. She puts dill in it, which I never thought would work, but it's amazing. She actually gave me the recipe, but I completely lost the index card she wrote it on. I put it in my glove compartment, and then when I went to look for it, all I found were these old toll receipts from when I drove up to see my aunt in upstate New York three years ago. The tolls up there are ridiculous, by the way. You can't even drive ten miles without hitting another plaza...

Wait, sorry. Alcohol. Yeah, no, I don't really drink much at all. None, really.

Depressed? No, not really. I mean, I get frustrated sometimes with things, but not depressed. Like yesterday, I was so annoyed because I had to go fix this shattered window in unit 2B. The tenant's kid threw a literal baseball right through the glass. I mean, who lets their kid pitch a hardball inside a living room? 

Anyway, the glass went everywhere, all over this really nice area rug they had. I was trying to sweep it up, but management just ordered these cheap new brooms and the bristles are way too stiff. They just flick the little glass shards around instead of actually sweeping them. I tried telling my supervisor, Carl, that we need the softer nylon ones for indoor jobs, but he barely even looked up from his phone. He's totally obsessed with this online auction site right now. They were shaped like little frogs, and their eyes lit up. I thought my sister would get a kick out of them because she just redid her whole backyard patio. She put down these really nice flagstones, but she had to hire this guy to level the ground first, and he took forever. He was always showing up late, driving this beat-up old truck that sounded like it was missing a muffler. I swear, the whole neighborhood knew when he was arriving. Oh, wait, sorry. Memory. Right. No, it hasn't gotten worse lately. It's just always been like this.

Oh... um, harm me? No, no one is trying to hurt me, I don't think. I try to be very nice to everyone who comes into the shop.

Well... I guess maybe a little? I feel terrible even admitting it, because I know I should be grateful for my work and I really don't want to sound like I'm just complaining.

I really hope you don't think I'm just being lazy. I still try to keep everything organized, I promise! It's just hard to find that same joy I used to have. Do you think it's okay to go through little phases like that, where you just sort of lose your spark for a bit?

Well... let's see. I'd say... maybe around a year and eight months? That's when I first started noticing the voices and... well, those strange smells I mentioned before, and getting so worried about the customers checking up on us. 

I know that sounds like a really long time to let something go on without saying anything. I'm sorry I didn't get help sooner. I just kept hoping it was stress from the shop and that it would pass, and I really didn't want to make a fuss or bother anyone about it. I hope it's not too late to try and figure it out? I really am trying to be proactive now, I promise.

I don't know, this charged up.

I just keep finding extra jobs for myself, constantly, like I'm on some kind of mission. 

Take my routes, for example. I’ve been staying up and completely rewriting all my route plans. And I don't mean just glancing at the GPS—I mean getting out the physical maps, cross-referencing the construction schedules, trying to shave off two miles here or avoid a tricky intersection there, recalculating all my fuel stops to save a couple of pennies a gallon... it’s a whole massive production. And then, even when I’m strictly off the clock, I’m calling up the new guys at the company. I'll just be checking on the new drivers after hours, calling them at 8 or 9 PM when I really should be winding down. I just feel like I have to make sure they know how to handle the steep grades, or asking if they actually manually checked their tire pressure, because these kids today just rely on dashboard sensors, you know? 

And if I’m not doing truck stuff, I’m tearing through the house. I fixed the loose floorboards on the back porch that have been sitting there for three years, I repainted the trim in the garage, I even started taking apart the lawnmower engine on a Tuesday night just to see if I could get it running a little smoother. My wife is looking at me like I’ve got two heads because I just can’t stop. If I try to force myself to just sit on the couch and watch a show with her, my leg starts bouncing, I get all jittery... I just feel completely antsy if I sit still for too long. I have to be moving, I have to be fixing something or planning something, or I just feel like I'm gonna crawl right out of my own skin. It's just go, go, go, all the time.

Well, I guess... I mean, "unlike my usual self" is a funny way to put it, because I still feel like me, you know? Just... maybe a louder, faster version of me. But if you ask my wife, or some of the guys at the depot, they might say something different. Like, I’ve been driving a truck for thirty years, right? You get a reputation for being steady. Reliable. You don't make waves, you just get the freight from point A to point B. 

But lately... I don't know, I haven't really noticed myself acting all that crazy or anything. I mean, sure, I'm doing more, like I said with the projects and the routes and all that, and I'm a little more irritable, but I wouldn't say I'm some completely different person. I'm just getting things done. But then again, my dispatcher did pull me aside the other day and asked if I was drinking too much coffee, which is ridiculous because I always drink the same amount of coffee, but he said I was talking so fast on the radio he couldn't understand me. And I guess I have been a little more... forward, maybe? Like, usually I just nod and take my paperwork, but last week I spent twenty minutes lecturing the shipping clerk about how inefficient their loading dock schedule is, and I drew up a whole diagram on the back of a manifest to show him how to fix it. He just looked at me like I was from Mars. 

So, I don't know if I'd say I'm noticeably unlike my usual self, because to me, it just makes sense in the moment. I'm just trying to improve things, you know? But I suppose other people are looking at me a little sideways. Does that make sense? I mean, what do you even consider "usual" when things are just running so much faster than they normally do?

Hearing or seeing things? No, no, definitely not. I mean, let's be real here, if I was seeing things that weren't on the road, I'd have handed over my CDL a long time ago. You can't be hauling eighty thousand pounds of freight down a steep grade in the rain if your eyes are playing tricks on you. The DOT doesn't mess around with that, and neither do I. I’ve passed every physical they’ve thrown at me since nineteen ninety-four. My vision is sharp, my hearing is fine... well, maybe a little ringing in the left ear from having the window cracked for thirty years, but I'm definitely not hearing voices or anything spooky like that. 

And as for special powers or some kind of secret mission? Nah, nothing crazy like that. I mean, I told you earlier that I feel like I could run the whole logistics company, but that’s not because I think I'm Superman or something. It’s just because I’ve been doing this for three decades and I actually pay attention to how things work. I see how the dispatchers mess up the routing, and I know exactly how to fix it. That's not a superpower, Doc, that's just good old-fashioned experience and elbow grease. 

Like, just last Thursday, I was explaining to the terminal manager—because he was trying to tell me my new route plan was too aggressive—I told him, "Look, buddy, I don't have a magic wand, I just know how to read a topographic map better than your computer program does." So, I don't think I'm on some divine mission or anything. I just think I'm the only one actually operating at a hundred percent right now while everyone else is sleepwalking through their shift. But no, I'm firmly planted in reality. I just happen to be moving through it a heck of a lot faster than the rest of them.

Hospitalized? Oh, lord, no. No, definitely not. I’ve never been in the hospital for anything except when I blew out my knee stepping off a loading dock back in '06. I'm not, you know, out of my mind or anything like that. 

But as for disrupting things... well, I guess if I'm being completely honest, it hasn't exactly been smooth sailing. Like I mentioned, I don't just drive, I do a lot of the driver-sales work too, right? So you're not just dropping a trailer and getting a signature; you're talking to the receiving managers, checking their inventory, trying to set up the next run or upsell a freight package. And lately... man, because my brain is just firing on all cylinders, jumping from the route plan to the fuel efficiency to the dock layout, I've been sort of dropping the ball on the basics. I’ll be on the phone with dispatch, or even right there standing in front of a client, and they’ll be giving me a gate code or a specific delivery window, and I’ll have to stop them and go, "Wait, hold on, run that by me again?" I'm having them repeat details that I absolutely should have tracked the first time. It's embarrassing, honestly. And a couple of my sales follow-ups—these are accounts I've been working with for years—they completely slipped through the cracks just because I was chasing way too many ideas at once. I get so wrapped up in reinventing the whole system that I forget to actually follow through on the day-to-day stuff. 

And then at home... man, that's the part that actually bothers me the most. Because in my head, I thought I was doing everybody this huge favor, right? Fixing the porch, tuning up the mower, getting all these projects done that have been sitting there forever. But I look around, and... I can see it. My wife, and my daughter too, they’ve just been walking on eggshells around me lately. My daughter usually jokes around with me the second I walk in the door, but now it's like they're both afraid to say the wrong thing, or they don't want to interrupt me when I'm in the middle of tearing through the garage because I'm so keyed up. I don't mean to be short with them, I really don't, but I'm just moving so fast. I'm supposed to be helping out around the house, being a good husband and taking the load off my wife, but I can tell I’m just adding strain. It's like my energy is just sucking all the air out of the room. So, yeah, no hospitals, but I guess... I guess it is messing things up a bit more than I wanted to admit.

Hi. It's nice to meet you too. 

Well, I'm here because I've been really bothered by this scar on my wrist lately. I mean, I know it’s probably not as bad as it looks to me, but... I just can't seem to stop focusing on it. When I’m at church, or sitting around the table playing bridge, I keep feeling like everyone’s eyes go right to it. It just feels like it’s the very first thing they notice about me now.

Yes, I do. Like I was just saying, deep down I know it's probably not as bad as my mind makes it out to be. But... yes, I think it looks very unattractive and abnormal. That's exactly why I feel like everyone's eyes go straight to it when I'm at church or sitting at the bridge table. Even if I try to tell myself otherwise, I just assume they see this ugly mark and it's the only thing they're looking at.

Yes, I do. Before I leave the house, I usually stop at the hall mirror and check my wrist a few times. I definitely try to hide it... I'll test out different sleeves, or put on a wide bracelet to see if that covers it up. And sometimes I'll ask my husband if it looks obvious before we go anywhere. He always tells me it’s barely there, but I still feel the need to check.

Yes, I do sometimes. I try not to let it stop me entirely, but... I have skipped some of my choir and theater volunteer commitments lately. I just get so caught up at the house trying to make sure my wrist won't be noticed, and sometimes it just feels easier to stay home. 

It’s actually affecting my job a bit, too. I do bookkeeping from home, and... well, I’ve been late turning in some of my work recently because I'm just so distracted by all of this.

No, I really don't think so. Um, the anxiety is pretty much just about the scar. If it were completely gone... well, I'm sure I'd feel fine. I've always enjoyed going to church and playing bridge, and I never used to get nervous about being around people before I started worrying so much about my wrist.

Hi, it's really nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for seeing me. 

Um... well, my manager actually suggested I come in. I hope that's alright. It's really not a huge deal, I promise, I've just been... well, I guess I sort of scared everyone at work recently. I didn't mean to, of course! I just, um... I started kind of freezing up in the middle of service. Or I'd do things a little out of order, I guess. 

Like, the other day, I was just standing over by the soda station holding the cash drawer key, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud instead of actually closing out the checks. It sounds so silly and embarrassing when I say it out loud, doesn't it? I think I just got a little overwhelmed or mixed up. Is... is that the kind of thing you need to know?

Oh, no, not at all. I really hope it didn't sound like I was having a panic attack or anything like that! I promise I'm not making a big fuss out of it. I don't really feel scared when it happens... I just feel kind of, um, blank, I guess? Or maybe just really distracted. But I definitely don't feel any intense fear. 

Is... is that an okay answer? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information and not making it sound worse than it actually is.

Oh, no, definitely not. I know exactly who I am and where I am, I promise! The restaurant feels completely real, and... and I still feel like myself. I'm really not losing touch with reality or anything scary like that. I just get... well, a little stuck, maybe? Like my focus just sort of wanders off for a minute and I forget what I'm doing. 

I hope that makes sense? I just really want to be helpful and give you the right answers, so please let me know if I'm not explaining things well enough for you.

Oh, no, definitely not. Um, I actually try to stay really upbeat! You know, working in a restaurant, you kind of have to keep a smile on for the customers, and I really don't mind it. I don't feel sad or depressed at all, I promise. 

I mean, everybody has a slightly off day sometimes, right? But nothing serious like what you're asking about. My mood is really, totally okay. I'm generally a pretty happy person! 

Is... is that helpful? I know you're trying to figure out what's going on with me, and I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right pieces to the puzzle. I hope it's okay that I don't feel down!

Oh, no, I don't think so. Everything has been... well, pretty normal, honestly! I mean, the restaurant gets a little busy sometimes, but it's really nothing I can't handle. I definitely wouldn't call it upsetting or, um, overly stressful or anything like that. 

I really hope that's okay? I know sometimes doctors look for a big stressful event to explain things, and I don't want to make your job harder by not having a good reason for why this is happening. But honestly, my life has been pretty good! Is... is that alright? I just want to make sure I'm giving you what you need.

Um... well... I really don't want you to think I'm, you know, crazy or anything. It's honestly probably just because I'm tired after a long shift, I promise! But... well, sometimes, like when we're closing up the restaurant, or when I'm just home alone in my kitchen, I... I do hear a woman's voice. 

She'll just say my name, or sometimes she tells me I'm doing the drawer count wrong. It sounds so normal and clear that I actually answer her out loud before I even realize that... well, that nobody else is there, and nobody else heard it. 

I mean, it's just my brain playing tricks on me because I'm working hard, right? I really hope that doesn't sound too strange or bad. I just want to make sure I'm being completely honest with you so you have all the right information to help me. Is... is it okay that I told you that?

Well, I came in because the doctor who did my insurance physical recently said my weight was too low. I don't really see it, though. To me, I just look lean. I mean, I'm a painter, so I spend my whole day up and down on ladders and working long hours. It just seems normal to me, but they told me I needed to come in.

I mean... yeah, I guess I am. Like, if I have a client dinner or eat something with bread, and I see the scale go up even just a little bit, I get pretty tense. I usually start cutting back the next day just to make sure it doesn't stick.

I wouldn't say I feel fat, exactly, but I definitely don't see what they see. It's more like... when I catch myself in a mirror, or if I see photos of myself standing next to one of my murals, I just really focus on my shape. I basically judge my whole day by whether my stomach and my face look sharp enough. If they don't look lean, it really bothers me.

Yeah, I suppose I do. Most days, I just keep it to coffee in the morning, and... maybe I'll have a protein bar between paint jobs. Then just a small dinner at night. I mean, eating a full meal during the day just feels like it would really slow me down, so it's easier to just keep it light. And it helps keep my weight where I want it.
No, I've never done that. If I feel like I ate too much, I just cut back the next day like I mentioned. But making myself throw up... no, that's not something I do.

Yeah, actually, that's why I came in to see you. I had to do a physical recently for my insurance, and the doctor there told me my weight was too low for my height. I don't really see it that way, to be honest. To me, I just look lean from being up and down ladders and working long days. But yeah, he was the one who brought it up and said it was an issue.

Well, it's not so much that I'm actively trying to lose more right now, but I definitely don't want to gain any. I mean, if the scale goes up even just a little bit... like after a dinner with a client or if I eat something with bread... I get pretty tense about it. So I just make sure to start cutting back the next day so the extra weight doesn't stick.

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my job is pretty physical—moving ladders around, painting all day—so I get tired at the end of a shift, sure. But I wouldn't say I feel weak or run-down from what I eat. I feel fine, honestly. I always seem to have plenty of energy to get my work done.
I'm about 5'10", and last time I checked, I weighed around 125 pounds.

Yeah, I guess I do. I mean, most days I just keep it to coffee... maybe a protein bar between paint jobs, and then a small dinner later on. Honestly, eating a full meal just feels like it would slow me down too much while I'm working. So sticking to that routine keeps my weight where it is, and I just prefer it that way.

Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I guess what brings me in is that... ever since I stopped working, I just can't seem to slow down. I'm up and moving from one little job to the next all day long. It's like I still have a crew waiting on me or something, and I just can't turn it off.

No, not really. I mean, I'm not running around because I'm thrilled about something. I don't get these big bursts of excitement or anything like that. It's just... I can't sit still. It's not a mood thing, it's just this feeling like I have to be doing something.

No, I wouldn't say that. I don't get, you know, strange thoughts or worries stuck in my head. It's not my mind telling me I have to do things to get rid of a thought... it's really just my body. I just feel restless if I'm not moving around and doing something, but there's no specific thought driving it.

No, I don't really worry all that much. I mean, everyday things are just... everyday things. I don't sit around stressing over bills or what's going to happen tomorrow. Like I said, it's more just this physical need to be moving, not that I'm anxious or worried about anything in particular.

Yeah, I was. I mean, even back in grade school, my teachers used to say I was bright but... scattered, I guess. I was always losing my pencils, or I'd just call out answers without waiting my turn. And they always had to give me reminders to actually finish my work before I could go out for recess. So, yeah, it's really been like this my whole life.

Well, it’s good to meet you too, Doctor. I suppose... well, I’m here because things at work have just gotten incredibly frustrating lately, and it's starting to cause a real problem on the floor. I’m a first-line supervisor in retail, you see. Have been for a good while. I got my bachelor's degree years ago and I’ve always prided myself on communication, running a tight ship, making sure the sales workers know exactly what they need to be doing before the doors open. 

But recently, it’s like... well, I came in because when I try to explain the inventory numbers to the team, or when I'm trying to go over the weekend schedule—which is always a massive headache to organize anyway with everyone wanting Saturdays off—my words just start jumping. I’ll start off talking about the delivery trucks out back, making sure they get unloaded properly, but then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, and then before I know it I'm bringing up the church grill from the Sunday cookout, and then I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice when he called me about the pallets last week. 

It makes sense while I'm saying it, but I look at my employees and they just stand there holding their clipboards. They look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. They get these wide, blank eyes, like I lost them three sentences ago. And I try to backtrack to get us back to the inventory counts, but there's just so much I need to communicate to them and it all just keeps tangling together when I speak.

Energized? High? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite. I’m just... I'm exhausted, Doctor. You have to understand, running a retail floor at my age—I'm 59, you know—it takes a lot out of you even on a good day. You’re constantly on your feet, walking the aisles, checking the end-caps to make sure the corporate promotional displays are set up exactly to the planogram, dealing with vendors coming in the back door... 

And lately, with all this trouble I've been having, with my words getting all tangled up and the employees just staring at me like I'm speaking a foreign language, well, it's incredibly draining. It takes so much mental effort just to get through a simple ten-minute morning huddle now. I go home at the end of my shift and I just want to collapse in my recliner. There's no extra energy, no feeling revved up or on top of the world or anything like that. I wake up at 5:30 AM every single morning, I have my one cup of black coffee—same routine I've had since I got my degree, really—and I just try to push through the day. 

So, no, definitely not energized. It's just a heavy, heavy feeling trying to keep the store running when I can't even get through the weekly numbers without my brain pulling my sentences in ten different directions. It just wears a person out.

Voices? Like... people talking when there's nobody there? No, Doctor, I haven't heard anything like that. The store is loud enough as it is, you know? Between the overhead music—which corporate insists on playing the exact same playlist every single day, I swear I hear those same twelve pop songs in my sleep—and the registers beeping, and the stockroom carts clattering over the tile floors, there's always noise. But it's all real noise, if you know what I mean. 

When I'm alone, like when I finally get home and sit down in my recliner... no, it's quiet. Well, I mean, the refrigerator hums, and sometimes I hear the neighbor's dog, but no voices. My problem isn't hearing things that aren't there, it's just... it's just getting the things that *are* in my head out of my mouth in an order that makes sense to my team. Like I was saying about the inventory counts, I know the numbers, I have the spreadsheets right there on my clipboard, but when I open my mouth to say "we're short on the seasonal end-cap displays," it just spirals into something else entirely. But nobody is whispering to me or talking to me when I'm by myself, no. Just my own thoughts, getting tangled up.

A stroke? Or a head injury? No, no, definitely nothing like that. I haven't hit my head, haven't been in any accidents. The last time I was in a hospital for anything physical was, oh, it must have been when I had my gallbladder taken out back in... well, that was a long time ago. But recently? No. 

I mean, I'm careful at work. We have strict safety protocols in the stockroom, you know, OSHA guidelines and all that. You can't just have people leaving pallets lying around or stacking boxes too high, especially the heavy liquid detergent boxes, those are a nightmare if they tip over. I always make sure the team is wearing their back braces if they're doing heavy lifting, and I certainly don't go climbing the tall ladders myself anymore, not at my age. We have the younger guys for that. 

And as for a stroke... well, I haven't had any of those warning signs they talk about on the television commercials, you know? My face isn't drooping, I can raise both my arms just fine, my vision hasn't gone blurry. I haven't collapsed or felt numb on one side. It's really just my speech, just the way my sentences get all scrambled up when I'm trying to direct the floor staff. It's not that my mouth isn't working, it's that the ideas just... they just run into each other. But physically, my head is perfectly fine. No bumps, no bruises, no strokes. Just a lot of frustration.

Plotting against me? Harm me? No, Doctor, no, I don't think anyone is out to get me. I mean, retail is competitive, sure, and sometimes the district manager comes down hard on us if the shrink numbers are too high or if the payroll percentage creeps up past the target... but that's just business, you know? That's just the nature of the beast when you're managing a big box store. They want results, they want the shelves faced perfectly, they want the seasonal aisles flipped overnight from Halloween straight into Christmas, and they want it done with a skeleton crew. It's stressful, absolutely, and sometimes I feel like corporate is completely disconnected from the reality of what happens on the floor.

But as far as people actually trying to harm me? Or some kind of conspiracy against me personally? No, I don't feel that at all. The team I have, well, they're good kids mostly. A lot of college students working part-time, some older folks who just want to get out of the house. They get frustrated with me lately, sure, because of... well, because of what I've been telling you about, how my words just sort of derail when I'm trying to give them instructions. I can see it in their eyes, they get confused, maybe a little impatient when I start talking about the end-caps and suddenly I'm bringing up the pallet jack maintenance schedule in the middle of a sentence about promotional signage. But they aren't malicious. They aren't plotting anything. 

Even the vendors, the guys who deliver the soda and the chips, they can be pushy about getting prime shelf space, but that's just sales. Nobody is sneaking around trying to hurt me. My life is pretty simple, really. It's just the store, my recliner, my coffee... and this awful, awful trouble I'm having with my thoughts getting all jumbled up before they make it out of my mouth. But no, no plots, no enemies. Just a lot of confusion on my end.

Sleep? Needing less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, I feel like I could use more sleep, what with how exhausting the days have been lately. I mean, my sleep schedule is pretty set in stone, you know? I usually try to be in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 at the latest, right after the late local news. I like to catch the weather report because it really affects our foot traffic at the store—if they're calling for snow, even just a dusting, everybody rushes in for rock salt and milk, and I have to make sure the front end is staffed for the rush. 

So I watch the news, I turn off the TV, and I'm usually up by 5:30 AM. My alarm goes off, and I have my routine. I make my coffee—just a standard drip maker, none of those fancy pod machines, I like the smell of the grounds in the morning—and I sit in my recliner for about twenty minutes just to wake up before I get in the shower. I get my solid six and a half, maybe seven hours most nights. And I definitely feel it if I don't. 

Like last week, the overnight crew had an issue with the alarm system—the motion sensor by the receiving doors kept tripping, and the monitoring company called me at 2:00 in the morning. By the time I got it sorted out over the phone with the shift lead and finally got back to sleep, it was almost 3:30. When my alarm went off at 5:30, I was dragging. I felt it all day long. I had to drink three cups of coffee in the breakroom just to keep my eyes open while I was trying to review the shrink report, and even then, my head felt heavy. So no, I definitely don't have that thing where I don't need sleep. I need it, and I'm tired just like anybody else if I don't get enough of it. It's just... the exhaustion makes the talking worse, I think. When I'm tired, the words get even more tangled up. But my sleep itself, the amount I need, that hasn't changed at all.

Understanding other people? Oh, no, no trouble with that at all. My hearing is fine, and my comprehension is perfectly fine. I know exactly what everyone is saying to me. When the district manager calls and tells me we need to push the loyalty program harder because our store's sign-up rate dropped by two percent last quarter, I understand him loud and clear. When the cashiers tell me their registers are out of receipt paper, or a customer comes up to me looking for the automotive section, I know exactly what they want. 

It's actually very frustrating, you see, because I take in the information perfectly. I process it. Someone asks me a question, say, about where we moved the clearance items, and in my head, the answer is right there. I know they're on the back wall near the seasonal department. I understand their question completely. But then, when I open my mouth to tell them, the words that come out... well, they just aren't the ones I meant to say. Or they are, but they're mixed in with thoughts about the inventory sheets or the squeaky wheel on the flatbed cart I was just pushing. 

So the problem isn't coming in, it's going out. I'm taking everything in just fine. I read the company memos, I listen to the morning huddle, I hear the complaints about the breakroom refrigerator smelling like old tuna—which, by the way, I've asked them to clean out every Friday, but nobody ever does—and I understand all of it. Every single word. It's just my own words that are betraying me. So, no, understanding people isn't an issue at all. I just wish they could understand me as well as I understand them.

Seizures? No, no. I've never had a seizure. Not recently, not ever in my fifty-nine years. I mean, physically, I'm actually in pretty decent shape, all things considered. You know, working retail, you're on your feet all day. Those concrete floors with just that thin layer of commercial tile over them—they absolutely destroy your knees and your lower back over the years. I've got a bit of stiffness, sure, and sometimes if I'm helping unload a truck because the receiving department is short-staffed again, I'll definitely feel it the next morning in my lumbar. I take an ibuprofen and I'm fine. But seizures? No. 

Like, falling down and convulsing? Never. We actually had an incident at the store, oh, it must have been three or four years ago now, right before the Thanksgiving rush. A customer had a seizure right in the middle of the baking aisle. Aisle four. She just completely collapsed, knocked over a whole display of condensed milk and pie crusts. It was terrifying, to be completely honest with you. I had to sprint over there, we called 911 immediately, and I had my shift lead block off both ends of the aisle with shopping carts so people wouldn't crowd around her, and we just tried to make sure she didn't hit her head on the metal base decks of the shelving until the paramedics arrived. 

So I know what a seizure looks like, and I know how serious they can be. But no, I haven't had anything even remotely like that happen to me. My body works just fine, my heart is good, my blood pressure is usually fine... it's really just, well, like I was saying before, it's just the words that get all scrambled up on the way out. My brain doesn't shut down or make me shake or pass out or anything physical like that. Just the talking. So, no, definitely no seizures.

Finding the exact word? No, it's not really like that. It's not that I'm standing there snapping my fingers trying to remember if it's called a 'pallet jack' or a 'hand truck.' I know the words. My vocabulary is perfectly fine, I've got a bachelor's degree in business administration, I know how to speak. 

It's more like... well, like I was saying before, it's not that I can't find the word, it's that the wrong ones come out with it, or they all come out at once. Like yesterday, I was trying to tell my assistant manager, Dave—Dave's a good kid, been with us two years, but he needs a lot of direction—I was trying to tell him to make sure the endcaps were faced before closing. And in my head, the sentence was, 'Dave, please face the endcaps.' Simple, right? But what came out was something like, 'Dave, face the endcaps, the truck is late, the squeaky wheel on the cart, the tuna in the fridge.' It just... spilled out. All these thoughts that were in my head, they just latched onto the sentence I was trying to say. 

So the words I want are there, I don't have trouble finding them. They just get buried under everything else. It's incredibly frustrating because I can see the look on people's faces when it happens. Dave just stared at me for a second, then nodded and walked away, and I knew he didn't understand the part that actually mattered. But no, I don't sit there forgetting the names of things or struggling to find a specific word. The words are all there. There's just too many of them trying to get out the door at the same time, if that makes sense. Like a bottleneck at the registers on a Saturday afternoon when you only have two cashiers scheduled. You know what needs to happen, you know who needs to go where, but it's just a mess.

Suddenly? No, no, it wasn't like a light switch flipping off, or on, I suppose. It wasn't like I woke up one Tuesday and suddenly couldn't give Dave a straight instruction about the endcaps. It's been more of a... a gradual slide, I guess you could say. Like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it right away, but eventually, you're driving on the rim. 

I'd say it's been going on for about six months now. That's when I really started noticing it, or at least, that's when it became impossible to ignore. Because before that, maybe I'd have a little slip of the tongue, or I'd lose my train of thought for a second—which happens to everyone, right? Especially when you're managing a floor with twenty different things happening at once. But about six months ago, that's when the jumbled explanations really started. Emotionally flat? Less able to show feelings? No, I wouldn't say that at all. If anything, I feel things too much right now, mostly just sheer frustration. I mean, how could you not be frustrated when you can't even get a simple sentence out without it turning into a complete disaster?

They actually pulled me off the high-voltage EV work because my supervisor said people were worried I wasn't being safe. And at home... things are really bad. The fighting with my husband got so intense over all of this that he actually took me in for an emergency evaluation. So, yeah, it's affecting pretty much everything.
It's been about ten months. The voice, and... well, the whole thing with them tracking me, it's all been happening for about ten months now.

Yeah, I have. There were periods... well, for weeks at a time, I'd sleep maybe two or three hours a night. I would wake up way before dawn, and my mind was already right back in the garage. I just felt so energetic that laying there trying to sleep more felt like it would just waste time.

Yeah, I guess you could say that. I'll feel like I'm just... flying high, you know? Like I have the energy and the know-how to fix every single car in town. But it can switch pretty fast. Like, if I'm feeling that good and my husband asks why the dishes aren't done, or one of the other techs moves my socket set at the shop... I just blow up. I get so angry, like they're trying to hold me back or slow me down when I'm on a roll.

Yeah, actually. Um, there was a stretch... maybe a few weeks where things felt a lot more normal. I was sleeping a regular amount, and I wasn't rushing around trying to do a million things at once. But even then, during that quieter time, I still heard the man's voice in the garage. And I still knew, I mean, I still believed that my husband and my boss were keeping tabs on me and tracking what I was doing. So, yeah, it didn't stop just because my mood settled down.

No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated or angry sometimes, like I mentioned before, but I don't really get down or sad. Definitely not for two weeks straight. I just haven't felt that way.

Yeah, I'd say so. Most of this past year, honestly, has been taken over by those stretches. The times where I'm just full of energy, talking too fast, taking on way too much at the shop... I just feel driven, like I can't slow down no matter what. So, yeah, that's been the majority of the time.

Well, they sent me here from the station. I was just... I was moving the airway bags into a pattern. I knew it was the right pattern. Airway bags are heavy if you pack them wrong, you know? We had this one rookie who used to stuff the oxygen tubing in the wrong pocket and it would always get tangled. I hate tangled tubing. It reminds me of Christmas lights. My dad used to make me untangle the Christmas lights every single year in the freezing cold out in our garage... 

But anyway, I was putting the bags in the sequence and repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Just saying them. You have to say them or they get lost in the air. Kind of like radio static. Do you ever just listen to the static on the radio? Sometimes it sounds exactly like ocean waves. I went to the ocean once in Florida when I was ten, got a terrible sunburn on my shoulders... 

But yeah, my lieutenant, he came over and told me to stop. He told me to step away from the bags. But I couldn't. I wouldn't step away because if I broke the sequence, the whole bay would go bad. The whole ambulance bay would just go completely bad. So... he made me come here.

Well, yeah, of course. It's not just a belief, it's a fact. If the sequence breaks, it all falls apart. You have to keep things exact, especially at the station. Like with the paperwork... I know the injury review people and some of the supervisors have been watching me through the station cameras. They watch me, and then they go in and change my triage notes. They do it on purpose to make me look unsafe on the job. They tell me, "Oh, it's just routine paperwork, don't worry about it," but I know they're altering my notes. 

Paperwork used to be so much simpler before they switched to those new tablets, anyway. The screens are always way too bright. It hurts your eyes if you stare at it too long, kind of like staring at the snow when the sun is out. We had this massive blizzard back in '09, and the snow was piled up completely past the headlights on the rig. We were slipping all over the roads. I had to shovel my entire driveway that week with this flimsy plastic shovel because my neighbor borrowed my good metal one and never gave it back. He said he lost it in his garage, but how do you lose a bright red snow shovel? You really can't trust people when you lend them tools.

Voices? No, I don't hear anybody talking when it's empty. Just the regular sounds, you know? Unless you count the dispatch radio, but that's a real voice. Although sometimes the static on the radio sounds a little bit like whispering if the volume is turned down too low. Whispering always reminds me of the library. I practically lived in the library when I was getting my associate's degree. They had these big, heavy wooden tables that always smelled like lemon polish. I really hate the smell of lemon polish. It smells exactly like those cheap air fresheners they hang in the station bathrooms. We ran out of paper towels in the bathroom last Tuesday and nobody even bothered to restock them. I had to dry my hands on my uniform pants, which is a terrible idea because then the fabric gets all stiff and uncomfortable. Kind of like when you wash your uniform and forget to use fabric softener. Do you use fabric softener? My mom always swore by the lavender kind, but I think it just makes the inside of the washing machine completely gummy.

Energetic? No, I don't... I don't really get like that. I'm mostly just tired from the shifts. A lot of the guys at the station drink those huge energy drinks to stay awake, the ones in the tall cans? I tried the green one once, but it made my teeth feel completely fuzzy. I really hate when my teeth feel fuzzy. It's exactly like when you eat too much spinach. My mom used to make this baked spinach casserole every single Thanksgiving and it was always so watery. I don't understand why people put vegetables in casseroles anyway, it just ruins the texture. Texture is really important with food. Like pudding, you know? I can't eat pudding unless it's completely smooth. They used to give us pudding cups in middle school, but the plastic spoons they had in the cafeteria were always so flimsy they'd just snap right in half if you pressed too hard. Have you ever tried to eat with a broken plastic spoon? It's basically impossible. You just end up getting it all over your fingers, and then your hands are sticky all afternoon. I hate having sticky hands, it makes it impossible to grip the steering wheel properly.

Friends? Um, I don't really know. I guess I didn't think about it much back then. I was mostly just doing my own thing, you know? Playing in the dirt, building forts... I built this really amazing fort once out of these old wooden pallets I found behind the grocery store. The grocery store near my house always threw out the best boxes, too. The thick cardboard ones they use for the bananas. Bananas are such a weird fruit if you think about it. They come in their own wrapper, but if you leave them on the counter for even one extra day, they get all brown and mushy. My partner at the station always eats brown bananas. He says they're sweeter, but I just can't get past the smell. It smells exactly like the inside of a dumpster in July. We had to park the rig next to a dumpster last week during a call, and the smell completely seeped into the cab. We had to drive with the windows down the whole way back, which was freezing because the heater on our side is completely busted. I told the mechanic about it three times, but he never listens to me. He just writes it down on his little clipboard and walks away. I hate clipboards. They always pinch your fingers if you aren't careful.

Exact way? Um, I don't... I don't really remember needing things to be exact when I was little. I was just a kid, you know? But my partner at the station, he's obsessed with exactness. He organizes the jump bag the exact same way every single shift. If I put the trauma shears in the wrong pocket, he loses his mind. Trauma shears are actually pretty incredible tools if you think about it. They can cut right through a leather boot or even a penny. I tried cutting a penny once just to see if it worked, but it just bent it in half and then the penny got stuck in the blades. Have you ever gotten a coin stuck in a machine? There's this vending machine in the breakroom that always eats my quarters. I lost three dollars trying to get a bag of pretzels last month. Pretzels are the worst snack anyway, they just make you incredibly thirsty. And the water fountain by the breakroom has been broken since October. It just drips this tiny, lukewarm stream that tastes completely like rust. I can't stand the taste of rust. It reminds me of when you accidentally bite your lip too hard and you get that metallic taste in your mouth. I bit my lip last night while I was trying to eat a sandwich and it swelled up so much I could barely talk on the radio. The dispatcher kept asking me to repeat myself, which is incredibly annoying because the radio static is already so loud.

Hard to follow? No, I... I don't think so. People usually know what I'm talking about. The only time people can't follow me is over the radio, but like I said, the static is just terrible. The dispatchers have it easy because they get those really expensive headsets with the noise-canceling foam. I had to wear one of those foam headsets once for a training module, but the foam makes your ears sweat so much. It's exactly like wearing a wool sweater indoors. My grandmother knitted me a wool sweater when I was a teenager, but it was this awful scratchy yarn. It was supposed to be red, but it looked more like tomato soup. Tomato soup is really only good if you have a grilled cheese sandwich to dip in it, but you have to use the right kind of cheese. If you use that cheap plastic-wrapped cheese, it doesn't melt right, it just turns into this weird oily plastic layer. I left a plastic spatula too close to the stove burner once and it melted into a puddle on the counter. The smell of melting plastic is impossible to get out of a kitchen. We had to keep the windows open for three days, and the screens on the windows were completely rusted out. Bugs kept flying in, especially those little fruit flies. Fruit flies are so pointless, they just hover around the sink drain no matter how much bleach you pour down there. Bleach gives me a terrible headache anyway. It smells exactly like the hospital corridors at county general. We do patient drop-offs there all the time, and the automatic doors at the ambulance bay are always getting stuck halfway open. It's a huge fire hazard if you ask me.

Not true? No, I... I know it is true. That's exactly why they sent me here in the first place. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern that I knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. Dispatch numbers are so incredibly long now, you know? They used to just be a few digits, but now they add all these letters and zone codes. It's exactly like reading a serial number off the back of a refrigerator. We had to move this massive refrigerator for a patient once, and the compressor on the back was completely coated in this thick, greasy dust. Dust always makes my nose itch right at the bridge, where my sunglasses sit. I have these polarized sunglasses that are great for driving, but they make all the windows on the other cars look like they have rainbows on them. 

Anyway, my lieutenant came over and told me to stop and step away from the bags, but I wouldn't do it. I couldn't step away. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. The bay is already in terrible shape as it is. There's this massive oil stain in bay three that nobody ever bothers to clean up. You're supposed to use cat litter to soak up motor oil, but the county only buys that cheap clay kind that doesn't even clump. It just turns into this awful gray paste if it gets wet. I stepped in some gray paste on a call last Tuesday and it completely ruined the treads on my boots. Good work boots are so expensive to replace on our salary, and the uniform allowance doesn't even cover half of it. They send the allowance as a separate paper check instead of direct deposit, which is so outdated. I always lose paper checks in the center console of my truck.

When did it start? Um, well, the stuff at the station... the behavior that got everybody all alarmed, and all the camera and paperwork stuff, that's been going on for about the last two months. Paperwork is just endless now, honestly. You have to fill out a triplicate form just to restock the oxygen tanks. The carbon copies always leave that weird blue smudge on the side of your hand. It's impossible to wash off with regular soap. You have to use that gritty orange pumice soap that mechanics use. My dad was a mechanic, he always smelled exactly like that orange soap and motor oil. He had this old Ford truck that he was always fixing up, but the transmission kept slipping. Transmissions are incredibly complicated, all those tiny gears and fluid. Transmission fluid is this bright cherry red color, it looks almost exactly like cough syrup. I took some cherry cough syrup last winter when I had a chest cold, but it just made me feel incredibly dizzy and I ended up sleeping for fourteen hours straight. Sleeping on the station cots is terrible for your back anyway. The mattresses are so incredibly thin you can feel the metal springs poking right through the vinyl cover. Vinyl gets so hot in the summer, you wake up completely drenched in sweat.

Before two months ago? Well, the whole thing actually started after I hurt my shoulder and ribs during an ambulance transfer about eight months ago. We were moving this bariatric patient down a narrow flight of stairs, and the stair chair completely jammed on the landing. Those stair chairs are supposed to have a smooth glide track, but the tracks get filled with all this grit and dirt from people's shoes. People wear the dirtiest shoes into their houses, it makes no sense to me. My mom always made us take our shoes off at the front door and leave them on this little rubber mat. The rubber mat had these little bristles on it that were supposed to scrape the mud off, but they just ended up trapping all the pine needles from the yard. Pine needles are impossible to sweep up, they just slide right under the broom bristles. You really need a good shop vac to get them all. Shop vacs are incredibly loud, though, they sound exactly like a jet engine taking off. I live right under the flight path for the regional airport, so I hear jet engines all day long. They rattle the windows so hard I had to put weather stripping around all the frames just to stop the shaking. Weather stripping is basically just sticky foam, and the adhesive always dries out and peels off after a few months. It's exactly like that cheap medical tape we use on the rig, the kind that won't stick to anything if the patient is even a little bit sweaty. Sweating is just a nightmare when you're wearing those heavy uniform shirts. The polyester blend they make us wear doesn't breathe at all.

Yeah, continuously. Ever since I messed up my shoulder and ribs on that transfer eight months ago, it's just been going on and on. My shoulder still clicks sometimes when I reach up, you know? Like when I have to grab the trauma shears off the top shelf in the rig. Those shears are supposed to be able to cut through a penny, but I've never actually tried it. Who has a penny just lying around anymore? Nobody uses cash. Everything is on those little plastic cards with the chips in them. The chips get scratched up so easily, though. I had to replace my debit card three times last year because the chip reader at the gas station kept rejecting it. Gas stations always smell so strongly of diesel and old hot dogs. Those hot dogs just roll on those metal heaters for hours, they must be completely dried out inside. I tried to eat one on a night shift once and it gave me the worst heartburn. Heartburn feels exactly like you swallowed a hot coal. We carry antacids on the truck, but they're the chalky mint kind. Mint flavor always reminds me of toothpaste, and eating toothpaste is just a terrible idea. My little brother ate a whole tube of sparkle toothpaste when we were kids and my mom had to call poison control. Poison control operators are so calm, I don't know how they do it. They just sit in a room with headsets all day. Headsets always give me a headache right behind my ears if I wear them too long.

Yeah, trouble working. I can't work the ambulance anymore. They tried putting me on desk duty, doing notes and equipment checks, but I guess I got so unreliable with it that they just took me off the schedule completely. Schedules are so rigid anyway, you know? Like, you have to clock in exactly at 0600 or the biometric scanner flags you. Those fingerprint scanners are terrible, half the time they don't even read your print if your hands are dry. My hands are always dry because of that awful hand sanitizer we use on the rig. It smells exactly like cheap tequila. I went to Mexico once, Cabo, and the tequila there was amazing, not like the stuff here. The beaches were beautiful, but the sand gets absolutely everywhere. You find sand in your shoes months later. Shoes with good arch support are so expensive now, easily over a hundred dollars. A hundred dollars doesn't buy anything at the grocery store anymore, either. I haven't even been going to the store much, honestly. I've mostly stopped seeing friends or keeping up with things at home the way I used to. My apartment is just... I don't know. The dust bunnies under the couch are getting huge. Dust is mostly dead skin cells, which is kind of gross when you think about it. Skin cells are constantly shedding, millions of them every day. It's like we're constantly falling apart, just leaving little pieces of ourselves everywhere we go.

I don't really know about my face, honestly, because I don't really see anyone for them to tell me. Most days I just sit in my apartment. There's trash just sitting in the corner, and all this food still in the fridge. I used to cook all the time, but I just can't get myself to care or start anything anymore. I don't even call the guys for basketball like I used to. We used to play at the community center, and the floors there are so polished. They squeak so loud when you run in rubber soles. Rubber comes from trees, originally, which is wild to think about. You just tap a tree and get tires. We blow out tires on the rig all the time because the city never fills the potholes on the east side. Potholes fill up with water when it rains, and then they freeze overnight and expand. Ice is one of the only substances that expands when it freezes. Most things shrink when they get cold. Like the thermal blankets we keep in the trauma bays, they always feel so thin and small when you pull them out of the warmer. Warmers are basically just giant incubators. Incubators always remind me of those little baby chicks they hatch in elementary school science class. We had a heat lamp for ours, and it gave off this intense red glow. Red is the longest wavelength of visible light, you know. That's why stoplights are red, so you can see them through the fog. Fog rolling in off the river is so thick here in November.

No, nothing like that before the injury. Everything was completely normal until I messed up my shoulder. Shoulders are such complicated joints, you know? It's a ball and socket, but the socket is really shallow, which is why they dislocate so easily. We had a call once for a guy who dislocated his shoulder playing rugby. Rugby seems so brutal, no pads or helmets or anything. Football players wear all that armor, but they still get concussions all the time. Concussions are weird because your brain basically bruises itself against the inside of your skull. The skull is supposed to protect you, but sometimes it's the thing that hurts you. Like when people don't wear helmets on motorcycles. Motorcycles are basically just engines with wheels. My uncle had a Harley, and it was so loud you could feel it vibrating in your chest from a block away. Vibrations can actually loosen screws over time, which is why you have to keep checking the mounting brackets on the stretcher in the ambulance. If the stretcher isn't secure, it's a huge liability. Liability insurance for EMS is insanely expensive. Everything is expensive now, though. Have you seen the price of eggs lately?

No, not right after. The injury was a while ago. The camera and paperwork stuff, and the station behavior that got everyone all alarmed, that's only been going on for about the last two months. Two months isn't that long, but they really do have cameras everywhere now. The lenses are getting so tiny, you can barely even see them. They hide them in smoke detectors and exit signs. Exit signs always have to be illuminated by law, you know. Fire codes are super strict about that. If a bulb burns out in an exit sign, the fire marshal will write you up instantly. We had a fire marshal inspect the station once who was absolutely obsessed with extension cords. You aren't allowed to daisy-chain extension cords because it creates a massive fire hazard. Fires burn so hot they can melt the structural steel right out of a building. Steel is an alloy, mostly iron and carbon. Carbon is what diamonds are made of, which is crazy. It takes millions of years of pressure in the earth's crust to make a diamond. And then people pay thousands of dollars for a shiny rock just to put it on a ring. Rings are actually really dangerous to wear on the job. In EMS, they tell you not to wear rings because you could get it caught on the stretcher mechanism and deglove your whole finger. Degloving is exactly what it sounds like, and it's horrible. Just... taking off a glove. The gloves they buy for us are always tearing anyway. The city switched to this cheap nitrile brand to save a few cents a box.

No, I don't think so. I mean, nothing stressful right before that. The shoulder thing was months before, like I said. Stress is such a weird concept anyway, right? Like, the body doesn't know the difference between good stress and bad stress. It's all just cortisol and adrenaline. Adrenaline is epinephrine, and we push that all the time during codes. It basically jumpstarts the heart. The heart is just a pump, really, just muscle and valves. Valves can get so calcified as people get older. Calcium is good for your bones, though. You're supposed to drink milk, but a lot of people are lactose intolerant. Lactose is a sugar, and the enzyme lactase breaks it down. If you don't have the enzyme, it just ferments in your gut and causes all this gas. Gas prices are ridiculous right now. I remember when it was under two bucks a gallon. Gallons are such a weird measurement, we really should just switch to the metric system like the rest of the world. The metric system makes so much more sense because everything is in base ten. Ten is a nice, round number.

Yeah, it's been like that. Most days I just sit in my apartment. There's trash in the corner, food still in the fridge going bad, and I just... I can't get myself to care or start anything. I don't even call the guys for basketball anymore, or cook like I used to. Cooking takes so much prep work, you know? Chopping vegetables and measuring spices. Spices used to be worth more than gold back in the day. People literally sailed across the ocean just to find peppercorns and nutmeg. Nutmeg can actually be hallucinogenic if you eat enough of it, which is crazy to think about. It's just sitting right there in the baking aisle next to the cinnamon. Cinnamon comes from the bark of a tree. Trees are amazing, how they pull water all the way up from the roots to the leaves against gravity. Gravity is a constant, 9.8 meters per second squared. That's why falls from a height are so dangerous in trauma calls. We had this one call where a guy fell off a roof cleaning his gutters. Gutters get so clogged with leaves in the fall. Fall is my favorite season because the air gets so crisp. Crisp apples are the best, especially Honeycrisp. They engineered Honeycrisp apples at a university in Minnesota, I think. Minnesota has all those lakes. They say it's the land of ten thousand lakes, but it's actually more than that. Water is so heavy, though. A gallon of water weighs over eight pounds.

No, it wasn't sudden like that. It wasn't just a few days. It kind of just... grew, you know? Like it crept up over time, over weeks. Weeks feel so long when you're just sitting there, but then you look at a calendar and realize how fast the year is going. Calendars are weird because we use the Gregorian one, but there are so many other ways to track time. Like the lunar calendar. The moon controls the tides, which is wild when you think about it. Just this giant rock in space pulling all the oceans back and forth. Oceans cover most of the earth, and we've barely even explored the bottom of them. There are fish down there that make their own light because it's so dark. Bioluminescence, they call it. Fireflies do that too, in the summer. I used to catch them in jars when I was a kid. You have to poke holes in the lid so they can breathe, obviously. Breathing is automatic, controlled by the brainstem. The medulla oblongata. We had to memorize all the parts of the brain for EMT training. Training was intense, lots of flashcards. Flashcards are made of paper, and paper comes from paper mills, and those places smell terrible. There was a paper mill a few towns over from where I grew up, and on windy days, you could smell it everywhere. Wind power is getting huge now, though. Those giant turbines they put up in fields. They look like they're moving slow, but the tips of those blades are actually spinning incredibly fast.

No, not six months. The camera stuff, the paperwork, and how everyone at the station started acting weird... that's been going on for about the last two months. Two months is a decent amount of time, I guess. Sixty days. It's crazy how we divide time into days based on the earth spinning. The earth spins at like a thousand miles an hour at the equator, but we don't feel it because everything is moving with us, including the atmosphere. The atmosphere is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen, which surprises a lot of people. We give 100% oxygen on the rig sometimes, like with a non-rebreather mask. Those masks have those little flaps on the side so the exhaled air can get out. Exhaling is just getting rid of carbon dioxide, which is a waste product of cellular respiration. Cells are basically tiny factories. Mitochondria is the powerhouse of the cell, everybody remembers that from high school biology. High school feels like a lifetime ago. I played football back then, defensive tackle. Football is rough on the joints, though. So many guys end up with bad knees. Knees are hinge joints, but they have a lot of complex ligaments holding them together. The ACL is the one everyone tears. Tearing a ligament is worse than breaking a bone sometimes, because bones heal better. Bones are constantly remodeling themselves, breaking down and building back up. It's called Wolff's law, I think. Law is a whole other field. Lawyers have to read so much case law, just stacks and stacks of books. Books are getting replaced by tablets now, though. Everyone just reads on a screen.

No, nobody said I was confused. I knew exactly what was going on, it wasn't confusion. My behavior changed because I was figuring it all out, not because I was losing my mind. The mind is a crazy thing, though. The brain uses about twenty percent of the body's energy, even though it's only like two percent of the weight. It runs on glucose. Glucose is basically sugar. We push D50, which is fifty percent dextrose, for diabetic emergencies when they're crashing. Crashing an ambulance is my biggest fear. You're driving this massive box on wheels, lights and sirens going, and people still don't pull over. They just stare at you in their rearview mirrors. Mirrors are coated with silver or aluminum on the back so they reflect light. Light travels at 186,000 miles per second. If you could travel at the speed of light, time would actually slow down for you relative to people on earth. Einstein proved that with relativity. Relativity makes you think about how everything is connected in the universe. The universe is expanding, they say, getting bigger every second. I wonder what it's expanding into, though. Like, what's outside of it? Space is a vacuum, so there's no sound. Sound needs a medium to travel through, like air or water. Water is H2O. Two hydrogens, one oxygen. Oxygen is what we need, but too much of it can actually be toxic. Oxygen toxicity can cause seizures. Seizures are terrifying to watch if you don't know what's happening. People bite their tongues and everything. Tongues are the strongest muscle in the body, pound for pound.

Hi, doctor. Well, I'm here because... I've been having some trouble with my eating. What happens is, once I start picking at the leftovers late at night, it feels like the sensible part of me is saying, 'That’s enough, Alejandro,' but... my hand just keeps going back for more anyway. I just can't seem to stop myself once I start.

Yeah, I do. Some nights after supper, when I’m supposed to be putting away the tamales or the mole, I’ll end up eating several servings of it right there. And then I'll usually have some pan dulce out in the garage, too. It's... well, it's definitely a lot more food than I’d ever actually put on a plate if my family was around watching me.

Yes, exactly. Like I was saying when we first sat down, I just can't seem to stop myself. It's like... my brain knows I should quit, and I tell myself 'that's enough,' but my hands just keep moving and grabbing more food anyway. I really do feel completely unable to control it once I start.

I don't know if I'd say they upset me a lot. I mean, it definitely bothers me... I feel pretty foolish afterward when I realize how much I actually ate. But it's not like I'm crying over it or anything like that. It's really just frustrating, I guess.

Yeah, that's right. A lot of the time I'm not even hungry. I mean, I usually just had a good, full dinner with everyone else. But then later on, I still find myself opening up the containers and just tasting one thing after another. It's not about being hungry at all.
No, I've never done anything like that. I mean, I just kind of sit there feeling overly full afterward... but no, I don't ever make myself throw up.
Well, looking back on it... these late-night leftover episodes have been happening at least once most weeks. Often two nights, actually. It's been going on like this ever since my cousin moved in.

Yeah, I do. I make sure I wait until the house is totally quiet, or sometimes I'll even take things out to the garage. I'd just be really embarrassed for my cousin or my family to see how much I'm eating. I mean, at my age, I'm supposed to be the disciplined one in the house. So, yeah, I definitely make sure I'm alone when I do it.
I'd say it's been about four months. Like I mentioned, that's when my older cousin came to live with us, so... yeah, right around four months now.

Well, I came in because... I just feel like I got a motor running inside me all day, you know? Like it never shuts off. It's real bad if I have to sit still. Like at church, or sitting out there in the waiting room, or even just at home trying to watch TV. I just feel trapped, like I'm gonna jump out of my skin, and I have to get up and do something. Speaking of church, Pastor Dave was talking about patience this Sunday, and I thought, man, I'd love to have some of that, but my buddy Earl—he sits two pews up—he bought this old Chevy truck he's been fixing up, and I told him he needs to check the carburetor because those things are always acting up, but he wouldn't listen to me. I used to work on cars all the time before... well, anyway, yeah, I just can't sit still. It's driving me crazy.

No, I ain't taking any new pills or nothing. I don't even really like taking medicine, to be honest with you. My aunt Linda, she takes a whole handful of 'em every morning. She’s got one of those plastic boxes with the days of the week on it, you know? Except the letters rubbed off hers, so she's always getting them mixed up. She had this little terrier dog that actually chewed on the Tuesday compartment once. Man, that dog was crazy... always digging holes under the fence. I had to go over there and put some chicken wire down in the dirt so it wouldn't get out into the street. Took me like three hours in the hot sun, and I didn't even have a proper pair of wire cutters, just these rusty old pliers. But uh... what were you asking? Oh, right, my medicine. Nah, I haven't started anything new.

Euphoric? Like... like super happy? Nah, I don't think so. I mean, I get in a good mood sometimes, sure, but not like... not like crazy happy or nothing. Like the other day, I found a twenty dollar bill in the pocket of my old winter coat. I was pretty happy about that. I was just digging in there looking for my keys because I locked myself out of the house again. I do that all the time. Last time I had to pry the screen off the bathroom window, and it bent the frame, so now the bugs get in. We had this huge moth in the living room last night, just flying around the lamp, driving me nuts. Well, hi there. It's nice to meet you too. I guess I'm here because... well, my daughter suggested it. I just feel like I’m always up and moving, you know? Euphoric? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I'm just... busy. I don't feel like I'm on top of the world or anything strange like that. I mean, I have my good days, of course!
