I actually went to the craft store on Monday to buy some paints to make my own, but they have so many different kinds of acrylics now, I couldn't decide. I ended up talking to the cashier for twenty minutes about her sister's cat who got stuck in a storm drain.
Oh my, yes. It’s funny you ask that, because even way back in grade school, my teachers used to tell my mother that I was a bright girl, but just completely scattered.

Worries? Oh, goodness no. I wouldn't say I'm a worrier at all. Now, Frank, my husband, he is the worrier in the family. Bless him, he watches that 24-hour news channel all day and gets so worked up about the weather reports. Just yesterday he was pacing around fretting about a storm coming in, and I told him, "Frank, we have a perfectly good roof!" 

Which actually reminded me, we really do need to get the gutters cleaned before all the oak leaves fall. I went into the kitchen to look for the number of that nice young man who did it last year—Jimmy, I think his name was? Or maybe Tommy. His mother goes to our church. Anyway, I was digging in the junk drawer for his business card, and I ended up finding

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. So, um, the reason I made the appointment... well, it’s honestly getting a bit embarrassing, but I just keep getting up when I am absolutely supposed to stay put. It sounds like something a restless kid would do, right? But I’m 49 years old, and I just can't seem to stay in my chair. 

I’m a private investigator, which means I do a lot of client interviews. People come to me, usually very stressed or upset, and they need to tell me all these highly sensitive details. I’m supposed to be this grounded, attentive professional. But right in the middle of them pouring their hearts out, I’ll just... stand up. I’ll start pacing behind my desk, or I’ll go fiddle with the window blinds, or I’ll offer them water for the third time just to have an excuse to move. 

And it’s not just at work! I do some tutoring on the side, and I’m constantly popping out of my seat and hovering around the room instead of just sitting next to the student. Even at my book club—we meet once a month, usually at my friend Diane's house, and she has these very comfortable couches—but I can't just sit on them. Everyone else is settled in with their wine, discussing the chapters, and there I am, wandering over to the kitchen island or standing behind the sofa. 

People are really starting to notice. My clients, my friends... they give me these looks, and it’s becoming really obvious to everyone that I just can't sit and listen. It makes it seem like I don't care about what they're saying, even though I *am* listening! I just can't seem to do it while sitting down. So, yeah, that's what brings me in today. I need to figure out why I can't just stay in my seat.

Antipsychotic or anti-nausea? Oh, um, no. No, definitely not. I haven't started anything new like that at all. I mean, I really don't take much in the way of medication anyway. Just a standard multivitamin in the mornings, usually with my coffee—which, I know, I read this article recently that said the tannins in coffee can actually block vitamin absorption, so maybe I should stop doing that, but it’s just so ingrained in my morning routine, you know? 

But no, absolutely no antipsychotics. And as for anti-nausea medicine, I actually have an absolute iron stomach. It’s a really good thing, too, because in my line of work, sometimes I end up doing surveillance from my car for hours on end, drinking lukewarm deli coffee, and if I got motion sickness or an upset stomach easily, I’d be in real trouble. My sister gets terribly nauseous just riding in the passenger seat of a car, and she takes those little motion sickness pills all the time, but me? Never. The last time I took anything for my stomach was probably... gosh, years and years ago, when I had food poisoning from this terrible seafood place downtown that isn't even open anymore. They got shut down for health code violations, which didn't surprise me one bit. 

So, yeah, no, nothing like that recently. Not a single new pill. Why do you ask? Can those types of medicines make a person completely unable to sit still? Because I'm definitely not taking anything that would cause this.

An intrusive thought or fear? Oh, gosh, no, no, it’s nothing like that at all. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, if I don't stand up right this second, something terrible is going to happen," or like I have to go check if the stove is on or the door is locked. I mean, my sister has a friend who does that, she has to check the locks exactly three times before she can even pull out of her driveway, and if she loses count, she has to start all over again. It sounds absolutely exhausting, honestly, but no, what I'm dealing with isn't like that. 

It’s really just this... this overwhelming physical urge. It's like my legs just decide they've had enough of the chair, completely independent of whatever my brain is doing. I'll be sitting there, listening to a client talk about a cheating spouse or a missing asset, and my mind is completely focused on the conversation, I'm taking notes, I'm fully engaged in the work—but my body just sort of rebels. It's almost like a pressure builds up in my muscles, and standing up is the only way to release the valve. 

There's no fear involved, no bad thoughts I'm trying to push away. I just suddenly feel like if I don't move, I'm going to jump out of my own skin. It's purely physical, just this restless energy that completely takes over. So, yeah, no intrusive thoughts or anything like that. Just an absolute inability to keep my bottom glued to the seat, no matter how much I want to or how inappropriate the timing is.

Oh, gosh, yes. Yes, I was exactly like this as a kid. It’s funny you ask that, because I was actually just talking to my mother about this the other day. We were going through some old boxes in her attic—she's finally downsizing, moving into a smaller condo, which is a whole other ordeal, let me tell you, trying to convince her to part with things she hasn't looked at since 1985. But anyway, we found this stack of my old report cards from elementary school.

And it was just... it was almost comical, reading them now. Every single one of them, from first grade all the way through middle school, basically said the exact same thing. The teachers would always write, "She’s very bright, grasps the material quickly," but then there was always the "but." "But she cannot stay in her seat," or "She has trouble waiting her turn." It was a constant theme. I mean, my mother still jokes about it. She says I treated every single classroom like a crime scene that I just had to pace through and investigate instead of just sitting at my desk like a normal student. 

I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade—she was this very strict, older teacher who always wore these brightly colored cardigans—she actually put a piece of masking tape around my desk. A literal square on the floor! And she told me I wasn't allowed to step outside the tape during lessons. It didn't work, of course. I'd just stand up and pace inside the little square, or I'd lean so far over the desk to talk to the kid next to me that I'd practically fall over. I just had this... this motor running inside me, even back then. I couldn't just sit and listen to the lesson. I had to be up, moving, checking out the pencil sharpener, looking out the window, seeing what the kid three rows over was drawing. So, yeah, this isn't a new thing at all. It's just that now, as a 49-year-old professional, it's a lot less cute and a lot more disruptive to my actual life and career.

Well... I guess I'm just here because I've been forgetting things. Important things, I suppose. Like... I missed a follow-up for my heart recently. And I forget to call the clinic back. Well, I came in because... it's my head. My mind just keeps going blank at the absolute worst times. Like, I'll be at work, and I'll look at the road-closure forms or even just holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I cannot remember the steps. And I've done this for years. But anyway, yeah, I just stand there holding the sign and my brain is just... empty.

Energized? No... no, I don't think so. Honestly, most of the time I just feel incredibly heavy. Like I'm walking through wet cement. I do try to drink coffee to get some kind of energy for my shifts, though. There's this little drive-thru espresso hut right by the intersection where I'm flagging this week, and the girl working there makes the best mochas. She actually brings her dog to work, this little terrier mix, and it just sits on the counter by the window. 

I always worry about the dog, honestly, because of all the cars idling right there in line. The exhaust can't be good for its little lungs. I read an article once about air quality and how it affects pets faster than humans because they breathe faster... or maybe it's because they're closer to the ground? I can't remember. My mom used to have a dog that had asthma, and they had to give it an inhaler, which just seems so strange to look at. 

But anyway... no. I never really get those big bursts of energy or feel high like you're saying. I'm usually just tired.

Trouble paying attention in school? I... I don't really remember having a problem with it. I was pretty quiet, mostly. I liked reading. I remember reading this one book about a girl who lived in a windmill, and she had to figure out how to grind the flour herself after her parents left. It was so detailed about the gears and the stones. I actually tried to build a little model windmill out of popsicle sticks and rubber bands for a science project after that. My dad helped me glue the base together because the glue gun was so hot. He used to keep all his tools in these old metal coffee cans in the garage, the kind that smelled like stale coffee and motor oil. He had this whole system for sorting the nails by size, but then my brother knocked one over once and they just went everywhere. It took us hours to pick them all up out of the sawdust on the floor. 

But no, I don't think I had trouble paying attention. I just kind of kept my head down and did my work.

Lose track of time? Um... yeah, I guess I do. It's like... I'll look at the clock on my phone, and it's 10:15, and then I blink, and my supervisor is tapping me on the shoulder to tell me it's time for my lunch break at noon. My phone actually has this really annoying crack right across the screen, right where the time is. I dropped it last week when I was trying to get my keys out of my pocket. My keychain is so heavy because I have all these little charms on it. There's a little Eiffel Tower from when my aunt went to Paris, and this plastic dinosaur that glows in the dark. I think it's a Stegosaurus, the one with the plates on its back. Did you know they think those plates were actually for regulating their body temperature, not just for defense? I read that in a waiting room magazine once. It's fascinating how much we've learned about dinosaurs just from fossils. They even found one recently that had preserved feathers, which completely changes how you picture them. It makes them seem more like giant, scary birds. 

But, um... yeah, the time just kind of vanishes when my head gets empty like that. I just don't know where it goes.

Aware? I... I don't think so. That's actually why I came in, to be honest. It's getting really bad at work. I'll be standing there, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms I have to sign, or even just holding my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I just... I cannot remember the steps. And I've done this job for years. But my mind just goes completely blank at the worst possible times. 

Like the other day, I was standing by the barricades, and they're those big orange plastic ones, you know? The ones you can fill with water or sand so they don't blow over. The crew usually fills them with water from the hydrant, which always makes me nervous because the water pressure from those things is incredible. I saw a video once where a fire hydrant broke and the water shot up higher than a three-story building. It completely flooded the street in like five minutes. Water damage is so hard to fix, too. My sister had a pipe burst in her basement last winter, and it ruined all her old photo albums. She had these beautiful leather-bound albums from our grandparents' wedding, and they just got completely soaked and warped. She tried to dry them out with a hair dryer, but the pages all stuck together. It was really heartbreaking.

But... yeah, when the blankness happens, I'm just gone. I don't know what's happening around me at all until I snap out of it and realize I don't know what I'm supposed to be doing with the paddle.

Remember what happened? No, not really. It's just a blank. Like I was saying, that's the whole reason I'm here. It's just so terrifying to be holding the stop-slow paddle, or staring at those road-closure forms, and I just completely forget the steps. Things I've done for years. It's like someone just hit erase. 

You know, those forms are always printed on this really cheap, thin paper that tears if you even look at it wrong. The ink smears, too, especially when it rains. We have to use these special waterproof clipboards, the ones that have a little plastic cover that folds down over the paper. My supervisor, Dave, he lost his clipboard last month and had to use a regular one during a downpour. The forms practically dissolved. Dave is always losing things, though. He lost his favorite sunglasses in a porta-potty once. He was so mad because they were those expensive polarized ones that cut the glare off the windshields. Glare can be really dangerous out on the road, especially right at sunrise or sunset. The light hits the asphalt and it just blinds you. 

But yeah, I don't remember anything from when it happens. Just... gone. And then I'm standing there holding the paddle like an idiot.

Emotional stress? I mean... maybe? I'm not really sure if it's stress causing it, but like I said, it just happens at the absolute worst times. I'll just be standing there, looking at the road-closure forms or holding my stop-slow paddle, and my mind just completely empties out. I suddenly cannot remember the steps for things I've done for years. It's so frustrating. 

Speaking of those road-closure forms, they changed the font on them recently. It used to be Arial, I think, but now it's something with those little feet on the letters... serifs, right? It makes it look so much more formal, almost like a legal document you'd get from a lawyer. My cousin is a lawyer, actually. She works in corporate law downtown. She has this amazing office on the thirtieth floor with floor-to-ceiling windows. You can see the whole city from up there. She says it's terrifying during thunderstorms, though, because the building actually sways a little bit in the wind. I don't think I could handle that. I get motion sickness just riding in the backseat of a car. I have to chew ginger gum whenever I take a cab. Ginger is supposed to be really good for your digestion, too. I buy these little crystallized ginger pieces from the health food store, but they're so spicy sometimes they make my eyes water. 

But, um... yeah, my mind just goes blank. I don't know if it's stress, but it's why I'm here. I just look at the paddle and I don't know what to do with it.

Shake or jerk? No, no one's ever said anything like that to me. I think I just stand there, completely still. Like a statue. Which is why I'm so worried about work, because if I'm just standing there frozen with the stop-slow paddle, someone could get hurt. I just... I forget the steps. 

I did see a statue once that looked incredibly real. It was one of those living statue street performers down by the harbor. He was painted completely bronze, head to toe, and he stood on this little milk crate for hours without blinking. I don't know how they do that without getting muscle cramps. I get a charley horse in my calf almost every night. My doctor told me to eat more bananas for the potassium, but I really can't stand the texture of bananas. They're just so mushy. I prefer apples, especially the Honeycrisp ones when they're in season. They're so expensive, though. I saw them for almost four dollars a pound at the grocery store last week. The prices of everything are just going up so fast. A carton of eggs is ridiculous now. 

But no, nobody has ever told me I shake or anything. I just... freeze up and my mind goes totally blank.

Fear or panic? Um... no, I don't think so. I don't feel anything coming on. It's just... one second I'm there, holding the paddle or looking at the forms, and the next second it's just blank. I don't get any kind of warning like that. 

Speaking of warnings, though, we have these new early warning signs for the work zones. They have these really bright, flashing LED lights on them now. They're supposed to be solar-powered, which is great for the environment, you know? I try to do my part, I recycle all my plastics and cardboard. Although, the recycling rules in my neighborhood keep changing. One week you can put glass in the blue bin, the next week you have to take it to a special drop-off center. The drop-off center is right next to this amazing little bakery, though. They make these blueberry scones that are just incredible. They put a lemon glaze on top that perfectly balances out the sweetness. I tried to bake scones at home once, but they turned out hard as rocks. I think my baking powder was expired. You really have to check the expiration dates on things. I drank some milk once that was a week past the date, and my stomach was upset for two whole days. 

But no, I don't feel any panic or fear right before it happens. It just... happens, and then I'm standing there, totally lost.

Lip smacking? No, I don't think so. None of the other flaggers have ever mentioned me doing anything weird like that. Although, my lips do get incredibly chapped out there on the road with all the wind and the dust from the construction. I have to carry this special beeswax lip balm in my safety vest pocket all the time. It has peppermint in it, which is supposed to be really soothing. Peppermint is great for headaches, too, you know. My aunt used to grow real peppermint in her garden. She had this massive garden in her backyard with all these wooden raised beds. She grew tomatoes that were the size of softballs, I swear. We used to make fresh salsa every single summer. I love a good salsa, but it absolutely has to have cilantro in it. Some people think cilantro tastes like soap, which I read somewhere is actually a genetic thing. I think genetics are so fascinating. Like how my sister and I both have the exact same freckle on our left wrist, right over the vein. 

But, um... what was it? Picking at things? No. Nobody has ever said I do anything like that when my mind empties out. I really think I just stand there frozen.

A head injury? No, I've never hit my head or been knocked out or anything like that. I've always been pretty careful. Even when I was a kid, I was the one who wouldn't ride my bike without a helmet. My mom bought me this bright pink helmet with little white stars on it. It was so ugly, but she made me wear it. 

I see kids riding around now without helmets all the time, and it just makes me so nervous. Especially with the way people drive these days. People are always looking at their phones while they're driving. Just yesterday, I was holding the stop sign, and this guy in a silver sedan drove right past me because he was texting. He didn't even look up! I had to blow my whistle so hard I thought I was going to burst an eardrum. Whistles are surprisingly loud when you blow them with all your might. I actually have a special whistle that's designed to cut through the noise of heavy machinery. It's made of this lightweight titanium, so it doesn't weigh down my lanyard. Lanyards can really chafe your neck if you wear them all day in the heat. I tried wrapping mine in a bit of felt, but then it just absorbed all my sweat and got really gross. 

But no, I've never had a concussion or hurt my head. My head is totally fine, except for... well, the blank spells.

Seizures? No, nobody's ever told me that. I've never had a seizure or epilepsy or anything. My health has always been pretty normal, honestly. Except for my allergies, I guess. I have terrible seasonal allergies, especially in the spring when all the pollen is out. The oak trees are the worst for me. There's this massive oak tree right outside my bedroom window, and it just dumps yellow dust all over my car every April. I have to run it through the car wash like twice a week just to see out the windshield. The car wash I go to has those really cool colorful foam soaps, you know? Like bright pink and blue. It smells like bubblegum. I used to love bubblegum when I was little, especially the kind that came in a long tape dispenser. You could just pull off as much as you wanted. I'd chew so much my jaw would ache. 

But yeah, no, definitely no seizures. Just the... the blanking out thing.

Traumatic? No, I don't think so. I've never been in a bad accident or a war or anything like that. I mean, standing out on the road with cars flying by can be a little scary sometimes, but you get used to it. You just have to stay alert and keep your eyes moving. That's what they taught us in the certification class. 

The instructor for that class was this really intense guy named Gary. He had this huge, bushy mustache that covered his entire upper lip. It looked like a caterpillar was just resting on his face. I could never grow a mustache, obviously, but sometimes I wonder what it would be like to have facial hair. Like, would it be itchy? My ex-boyfriend had a beard, and he was always scratching it. He used this special beard oil that smelled like cedarwood and vanilla. It was actually a really nice smell. We used to go camping a lot, and the smell of the cedarwood always reminded me of being out in the woods. I love camping, especially in the fall when the leaves are changing colors. The reds and oranges are just so vibrant. I tried to paint a picture of a forest in the fall once, but I'm not very good at watercolors. They always just bleed together and turn into this muddy brown mess. You have to have a really light touch with watercolors, I think. 

But um... no, nothing extremely frightening or traumatic has ever happened to me. Just a normal life, really.

A brain infection or a tumor? No, nothing like that. I've never had a stroke, either. Physically, my brain is fine. I did get a really terrible headache once, but that was just because I forgot my hat at work. Being a flagger, you're just standing out there baking in the sun for hours, so you really need a good hat. I usually wear this wide-brimmed straw one. It has a little toggle string under the chin so it doesn't blow away when the big semi-trucks go past. 

The wind from those trucks is incredible, honestly. One time a truck went by so fast it actually blew my sunglasses right off my face, and they skittered across the asphalt and got completely scratched up. They were my favorite pair, too. They were polarized, which you really need so it cuts the glare off all the car windshields. It is so hard to find good polarized sunglasses that don't cost an absolute fortune. I ended up having to go to this little kiosk at the mall to get a replacement pair. The mall is always so dead these days, though. Half the stores are just empty and gated up. I remember when the mall used to be the place to go on a Friday night when I was a teenager... you'd get a soft pretzel and just walk around looking at things. I love those pretzels with the big chunks of salt on them, especially if you dip them in that fake yellow cheese. 

But um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, the brain thing. No, no tumors or infections or anything like that.

No, I don't think so. I mean, I told you I haven't really had any bad or painful events like that, so there's nothing to be reminded of. The blank spells just kind of... happen. Usually when I'm just standing there holding the stop sign. It gets so heavy after a while, you know? The pole is made of this thick aluminum, and your arm just starts to ache right around the shoulder joint. I tried switching arms, but I'm so right-hand dominant that it feels incredibly awkward to hold it with my left. 

My left hand is basically useless. I tried to teach myself to write with my left hand once when I was in college, just as a brain exercise. I read this article that said it builds new neural pathways or something. I bought this really nice fountain pen to practice with. It had blue ink, like a really deep cobalt blue. I love that color. I actually painted my living room that color a few years ago, but it ended up making the room look way too dark because I don't get a lot of natural light in there. My apartment only has windows on the north side, so it's always kind of gloomy. My houseplants hate it. I've killed like three ferns already this year. Ferns are so finicky, they need just the right amount of humidity. 

But yeah, the blank spells don't have anything to do with upsetting memories or anything. They just happen out of nowhere.

New medicines? No, I haven't started anything new. I don't really like taking a lot of pills anyway. Even when I get a cold, I try to just drink a lot of tea. Peppermint tea is my favorite. It really clears out your sinuses, you know? I buy it in bulk from this little co-op down the street from my apartment. They have these huge glass jars filled with all kinds of loose leaf teas and herbs. It smells amazing in there, like dried flowers and spices. 

The woman who runs the co-op is so nice, she always gives me a little extra scoop of the peppermint. She has these really beautiful silver rings on every single finger. I always wonder how she manages to do anything with all those rings on. I feel like they would get caught on everything. I used to wear a ring on my thumb when I was in my twenties, but I lost it at a concert. It was a general admission show, and everybody was just packed in so tight. The band was okay, but the bass was so loud it made my teeth rattle. I hate when the bass is that loud, it just vibrates right through your chest cavity. 

But um, no, no new drugs or medicines or anything like that. Just the same old me.

Detached? Like things aren't real? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, the world is definitely real. The pavement gets so hot you can literally see the heat waves coming off it, making everything look all wavy and distorted. It's like looking through a funhouse mirror. 

I went to a funhouse once at the state fair when I was a kid. They had this whole hall of mirrors where you looked super tall and skinny, and then the next one made you look short and round like a beach ball. The fair is always so crowded, though. You can barely walk without bumping into someone eating a giant turkey leg. I don't understand how people can eat those things while walking around. They're so messy, and the grease gets everywhere. I prefer cotton candy. The blue kind, not the pink. It just tastes better, even though I know it's probably just the same sugar with different food coloring. I read once that red food dye is made from crushed up beetles. Isn't that disgusting? I try to check the labels on everything now, but the print is always so tiny. I should probably get reading glasses, but I feel like I'm too young for that. My mom started wearing reading glasses when she was forty, and she had them attached to this sparkly beaded chain around her neck so she wouldn't lose them. 

But no, I don't feel detached or anything during the blank spells. I'm just... blank.

An EEG? No, I've never had any kind of brain scan or anything like that. I've actually never even been in a hospital, except for when my sister had her baby. She had a little girl, Emily. She's five now, and she is just a handful. She has this curly hair that is impossible to brush. My sister buys all these expensive detangling sprays, but I swear none of them work. They just smell like artificial green apples. 

I actually really hate artificial fruit smells. Like those car air fresheners shaped like little trees? The cherry one gives me an instant headache. My ex-boyfriend used to have one of those in his truck, and I made him throw it out the window one time when we were driving on the highway. I know that's littering, and I felt bad about it later, but the smell was just so overwhelming. His truck was always a mess anyway, fast food wrappers everywhere. He used to eat those spicy chicken sandwiches from the drive-thru like every other day. I don't know how his stomach handled it. Spicy food always gives me terrible heartburn. I have to sleep propped up on two pillows if I even look at a jalapeño. 

But um, no, no brain scans or EEGs for the blank spells. Nobody's ever suggested that before.

Stare off into space? I mean, I guess so. I came in because my mind just keeps going completely blank at the worst possible times. Like, I'll be at work—I'm a crossing guard, well, a flagger really, for the construction sites—and I'll look down at the road-closure forms or even just my stop-slow paddle, and suddenly I cannot remember the steps I've done for years. It's just... gone. Like someone wiped a chalkboard clean. 

Chalkboards always remind me of elementary school. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she used to make us go outside and clap the erasers against the brick wall of the school to get the dust out. We'd be covered in this fine white powder by the time recess was over. It was so bad for our lungs, probably. I read an article once about how much dust we breathe in every day, mostly just dead skin cells. It's horrifying when you really think about it. I bought one of those fancy HEPA air purifiers for my apartment, but the filter replacement costs are just ridiculous. They get you on the refills, you know? It's like printers and ink cartridges. I haven't printed anything in years because the ink dried up and it costs more to buy new ink than to just buy a whole new printer. It's so wasteful. 

But yeah, I don't know if I'm staring into space, exactly, it's just that my mind goes completely blank and I forget what I'm supposed to be doing with the paddle.

While I'm asleep? I'm not really sure how I would know if my mind goes blank while I'm sleeping. I mean, you're unconscious, right? So you wouldn't know. I guess I don't really remember my dreams most of the time anyway. Sometimes I'll wake up and know I had a bad dream, but I can't remember any of the details. Just this lingering feeling of dread, like I forgot to do something really important. 

I hate that feeling. It's like when you leave the house and you're halfway down the street and you suddenly panic because you can't remember if you locked the front door or turned off the stove. I do that with my curling iron all the time. I'll actually turn the car around and drive all the way back home just to check, and it's always unplugged. I should really just start taking a picture of the unplugged cord on my phone before I leave, but then my camera roll would just be hundreds of pictures of a curling iron on a bathroom counter. My phone is already out of storage space anyway. It keeps giving me that annoying pop-up message saying I need to manage my storage, but I don't want to delete any of my pictures. I have all these photos from a trip I took to the Grand Canyon like ten years ago. It's so beautiful there, but the lack of guardrails is terrifying. You just walk right up to the edge and look down. I felt dizzy just standing there. 

But um, no, I haven't noticed them happening when I'm waking up or anything. Just mostly when I'm awake and trying to do things.

Hi, yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, well, what finally made me come in is that I just keep forgetting basic adult things, you know? Like paying bills, returning emails for job interviews, actually showing up for appointments, or even just following through on simple errands. It's really starting to cost me real opportunities, especially since I just graduated. Which, honestly, graduation was a whole other disaster. I almost missed the ceremony because I couldn't find my cap and gown until the absolute last second. My mom was so mad, she kept saying I was going to be late to my own funeral one day. We had this huge argument in the car on the way there, and then the AC broke in her Honda, so we were just sweating and yelling. But anyway, yeah, the emails and the bills... it's just getting really bad.

Oh, yeah, definitely. I mean, my mom actually kept all my old report cards from elementary school in this big plastic bin in the basement. Which, by the way, got totally ruined when our water heater broke last winter. It was this massive flood, and we had to rip up all the carpet down there. The carpet was this awful green color anyway, so it wasn't a huge loss, but it smelled like mildew for weeks. 

But um, before they got ruined, I remember looking at them and every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. They'd say I was bright, but I constantly lost my worksheets and just rushed through all the directions. And they always complained that I talked out of turn. Oh, and my desk! My desk was a complete disaster area. It was so messy I could never find my actual assignments in there. I used to just stuff everything inside. I actually found a half-eaten sandwich in the very back of it once in third grade. It was practically fossilized. I remember it was peanut butter and jelly because my mom bought that weird Goober grape stuff where the peanut butter and jelly are striped in the same jar? Have you ever had that? It looks cool on the commercial but it actually tastes kind of terrible because the jelly ratio is just way off...

Yeah, oh my gosh, yes. Sitting still is... it's honestly agonizing. Like if I'm in a job interview or a meeting, or even just trying to watch a movie, I get this intense pressure building up inside my body. It feels like I literally have to get up, or shift around, or at least do something with my hands, otherwise I'm going to crawl right out of my skin. 

Actually, I went to see that new superhero movie last week with my friend Sarah. You know, the one that's like three hours long? I don't know why movies are getting so long these days. It's ridiculous. Anyway, Sarah loves getting those massive tubs of popcorn, the ones where they layer the butter in the middle. But the guy at the concession stand was so slow, and I was just bouncing on my heels the whole time waiting. And then during the movie, I must have crossed and uncrossed my legs a hundred times. I ended up shredding my napkin into tiny little pieces and leaving them in the cup holder. Sarah got so annoyed with me because I kept kicking her seat by accident. She actually made us switch seats halfway through, which was super awkward because the guy next to us had to stand up to let us shuffle past, and he spilled his soda. It was Diet Coke, I think. But yeah, sitting still is just really, really hard for me.

Oh, absolutely. It's actually a huge problem for me, especially with these job interviews I've been trying to do. I have this terrible habit where, in conversations, I just jump right in before the other person is even finished talking. It's like my brain just assumes I know exactly where they're going with the sentence, so I just blurt it out. And then half the time, I realize I completely cut them off or I answered the wrong question entirely. 

It happened just last week on a Zoom interview for this marketing assistant job. Zoom is already the worst, right? Because you have that weird audio delay and you never know when someone is actually done speaking. Plus, I had to use my roommate's laptop because mine completely died. It's a MacBook, and the screen just went black. I took it to the Genius Bar, and the guy—he was wearing this really cool vintage band tee, I think it was Fleetwood Mac—he told me the logic board was fried. Which, of course, costs as much as a new computer to fix. So I'm using my roommate's Dell, which has the webcam at the bottom of the screen, so it's constantly looking up my nose. It's the most unflattering angle ever. 

But anyway, in the interview, the hiring manager was asking me something about my experience with social media campaigns, and I just completely interrupted her to talk about this one Instagram project I did in college. But she wasn't even asking about that! She was trying to ask about analytics software. It was so embarrassing. I could see her face just kind of freeze, and then there was that horrible awkward silence. I didn't get a call back for that one.

Oh, um... wait, what was the question? Like, do they happen everywhere? Honestly, I'm not really sure. I mean, obviously they happen at interviews, like I just said, and um... oh, and at home with my roommate. She gets so mad at me because I'll start cleaning the kitchen, right? And then I'll see a piece of mail on the counter, and I'll open it, and it's a bill, so I'll go to my room to get my wallet to pay it online. But then I see my laundry basket is overflowing, so I start sorting the darks and lights. And she'll come home like three hours later, and there's just soap suds drying on the dishes in the sink, my wallet is on the floor, and I'm like... repotting a houseplant in the living room. 

I bought this Monstera plant from this little nursery downtown. Have you been there? It's right next to that bakery that makes those incredible sourdough croissants. I went in there just to get a coffee, but the smell of the bread was so amazing I ended up buying like four pastries. I ate two of them in the car on the way home, which was a terrible idea because the flakes got absolutely everywhere. My car seats are black, so you can see every single crumb. I really need to vacuum my car. They have those drive-thru car washes where the vacuums are free at the end, but the suction on those things is always so weak, you know? Like, it doesn't even pick up the tiny pebbles from your shoes. 

But yeah, I don't know if I'd say it happens everywhere. Maybe? I guess I haven't really kept track of it like that.

Yeah, it really has. I mean, it's pretty bad. Like, since I got fired from my last job, I've just been... stuck. I keep missing follow-up emails for interviews, or I forget to send the thank-you notes, which I know is like, Interviewing 101. My mom is always telling me how important thank-you notes are. She buys these really expensive, thick cardstock ones from this boutique stationary store near her house. The envelopes have this beautiful gold foil lining inside. They're gorgeous, but they're like, five dollars a card, which is insane. Who spends that much on a piece of paper you're just going to throw away? 

But anyway, yeah, I'm totally unemployed right now, and it feels like I just can't manage the basic steps to get my life moving again. I even had to step back from this volunteer project I was doing, which really sucked because I actually cared about it. We were organizing this community garden downtown, right by the library. The library there is amazing, by the way. It has this huge glass atrium where you can just sit and read, and the light is perfect. I used to go there all the time in college to study, well, "study," mostly I just ended up looking at the architecture books because the pictures were so cool. 

But yeah, the garden project... I just kept missing the planning meetings, or I'd show up without the stuff I was supposed to bring, so I finally just had to quit. It's really frustrating. I just feel like I can't rely on myself to do the things I actually need to do.

I mean... down? I don't know if I'd say depressed, exactly. Just... really frustrated with myself, you know? Like, I'm just so annoyed that I can't seem to get it together. I guess sometimes I feel a little bummed out when I think about my friends who all have these real jobs now. My friend Sarah just got hired at this huge PR firm in Chicago. She moved there last month, and her apartment is incredible. It has exposed brick walls and these massive industrial windows. I've always wanted to live in a place with exposed brick. It just feels so much warmer than regular drywall, right? Plus, she’s right near this deep-dish pizza place she keeps posting about on her story. I love deep-dish pizza, even though some people say it’s more like a casserole than a pizza. But honestly, if it tastes good, who cares what you call it? 

But yeah, I don't think I'm depressed. Just... stuck in this really annoying rut and kind of mad at myself about it.

With friends? Um, I guess so? I mean, I don't really know what you mean by "problems" with them. Like, we hang out and stuff. We went to this trivia night on Tuesday at this pub downtown. They have the best sweet potato fries there. They serve them with this marshmallow dipping sauce, which sounds super weird, I know, but it is actually incredible. The saltiness of the fries and the sweetness of the marshmallow just... it works perfectly. My friend Jess refused to try it because she hates marshmallows. She had this traumatic experience at a campfire when we were in middle school where a roasted marshmallow fell off her stick and landed right on her leg and gave her this nasty burn. She still has the scar, actually. It's shaped kind of like a crescent moon. 

But anyway, what was the question? Like, do I have problems with them? I don't know, we get along fine mostly. I guess I'm always late when we meet up, but they're used to it.

Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, I don't sit around stressing about things that haven't happened. My mom is a huge worrier, though. Like, she worries about everything. If I don't text her back within an hour, she thinks I've been kidnapped. She watches a lot of those true crime documentaries, you know? The ones on Netflix where there's always some crazy twist in the third episode. I started watching one with her last week about this guy who forged all these rare documents. It was actually fascinating. He used tea bags to stain the paper so it would look old, which is so clever. I tried doing that once for a history project in high school, but I left the paper in the tea way too long and it just disintegrated. My teacher was not impressed. He was this really strict guy, Mr. Henderson, who always wore these horrible plaid ties. Like, every single day, a different plaid tie. 

But no, I don't really worry like that. I'm usually just dealing with whatever mess I've already made right in front of me, you know?

Before age 12? Oh, definitely. Yeah, even back in elementary school. I remember my mom showing me these old report cards, and every single teacher wrote the exact same thing. Like, "She's very bright, but..." And then it was always about how I constantly lost my worksheets or how I'd rush through the directions and do the whole thing wrong. Or how I'd just blurt things out and talk out of turn. 

Oh, and my desk! My desk was a disaster zone. I remember in third grade, my teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was so nice, she always smelled like lavender and she had this really fluffy golden retriever that she brought in for show-and-tell once. His name was Barnaby, and he was the softest dog I've ever pet. I begged my parents for a golden retriever after that, but my dad is super allergic to dogs. Like, his eyes swell up and he gets hives. So we ended up getting a lizard instead. A bearded dragon named Spike. He was cool, I guess, but you can't really cuddle a lizard, you know? They just kind of sit there under their heat lamp looking grumpy. 

But yeah, Mrs. Gable used to make me stay inside during recess sometimes just to clean out my desk because it was so stuffed with crumpled papers and broken crayons that I couldn't even find my assignments. So, yeah, it's definitely been happening since I was little.

At home? Um, trouble at home... I don't know, maybe? I mean, my room was always a mess, but I feel like every kid's room is a mess, right? My mom used to get so mad about the laundry. Like, I'd bring it up from the basement and just leave the basket in the hallway for days. Our basement was so creepy, by the way. It had these weird, flickering fluorescent lights that buzzed, and there were always spiders in the corners. I am terrified of spiders. Once, I was down there looking for my rollerblades—I went through this huge rollerblading phase in fifth grade, I even had the neon pink knee pads and everything. We used to skate down this big hill near my house, which was probably super dangerous because there was a busy intersection right at the bottom. My friend Mark actually wiped out there once and scraped his whole arm up. He had to wear this bandage for weeks and he milked it for all it was worth, making everyone carry his books at school. 

But anyway, I was in the basement looking for my skates, and this massive spider dropped right onto my shoulder. I screamed so loud my dad thought someone broke in. He came running down the stairs with a golf club. A golf club! He doesn't even play golf, he just found it at a garage sale once. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Trouble at home? I don't really know if I got in trouble for the same stuff as at school. I guess my parents just yelled at me to clean my room a lot.

I mean, like I said, I'm not really sure. I don't know if I noticed the exact same issues at home, just because it wasn't like sitting at a desk all day, you know? At home, I mostly just hung out in the kitchen while my mom cooked. She made this incredible lasagna from scratch. It took her literally all afternoon because she made her own pasta and the sauce had to simmer forever. 

I actually tried to make it once when I was in college, but my dorm kitchen was absolutely disgusting. Like, nobody ever cleaned up after themselves. My freshman roommate, Chloe, she was an art major and she used to leave all her weird project materials all over our tiny counter. She made these giant sculptures out of recycled trash, which I guess is great for the environment, but it meant we always had empty milk jugs and egg cartons everywhere. She once glued a bunch of plastic spoons together to look like a chandelier and hung it from our ceiling. It was kind of cool, actually, but the tape gave out and it fell down in the middle of the night and scared me half to death. I thought the ceiling was caving in. The dorms were so old, they honestly could have caved in at any minute. They didn't even have air conditioning, which was brutal in September. 

But um, yeah, I really couldn't tell you. I just don't remember noticing the attention stuff as much when I was just hanging around the house.

I really don't think so. I mean, maybe my parents would say something different, but to me, it didn't feel like it caused actual problems. Like, we didn't have huge fights about it or anything. Mostly my dad was just out in the garage working on his car. He had this vintage Mustang that he bought as a total rust bucket, and he spent every weekend trying to fix it up. He was always covered in grease. He actually taught me how to change the oil once, which was kind of fun, but I got oil all over my favorite pair of jeans. They were these light wash flared jeans that I wore literally every single day. I was so upset. My mom tried all these different stain removers, but it never came out. She even tried this weird trick with baking soda and vinegar that she found on the internet. Have you ever tried that? It fizzed up like a volcano project. I actually won second place in the science fair with a volcano project in fourth grade. I used papier-mâché and painted it to look super realistic. The kid who won first place did something boring with magnets, which I still think was rigged because his mom was the PTA president. She was always bringing in these huge trays of cupcakes for the teachers... Wait, did that answer your question? I just don't remember it being a big issue at home.

With other kids? Um, I mean, I guess I was kind of a handful. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was bright, but I was constantly losing my worksheets. I'd rush through the directions and just talk out of turn all the time. And my desk—oh my gosh, my desk was a disaster zone. I could never find my assignments in there. It was just crammed full of crumpled papers and broken crayons. 

I actually used to collect those little erasers shaped like animals? I had a whole zoo in my desk. There was this one turtle eraser that I loved, it had a little shell you could take off. My friend Jessica tried to trade me her sparkly unicorn eraser for it, but I said no. Jessica was always trying to trade stuff. She brought these amazing lunches to school, like her mom would cut her sandwiches into star shapes and pack these little containers of hummus and pita chips. My mom just gave me a squished bologna sandwich and a bruised apple every single day. I hated bologna so much. I tried to feed it to the stray cat that hung around the playground once, but even the cat wouldn't eat it. That cat was so mean, too. It scratched Jimmy Henderson right on the nose. Jimmy was the kid who always wore shorts, even in January. Like, it would be snowing, and he'd be out there in cargo shorts and a t-shirt. 

But yeah, I guess I did interrupt a lot and talk out of turn. I just couldn't keep my desk clean to save my life.

No, I don't think so. I still like doing the things I usually do. Like, I love going to thrift stores. I could spend literally hours just looking through all the racks of clothes. Last week I found this amazing vintage denim jacket that fits me perfectly. It has these really cool embroidered roses on the back. It reminds me of this jacket my aunt used to wear in the 90s. She was in a band and they actually played a few shows at this local dive bar. She played the bass, which I always thought was the coolest instrument. I tried to learn the guitar once, but my fingers hurt so bad from pressing down on the strings. I gave up after like two weeks. The guy who taught the lessons was so weird, too. He smelled like old coffee and patchouli, and he kept talking about how music is just math with feelings. Which, I mean, maybe it is, but I just wanted to learn how to play Wonderwall. Everyone learns Wonderwall first, right? It's like a rule. But anyway, yeah, I still enjoy things just fine.

I came in because... well, I just keep thinking it would be better if I didn't wake up in the morning. It's been heavy on my mind. Sometimes I honestly feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to my family, and to my crew at work. I just don't know what else to do anymore.

Not right this exact minute, no. But... like I was just saying, the thought of just not waking up tomorrow is constantly there. I don't have a specific plan to do it right now, but I just really feel like dying is the only fair punishment left for what I've put my family through, and the guys on my crew. I just want it to be over.

Yes. I really do. I just keep thinking that I'm the reason my husband got worse. And at work... my crew lost work because of me, and clients' homes got messed up. It's like I just poisoned everything I touched. So, yeah, I feel like I deserve whatever happens to me.

Yes, they have. My husband tries to tell me that, and some of the guys. But... I know I am. Because even when I'm not crying or just stuck down in bed, I know what's going on. 

I am absolutely certain that the homeowners and the suppliers are tracking me. They use the floor patterns we lay down, the text messages, the permit calls... they use all of that to track whether I'm ruining the jobs on purpose. People try to tell me that's not happening, but no one can talk me out of it. I just know they're doing it.

No... no, I haven't. I don't really get energized or... euphoric. Honestly, I'm usually just exhausted. I've never had a time where I felt really high or full of energy for days like you're saying. It's pretty much just the opposite.

Yes. Actually, there was a stretch... maybe a few weeks, where I was doing a bit better. I was getting up out of bed, eating a little more normally, and I wasn't crying all day long. But even then, I still heard the voice when I was at work, and I was still completely convinced that the clients and suppliers were tracking me. So, yeah, it didn't go away even when my mood lifted a bit.

I suppose... I just feel like the part of me that used to reach out to people has gone very quiet lately. I don't really take pleasure in things anymore. My work... yoga, going to galleries. Even just journaling. It's... I don't know. I'm mostly just moving through my obligations right now. So... I guess that's what brought me in.

I'm not sure if you'd call it significant, but... it's been about eight months. We took an older relative into our apartment around then. I suppose that's when this whole change in how I'm thinking... and working, and connecting with people really started.
I... I don't really know. I wouldn't necessarily say it's because of them. It's just... that's just around the time I noticed things changing.
Like I said... I really couldn't tell you. It's just the timing of when I started noticing things. I wouldn't necessarily call it the cause.
I... no, I don't think so. I haven't really noticed feeling down for two straight weeks like that. It's... it's not really like that.
Two years? No... I haven't felt like this for that long. It's... no.

I mean... I guess it has a little. I'm still going to work. But... I've missed a few grant deadlines. And my supervisor... she quietly moved some of my more demanding clients to other clinicians. I suppose I'm just... not functioning at my usual level right now.
No... I don't think so. I can't really remember another time where I felt... quite like this. It's just been recently.
I don't know... not really. I wouldn't call it distress. It's just... kind of how things are right now. I'm not really upset about it.
No... I'm not sure what you mean. I don't have any older relatives moving in with me. So... no.

Well... I mean, nobody is moving in right now. But... I guess we did take my older relative into our apartment. That was about eight months ago. So... that's about how long all of this has been going on. The changes in how I'm thinking, and working... and connecting with people.

Lost interest? Yeah, I'd say so. I'd say I've lost interest in just about everything, honestly. And cooking, too. I used to love making this big pot of beans every Sunday. I even used to do little repair jobs for folks around the building, you know? Fixing a leaky faucet, tightening up a loose cabinet hinge. I liked feeling useful. I liked working with my hands. 

But now? Now I don't do any of it. None of it. The choir director called a few times, left messages, but I just let the phone ring. I sit there on the couch and watch it ring, and I just tell myself there's no point in going. There's just no point. The bridge group probably found a replacement by now, and I haven't cooked those beans in months. The thought of chopping the onions, standing over the stove... it's just too much. Why would I help them? But even if they weren't, I just... I don't care anymore. The things that used to bring me a little bit of joy, a little bit of satisfaction, they just feel empty now. Two weeks? Oh, Lord, if it was only two weeks, I’d count my blessings. Two weeks is just a bad mood or a rough patch. No, doc, it’s been way, way longer than that. If I really sit and trace it back... it's been about a year and two months. Yeah, a year and two months of this.

So I end up putting it all right back down in the pile and walking away. It's just... it's exhausting, you know? I actually had to go to the dentist last month because of a terrible toothache. Dr. Evans. He’s got this big beautiful aquarium in his waiting room with these little neon fish that glow in the dark. The grandkids just love watching them dart around. My youngest grandson, Tommy, he begged for a fish tank for his birthday, but his mother said absolutely not, she wasn't going to be the one cleaning the green algae out of it every week. Which is fair, I suppose. I had a goldfish when I was a little girl, won it at the county fair tossing ping pong balls into those little glass bowls. It only lived for about a week, though. We flushed it down the toilet and I cried all afternoon... 

But anyway, yes, the business decisions and the money. That is exactly what she is doing.

Well, hello. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose... well, I came in because things have just been so incredibly tense at work lately, and I just don't know how to process it all anymore. I’m a secondary school teacher—history, mostly the older years, which is a handful on its own, as you can imagine. I've been teaching for over thirty years now, so I know how schools operate. I know the rhythms of the day, the administrative side of things, all of it. 

But recently, maybe over the last few months or so, there’s been this... well, a shift. It started with the morning announcements over the PA system. You know, the usual things the headmaster reads out about assembly times or parking lot rules or cafeteria menus. But I started noticing—and I still can't shake this feeling, no matter how much I try to just sit at my desk and focus on my lesson plans—that they aren't just general announcements. The phrasing they use, the specific pauses, the choice of words... it feels quite clearly like they are actually coded messages directed specifically at me. Like a warning, or some sort of commentary on what I'm doing, hidden right there out in the open where the students can't catch on but I'm supposed to. 

And it’s not just the intercom, either. It’s the staff emails. I’ll read a memo about, say, the new grading software or a reminder about locking the supply cupboards, and I can just tell that between the lines, it’s a message meant only for me. I actually brought it up in the staff room the other day to Margaret—she teaches geography next door to me, lovely woman, we’ve shared a wall for a decade—and she was very gentle about it. She actually pulled up her laptop right there by the kettle and showed me the header of the email, pointing out that it was sent to the entire "All Staff" mailing list. She kept saying, "Look, we all got the exact same email, it's just standard administrative nonsense." 

And logically, I look at her screen, I see the email addresses... but the feeling just doesn't go away. Even when they show me it went to everyone, I can't stop feeling like the message itself was written *for* me, and just disguised as a mass email to throw me off. It's just exhausting, frankly, trying to decipher what they really want from me from the moment the first bell rings to the end of the day.

No, no, nothing of the sort. I mean, I suppose it’s almost a miracle, given the environment I work in. You’d think being surrounded by hundreds of teenagers for three decades would leave you with every ailment in the book, but I’ve always been very diligent about my health. 

I see my regular GP—Dr. Evans, he’s been my doctor for ages—every August right before the autumn term begins. I always do it then because once September starts, well, you know how it is, there’s simply no time to be sitting around in waiting rooms when you have a syllabus to launch. And he’s always told me my health is perfectly fine. My blood pressure is excellent, surprisingly, especially for a teacher, and I’ve certainly never had to see a neurologist or get any sort of brain scan or anything like that. 

There's no history of seizures or strokes or... well, whatever else falls under that umbrella. I don't even get headaches, really, unless I've been staring at Year 11 essays for too many hours without my reading glasses. So physically, medically speaking, my record is completely clean. I haven't even taken a sick day for a physical illness since a rather nasty bout of bronchitis back in, oh, it must have been 2017. So no, absolutely nothing diagnosed. My brain and my body are perfectly healthy. It’s really just this... this intense, exhausting situation with the messages at the school that’s wearing me down, not my physical health.

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... let me think. We are in late summer now, so... it would have been right around the middle of the spring term. Yes, just before the Easter holidays, actually. I remember it quite vividly because I was in the thick of marking the Year 11 mock exams—which is always an incredibly demanding period, as you can imagine, just mountains of paper everywhere on my desk—and that’s when the worries about the coded messages really began to take hold. 

So, let's see... April, May, June, July... it’s been about four months. Four months of this constant, daily analyzing of every single word that comes out of that PA system or lands in my inbox. And, actually, now that I’m really thinking about that specific timeframe and how it all started, it wasn't just the messages that began then. It was also right around that exact same time, maybe just a week or so after the intercom announcements started feeling so pointed, that I started... well, I started noticing this voice. 

It's just a voice, and I find myself sometimes answering it, just talking back to it when I'm alone in my classroom after the students have gone home for the day and the corridors are finally quiet. It’s a bit strange to admit out loud, I suppose, but yes, both the worries about the coded messages and that voice I sometimes answer, they’ve both been happening for about four months now. 

And I must say, these last four months have felt much more like four years, what with the constant vigilance it all requires. You just never really get a moment's peace when you're constantly trying to figure out what they are trying to tell you through the morning announcements, or when you're suddenly responding to someone who isn't standing there in the room with you. It really takes a toll on your energy, especially when you still have to stand up and deliver a comprehensive lecture on the Tudor dynasty the very next morning...

Yes, oh absolutely, yes. It hasn't stopped at all. Like I said, it started right around the Easter holidays, which feels like a lifetime ago now, but it's been about four months. Four entire months of this. And it hasn't been something that comes and goes, you know? It's not like I have a good week where I don't hear the voice or where the morning announcements just sound like normal announcements. It is every single day. 

I wake up, I have my tea, I drive to work, and from the absolute second I step out of my car in the staff car park, I am on edge, waiting for the PA system to crackle to life, waiting for that voice to chime in while I'm trying to organize my desk. It’s a continuous, unbroken chain of days. I mean, even on the weekends, when I'm not at the school, I'll be at home trying to grade papers or do a bit of gardening, and the voice is still there, and I'll find myself answering it while I'm pruning the hydrangeas. And I'll still be agonizing over an email that was sent on Friday afternoon, trying to decode it. So yes, it has definitely been well over a month. Four months, continuously, without a single day's reprieve. It’s just relentless, really.

Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have. Though it's difficult to pinpoint exactly when it started, but it's been going on for many months now. I still care, you know? I really do. I care deeply about my students—I always have, that's why I've stayed in the profession so long—and I care about my friends. I just let it all slide. I haven't attended book club since... oh, it must be before Christmas. I just couldn't muster the energy to read the book, let alone go and discuss it. And the theater committee... I just quietly stopped going to the meetings. 

Even simple things, like making a phone call to my sister on a Sunday afternoon, which used to be a weekly ritual for us. Now, I just... I look at the phone and I can't bring myself to dial the number. I just sit there. Unless someone really pushes me, unless someone physically comes up to me and says, "We need you to do this right now," I just don't have the motivation to initiate anything anymore. It’s not that I don't want to see my friends or talk to my family, it’s just this... this profound emptiness, like my battery is completely flat and refuses to recharge. I just feel so incredibly flat, emotionally speaking, like all the color has washed out of everything. It’s quite sad, really, when I say it out loud like that, but yes, it’s been months of just feeling completely depleted of any sort of spark or enthusiasm.

My whole life has basically narrowed down to just barely getting through the school day, and then going home completely exhausted.

Yes, definitely. I mean, I've been teaching for a while now, so I know what normal work stress feels like. There are always busy times and extra workload. But this... it just feels completely different. It's a lot heavier than that, and I've never reacted to a heavy workload like this before. It doesn't feel like it's just about the work.

Well, yeah, I guess so. I mean, lately I can sleep maybe two or three hours, and I'll wake up way before dawn just... completely ready to go. The only thing you hear is the paper delivery guy. He comes around 4:30 on this vintage Schwinn bicycle. I had a bike exactly like that when I was a kid, cherry red with the silver fenders. But yeah, I'll just be up in the dark, feeling fantastic, mapping out this whole new deck I want to build out back. You know the price of treated lumber is just through the roof right now? It's unbelievable.

Well, yeah, it definitely feels different. Like, usually I'm just, you know, normal. I snapped at the guy at the hardware store yesterday just because he didn't know where the galvanized screws were. I mean, how do you work in a hardware store and not know that? But no, I haven't been doing anything crazy or risky. Just... getting ready for the projects.

Depressed? Like, down in the dumps? No, I don't really get like that. I mean, sure, everyone has a bad day here and there, but not for two whole weeks. Two weeks is a long time. I learned that when I was helping my buddy pour a patio behind his place. We mixed all the bags by hand in this old wheelbarrow. My arms were killing me the next day. Well, yeah, actually... when I get in those fired-up stretches, you know, when I'm only sleeping a couple hours and making all these big plans for the deck and everything... Well, you know, it’s funny you put it that way, because... well, yes and no. It’s not just a simple "high," it’s more like... it’s like the whole world is just humming, you know? Well, like I was just saying, it’s... it's a bit of both, really, and it takes up the whole day. It's not just a passing thing. Well, it’s not so much a "power" like in a comic book, but... yes, a mission, absolutely. See, I’ve been working this land for forty years, and you get to know the dirt. You get to know how it breathes. And lately, it’s become clear as day to me—crystal clear—that I am the one farmer in this entire county, maybe the whole state, who actually understands what needs to be done. I’ve figured out this entirely new way of growing, a whole new system of crop rotation and soil turnover that works with the natural magnetic pull of the earth. 

I’ve been trying to explain it to people. I sat down and drew up these charts—beautiful, detailed charts showing the yield projections—and I took them down to the university extension office. And you know what they did? Those kids in their clean button-down shirts, who probably couldn't tell a soybean from a pinto bean if it bit them, they just smiled at me. Patted me on the head, practically. And the lenders at the bank, same thing. I went in to get a loan to overhaul the combines for this new method, and they looked at me like I was speaking Greek. 

But I know I'm right. I feel it in my bones. I am absolutely sure I can prove this new way of growing, and those university people and the bankers, they ought to be sitting down and taking notes from me instead of doubting me and looking at their watches. They should be begging me for the secret! Because once I get the machinery moving in that new pattern—like I was trying to show them at the fair—it’s going to revolutionize agriculture. I just need them to stop getting in my way and listen for five minutes, because I’m the only one who sees the big picture here. The only one.

Well, it’s... you see, that’s another thing entirely. Now, I don't know about seeing things, my eyes are as good as they were when I was twenty, but hearing... well, yes. But it’s not just random noise, Doc. It's very specific, and it's important. 

You know my north pasture? The one that slopes down toward the old creek bed? We put in a new set of irrigation lines down there about, oh, must be five years ago now. Good quality aluminum. Anyway, lately... especially right around dusk, when the sun is just dipping behind the ridge and the light gets all long and orange, and the wind dies down so it's just dead quiet out there... I’ll go out to check the valves. And I hear them. Voices. Clear as a bell, coming right out of the metal of those irrigation lines. 

At first, I thought maybe it was just the water pressure whistling, you know how pipes do, or maybe the metal catching a radio frequency somehow. But no, it’s voices. Real, distinct voices. And they’re talking to me about the dirt, about the crops. They tell me exactly which rows are blessed—which ones are going to yield up strong and pure—and which rows are poisoned. Just straight up poisoned from the roots. And I have to listen, because if I don't mark off the poisoned rows, the whole harvest could be compromised. 

And the strange thing is, Mary thinks it's just because I've been working too hard, or because I've been running hot with all that energy I was telling you about earlier. She thinks I'm just overtired and wound up. But I've been keeping track, Doc. I hear those voices in the pipes even on the weeks when I'm perfectly calm. Even when I'm not all fired up and pacing the floorboards, when I'm just having a regular, slow, quiet week... I can walk out to that north pasture at sundown, and they are still there. Still telling me what's blessed and what's poisoned. So it's not just the energy, you see? It doesn't matter if I'm flying high or just resting easy, the lines still speak to me.

Well, yes, exactly. That's just what I was trying to explain, Doc. You see, I've really been paying attention to this, because Mary kept insisting it was just me being wound up. So I started keeping track. And there was this stretch, oh, maybe a month or so ago, where I was just... normal. I wasn't waking up with that buzzing energy, I wasn't feeling irritable or grand, I was just doing my chores at a regular pace. Eating my meals, sitting on the porch after dinner, sleeping a solid eight hours. Just a quiet, completely normal couple of weeks. 

But even then, during those quiet weeks, if I went down to the north pasture at dusk, I still heard the lines talking. Clear as day. And it wasn't just the voices, either. I'd be sitting at the kitchen table with my ledger, looking over the farm data, the yield reports, and I still knew—I still believed with absolute certainty—that the numbers were carrying hidden warnings about the poisoned rows. Even when my mood was as steady as a rock, those warnings were there, and the voices were there. It doesn't seem to matter if I'm flying high or just having a regular old Tuesday, the truth about the land doesn't change.

Nice to meet you, too. Well, I’m here because... I’ve gotten to the point where I basically plan my whole summer around avoiding wasps. It's just become too much.

Hi, yeah, it's good to meet you too. Um, well, I guess the main reason I’m here is that I’m just having a really, really hard time getting through my work. I’m a secondary school teacher, and obviously, that comes with a lot of grading and lesson planning outside of actual classroom hours. And I really care about my job, I do, but... I’ll set myself up to work, right? I'll make a cup of coffee, clear off my desk at home, and I'll sit down with a stack of essays from my students, or maybe a massive curriculum document the administration wants us to review for the new term. 

I sit down fully intending to work. Like, I am completely ready to just power through it and get it done. But then... I don't even know how it happens, really. Within ten minutes, I'll suddenly sort of snap back to reality and realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the entire time. I'll be looking right at the words, but I'm actually thinking about three completely different things—like if I need to get my car's oil changed, or a random documentary I watched last week, or what groceries I need to buy later. I'm just barely taking in what’s actually right in front of me. 

And it’s so frustrating because I sit there thinking, "just read the paper, it's right there," but my mind is already a million miles away again before I even finish the sentence. It ends up taking me hours to do what should be a fairly quick task, just sitting there fighting with my own head to read a single page. So, yeah, I just... I can't keep doing it like this, which is why I finally made the appointment.

Yeah, actually... it’s funny you ask that, because I've been thinking about that a lot lately. It goes all the way back to, well, even in primary school. My parents kept all my old report cards in this big filing cabinet at their house, and if you go back and read them, it’s almost comical how consistent the comments are. Every single year, different teachers would write the exact same things, like “bright but careless,” or they’d specifically note that I “doesn’t finish work unless closely supervised.” 

Like, they knew I understood the material, but if the teacher walked away from my desk to help someone else, I'd just drift off into space or start staring at the grain on my desk, just like I do now with my grading. And my parents... oh man, they used to get so frustrated with me about my backpack. They were always, and I mean *always*, finding these old worksheets just completely crumpled up at the very bottom of my bag. Like, shoved under a jacket or crushed under a textbook. I would do the work, or at least start it, and then I’d just completely forget to actually turn it in. 

My mom used to pull out these incredibly wrinkled pieces of paper and try to flatten them out on the kitchen table, just asking me why I couldn't just walk up to the teacher's desk and hand it in when everyone else did. And I never had a good answer for her. It just ceased to exist in my brain the second I put it in my bag. So, yeah, I guess this isn't exactly a new problem for me. It's just... it's a lot harder to manage now that I'm the adult in the classroom and there's nobody there to supervise me and make sure I'm doing what I'm supposed to be doing, you know?

Um, that's a good question. I guess... no, not really. I mean, if it's something I'm really into, it's almost the exact opposite problem, to be honest. Like, if I'm reading a book I actually chose to read—like a really good sci-fi novel, or even just researching something random I got curious about online, like the history of cartography or something—I can do that for hours. 

Actually, it can get kind of ridiculous. My partner gets so annoyed with me sometimes because I'll start doing something I enjoy, like working on this little woodworking project I started in the garage, and I'll just completely lose track of time. I'll go out there at like 2:00 PM on a Saturday, just intending to sand down a piece of wood for twenty minutes, and suddenly it's 7:00 PM, it's pitch black outside, I haven't eaten dinner, and I haven't heard them calling me to come inside because I was just so intensely locked into what I was doing. 

It's like I have two modes: either I can't focus on it for more than ten seconds to save my life, or I'm so hyper-focused on it that a bomb could go off next to me and I wouldn't even flinch. And it's so weird, right? Because you'd think if I can focus that intensely on building a birdhouse, I should be able to focus on grading a tenth-grade history essay. But it just doesn't translate. If the interest isn't there, naturally, organically there... my brain just refuses to engage with it. So, yeah, if I enjoy it, I'm locked in. Maybe too locked in sometimes.

Oh, man. Yeah. Yes, absolutely, it spills over into everything else. It’s not just the grading, though that’s bad enough. Like I mentioned, at work, it’s gotten to the point where my department chair actually had to pull me into her office last month.
