And then at home... well, it’s not much better. My wife is amazing, she really is, but she's just reached her breaking point with me lately. It used to be that we’d split the household stuff, you know? Like I’d handle the utilities and the car registration, and she’d do the mortgage and the insurance. But I kept missing due dates. Not because we didn’t have the money, but literally just because I would look at a bill, think, "I need to pay that on Tuesday," put it down on the counter, and then it would just cease to exist in my reality until we got a late notice in the mail. Or she'd ask me to call the plumber, and I'd say yes, and then three days later the sink is still leaking and I haven't even looked up a number. 

So now, she’s basically just taken over all of it. All the bills, all the appointments, all the reminders. She even has this shared calendar app on our phones now where she inputs everything because she said she just can’t count on me to keep track of any of it anymore. And I hate it. I hate that she has to take on that mental load because my brain just won't hold onto the information. I feel like I'm failing at work and I'm failing as a partner, all because I just can't seem to keep my focus where it needs to be to just... do the normal, basic things adults are supposed to do.

Um, anxious? No, not really. I mean, not in the moment when I'm actually drifting off. It's more like... well, it's almost like my brain just quietly changes the channel without me even noticing that the remote was pressed, if that makes sense. Like, I don't feel a sense of dread or worry that pulls me away from the grading. I'm not sitting there thinking about my department chair or the support plan or, you know, stressing about whether I'm going to get fired. 

It's more like... I'll be reading a paragraph about the causes of World War I for the fifteenth time, and then suddenly I'm looking out the window at a squirrel on the fence, and I'm wondering what kind of squirrel it is, and then I'm thinking about how I read somewhere that squirrels plant thousands of trees every year because they forget where they buried their nuts, and then I'm wondering if I could build a squirrel feeder in the garage... and it's all very calm. Almost peaceful, honestly. It's just my brain wandering down this totally random path of thoughts. 

The anxiety only hits later. Like, *much* later. It's when I suddenly snap back to reality and look at the clock and realize that forty-five minutes have gone by and I haven't graded a single paper. *That's* when the panic sets in. That's when my heart starts racing and I get that awful, sinking feeling in my stomach, and I start beating myself up, thinking, "Why do you do this? Why can't you just sit here and do the work like a normal person?" But the actual drifting part? No, there's no worry there at all. It's just... a complete absence of focus on the task at hand. It's like I just float away.

Um, physically restless? Like, needing to move around? No, not really. I mean, I can sit still just fine. It's funny you ask that, actually, because my mom used to tell me stories about my cousin, David—he’s a few years younger than me—and when he was little, he literally could not sit in a chair for dinner. He’d be bouncing off the walls, running around the table, tapping his fork on everything. They had to get him one of those special wobble stools for school just so he wouldn't disrupt the whole class. But I was never like that. I was the quiet kid in the back of the room, you know? 

Even now, sitting at my desk to grade or whatever, my body is perfectly still. I'm not fidgeting or tapping my foot or feeling like I need to get up and run a marathon. I can sit in one spot for hours, especially if I'm doing something I like, like that woodworking I mentioned. My body just stays put. It’s entirely in my head. My brain is what’s doing the running around, jumping from the grading to the squirrel to the history of cartography. So, yeah, physically, I'm pretty stationary. I don't get that urge to move or that feeling like I have a motor running inside me. It's just my thoughts that won't stay in their seat, if that makes sense.

I mean... I suppose everyone walks into a room and forgets what they went in there for once in a great while, right? But I certainly don't just lose track of what I'm doing in the middle of a routine. I have my little daily habits, and I stick to them very well. 

I wouldn't want you to worry that I can't manage on my own or that I'm just wandering aimlessly around the house. I take a lot of pride in keeping things running smoothly, especially with my cousin living here now. I hope that's the kind of answer you were looking for? I just really want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture of how things are.

Well, um... I suppose it's mostly... mostly when it's about my cousin's care. That's really the main thing, to be honest. It's actually sort of what brought me in to see you today. 

My wife, she's so wonderful and organized, and she'll be telling me about his upcoming appointments, or who is giving him a ride on what day, and... well, I'm looking right at her, nodding along, trying to be a good listener. But then, maybe a minute later, I realize I didn't actually take in half of what she just said. 

I feel just terrible about it when it happens! I don't want her to think I don't care, because I do, very much. It's just... well, it's a lot of details to keep straight all of a sudden, you know? With the schedules and the times. I'm sure anyone would get a little overwhelmed by all those logistics, right? I really hope that doesn't make me sound like a bad husband. I do try my very best to pay attention. Is that... is that the sort of thing you were asking about?

Oh, no, no, not really. Before he moved in, things were quite manageable, they really were. We've always had wonderful conversations, my wife and I. 

It's just... well, it's really just been the last 11 months or so that it's gotten noticeably harder. Ever since my cousin had his surgery and came to stay with us. It's just been such a big change to our routine, you know? So many new things to keep track of all at once. 

Before that, I was always very attentive. I still am, mostly! It's just this one particular area that's been a little tricky lately. I'm sure it's just the stress of the adjustment, don't you think? I mean, anyone would struggle a little bit with such a sudden change in the household, right? I just want to be sure I'm explaining it clearly so you don't think I've always been this way.

They... my lieutenant sent me here. I was at the station. Just moving the airway bags around. I had to put them in a pattern I knew was right. And... I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. 

He told me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't. If I broke the sequence... the whole bay would go bad. So they made me come here.

It wasn't my mind. I was certain. 

Because I... I already know what they're doing to me. The injury review people. Some of the supervisors, too. They've been watching me through the station cameras. And they... they go in and change my triage notes. Just to make me look unsafe. They keep telling me it's just routine paperwork, but... I know. I know they're doing it. So, yeah. I was certain.
No. I don't... no. I haven't heard anything like that. Just the people who are actually there.
No. I don't... I don't really know what you mean by intrusive. It wasn't unwanted. I just... I had to do it. That's all.
No. I don't... no. Nobody's putting things in my head. They're just watching me. That's all.
No. I don't... they aren't sending signals or anything like that. They just... they just record what I'm doing. That's it.
It makes sense to me. I don't... I don't think it's wrong or anything. It's just what I have to do.
About two months. That's... that's when the camera and the paperwork stuff started. And the things at the station that got everyone all alarmed. Just the last two months or so.
I'm not... I don't really know. It just sort of... happened. I wasn't keeping track of the days or anything.

Yeah. Like I said... it's been about two months. That's how long the camera and the paperwork stuff has been happening... and the things at the station that got everyone so alarmed. So, yeah, more than a month.

No. I... I can't work the ambulance anymore. They put me on desk duty for a bit, just doing notes and equipment checks, but... they said I was unreliable. So they took me off the schedule. I don't really go in now. I've mostly just... stopped seeing friends, too. Haven't been keeping up with things around the house much either. Just... keeping to myself.
No... it's been longer. It all started... well, I hurt my shoulder and my ribs. It was during an ambulance transfer. That was... about eight months ago. So, no, it's been longer than three.
No... I told you. The camera stuff... it's only been about two months. Not three.
No. I... I don't think so. Like I said, I don't really talk to people much right now anyway. But... no, no one's told me that.
No. They're always doing it. I haven't had a day where they weren't.
No. I haven't... I don't feel like that.

Hi. It's nice to meet you too. 

I’m here because... well, for months now, I’ve been seeing this exact same pattern in my project files at work. I work as a translator, and certain subcontractors, along with one colleague in particular, keep making these tiny changes to the translation memory and the file timestamps. 

It's set up specifically to make it look like my quality control failed. I actually brought it up to our IT department, but they told me the audit trail is clean. But I know what I'm seeing. I know the digital record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me for these errors, and it's just becoming impossible to deal with on my own.

Yes, I am completely certain. I know what IT told me about the audit trail being clean, but... well, they are just looking at the standard logs. 

I've been a translator for a long time, and I know exactly how our translation memory works. These subcontractors and that one colleague are making tiny, very specific changes to the files. It's not a glitch or a mistake. Even if they managed to make the timestamps look normal to the IT department, I know what I'm looking at. The digital record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me for those errors. So, yes, I have no doubt they are still doing it.
No, I haven't experienced anything like that. I haven't felt unusually high or irritable, just... frustrated by what's happening at work. But my mood itself has been pretty normal.
No, I haven't heard any voices. Nothing like that. It's just the files and the changes they're making to them. My hearing is perfectly fine, and I don't hear things that aren't there.

No, definitely not. I've never felt like anyone is messing with my mind or my thoughts. My thoughts are my own. The issue is entirely with the computer files and what my colleague is doing to them, not anything inside my head.

No, not at all. Outside of this whole project issue, things are pretty much normal. I still translate, manage my team’s workflow, pay the bills, and keep up with all my usual family routines. I haven't lost interest in any of that. 

The only place things really go off track is when the file history or certain coworkers come up. But other than that, my life is exactly the same.
No, I haven't. I've never had any issues with my brain or my nervous system. I'm completely healthy in that regard. Like I said, the only problem is what's happening at work with my files.
No, I haven't. I've never seen anything that wasn't actually there, or that other people couldn't see. My vision is perfectly normal, I just see what everyone else sees.
It's been about 11 months now. It started shortly after I was put in charge of the new localization project.

No, no one has ever said anything like that. I mean, as a translator, my whole job relies on clear communication. I haven't noticed any issues with how I speak, and no one else has mentioned that I'm hard to follow or... disorganized. I express myself just fine.

Well, I'm here because... everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, normal paperwork and missed payments. But I know the truth. I know the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job—my cashiers have been acting so strange lately, whispering when I walk by the breakroom. It's like that time I found all those receipts stuffed behind the register, just completely out of order. I had to spend three hours sorting them, and my manager didn't even care. But anyway, they've all been quietly working together to push me out of my house. And no amount of papers they show me changes what I’ve been seeing for almost two years. It's just like how they keep rearranging the endcaps at the store without telling me, just to see if I'll notice. But I notice everything.

Voices? No, no, I don't hear things that aren't there. I just hear exactly what people actually say, even when they think I'm out of earshot. Like... well, take yesterday. I was in the back stockroom—which isn't even a proper stockroom anymore since corporate made us condense the steel shelving to fit those massive seasonal displays. Which, by the way, arrived three weeks late. I kept telling the district manager that you can't just shove all the summer clearance into the corner without a plan, but he just sends these generic automated emails back. It drives me crazy. 

Anyway, I was back there, and I heard Brenda—she's one of my cashiers, just got hired in April—complaining about her shifts to the vendor. So no, it's not imaginary voices. It's real people, whispering and messing with things. Do you have any idea how hard it is to write a floor schedule when half the staff is actively trying to undermine you and requesting the same weekends off?

High? Energetic? I mean, I guess I have normal energy. I drink coffee, like anyone else. But no, I don't feel "on top of the world." How could I, with everything going on? Honestly, it's exhausting just trying to keep up. Just yesterday, I was trying to reorganize the backroom because corporate decided to send us three pallets of back-to-school supplies in May. May! Who buys notebooks in May? 

And the worst part is, they didn't even send the right signage. I spent two hours on hold with the distribution center, and the guy on the phone—I swear he was pretending not to hear me. He kept saying, "Can you repeat that?" like he was stalling. Just like the bank does when I call about the mortgage. They all use the same script. But no, I don't feel unusually high or whatever you said. I'm just trying to do my job while everyone else is playing games. Do you know how hard it is to build an endcap when the shelves don't even lock in properly anymore?

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm stressed, obviously. Anyone would be stressed if they were dealing with what I'm dealing with. But I'm not sitting around crying all day, if that's what you mean. I have too much to do. Like, I have to make sure the store opens on time, and honestly, if I wasn't there, the whole place would fall apart. 

Just last week, the alarm company called me at 3:00 AM because someone didn't secure the loading dock doors properly. 3:00 AM! I had to drive all the way down there in my pajamas. And you know what? It was the new shift lead, Marcus. He said he "forgot" to pull the latch all the way down. Forgot. Right. Just like the bank "forgot" to apply my payment to the principal last month. It's always these little "mistakes," you know? But anyway, no, I'm not depressed. I'm just tired of having to double-check everyone's work because nobody else pays attention to the details. Like the price tags on the clearance aisle—they're supposed to be yellow, not red, and I had to reprint fifty of them yesterday. It just never ends.

Brain problem? No, no seizures or anything. My brain works perfectly fine. Better than most people's, honestly, considering everything I have to keep track of. I mean, I did bump my head on the new sunglass carousel they installed by register four last week, but that wasn't a real injury. That was just because the vendor didn't measure the aisle clearance properly. 

I specifically told them, I said, you can't put a spinning metal rack two feet from the impulse bins, people are going to knock into it. But do they listen? No. They just drop the boxes, get their signature, and leave. And then I'm the one who has to clean up all the cardboard and plastic wrap they leave behind. We go through so many trash bags because Dave, our maintenance guy, keeps taking the heavy-duty ones to cover his car windows because his passenger window won't roll up. Which is technically theft of company property, by the way. I've sent three emails to HR about it, but they just tell me to "monitor the situation." Monitor it! I'm trying to run a whole store, I don't have time to monitor Dave's Honda Civic. So... what were you asking? Oh, right. No, no medical issues or head injuries. I'm perfectly healthy.

Disorganized? Hard to follow? No, nobody's ever said that. I speak very clearly. I have to, right? If I don't give exact instructions, nothing gets done right. Like yesterday, I told Jessica—she's the new cashier—I told her, "Make sure you face the candy aisle before you clock out." Facing, you know, pulling all the product to the front so it looks full. It's retail 101. 

But I come in this morning, and the Reese's are pushed all the way to the back, and someone put the king-size Snickers in the fun-size slot. It's not that hard to follow a simple instruction. But she said she didn't hear me because the PA system was crackling. Which, to be fair, it has been doing that weird static thing again. Every time someone pages for a price check, it sounds like a walkie-talkie from a war movie. I told the district manager about it three weeks ago, but he just said to put in a work order. Put in a work order! The portal for the work orders has been down since Tuesday. Every time I try to log in, it gives me an error code 404. I even tried clearing my cache, but you know how the company computers are. They run on Windows 7, I swear. It takes ten minutes just to boot up the scheduling software. So no, my speech isn't hard to follow. People just don't listen.

Less interested? No, I wouldn't say I'm less interested. I mean, I still like doing things. It's just that I literally don't have the time anymore. Between the store and... well, everything else, my schedule is packed. Like, I used to go to this pottery class on Thursday nights. It was nice, you know? Getting your hands dirty, making something from scratch. I made this really beautiful ceramic bowl, glazed it this deep cobalt blue. 

But then they changed the class time to 6:00 PM, and I can never leave the store by 5:30. Not with the way the evening shift operates. If I don't stay to count down the registers myself, the drawers are always short. Just last Tuesday, register three was off by twelve dollars and forty-two cents. Twelve dollars! And when I asked Kevin about it—he was on three that night—he just shrugged and said someone must have given the wrong change. How do you give exactly twelve dollars and forty-two cents in wrong change? It doesn't make sense. It's like the time the regional manager came in for a surprise inspection and found three expired bags of chips on the endcap. Three bags! Out of a whole store. And suddenly I'm getting written up for "poor inventory management." It's ridiculous. The vendor is supposed to rotate the stock, but they just shove the new boxes in front of the old ones. I've watched them do it. They think I don't see them, but I see everything. I have to. So, yeah, I still enjoy things, I just have to be at the store.

Controlling my thoughts? No, nobody is putting thoughts in my head. My thoughts are completely my own. Though corporate certainly tries to dictate every single thing we do, if that's what you mean. They send down these planograms—you know, the visual maps for where the product goes on the shelves—and they expect us to follow them like robots. 

Just yesterday, I got a memo saying we need to move all the seasonal allergy medication to the front endcap. But we already have the back-to-school clearance there! Where am I supposed to put three hundred boxes of discounted highlighters and spiral notebooks? The backroom is already full of those giant plush bears from Valentine's Day that never sold because they priced them at forty-nine ninety-nine. Who spends fifty dollars on a stuffed bear at a pharmacy? You could get a nice dinner for that. 

I told Mark, our district manager, I said, Mark, nobody is buying these bears. But he just sends me these generic emails about maximizing floor space. Maximizing floor space! The only thing getting maximized is my headache. And then the delivery guys just dump the new merchandise totes right in front of the fire exit, which is a massive OSHA violation. If the fire marshal walked in, I'd be the one getting the citation, not Mark. The delivery guys know better, too, but they're always rushing because they get paid per stop. 

So... yeah, no one is controlling my mind. They can't even control the backroom inventory properly, let alone my brain.

Harder to feel emotions? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still get mad, obviously. Like with the whole inventory thing. And I still care about things that matter. But honestly, what really matters anymore? Because it feels like nobody cares about quality control. 

Like the new store shirts they sent us last week. They changed the fabric. The old ones were a nice cotton blend, breathable, you know? But these new ones are some cheap polyester. You wear it for ten minutes in the stockroom and you're sweating. And the logo is printed crooked on half of them. I had to send an email to HR about it, because I'm not having my team walk around looking like we bought our uniforms out of the trunk of a car. 

And HR, of course, they take three days to reply, and when they do, it's just an automated ticket number. Ticket number 88402. Like that helps me. Meanwhile, I have Jessica wearing a shirt that looks like it's sliding off her left shoulder because the seam is completely off-center. And she doesn't even care! She just tied it in a knot at the bottom like it's some kind of fashion statement. I told her, "Jessica, this is a professional environment, not a music festival." But she just rolled her eyes. The lack of professionalism in the younger generation is just... it's exhausting. So, no, I definitely still feel things. Mostly frustration, if I'm being honest.

Harder to function? No, not really. I mean, I still get up every day, go to the store, supervise the team, do the schedules... I handle the customer complaints, which are endless, by the way. Like yesterday, a woman wanted to return a half-eaten bag of gummy worms because she said they were "too chewy." They're gummy worms! What did she expect? I swear, people just want something for nothing. 

But anyway, no, I take care of myself, I do my job. It's just... the only time things get really difficult is when the mail comes, or the bank calls, or I have to deal with certain paperwork at the store. Because I know it's all connected to the foreclosure. They're trying to hide it in the regular mail, you know? They send these letters that look like credit card offers, but if you hold them up to the light, the watermark is completely different. I showed one to the mail carrier, Dave. Dave’s been on our route for six years, always wears shorts even when it’s freezing out. I asked him, "Dave, why are these envelopes heavier than the normal junk mail?" And he just looked at me like I was crazy and said he just delivers what's in the bag. But someone has to be sorting it at the post office. The sorting machines don't just magically put the foreclosure documents in the middle of a stack of grocery circulars. 

So, yeah, when that stuff happens, it throws me off a bit because I have to document everything. But otherwise? I'm functioning perfectly fine. Better than most of the people I work with, honestly.

Less sleep? No, I sleep fine. I usually get my seven hours, unless I'm closing the store and have to open the next morning, which is a scheduling nightmare. They call it a "clopening" shift, and it should be illegal. You leave at 11 PM and have to be back at 6 AM to let the vendors in. 

And speaking of vendors, the guy who delivers our greeting cards—I don't know his name, tall guy, always chewing gum—he came in yesterday and just completely messed up the Mother's Day display. I had spent two hours making sure all the "To a Special Aunt" cards were separated from the "To a Wonderful Grandmother" cards, because people get very upset if they buy the wrong one. Last year, a customer came in screaming because she accidentally bought a "Sympathy on the Loss of Your Pet" card for her sister's wedding. I mean, read the card before you buy it, right? But no, it's always our fault. 

So this vendor just shoves the new stock wherever it fits. I told him, "You can't just put the musical cards next to the blank ones, they have different price points!" The registers won't scan them right, and then the cashier has to do a price override, and if they do too many overrides, the system flags it for loss prevention. And loss prevention is already breathing down my neck because our shrink was up 2% last quarter. Shrink! Half of it is just cashiers forgetting to scan the bottom-of-the-basket items like cases of water. 

But anyway, yeah, I sleep normal. When I actually get to go home and sleep, that is.

My mood? Yeah, my mood is totally fine. I mean, I'm just a normal person going about my day when all this stuff happens. Like, I'll be perfectly fine, having my morning coffee—I always get the hazelnut blend, not the French roast, because the French roast gives me heartburn. I told the girl at the cafe down the street, "Just one pump of hazelnut," but she always puts in two, and it makes it way too sweet. You'd think it wouldn't be that hard to follow a simple instruction, right? It's like nobody listens anymore. 

Just like at the store. I'll be having a great day, totally normal mood, and then I'll find out someone left the freezer door cracked in the back room. Do you know how fast a pallet of frozen pizzas thaws? Fast. And then we have to damage it all out. The paperwork for damaged goods is ridiculous. You have to scan every single barcode, and the scanner gun we have in the back is held together with duct tape. Literally, silver duct tape wrapped around the handle because someone dropped it on the concrete floor two months ago. I put in a requisition for a new one, but corporate rejected it. They said we haven't met our equipment depreciation threshold yet. What does that even mean? It's broken! 

So, yeah, my mood is fine. I'm not depressed or anything when I notice what they're doing with the mail or how people are acting. I'm just paying attention. Someone has to pay attention, especially when corporate won't even buy us a new scanner gun.

Messages on the TV or the internet? No, I haven't seen anything like that. I mean, I watch TV to unwind, mostly those home renovation shows. Have you seen the one where they flip the houses in Texas? The couple that does it, they always want to knock down every single wall to make an "open concept." I don't get it. Where do you put your furniture if you don't have any walls? And the smells! If you're cooking fish in the kitchen, the whole house is going to smell like fish if there are no walls to stop it. 

I was telling my sister that the other day. She called me while I was watching it, complaining about her HOA again. Her homeowners association is ridiculous. They sent her a warning letter because her trash cans were visible from the street for two hours after the garbage truck came. Two hours! She was at work, how was she supposed to bring them in? I told her she should just paint them the same color as her house so they blend in. Her house is this awful shade of beige, though. Builder's beige, they call it. 

But anyway, no, the TV is just regular shows. And the internet is mostly just me checking the store's inventory system from home, which I'm not supposed to do off the clock, but if I don't check it, the morning shift will completely mess up the restocking. Last week they put all the seasonal allergy medicine in the clearance bin. It's April! That's prime allergy season! I had to pull it all back out and re-tag everything. So, yeah, no special messages or anything, just the usual headache.

No, definitely not. People can't hear what I'm thinking. If they could, I probably would have been fired from my job a long time ago with the things I think about my district manager. He came in last Tuesday for a walkthrough, wearing these ridiculous loafers without socks. Who wears leather loafers without socks? It just seems so unhygienic. And he was pointing out every little thing, like the dust on the top shelf of the greeting card aisle. 

I mean, nobody looks up there! Unless you're seven feet tall, you can't even see the top shelf. But he made me get the ladder out right then and there. The rolling ladder we have is so wobbly, I always feel like I'm going to break my neck. The right wheel gets stuck because a piece of a plastic hanger got jammed in the caster like three years ago and nobody can figure out how to pry it out. I've tried needle-nose pliers, tweezers, even a screwdriver. It just drags across the linoleum and leaves these black scuff marks that the night crew complains about. 

The head of the night crew, Gary, he leaves me these passive-aggressive Post-it notes on my desk about the scuff marks. He writes them in red Sharpie. Who uses red Sharpie for a casual note? It feels like I'm being graded. I should just buy him a pack of blue pens and leave them on his cart. But anyway, no, my thoughts are private. If Gary could hear what I think about his Post-it notes, things would be a lot more tense around the store.

Physically impossible? Like... sci-fi stuff? No, definitely not. There aren't any secret devices or forces or whatever. I mean, the only devices monitoring me are the security cameras at the store, and honestly, half of those don't even work. 

Our Loss Prevention guy, Kevin, he just sits in the back office all day eating those little powdered mini donuts. You know the ones that come in the crinkly white bag? He gets powdered sugar all over the keyboard. I had to use his computer last week to fix a time punch for one of my cashiers, Brenda. Brenda is always clocking in exactly four minutes late because she insists on parking under the one oak tree in the plaza lot so her car doesn't get hot. But the tree is at the very back of the lot! It takes her five minutes just to walk to the front doors. 

I told her, "Brenda, just buy a windshield sun shade." You can get them for like five dollars. I bought one last summer that has a picture of a beach on it. It really does keep the steering wheel from burning your hands, especially with those black leather steering wheels. Mine was starting to crack from the sun anyway, which is annoying because I just paid off the car last year. It's a Honda, so it'll run forever, but you still want the interior to look nice, you know? 

But no, no weird forces or impossible devices. Just the broken cameras and Kevin.

Motivate myself? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still get up and shower and go to work every day. I have to, right? If I don't open the store, nobody will. I'm the one with the master keys. Well, me and the district manager, but he's obviously not going to come down at 6:30 in the morning to unlock the doors. He's probably still asleep in his fancy house, you know? 

I actually saw a house like his on Zillow the other day. I wasn't looking to buy, obviously, retail doesn't pay that well. I just like to look at the pictures sometimes. This one had a huge kitchen island. It was marble, I think. Or maybe quartz? People are really into quartz right now because it doesn't stain like marble does. My sister's friend got marble countertops and spilled red wine on them the first week. You can't get red wine out of porous stone. I told her she should have gone with butcher block, it's so much warmer looking anyway. 

Butcher block does require maintenance, though. You have to oil it, like, once a month with food-grade mineral oil. I bought a bottle of it once for my cutting board, but I always forget to use it. It's sitting under the sink right next to the dish soap. I buy the bulk size dish soap from Costco and refill the smaller bottle by the sink. It saves so much money, honestly. 

But yeah, chores and stuff? I get them done. I mean, the laundry isn't going to wash itself, right?

Impossible in real life? Like magic or something? No, of course not. The bank is just a bank. They just use regular computers and paperwork, you know? Though, honestly, their paperwork is a mess. I had to go in there last month to update my address because I moved to that new apartment complex off Route 9. 

The teller, she had these really long acrylic nails. Like, the kind with the little rhinestones glued to them? I don't know how she types with those. I tried getting acrylics once for my cousin's wedding, but I couldn't even text on my phone properly. My cousin had this huge outdoor wedding in August. It was so humid, everyone's hair was just completely frizzy by the time the reception started. They served this chicken dish that was so dry, I had to ask for extra sauce. And the sauce tasted exactly like the kind you get in those little packets at the drive-thru. 

Which reminds me, the drive-thru at the bank is always broken. The little pneumatic tube thing? It gets stuck halfway up. One time I sat there for ten minutes just watching my deposit slip hover in the middle of the plastic pipe. The teller had to come out the side door with a broom handle to poke it down. 

But no, nobody at work or the bank is doing anything impossible. It's just regular people being incompetent, mostly.

Heard my thoughts out loud? Like... echoing around the room? No, I've never had anything like that happen. My thoughts stay in my head where they belong. Though sometimes I wish people could hear what I'm thinking, especially at work. Like when a customer asks if we have something in the back. 

"The back" isn't some magical warehouse, you know? It's just a tiny stockroom with a broken step stool and a bunch of empty cardboard boxes we haven't crushed yet. Our baler has been broken for three weeks. The repair guy came out on Tuesday, but he said he had to order a part from Germany or something ridiculous. Why would a cardboard crusher need German parts? It's not a BMW. 

My uncle used to drive a BMW. One of those vintage ones from the 80s, the boxy kind. He loved that car more than his kids, I swear. He spent every weekend waxing it in the driveway. He used this specific turtle wax that came in a green tub. It smelled like coconuts. I always thought it was weird for car wax to smell tropical. You'd think it would smell like chemicals or something. 

I bought a coconut-scented candle from Bath and Body Works last week because they were having their semi-annual sale. You really can't beat those prices when they do the buy three, get three free deal. I gave two of them to Brenda for her birthday. 

But yeah, no, I don't hear my thoughts out loud. Just my own voice when I'm actually talking.

Flatter? Like I don't show emotion? I don't think so. I mean, I still get upset when things go wrong, or laugh when something's funny. Speaking of funny, Brenda brought in this video of her cat yesterday. The cat was trying to jump from the sofa to the top of the bookshelf, but it totally miscalculated and just slid down the wall. It was hilarious. 

Brenda has three cats, actually. Two tabbies and a calico. The calico has this weird patch of fur over its eye that makes it look like a pirate. I told her she should get it a little eye patch for Halloween, but she said cats hate wearing costumes. Which makes sense. I tried to put a sweater on my sister's dog once, a little chihuahua mix, and it just froze. Like, completely stiff, wouldn't move an inch until I took it off. It was a really cute sweater, though. Hand-knitted, I found it at this craft fair downtown. 

They have that craft fair every September, and they always have the best kettle corn. The line for the kettle corn is always a mile long, but it's worth it. They pop it right there in this huge copper kettle. Copper is so expensive these days, people are actually stealing it out of abandoned houses. Did you see that on the news? Um, I'm not really sure. I haven't exactly been marking it on a calendar or anything to see if it stops for a whole month. It just kind of blends together, you know?

No, not really. I mean, I'm just tired, like I said. I don't get super down or anything, just exhausted from the restaurant.

I don't really remember ever feeling like that. Not before everything started, anyway. I was just, you know, living my life, going to classes back when I was taking a few courses at the community college.

I... I really don't know. Like I said before, I don't really track my mood like that. I don't know what "completely normal" is even supposed to feel like, honestly. It's just hard to say.

We have these giant plastic cups for the staff, the ones that are red and pebbled on the outside, like the kind you get at a pizza parlor. They're basically indestructible. They always peel off at the edges and get all gross and gray...

I just want to make sure I'm doing a good job and being there for the people who need me. That's a pretty normal amount of worrying, isn't it? I just want to make sure I'm not making a big deal out of nothing.

Well, um... I wouldn't say it's interfering, exactly. I mean, I'm still getting everything done, and my clients are all taken care of. I just... I want to make sure I'm doing things right, you know? 

So, um, I have been asking some of my coworkers to just double-check my documentation lately. Just to be safe, because I want to be thorough. And, well, at home, my wife has been helping out a little more with the bills and the scheduling. I just haven't felt quite as sharp with all those little details, so she offered to take over for a bit. It's really nice of her, and I think it's good to ask for help when you need it, right? I just want to make sure I'm not letting anything slip through the cracks. That's a responsible way to handle it, don't you think?

Well, um... I guess you could say that, yeah. It hasn't been going on forever or anything. Just, um... well, my uncle passed away about two weeks ago. 

It was a bit of a shock, and, you know, we were pretty close. So I think it's just natural to feel a little off after something like that, right? Anyone would be a bit distracted or foggy while they're processing a loss. I just... I really think it's just a normal reaction to grief, don't you? It's only been a couple of weeks, so I'm sure it'll pass once things settle down a bit.

Well, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, of course I miss him, because we were close, but I'm not... I'm not just sitting around dwelling on it all day or anything. 

I really try to keep my focus on my clients and my family. I'll think about the good memories we had sometimes, sure, but it's definitely not a preoccupation. I'm just trying to keep moving forward and handle it the best I can. That's the healthiest way to grieve, isn't it? I just wouldn't want you to think I'm falling apart or letting it take over my life. I think I'm managing it pretty normally, right?

Well, um... I guess I have been feeling a little down, yeah. But not, like, completely falling apart or anything! I mean, I still go to work, I still talk to everyone... I'm getting through my shifts just fine. 

It's just... lately, when I wake up, there's this sort of... heavy, empty feeling in my chest? Like, I can put on a smile for my clients, but inside I just feel kind of sad and... flat, I guess. But I think that's pretty normal when you're grieving, right? It's okay to feel a little sad for a while after losing someone, don't you think? I just wouldn't want you to worry that I'm not handling it well, because I really am trying my best to stay positive.

Oh, no, no, I would never... I mean, I don't have any plans to do anything like that. I really don't want you to think I'm, you know, a danger to myself or anything. I know how important it is to keep going for my family and my clients. 

But, um... I guess... well, there have been a couple of mornings lately where... where I just sort of think, maybe it wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I just... didn't wake up? Just to not have to feel that heaviness for a bit. But it's just a fleeting thought, you know? It actually kind of scares me when it happens, because that's not who I am at all. I'm usually such a positive person. That's just the grief talking, right? It doesn't mean there's something horribly wrong with me, does it?

Well, um... no, not really. I think I'm eating about the same as I always do. I mean, I might not have the biggest appetite right now, but I'm definitely still eating. 

I make sure to have my meals because I need the energy for work, you know? My clients rely on me, so I can't just skip eating. I guess maybe I'm not craving my favorite foods as much, but I'm still getting enough nutrition and everything. That's the important part, right? As long as I'm keeping my strength up, a little change in appetite isn't anything to worry about, is it? I just want to make sure I'm doing all the right things to take care of myself.

Oh, well, I wouldn't say I feel *worthless*, exactly. I mean, I know I do good work with my clients, and I try to be a good person... I really don't want to sound like I'm just sitting around throwing a pity party for myself. 

But, um... I guess... well, since my tío passed, I have been having a hard time with... just thinking about things I could have done better. Like, I keep replaying it all in my head, you know? Thinking I really should have called him more often, or... or made the time to visit him sooner before things got bad. And sometimes I just end up feeling like... like I really let him down. Like I failed him as family. 

But I know everyone has regrets when someone passes away, right? It's normal to wish you had done more, isn't it? I'm trying not to be too hard on myself, because I know he wouldn't want me to feel guilty. I just want to make sure I'm processing it the right way... does that make sense?

Well, um... I wouldn't say it's making it *hard* to function, exactly. I mean, I'm still going to work every day, still taking care of my clients. I would never just stop doing my job, you know? They really need me.

But, I guess... well, I have been leaning on people a little bit more than usual. Just to be safe. Like at work, I've asked some of my coworkers to just double-check my client documentation for me. Not because I can't do it, but just... just to make sure I haven't missed any small details while my head's a little foggy from the grief. And at home, my wife has been so great, she's taken over paying some of the bills and doing the scheduling for a bit. Just because I haven't been quite as reliable with keeping track of all those little things right now. 

But I'm still doing the important stuff, you know? It's okay to ask for a little help when you're going through a tough time, right? I just want to make sure I'm doing everything right so nobody else is affected by what I'm going through. That's the responsible thing to do, isn't it?

Oh, no, definitely not. Um... I know sometimes people isolate themselves when they're grieving, but I really try not to do that. It wouldn't be fair to my wife or my friends to just shut them out, you know? 

I'm still talking to my coworkers every day, and I make sure to spend time with my family in the evenings. Like I said, I've actually been leaning on them a little bit more lately, so I'm definitely not hiding away or anything. I think it's really important to stay connected to your support system when things are tough. That's the healthiest way to handle it, right? I just want to make sure I'm dealing with everything the right way so I don't become a burden to anyone.

Well, um... I wouldn't say I'm completely drained or anything like that. I still get up and go to work, and I try my best to keep up with everything. I really don't want to sound like I'm complaining or just being lazy. 

But, I guess... well, I have noticed that even on days when I don't do a whole lot, my body just feels... kind of worn out. Like, even simple things at work, like helping one of my clients with a shower, or just bringing the groceries in at home... it just seems to take a lot more out of me than it usually does. 

I know grief can take a physical toll on a person, right? It's pretty normal to feel a little more tired when you're going through something emotional, isn't it? I'm just trying to push through it and make sure I'm still doing what I need to do. I hope that makes sense.

Oh, um... no, I really don't think so. Before he passed, I was doing just fine. I was keeping up with all my clients and everything at home was perfectly normal. I didn't feel like this at all. 

It's really just been since we lost him. I mean, losing a family member is a big shock, right? I'm pretty sure anyone would feel a little sad and out of sorts after something like that. It's just a normal reaction to grief, don't you think? I really believe I'd be my usual self right now if he were still here. I just need a little time to process it all, that's all.

Um... no, I don't think so. I haven't really been feeling nervous or, you know, jittery at all. 

I mean, obviously it's been a tough time, but I'm not walking around on edge or snapping at anyone or anything like that. I try really hard to stay calm, especially for my clients at work. They rely on me to be steady, you know? So I just make sure to keep a level head. 

I hope that's okay—I know everyone handles loss differently, but for me, anxiety hasn't really been an issue. It's really just the sadness and feeling a bit worn out, like we talked about. That's still a pretty normal way to grieve, isn't it?

Well, um... hopeless is a pretty strong word, isn't it? I wouldn't say I feel hopeless. I mean, I still get up every day and do my job, and I know things will eventually get better. I'm not giving up or anything like that. 

I guess... sometimes I have moments where it feels like the sadness is going to last a long time, but that's just because I miss him so much. It's not like I don't see a future or think everything is ruined. I just take it one day at a time, you know? That's the right way to handle it, isn't it? Just keeping a positive outlook as best I can?

Oh, um... no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm still doing all the things I usually do. I still like watching my shows in the evening and, you know, keeping up with my normal routine. 

Obviously, I'm grieving, so maybe I'm a little quieter than usual, but I haven't lost interest in my life or anything. I still get enjoyment out of my hobbies. I think it's really important to keep doing the things you love when you're going through a tough time, don't you? It helps keep you grounded. So, yeah, I'm still enjoying things just fine. That's a good sign, right?

Well... I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by most of the day. I definitely don't want to sound like I'm just sitting around crying all the time, because I'm not. I still go to work and take care of my clients, and I can talk to them and be cheerful when I need to be. 

But... lately, I guess I do wake up with this kind of heavy, empty feeling in my chest. It's like... I can get through my shift just fine, but underneath it all, I just feel kind of sad and flat. It's not like I'm letting it ruin my day or affect my work, though. I still push through. That's pretty normal when you've lost someone, right? Just feeling a little heavy for a while?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what really brought me in is... my wife, mostly. She gets pretty frustrated with me. Like, she’ll be telling me about my cousin’s appointments or rides he needs to get to the doctor. 

My cousin Bob, he's been having a lot of trouble with his knee lately. He actually tore his meniscus way back in, gosh, must have been '98? We were playing in this church softball league and he slid into second base—which was ridiculous because we were up by ten runs anyway—and his knee just popped. Ever since then, it acts up, and he can't drive his truck when the arthritis flares up. It's a manual, you know, an old Ford. Beautiful truck, cherry red, but that clutch is incredibly stiff. 

But anyway, where was I? Oh, right, so my wife will be talking about his schedule and who is driving him, and I’m looking right at her, nodding along, but then a minute later I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said. It's like the words just go right past me.

Yeah, actually, I did. Even way back in grade school, well before I was 12, my parents used to hear it from my teachers all the time. They'd always say I was a bright kid but I was just constantly daydreaming. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she was this really tall woman who always wore these bright floral dresses, and she had this huge collection of ceramic owls on her desk. I don't know why owls, maybe she just liked them, but one of them had a chipped beak from when Tommy Henderson knocked it over during indoor recess. Anyway, she was always having to remind me to finish my classwork, and I was notorious for leaving my homework shoved in the back of my desk. My desk was always a disaster zone, honestly. I’d find assignments from a month ago crammed in next to my math book.

Well, I'm actually not working right now. I retired a few years ago, mostly because I just wanted to slow down. But I do help out with a little catering business my friend runs. It’s mostly just small gigs, you know, backyard barbecues, graduation parties, that sort of thing. My friend, Dave, he makes the best pulled pork you will ever have in your life. He smokes it for like fourteen hours over hickory wood. He actually built the smoker himself out of an old oil drum. It’s a real piece of work, but man, does it get the job done. We did a party last weekend and went through forty pounds of the stuff. 

But, uh, yeah, when I'm helping him, I definitely have to double-check things or even redo some tasks because I'll get mixed up. Like, I’ll forget if I already loaded the napkins or which cooler has the potato salad. And like I said, it’s really causing some tension at home. My wife feels like she just can’t count on me when it comes to helping out with Bob's care. She gets so frustrated when I drop the ball on who is driving him where.

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I'm depressed. I get frustrated with myself sometimes, sure, especially when my wife gets upset with me. But down? No. I actually try to stay pretty positive. My neighbor, Frank, now he gets down. He's always complaining about the weather or his lawn. He's obsessed with his lawn, honestly. He spends every Saturday morning out there with this little edger, making sure the lines are perfectly straight. It's Bermuda grass, which is tough to keep looking nice around here because the soil is so clay-heavy. I tried to tell him he needs to aerate it more, maybe put down some gypsum to break up the clay. I read this whole article about soil composition in this gardening magazine I picked up at the dentist's office. It was a really fascinating read, actually, about how the pH levels affect nutrient absorption. The dentist, Dr. Miller, he's a great guy. Always has the best magazines in his waiting room. Not just the usual old issues of Time or whatever, but really niche stuff. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling down. No, I'm generally pretty content, just... scatterbrained, I guess.

Yeah, everyday tasks can be a real headache. Lately I’ve been forgetting things I really meant to do. Like, just last week, I was supposed to return a call from the doctor’s office—my primary care guy, Dr. Evans. He’s got this new receptionist, I think her name is Brenda or maybe Linda. She’s got this very distinct voice, kind of high-pitched, almost like a cartoon character. She always wears these huge, colorful statement necklaces. I don't know where she finds them, probably at those little artisan craft fairs they have downtown on the weekends. My wife loves those fairs. We went to one last fall and she bought this incredible hand-blown glass vase. It’s got these swirls of cobalt blue and emerald green in it. We put it on the mantle right next to the clock we got for our anniversary. 

Anyway, I forgot to call her back. And picking up prescriptions? Forget about it. I went to the pharmacy the other day and totally walked out without the main thing I went in for because I got distracted looking at the new display of reading glasses. And then there's getting out the door. I'm always running late, especially when I have to leave on time for one of my cousin’s appointments. He’s got this old Buick, a '98 LeSabre, and the passenger side door sticks, so you have to yank it just right to get it open. It's a whole production just getting him in the car.

Well, I guess... I mean, I told you about helping Dave with the catering, right? So it happens there. And then, well, I don't really do a whole lot else these days besides helping with my cousin Bob. I go to the grocery store, I guess. Though I'm terrible at the grocery store. I always forget the list on the counter. The other day I went in for milk and came out with three boxes of those little powdered donuts. You know the ones? They come in that crinkly white bag. My grandfather used to eat those all the time. He'd sit on the porch with a cup of black coffee and a bag of those donuts every Sunday morning. He had this old wooden rocking chair that squeaked every time he moved. My dad tried to oil it a million times, but it never helped. I think the wood was just warped from being out in the humidity for so long. 

But, uh, anyway. Other parts of my life? I don't know, I'm just kind of scattered wherever I am, I suppose.

No, I don't think so. I mean, if I'm actually paying attention, I remember it fine. Like, I can tell you all about this documentary I watched last night on the History Channel. It was about the construction of the Hoover Dam. Did you know they had to pour the concrete in these separate blocks because if they poured it all at once, the chemical reaction would have created so much heat it would have taken 125 years to cool? It's fascinating. They had this whole system of pipes running cold water through the concrete to speed up the cooling process. My uncle Arthur was an engineer, actually. Not on the dam, obviously, but he worked on some big bridges out in California. He always said the real trick to engineering isn't the math, it's the materials. He used to build these intricate model airplanes in his basement. He had a whole setup down there, with these tiny little tools and a magnifying glass on a stand. It smelled like glue and balsa wood. 

So, yeah, if I'm focused, I remember stuff. It's just getting focused in the first place that's the trick.

Well, friends... I don't really see a lot of friends these days, mostly just Bob and Dave. But hobbies, sure. I try to read, but I end up reading the same paragraph over and over. Or I'll sit down to do a crossword puzzle. I used to love crosswords. My wife and I used to do the Sunday Times one together. We had this whole routine. We'd make a pot of Earl Grey tea—loose leaf, not the bags, she was very particular about that—and we'd sit at the kitchen table. It’s this beautiful old oak table we found at an estate sale. The guy selling it said it belonged to a ship captain in the 1800s. You can actually see these faint rings on the wood where I guess he used to set his mug. We had to rent a U-Haul just to get it home because it was so heavy. 

But anyway, yeah, I'll start a crossword now and just sort of stare at it, and then I'll realize I've been looking out the window for twenty minutes watching the squirrels. So I guess it happens then, too.

Well, you know, it's hard to say for sure. I think I've always been a little scattered, but... I mean, maybe it's gotten a bit worse lately? Or maybe I just notice it more now because I have more time on my hands since I stopped working. I used to work at this hardware store downtown, Nelson's Hardware. It's closed now, they put a coffee shop in that building. It's a shame, really, Mr. Nelson was a great guy. He knew everything there was to know about plumbing fixtures. I remember one time this lady came in with a broken piece from a toilet that had to be at least fifty years old, and he just looked at it for two seconds and knew exactly what aisle and bin to find the replacement in. He had this incredible memory for things like that. He always wore these blue suspenders, every single day. I asked him once if he owned any belts, and he just laughed and said belts were for people who didn't trust their own pants. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my attention. Yeah, I don't know, it's probably been about the same, just... more obvious now, maybe.

Fidgety? No, I don't think so. I was actually a pretty quiet kid. I'd just sit at my desk, mostly. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she was incredibly strict, so you didn't dare get out of your seat in her room anyway. She had this heavy wooden yardstick she'd smack against the chalkboard if anyone even whispered. It had "Smithson's Lumber" printed on the side in these faded red letters. 

Smithson's was this big lumber yard on the edge of town, right next to the railroad tracks. We used to walk down there in the summer and put pennies on the tracks to let the freight trains flatten them out. You had to be quick about it, though, because the switch operator would yell at you if he caught you trespassing. One time my buddy Jimmy—he ended up moving to Florida in middle school, his dad got a job at a citrus plant or something—but Jimmy put a whole silver quarter on the track. We searched for an hour in the gravel after the train went by and never found it. I always wondered if it stuck to the wheel or if it just got launched into the bushes. 

But, um... no, I wasn't bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I mostly just stayed put.

Oh, absolutely. It's a daily struggle. I'm always putting down my keys, or my phone, or the garden clippers somewhere in the house and then I end up spending ten minutes just retracing my steps to find them. Or those catering receipts! My wife does a bit of catering on the side, mostly small events, you know, baby showers, retirement parties. She makes these incredible mini quiches. They have gruyere cheese and just a hint of nutmeg. She learned the recipe from her grandmother, who actually grew up in France before moving here after the war. 

Her grandmother was a fascinating woman. She had this huge collection of vintage thimbles. Hundreds of them, displayed in these little wooden shadow boxes all over her living room. Some were porcelain, some were silver, one even had a tiny piece of turquoise set into it. I always wondered how you'd actually sew with something that fancy without ruining it. 

But anyway, she asks me to hold onto her receipts for her taxes, and I'll just set them down on the counter, or maybe on top of the microwave, and then they're gone. Just vanished. So yeah, I lose things all the time.

Well, I suppose they have, yeah. It's definitely causing some tension at home lately. My wife feels like she can't really count on me when it comes to helping out with my cousin's care. He moved in with us a few months ago after he had a fall. Nice guy, my cousin Arthur. He used to be a jazz musician, played the upright bass. He actually toured with some pretty big names back in the seventies, though you wouldn't know it to look at him now. He's got these great stories about playing in smoky little clubs in Chicago and New York. He said he once played a set with a drummer who insisted on wearing a full tuxedo, even in the dead of summer when the AC was broken. Sweated right through it, but wouldn't take the jacket off. Arthur said the guy was a fanatic about presentation. 

But, uh, yeah, my wife gets frustrated because I'll forget to give Arthur his afternoon pills, or I'll get distracted and leave his lunch sitting on the counter. And then with her catering stuff, I've had to start double-checking or redoing tasks so her small jobs don't get mixed up. I was supposed to sort the napkins for this retirement party last week, and I completely zoned out and mixed the cocktail napkins with the dinner ones. She was not happy about that. So, yeah, it's definitely causing some problems.

Careless mistakes? Hmm. No, I don't really think so. I actually took a lot of pride in my assignments back then, especially my handwriting. We had to learn cursive, you know, the Palmer Method, and the teacher made us do these endless loops on our lined paper. He was a real stickler for penmanship. 

He drove this ancient powder-blue Studebaker to school every day. You really just don't see cars like that anymore. The chrome on the front bumper was so polished you could see your reflection in it from across the parking lot. My older brother actually tried to buy a car like that once, a classic, but the transmission blew out on the drive home from the dealership. Left him stranded on Route 9 for four hours in the pouring rain. A tow truck finally got him, but the driver charged him double because it was a Sunday. Which is just highway robbery, if you ask me. He ended up having to sell it for scrap a few months later because the parts were just impossible to find. 

But, uh... what were we saying? Schoolwork. Right. No, I don't remember making a bunch of careless mistakes or anything like that. I think I did alright with it.

Well, at home... I mean, my parents definitely knew about it, mostly because they heard it from the school. Even back in grade school, you know, way before I was 12, the teachers were always telling my parents that I was a bright kid, but I was just constantly daydreaming. 

I'd be staring out the window, probably thinking about those model airplanes I used to build. I had this whole fleet of balsa wood planes. You had to use this special model cement, smelled incredibly strong, but it held those tiny little wooden wing ribs together perfectly. My dad helped me hang them from my bedroom ceiling with fishing line so they looked like they were flying. He used this old metal step stool to reach the ceiling, and it had one wheel that squeaked so loudly it would drive my mother absolutely crazy. She eventually gave that stool away to our neighbor, Mr. Henderson. He spent all his time out in his greenhouse trying to grow prize-winning beefsteak tomatoes. He actually won a blue ribbon at the county fair one year, if you can believe it. He used this special fertilizer made from seaweed or something.

But, uh, anyway... my parents. Right. The teachers told them I was always daydreaming, and that I was always leaving my homework stuffed inside my desk. We had those heavy wooden desks where the whole top lifted up on hinges, and I'd just shove everything in there and completely forget about it. And they said I always needed reminders just to finish my regular classwork. So, even if I wasn't doing the work at home, my parents definitely knew I wasn't paying attention.

At home? Hmm, no, I don't think so. I mean, my mom ran a pretty tight ship, so things were usually pretty organized around the house. She had this whole system for chores, with a chart on the fridge and everything. We had one of those old Frigidaires, the kind with the heavy latch handle that you really had to pull on. It was this awful avocado green color that was so popular back then. 

My aunt had an entire kitchen in that color—the stove, the fridge, even the blender. She used to make these incredible milkshakes with that blender. She'd use fresh strawberries from her garden. She had this massive garden in her backyard, grew all sorts of things. Zucchini the size of baseball bats. She'd try to pawn them off on anyone who came to visit because she just had too many. My uncle started making zucchini bread just to use them up, and he actually got pretty good at it. He'd put walnuts in it, and sometimes a little bit of orange zest. He said the secret was not overmixing the batter, otherwise it gets too dense. 

But, uh... daydreaming at home. No, I don't really remember that being an issue there. Just at school, mostly.

Chores or conversations? Hmm. Well, with chores, like I said, my mom's chart kept us pretty in line. I'd do my chores, usually. I had to take out the trash, which wasn't too bad, except in the winter when the snow would pile up against the side gate. We lived in this house that got terrible snowdrifts. One year, it snowed so much the city plows pushed a mountain of it right at the end of our driveway. 

My dad had this old snowblower, a Toro, I think. Red and white. It was loud as a jet engine and always smelled like gasoline and hot metal. He'd spend hours out there clearing the driveway, wearing these giant leather mittens that looked like bear paws. He bought them at an army surplus store downtown. That store was amazing, actually. They had old helmets, canteens, even those big canvas tents. I bought a compass there once, thought I was going to be some great explorer. I took it into the woods behind our subdivision, ended up getting totally turned around and had to follow the creek back to the main road. Got my boots completely soaked in the mud. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Conversations at home? No, I don't think I had trouble paying attention to those. I mean, I'm pretty sure I listened just fine when people were talking to me at the house.

Trouble following what they were saying? No, I don't think so. We usually talked the most during dinner, and I could follow along just fine. Every night at six o'clock sharp, we'd sit down. We had this big, heavy oak table that my grandfather actually built by hand. 

He was a master carpenter, worked for the railway for, gosh, almost forty years. He helped lay down tracks all over the state. He had this massive collection of vintage railroad spikes that he kept in a glass display case in his den. That den always smelled like pipe tobacco—Cherry Cavendish, I'm pretty sure it was. He smoked it out of this beautiful briar wood pipe that he bought when he was stationed in France. He brought back a lot of stuff from Europe, actually, including this old brass pocket watch that he ended up giving to my older brother for his birthday. My brother completely ruined it, though. He took it apart trying to see how the little gears and springs worked and could never figure out how to get it back together. He was always doing that, taking apart radios, toasters, the lawnmower... drove my mom absolutely up the wall. 

But, uh... yeah, to answer your question, I didn't really have a problem following my parents when they talked to me at the house. I heard them just fine.

Trouble outside of school? Like getting into trouble? Hmm, no, I don't really think so. I mean, I wasn't a bad kid or anything. I didn't go around breaking windows or getting into fights. We did have a neighbor, Mr. Henderson, who was always convinced us kids were up to no good. 

He lived in this two-story colonial at the end of the cul-de-sac and he was obsessed with his lawn. It was like a golf course, perfectly manicured Kentucky bluegrass. He had this whole sprinkler system installed, which was pretty fancy for our neighborhood back then. The sprinklers would pop up right at 5:00 AM every single morning. You could hear the *ch-ch-ch-ch* sound they made if you had your window open. My window faced his house, and I used to keep it cracked in the summer because the air conditioning in our place was practically useless. We had this huge unit in the living room window, but it rattled so loud you couldn't hear the television over it. We used to watch a lot of those old westerns, my dad loved them. John Wayne, Clint Eastwood... my dad actually had a cowboy hat he'd wear when he was out grilling on the patio. 

But, uh, anyway... getting into trouble outside of school because of my attention? No, I can't really think of anything like that happening. I was pretty well-behaved, all things considered.

Problems at home because of paying attention? No, I wouldn't say that. Like I said, my mom's chore chart kept things pretty organized. She was a stickler for organization, actually. 

She used to color-code everything in the kitchen. The spices were alphabetical, and all the Tupperware had to be stacked by size with the lids in a separate little wire rack. She bought that rack at a yard sale down the street. The Millers' yard sale, I think it was. They were moving to Florida because Mr. Miller retired from the auto plant. He worked on the assembly line for years, putting in windshields. He always said his back was shot from bending over those cars all day. He had this old Chevy pickup truck he was always tinkering with in his driveway. It was a beautiful robin's egg blue, but the rust was starting to eat through the wheel wells. He used to let us kids sit in the back and pretend we were driving across the country. We'd pack these little bags with peanut butter sandwiches and a thermos of Kool-Aid.
