Oh, my stars. I've wandered completely off the path again, haven't I? Tommy and the watering can... I'm so sorry. You were asking if I still enjoy things. But yes, like I said, I just leave my bag by the door these days. The interest just isn't there.

Well, like I was saying before, nobody has actually taken over the bills for me. I still manage to stay in my own home, which is a blessing. But I suppose I do let things slide more than I used to. I rely a lot more on little reminders from my daughter, and I put off things that used to just be routine. I've missed some calls and appointments lately, and family tasks I used to handle so carefully... and like I mentioned, I even stopped teaching my craft classes at the community center. 

Those classes were always on Tuesdays. I always wore my favorite yellow cardigan on Tuesdays. I bought it at a little boutique downtown that closed years ago... they used to wrap everything in this lovely lilac tissue paper before they put it in the bag. The woman who owned the shop, Mrs. Gable, she had the most beautiful handwriting. She would write little thank-you notes on heavy cream cardstock and slip them into the bag. She used a real fountain pen, the kind you have to fill from a little glass bottle of ink. My father had a fountain pen just like it. He kept it in the top drawer of his oak desk, right next to his collection of old silver coins. He had this one coin from 1899, an old Morgan silver dollar. He always said it was his lucky coin, and he'd rub his thumb over the eagle on the back whenever he was thinking hard about something...

Oh, dear me. I'm doing it again, aren't I? My father's silver dollar... I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked about my bills again. But yes, I still handle them, I just... I'm just not as careful with things as I used to be.

Well, no, I haven't had to stop driving. I still have my car, and I drive myself when I really need to. It's a Buick. A LeSabre. My husband bought it for me right before he passed. He always loved Buicks. Said they rode like you were floating on a cloud. He used to wash it every Saturday morning, right out there in the driveway, with a big yellow sponge and a bucket of warm soapy water. He'd always use Palmolive dish soap, the green kind, because he said it cut the grease on the hubcaps better than anything else. He'd scrub those hubcaps until you could see your face in them. He was so particular about his cars. Before the Buick, we had this old station wagon with the wood paneling on the sides. We took the kids all the way to Mount Rushmore in that car. It was the summer of '76, the Bicentennial. The kids in the back seat were eating those red, white, and blue popsicles, the Bomb Pops, and my son dropped his right on the upholstery. It left this awful sticky red stain that never did come out, no matter how much carpet cleaner I used on it... 

Oh, for heaven's sake. Listen to me. The Bomb Pops and the station wagon. I apologize, doctor. My mind just wanders off like a loose balloon. You were asking about driving. No, I haven't had to stop because of my memory or anything like that. I just don't go out as much as I used to.

Well, no, not completely unpaid, but like I was saying earlier, I do rely on my daughter to remind me about them. I haven't lost the house or anything... I still manage to stay here, thank the Lord. But I just put things off. It's like I mentioned before, I've missed calls and appointments, and those family tasks I used to be so careful with. I even stopped teaching my craft classes at the community center. 

I really miss the community center sometimes. The floors there were this polished linoleum, always smelled a bit like lemon wax and old paper. The janitor, Mr. Henderson, he must have been eighty years old if he was a day, but he pushed that big wide dust mop up and down the halls every single afternoon. He wore these navy blue coveralls with his name embroidered over the pocket in red thread. My husband had a shirt with his name on it like that when he worked at the hardware store. It was a bowling shirt, actually, from when they sponsored a team. The "Hardware Hitters," they called themselves. They had these shiny satin jackets, bright emerald green with a big white bowling pin on the back. He brought one home for our son once, but it was miles too big. The sleeves hung down past his little hands, and he ran around the living room pretending he was a ghost...

Oh, my goodness. The bowling shirts. I'm so sorry, doctor. I've completely lost the thread again. You were asking about the bills. I haven't let them go completely unpaid, no, I just... I need more reminders now, and I put off the routine things.

Well, nice to meet you too, doctor. I suppose what brings me in is... well, I just don’t have the push I used to have. For anything, really. Like my choir... I used to never miss a Sunday. Brother Thomas leads it, and he always wears these real loud yellow ties. I told him once, I said, 'Thomas, that tie is brighter than the morning sun.' He’s a good man, though. His wife makes the best potato salad for the church picnics, she puts that sweet relish in it. I always ask her for the recipe but she won't give it up. 

But anyway... I just don't go to choir now. Or do my quilting. I was working on a nice quilt, but I ran out of the blue thread, and the sewing store downtown closed up a few years back. It used to be a bakery before that, they had these little cherry tarts. So now... most days I just sit at home. I keep the TV on real low... usually just the game shows. The commercials are so loud these days, aren't they? Selling all sorts of mops and car insurance. But I just sit there with it on low, even though I know folks are expecting me to come visit or show up to things. I just can't seem to get up and go anymore.

Depressed? Well, I don't think so. I'm not crying into my soup or anything like that. Not like my neighbor Shirley. Now she gets real depressed. She lost her little dog last spring and she just wept and wept. It was a Pomeranian, I think. Fluffy little thing, but it had a mean streak. It used to nip right at the mailman's ankles every single morning. The mailman, Gary, he was such a nice boy, too. He always made sure to put my magazines inside the screen door so they wouldn't get wet when it rained. It’s been raining so much lately, hasn't it? My grandmother used to say too much rain makes the tomatoes split right on the vine, and she was right. She grew the biggest tomatoes you ever saw. But no... I wouldn't say I feel sad or blue myself. I just don't have the get-up-and-go anymore.

Memory? Oh, no, I don't think so. My memory is still sharp as a tack. I remember all sorts of things just fine. Like just yesterday I remembered to water my African violets. I've had those violets for near on ten years now. My sister gave them to me in this little ceramic pot that looked like a frog. She always liked frogs... used to collect them. Glass ones, wooden ones, she even had a stuffed one that croaked when you squeezed its belly. She moved down to Florida a while back. Tampa, I think it was. Or maybe Pensacola. They get terrible hurricanes down there, just awful. The wind blows the roofs right off the houses, I saw it on the news. The newsman had on a very nice raincoat, though. Bright yellow... kind of like Brother Thomas's tie, actually. But, um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, remembering things. No, my memory is perfectly fine.

What month? Well, it's October. I'm pretty sure it's October. I just flipped the page on my calendar in the kitchen a few days ago. The bank gives them out for free if you ask nice, the teller with the curly hair always saves me one. This year they have pictures of covered bridges. I always liked covered bridges... my uncle Henry lived out near one in Pennsylvania. Or maybe it was Ohio. He raised pigs out there. Big, muddy things, they smell just awful in the summer heat. But he made his own sausage, and let me tell you, you haven't lived until you've had Uncle Henry's breakfast sausage with a little maple syrup poured over it. Real maple syrup, not that fake stuff in the plastic bottles they sell now. The real stuff comes in glass, sometimes shaped like a little log cabin. My sister had a cabin up by the lake, actually... but yes, I know what month it is.

The year? Well, they do tend to blend together a bit these days. I was just thinking about New Year's, actually. When I was a little girl, my father would bring out the good radio for New Year's Eve. It was one of those big wooden ones that sat right in the parlor, with the glowing glass tubes in the back. I used to just sit and watch them glow, they got so warm. Our cat, Barnaby—he was a big orange tabby—he loved to sleep right behind that radio to soak up the heat. He was a wonderful mouser, that cat. He caught a mouse right in our pantry once, right next to the flour bin. We had to keep the flour in a big metal tin back then, otherwise the weevils would get into it. Have you ever seen a weevil? Just nasty little bugs. They'll ruin a whole batch of biscuits if you aren't paying attention. My mother made the best biscuits, though. She used a whole lot of buttermilk. We'd get the buttermilk from the milkman, he had a little truck that rattled down the dirt road... but what was it? Oh, the year. Honestly, I'd probably have to look at the top of the newspaper to tell you the exact number. They just fly by so fast now.

Where we are? Well, we're in this room right now. It's a nice enough room, I suppose. The chairs are comfortable. Not like the chairs at the dentist's office. Oh, those are just dreadful, aren't they? They lean you so far back you feel like all the blood is rushing right to your head. And that bright light shining right in your eyes... it always gives me a headache. I used to take aspirin for headaches, but then my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she told me that peppermint tea is much better for that sort of thing. She grows her own peppermint in little window boxes. They smell wonderful in the summer. She gave me a cutting once, but I think I watered it too much. I'm usually so good with plants, you know, with my African violets and all, but herbs can be fussy. Some of them like the soil dry, some like it damp... it's a lot to keep track of. But, um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, where we are. I know it's a doctor's office of some sort, but I couldn't tell you the exact name of the building or anything.

Paying my bills? Oh, well, I suppose I manage alright with the mail, though I have had to step back a bit from things lately. I used to be the one leading the church choir, you know. Every Sunday, standing right up there in the front. I had this beautiful navy blue dress I wore for the big performances, the one with the little pearl buttons down the sleeves. I bought it at a department store downtown... oh, what was the name of it? They had the most wonderful perfume counter right when you walked in. It always smelled like roses and powder. My mother loved rose water, she used to dab it on her wrists before church. She had a little glass bottle with a silver stopper. Anyway, I had to stop doing the choir, and I stopped helping out with the projects at the senior center, too. I just couldn't seem to keep up with what I'd promised to do, and I'd forget the sheet music or the meeting times. Now my friends from church, they come by and check on me a lot more than they used to. They bring casseroles sometimes. Martha brought a tuna noodle one last week, but she uses those crushed potato chips on top instead of breadcrumbs. I always think breadcrumbs are much better, especially if you toast them in a little butter first with some parsley... but yes, I've had to take a step back from my activities.

Feeling down? I don't think so, really. I mean, some days are quieter than others, I suppose. I like to sit by the window when it's quiet. I have a bird feeder right out there, a nice wooden one shaped like a little barn. I put out black oil sunflower seeds because the cardinals just love those. They're such beautiful birds, aren't they? That bright red against the snow in the winter, it's just lovely. My husband, God rest his soul, he built that bird feeder for me. He was always tinkering in the garage with wood. He made a beautiful cedar chest for our bedroom, too. It still smells like cedar when you open it up, even after all these years. I keep my winter quilts in there. You have to keep them packed away properly or the moths will get them. Moths can just ruin a good wool blanket in no time at all. My grandmother used to put mothballs in everything, but oh, that smell is just awful. It gets right into the fabric and you can never wash it out... but no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling down. Just watching the birds, mostly.

Getting lost? Oh, no, I don't think I've gotten lost. I know my way around the neighborhood well enough. I've lived in the same house for... oh, it must be over forty years now. It's the one with the big oak tree in the front yard. That tree drops so many leaves in the autumn, it's a real chore to rake them all up. My grandson used to come over and help me rake them into big piles, and then he'd jump right in! He was such a rambunctious little boy. Always had scraped knees from climbing things he shouldn't. I used to keep those character band-aids in the bathroom just for him. The ones with the little cartoon dogs on them. He wouldn't let me put a plain one on, no sir. It had to be the cartoon dogs. They don't make band-aids like they used to, though. They just don't stick right if you get them even a little bit wet. I was washing dishes the other day—just a few plates, I don't use the dishwasher much anymore since it's just me—and the band-aid came right off in the soapy water. It was a lemon-scented dish soap. I always buy the lemon kind, it smells so clean. But anyway... no, I haven't been getting lost.

Manage my medicines? Oh, well... I don't think I need anyone to do that for me. I have them all lined up on the kitchen counter, right next to the toaster. It's one of those shiny chrome toasters, the kind that pops up with a real loud clank. My sister gave it to me for Christmas a few years back. She always wraps her presents so beautifully, with those big velvet bows that she ties herself. She learned how to make them at a craft store down in Florida when she lived there. Florida is so humid, though, I could never stand the heat. My hair just frizzes up into an absolute mess the minute I step off the plane. I used to use those big pink curlers to try and tame it, the ones you sleep in? Goodness, they were uncomfortable. Like sleeping on a pile of rocks. But yes, I just take my pills myself when I have my morning tea.

Wrong with my thinking? No, no, I don't think so. My memory is just fine. I was just remembering the other day about the time my cousin came to visit from upstate. She brought this huge basket of apples from an orchard near her house. Honeycrisp, I think they were. They make the best pies, they really do. You have to peel them just right, though, or the texture gets all mushy when you bake it. I have this little paring knife with a wooden handle that I've used for years, fits right in the palm of my hand. The blade is getting a bit dull, I suppose, but I don't know how to sharpen it. My husband used to do all the sharpening out in the garage on his grinding wheel. Sparks would just fly everywhere! It always made me nervous he was going to catch his shirt on fire. He wore those thick flannel shirts all winter long, the plaid ones. Red and black, mostly. They were so warm, but they took forever to dry on the line. I always loved the smell of clothes dried outside in the fresh air, though... much better than the dryer. But anyway, no, my memory is just fine.

More trouble? Oh, I wouldn't say that. I think I remember things just as well as I ever did. Like yesterday, I remembered to put the trash out right on time. The garbage truck always comes so early on Tuesdays, before the sun is even fully up. It makes such an awful racket, clanging those big metal bins against the side of the truck. I don't know how the driver stands the noise all day long. He must wear earplugs, don't you think? Those little foam ones you roll up between your fingers. I tried wearing those once when my neighbor got a new dog that barked all night. It was a little terrier mix, cute as a button but just wouldn't stop yapping at every shadow. I think it was afraid of the dark. Some dogs are like that, you know. They need a little nightlight just like children do. I always kept a nightlight in the hallway when my kids were small. It was shaped like a little seashell, plugged right into the wall. Gave off the softest pink glow... But no, I don't think I'm having any more trouble than usual.

A medical condition for my brain? No, no doctor has ever said anything like that to me. I haven't been to the doctor much lately anyway, except when I went to see Dr. Evans for my bad knee a while back. He has this huge aquarium in his waiting room, right against the wall. It’s full of those little blue and red fish... neon tetras, I think they’re called. They just dart around so fast, back and forth, back and forth. I always wonder who cleans that tank. It must take hours to scrub all that green algae off the glass and clean the little pebbles at the bottom. I had a goldfish bowl once when the kids were little, just a small round glass one we won at the county fair. We named him Barnaby. He lived for a really long time for a fair fish, almost two years! We buried him out by the rosebushes when he finally passed on. Those rosebushes grew so tall that next spring, with these beautiful yellow blooms. They smelled just like lemon drops, so sweet and bright. But no, nobody's told me I have any kind of memory condition.

Finances? Oh, well, I suppose I haven't been keeping track of things quite the same way. The ladies from church have been checking on me a lot more lately, making sure I have what I need. I actually had to step back from leading the choir. And the projects at the senior center, too. I just couldn't seem to keep up with what I promised to do. It’s a shame, really, because we were working on this beautiful quilt for the charity auction. All these little squares of fabric, donated by people all over town. Mrs. Higgins brought in a whole bag of old calico dresses she didn't wear anymore. They had the sweetest little floral prints on them, tiny pink and yellow daisies. I always loved calico, it reminds me of the aprons my grandmother used to wear when she baked bread. She’d get flour all over the front of it, just covered in white dust. Her bread was the best, though. So crusty on the outside and soft in the middle. We'd eat it warm with butter and that homemade strawberry jam she kept in the cellar. The cellar was always so cool and damp, smelled like earth and old potatoes... but anyway, yes, I've had to stop helping out as much because I just can't keep my promises straight.

Paying my bills? Oh, well... no, I don't think I need help with that. I still write the checks out myself every month. I sit down at the kitchen table with my special blue pen. It's one of those gel pens, you know? It writes so smooth, just glides right across the paper. My granddaughter gave it to me for my birthday last year. She’s such a thoughtful girl, always finding little things she thinks I'll like. She just started her first year of high school, can you believe it? Time goes by so fast. It feels like just yesterday she was running around the yard catching fireflies in a glass jar. We used to poke holes in the lid so they could breathe, and she’d keep them on her nightstand until they stopped glowing. Then we'd let them go in the morning. The dew would still be on the grass, getting our slippers all wet. I always wore those fuzzy pink slippers, the ones with the little pom-poms on the toes... but no, I manage my bills just fine.

Sad or low? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, everybody has their days, but I haven't been feeling down like that. Mostly I just sit on the porch in the afternoons and watch the neighborhood. The Miller boy across the street got a new bicycle, one of those bright red ones with the shiny chrome handlebars. He rides it up and down the sidewalk, ringing the little bell. It reminds me of the bell on the ice cream truck when I was a little girl. We used to hear it from three streets over and go running inside to beg my mother for a nickel. A nickel could get you a whole twin popsicle back then! We’d split it down the middle, me and my brother. He always wanted the cherry side, and I liked the orange. Orange always tasted like sunshine, you know? Like those hot July days when the tar on the road would get all soft and stick to the bottom of your bare feet. My mother would scold us for tracking black marks onto her clean linoleum floor. She kept that floor so spotless you could eat off it... but no, I haven't been feeling sad or anything like that.

Missing payments? Oh, well... no, I haven't missed any. I always make sure they go out on time. I walk them down to the blue mailbox on the corner every Tuesday morning. It's a nice little walk, past the Henderson's house. They just planted the most beautiful hydrangeas along their fence. Huge, blue blooms, like giant cotton candy but blue, you know? They remind me of a dress I had when I was a young woman. I wore it to a dance at the VFW hall, it had this full skirt that would just twirl and twirl when you spun around. The band was playing Glenn Miller that night, and the trumpet player had the shiniest shoes I'd ever seen. You could see the lights reflecting right off the toes of them. They must have polished them for hours. My husband used to polish his shoes like that every Sunday before church. He'd lay out a newspaper on the floor so he wouldn't get polish on the rug... but yes, my bills always get mailed right on time.

Cooking meals? Oh, no... I don't need any help with that. I still do all my own cooking. Just the other day I made a big pot of beef stew. I let it simmer on the stove for hours, and the whole kitchen smelled like carrots and thyme. I always use fresh carrots, the ones with the green leafy tops still on them. They remind me of the garden my grandfather used to keep behind his house. He grew tomatoes as big as softballs, I swear. We used to eat them right off the vine, still warm from the sun, with just a little sprinkle of salt from a glass shaker. He kept that salt shaker right in the front pocket of his overalls. Those overalls were so faded, almost white at the knees from where he'd kneel in the dirt all day. He had this old hound dog named Buster that would follow him up and down the rows, just sniffing at the dirt and trying to catch the big fat bumblebees in his mouth... but no, I manage the cooking all by myself just fine.

Drive? Oh, yes, I still drive myself. I take my little Buick out when I need to go to the market. It's a very reliable car, that Buick. The color is a lovely shade of silver, almost like the color of the moon on a really clear, crisp autumn night. You know those nights when the air is so sharp it almost hurts to breathe, but it smells like woodsmoke? My father used to build the most wonderful fires in our fireplace on nights like that. He’d bring in these huge oak logs, and they’d crackle and pop, sending little orange sparks flying up the chimney like tiny fireflies. We used to catch fireflies in glass jars during the summer. We’d punch holes in the metal lids with a nail and a hammer so they could breathe. The hammer had a wooden handle that was all smooth and worn down from years of use... but yes, I do drive myself around just fine.

Handling my finances? No, no, I still do all that myself. Nobody else touches my checkbook. I keep it in the top drawer of my desk, right next to the stationary. It's this beautiful heavy paper, cream-colored, with my initials embossed at the top in gold ink. I bought it at a little stationery shop downtown years ago. The shop owner was this sweet man who wore a bowtie every single day. He had a whole collection of them, polka dots, stripes, little paisley patterns. He told me once he bought them all on a trip to London. Oh, I've always wanted to go to London and see the changing of the guard. The soldiers in those tall, fuzzy black hats... they must get so dreadfully hot in the summertime. I wonder what they're made of? Bear fur, maybe? That seems so heavy to wear on your head all day... but anyway, no, I take care of all my own money. Nobody else handles it.

Well, I came in because... people have been telling me they can actually see something's off with how I'm moving. Like I'm moving like I'm underwater, you know? Taking forever to just answer a question or even get out of a chair. Which is weird because usually I'm pretty quick. I work in customer service, so you have to be fast on the phones. Sometimes I get these callers who just want to complain about the shipping times, and I'm like, "Ma'am, I don't drive the delivery truck." But anyway, yeah, either I'm super slow, or else I'm just pacing my apartment for hours, rubbing my hands together like I'm trying to shake off a bad call. It's really frustrating. My cat, Mr. Whiskers, he just sits there watching me pace. I think he judges me, honestly. He's an orange tabby, very vocal. But yeah, the moving too slow or too fast thing is why I'm here.

Depressed? I don't really think so... I mean, I haven't noticed feeling sad most of the day or anything like that. Though I do get a little bummed out when I see those sad animal rescue commercials, you know the ones with the Sarah McLachlan song? Man, those are just brutal. Mr. Whiskers usually just leaves the room when they come on. I actually ended up upgrading my streaming service to the ad-free tier just to avoid them entirely. It's like four extra dollars a month, which doesn't sound like a lot, but when you add up Netflix, Hulu, and all the others, you're basically just paying for cable all over again. My buddy Mark was just complaining about that the other day. He works in IT and keeps trying to show me how to pirate movies, but I really don't want to risk getting a virus on my work laptop, you know? The IT department at my job is super strict about what we do on our machines, and if I get locked out, I can't take any calls. But, um... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling depressed. Yeah, no, I don't really feel like that.

Energetic or high? No, not really. I mean, I drink a lot of coffee, but that's just because I work the early shift. I have to be logged on by 7 AM, which means I'm up at 5:30. I got this new coffee maker, actually, one of those fancy ones that grinds the beans right before it brews. It's supposed to be better for the flavor profile or whatever. My sister got it for me for my birthday. She's really into all that artisanal stuff. She actually lives in Portland now, which makes sense, right? Everyone there is super into coffee and, like, knitting their own sweaters. She keeps trying to get me to come visit, but flights are just so expensive right now. I was looking on Expedia the other day, and even with the budget airlines, it's crazy. Plus, you have to pay for carry-on bags now! Can you believe that? It's like they nickel and dime you for everything. I remember when you could just bring a bag and they'd even give you a little pack of peanuts. Now you're lucky if you get a half-cup of water. But, uh, yeah, no, I don't get unusually energetic or anything like that. Just the normal caffeine buzz, you know?

Voices? Well... it's kind of weird you bring that up. I actually have been hearing stuff from work when I'm not even working. Like, I'll hear my old headset beep—you know that little electronic chime it makes when a call drops in?—and then I'll hear this supervisor-type voice just say my name, or tell me I'm being "too slow." And the thing is, my laptop is completely closed and there’s no phone ringing at all. 

It's really annoying because supervisors are always on you about being too slow anyway. My old manager, Greg, he used to monitor our average handle times like a hawk. He had this massive Excel spreadsheet, color-coded and everything. I don't know how these middle managers have the time to just stare at spreadsheets all day, you know? Like, don't you have actual work to do? He would literally ping me on Teams if my wrap-up time went over thirty seconds. Wrap-up time is when you type the notes after a call, and you have to be really detailed, otherwise the next rep gets completely confused when the customer calls back. And the system we use is so clunky, it takes forever to load the customer's profile anyway, so it's not even my fault if it takes a minute. But yeah... I'll just be sitting there in my living room with the computer shut, and I'll hear that beep and the voice getting on my case.

Yeah, actually... I've had stretches, like a few weeks here and there, where my mood was totally fine. Like, closer to normal, and I was actually getting things done around the apartment. I even finally cleaned out the lint trap in my dryer. You know how dangerous those things are? My buddy Mark—the IT guy I mentioned—his cousin's entire apartment building almost burned down because someone didn't clean their lint trap. It's crazy how something so small can cause so much damage. It's like those little space heaters people bring into the office during the winter because the AC is always blasting. I used to sit right under a vent at my last job, and I swear I had a cold from October to March. I brought in this little ceramic heater, and Greg—my old manager—made me take it home because it was a "fire hazard." Meanwhile, the microwave in the breakroom sparked every time someone tried to heat up a Hot Pocket, but that was totally fine, apparently. Hot Pockets are terrible for you anyway, just pure sodium. But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Even during those good weeks when I'm feeling fine and getting stuff done, I still hear that supervisor voice. Or I'll just feel absolutely certain that the old ticketing software is flagging my account for some reason, even when I'm not working.

Less sleep? No, I usually need my full eight hours, otherwise I'm completely useless the next day. Sometimes nine if I can swing it. I actually bought this really nice weighted blanket a few months ago to help me sleep better. It's like fifteen pounds, which sounds heavy, but it's supposed to simulate a hug or something? I don't know the exact science behind it, but it really works. My buddy Mark told me about it. He's always researching random biohacking stuff. Like last month, he was trying to convince me to start taking these mushroom supplements—not the psychedelic kind, just like, lion's mane or whatever. He said it improves cognitive function and helps with brain fog. But I don't know, those supplements are completely unregulated by the FDA. You could be taking literally anything. I watched this documentary on Netflix about the supplement industry, and it's wild. They can basically put whatever they want in those capsules as long as they don't claim it cures a disease. It's just like the diet pill craze in the 90s, remember that? People were having heart attacks from ephedra. My aunt tried all those crazy diets back then. Cabbage soup, grapefruit... she even did that one where you only eat meat and cheese. But yeah, no, I definitely need my sleep. I've never had a time where I didn't need it.

Irritable? I mean... I don't think so. Not unusually, anyway. Like, I'll get annoyed at normal things, but I've never had days where I'm just snapping at everyone for no reason. Though, speaking of getting annoyed, the traffic around my apartment complex has been absolutely insane lately. They decided to repave the main road right at the entrance, and they only have one lane open. So you have to sit there waiting for this guy with a stop sign to flip it to "slow." And half the time, the guy isn't even paying attention. He's just looking at his phone. I swear, nobody has any work ethic anymore. It's just like when I call my internet provider. I was on hold for forty-five minutes last Tuesday because my Wi-Fi kept dropping. Forty-five minutes! And when I finally got someone, they just told me to unplug the router and plug it back in. Like I hadn't already tried that ten times. It's a standard script, I know, I used to do it, but come on. And then they try to upsell you on a faster package while your current one doesn't even work. It's a total scam. Cable companies basically have a monopoly in most areas, so they can treat you however they want. My buddy Mark actually set up his own mesh network at his house, and he says he never has dead zones anymore. I might have him come over and help me set one up. But um, yeah, no, I wouldn't say I get unusually irritable. Just the normal amount when things are frustrating.

Depressed for two weeks straight? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, I get down sometimes, sure, but not like every single day for weeks. It's more like... I'll just have a bad day here and there. Like last week, I was feeling pretty bummed out because I went to the grocery store to get those specific jalapeño kettle chips I like, and they were completely sold out. Again. It's the third time this month. I don't understand how a major grocery chain can't keep their inventory stocked properly. It's all automated now, right? The system should know when they're running low and just order more. My buddy Mark was telling me about this new supply chain software his company is implementing, and it uses AI to predict buying patterns based on weather and local events. Like, if it's going to rain, it automatically orders more umbrellas and soup. It's actually kind of creepy when you think about it. The computers know what we want before we even know we want it. It's just like how you talk about something near your phone, and suddenly you're getting ads for it on Instagram. I was literally just talking to my mom about getting a new coffee maker, and bam, ten different ads for espresso machines. I don't even drink espresso, it makes my heart race too much. But yeah, no, I haven't been depressed like that. Just regular bad days, you know?

Seizures? No, definitely not. I've never had anything like that happen to me. My cousin's dog actually has seizures, though. It's really sad. He's this little Jack Russell terrier mix, super high energy usually, but then he'll just drop and start shaking. They have him on some kind of medication for it now, pheno-something, I think? But they have to hide the pill in a scoop of peanut butter or he'll just spit it right back out. Dogs are so smart like that. Like, they know when you're trying to trick them. My old roommate had a cat that figured out how to open the cabinets in the kitchen. We'd wake up and all the Tupperware would be all over the floor. We had to put child locks on everything, which was honestly super annoying because I could barely figure out how to open them myself when I was half asleep trying to get a bowl for cereal. I'm a big cereal guy. Cinnamon Toast Crunch is top tier, but honestly, a good bowl of Honey Nut Cheerios just hits different sometimes. Mark says cereal is basically just eating dessert for breakfast because of all the sugar, but whatever. Anyway, no, no seizures for me.

Brain injury? Um... no, I've never hit my head that hard or had any neurological stuff. I mean, I bumped my head on the open trunk of my car a couple weeks ago, but that was just because I was rushing to get my groceries inside before the ice cream melted. It was that really hot day we had, remember? Like 95 degrees in early May, which is just ridiculous. I bought this new brand of pistachio gelato, and it was pretty expensive, so I didn't want it turning into soup. I actually watched a documentary the other night about how gelato is made differently than regular ice cream. They churn it slower, so there's less air whipped into it, which makes it denser and more flavorful. Plus they serve it at a slightly warmer temperature so your taste buds don't get numbed by the cold. It's fascinating how much science goes into food. Like baking—baking is basically just chemistry. If you mess up the ratio of baking soda to flour, your cookies turn out like little hockey pucks. My mom used to make these incredible chocolate chip cookies when I was a kid, but she never wrote the recipe down. She just kind of threw things in a bowl. I tried to recreate them once, and I totally forgot the vanilla extract. You wouldn't think one little teaspoon of liquid would make such a huge difference, but they tasted completely flat. Anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, brain injuries. Yeah, no, nothing serious like that. Just the occasional bump on a car trunk.

Well, yeah, actually. There have been stretches, like a few weeks here and there, where I actually felt pretty okay. My mood was closer to normal, I was getting up, getting things done around the apartment, doing my laundry... which, by the way, the dryer in my building is completely useless right now. You have to run it through three cycles just to get a load of towels dry. I told the landlord about it, but he's always dragging his feet. He says it's an issue with the lint trap ventilation or something, but I think he just doesn't want to pay for a repair guy. Repair guys charge like, what, a hundred bucks just to show up? It's a total racket. My uncle used to do HVAC repair, and he told me half the time he'd just go to a house, clean off a sensor with a Q-tip, and charge them for a full service call. He said people just don't want to learn how their own appliances work. It's like cars. I don't know the first thing about cars. If my check engine light comes on, I just put a piece of black electrical tape over it so it stops glaring at me at night. But anyway, yeah, even during those couple of weeks when I was feeling fine and getting my chores done, I still heard that supervisor voice talking to me. And I was still completely sure that the old ticketing software at work was flagging my account. So the mood stuff was fine, but the other stuff was definitely still happening.

Um... holding the same position? I mean, I guess sometimes when I get really overwhelmed with everything, I'll kind of just freeze up. Like, I'll catch myself standing in the kitchen with my coffee mug just hovering halfway to my mouth, and I won't even realize how long I've been standing there. Or I'll start walking this same little loop back and forth by the couch for no real reason. I actually got that couch at a thrift store, believe it or not. It's this really cool mid-century modern style, kind of a mustard yellow color. Mark hated it when I first brought it home. He said it looked like it belonged in a 1970s bowling alley, but I think it gives the living room character. Plus, it's surprisingly comfortable once you break it in. The only problem is the fabric is a magnet for pet hair, which is weird because I don't even have any pets. But somehow, every time I sit down in black sweatpants, I stand up looking like I just hugged a golden retriever. I've gone through so many of those sticky lint rollers. The ones from the dollar store are terrible, by the way. The paper just rips in these tiny diagonal strips instead of peeling off in one clean sheet, so you spend ten minutes just trying to find the edge. It's infuriating. But yeah, sometimes I just stand there with my coffee, or do the pacing thing by the couch when things feel like too much.

Resist when they try to move me? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, nobody's really tried to physically move me around like that. I live by myself, so there's not really anyone around to do that anyway. It's just me and the apartment, which honestly is getting a little cramped. I've been thinking about trying to find a bigger place, maybe something with a balcony. I saw this one listing online the other day that had this amazing little terrace overlooking a courtyard, but the rent was just outrageous. It's crazy how much they charge for a tiny square of outdoor space in this city. And the deposit they wanted was equal to two months' rent, plus a non-refundable application fee. Application fees are such a scam. You pay fifty bucks just for them to run a credit check that costs them like two dollars, and then they don't even call you back if they pick someone else. I had a friend who spent almost three hundred dollars just applying to places before she finally got one. She works at a bakery downtown—well, she used to, before they downsized. She made these amazing sourdough loaves. Sourdough is so tricky to get right, you have to feed the starter every day and keep it at the perfect temperature. If it gets too cold, the yeast just kind of goes to sleep and the bread turns out flat. I tried making it once during that phase when everyone was baking bread, but my starter just smelled like old gym socks, so I threw it out. But anyway, no, nobody has tried to physically move me or anything like that. I just do my own thing.

Important or powerful? No, definitely not. I mean, I'm just a customer service rep, you know? You pretty much feel like the least important person on the planet when you're doing that job. People call in and yell at you over the smallest things, acting like *they're* the king of the world. Like this one guy last week, he was screaming at me because his account update was delayed by an hour. An hour! And it's not like I personally control the servers. 

Speaking of servers, my laptop has been acting so weird lately. The fan just spins up and sounds like an airplane taking off, even when I only have one browser tab open. I think it might be full of dust. I tried to buy one of those cans of compressed air to clean it out, but they lock them up behind glass at the pharmacy now. You have to press a little red button and wait for an employee to come unlock it. I stood there for like fifteen minutes the other day, pressing the button, and the overhead speaker just kept saying "Customer assistance needed in aisle four." Over and over. Nobody ever came. I ended up just giving up and buying a candy bar at the front register instead. It was one of those ones with the almonds in it. I usually prefer peanuts, but peanuts have been giving me heartburn lately. Actually, almost everything gives me heartburn lately, which sucks because I love spicy food. There's this great Thai place down the street... 

Wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, feeling powerful. Yeah, no, I don't get feelings like that. I'm just a regular guy.

Um, a month? No, it's been a lot longer than that. I think... yeah, it's been about a year and eight months now that I've been hearing them and knowing the software is watching me. And it's not just when I'm feeling really down or anything, it's just kind of always there. 

Like, even when I had that brief period where I tried to get back into running—which didn't last long, by the way. I bought these really expensive running shoes, the kind with the extra thick foam on the bottom that are supposed to be like running on clouds. They were neon green. I thought maybe a bright color would motivate me to put them on in the mornings. But the laces were those weird elastic ones that you don't tie, you just pull them tight with a little plastic toggle thing. I could never get the tension right. They were either cutting off the circulation to my toes or slipping off my heel with every step. I ended up getting this massive blister on my right heel after just two miles. Blisters are the worst, especially when you have to wear dress shoes for a cousin's wedding or something. My cousin Sarah got married last October in this beautiful outdoor ceremony, but it rained the whole time. They had to rent this huge tent at the last minute, and the ground was so muddy. Everyone's shoes were ruined. They had a taco bar for the reception, though, which was pretty cool. I love tacos, especially the al pastor kind with the little pieces of pineapple mixed in. The sweetness really balances out the spice. 

But yeah, anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right, the voices and the software thing. Yeah, it's been going on for like a year and eight months, not just when I'm super depressed.

Go mute? Like, just stop talking entirely? No, I don't think so. I mean, I talk all day for my job, so I can't really get away with that. Though sometimes I definitely wish I could just hit a mute button on myself, or on the customers. My throat gets so dry by the end of my shift. I started drinking that throat coat tea, the one with the slippery elm in it? It's supposed to be really good for your vocal cords, but it tastes exactly like black licorice. 

I absolutely hate black licorice. When I was a kid, my grandma used to keep this crystal bowl of black jelly beans on her coffee table. Who even likes the black jelly beans? They just sat there for years, I swear they were practically fossilized. Her house always smelled like mothballs and peppermint. She had this massive grandfather clock in the hallway that chimed every fifteen minutes, day and night. It drove me crazy when I had to sleep over. The pendulum was made of this really shiny brass, and I remember trying to polish it with my sleeve once. Brass tarnishes so fast if you don't keep up with it. I have a brass lamp on my desk right now, actually, and it's looking pretty dull. I should probably buy some Brasso. You can get it at the hardware store, but the mom-and-pop hardware store near my apartment just closed down last month. They're turning it into a boutique pet bakery. A bakery for dogs! Can you believe people spend eight dollars on a cupcake for a pug? It's wild. 

But anyway... no, I don't ever just go completely mute. I always answer when people talk to me, even if it's just to say yeah or whatever.

Lost interest? I guess... I mean, my friends keep telling me I sound totally flat these days, like I'm hard to read or something. And even when they're talking about stuff I actually care about, I just end up giving these really short answers and I avoid making plans to hang out. 

Making plans is just so exhausting anyway. You have to coordinate schedules, and then someone always cancels at the last minute because they forgot they had a dentist appointment. I hate the dentist. The last time I went, the hygienist kept talking to me while she had her hands in my mouth. How are you supposed to answer when someone has a metal hook scraping your molars? She was telling me all about her son's travel baseball team. Travel sports are so intense now. Parents spend thousands of dollars just so their ten-year-old can play in tournaments three states away every weekend. It's ridiculous. I played little league when I was a kid, but we just played at the park down the street. The snack shack there had the best soft pretzels. They were always super salty, and they came with this little plastic cup of neon yellow cheese. I used to dip my pretzels in it until the cheese was totally gone, and then I'd try to scrape the rest out with my finger. You can't really get good pretzels like that anymore, except maybe at the mall. But the mall is always so crowded, especially around the holidays. The parking lot is a nightmare... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, being around people. Yeah, I just kind of keep to myself and give short answers now. I don't really make plans with anyone.

Freeze in the same position? I mean... I don't know about staying completely frozen like a statue for a really long time. But when I get really overwhelmed with everything, I do catch myself doing weird things. Like, I'll be standing in the kitchen with my coffee mug just hovering halfway to my mouth, just kind of stuck there. Or I'll find myself walking the exact same little loop around my couch over and over for no real reason. 

My couch is this dark gray sectional I got off Craigslist a couple years ago. The guy who sold it to me said it was barely used, but there's definitely a dip in the middle cushion where you can tell someone sat all the time. It came with these terrible mustard yellow throw pillows that I immediately threw in the closet. Mustard yellow is just such an aggressive color, you know? It reminds me of the uniform I had to wear at my first job in high school. I worked at this hot dog stand at the local fairgrounds. We had to wear these bright yellow polo shirts with a cartoon hot dog embroidered on the pocket. The hot dog was wearing sunglasses and giving a thumbs up. It was so embarrassing. The worst part was that the stand didn't have air conditioning, and in August it would get up to like a hundred degrees in there. The smell of boiling hot dogs and stale buns just baked into my clothes. I must have washed that uniform a hundred times, but I could never get the smell out. I actually had to throw the shirts away when I quit because even my mom said they were making the whole laundry room smell like cheap meat. I haven't been able to eat a hot dog since then. 

But yeah, what were we talking about? Oh, freezing. Yeah, I just kind of get stuck holding my coffee or pacing around the couch sometimes when it's all too much.

Placed my arms in a position? Like... like someone else moving my body for me? No, nobody does that. I live by myself, so there's no one around to even try that, you know? It's just me and my cat, Barnaby. 

Barnaby is a Maine Coon mix, so he's absolutely massive. He's got these giant tufted ears and paws the size of baseballs. He's actually the reason I had to buy a new vacuum cleaner last month. He sheds so much, it's like a second cat is forming on my rug every week. I ended up getting one of those Dyson stick vacuums. They're so expensive, but everyone says they're the best. I don't know though, the battery only lasts like twenty minutes on the highest setting. By the time I finish the living room and the hallway, it's dead. Then I have to wait three hours for it to charge just so I can do my bedroom. It's so annoying. I should have just bought a regular plug-in one. My mom has this old Hoover from the nineties that still works perfectly. It's this ugly teal color, and it's super loud, but it sucks up everything. She used to make me vacuum the stairs every Saturday morning when I was a teenager. The cord was never quite long enough to reach all the way to the top, so I always had to unplug it halfway up and find another outlet. We lived in this split-level house, and the layout was just so weird. The kitchen was basically on a landing between the living room and the bedrooms...

Wait, sorry. No, nobody poses my arms or anything like that. I just move myself.

Repeated other people's words? Like, repeating them back? No, I don't think I do that. Unless you count when I'm on the phone at work. I work in customer service for this internet provider, and we actually have to repeat the customer's issue back to them as part of our script. It's supposed to show "active listening" or whatever. So if they say, "My router keeps dropping the signal," I have to say, "I understand your router keeps dropping the signal." 

It honestly just makes people mad half the time. They think I'm being condescending. People get so angry about their internet. I had this one guy yell at me for twenty minutes last week because his Netflix was buffering. He kept saying he paid for high speed and I was personally stealing from him. He lived out in this super rural area, too. Like, you can't live in the middle of a forest and expect gigabit speeds, you know? I actually went camping in a forest once, up in the mountains. It was supposed to be this relaxing weekend, but it rained the entire time. The tent leaked, and all my extra socks got soaked. There is nothing worse than wet socks. We tried to make a fire, but the wood was completely saturated. We ended up just sitting in my friend's car eating cold cans of baked beans and listening to the radio. They were playing this weird marathon of 80s synth-pop... 

But no, I don't just repeat what people say to me in normal life. Just when my boss makes me.

Well, I suppose it's because of what happened at the restaurant. I mean, I didn't think it was that big of a deal at first, but my manager insisted I come see someone. I've been waitressing for years, you know? It's usually second nature to me, the flow of it all, carrying the trays, remembering who had the side salad and who wanted extra ranch. But lately... well, what scared everyone at work is that I started freezing up in the middle of service. Just... stopping. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. Like, the other day, during the lunch rush—which is always crazy, right?—I found myself just standing by the soda station. I was holding the cash drawer key, which I wasn't even supposed to have right then, and I was just repeating table numbers out loud. "Table four, table seven, table nine..." just over and over, instead of actually closing out the checks like I was supposed to be doing. And I couldn't seem to snap out of it right away. My coworker, Sarah, she had to physically tap me on the shoulder to get me to move. She said I looked like a statue. It's just... it's really embarrassing, honestly, and it's making everyone nervous.

Am I aware? I mean... it's hard to say, really. Because, well, you'd think I'd know, right? You'd think if you're standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, with the clinking of the silverware and the kitchen bell ringing—our line cook, Tony, is always ringing that bell, it's so loud, he hits it like three times for every single order just to rush us—you'd think I'd be completely aware of all that noise and chaos. But when I freeze like that... I don't know, I'm really not sure what I'm processing. 

It's almost like I'm there, but I'm not *there*. I don't remember seeing Sarah actually walk up to me. I just remember the sudden feeling of her hand on my shoulder, and it startled me, almost like waking up from a nap you didn't know you were taking. But I wasn't asleep, obviously, I was standing right there by the soda machine, holding that cash drawer key. So I guess... I really don't know if I'm aware of my surroundings or not. It's not like I'm passed out on the floor, but I'm definitely not paying attention to the lunch rush either, which is just so weird for me because I'm usually the one keeping everyone else on track, you know? Like, I'm the one who always remembers that the regulars at table four need extra lemons for their iced tea, and I never drop the ball on that. But during those moments, it's just... I couldn't tell you what was happening right in front of my face.

I mean, I don't think I'm actually forgetting anything, really. It's not like I have amnesia or anything dramatic like you see in those soap operas my mom watches—she's obsessed with them, always has them on in the background, and someone's always getting hit on the head and forgetting their whole life. It's definitely not like that. It's more just... well, like I said, I'm not really sure what I'm taking in during those moments anyway. So it's not that I can't remember what happened, it's more like I wasn't really recording it in the first place, if that makes sense? 

Like, if you asked me what Tony the cook was yelling about while I was standing by the soda machine, I couldn't tell you. But I don't think I *forgot* what he was yelling, I just don't think I heard it at all while I was stuck like that. Because usually, I remember everything. I have to! In my job, if you forget that the guy at table six wanted his dressing on the side, he'll send the whole salad back and then the kitchen gets backed up, and Tony starts slamming pans around, and it throws off the whole rhythm of the shift. I'm usually so sharp with my memory. I can remember orders from regulars who haven't been in for months. But with these... these freezing things... I don't feel like I'm losing memories. I just feel like there's a gap where I wasn't really paying attention to anything except whatever table numbers I was mumbling. So, no, I wouldn't say I can't remember parts of it, because there isn't really anything *to* remember from my end, you know? Just... blank space until Sarah touches my shoulder.

Confused? Well, I wouldn't really use the word confused. I mean, when I think of being confused, I think of, you know, when they change the menu on us without telling us—which management actually did last month, they swapped out the seasonal vegetables and completely changed the POS system layout overnight. *That* was confusing. Everyone was running around trying to figure out where the button for the sweet potato fries went. But after these... these spells... it's not like that. 

It's more just... jarring, I guess? Like I said, when Sarah touched my shoulder, I jumped. It was like I was suddenly just *back*. I knew exactly where I was, I knew I was at the restaurant, I knew I was holding the cash drawer key—even though I still don't know why I grabbed it in the first place—and I knew it was the lunch rush. I wasn't disoriented about my surroundings or who I was or anything like that. I just felt... embarrassed, mostly. And maybe a little frustrated, because I knew I was holding up the line and I had tables waiting. So, no, I don't feel confused like my brain is scrambled. I just feel like I was paused, and then someone hit play again, and I just have to catch up to the speed everyone else is already moving at. But I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing once I'm back. I just get right back to it, or try to, anyway, once the embarrassment wears off a little.

A warning feeling? Hmm. No, I don't think so. I mean, it's not like I get a headache first, or my vision goes blurry, or anything like that. You know how some people say they can feel a thunderstorm coming because their knees ache? My aunt used to say that all the time, she'd sit on the porch and say, "It's gonna pour, my left knee is acting up," and sure enough, twenty minutes later, it would be raining. It's definitely not like that. There's no physical sign or... or weird feeling that tells me it's about to happen. 

It's really just... sudden. One second I'm walking toward the back station to grab extra napkins for table nine—because table nine always asks for extra napkins, it's a family with three little kids and they make such a mess, but they tip well so I don't mind—and the next thing I know, I'm just stuck there, mumbling numbers. I don't feel a shift in my mood, I don't feel dizzy, I don't feel like the room is spinning. I'm just doing my job, going about my shift, trying to keep up with the lunch rush, and then... bam. I'm paused. So, no, I wouldn't say there's any kind of strange warning or premonition or whatever you want to call it. It just sort of sneaks up on me, which honestly makes it even more frustrating because I can't prepare for it or tell someone to cover my section for a minute. It just happens right in the middle of whatever I'm doing.

Repetitive movements? Like... like chewing or picking at things? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I'm already stuck there like a statue, right? It's not like I'm doing a whole routine. I'm just frozen. 

Except for the mumbling, of course, which I already told you about. The table numbers. But my hands? No, they just stay wherever they were. Like when I had that cash drawer key—my hand was just clamped around it. I wasn't fumbling with it or tossing it up in the air or anything. And I definitely wasn't smacking my lips or chewing. I mean, can you imagine? Standing in the middle of a busy restaurant, staring into space, mumbling numbers, and smacking my lips like I'm eating invisible food? It's embarrassing enough just freezing. If I was doing all that extra stuff, Tony would probably throw a spatula at me. 

So, no, my body is just... still. Rigid, almost. It's not like when my cousin gets nervous—she has this awful habit where she picks at her cuticles until they bleed. She does it without even realizing it, especially when we're watching a tense movie or something. I always have to swat her hand away. But this isn't like a nervous habit or a fidget. I'm not fidgeting at all. I'm just completely stopped in my tracks. Like, if I'm holding a tray, the tray just stays there. I'm not tapping my fingers on it or adjusting my grip. It's just... nothing. Just the freezing and the mumbling.

Fallen down? Or shaking? Oh, gosh, no. No, thank goodness. I mean, can you imagine? The floors at the restaurant are already such a hazard on a normal day. They mop them, sure, but they use this cheap, greasy cleaner, and even with those mandatory non-slip black shoes we have to wear—which, by the way, are incredibly uncomfortable, they have absolutely zero arch support and my feet are just screaming by the end of a double shift—people slip and fall all the time. Just last week, one of the bussers went down hard near the dish pit. But during these spells of mine? No, I stay right on my feet. I don't collapse, I don't faint, I don't even lose my balance. If I did, I would have definitely ended up in the hospital by now, because falling in that dining room means you're probably taking a tray of hot soup or a stack of heavy ceramic plates down with you, and that would be a total disaster. 

And shaking? No, definitely not shaking either. Like I was trying to explain a minute ago, I'm just completely still. Like a statue. If I was shaking or trembling, I'd probably drop whatever I was holding. My aunt has this little dog, a tiny Chihuahua mix, and he shakes all over whenever there's a thunderstorm or a loud noise, just his whole body vibrating. It's nothing like that. My body doesn't jerk around or shiver or anything. I just... lock up. I stand there perfectly upright, completely frozen, not moving a single muscle except for my mouth doing that mumbling thing with the numbers. So, yeah, no falling, no shaking, just... standing there stuck in place.

Sleepy? Um, well. I mean, I'm a waitress working double shifts, so I'm pretty much always some level of tired, you know? It's just the nature of the job. You're on your feet all day, running back and forth from the kitchen to the floor, dealing with demanding customers, carrying those heavy trays... by the time I clock out, I'm completely exhausted. 

But unusually sleepy right after one of those freezing spells? No, not really. It's not like I suddenly need to take a nap or anything like that. When it ends, it's just... over. Like somebody finally hit the play button again. I just blink, realize I've been standing there stuck, and then I just have to jump right back into whatever I was doing because, like I said, the lunch rush doesn't wait for anybody. If I got sleepy every time it happened, I wouldn't even make it through my shift. I'd be trying to doze off in the breakroom. And you really can't do that at my restaurant anyway. The breakroom is ridiculously tiny, it barely fits two chairs, and the ice machine is right next to the wall and it is so loud it sounds like an airplane taking off every time it cycles, so nobody really rests in there even if they wanted to. 

So, yeah, back to your question, no sudden exhaustion or sleepiness. I might feel a little flustered or, I don't know, annoyed that it happened again, especially if I think Tony or one of the other servers noticed me just standing there staring into space. But physically? I'm totally awake. My energy level doesn't just drop off a cliff. I just pick up my tray or my notepad, take a breath, and keep moving. So no, no weird sleepiness. Just the regular, everyday exhaustion of the job.

How long do they last? Well, it's hard to say exactly, because when I'm in it, time sort of... I don't know, it feels different. But it's long enough. It's long enough that people notice, and that's the part that really scares everyone at work. I mean, it's not just a quick second where I zone out. It's a whole thing. 

Like, what really freaked everyone out was when I started freezing up right in the middle of a busy service. I'd just be standing there, completely locked up. Or I'd start doing things completely out of order. There was this one time, and this is what really got Tony on my case, I was standing over by the soda station—which is always a chaotic mess anyway, because the Diet Coke syrup is always running out and nobody ever changes the box—and I was just standing there, holding the key to the cash drawer. I was supposed to be closing out checks for my section, right? Because table 12 was waiting to leave and they had theatre tickets. But instead of going to the register, I'm just standing by the soda fountain, clutching this key, and repeating table numbers over and over. "Table 4, table 7, table 12..." Just mumbling them. 

And I was stuck like that for... I don't know, it felt like forever, but Tony said it was a good couple of minutes. Two or three minutes of just standing there, holding a key I wasn't using, not closing the checks, just repeating numbers while the ice machine is roaring next to me. So it's long enough to completely derail what I'm doing and make everyone stare at me like I've lost my mind. It's just so embarrassing, you know? Because I know I have a job to do, and I'm a good waitress, I really am, I can balance four plates on one arm, but when I get stuck like that, I just... I can't do anything until it passes.

Well, honestly, my sleep has just been all over the place lately. It's really frustrating, to be honest with you. Well, that's... that's a heavy question, I guess. It's hard to even say it out loud, to be honest. Um... no, I haven't... I haven't had any actual plans to hurt myself or anything like that. Well, my appetite... you know, I haven't really noticed any big changes there. I mean, I'm still eating. I have to eat, right? Especially with the work I do. Yeah, actually, that's... that's a big part of why I decided I needed to come in and talk to somebody, to be honest. It's like I was saying earlier about that heavy, foggy feeling? It's not just physical exhaustion, it's... my actual head feels foggy. Like my brain is wrapped in thick cotton or something, and I just can't think straight.

I'll walk from Mr. Henderson's living room into his kitchen because I know I need to grab something, maybe a fresh dish towel or a glass of water for him, and I'll get into the kitchen and just stop dead. Just completely blank. I'll stand there looking at the fridge, looking at the counter, and I have absolutely no idea what I walked in there for. I literally have to walk all the way back into the living room and look at him to trigger the memory of what I was about to do. 

And that... that just isn't like me at all. I'm the guy who remembers everyone's schedule, everyone's appointments, who likes what on their sandwich. I usually have a mind like a steel trap because in my line of work, you really can't afford to be scatterbrained. People are relying on you. So having this constant fog, making these little errors, forgetting what I'm doing right in the middle of doing it... it's incredibly frustrating. It makes me feel like I can't trust my own brain right now.

Well, honestly... I don't think I'm moving or talking slower. And as for moving around... I'm still doing the laundry, still getting the meals prepared, still helping them transfer from the bed to the wheelchair. I might feel completely drained on the inside, like I'm running on empty, but on the outside, my body is still doing the motions at the same speed. Well, actually, it hasn't quite been a month. I know I might have made it sound like it's been going on longer, probably just because every single day feels so incredibly long and drawn out right now, but... it was really just about two weeks ago.

He was my mom's younger brother, and they were really close, so when he passed, it just kind of shattered her. And because of what I do for a living—you know, being a care aide, being used to dealing with medical situations and just managing people's needs—my whole family just kind of defaulted to me to handle everything. I had to be the strong one, the one holding it all together. 

I was the one making the calls to the funeral home, driving over to his apartment, packing up decades of his life into these little cardboard boxes, all while trying to make sure my mom was actually eating and sleeping. And I was doing all of that on top of still going to work every day for Mr. Henderson and Mrs. Gable, because I couldn't just abandon my clients. Like I said, they really rely on me. So I was just running on pure adrenaline, I think, just pushing and pushing through the exhaustion to get my family through the service and the burial. 

But then the funeral ended, the relatives went home, everyone went back to their normal routines, and... that's when it hit me. This whole shift really started right after my uncle died, about two weeks ago. Once the immediate crisis was over and I didn't have to be in go-mode anymore, it was like my brain and my body just completely gave out. That's exactly when that heavy, foggy feeling I've been telling you about just settled right over me, and it just hasn't lifted since. So, yeah, it was two weeks ago, not a month, but that was definitely the turning point.

I... gosh, I'm really not sure. I don't think so? Or at least, I haven't really noticed feeling anything like that.

It was shoved way in the back behind this stack of old bowling trophies he had from a league in the 90s, and I just stood there in his kitchen for what felt like an hour, staring at the trophies and the knife, trying to figure out if my mom would want to keep them or if I should put them in the donation pile. 

So, yeah, I haven't really noticed any positive feelings breaking through. It's like I was saying earlier about that fog. The fog just kind of coats everything right now, even the past. When I pull up a memory of him, I don't feel the joy of it. I just feel the heavy, exhausting weight of packing up his apartment, or I just see the funeral director's face, or the stack of cardboard boxes in his living room. I want to feel those warm memories, I really do, but right now... I just don't know. I'm just not feeling it.

Well, no, not really. I mean, you'd think that being around people would help, right? That's what everyone says—you know, "don't isolate yourself, lean on your support system." And I've certainly been around people. Between work and checking on my mom, I'm rarely completely alone. 

Like, just this past Sunday, my sister came into town to check on my mom, and she brought over this massive tray of baked ziti from that Italian place down on 4th Street—the one with the red and white checkered awnings? We used to go there for every single birthday when we were kids, and that ziti is usually my absolute favorite thing in the world. Normally, just the smell of the garlic and the melted mozzarella would instantly put me in a good mood, no matter how bad my day was. And she even brought my nephews, who are usually just a riot. They're seven and nine, and they were running around the living room, building this huge fort out of my mom's couch cushions and couch blankets, just giggling and being kids. 

And I sat there on the recliner, eating the ziti, watching them play, and my sister was trying to tell me this funny story about how her dog got loose in the neighborhood... and I just felt absolutely nothing. The ziti just tasted like cardboard, honestly. I was chewing it, but there was no comfort in it, no enjoyment. And watching the boys... I knew they were being cute, I knew I should be smiling or laughing with my sister, but it was just like I was watching them through a thick pane of glass. I couldn't connect to the warmth of the room at all. 

So, I don't know... I guess the answer is no. Even when I'm doing something that's supposed to be comforting, or I'm surrounded by my family trying to cheer me up, that heavy, empty feeling just doesn't budge. It's like I'm there physically, but the part of me that actually feels the comfort or the connection is just totally switched off right now.

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my brain definitely feels like it's wading through thick mud right now, just with that heavy fog I was talking about, but the actual facts and figures? They're all still locked in there. I haven't forgotten anyone's name or where I live or anything major like that. 

Honestly, with what I do for a living, I really can't afford to let things slip through the cracks, so my brain is kind of trained to hold onto schedules. Like with Mr. Henderson, one of my main clients, he has this very strict medication regimen. He takes his blood pressure pill at exactly 8:00 AM, and then he has a water pill at noon, and if I forget those, it throws his whole day off. And Mrs. Gable has her mobility exercises every Tuesday and Thursday at 1:15 PM sharp. I haven't missed a single one of those, even with everything that's happened over the last couple of weeks. 

And even with my family, I'm the one remembering all the details for my mom right now. I remember the name of the funeral director—Mr. Abernathy, over at the place on Elm Street, right past the old post office—and I've got all my uncle's account passwords written down, but I actually have most of them memorized already just because I've had to log into them so many times to help settle his bills. I can even tell you the exact address of his apartment building, it's 442 West Oak, apartment 3B. 

So, no, the memory part is completely intact. I know exactly where I'm supposed to be, I know my address, I know who everyone is. It's just that going to those appointments and seeing those people feels like I'm dragging a hundred-pound weight behind me. But the information itself? No, I haven't forgotten any of that. I'm still keeping the whole schedule running for everyone, even if I feel totally empty doing it.

It’s definitely there pretty much all day. It’s not just a wave that hits me when I see a picture of him or find something of his in a box. Honestly... lately I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling in my chest. Before I even fully open my eyes, before my brain even has a chance to remember that he's gone or think about the estate stuff, that weight is just already sitting there. 

Like yesterday, my alarm went off at 6:15 AM, just like it always does, and usually I'm up right away, making my coffee—I get this dark French roast that I usually love—but I just laid there for a minute, feeling that emptiness. And it just stays with me the whole day. Like, I can get through my shift, you know? I go over to my clients' houses, I help Mr. Henderson with his meds, I talk to people, I make the polite small talk about the weather or whatever is on the morning news. I do all the things a good aide is supposed to do. But inside? Even when I'm nodding and holding a conversation and doing my job, inside I’m just sad and flat. 

It’s just this constant, dull background noise that doesn't care what I'm doing. I could be driving down the interstate or standing in the grocery store aisle looking at oatmeal, not thinking about my uncle or the funeral at all, and I still just feel that heavy flatness. It's like wearing one of those lead aprons they put on you at the dentist's office, but you have to wear it all day long, from room to room, from client to client. You just carry it everywhere. So, yeah, it's not just when I'm specifically reminded of him. The sadness is just... it's just always there right now, from the second I wake up to the minute I go to bed.
