But I always try to keep a lid on it and just use it to get more stops done on my route. It's not like I'm out of control for that whole time, just... running a little hotter than usual. That's not too bad, is it? Just a few days of being extra productive?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I try really hard to keep a positive attitude, you know? I think it's important to be a cheerful guy, especially for my family and the customers on my route. I'd never want to be a burden or bring everyone else down by moping around for weeks on end. 

Sure, everybody has a bad day here and there, maybe feels a little tired after a long shift, but... two whole weeks of just feeling down and not caring about anything? No, sir. I always make sure to get up, go to work, and take care of my responsibilities. I try to be dependable like that. That's the right way to handle things, isn't it? Just keeping your chin up and pushing through?

Oh, goodness, no. Hospitalized? No, I've never had anything like that happen. I mean, I would never let things get so out of hand that I'd need to be in a hospital. I always make sure I'm taking care of myself and staying out of trouble, you know? 

Like I said, when I get that extra energy, I just put it into my work. I'd never want to cause a scene or make my family worry to the point where they'd think I needed to be locked up somewhere. I'm a responsible guy, I promise. It's just a little extra pep in my step sometimes, nothing that requires a doctor or a hospital bed. That shows I'm handling it okay, right? If I've never had to go to the hospital for it?

I just... I've been having a hard time lately. I feel like I can't settle down. It's like my own skin is too tight or something. I just always feel like I have to jump up and do the next thing, even when I'm completely worn out and know I should just be sitting still.
No... not really. I haven't noticed anything like that. I don't get scared, just... what I mentioned before.
No, I wouldn't say that. I don't get... wired like that for days. It's just a constant feeling, not a special period of time.
No, I... I haven't started taking anything new. It's not from that.

I suppose... yes. Even back in grade school. The teachers used to write on my report cards that I was bright but... careless. I was always losing papers, or... talking out of turn. They had to keep reminding me to stay in my seat and just... finish my work. So... yes. It's always been like that.

Yes... I do. I help with a quilting charity, and... well, if someone gives me three or four things to do, I might start the first one right away. But then... I just wander into another chore. The last steps just never get done.
No... I don't think so. I mean, I worry about things sometimes, like anyone, but... not excessively. Just normal things, I suppose.

Hi. Nice to meet you too. 

I came in today because... well, I just can't stop worrying about everything at once. It's just constant. I'm constantly worrying about my marriage, whether my performance is slipping at work, paying the bills... even the house projects I keep starting and then dropping. I just get stuck worrying about whether I'm basically failing as a husband and a father. It's just taking over everything.

Yeah, it's really hard to stop. I try to control it, but... even when I tell myself to just focus on the code in front of me at work, or try to breathe through a workout, it doesn't work. 

One concern just hooks another. Before I know it, I'm twenty steps ahead, imagining a bad review turning into losing my job, and then my family being worse off because of me. I just can't shut it down once it starts.

It's been going on for about nine months now. I think it really started when the cloud migration project at work ramped up, and right around the same time, the arguments at home started becoming a regular thing. Since then, it's just been constant.

Well, I mean... those things definitely kicked it off, but no, it's not just tied to that anymore. 

Like I said, I worry about everything now. Even if work is going okay for a day, or things are quiet at home, my brain just finds something else. I'll worry about the bills, or those house projects, or just... whether I'm doing enough in general. It's like the worry just spread to every part of my life, even the stuff that isn't actually a problem right now.

No, not really. I don't have any... rituals or anything like that. I mean, I don't count things or have a specific routine I have to do to make the anxiety stop, if that's what you mean. 

I mostly just sit there and let the thoughts run, or I try to force myself to look at my screen and keep coding. But there's no repetitive action or mental checklist I'm doing to try and cancel the worry out. It just stays stuck in my head.

No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. I mean, I'm definitely exhausted from all the worrying, and that can drag me down, but I don't feel sad or... hopeless, if that makes sense. It's just the constant anxiety that's the issue, not feeling down.

Yeah, definitely. I feel wound tight almost all day. It's like... my shoulders are just locked up, and I'm constantly bracing for something bad to happen. 

And sitting still is really hard. I catch myself pacing around the house between work meetings. Even when I try to do something I enjoy, like going to chess club, I can't just sit there. I end up tapping the pieces or fidgeting the whole time because sitting still just feels impossible right now.

No, I wouldn't say so. I know I mentioned earlier that I feel exhausted, but that's more of a mental drain by the end of the day from being so tense. As far as just getting tired easily physically during the day... no, I haven't really noticed that. If anything, I'm usually too wired to feel sleepy.

Yeah, definitely. It's actually been a real problem at work lately. During sprint planning or when I'm doing code reviews, I'll catch myself reading the same design note three or four times. And I still end up missing details because... well, part of my mind is just off somewhere else. I'll be sitting there, but in my head, I'm calculating what I might have forgotten at home, or worrying about how badly the next argument with someone is going to go. It's like I just can't keep my focus on what's right in front of me.

Yeah, sleep has been really rough. Most nights, I'll get into bed and I'm just physically exhausted, but my brain... it just won't shut off. I just lie there running through all the risks on my current project at work, or worrying about money, or agonizing over something I said to my wife earlier. 

And then, even when I finally do manage to drift off, I almost always wake up around 3 or 4 in the morning. Once I'm up, that's it. I can't get back to sleep because I'm already lying there rehearsing all the problems I have to deal with the next day. It's just a constant cycle.

No, not really. I know I mentioned agonizing over an argument with my wife earlier, but that's... well, it's not really because I'm snapping at her or feeling angry. It's more about me just being overwhelmed with worry. As far as feeling irritable or short-tempered in general, no, I haven't really noticed that. I'm mostly just anxious.

No, I don't think so. I still enjoy the things I usually like doing. I mean, sometimes it's a little hard to fully relax and just get into a game or a project because my mind is still racing with all the stuff I'm worried about, but... the actual interest is definitely still there. I haven't lost the desire to do my hobbies or anything like that.

I... I don't really think so. I'd like to say yes, but honestly, probably not. 

It seems like even when things are actually going fine at work, and there aren't any immediate issues at home, my mind just finds something else to latch onto. It's like my brain just always needs a problem to fixate on. If it's not a software deployment, it'll be, you know, worrying about the car breaking down, or a bill, or just something completely random. 

So... no, I don't think it would just disappear. I'd probably just shift to worrying about whatever is next on the list.

Well, it’s good to meet you too, Doc. I, uh, I guess I'm here because of this thing I've been noticing lately. I spend a good amount of time down at the local art museum these days, just helping out and keeping busy now that I'm not working anymore. It's a great place, really wonderful people. But lately, we've been getting ready for this next art walk. It's a pretty big deal for us, lots of local artists, a whole mapped-out route through the downtown area, so there's a lot of coordination and planning involved. 

And what brings me in is that people at the museum, the other folks helping out, they will be talking right to me about the plans for this art walk. I mean, they are standing right there, maybe two feet away, and I’ll be looking right at them, making eye contact, nodding along, thinking I'm completely engaged in the conversation. But then... I don't know, it's like a radio station just cuts out to static in my head for a minute. I'll suddenly realize I completely missed the entire middle of what they just said. The beginning is there, the end is there, but the actual meat of the instructions is just gone. 

And then I have to stop them, which is always awkward, and say, "Hey, I'm so sorry, can you run that by me again?" It's getting a bit embarrassing, to be honest with you, having to constantly ask people to repeat themselves when I was looking right at them the whole time. You start to feel like people think you don't care about what they're saying, but I do! I really do. So I figured I should probably come in and talk to somebody about it, just to see what's going on.

No, no, it's not that. My hearing is actually pretty darn good for a guy my age. I mean, I had it checked a few years back when they had one of those free clinics at the community center, and the fella there told me my ears were doing just fine. So it's not the volume, and they don't sound muffled or like they're underwater or anything like that. 

Take Martha, for instance—she’s the volunteer coordinator down at the museum, wonderful lady, used to be a high school drama teacher, I think. Anyway, she has this really booming, theatrical voice. She really projects, you know? When she's standing right next to me talking about the city permits for the food trucks or where we're going to put the street barricades for the art walk, she is loud and clear. Crystal clear. You could probably hear her from the parking lot. 

But even with her, I'll be listening, and the sound is going into my ears perfectly fine, loud as day, but then... it's like my brain just decides to take a little coffee break. I hear the noise she's making, I can hear the tone of her voice, but the actual words, the meaning of what she's trying to tell me, just completely slips right past me. So, no, it's definitely not that they sound faint or unclear. It's just... I don't know, a disconnect somewhere after the sound gets in.

Well, now that you mention it, yes, I suppose I have been. And it's funny you ask, because it's been driving me absolutely up the wall lately, especially down at the museum. You see, since I'm helping out with this art walk, they've given me a few extra little responsibilities. Nothing too crazy, but I'm sort of the unofficial photographer for the prep work, just snapping pictures of the setup for the community newsletter. 

So I have this digital camera they let me use, and I'm always taking the battery out to charge it. I'll tell myself, "Okay, I'm putting the camera battery right here on the breakroom counter, nice and safe, so I don't forget it." But then I turn around, go talk to Martha or somebody, come back, and I can't for the life of me remember where I put it. 

And it's not just the battery, either. It's the name tags for the volunteers, too. We have these little plastic clip-on ones, and I'm supposed to keep track of them. The other day I had them, and I also had this big manila envelope with all the sign-up sheets for the different volunteer shifts. I always do this thing where I set them down somewhere safe—you know how you do that? You think, "This is a perfectly safe spot, I couldn't possibly lose this." Well, I do. I’m always putting down the camera battery, the name tags, or that envelope with the sign-up sheets somewhere safe, and then I end up spending half the morning just wandering around the museum, poking my head into the gallery, checking the front desk, just completely retracing my steps trying to find them. 

It's ridiculous, honestly. I'll spend an hour looking for something I swear I just had in my hands five minutes ago. I eventually find them, usually in some spot that makes absolutely no sense, like on top of the mini-fridge or next to the mop bucket, but it just eats up so much of my day. So, yeah, I guess outside of the conversation thing, I have been pretty forgetful with my hands, so to speak. It's just frustrating to lose so much time to it, you know?

Well, as far as the house goes, paying the bills and the medications and all that... no, not so much. I mean, the bills are mostly on that automatic pay thing through the bank these days anyway, which my daughter set up for me a couple of years back. She said it would save on stamps, and she was right about that! And as for my medication, I only

...take a little pill for my blood pressure, just the one in the morning. I keep the bottle right next to the coffee maker, so I see it when I'm getting my morning cup ready. It's part of the routine, you know? Get up, put the grounds in the filter, pour the water, take the pill, wait for the coffee. So, no, I've never forgotten to take it or taken it twice or anything dangerous like that. 

And the bills, like I was saying, it's all automated. My daughter, Sarah—she's a financial planner over in the next county—she came over one Sunday afternoon with her laptop and just spent a good two hours getting everything set up. The electric, the water, the property taxes, even my subscription to the woodworking magazine I get every month. She linked it all up to my checking account. She said, "Dad, this way you don't even have to think about it." And she was absolutely right. It just comes right out. I get an email receipt, which I usually don't even open, to be honest. 

So, no, as far as the important stuff at home, the medications and the bills and keeping the lights on, I'm doing just fine. It's really just the little things, like the camera battery or the name tags down at the museum, that seem to slip my mind. The big things, the things that keep the wheels turning, so to speak, those are all perfectly fine. I haven't messed up any of that.

Well, no, not really. I mean, like I said about the bills, Sarah did set that up, but that was just her being helpful, you know? It wasn't because I couldn't do it. I used to sit down every first of the month with my checkbook and a roll of stamps at the kitchen table. It was a whole routine. I'd have my coffee, maybe a slice of toast with that marmalade I like—the thick cut kind, not the jelly—and I'd go through the stack. But she just thought the computer way was more efficient. 

But as for needing help because I can't manage? No, no. I still do my own grocery shopping every Tuesday morning. I like to go early, right when they open, before it gets crowded and they haven't picked over all the good produce. I still cook my own meals, keep the house tidy enough for my liking. I mow the lawn, although I did hire the neighbor's boy to do the edging last summer, but that's just because my knees don't like all that bending anymore, not because my brain couldn't figure out the weed whacker! 

So, I'm still very much my own man, taking care of my own business. It's just... it's really just those little things, those momentary lapses where I put something down and poof, it's gone from my mind. But the day-to-day living, the actual running of my life? No, I haven't needed anyone to step in and take over for me. I'm doing all right there.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, my vocabulary is just as good as it ever was. I've always been a reader, you know. Even back when I was working at the plant, I'd bring a paperback with me to read in the breakroom while the other guys were playing cards or complaining about the foreman. Mostly history, biographies, that sort of thing. I just finished a fascinating one on the building of the Brooklyn Bridge, actually. The engineering involved in that, back in those days, it's just incredible. 

So, no, the words are all still up there in the old filing cabinet. Sometimes, sure, I might pause for a second to think of the best way to phrase something, but that's just because I like to be precise. I don't like to just babble, I want to make sure I'm saying exactly what I mean. Like the other day, I was talking to my neighbor, Tom, about his new truck, and I wanted to ask him about the torque, not just the horsepower. There's a difference, you know. Horsepower is how fast you hit the wall, torque is how far you take the wall with you! 

But as far as forgetting common words, or calling a spoon a fork, or just standing there with my mouth open unable to think of what to say? No, nothing like that. The words come to me just fine. It's just the keys, or the battery, or where I put my glasses when they're sitting right on top of my head. The talking part, the words themselves, those are working just perfectly.

Well, no... no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, I don't really get all that worried or tense these days anyway. I mean, back when I was working at the plant, sure, especially if we had a big order to push out and one of the machines went down, you'd feel your blood pressure go up. You'd get that tight feeling in your chest. But now? Now I'm retired, I've got all the time in the world. I'm usually pretty relaxed. 

Take last Thursday, for example. Beautiful afternoon, not a cloud in the sky. I was out in the garage, just tinkering with this birdhouse I'm building for the backyard—I'm using cedar, by the way, because pine just rots too fast if you don't treat it right, and I don't want to be painting the thing every two years. Anyway, I was feeling great, just whistling along to the classic rock station on the radio, totally at peace with the world. I set down my measuring tape on the workbench to grab a handful of brad nails, turned back around, and... poof. The tape was just gone. 

I spent a good twenty minutes looking for it, and I wasn't stressed or worried in the slightest before that happened. I finally found it sitting right inside the roof of the birdhouse! So, no, it's not nerves or being tense. It just happens completely out of the blue, even when I'm as calm as a cucumber. It doesn't seem to matter what kind of mood I'm in, the little things just slip away from me all the same.

Well... you know, Sarah hasn't said anything directly. She's a good girl, she doesn't want to make her old man feel bad, I suppose. But the folks at the museum... that's a little different. I wouldn't say they've sat me down and had an intervention or anything dramatic like that. But, well, I've noticed a shift. 

I used to be the one who organized the schedule for the volunteer docents, making sure we had coverage for the weekend rushes and the school field trips. It was a bit of a puzzle, but I enjoyed it. I'd sit there with my big wall calendar and a handful of different colored highlighters—yellow for mornings, green for afternoons, pink for the special exhibits—and I'd get it all sorted. But lately... well, a few months ago, Margaret—she's the volunteer coordinator, lovely woman, makes a fantastic rhubarb pie—she just sort of quietly took that over. She said they were moving to a new digital system and it would just be easier if she handled it from her desk. I didn't argue, but... I know I'd double-booked a couple of folks the month before, and I completely forgot to schedule anyone for the Impressionist wing during a Tuesday morning senior tour. 

And the art walks... I used to love leading those. We have this beautiful sculpture garden out back, and I had this whole route planned out. I'd talk about the bronzes, the way the patina changes with the weather, the history of the artists... I had all these wonderful little anecdotes. But the last couple of times I tried to do it, I just... I lost my train of thought halfway through explaining the casting process for the Rodin replica. I was standing there, looking at this group of eager faces, and I just couldn't remember where I was going with the story. I had to sort of laugh it off and move to the next piece, but I felt like a fool. 

So, I haven't really volunteered to lead one of those in a while. I just tell them my knees are acting up and I'd rather stay inside at the information desk. It's easier that way. I just don't feel that same confidence anymore, you know? It's like I'm walking on thin ice and I'm just waiting to hear a crack. So, they haven't explicitly said, "Hey, your brain's getting fuzzy," but they've definitely started shifting the load, and I can't really blame them.

Lost? Oh, no, definitely not. I've got a built-in compass, always have. Even when I was a kid, growing up over on the east side—before they put the new highway in and tore down half the old neighborhood, mind you—I knew every alley, every shortcut, every dead end. I used to ride my Schwinn all over the county and never once had to ask for directions. 

And it’s still like that today. I know this town like the back of my hand. I mean, sure, they keep building these new subdivisions out past the old county line, all these winding streets with names like "Whispering Pines" or "Meadowbrook Lane" that all look exactly the same, but even then, I can figure it out. If I'm going to the grocery store, or the hardware store, or the museum, or over to Sarah's house... I could drive there blindfolded. Well, not literally, obviously, that would be terrible, but you know what I mean. 

Just the other day, actually, they had a detour set up on Elm Street because of a water main break. Huge mess, water everywhere, guys in hard hats standing around looking at a hole in the ground. The detour signs were completely confusing, pointing people down a one-way street the wrong way—typical city planning, right? But I didn't even need the signs. I just took a quick left on Maple, cut through the alley behind the old movie theater—the one that closed down back in '98 and is just sitting there rotting, which is a real shame because they used to have the best popcorn—and I was back on the main road in two minutes flat. 

So, no, getting lost isn't an issue at all. My internal map is perfectly intact. It's just the little things right in front of me that go missing, like my glasses or that tape measure I told you about. But as far as knowing where I am or how to get where I'm going, I'm sharp as a tack. I've never once found myself sitting at an intersection wondering which way is home.

Well, yes and no. I mean, I suppose it might have been creeping up on me before then, but there’s a very specific point where it really started becoming a genuine problem. If I trace it back... it’s been noticeably causing trouble for about two years and four months. I know the exact timeline because, well, it was right after my friend Arthur passed away. 

Arthur and I, we were sort of the dynamic duo down at the museum. We handled all the community liaison duties together. He was a retired accountant—wore these little wire-rimmed glasses, always had a pocket protector, real classic type—so he loved keeping track of the spreadsheets and the fine print. I was the one who liked going out and talking to the schools, setting up the big group tours, you know, the social stuff. We had this perfect rhythm going for years. 

But then Arthur died. Just totally unexpected, a real shock to all of us. And after he passed, I just... well, I couldn't

Well, depressed... that's a strong word, isn't it? I mean, I was sad, of course. Terribly sad. Arthur was a good man, a fixture in my life. You don't just lose someone you've spent every Tuesday and Thursday with for a decade and not feel a profound sense of loss. I missed him terribly. I missed his dry sense of humor, the way he'd always complain about the coffee in the breakroom but drink three cups anyway. 

But depressed? Like, couldn't get out of bed, pulling the shades down, crying all day kind of depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I still got up, I still made my oatmeal—steel-cut, mind you, I never touch that instant stuff, it turns to absolute mush—and I still went down to the museum. I tried to keep the routine going, because that's what you do, right? You put one foot in front of the other. 

It was just... the joy was sort of sucked out of it for a while. The museum felt hollow without him sitting at his desk, tapping his pen on his clipboard. But I didn't feel that heavy, dark cloud that people talk about when they say they're depressed. I was just grieving an old friend. It was more of a lonely feeling than a depressed feeling, if that makes sense. I just felt a bit adrift without my anchor there to handle all the paperwork while I did the talking. So, no, not depressed most days. Just... adjusting to a new, quieter normal, I suppose.

Repeat stories? No, no, I don't think so. I mean... well, if you were to ask my sister, Martha—she lives out in Dayton now, moved there back in, oh, it must have been 2004 when her husband got transferred with the tire company, which is a whole other saga let me tell you—she might tell you I tell the same stories over and over. But that's not because I forgot I told them! It's just because they're good stories, you know? 

Like the one about the time a family of raccoons got into the museum's basement and Arthur and I had to chase them out with push brooms before the third-grade field trip from Lincoln Elementary arrived. I tell that one all the time. But I know exactly who I've told it to. I'll even say, "Martha, I know I've told you this," but I tell it anyway because I just enjoy the memory of it, and frankly, she needs a good laugh these days with her bad knees acting up. 

But as far as genuinely forgetting that I just asked a question? Or telling you a story and then, I don't know, twenty minutes later telling it again because my brain just wiped the slate clean? No, absolutely not. My memory for conversations is actually quite sharp. If I ask you what time the hardware store closes, and you tell me six o'clock, I lock that in. I'm not going to come back ten minutes later and ask you the exact same thing. 

It's really just the physical items, the little objects right in front of me, like that tape measure I was telling you about earlier, that give me grief. But I keep track of what I've said to people. You really have to when you do community liaison work, right? You can't go pitching the same middle school principal the exact same field trip package two days in a row, they'd think you were completely off your rocker! So no, I don't have that problem at all. My conversations stay right up here where they belong.

Well, planning... no, I wouldn’t say that’s an issue at all. I haven’t noticed any real change in how I put things together or map things out. I’ve always been a fairly methodical fellow when it comes to knowing what needs doing and in what order. I mean, Arthur was the one with the color-coded spreadsheets, sure, but I still had to organize all the actual logistics for the school groups, making sure the buses had a place to park and the docents were all at their stations. 

And even now, at home, I keep a very tight ship. Take my Wednesday routine, for example. I wake up, make my steel-cut oats—like I mentioned before—and then I have a very specific system for the errands. Hardware store first, because old man Henderson gets his deliveries on Tuesday afternoons, so Wednesday morning is when the shelves are fully stocked with those specific brass screws I like for the birdhouses I build. Then the post office, then the grocer. I write it all down on a little yellow legal pad. Always yellow, the white paper just glares too much in the kitchen light, I find. 

So, no, organizing the steps of a task or planning out my week, that hasn't slipped at all. I still know exactly how to get from A to B to C without getting things muddled. If anything, since Arthur passed, I’ve had to be a bit more rigid about my planning just to make sure the museum tours don’t fall apart without him double-checking my work. I sit down every Sunday evening after dinner—usually just a nice piece of baked cod and some green beans—and I map out the whole week. So the planning part of my brain is working just as well as it did twenty years ago, I assure you. It's really just the... well, like I said, setting down the tape measure and it vanishing into thin air, that sort of thing. But the actual planning of a project? No, no trouble there whatsoever.

Finances? Oh, no, not at all. My finances are... well, they're quite simple, really, but I keep them in perfect order. I've always been very particular about my money. I suppose that comes from growing up when I did, you know, my parents lived through the Depression, so they drilled it into me: "Watch the pennies and the dollars take care of themselves." 

I still balance my checkbook by hand, every single Friday morning right after breakfast. I sit at the little desk in the corner of the living room—the one by the window where the morning light comes in just right—and I go through every receipt from the week. The hardware store, the grocer, the electric bill. I check it against the bank statement that comes in the mail. I don't trust any of this online banking nonsense. My nephew, Steven—he's the one who works in IT down in Columbus—he's always trying to get me to set up an app on my phone for the bank. He says, "Uncle, it's so much easier, you just look at the screen." And I tell him, "Steven, if I can't hold the paper and see the ink, I don't trust the numbers." 

So no, I haven't been making mistakes with the checkbook. The math is always right. Sometimes it takes me a moment to find my reading glasses before I sit down to do it, or I'll misplace the specific blue pen I like to use for the ledger—it has to be blue ink, black just looks too severe on the page—but once I sit down and actually do the arithmetic? Perfect. To the penny. I haven't bounced a check since 1982, and that was only because the dealership took three weeks to cash the check for the down payment on my old Ford Fairmont, and I had forgotten to carry the balance over to the next page of the register. But since then? Absolutely flawless. So, no trouble with the finances whatsoever.

Stopped doing things? Well... I suppose if I’m being completely honest with myself—and with you, of course, which is why I’m here—there have been a few changes down at the museum. I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped going entirely, I’m still very much a presence there, but... well, the museum group has had to quietly shift some of the planning pieces away from me. 

It started maybe a few months back. Susan—she’s the new volunteer coordinator, a lovely woman, moved here from Peoria, makes a truly spectacular rhubarb pie for our seasonal bake sales—she started stepping in. She’d say, "Oh, let me handle the vendor calls this time," or "Why don't I take care of organizing the docent clipboards?" And at first, I thought she was just being neighborly, you know, trying to ease my load since Arthur isn't around to help me keep the desk tidy anymore. But then I realized they were doing it because I kept misplacing the physical files, or setting down the contact sheets and losing them under a pile of brochures. They didn't make a big fuss about it, they just quietly took those responsibilities over. And I have to admit, it stings a little bit. I’ve managed those logistics since 2008! 

And then... well, there are the art walks. I used to lead the downtown architectural art walks every second Saturday of the month, rain or shine. We’d start at the old courthouse, walk down Elm Street, and I'd point out the Art Deco detailing on the old post office—it's a fascinating building, really, built in 1933, they used a very specific Indiana limestone that just glows in the late afternoon sun. But lately... I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to. 

I’d be standing there in front of a group of fifteen eager people, and I'd realize I'd completely misplaced my telescopic pointer, or I couldn't find the binder with the historical reference photos that I literally just had in my hands two minutes prior. I'd be patting down my pockets, looking around the pavement, getting all flustered while everyone just stared at me. It just got to be too embarrassing. So, I told the board my knees were acting up—which isn't entirely a lie, the damp weather does get to them in the mornings—and I stepped back from leading. It’s a terrible shame. I really do miss it. I even had a special pair of walking shoes just for those tours, New Balance, very supportive arches. But yes, to answer your question, I suppose I have had to give up a few of the things I used to run all on my own.

Help with daily life tasks? Oh, heavens no. No, no, I am completely self-sufficient when it comes to the day-to-day running of the house. I mean, I know I was just saying how the museum folks stepped in with the clipboards and the phone calls, but that’s volunteer work, that’s a different beast entirely. Here at home? Absolutely not. I don't need anyone coming in to cook for me or help me, you know, manage my chores or anything of that sort. 

I still do all my own laundry, for instance. Tuesdays are laundry days. I separate the whites and the darks meticulously, always have. I still use that powdered detergent, the one in the big orange box, because the liquid stuff just gets everywhere and leaves a terrible sticky ring on the washing machine lid. Arthur used to just throw everything in together on whatever temperature the dial was stuck on—drove me absolutely up the wall, bless his heart. But I have my system. And I do my own grocery shopping, I cook my own meals... like that baked cod I mentioned, and I make a wonderful roasted chicken on Sundays with carrots and those little red potatoes, the waxy ones that hold their shape in the oven. 

I keep the house spotless, too. Now, I might... well, I might misplace the feather duster for twenty minutes while I'm in the middle of doing it, mind you, and I might eventually find it sitting on top of the refrigerator for some completely inexplicable reason, but I still get the dusting done all by myself! I don't need a home aide or my nephew Steven coming over to babysit me. I'm only 63, after all. I can still manage my own life and my own house just fine. It's really just the losing things that's the bother, the... the objects themselves wandering off, as it feels. But the actual doing of the daily tasks? No, I don't need a lick of help with any of that.

Hi. Good to meet you too. I came in because... well, I just can’t shut my brain off anymore. 

It usually starts with one small concern, like a client not responding to a message. But then, within minutes, I’m completely convinced I’m going to lose the contract. And from there my mind just spirals—I start thinking I'll fall behind on my divorce payments, and that I'll never get back to a real leadership role. It just keeps going like that, and I can't seem to stop it.

Yeah, it's... it's definitely not just work. It's really everything. My mind just keeps jumping around. 

I'll go from stressing out about my contract work to panicking over the mortgage payments. And then... well, then I'll start worrying about my reputation, like whether people in the Bethesda tech circles think I’m damaged goods now. It's exhausting. Even something small, like a delayed email from a recruiter... it can honestly feel like proof that my whole career is closing down. So, yeah, it hits pretty much every part of my life right now.

No, I wouldn't say I have panic attacks or anything like that. It's not a sudden spike of fear that hits me out of nowhere. It's more of a constant, low-level dread that just runs in the background all the time. It builds up and spirals, like I said, but it's not like a sudden, intense episode that peaks in a few minutes. It's just... always there.

Yeah, I guess there was a starting point. It really kicked off when I was fired from my job... that was about thirteen months ago. I figured the stress would pass once I got some income flowing again, but... it never really let up, even after I landed this contract work. It just kind of settled in and stayed.

No, not really. I mean, I'm definitely stressed and worn out from all the worrying, but I wouldn't say I feel depressed or down. It's not like a sadness... it's just this constant tension and fear about everything that could go wrong. So, no, I don't think I'm depressed.

Yeah, definitely. Like I mentioned, it started about thirteen months ago, and... well, it's been pretty much every single day since then. So, yes, definitely more days than not. Honestly, it's a rare day when I'm not worrying about something.

Hey, yeah, good to meet you too. Thanks for fitting me in. So, look, I’m not usually the type of guy to come sit in a doctor's office, you know? I’ve always just powered through things. I mean, I didn’t even finish high school, just got straight to work, built my business from the ground up, and now I’m the CEO. So I'm used to handling a lot on my plate and just dealing with it. 

But what made me finally come in today is that... well, for the past year or so, it’s just been getting ridiculous. The absolute smallest things are throwing me off, and it's driving me crazy. I'll be sitting at my desk trying to review something important, and my phone will give that tiny little half-second buzz—not even a call, just a buzz from some useless app notification—and boom, my focus is completely gone. Or, you know, my office has these big glass walls. I thought it was a great idea for company culture, transparency, all that. But now, if somebody just walks past my office heading to the breakroom, I’m watching them, wondering what they're working on, and I've completely lost my place. 

And it’s not even just stuff happening around me, either. It’s my own head. I’ll be sitting there, trying to work, and suddenly I’ll have this totally random thought about my in-laws—like, some offhand comment my wife's dad made at a barbecue three weeks ago—and before I can even stop myself, I’m off down this mental rabbit hole and completely pulled off what I was doing. It just rips me right out of my work before I can even hit the brakes, and I just can't seem to get a handle on it lately.

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because... well, I haven't thought about my school days in a long time. Like I said, I got out of there as soon as I could and just started working. But looking back... yeah. Yeah, this actually was around when I was a kid, too. I mean, it was a whole thing. My teachers were just constantly, and I mean constantly, moving my seat. It was like a game of musical chairs but just for me. They’d put me in the back, then I’d be too distracting, so they’d move me right up to the front, literally touching the teacher's desk, thinking that would fix it. 

But it didn't really matter where they put me, because I just... I talked way too much. I'd talk to the kid next to me, the kid behind me, whoever would listen, really. I just always had something to say. And I could never just stay put. I'd just get up without asking. I wouldn't even think about it, I'd just suddenly be out of my chair walking to the pencil sharpener or going to look at something on the bulletin board while the teacher was right in the middle of a lesson. They hated that. 

And the other thing that drove them absolutely up the wall was that I would just blurt things out. A teacher would be standing there, halfway through asking a question to the class, setting up a whole math problem or something, and before they could even finish getting the words out, I was already shouting out the answer. Or just a comment. Whatever popped into my head. It was like I couldn't hold it in for even a second to let them finish the sentence. So... yeah, I guess the more I think about it, I was definitely a handful back then with all that. It just felt like I had this motor running that I couldn't shut off.

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm a high-energy guy, right? You don't build a company from nothing without having some drive. I'm always on the go, always thinking about the next quarter, the next product launch, dealing with vendors, managing my team... it's just non-stop. So I guess you could say I'm always a little wired, just by the nature of the job. But not in some weird, unusual way that lasts for days where I'm suddenly, I don't know, bouncing off the walls more than my normal baseline. 

Like, last week, we had this massive pitch to a new investor group, and yeah, I was pumped up. I stayed late at the office three nights in a row, drinking probably way too much espresso, just tweaking the slide deck and making sure every single financial projection was bulletproof. My wife kept texting me, asking when I was coming home, and I just couldn't pull myself away because I had that adrenaline going. But that's just business, you know? That's just doing what it takes to close the deal. It wasn't some strange phase where I felt completely out of control or anything like that. Once the pitch was over—we nailed it, by the way—I went right back to my normal level of busy. So, no, nothing like what you're describing, just the usual hustle.

Well, yeah, actually, now that you mention it... remember how I brought up my father-in-law earlier? The whole barbecue thing? Yeah, so, it’s not just a one-off comment. It’s been this whole massive, ongoing ordeal. I'd say this whole thing—my focus just being completely shot and noticeably harder to manage—it's been going on for about a year and two months now. 

And I know exactly how long it's been because that’s exactly when this huge conflict with my in-laws really started blowing up and just completely taking over our family life. Like, they've always been a little demanding, sure, always had opinions, but a little over a year ago, it just escalated. They started getting way too involved in how my wife and I are running our household, questioning my work hours, making these little passive-aggressive comments about how much time I spend at the office. Which, by the way, you don't become a CEO by working nine to five, and I've tried explaining this to them a hundred times, but it just doesn't compute. 

So it created this constant, heavy tension. My wife is stressed out about it, which obviously stresses me out, and then I'll be sitting at my desk trying to look at a P&L statement, and instead of doing my job, my brain is just suddenly replaying some stupid argument we had in their driveway fourteen months ago. It’s just... it’s exhausting, honestly. It’s like the volume on all the distractions just got cranked all the way up right around that time, and I just haven't been able to tune any of it out since. It's just bleeding into my work, my headspace, everything.

No, no, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier in general. I mean, look, as a CEO, you have to anticipate problems, right? You have to look down the road and see where the potholes are. So sure, I think about supply chain issues, or whether a competitor is going to undercut us, or if inflation is going to mess with our margins. But that's just strategic planning. That's just part of the job. It's not like I'm sitting around biting my nails about every little thing in the world. 

The in-law thing, though, that's different. That's personal, and it's in my house, and it affects my wife, so yeah, that takes up a lot of mental real estate. But outside of that specific mess, and just the normal day-to-day pressure of running a company, I'm not really losing sleep over a bunch of random other things. I don't sit there worrying about my health or the news or if I left the stove on or whatever. I'm too busy for that kind of worry, honestly. I've got a business to run and a team of forty people relying on me to make payroll, so my focus—when I can actually get it to cooperate—is pretty much locked on the immediate fires I need to put out, not just free-floating anxiety about everything under the sun.

Yeah, all the time. It's actually a huge problem, especially when I'm not the one running the show. Like, if I'm at work pacing around the boardroom, that's fine, it looks dynamic, right? But put me in a situation where I'm just supposed to sit there and be quiet? Forget it. 

Like, take family dinners, for example. My wife loves these big, sit-down Sunday dinners. We get the nice plates out, the whole nine yards. And I love my family, I really do, but sitting there for an hour, an hour and a half, just making small talk while we eat roast chicken... it's torture. Honestly, it feels like there is this actual, physical motor running inside my chest, just humming away, telling me to get up, move, do something. I end up bouncing my leg under the table so hard I shake the glassware, or I'm constantly getting up to refill water glasses or clear plates before people are even done eating just so I have an excuse to be on my feet. 

And it's not just at home, either. I got roped into being on this volunteer committee for our church—which, don't even get me started on how inefficiently those meetings are run. We sit in these little folding chairs in the basement for two hours every Tuesday night, going over the budget for the bake sale or whatever. And I'm sitting there, and I literally cannot keep my hands still. I'm clicking my pen until the guy next to me gives me a look, or I'm tearing my styrofoam coffee cup into tiny little pieces, or I'm checking my phone under the table. I just have this overwhelming urge to be doing something, anything, other than just sitting there. It's like my body physically rejects the idea of being stationary for more than ten minutes unless I'm dead asleep.

Emotional distress? I mean... no, I wouldn't use that word. "Distress" makes it sound like I'm, I don't know, sitting in the dark crying about it or something. It’s not like that at all. It’s more just... extreme, mind-numbing frustration. 

Because, look, I’m not heartbroken that my father-in-law doesn't get me. The guy worked a comfortable middle-management job for thirty-five years, punched a clock, went home. Which is fine! Respectable. But he has absolutely zero concept of what it takes to build a company from nothing. I mean, I left high school in the eleventh grade. I didn't have a safety net, I didn't have a diploma to fall back on. I had to hustle, I had to fight for every single inch of ground I have to get to where I am today. So I don't exactly value his opinion on my work-life balance, you know? Emotionally, his approval means absolutely nothing to me. I'm not distressed by the lack of it. 

But what it *does* do is create this incredibly annoying, constant friction. It’s like... it's like a mosquito buzzing right in your ear when you're trying to read a complicated contract. You aren't emotionally devastated by the mosquito, right? You’re just intensely irritated because it won't go away and it’s completely breaking your concentration. That’s what this is. I just get so fed up with the sheer audacity of them coming into my house, drinking my wine, and making these passive-aggressive little jabs about how I'm on my phone too much. 

My wife gets emotional about it, sure, because they're her parents, and I hate seeing her upset. That part bothers me, obviously, because I'm protective of her. But for me personally? No deep emotional trauma here. I'm not depressed over it. I just want the noise to stop. I just want to be able to focus on the things that actually matter, like scaling my business and providing for my family, without this constant, ridiculous peanut gallery chiming in every five minutes and completely derailing my train of thought. So yeah, annoyance? Off the charts. But emotional distress? No, definitely not.

Well, nice to meet you too. I guess I'm here because I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting. Important stuff, you know? Like my heart follow-up appointments, or remembering to call the clinic back. 

Speaking of that clinic, they have this absolute racket they play for their hold music. It’s this smooth jazz saxophone that just loops every thirty seconds. It drives me up the wall, but it actually reminds me of this little club my buddy Lou used to drag me to back in the 80s. Lou played the trumpet, actually. Not professionally, but he was pretty good. We used to go down there on Tuesdays... wait, maybe it was Thursdays? They had 50-cent wings on Thursdays. 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, forgetting things. Yeah, it's not just the doctors. Like the other day, I went over to help my neighbor with a repair job on his back deck, and I showed up without any of the right tools! I was standing there empty-handed. Just completely slipped my mind. So, yeah, that's what brings me in.

Bills and medications? Uh, I'm not really sure, I haven't really noticed any big issues with that, I guess. I just kind of toss the mail on the kitchen counter when it comes. 

Speaking of the mail, they completely changed our route times recently. We used to get it right at 11 AM, like clockwork. Now it's just whenever they feel like it. The regular guy, Gary, he retired a few months back. Great guy. He used to drive this old Chevy Nova on his days off. Beautiful car, cherry red. I had a buddy in high school with a Nova, and we used to take it down to the lake on weekends. We'd fish for bass for hours. Never caught much, but it was a good time, you know? I haven't been fishing in years, though. I should really get my old tackle box out of the garage... but man, that garage is an absolute disaster area right now. I was supposed to organize it last spring and just never got around to it. 

Anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the bills and stuff. Yeah, I don't know, I guess I get to them eventually when they're sitting right in front of me.

Help with my meds? No, I don't think so. I just take them myself. I keep the bottles right next to the toaster so I see them when I'm making breakfast. 

I've been eating the exact same thing for breakfast for, oh, it's gotta be twenty years now. Two slices of sourdough toast and orange marmalade. You know, they actually stopped selling the good brand of marmalade at my local grocery store. The one with the little gingham lid? Now it's all that cheap high-fructose stuff. I tried complaining to the manager—young kid, couldn't have been older than nineteen. Nice enough kid, but he looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Kids today just don't get customer service, do they? 

Back when I worked at the hardware store right out of high school, we would walk the customer right to the exact aisle if they needed something. We had these heavy green aprons with the big pockets for nails and screws. My buddy Dale and I used to see who could ring up a register the fastest... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, the pills. Yeah, no, nobody helps me with them, I just do it myself.

Missed paying bills? Well, like I said earlier, I just kind of leave them on the counter. But honestly, that's exactly the kind of thing I'm talking about. The forgetting. It's why I came in today. I just keep forgetting things I really shouldn’t be forgetting at my age. 

Like my heart doctor—I'm supposed to have these follow-up appointments, and I just completely blank on them. Or I'll tell myself I need to call the clinic back, and then... nothing. Poof. Gone from my brain. 

It's just like that deck repair I was telling you about with my neighbor. Showing up without the right tools! I mean, I used to work at a hardware store, for crying out loud. You'd think I'd know better. We used to sell these beautiful Craftsman tool sets back then. Real heavy-duty steel, not like the cheap plastic handles they make everything with now. I bought my first set with my third paycheck. Kept it in the trunk of my car for years. 

Actually, I think my son has that set now. He lives out in Colorado. Beautiful out there, the mountains and all. He went out there for college and just never came back east. He likes to hike... 

Anyway, what was the question? Oh, the bills. Yeah, the forgetting is just... it's getting to be a real problem with the important stuff, like the doctors and the tools.

Take over the bills? Uh, no, nobody's taken them over. I'm still doing them myself. Well, I mean, I try to. Like I said, they just kind of pile up by the fruit bowl. 

Speaking of fruit, I bought these peaches the other day from that little stand out on Route 9. You know the one? The guy with the overalls always sits out there reading a paperback. Anyway, they looked great, but they were hard as rocks. I left them in a paper bag to ripen—my mother always swore by the paper bag trick. She used to can her own peaches every August. The whole house would smell like sugar and summer. We had this enormous copper pot she only brought out for canning season. I wonder whatever happened to that pot? My sister probably took it when they sold the house. She always had an eye for the antiques. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Someone taking over? No, no, it's just me handling the bills. For better or worse, I guess.

Unpaid? Well, I mean, they're late sometimes, sure, but I always get to them eventually. They don't shut the lights off or anything. I just wait until they send those pink envelopes, you know? The ones that say "Past Due" in big letters. 

I remember when the electric company used to send a guy out to actually read the meter on the side of the house. Our guy was named Frank. Big guy, always wore a gray uniform and carried this heavy flashlight, even in the middle of the day. He had a golden retriever that would sit in his truck while he did his rounds. Beautiful dog. Max, I think his name was. Or maybe Buster? No, Buster was the dog my uncle had when I was a kid. Buster was a terror, always digging up my aunt's petunias. She used to chase him around the yard with a rolled-up newspaper...

Oh, but no, they haven't shut anything off. I always manage to send a check before it gets to that point. I just... I need the pink envelopes to remind me.

Lost driving? No, no, I know my way around town just fine. I've been driving these roads for... gosh, forty years now? 

Though I will say, the traffic has gotten just terrible lately. They put in that new roundabout over by the old high school, and nobody knows how to use it. It's a free-for-all! I was sitting there the other day in my Buick—it's a '98 LeSabre, runs like a top, they really don't make them like that anymore. The seats are like sitting on a living room sofa. My wife hated the color, it's this sort of seafoam green, but she admitted it was comfortable on long trips. We drove it all the way down to Florida once, back in... oh, must have been 2004. Stopped at South of the Border on the way down. You know, with the giant sombrero? Pedro! It's so tacky, but the grandkids loved the bumper stickers. We bought this awful neon pink flamingo for the yard, but the wind blew it away during a storm a few years back. 

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, getting lost. No, I don't get lost. I know exactly where I'm going, even if I have to deal with that darn roundabout.

Month? Oh, it's October. 

My favorite time of year, honestly. The leaves are just starting to turn over on Elm Street. We used to have this massive oak tree in our front yard when I was growing up. Every October, my dad would rake all the leaves into this huge pile, and my brother and I would jump in it until we were covered in dirt and little bits of dried leaves. My mother hated it because we'd track it all into the house. She had this vacuum—an old Hoover, heavy as a tank. Sounded like an airplane taking off. She'd be vacuuming and yelling over the noise about how we were turning her living room into a forest floor. 

My brother, he lives out in Arizona now. No autumn leaves out there, just rocks and cactus. I went to visit him a few years ago, and I swear, I don't know how he stands the heat. We went to this diner, and I ordered a slice of cherry pie... 

Wait, did you just need the month? Yeah, October.

The year? Oh, it is 2024. 

It is funny, I still write 2023 on my checks sometimes. Well, the few checks I still write anyway. Everything is on the computer now, which is just... I mean, I remember when the year 2000 sounded like a science fiction movie. Everyone was in such a panic about the computers crashing for Y2K. My neighbor Phil bought a generator and about fifty cans of baked beans. He stacked them all up in his garage next to his riding mower. 

Phil was a bit of a character, always getting into these wild schemes. He tried to start a business selling those metal detectors you use at the beach. We took one out to the coast once, didn't find a single coin, just bottle caps and a rusty pair of sunglasses. I think they were aviators. I used to have a pair of aviators... loved those glasses. I wore them until the arm snapped off. Tried to tape it back together with duct tape, but my wife told me I looked like a lunatic, so I had to throw them out. I always meant to buy another pair, but you know how it goes. 

Anyway, what was I... right, the year. 2024.

Finances? Oh, no, I handle all my own money. Memory's got nothing to do with it, I'm sharp as a tack when it comes to the bills. 

Though, honestly, paying bills used to be an event, you know? Sitting down at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning with a cup of black coffee. My wife used to make these incredible blueberry muffins on Sundays. Real blueberries, none of that canned nonsense. She'd get them fresh from the farmer's market downtown. We'd walk down there early, before it got too crowded. There was this one fella who sold the most amazing honey, kept his own bees out past the county line. I bought a jar once and left it in the pantry so long it crystallized. Did you know you can just put the jar in warm water and it turns right back to liquid? Fascinating stuff, honey. Never goes bad. They found it in Egyptian tombs, you know. Imagine eating thousand-year-old honey! 

But yeah, the bills. I still do them myself. No problem at all.

Medications? No, no, I handle all that myself. I've got one of those little plastic pill organizers, you know the ones with the days of the week stamped on the lids? 

Mine is bright blue. I picked it up at the pharmacy down on Main Street. That place has been there forever. Old Mr. Henderson used to run it when I was a kid. He always had a jar of butterscotch candies on the counter. You don't see that anymore, do you? Now it's all chain stores and self-checkout lines. I can never get those machines to scan right. The last time I went, it kept yelling at me about an unexpected item in the bagging area. It was just my umbrella! I always carry an umbrella if it looks even a little gray out. Better safe than soggy, my grandfather used to say. He lived in Seattle for a few years, so I guess he knew a thing or two about rain. He had this amazing old trench coat he wore everywhere... 

But no, nobody needs to help me with the pills. I do it all myself.

Help with shopping and cooking? Oh, no, I do all of that just fine on my own. My memory doesn't get in the way of any of that. I still drive myself to the grocery store every Tuesday morning. 

Tuesday is the best day to go, you know. They restock the produce overnight on Mondays, so everything is crisp. I like to get those big honeycrisp apples. They are so expensive now, though! I remember when you could get a whole bag of apples for a couple of bucks. Now they charge by the pound, and it's like buying gold. Speaking of gold, I saw this documentary the other night about the Gold Rush out in California. Those poor guys panning in the freezing rivers for months on end, mostly finding nothing but fool's gold. Pyrite, I think it's called. My grandson had a little chunk of it he bought at a museum gift shop. Kids love those gift shops, don't they? They always want the shiny rocks or those astronaut ice cream packets. I tried one of those once... tasted like sweet chalk. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, I don't need any help getting around or cooking. I manage all that just fine.

Down? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm in pretty good spirits, really. I mean, it's hard to be too down when you've got things to keep you busy. I've been spending a lot of time out in the garage lately, trying to fix up this old push mower. It's a Briggs & Stratton, a real sturdy machine. They just don't make them like that anymore, you know? Everything you buy now is just cheap plastic that cracks if you look at it wrong. 

My neighbor, Gary, he just bought one of those fancy electric mowers. Sounds like a giant hairdryer! He loves it, though. Gary's a good guy, he used to work down at the bottling plant before it closed up in the nineties. We went fishing a couple times up at Miller's Pond. Caught a nice sized bass once, but mostly it's just bluegill in there. Bluegill are feisty, though, they put up a real good fight for their size. Have you ever been fishing up there? It's so peaceful early in the morning, right when the mist is still sitting on the water and the sun is just coming up over the pines. I used to take my kids there when they were little... 

But anyway, what were you asking? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no, I feel fine. Just keeping busy.

Worse? No, I don't think so. I'd say it's about the same as it was a few years ago. Let's see, a few years ago... that was right around the time my brother Frank finally sold his old Chevy. 

It was a '69 Chevelle, beautiful thing. Painted this deep, metallic blue. He kept it sitting under a tarp in his garage for practically a decade. I used to tell him, "Frank, you gotta take that thing out, engines need to run!" But he was always so paranoid about getting a rock chip on the highway. You know how guys get with those classic cars, they treat them better than their own kids! Speaking of which, his youngest, Tommy, just got his driver's license. Terrifying thought, honestly. The way people drive out there today, everybody's just staring down at their phones instead of the road. I saw a guy the other day drift right into the rumble strip because he was texting. Scared the living daylights out of him, I bet. Serves him right, though, you really shouldn't be messing with those things behind the wheel. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, my memory. Yeah, no, I remember all that stuff just fine. It hasn't gotten any worse.

My family? No, nobody's said anything like that to me. My wife, Mary, she's the one who usually keeps track of everything anyway. She's got this big calendar in the kitchen, writes everything down in red ink. 

She's always been organized like that, ever since we first got married. We had this tiny little apartment over on 5th Street, right above a bakery. Oh, the smell of that bread every morning! It was wonderful, but it made you hungry all the time. The baker, Mr. Rossi, he used to give us the day-old loaves for half price. He was a sweet old man, had this big bushy mustache that would get powdered sugar all over it when he made the cannolis. I haven't had a good cannoli in years. The bakeries around here now, they just don't do it right. The filling is always too sweet, or the shell is soggy. You need a nice, crisp shell that shatters a little when you bite into it. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my family saying something about my memory. No, nobody's mentioned anything to me. I think I'm doing alright.

Help with everyday tasks? No, I don't need any help like that. I do everything I've always done. I mean, I was just out back this morning pulling weeds in Mary's garden. She loves her tomatoes, got these big beefsteak ones growing this year. 

She's been trying to get the soil just right for ages. We went down to the garden center over on Route 9 a few weeks back to get some of that special fertilizer. The guy working there, young kid, maybe eighteen, he had no idea what he was talking about. Kept trying to sell me on this organic compost stuff that smelled like a wet dog. I told him, "Listen, son, I've been growing tomatoes since before you were born." You just need a little bit of bone meal and some good old-fashioned sunshine. We used to have a huge garden when we lived out in the country. Grew all our own corn, squash, beans... the deer would always get into the beans, though. You'd wake up in the morning and half the row would just be gone, chewed right down to the nub. We tried everything to keep them out—pie tins on strings, Irish Spring soap, you name it. Nothing works on a hungry deer. Beautiful animals, though. I saw a ten-point buck out there once, just standing in the mist... 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, needing help with things. No, no, I'm still doing everything myself. Weeding, fixing the mower, all of it. I don't need any help.

Great fishing spot, right off the dock. You could catch largemouth bass all day if you used the right lure. I always preferred those rubber worms, the purple ones with the little white tails. My buddy Al used to swear by spinnerbaits, but I told him they just get caught in the weeds. 

Speaking of Al, he moved down to Florida a few years back. Bought a condo down in Boca. Says the humidity is terrible for his joints, but he plays golf every single Tuesday. I tried golf once, couldn't stand it. Too much standing around, waiting for people to hit a little white ball. I'd rather be doing something, you know? Keeping my hands busy. I built this beautiful cedar birdhouse last spring instead of taking up golf. The blue jays absolutely love it, though they chase all the smaller birds away. Mean birds, blue jays. Beautiful, but mean. They sound like a rusty pump handle when they squawk.
