Well, it is nice to meet you too, doctor, though I must admit I'm quite overwhelmed right now. What brings me in... well, I suppose it's the voices. I just keep hearing these very, very clear voices, and it’s becoming impossible to manage. 

I live in a fairly quiet building, you see, but lately, in my apartment, I hear them constantly. It sounds exactly like a group of women whispering right from behind the walls. Just murmuring and whispering through the drywall. And the strange thing is, it’s not just at home. I try to get out, I go to the art museums downtown because I’ve always loved the quiet there—I got my degree years ago and I've always appreciated the atmosphere—but even there, when I wander into one of those large, empty museum rooms where there's absolutely no one else around, I hear them again. The exact same women, whispering from behind the gallery walls. 

And they are so specific about what they want to say. They just keep telling me which photographs belong in the archive. Over and over, discussing this archive and dictating to me which specific photographs need to be placed in it. I try to focus on other things, I try to just sit in my living room and read, or look at the museum exhibits, but their voices are so clear, and they just won't stop whispering about the photographs and the archive... it's just exhausting, to be honest with you.

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I've seen my regular doctor for years—decades, really, ever since I moved into that quiet building I mentioned. And he always does the standard physicals, you know, checks my reflexes with that little rubber hammer, looks in my eyes with the light, and he’s never once said a single word about my brain or my nervous system being damaged. 

I don't have Parkinson's or dementia or anything of that sort. My mother, bless her heart, did have some nerve pain in her legs when she got to be about my age, but my nerves are perfectly fine. I don't get migraines, I've never had a seizure, and my memory is just as sharp as it ever was when I was getting my bachelor's degree. I still remember all the historical dates on the placards at the museum, clear as day, without even having to write them down. 

So physically, my brain is completely healthy. No doctor has ever told me otherwise. Which makes it all the more baffling, you see, because if my brain is perfectly fine and my nervous system is intact, why am I the only one who can hear them? Why are these women so fixated on me and the archive? It just doesn't make any sense if there's no physical illness, but they just keep whispering anyway...

Well, let me think back... it’s been quite a while now, hasn't it? I remember exactly when it started because it was right around the time the weather was turning, and the heating pipes in my building usually make such a racket, but this... this was completely different. It has been about eight months now. Yes, eight solid months. 

I thought at first, maybe it's just the neighbors, maybe someone new moved in next door and they just talk very softly. But then it just kept going, day in and day out, every single day for the last eight months. And it's not just the whispering, doctor. For that exact same amount of time, I've had this... this absolute certainty, this undeniable knowledge that people are watching my archive. I don't know how they know about it, or how they're doing it, but they are watching it. I can feel it. 

I’ve tried to figure out how they could possibly be monitoring the photographs. I check the locks on my door, I make sure the blinds are drawn tight, especially in the evenings when the streetlights cast those long shadows into the living room, but it simply doesn't matter. For eight months, the women have been whispering, and I just *know* there are people watching the archive. It's a terrible, heavy feeling, really, knowing you're being observed like that in your own private space. And like I said, even when I go to the museum to escape it, it's the exact same feeling, the same voices, the same watching... I just can't seem to get a single moment of peace from it, not once in eight months.

Oh, it’s completely fallen apart, doctor. Just... terribly worse. I used to be so organized, you know. I was always very involved with the local historical society and the museum boards, always the one they relied on for things. But lately, with the whispering and the constant feeling of the archive being watched... I just haven't been able to go. I’ve missed so many board meetings. It’s embarrassing, really, because I know I’ve lost the trust of my colleagues. I can just feel it; they think I'm completely unreliable now. 

And it’s not just the meetings, it’s the daily things right inside my own home. The mail comes, and I just stare at the envelopes, and... well, I've missed paying my bills. The electric, the water... I used to be so meticulous with my checkbook, balancing it to the penny every Sunday evening at my kitchen table, but now I just can't manage the money at all. I get too distracted by what the voices are dictating to me.

It actually got to the point where my cousin had to get involved. She lives a few towns over—usually we just exchange letters or Christmas cards, but she had to come down. She and... well, one of the museum administrators actually had to step in together to help me. It was quite overwhelming, having them both there, going through my mail and my calendar. They realized I couldn't manage my appointments anymore, or handle my finances, or even attend those public gallery events safely on my own. They were so worried I might get confused or overwhelmed in public, or that I wasn't safe. It’s just humiliating, honestly, to have someone else have to take over your life like that, at my age, after being independent for so long. But I just couldn't keep up with any of it, not with those women constantly whispering.

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, I guess what brings me in is... I just can't seem to shake this really heavy mix of fear and guilt lately. It's like I'm just tense all day, waiting for something else to go wrong. And I just keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened.
Yeah, it did. Um... this has been going on for about four months now, ever since my husband had a bad fall during the porch repair.

Yeah, they do. Um... especially since I work around that kind of stuff. I'll just be at work, measuring a railing or maybe just hearing a ladder scrape against a wall, and out of nowhere I can see him falling. It's like it's happening right in front of me all over again. My stomach just drops and my hands get all shaky.

Yeah, I have. Um... I've actually started turning down jobs if they involve raised porches or second-story decks. I just can't really do them right now. And even at home, I just... I find excuses not to talk about the repair. I don't even look at the spot where it happened. I just try to stay away from it.

No, I haven't really noticed that. I mean... I don't feel jumpy or constantly on edge or anything. It's really just when I'm around those specific things at work or the porch that I get upset. But in general, no, I wouldn't say I'm easily startled.

No, not really. I mean, I still talk to my friends and my family just like I always have. I don't feel disconnected from them or anything. It's really just the stuff related to the accident that bothers me.

Yeah, I do. I mean, I do building inspections for a living, so... I keep thinking that if I missed something that important at my own house, then maybe I'm not as careful or competent as I thought I was. I know my work reports don't show that I'm doing a bad job or missing things, but... I just feel like I really should have caught it.
No, I didn't see it actually happen. I was inside the house when the railing broke. I just heard the crash and... and then I ran out and saw him on the ground.

Yeah, I have. Most nights I just lie there in bed for an hour or two, just... replaying everything in my head. And even when I finally do fall asleep, I'm waking up at every little creak the house makes. Or I wake up from these dreams where I just keep hearing the sound of him hitting the ground over and over again.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, things have been stressful, obviously, but... I still feel happy when good things happen, and I still love my husband just as much as I always have. It's just... the anxiety about the accident that's the problem, not really my other emotions.
No, it wasn't life-threatening. He broke his arm and had a concussion, which was scary enough, but... the doctors said he wasn't in any real danger of dying. It was just a really bad break.

Yeah, thanks. Well, I guess what brought me in is... I just can't stop jumping out of my skin. I do maintenance work, and if a breaker snaps loud, or somebody drops a tool, or even if a guy just comes up behind me unannounced, I practically jump out of my boots. 

And it's not just a quick scare, you know? My heart just keeps hammering in my chest long after everyone else has already moved on and gone back to work. I just can't seem to shake it.
Yeah. Um... there was an arc-flash accident on this retrofit job I was working on. That's when all this started. It's been going on since that happened, so... about a year and a month now.

Yeah, all the time. It's like... out of nowhere, I'll just see that bright flash right in my head. Or I'll hear the new guy yelling. It doesn't even matter what I'm doing. I could just be loading up my tools in the back of the truck, and boom, it just pops up. It knocks me sideways, man. It honestly feels like I'm right back there and it's happening all over again.

Yeah, I do. I mean, I make excuses not to go near certain panels or breakers now. If a job site looks too much like that one, I'll try to get out of it. And I definitely don't want to talk about that day. If I even get close to thinking about it or talking about it, it just starts up in my head and I can't shut it off. So I just try to stay away from anything that reminds me of it.
No, I don't think so. I mean, I still talk to my family and the guys on the crew just fine. I don't really feel disconnected from them or anything like that.
No, not really. I mean, it was an accident. The new guy made a mistake, but I don't sit around blaming him for it. And I don't really blame myself either. It just... it just happened.

Yeah, I do. I just... I walk around mad all the time now. And guilty, too. It's like I failed that kid, you know? Since I was the experienced guy on the job. And it feels like everybody can see it on me, like they know. So yeah, I just feel angry and guilty pretty much all the time.

Well, I’m here because... dispatch and compliance have been tracking my route changes. They do it through the computer system and, like, they make these little comments on the radio. Actually, the radio in my cab is one of those really old models. It gets this awful static. When I was getting my associate's degree, I took this communications class and the professor talked about radio frequencies all the time. He always wore these really loud plaid shirts, every single Tuesday... I don't even use that degree now, obviously, since I'm driving all day. 

But anyway, even when people tell me it’s just normal oversight from management, I know it's not. I can tell certain drivers are reporting on me.

Voices? No, not really. I mean, I hear dispatch over the radio, but that's a real person. When it's quiet, it's mostly just the road noise. You know, the tires on the highway. I drive the interstate a lot, and there's this one stretch right near the county line where the pavement changes and it makes this weird, loud humming sound. It actually reminds me of this giant box fan my grandmother used to keep in her living room window during the summer. She lived in this old house that didn't have central air, and she would make pitcher after pitcher of iced tea with fresh mint from her garden. I actually tried growing mint once in a little pot in my apartment, but it completely died. I think I overwatered it, or maybe it didn't get enough sun because my window faces the brick wall of the building next door... But yeah, I don't hear anyone talking to me if they aren't actually there. Just the normal traffic sounds.

Well, like I was saying earlier, it's not really the static itself. It's the little comments they make on the radio, and how dispatch and compliance are tracking all my route changes through the computer system. I know people try to tell me it’s just normal oversight from management, but I can just tell that certain drivers are reporting on me. It's all connected through that computer... which, by the way, they just updated the screens in our cabs last month. 

The new screens are incredibly bright, especially when you're driving at night. It actually reminds me of this huge neon sign outside a diner I used to hang out at when I was a teenager. We used to go there and get milkshakes all the time. Strawberry was my favorite. I haven't had a good strawberry milkshake in years, honestly. You know how they always taste so artificial now? Like they just use that fake red syrup instead of real strawberries. My mom used to make jam from scratch, so I guess I'm just picky about it... but yeah, they're definitely tracking me on that screen.

Energized? No, not really. I mean, I don't get like that unless I drink way too much coffee. Sometimes when I'm on a long route I have to stop at this specific truck stop off Exit 42, and they have this really strong cold brew. It comes in these massive plastic cups with bright orange lids. Orange is actually my least favorite color. When I was in middle school, my aunt knitted me this bright orange sweater for picture day, and it was made out of this really cheap wool that was so itchy. I had to wear it because she was visiting us that week, and I was just scratching my neck the entire time they were lining us up for the photos in the gym. The photographer kept waving this little squeaky toy to make people smile, which was super weird because we were in seventh grade, you know? Like we weren't toddlers, we didn't need a squeaky toy... But no, I haven't had any days where I felt unusually high or irritable or anything like that. Just regular tired from driving.

I'd say... it's been really clear to me for about the past two months. Yeah, two months of the tracking through the computer system and those little radio comments. I remember because it started right around the time I had to take my personal car in for its annual inspection. I went to this little garage off Elm Street, and the mechanic there tried to tell me I needed brand new windshield wipers to pass, which was completely ridiculous because I had just bought a set at AutoZone like a week before. I got those really expensive silicone ones, you know? The ones that come in the bright yellow packaging and are supposed to last for years. They actually work incredibly well. I drove through this massive downpour going to my sister's house last spring, and the water just beaded right off the glass. She lives way out in the country, and her driveway is this really long gravel road, so my car was completely covered in this thick white dust by the time I got to her place. We ended up spending the whole afternoon washing it in her front yard with this cheap green garden hose that kept kinking every five minutes. It was so annoying, I kept having to walk back to the spigot to unkink it... but yeah, about two months, I think.

Medical illness? No, no, I've been perfectly healthy. No head injuries or anything like that, and I don't really take any medications. Well, I guess I take a multivitamin sometimes, the gummy kind. I usually get them at this pharmacy right by my apartment, but the last time I went in there, they had completely rearranged all the aisles. It was so confusing. I spent like twenty minutes just looking for the vitamins, and I ended up in the hair care section. Which actually reminded me I needed new shampoo, because the one I was using had this really overpowering coconut smell. I bought it on sale, but it smelled exactly like those cheap air fresheners people hang from their rearview mirrors. You know the ones shaped like little pine trees? My dad used to have a vanilla one in his old pickup truck, and the smell would just bake into the upholstery during the summer. We drove all the way down to Florida in that truck once, and the AC was broken the whole time. My brother kept complaining about the heat, and he would roll the window down, but the wind was so loud we couldn't even hear the radio playing... But yeah, no new medications or sicknesses or anything.

Well, yeah, I guess I have been pulling away. I don't really feel like singing with the choir anymore, or having the softball team over to my place. Actually, the last time I had the team over, I made this massive batch of chili in my slow cooker. It was this recipe I found in a magazine at the dentist's office. The waiting room there always has the oldest magazines, I swear I saw one from like 2018 last time I was there. Anyway, I used this specific kind of smoked paprika that gave it this really deep, rich flavor, but I accidentally spilled half the bottle on the counter because the little shaker lid popped off. Those plastic lids are always so flimsy, you know? Like the ones on the Parmesan cheese shakers at pizza places. There's this little pizza place downtown that has the best garlic knots, but they always burn the bottoms just a tiny bit, which I actually kind of like. But yeah, most days after my shift, I just sit at the kitchen table with my planner open. I just sit there, and I can't even make myself start dinner, or make any calls, or do anything else really. Just sitting there.

Yeah, like I was saying earlier, the tracking through the computer system and all those radio comments... it's been really clear to me for about the past two months. Continuously, every single day. I know for sure because I've been looking at my calendar a lot lately. I have this really nice wall calendar in my kitchen with pictures of different national parks. My aunt got it for me for Christmas. She always gets me the most thoughtful gifts, actually. Last year she got me this incredible wool sweater that she knitted herself. It was this deep maroon color, which is my absolute favorite, but I accidentally shrank it in the wash because I completely forgot to check the tag before throwing it in. I was so upset about it. I tried stretching it back out while it was wet, you know, pulling on the sleeves and the bottom hem, but it just ended up looking all lopsided and weird. I ended up giving it to my neighbor's daughter. She's like eight, and it actually fit her perfectly. I saw her wearing it when they were walking their dog the other day, this little golden retriever mix that barks at literally every single squirrel it sees... but yeah, definitely the last two months, non-stop.

Well, I guess... I don't know if anyone's said anything about my face or my voice, exactly. But like I was saying before, I just don't have the energy for things. I don't feel like singing with the choir anymore, or having the softball team over. And the softball team, we used to have so much fun. We had this one game last summer where it rained so hard the field turned into absolute mud. Like, thick, brown sludge. My cleats got completely stuck when I was running to second base, and I ended up sliding face-first into the dirt. It took me like three showers to finally get all the grit out of my hair. I was using this really cheap shampoo back then, the kind that comes in those massive pump bottles at the drugstore. It was supposed to smell like green apple, but honestly, it just smelled like floor cleaner. You know that industrial stuff they use in the subway stations? I smell it all the time at work. It's so strong it practically burns your nose when you walk past the janitor's cart. They always seem to be mopping right when the rush hour crowd is coming through, which makes no sense because everyone just tracks dirt right back over the wet floor... But yeah, most days after my shift now, I just sit at the kitchen table with my planner open. I just sit there and stare at it. I can't even make myself start dinner, or make any phone calls, or do anything else. Just... sitting.

Well, I don't think anyone has said exactly that. People don't really say my answers are hard to follow. Sometimes they look at me a little funny, I guess, but nobody really says anything. Mostly people just want to talk about themselves anyway, you know? Like my supervisor at the depot, he's always going on about his boat. It's this pontoon thing he bought used, and he spends every weekend fixing the motor. He actually showed me a picture of the carburetor the other day, completely taken apart on his garage floor. His garage is huge, by the way. He's got this whole pegboard system for his tools that he painted bright orange. I tried organizing my tools once, but I just bought one of those cheap plastic toolboxes from the hardware store on 4th street. The latch on it is broken, so if you pick it up by the handle, everything just dumps out onto the floor. I dropped a whole container of drywall screws that way last month, and I'm pretty sure I'm still finding them under the refrigerator. They just roll everywhere, like those little beads from that necklace I broke when I was in high school... but no, nobody's told me I go off track.

No, I wouldn't say depressed. I just... I don't feel much of anything, like I said. Just empty, I guess. Not sad, really. Sad is how I felt when they cancelled my favorite TV show last year. It was this baking competition where they had to make everything out of, like, historical recipes. They made this one pie from the 1700s that had actual meat mixed with fruit, which sounds completely disgusting, but the judges loved it. I tried baking bread once, during that whole sourdough craze, you know? I had this starter bubbling away in a jar on my counter for weeks. I named it 'Dough-lores.' You're supposed to name them, apparently. But I forgot to feed it one week because I got put on the overnight shift at the depot, and it just died. Turned this awful gray color and smelled like old beer. The overnight shift is the worst, honestly. The breakroom vending machine is always out of the good snacks by 2 AM, and you're just left with those weird off-brand cheese crackers that stick to the roof of your mouth. I chipped a tooth on one once, right in the back. The dentist said I grind my teeth anyway, so it was bound to happen. He gave me this plastic guard to wear at night, but I keep losing it in my sheets... so, yeah, no, not depressed. Just... blank.

Hopeless? Um, no, I wouldn't say hopeless. Like I said, it's more just... nothing. Not down. The only thing that's really hopeless is trying to get the Route 4 bus to run on time at work. They had to detour the whole line last month because of this massive water main break over on Elm Street. The water was just gushing right up through the asphalt like a fountain. I saw a video of it on the local news, and the reporter standing there was wearing this incredibly bright neon yellow raincoat. It was so bright it actually hurt my eyes a little through the TV screen. I bought a raincoat once that was supposed to be clear, like transparent plastic, you know? But it just ended up fogging up on the inside from my body heat so I looked like I was wrapped in a foggy shower curtain or something. I ended up leaving it on a bench at the transit center. Somebody probably took it. People leave the weirdest things at the depot, honestly. Last week someone left a single roller skate. Just one. It had these bright pink wheels that actually smelled like bubblegum when you got close to it. I don't know how you lose just one skate, you'd think you would notice walking away with one shoe on... but yeah, no, I haven't really felt down.

Hear my thoughts? No, I don't think anyone can hear what I'm thinking. That would be pretty weird, wouldn't it? Like if my thoughts were just broadcasting out loud. I did have a radio that used to pick up some weird interference once, though. It was this old silver boombox I got at a garage sale for five dollars. The antenna was bent at this really sharp angle, almost like a lightning bolt. Whenever I put it on the windowsill in my kitchen, it would pick up what sounded like police dispatch calls, but only on Tuesdays. It was the strangest thing. I tried recording it once on a cassette tape, but the tape got all chewed up in the player. You know how those old tapes used to just unspool and get tangled around the little gears inside? I spent an hour trying to pull it out with a pair of tweezers, but it just snapped. The tweezers I used were actually for my eyebrows, but they were so dull they wouldn't grip anything anyway. I really need to buy a new pair, maybe those slant-tip ones they sell at the pharmacy. The pharmacy by my apartment just remodeled, actually, and they moved the entire beauty section to the back corner near the greeting cards. It's so confusing now, I couldn't even find the toothpaste last time I went in. I had to ask this clerk who looked like he was about twelve years old, and he just pointed vaguely toward the middle of the store. So, no, people can't hear my thoughts.

Yeah, I guess so. It's just... I don't feel like singing with my choir anymore, or having the softball team over to my place. I used to love hosting the softball team. We had this one game last summer where it started pouring rain right in the middle of the third inning. We all got completely soaked, and the mud out by second base was so thick my cleat actually got stuck in it. I had to hop back to the dugout with only one shoe on. It reminded me of that roller skate someone left at the depot, just sitting there all by itself. Anyway, we ordered pizza after that game from this place downtown that makes these huge, foldable slices. The crust was perfectly crispy, but the cheese slid right off when you picked it up. You had to do this weird head-tilt thing just to eat it without making a mess. I spilled tomato sauce all over my white jersey, and no matter how much bleach I used, there was always this faint orange stain right near the collar. I tried using this eco-friendly stain remover I found online, but it smelled strongly of pine needles, almost like a car air freshener. I hate those pine tree air fresheners, they always give me a headache. My dad used to hang one in his old pickup truck, and the smell would just bake into the upholstery during the summer. So, yeah, most days after my shift now, I just sit at the kitchen table with my planner open. I just stare at it, but I can't make myself start dinner, or make any calls, or do anything else, really.

Put into my mind? No, I don't think so. My thoughts are my own, they just feel a bit... slow lately. But no one is putting them there. I did read this article once about how advertisers try to put thoughts in your head, though. It was in this magazine I picked up at the dentist's office. The waiting room there is always freezing, they keep the AC blasting even in November. I always have to bring a sweater, usually my green cardigan. It has these big wooden buttons that look like little tree stumps, with the rings and everything carved into them. I found it at a thrift store near the depot for like three bucks. Thrift stores are great, but sometimes the clothes have that weird dusty smell, like old books. I love the smell of old books, though. There's this used bookstore downtown that has a whole basement full of first editions, and it smells exactly like vanilla and dust. The stairs going down there are super steep and creaky, and the wood is all worn down in the middle from people walking on them for years. I tripped on the bottom step once and dropped my coffee everywhere. It was a hazelnut latte, and I felt so bad because the owner had to bring out this giant mop to clean it up. The mop bucket was bright yellow, kind of like that raincoat I saw on the news. But yeah, nobody is putting thoughts into my head.

Controlling my actions? No, I'm the one in charge of what I do. I'm in the driver's seat. Literally, since I drive the shuttle routes down at the transit depot. Though, the steering on the new shuttles is so sensitive, sometimes it feels like the bus is driving itself if you hit a pothole. The potholes are getting so bad on 4th Street. I hit one last week that completely rattled my teeth, and it spilled my travel mug everywhere. It was this insulated metal mug I got for Christmas, the kind with the little plastic slidey lid, but the lid never really seals right. If you tip it even a little bit, coffee just seeps out the edges. It stained the cup holder in my own car, which is so annoying because I had just paid to vacuum the interior. I used those little crevice attachments they have at the self-serve car wash, the ones with the stiff bristles. The vacuum there is incredibly loud, it actually sounds like a jet engine taking off. I always have to wear my earbuds when I go there, usually listening to a podcast. I started this new podcast about deep sea diving, and it's crazy how dark it gets down in the ocean. Just pitch black, like you wouldn't even be able to see your own hand in front of your face if you were down there. But yeah, no one is controlling me or my actions.

Stuck? No, I've never had that happen. I can always move my arms and legs just fine. Sometimes my legs get a little stiff if I've been sitting in the driver's seat for too long without a break, especially on the longer routes out to the suburbs. The seats in the older shuttles don't have good lumbar support, so you end up slouching. I tried bringing a little throw pillow from my couch to put behind my back, but it kept sliding down. It was this ugly mustard yellow pillow my aunt gave me when I moved into my first apartment. She got it at a garage sale, I think. I love going to garage sales on Saturday mornings, you never know what you're going to find. Last summer I found this incredible vintage blender with a glass pitcher. The base was chrome and it weighed an absolute ton. I tried to make a smoothie in it once with some frozen strawberries, but the blades were so dull it just kind of mashed them around instead of blending them. It made this awful grinding noise, too, like metal scraping on metal. It sounded just like the brakes on my neighbor's old sedan. He leaves for work at 5 AM every day and the squeal wakes me up every single time. So, no, I don't ever feel stuck or anything like that.

Energetic? Like, not needing sleep? No, I don't think so. I mean, I sleep pretty normally, usually. Although, lately, it's been a bit hard to fall asleep because of the streetlights outside my bedroom window. They installed these new LED bulbs on our block last month, and they are so incredibly bright. It's like having a stadium light shining right through my blinds. I tried to buy blackout curtains, but I couldn't find the right length at the store. The ones they had were either way too short or dragging on the floor. I ended up getting these dark blue ones that have little silver stars on them. They were in the kids' section, actually, but I thought the stars were kind of cute. They remind me of this planetarium I went to on a field trip in middle school. The seats leaned way back and they projected the night sky on the ceiling, and the guy talking had this really deep, soothing voice. I actually fell asleep during the presentation because it was so dark and relaxing. My friend Sarah had to poke me in the ribs to wake me up when it was over. Sarah always used to wear this strong vanilla perfume, it was almost overpowering. I can't even smell vanilla now without thinking of her. We used to go to this bakery that made the best vanilla bean scones, they had this thick white icing on top that would crack when you bit into it. The icing was so sweet it almost made your teeth hurt. But yeah, no, I haven't had days where I didn't need sleep or felt super energetic.

A voice talking about me? No, I don't hear anything like that when it's quiet. I actually like it when the radio is off, it gives me a chance to just think. I used to listen to the radio all the time when I was a teenager, especially this one station that played alternative rock. I had this little boombox in my room that took like eight D batteries. It was silver and had this weird shaped handle on top. I used to record songs off the radio onto cassette tapes, and you had to sit there with your finger hovering over the record button so you didn't miss the beginning of the song. But then the DJ would always talk over the intro, which was so frustrating. I had this one tape that I labeled with a purple sparkly gel pen, and I listened to it until it finally snapped. It just got tangled up in the tape deck of my mom's station wagon. That car was huge, it had that fake wood paneling on the side and the seats in the very back faced backwards. Riding back there always made me feel a little car sick, especially if I was trying to read a book. I loved reading those mystery novels where the kids would solve crimes in their neighborhood. But no, I don't hear any voices or anything when I'm alone.

Outside forces? Like someone else putting things in my head? No, I don't think so. My thoughts are just my own, you know? Sometimes I wish someone else would take over, though, especially when I'm trying to figure out what to make for dinner. I get so tired of cooking the same things every week. I tried to make this eggplant parmesan last Tuesday, but the eggplant came out really rubbery. I don't think I salted it right before I fried it. My grandmother used to make the best eggplant parmesan, she had this huge cast iron skillet that she swore by. She said the trick was letting it simmer in the sauce all afternoon. Her kitchen always smelled like garlic and oregano. She grew her own herbs in these little terracotta pots on the windowsill. The pots had these tiny painted flowers on them, mostly daisies, I think. Daisies are so cheerful, they always make me think of spring. Last spring I bought a bouquet of them at the farmer's market, the one downtown near the river. They had this amazing honey vendor there who sold different kinds of local honey. I bought a jar of clover honey that was so light and sweet, it was perfect in my tea. I drink a lot of chamomile tea in the evenings, it helps me wind down. The brand I buy has these little string tags with inspirational quotes on them, which is kind of cheesy but I read them anyway. So, yeah, no outside forces or anything messing with my thoughts.

Um, hi. I'm here because... well, I'm having trouble at work. I work at a meat processing plant, and... I keep messing up the paperwork. Like, I'll start the sanitation steps, or the batch logs, or the end-of-line stuff, and I just... I somehow leave out the last parts. Even though I know I have to finish them right. It's becoming a problem.

Um... yeah, I guess so. My mom actually still has some of my old report cards from around fourth grade. They said I was bright, but... I always needed constant reminders to finish things. Like classwork, or turning in my homework. 

I understood the lessons fine, I just... I'd miss chunks of the instructions. Unless the teacher was standing right next to me, I guess.

It's supposed to be scratch-resistant, but the maintenance guys wipe them down with paper towels, which is the worst thing you can do. Paper towels are made of wood pulp, so they leave these microscopic scratches on the plastic or glass, and over time it gets all cloudy. You're supposed to use a microfiber cloth. I bought a whole pack of them at the auto parts store. They were on sale, buy one get one free. I gave a few to my neighbor, he drives this old Buick that he's always polishing... 

But yeah, to answer your question, yes. Even during those weeks when I wasn't feeling depressed at all, the voice in the stairwell and the cameras watching me... that didn't stop. It just kept right on going.

Hi, yeah, it's good to meet you too. So, um, I guess the main thing... well, it's been building up for a while, honestly. I work as an insurance claims clerk, so it's a lot of desk work. You know, processing policies, staring at dual monitors, cross-referencing policy numbers, making sure the coverage dates match up with the incident reports. It's tedious, but it pays the bills, and since I didn't finish college, it's a pretty decent gig for me right now. 

But the main thing that finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I just keep getting up from my workstation during the day. Like, constantly. And I know I’m supposed to stay put. I have a quota of claim reviews I need to finish by the end of my shift, and every time I sit down, I tell myself, 'Okay, just power through this batch.' But then, I don't know, a few minutes later I'm up again. I'll go to the breakroom to get water, or I'll walk over to the printer even if I didn't actually print anything, or I'll just stand up to stretch and end up wandering down the hall. It's like my legs just decide they're done sitting. My supervisor walked by yesterday and I wasn't at my desk again, and I could tell she was annoyed. I just sit there, knowing I absolutely need to finish these reviews, and I still just get up and walk away. It's getting to be a real problem.

No, no, it’s not really... it’s not like a pain or a creepy-crawly feeling in my legs, if that’s what you mean. It’s not uncomfortable like my muscles ache or anything like that. It’s more just... I don't know, this constant restless energy? Like, even when I am forcing myself to stay in the chair, I’m not actually sitting still. 

For example, we have these quarterly compliance trainings, right? And they are just absolutely brutal. They put us in this stuffy conference room on the second floor, and the chairs are those cheap mesh ones that squeak if you move too much. And I swear, in those trainings or during our longer team meetings—like the ones where the managers just drone on about new underwriting guidelines for what feels like hours—I’m usually bouncing my leg the entire time. Like, my heel is just going up and down, a mile a minute. I don't even realize I'm doing it until the person next to me gives me a look because I'm shaking the whole table. 

And if I try to stop the leg bouncing, like if I really force myself to keep both feet flat on the floor, I just end up doing something else. I'll start clicking my pen. I actually had to switch to using those cheap pens with the caps instead of the retractable ones because my coworker got so annoyed with me clicking it during a presentation last month. Or I'll just be constantly shifting around in the chair, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. And the whole time, I'm genuinely trying to look focused! I'm staring right at the speaker, nodding, trying to look like the perfect employee who is absorbing every single word about the new policy updates, but my body just refuses to stay at rest. It's just this constant need to be doing something with my hands or my feet, even when I'm trying my hardest to just be normal and sit there.

Yeah, actually, looking back... it really isn't a new thing at all. It's funny you ask about when I was a kid, because my mom actually kept a bunch of my old report cards and parent-teacher conference notes in this big plastic bin in her attic, and I was looking through them a couple of years ago when I was helping her move. And, man, it was like reading a script of my life right now, just scaled down to a third-grade level. 

Like, my teachers would always write these really specific notes. They'd say things like, "He's a very bright boy, very capable," which was always nice, but then there was always a "but." It was always, "but he loses his worksheets constantly." And it was true! I remember having this red folder that was supposed to be for homework, and somehow the papers would just vanish between my desk and my backpack. Or they'd say I missed instructions. Like, the teacher would stand at the front of the room, explain exactly how to do the diorama project or the math assignment, and I’d just be sitting there... maybe looking out the window, maybe drawing on my desk, and then suddenly everyone is working and I have absolutely no idea what we're supposed to be doing. 

And the reminders... oh man. They were always saying I needed constant reminders to actually finish my classwork. I'd start a worksheet, get through maybe the first three questions, and then I'd just drift off. I'd start organizing my crayons, or I'd be trying to see what the kid next to me was doing, or I'd just be staring into space thinking about a video game. The teacher would have to come tap on my desk and say, "Focus, we need to finish this before recess." So, yeah, the fidgeting and the not staying on task... it's definitely been there since elementary school. It's just that back then, the consequence was missing five minutes of recess, and now the consequence is my supervisor glaring at me because I haven't processed enough insurance claims. But the underlying feeling? The getting distracted and needing someone to basically herd me back to what I'm supposed to be doing? That's been happening for as long as I can remember.

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, sure, I have to double-check my work sometimes, right? Like with the claims, if I’m entering a policy number, I might look back at the source document just to make absolutely sure I didn’t transpose a 7 and a 9, because doing that messes up the whole system and then the adjusters get mad. But that’s just, you know, normal job stuff. It’s not like I feel this intense, overwhelming urge to do it over and over again until it feels "just right" or anything like that. 

I don't really have any weird rituals or anything. Like, I don't need to tap the doorframe three times before I leave a room, and I'm definitely not a germaphobe. My apartment is actually a bit of a mess, to be honest. I mean, my desk at work is pretty cluttered too, with sticky notes and half-empty coffee cups. I definitely don't spend time arranging things perfectly. If anything, my problem is the exact opposite—I can't seem to keep things organized or stick to a routine to save my life. So, no, I don't get those urges to repeat things or wash my hands constantly or anything like what you're describing. It's really just the distraction and the restless energy that are the main issues for me.

Hi, yes, it is nice to meet you too. Thank you for seeing me. I, um, well, I guess the main reason I am here, and it took me a little while to actually make the appointment to be honest, because I kept thinking oh it is just a phase, I am just tired or whatever. But what finally made me actually ask for help is that I just keep forgetting all these little things. And I mean things I normally handle with absolutely no problem at all. 

I work as a secretary, so my entire day is basically about managing details and keeping things running smoothly, you know? But lately, it is like my brain just drops things completely. I will forget to return calls, which is so embarrassing when someone has to follow up with me because that is literally my job. Or, for example, I had this registration form recently that I just needed to fill out and turn in, and it just sat there. I kept meaning to do it and then completely forgetting about it the second I walked away or got distracted by something else. 

And it is happening on my commute, too. I will tell myself all day that I need to remember to stop for an errand on the way home, like picking something up at the store or dropping something off, and then I just drive straight home on autopilot and do not even realize I forgot until I am walking through my front door. It is just getting so frustrating because I am usually the one who keeps everything organized, so having all these little slip-ups is really starting to bother me and I figured I should finally talk to someone about it.

Worrying? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, not about a lot of different things, anyway. Like, obviously I get frustrated with myself about the things I just mentioned, the dropping the ball at work and forgetting my errands, because that's just so unlike me and it's super annoying. But I wouldn't call it worrying, exactly? 

Like, my mom is a huge worrier—she will literally lose sleep over whether she left the coffee maker on or if the neighbor's dog is eating enough, just random stuff all the time. But I've never really been like that. I'm usually the one telling everyone else to just take a breath and calm down. I don't sit around stressing about finances or health or, I don't know, what people think of me. If I forget to return a client's call, I don't agonize over whether they're secretly mad at me or if I'm going to get fired, I just think, 'Ugh, seriously, again?' and I fix it and apologize. 

So it's more just... irritation with my own brain right now, rather than feeling anxious or worried about life in general. I just like things to be handled, and when they aren't, I get annoyed at myself, but I definitely don't spend my day worrying about everything under the sun. I've always been pretty even-keeled that way, which is why this whole forgetting phase is so baffling to me, because I don't even have the excuse of being stressed out about a bunch of other things, you know?

Well, see, that's the thing. I've been thinking about this a lot lately, trying to figure out if this is really a new thing or if it's always been there, just hiding, you know? And when I really look back, I mean really look back to when I was little, like elementary school age... yeah, I guess I kind of was that kid. 

I was always the one who forgot to bring home the permission slip for the field trip until the absolute last second, or I'd bring it home and leave it on the kitchen counter and forget to bring it back to school. My mom used to get so exasperated with me. And my backpack... oh my gosh, my backpack was like a black hole. I would do my homework, I swear I would do it, but then it would just disappear into the abyss of crumpled papers and old snack wrappers at the bottom of my bag, and I wouldn't be able to find it when the teacher asked for it. 

And projects! Don't even get me started on projects. The science fairs, the book reports... I could never just sit down and do them. I always needed my mom or my teacher to basically hold my hand and walk me through it step by step. Like, "Okay, first we need to get the poster board. Now we need to outline the title." If they didn't break it down for me and constantly remind me what the next step was, I'd just wander off and start playing with the dog or reading a book that had nothing to do with the assignment. 

So I guess, yeah, I've always been a little scattered. But I always thought I grew out of it! I mean, I made it through high school, got my job, and I've been doing fine for years. I developed all these little systems to keep myself on track, like color-coded folders and sticky notes everywhere. But now, it's like my systems are failing me, or I'm failing the systems, and I'm right back to being that little girl who can't remember where she put her math worksheet. It's just so bizarre to feel like I'm regressing, you know? Like, why now? Why is it suddenly becoming an issue again when I've managed it for so long?

Interrupt people? Um, no, not really. I mean, I don't think I do that. It's actually kind of funny you ask that, because my husband is totally the one who does that in our house. He gets so excited about a story or an idea, and he just jumps right in before you've even finished your sentence, and I'm always having to tell him, "Hey, let me finish, please!" So I'm pretty hyper-aware of it when other people do it, which probably makes me less likely to do it myself, you know? 

I'm usually more the listener type anyway. Especially at work. As a secretary, a huge part of my job is just letting people talk, taking down the information, and making sure I get all the details right. If I was constantly interrupting my boss or the clients, I'd probably miss something important, or they'd get annoyed with me. So I've really trained myself to just sit back, nod, take notes, and wait for the natural pause in the conversation before I chime in. 

And even outside of work, like with my friends, I'm usually the one who just kind of absorbs what everyone else is saying. Sometimes I actually have the opposite problem, where I wait too long to say something, and by the time I finally have a thought put together and I'm ready to speak, the conversation has already moved on to something else entirely! So then I just keep it to myself because it would be weird to bring up a topic from five minutes ago. But no, blurting things out or talking over people... that's definitely not one of my struggles right now. The forgetting things, yes, absolutely, but I'm pretty good at waiting my turn to talk.

Trouble staying focused... um, no, I wouldn't say that. Especially not with conversations, like I was just saying about how I'm the listener of the group. When someone is talking to me, I'm fully there. 

Take my sister, for example. She calls me almost every Sunday, without fail, usually right after she gets back from church, and she will just talk for an hour straight about absolutely everything under the sun. It's her kids, the PTA drama, what her husband is doing with the garage renovation—he's been trying to put in these custom cabinets for like six months now and it's a whole ordeal. But anyway, I listen to every single word. I'm not zoning out or secretly making my grocery list in my head while she talks. I'm actually the one who remembers the details from last week and asks, you know, how the neighbor's dog is doing or if her youngest passed his spelling test. So I definitely pay attention to people. I've never been one to just drift off when someone is looking right at me.

And with tasks, it's honestly kind of the same thing. Once I'm actually doing the task, I'm completely locked in. At the office, I have to do a lot of data entry and calendar management. Juggling the schedules for the different managers is a lot, but when I sit down to sort out a scheduling conflict, I am focused. I have this whole little routine where I get my cup of tea—usually peppermint, I try to avoid too much caffeine in the afternoon because it makes me a little jittery and messes with my sleep—and I just power through it. I don't get distracted by the hum of the air conditioner or people walking by my desk to go to the breakroom. I can just zero in and get the work done. 

So, no, the focus itself isn't the issue at all. Like I was saying earlier, it's more... remembering to start the task, or remembering where I put the physical piece of paper I need for the task. If I have the file right in front of me, boom, I

When did it start getting worse... well, it's actually pretty easy to pinpoint, now that I think about it. It was about 15 months ago. 

That was when I decided to take on this evening certificate program. I've been a secretary for a long time, and I really like my job, but I thought, you know, maybe if I get this business administration certificate, I could eventually move up to an office manager position. It seemed like such a great idea at the time. My husband was super supportive, he was like, "You'd be great at that, you're so organized at work!" Which is ironic now, right? 

But almost as soon as I started those classes, everything just started slipping. Because suddenly, I'm working my full shift at the office—which, like I said, I have my whole routine for—but then I have to rush straight over to the community college on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and then I have coursework on the weekends. It's just like my brain hit a wall. 

The sticky notes and the color-coded folders I mentioned earlier? They just aren't enough anymore. I'm trying to juggle the office managers' schedules, my own homework, reading assignments, and just regular life stuff like grocery shopping and laundry, and that's when I really noticed that my attention and my organization were just... tanking. It's been noticeably harder to manage everything since I started that program. I just feel like I'm constantly dropping the ball now, leaving things behind or forgetting what I was supposed to be doing, whereas before I had it all perfectly balanced. So, yeah, it's been about a year and three months of just feeling completely overwhelmed by it all.

Well, I'm here because... well, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I'm absolutely sure the contractor we hired and some of the people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And you know, kitchens are so important. I remember when I was a little girl, my mother's kitchen was the heart of the house. She had this beautiful yellow wallpaper with little roosters on it. I always wanted a kitchen like that, warm and inviting. But anyway, no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many excuses they all give, I know what they're doing. They think I don't see it, but I do. My husband, bless him, he just doesn't understand. He bought me this lovely set of mixing bowls for my birthday last year, blue ceramic, just gorgeous, but I can't even enjoy using them in that kitchen. They're all in on it, I just know it.

Unusually energetic? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I definitely need my sleep. I usually get my eight hours, well, unless Arthur's snoring wakes me up. He sounds like a broken lawnmower sometimes, bless him. We actually bought a new mattress last year to see if it would help him sleep quieter, one of those thick memory foam ones? The salesman at the furniture store was so pushy about it. He was a young man, wore far too much cologne. I really can't stand strong cologne, it just lingers in the air forever. My father used to wear Old Spice, and that was just a nice, clean, subtle smell, you know? But this young man at the store smelled like a whole department store counter... anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, sleep. No, I don't have times where I'm bursting with energy or staying up all night. I just go to bed at my regular time.

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. I don't hear anything that isn't there. Although, speaking of hearing things, the walls in our house are so terribly thin. We bought the place back in '82, and it's a lovely split-level, but you can hear every little thing from the street. The neighbor's dog, a little terrier mix, barks at absolutely every car that goes by. Yap, yap, yap, all afternoon. I tried talking to Susan about it—she's the owner, a nice enough woman, makes a wonderful pecan pie for the block party every summer—but she just says he's 'protecting the house.' Protecting it from the mailman, I suppose! The mailman we have now is always running late, too. Not like Mr. Henderson from when my kids were little. You could set your watch by Mr. Henderson. But no, I don't hear voices or anything strange like that. Just the usual neighborhood racket.

Hard to follow? Well, Arthur tells me I talk a lot, but husbands always say that, don't they? He's always been a man of few words. When we first started dating, I thought he was just mysterious, you know? We met at a church social, and he just stood by the punch bowl, looking so handsome in his brown suit. They don't make suits like that anymore, the fabric was so sturdy. Now everything you buy at the department store is so thin, it falls apart after three washes. I bought a blouse at Macy's last month, a lovely peach color—peach always washes me out a little, but I liked the collar—and the button popped right off the first time I wore it. I had to dig through my sewing tin to find a match, and you know how impossible it is to find the exact right shade of thread. My grandmother had this huge collection of thread on wooden spools. Wooden spools! You never see those anymore... but no, nobody has ever told me I'm hard to understand. I speak perfectly clearly, if you ask me. I just have a lot to say.

Depressed? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, everyone gets a little blue sometimes, especially in the winter. The winters here feel so much longer than they used to. I remember when the kids were young, we'd get a good snow in December and it was just magical. We had this old wooden toboggan, the kind with the curled front? Arthur spent a whole weekend sanding and varnishing it one year. He was always so good with his hands. He built a birdhouse for the backyard, too, painted it a bright robin's egg blue. The blue jays absolutely loved it, but the squirrels, oh my goodness, the squirrels would just hang upside down and steal all the suet. We tried everything to keep them away—greasing the pole, putting little baffles on it—but those creatures are like acrobats. I saw a special on PBS once about how smart squirrels actually are, they can solve puzzles and remember where they hid nuts for months. Isn't that incredible? I can barely remember where I put my reading glasses half the time! I had a lovely pair with little rhinestones on the corners, but I left them at the grocery store checkout last Tuesday. The cashier was a new girl, very sweet, but she bagged my bread under a heavy bottle of laundry detergent. It was completely squished by the time I got home. But no, I haven't been depressed for two weeks or anything like that. Just the normal ups and downs, you know.

Brain illness? No, no, I've never had anything wrong with my brain. Thank goodness for that. My memory is sharp as a tack, except for the reading glasses, of course. My Aunt Clara, though, she had terrible trouble with her memory toward the end. We had to move her into one of those assisted living places over in Westbridge. It was a very nice facility, they had a beautiful garden with these big, blooming hydrangea bushes. I've always wanted to grow hydrangeas, but the soil in our yard is just too acidic. I read in a magazine—Better Homes and Gardens, I think it was, or maybe Southern Living—that you can change the color of the blooms by putting coffee grounds or rusty nails in the dirt. Isn't that funny? Rusty nails! Arthur used to keep coffee cans full of rusty nails and screws in the garage. He never threw anything away, said you never know when you might need a two-inch wood screw. When we finally cleaned out the garage last spring, we found things we hadn't seen since 1990. We even found the old croquet set we used to play with on the Fourth of July. The kids would get so competitive, especially my son, David. He always had to have the blue mallet. He was so particular, even as a little boy. He wouldn't eat his peas if they touched his mashed potatoes. I had to buy those special plates with the little dividers in them. But no, no brain problems for me. Just regular doctor checkups, that's all.

Controlling my thoughts? Goodness, no, nobody can do that. That sounds like something out of one of those science fiction movies my grandson likes to watch. He came over last weekend and had me sit through this whole film about people living in a computer simulation. It was so loud, all explosions and flashing lights. I told him, "Tommy, my ears are ringing!" He just laughed. He's such a sweet boy, though. He's starting college in the fall, going all the way up to State. I can hardly believe it. It feels like just yesterday he was running around the backyard catching fireflies in a mason jar. We used to poke holes in the lid with an ice pick so they could breathe. You have to be so careful with an ice pick, Arthur always warned me about that. He had an uncle who actually punctured his own hand trying to chip ice for a punch bowl back in the fifties. Can you imagine? They didn't have those fancy refrigerators with the ice makers built right into the door back then. My neighbor, Susan, just remodeled her kitchen and she got one of those refrigerators. Stainless steel, she calls it, but I swear it shows every single fingerprint. I told her, "Susan, you're going to be wiping that thing down three times a day." She's always cleaning, that woman. I think she vacuums her driveway. But no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head or controlling them or anything silly like that. My thoughts are my own.

New medicines? Let me think... no, no new pills or anything like that. I've been taking the same blood pressure pill for, oh, it must be five years now. Dr. Evans prescribed it right before he retired. Such a shame he retired, he had the best bedside manner. His office always smelled like peppermint, he kept a bowl of those little red and white striped candies on his desk. The ones wrapped in clear plastic? I used to take two, one for me and one for Arthur. Arthur loved peppermints, he said they settled his stomach after dinner. We used to have pot roast every Sunday, with carrots and potatoes roasted right in the pan juices. I'd make a gravy from scratch, none of that powdered stuff from a packet. My mother taught me how to make a proper roux. You have to stir it constantly or it burns, and once it burns, you just have to throw the whole thing out and start over. It takes patience, which is something young people just don't seem to have these days. Everything is microwave this and instant that. I saw a commercial the other day for a machine that makes a whole cup of coffee in thirty seconds. Thirty seconds! Where's the joy in that? I still use my old percolator. It makes this wonderful bubbling sound in the morning, it's so comforting. But no, to answer your question, I haven't started any new medications. Just the same old routine.

Less interested? Oh, no, not at all. Outside of dealing with the remodel, I still keep up with my church gatherings, my book club, all my household routines, and family plans the way I usually do. I wouldn't miss book club for the world. We're reading that new mystery novel, the one set in the English countryside? The author describes the gardens so beautifully, it makes me want to plant roses. I tried growing roses once, those lovely climbing ones, but the aphids got to them. Just covered the stems, little green bugs everywhere. I tried spraying them with soapy water, which is what my neighbor Susan told me to do. She swears by Dawn dish soap for everything. She even uses it to get grease stains out of her husband's work shirts. He works down at the auto body shop on Main Street. He's the one who fixed the dent in my bumper when I backed into that mailbox last winter. The snow was piled so high, I just didn't see it! It was a terrible sound, that crunch. The postmaster was very understanding about it, though. He said it happens at least three times a winter on that route. But anyway, yes, I still see everyone just the same. I'm as busy as ever.

Off track? I don't think so. I mean, my daughter sometimes tells me I talk too much when she's trying to get the kids ready for school, but she's just always in a rush. Those mornings are so chaotic at her house. The youngest, little Lily, she refuses to wear anything but purple. Every single day, it has to be purple. We went shopping for her birthday last month, and we had to go to three different stores just to find a purple winter coat. It’s hard to find a good coat these days that isn’t too bulky, you know? You want them to be warm, but if it’s too thick, they can’t even bend their arms. It looks like they’re little snowmen waddling around. When my children were little, I used to knit their sweaters. I made this beautiful cable-knit cardigan for my son—it took me three months! I used this lovely forest green yarn I found at a little shop downtown that closed years ago. It’s a shame how many local shops have closed down. There used to be a wonderful bakery on the corner that made the best eclairs. The custard inside was just perfect, not too sweet. But no, nobody has ever told me I go off track. I just like to share stories.

A head injury? Oh, goodness, no. I've always been very careful, well, except for that time I slipped on the ice outside the grocery store, but I just bruised my hip then. Ice is so treacherous around here. The city really doesn't salt the sidewalks enough, if you ask me. I remember one winter, it must have been '98, the ice storm was so bad the power was out for three days. We had to bring all the perishables out to the garage just to keep them cold. And we huddled around the fireplace in the living room, wrapped in every blanket we owned. My husband built this roaring fire, and we actually toasted marshmallows right there in the house. It felt like camping, but without the mosquitoes. I can't stand mosquitoes. They always seem to bite me more than anyone else. My sister says it's because I eat too many bananas, but I don't know if I believe that. She reads all sorts of strange things in those magazines she gets at the checkout line. The ones with the big bold headlines about aliens and celebrities. I just buy the ones with the recipes. There was a lovely recipe for a lemon pound cake in one last month, but I haven't gotten around to baking it because of all this mess with the house. But no, to answer you, I haven't hit my head or had any injuries like that.

Harder to feel emotions? Oh, no, I feel everything just as much as I always have. I still get so happy when I see my grandchildren, and I certainly get upset about this whole mess with the house. Honestly, sometimes I think I feel things too strongly, like when I watch those commercials on television with the sad animals in the shelters. The ones with that Sarah McLachlan song playing in the background? They just break my heart. I always have to change the channel or I'll start crying right there in the living room. I love animals, you know. We had a golden retriever named Buster when the kids were growing up. He was the sweetest dog, just a big goofball. He used to chase his own tail until he'd get dizzy and fall over on the rug. That rug was a nightmare to keep clean, though. It was a cream color, which was a terrible mistake with a dog and three kids. I spent half my life on my hands and knees with a bottle of carpet cleaner, scrubbing out mud and spilled juice. Kids always seem to spill the brightest colored drinks, don't they? Fruit punch, grape juice... it's never just water. I remember one time my son spilled a whole pitcher of cherry Kool-Aid during a birthday party. We ended up having to put a big armchair over the stain. It actually looked quite nice in that corner, now that I think about it. But no, my emotions are perfectly fine. I feel things just like I always have.

Harm me? No, no, it's really just the contractor and those neighbors who are in on it. I don't go around thinking the whole world is out to get me, I'm not crazy. I mean, the mailman is perfectly nice, he always waves when he drops off the letters. Although, the mail service isn't what it used to be, is it? Sometimes my magazines come a week late, and the edges are all bent. I hate when the pages are creased before I even get to read them. I subscribe to this lovely gardening magazine, *Better Homes and Gardens*, I've been getting it for, oh, thirty years now. They had this wonderful spread last month on growing hydrangeas. I tried to grow hydrangeas in the front yard a few years ago, but the soil here is just too alkaline. They turned out this pale, washed-out pink instead of that beautiful deep blue. You have to add aluminum sulfate to the soil to get the blue color, but I always forget to buy it when I'm at the garden center. The garden center on Elm Street is so nice, though, they have this big orange cat that just sleeps on the bags of potting soil all day. I love cats, but my husband was allergic, so we could only ever have dogs. Buster, the golden retriever I told you about, he was terrified of cats anyway. One time a stray cat hissed at him from the top of the fence, and Buster hid under the porch for three hours. We had to coax him out with a piece of sliced ham. Ham is getting so expensive at the deli counter lately, have you noticed? But anyway, no, I don't think anyone else is trying to cheat me or anything like that. Just the people involved with the house.

A change in my personality? Oh, goodness, no. My kids and my sister, they'd tell you I'm exactly the same woman I've always been. I mean, my sister Linda might say I'm stubborn, but she's been saying that since we were little girls sharing a bedroom. We had this awful floral wallpaper in that room... big yellow and orange daisies. It was the seventies, I suppose, so everything was yellow and orange and avocado green.

A fever? Oh, heavens no, nothing like that. I haven't had a real fever since... oh, it must have been the winter of '98. Or was it '99? The dog was barking... oh, we had a golden retriever back then named Buster. He was such a good boy, but terrified of loud noises. So now I just buy the glass jar with the little gingham lid at the supermarket. It's much easier. 

But no, nobody has ever told me my thinking is disorganized. I keep everything perfectly straight up here.

Well, yes, actually. Well, yes... yes, I do.
