And it's not just my family, doctor. My so-called friends are doing the exact same thing to me. We used to do things together. Like, my friend Brenda, she's always organizing these little community fundraisers, or they'd put together these group travel plans, like taking a bus trip down to the lake for the weekend. But they stopped including me. Just completely cut me out. I had to find out from looking at pictures online that they went on a whole trip last month and didn't even invite me! 

When I finally cornered Brenda and asked her why, she actually had the nerve to say it's

Well, no, not really. I mean, aside from the arguments—which, like I said, are completely justified because they are taking my money—I'm still doing everything I need to do. It's not like I'm sitting around staring at the wall all day. I have to keep my life running, right? 

I still handle all my own meals, for one thing. I go to the grocery store, I make my list, I check the prices, I cook my food. I have to be careful about what I buy now, obviously, because of the situation, but I'm still feeding myself just fine. I make a really good chicken stew, actually, and I still make that. And I get myself to the county clinic when I need to, and I never miss my assistance appointments. You can't miss those, or they cut you off, and I'm not giving anyone an excuse to say I'm not capable of taking care of myself. 

And my room? My things? I keep everything in order the exact same way I always have. Honestly, probably even better than before, because I have to be so meticulous now. I know exactly where my clothes are, my shoes, my paperwork. I have a system for everything. So, no, my daily functioning is perfectly fine. I'm just a person trying to live my life while dealing with thieves, that's all. I'm still me. I'm still doing what I've always done.

See things? Like what, like ghosts or something? Or like, like hallucinations? No, no, absolutely not. I don't see things that aren't there. My eyes work perfectly fine, doctor. Better than fine, actually, because I have to keep them peeled all the time. 

I mean, if you're asking if I see things other people don't see, well, sure, I see the truth! I see what's really going on when everyone else is acting like everything is just perfectly normal. I see the little smirks my sister gives when she thinks I'm not looking, or the way the lock on my box looks just a tiny bit scratched, like someone was messing with it while I was in the bathroom. I see all of that. But I'm not seeing things that don't exist. Everything I see is completely real. 

It's actually kind of funny that you ask that, because my aunt—the one who won't help me with my electric bill anymore—she tried to pull that on me once. She was like, "Oh, you're just seeing things, nobody took your twenty dollars." And I told her, I said, "I am not seeing things, I had two twenties in that envelope on Tuesday, and on Thursday there was only one, and nobody else has a key to this apartment but me and the landlord, and the landlord didn't come in, so you tell me where it went!" 

People love to say you're "seeing things" when they want to make you sound crazy, you know? It's a very common tactic. They want you to doubt your own eyes. If they can make you think you're seeing things, then they can get away with whatever they want. They can walk right in, take my ledger, take my cash, and then just pat my hand and say, "Oh honey, you're just seeing things." Well, I'm not falling for it. I have 20/20 vision. I had it checked at the free clinic two years ago, and the guy told me my eyesight was perfect. So no, I don't see things that aren't there. I only see exactly what is right in front of my face.

Put thoughts into my mind? Or take them out? What, like... like mind control? Or like some kind of sci-fi movie with people wearing tin foil hats? No, no, no, doctor. That's just silly. Nobody is putting thoughts in my head. My thoughts are my own. They always have been. 

I mean, look, my sister might be a thief, and she might be incredibly sneaky about how she gets into my room to take my money, but she's not a psychic. She can't read my mind, and she certainly can't change what I'm thinking. If she could, don't you think she would have made me forget about the money she stole by now? She'd just zap my brain and make me think I spent it all at the grocery store on... I don't know, fancy cheeses or something. But she can't do that. She has to resort to all this sneaking around and lying because my mind is perfectly sharp. I remember exactly what I have and where I put it. 

And as for taking thoughts out... well, sometimes I might walk into the kitchen and forget why I went in there, but that's just normal, right? Everybody does that. You get distracted because you're thinking about how you need to check the lock on the window again, and you forget you went in there for a glass of water. That's not someone taking a thought out of my head. That's just being busy and having a lot on my plate because I have to be so vigilant all the time. 

It's actually really frustrating when people try to act like my thoughts aren't my own, though. Like, my cousin, he told me once that I was only thinking these things about my sister because I was stressed out. Like the stress was somehow putting the thoughts there! I told him, "Stress didn't make my twenty dollars disappear, Kevin!" But they just want to find any excuse to say my thoughts aren't real, valid thoughts. They want to say it's stress, or it's lack of sleep, or it's whatever. But it's not. My thoughts are perfectly clear, and they belong entirely to me. Nobody is tampering with my brain, doctor. Just my belongings.

Messages? Like... like secret codes on the news or something? No, doctor, definitely not. 

I mean, I watch TV, sure. I have this little flat screen in my room, it's not very big, maybe nineteen inches, and I mostly just watch the game shows in the morning. You know, to pass the time while I'm keeping an eye on things. I watch the people guessing how much a can of soup or a bottle of laundry detergent costs. Nobody on those shows is talking to me. They're just actors and contestants trying to win a car. The man on the local news is just telling me if it's going to rain, he's not sending me a special signal. 

And the radio? I don't even own a radio anymore. I used to have one of those little alarm clock radios, the black plastic ones? But it broke a few years ago. The dial just snapped right off when I tried to change the station, so I threw it in the dumpster out back. So I definitely couldn't get messages from that even if I wanted to. 

As for the internet... well, I have a cheap smartphone, but I don't even have a data plan on it right now. I can't be paying forty or fifty dollars a month for internet when I'm constantly having to replace the cash my sister takes from me. I have to pinch every single penny. So I only use the internet when I can get free Wi-Fi, like here at the clinic or if I go sit outside the library. And when I do use it, I'm just doing regular things. I check my bank account balance—which I check three times a day now, just to be absolutely certain nothing is missing from there, too—or I look up a recipe for dinner. 

I don't have time for nonsense like secret messages. Why would anyone on the TV or the internet care about me anyway? I'm just a regular person trying to hold onto the little bit of money I have. The only messages I get are the ones right in real life, like when I see my sister's car parked a block away when she told my mom she was going to be at work all day. That's a message, alright. It tells me exactly what she's up to. But no, nothing coming out of a screen. That's just silly.

Well, I came in because... honestly, it’s getting completely impossible to run my company. I mean, when you're the chief executive, you expect a certain amount of gossip, you know? Office politics, people whispering behind your back, that’s just part of the job and you learn to deal with it. But this is... this is constant, and it's so invasive. 

I keep hearing people talking about me, specifically about me, right through the walls of the main conference room. And it’s not just muffled sounds where you can't make out the words, it’s my board members, or my senior staff, and they are saying horrible things. They keep saying I’m completely ruining the company, that I'm driving the whole operation into the ground. And I hear it from my phone, too. Which is the part I just cannot figure out because I’ll actually power the phone completely down—screen black, totally off, sitting right there on my desk—and their voices still come pouring out of the speaker. 

It sounds so incredibly clear and real that I actually answer them. I’ll speak up and defend my quarterly decisions out loud, or I'll tell them I can hear them and they need to stop, and I'll be halfway through my sentence before I look around and realize... I'm totally alone in the room. Or my assistant is standing in the doorway staring at me, and I realize absolutely no one else heard a single thing. It’s just... how are you supposed to focus on margins and lead a company when your own board is constantly whispering through the electronics and the drywall all day? It's exhausting, it really is.

Energetic? God, no. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite right now. I mean, people always assume that when you’re running a company you must be this endless well of energy, you know, the type of person who’s up at 4 AM hitting the treadmill and answering emails before the sun even comes up. And sure, I have my routine, and I work long hours—you have to, it's just the nature of the beast when you're at the top—but I’ve always, always needed a solid seven or eight hours of sleep to actually function properly. Especially when I'm dealing with complex things like our quarterly projections or investor relations. 

But lately... I mean, there is absolutely no burst of energy, no feeling like I just don’t need to sleep. I *want* to sleep. I desperately want to just close my eyes and have it be completely quiet for once. But how are you supposed to get any rest when your own senior staff is practically shouting at you through the bedside lamp? So, yes, I might be awake, I might be lying there at 2 AM just staring a hole into the ceiling, but it is definitely not because I have too much energy. It’s because I’m completely drained, just utterly depleted, and I'm lying there trying to figure out how to protect my company from these people who won't stop talking. So no, I've never had a time where I felt like I didn't need rest... I just can't get any peace to actually take the rest, if that makes sense.

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say depressed. I mean, sure, I'm stressed. Anyone would be stressed in my position. When you're the chief executive, you're carrying the weight of the entire organization on your shoulders, and that's a heavy burden even on a good day. You've got shareholders breathing down your neck, employees looking to you for direction, and then, on top of all that, you have your own board members constantly undermining you, whispering through the walls, telling you you're ruining everything. It's incredibly stressful. It's frustrating. It makes me angry, honestly, because I've worked so hard to build this company up, to get it to where it is, and they just don't see that. Or maybe they do see it and they're just trying to tear me down out of spite. 

But depressed? Like, sad and crying all day? No, absolutely not. I don't have time to be depressed. I have a company to run. I have to stay sharp, I have to stay focused, even when it feels like the whole world is conspiring against me. I mean, there are moments where I feel completely overwhelmed, where I just want to lock my office door and hide under my desk because the voices are just so loud and so relentless. But that's not depression, that's just... survival, you know? It's self-preservation. I'm trying to protect myself and my company from these people. So no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. Just incredibly, incredibly stressed and exhausted by the whole situation. It's like fighting a war on two fronts—the actual business challenges, and then this constant psychological warfare from my own team. It's just too much sometimes, but I'm not depressed. I'm just trying to hold it all together.

Medical illness? No. Head injury? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I try to take very good care of myself, physically at least. You have to, right? Like I said, the demands of being a chief executive are just astronomical. You can't afford to be out sick, you can't afford to have a fuzzy head because you bumped it or something. So I'm very careful. I get my annual physicals, my blood work is always perfect—my GP says I have the cholesterol of a twenty-year-old, actually, which is amazing considering the stress I'm under. 

But as far as anything neurological, seizures, head trauma... no, nothing like that. I haven't been in any accidents, I haven't fallen. The only thing that's wrong with my head is that it's constantly being bombarded by these voices from my board members. And I know people might think, "Oh, she's hearing things, she must have a brain tumor," because that's what happens on those medical TV shows, right? Someone starts hearing the radio in their teeth and it turns out to be a massive tumor pressing on their temporal lobe. But I haven't had any headaches—well, aside from tension headaches from the stress of it all, but not, like, medical headaches. No dizzy spells, no passing out, no seizures. My brain is physically completely fine. It's just... it's the environment. It's the technology they're using, or the acoustics of the building, or however they are managing to project their voices into my space. It's an external problem, a personnel problem, really, not a medical one. So, no, physically, neurologically, I am completely healthy. It's just my company that's sick, and they're the ones making it that way.

Interested? I mean... I don't know if 'interested' is the right word, but... yes. Yes, I suppose that's exactly what's happening. It’s actually... it’s really strange, if I’m being completely honest with you. Because I used to be the person driving absolutely every single idea in this company. I mean, I was the engine. If we had a new branch opening or a major launch, I was the one on the phone at ten o'clock at night, calling people right after the openings, getting the immediate feedback, analyzing the numbers, just buzzing with the energy of it all, you know? I thrived on that connection. I absolutely loved my work. It wasn't just a job, it was my entire identity, my passion. 

But now... I don't know what's happened to me. The drive is just gone. Completely gone. I go into my office, and I shut the heavy oak door to try and block out the noise, and I can literally just sit at my desk for hours. Just sitting there in the leather chair, staring at the printed agenda for the day. I don't even really read it. I just stare at the bullet points until they blur into little black lines on the paper, and hours will go by. And I don't do anything. I don't call anyone. I barely even speak to my staff anymore—my executive assistant just leaves folders on the edge of my desk now because she knows I don't want to engage, I don't want to talk. 

And it’s not just at the office, either. It bleeds into everything. I go home and I barely speak to my husband. He tries, you know, he’s a good man, he asks me about my day, asks what we should do for the weekend, and I just... I have absolutely nothing to give him. I don't want to see our friends, I don't want to go to the dinners we used to enjoy. I just don't want to talk to anyone. I just feel... nothing. I look at the quarterly reports, the things that used to get my blood pumping, and I feel almost nothing about the work I used to love so much. It's like all that passion, all that fire that got me to the top in the first place, it just evaporated. I just sit there staring at the paper, feeling completely empty.

Express my emotions? I... well, it goes right back to what I was just saying, really. How can I express emotions when I don't have any left to express? I mean, think about it. I just told you how I used to be the one driving every single idea, right? Back then, my face, my voice... they were alive. When I was calling people right after those new branch openings, my voice was probably bouncing off the walls. I was animated, I was passionate, I was smiling so much my jaw would hurt by the end of the day. People fed off that energy. I was expressive because I cared so deeply.

But now... now that I feel almost absolutely nothing about this work I used to love so much... my face just kind of matches that nothingness. When I'm sitting at my desk for hours, just staring at that printed agenda like I mentioned, my face is just... blank. It feels heavy, almost like it's made of stone. I don't smile. I don't frown. I just stare. And my voice... on the rare occasions I actually do speak, since I barely speak to my staff or my husband anymore... it just comes out completely flat. Like a dial tone. 

My husband actually asked me the other night if I was furious with him because I sounded so cold, so monotone when I answered a simple question about dinner. But I wasn't mad. I wasn't anything. It’s just that the fire is gone, so there’s no spark left to put into my words or my expressions. I don't have the energy to fake a smile for my assistant, and I don't have the inflection in my voice to pretend I care about the quarterly reports. You can't project warmth or enthusiasm on the outside when you're just feeling completely empty on the inside, you know? It all just feels completely disconnected.

Three months. It’s been going on for about the past three months now. I mean, I remember when it first started, I genuinely thought there was just a technical issue, like a crossed wire or something with the telecommunications setup in the executive suite. Because at first, it was just coming through my phone. I would be sitting there, and my smartphone would be completely locked, screen totally dark, just sitting there on my desk, and I would hear them. The board members. Whispering about me, criticizing my decisions, right through the speaker of a turned-off phone. 

And I thought, well, maybe it’s a glitch, maybe someone left a secure line open or hacked into the microphone. But then... then it wasn't just the phone anymore. It started coming from the walls. The actual walls of my office. It’s been three solid months of this happening. I even had the building maintenance manager come up during that first month because I was convinced the HVAC system or the acoustics were somehow carrying their conversations from the boardroom directly into my space. They poked around the vents, they tapped on the drywall, and they tried to tell me there was nothing there, no sound carrying over. But I know what I'm hearing. 

It’s been about three months of them using the walls and my phone to project their voices at me, just constantly bombarding my space. Which, like I was saying before, is probably why I just shut down and stare at my desk now. You can't think, you can't lead a company when the walls are literally talking to you with the voices of people trying to undermine you. It's exhausting. But yes, to answer your question, it's been roughly three months of this.

No, no, they've always... they've been tied together this whole time. I mean, think about it from my perspective. How could I possibly feel anything but completely empty when this has been happening? From the very first week, the very first time I heard them coming through my locked phone—the board members, whispering, plotting—that was when the fire just went out. It was immediate. I remember it so vividly. It was a Tuesday, I had just finished reviewing the Q3 projections, and then... the whispers started. And right then, it was like someone just flipped a switch inside me. 

There hasn't been a single day, let alone two weeks, where I was hearing them but still felt like my old self. How could there be? You can't be the engine of a company, you can't be buzzing with energy and calling people at ten o'clock at night when you know, you absolutely know, that the people you're working for are projecting their voices through the HVAC system to criticize you. The emptiness, the staring at the agenda until the lines blur, the complete inability to talk to my husband or my staff... it all started exactly when the voices started. It’s been three months of both. They are completely intertwined. The voices started, and the passion died. Just like that. There hasn't been any break or any period where one was happening without the other. It's just been three solid months of this heavy, blank nothingness while they whisper at me from the walls.

I... wait, didn't I just say that? I mean, I'm sorry, I don't mean to be rude, but I feel like I just explained that exact thing. No. The answer is no. There hasn't been a two-week period, or a one-week period, or even a two-day period where the voices were there but I felt fine. 

I just... I don't think you're understanding the timeline here, or maybe I'm just not explaining it right, even though I feel like I am. It's like I was saying about that Tuesday, when I was looking at the Q3 projections. Before that moment, I was me. I was the CEO, I was driven, I was the woman who built this regional division from the ground up. And then the phone started whispering. The locked, dark phone. And the very second that happened, the second I realized the board was monitoring me, criticizing me, projecting their voices into my private office... that was it. The emptiness was immediate. 

It's not like the voices started and then a month later I got depressed or flat or whatever you want to call it. It was instantaneous. The voices started, and the fire went out. So, no, there hasn't been any two-week gap. It's been three months of the voices, and three months of the emptiness, happening at the exact same time, every single day. I just... I don't know how else to explain that they are completely tied together.

No, never. Never in my life. I mean, I'm forty-three years old, and up until three months ago, my mind was... it was a fortress. It was sharp. I built my career on being able to focus, on being the person in the room who could tune out the noise and just get things done. I mean, I didn't finish college, I dropped out because I was already managing a team and making more money than my professors, so I've always trusted my instincts and my mind. 

I've never experienced anything even remotely like this. Not in my twenties when I was working eighty-hour weeks to prove myself, not in my thirties when I took over the regional division... never. There was never a time when I heard things that weren't there, or, well, heard things that other people claim aren't there. I never had voices coming out of my electronics, I never had the walls whispering at me. 

My home, my office, my car... they were all just quiet, normal spaces until that Tuesday three months ago. Before that, the only voices I heard in my office were the ones coming out of the speakerphone when I actually dialed someone. I was completely fine. My head was clear. I was driven. This... this whole nightmare with the board members projecting into my space, this is completely new. It started three months ago, out of nowhere, and it hasn't stopped since. But before that? No. Never. Not once.

Yes, absolutely. A month after it all started, the voices were... they were still there. They were relentless. I remember it was right around the time I was supposed to finalize the annual budget, which is usually my favorite time of year, you know? I love diving into the spreadsheets, finding the efficiencies, moving the numbers around until everything clicks into place. It's like a puzzle, and I've always been brilliant at it. But a month in, the emptiness was so heavy, it was like I was moving underwater. I'd sit at my desk, staring at the monitor, just feeling absolutely nothing, no drive, no spark. 

And while I was sitting there, feeling like a ghost in my own office, the voices were still coming through the vents. It was the board members, always the board members. They were whispering about my budget proposals, laughing at my allocations, telling each other I was losing my edge. I could hear them so clearly, even when I felt completely numb to everything else. I tried to focus, I really did, I tried to push through the flatness and just do my job, but they wouldn't stop. They were there a month in, they were there two months in, they're here right now. So yes, to answer your question, a month after the fire went out, the voices were still burning me alive.

Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I came in because... I keep steering clear of my own workshop. And any family get-together where my brother-in-law might show up, I avoid those too. Yeah, it was both, actually. We had a... well, a confrontation out in the workshop. This whole thing has been going on ever since that happened, which was about two years and four months ago now.

Yeah, they do. Out of nowhere, really. I'll just be standing there, maybe shaving or... or working on one of my paintings, and suddenly I see his hand holding that heavy tool again. It's like a picture that just pops right into my head. Even after all this time, it still makes my chest tighten up when it happens.

Yeah, I do. Most nights I can get to bed okay, but... well, I just lie there listening for noises in the house. Or I'll wake up from a bad dream about the workshop. And once that happens, I'm usually wide awake for an hour or two before I can settle back down.

Yeah, I do. Even when I'm somewhere completely safe, like at the senior center or down in the church basement, I find myself checking who just came in. I always make sure I know exactly where the door is... and I'm constantly checking whether anyone is standing too close behind me. I just can't seem to drop my guard.

No, I wouldn't really say I get very upset. I mean, like I mentioned before, my chest might get a little tight if the memory just pops into my head, but... I don't get all emotional or break down if I see something that reminds me of it. I just kind of brush it off and keep doing whatever I'm doing.

No, I didn't think he was going to kill me or anything like that. I mean, it was tense, and he was really in my face yelling, but... I didn't think I was in any real physical danger of being seriously hurt. It was just a very ugly situation.

No, he didn't. I mean, he was shouting and saying a lot of nasty things, but... he never actually said he was going to hit me or put me in the hospital or anything. It was just a lot of loud, angry talk, no actual threats like that.

No, it's not that. I'm not worried about being embarrassed or what other people might think of me. At my age, I don't really care much about that sort of thing. It's just... I'd rather avoid the headache of being around him, you know? It doesn't have anything to do with the rest of the family judging me.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have my moments, but... I don't feel down or depressed most days. I get up, do what I need to do around the house. It's not like a dark cloud hanging over me all the time or anything.

No, not really. I mean, I worry about normal things now and then, like the bills or the car needing work, but... I don't sit around worrying all day about everything under the sun. It's just the usual stuff, nothing out of the ordinary.

Afraid? No, I wouldn't use that word. I mean, I'm not scared of my brother-in-law, and I'm certainly not scared of my own workshop. It's just... I just really don't want to be around him or in that space. Like I said before, it's more about avoiding the whole headache of it all. So no, I don't feel afraid.

They told me I had to come see you because... well, they say my talking gets all mixed up. Like, I'll just be trying to explain about the keys. I have this heavy ring of keys for the night shift, cleaning the offices, you know? And the metal clinking, it always makes me think about the jail. Which is funny because I was just telling my supervisor about the jail, and then the prayer rug. You ever see a real woven prayer rug? The patterns on them are exactly like how chess pieces move. The knights, specifically, they do that L-shape jump. I used to carve chess pieces out of soap a long time ago, back before I dropped out of school. 

But anyway, I try to explain all this to people—the keys, the jail, the rug, the chess pieces—and they just look at me blank. They tell me they cannot follow what I am saying at all. So I guess that's what brings me here.

High? Yeah, I guess you could say that. There are days, you know, where I just feel... powerful. Like I'm vibrating with it. I'll be laughing, talking loud to everyone in the building, just feeling on top of the world. But then, you know, if someone looks at me wrong or questions what I'm doing, I just snap. I'll start shouting over the littlest things. Like the other day, this guy asked me why I was using the blue mop bucket instead of the yellow one. The blue one, it’s got these wheels that squeak, and the squeak sounds exactly like a mouse I used to have when I was a kid. A white mouse with red eyes. I kept him in a glass tank, and he'd run on that wheel all night. Squeak, squeak, squeak. My mom hated it. She said it kept her up, but she was always up anyway, smoking cigarettes in the kitchen. She smoked those long ones, the 100s. The smoke would just hang there in the air, like a ghost. I always thought smoke looked like ghosts trying to form a shape, you know? But yeah, the bucket... I just yelled at him. Over a bucket.

Voices? Yeah, I do. Sometimes when I'm working, I'll hear this man's voice. It comes right out of the air vents, or sometimes when I'm alone in the mop closet. He says my name, or he tells me that I ruined everything. And it's not like a thought, it sounds exactly like someone is standing right next to my ear. Which is crazy because the mop closet is so small, you know? It's barely big enough for the buckets and the industrial floor wax. That floor wax smells terrible, by the way. It smells like old lemons and chemicals. Reminds me of the time I tried to fix up this old Chevy Nova I had. I bought it off a guy who lived two towns over. He had this huge dog, a Mastiff, I think. Thing weighed more than I did. It just sat on the porch the whole time we were doing the paperwork. I never did get that car running right. The carburetor was completely shot. You need a good carburetor if you're gonna go anywhere, otherwise the engine just floods. But yeah, the voice in the closet... it's just as real as you talking to me right now.

Yeah, I still hear him then, too. Like, there was a stretch... maybe a month ago? I wasn't feeling all wired up and powerful, and I wasn't feeling totally dragged down either. Just sort of regular, you know? Just doing my shift. But even then, for like two or three weeks straight, I still heard the man in the vents. And it wasn't just him, I also knew the people in the building were signaling each other about me. They do this thing with their coffee cups when I walk by. Coffee cups... you know, I found this mug in the trash once, perfectly good ceramic mug. It had a picture of a lighthouse on it. I always wanted to visit a lighthouse. They have those big spiral staircases inside. Must take forever to walk up all those steps. Imagine carrying a bucket of paint up a spiral staircase. I painted my aunt's house once. It was this awful shade of green, like pea soup. She loved it, though. Made me meatloaf every night I worked on it. Meatloaf with ketchup on top. I don't really like ketchup, it's too sweet. But anyway, yeah, even when I'm feeling calm, the voice is still there, and the signaling with the cups.

Depressed? Yeah... yeah, there are times like that. On my bad days, I just... I sit on the edge of the bed right after my morning prayer, and I just feel so heavy. Empty, you know? Like there's absolutely no point in even cleaning myself up or walking out the front door. I just stare at the floorboards. My floorboards are that cheap laminate stuff, you know the kind? Keeps it hot for hours. But yeah, I just can't sit still for very long without feeling like I need to jump out of my skin.

Yeah, pretty much every single day. It's just a constant thing. Like yesterday, I was trying to get through this stack of performance reviews for my team, and I just couldn't keep my eyes on the screen. Which is bad, because I really need to get them done before Friday. We're having this big team lunch on Friday at this new Italian place that opened up down the street. Supposedly they make all their pasta from scratch right there in the window. My buddy Dave went last week and said the lasagna was unbelievable, but he said parking is a total nightmare. You have to park like three blocks away and walk, which I don't mind, but you know how it is when you only have an hour for lunch. Plus, it's supposed to rain on Friday, so walking three blocks in the rain just for some lasagna seems like a lot of effort. I might just order a sandwich from the deli instead. They do this turkey club that's really good, they use that thick-cut bacon. But yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely an everyday struggle for me.

Yeah, organization is... well, honestly, I don't really know if I have trouble with it or not. I mean, my desk at work is pretty messy, but I usually know where things are, mostly. It's like organized chaos, you know? My boss hates it. He's one of those guys who needs everything completely spotless. He actually came in on a Saturday once just to reorganize the supply closet because he couldn't stand how the printer paper was stacked. He's a good guy, though. He let me leave early a couple of weeks ago when my car broke down. The alternator just completely died on me right on the highway. I had to get it towed to this shop near my house, and the guy there tried to charge me like eight hundred bucks. I told him he was crazy, you can get a remanufactured one online for like a hundred and fifty. My brother-in-law is a mechanic, so I usually just have him look at stuff, but he was out of town on a fishing trip. They go up to this lake in Wisconsin every year for walleye. He caught a huge one last time, mounted it in his basement. His wife hates it, says it smells, but I think it looks pretty cool. But yeah, organization... I'm not really sure if it's a huge problem for me or just how I do things.

Yeah, it definitely has. It's actually gotten to the point where my manager put it in my formal review, which was really stressful. We had the review in that little glass conference room near the breakroom, the one where the AC is always blasting. I swear it's like forty degrees in there. I had to wear my heavy winter coat inside just to stop shivering. It's this North Face jacket I got on sale last Black Friday, actually a really good deal. I stood in line for like three hours outside the mall, which was crazy because it was snowing, but they were giving out those free hot chocolates from the kiosk, so it wasn't too bad. But yeah, the review was rough. And at home, it's causing issues too, because people feel like they can't count on me to follow through on things. It just adds to the conflict, you know? Like my sister was supposed to come over for dinner on Sunday, and she got all mad because she said I always forget to pick up the stuff she likes. She's doing this keto diet right now, which seems impossible to me. She's eating like, blocks of cheese and bacon, but no bread. I couldn't live without bread. There's this bakery near my house that makes these fresh sourdough loaves on weekend mornings, and the smell is just incredible. But yeah, it's definitely causing some real problems for me.

I mean, I don't really know if I have trouble focusing on fun stuff. I guess it depends on what it is. Like, if I'm watching a movie, sometimes I'll pull out my phone and start scrolling, but everyone does that now, right? My wife and I were trying to watch that new superhero movie on streaming the other night, the one with the guy from that old sitcom. He looks so different now, I think he got hair plugs or something. Which is fine, no judgment, but it just looks a little unnatural around the hairline, you know? Anyway, we were watching it, and the dog started whining to go out. We have this golden retriever mix, Buster, and he's got this stomach thing where he can only eat this super expensive prescription food. We tried switching him to a cheaper brand once, and it was a disaster. I had to rent one of those carpet cleaners from the grocery store. Have you ever used one of those? They're incredibly heavy, and getting it into the trunk of my sedan was a whole workout. I really need to get an SUV, especially with winter coming. My buddy just bought a used Tahoe and he loves it, says it handles the snow like a champ. But yeah, for fun stuff... I don't know, I guess I haven't really paid attention to whether I lose focus or not.

Yeah, I was definitely like this as a kid, too. My mom actually still brings it up. She kept all these old report cards and notes from my teachers in elementary school, and they all said the same thing—that I'd rush through my work, lose my homework, talk out of turn, and just couldn't stay in my seat without them constantly reminding me. She keeps them in this giant plastic tub in her basement, right next to her sewing machine. She's super into quilting right now. It's wild, she spends hours matching up these tiny little squares of fabric. She made me this huge quilt for my bed last Christmas, all in these dark blue and gray colors. It's really warm, actually, maybe a little too warm. I had to kick it off the bed in the middle of the night last week because I woke up sweating. I usually sleep with a fan on, even in the winter, just for the white noise. I bought this tower fan from Costco a few years ago, and it has this little remote control that I always lose in the couch cushions. Our couch is one of those deep, squishy sectionals, and it just eats everything. I found like three dollars in quarters and a dog toy down there the other day. But yeah, the stuff at school and home... it's been happening since I was little, for sure.

Well, it's... it's a lot, honestly. I came in because, well, I keep hearing these voices. And I don't mean like a passing thought or, you know, how sometimes you think you hear something when the wind blows. I mean it's as clear as somebody standing right there in my little studio apartment. It's just a small place, you know, so when I'm there, I know I'm alone. But then, right out of nowhere, even when the house is completely quiet and there's absolutely nobody there, I hear them. They say my name, just clear as day, and they keep telling me that my work is being judged. I'm a personal care aide, you know, and I try so hard to do a good job for the people I look after, but these voices, they just won't stop talking about how I'm being watched and judged. It's been so exhausting, and I just... I don't know how to make it stop or why it's happening when I know nobody else is in the room with me.

Well, it’s funny you say that, because... yes, actually. But it's a strange kind of feeling. Sometimes I wake up and I just feel so... so bright, you know? Like I’ve been chosen for something incredibly important. I get all these ideas rushing through my head, these huge, magnificent plans, and I swear to you, I feel like the whole town of Greenville just cannot hold me or everything I'm meant to do. I feel like I could conquer the world before breakfast and I have all this energy just buzzing in my veins. 

But then... it doesn't always stay a good feeling. It turns on me. I'll be flying high with all that energy and those big thoughts, and then I just snap. I mean, I snap *hard* at people over the smallest, most ridiculous things. Like just the other day, I was at work, and one of my clients—a sweet older lady who can't help it, she's hard of hearing—she just asked me to repeat myself because she didn't catch what I said about her lunch. Just a normal thing to ask, right? But I just lost it. I snapped at her so badly, my heart was just pounding with anger over this tiny little question. It's like I go from feeling like this glowing, chosen person with all these massive plans, straight to being furious just because someone needs me to say a sentence twice. It’s so exhausting, going back and forth like that, and I don't want to be mean to my clients, I really don't, I need this job, but that energy just gets so sharp and I can't keep it inside.

Well, yes. Yes, they did. And that's what really scared me, to be perfectly honest with you. Because you'd think, wouldn't you, that if the voices and the feelings were tied to being so wound up and full of all those big ideas, that when that finally stopped, the voices would stop too? But they didn't. 

There was this stretch—it was a little while back, maybe a couple of months ago—where all that buzzing, frantic energy finally just drained right out of me. I wasn't having those huge thoughts about being chosen anymore, and I wasn't snapping at my clients like I told you about. I was actually sleeping through the night again, waking up at a normal time, going to work, coming home... just feeling, well, normal. My mood was completely flat, just average, everyday normal. No highs, no anger. 

But the voices... they stayed. They just kept right on going. Every time I was in my apartment, even though I felt fine otherwise, there they were, clear as a bell, telling me my work was being judged. And I still had this awful, sinking feeling that people were tracking what I was doing, like someone was keeping a tally of every little move I made at my job. It didn't make any sense because my mood was fine, I was resting, I wasn't buzzing, but I still had to listen to them talking about me. It went on like that for several weeks, just me feeling totally normal in my own head, but still having to deal with these voices and that terrible feeling of being watched and judged. It makes you feel like you can't even trust your own quiet moments, you know? Because even when I'm calm, they're not.

Well, depressed... no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I've felt deeply depressed or anything like that. It's not like I'm sitting around crying all day or feeling like life isn't worth living, you know? It's more just... well, it's the voices, and that buzzing energy, and then the snapping. But as for being down in the dumps for weeks on end, no. 

I mean, sure, I get tired. Anyone would get tired doing what I do. Being a personal care aide is hard work, especially when you're 55 and you've been on your feet all day, lifting people, helping them bathe, making sure they eat. It wears you out. And when you come home to a tiny apartment and have to listen to voices judging you on top of all that, well, it's exhausting. But it's an exhausted feeling, not a depressed feeling, if that makes sense. I still get up, I still go to work, I still try my best to take care of my ladies. I don't just lay in bed unable to move from sadness. It's just... it's just a lot to carry, but I wouldn't call it depression. I just want the noise to stop and the buzzing to go away so I can just do my job and live my life in peace.

Seizures? Oh, no, no, nothing like that. I mean, I’ve seen people have seizures—working in personal care, you see a bit of everything, you know? I had a client a few years ago, a lovely gentleman, Mr. Henderson, who had epilepsy, and I remember exactly what that looked like. It’s frightening to watch, let me tell you, just awful to see someone lose control of their body like that. But me? No, I’ve never had anything like that happen to me. 

My body is perfectly fine, really. I mean, sure, my back aches from lifting clients, and sometimes my feet swell up if I’ve been doing back-to-back shifts, but my brain doesn't... short-circuit like that, if you know what I mean. The buzzing energy I told you about, that feels like it’s in my blood, like I’m vibrating from the inside out, but it doesn’t make me pass out or shake or anything. I’ve never lost consciousness or had any kind of fit. It’s just the thoughts, the rushing ideas, and those awful voices. But physically, aside from being worn down to the bone from the work and the stress of it all, my body doesn’t do anything strange like seizures. Thank goodness for that, at least, because I don't know how I'd manage to keep working if I had to worry about collapsing on the job. No, definitely no seizures.

Well, let's see... I'm 55 now, and this all started... gosh, it feels like it's been going on forever, but if I really sit down and trace it back, it's been about nine months. Yes, nine months. I remember because it was right around the time the weather started turning cold last year, right after Thanksgiving. 

I was working a double shift at Mrs. Gable's house—she's one of my tougher clients, bless her heart, but she needs a lot of turning and positioning—and I was just so exhausted. I remember walking back to my apartment, the wind was just howling, and that's when I first heard them. Just a whisper at first, but clear, you know? Telling me I hadn't cleaned Mrs. Gable properly, that I was cutting corners. And then that feeling settled in, that heavy, awful feeling that someone at the agency was watching me, keeping a file on me. 

And it hasn't stopped since. Nine whole months of these voices and this constant fear that my work is being monitored. I mean, I've been doing this job for years, I don't even have my high school diploma, but I know how to care for people. I know how to do my job. But for nine months, every time I go to work, every time I come home, it's there. The voices judging me, the feeling of being tracked... it's just exhausting. Nine months of not being able to just do my work in peace without feeling like I'm under a microscope. It really takes a toll on a person, it really does. You try to push through it, you try to just focus on the clients, but when it's day in and day out for nine months... well, it just wears you down to the absolute bone.

Hard to follow? Jumbled? No, I don't think so. I mean, nobody has ever come right out and said, "I can't understand a word you're saying," or anything like that. I talk the way I've always talked. When I'm at work, I have to be very clear, you know? If I'm telling Mrs. Gable she needs to sit up so I can adjust her pillows, I have to speak clearly and plainly, otherwise she gets confused. And my supervisor at the agency, she's never called me into the office to say my reports don't make sense or that I'm talking in circles. 

Now, sometimes when that buzzing energy gets going, the one I mentioned before, my thoughts do start racing. It's like a train going too fast down a hill, and I have all these ideas about how to reorganize the supply closet or a new schedule for bathing the clients, and I might talk a little faster than usual because I just have to get it all out before I lose it. But even then, I'm making perfect sense to myself, and nobody has ever stopped me to say I'm talking gibberish. I just have a lot to say in those moments. 

But jumbled? Like I'm mixing up my words or not making sense? No, I don't think anyone has ever accused me of that. I might talk a lot, especially when I'm feeling that pressure, that buzzing, but I'm always clear about what I'm trying to communicate. I have to be, in my line of work. You can't be mumbling or talking nonsense when you're responsible for someone's well-being. So no, nobody has ever told me my speech is hard to follow. I think I communicate just fine, even with everything else going on.

Well, let me think about that... yes, definitely. Actually, it was longer than two weeks, I can tell you that for sure. 

You see, there was this stretch... I remember because that buzzing energy I was telling you about, the vibrating in my blood and all those racing thoughts, well, it finally just settled down. My energy dropped back to my regular level, and thank goodness, because I actually started sleeping normally again. For a while there, I was just running on fumes, but then my body just kind of regulated itself. I was getting my solid seven or eight hours, waking up feeling rested, making my morning coffee without feeling like I was being driven by a motor, you know? I felt like my usual self again, just a regular fifty-five-year-old woman getting ready for her shift. 

But the thing is, even though my mood leveled out and I was resting so much better, the rest of it didn't stop. Not at all. I’d be standing there in my kitchen, feeling perfectly calm, and there the voices were, still whispering about how I was cutting corners or messing up with the clients. And that awful, heavy belief that the agency was keeping a file on me, that they were judging my work and tracking my every move? That stuck right with me. 

I would go into work, feeling physically fine, not sped up or exhausted or anything, but I'd still be looking over my shoulder the whole time. I'd be turning Mrs. Gable or fixing her meals, and I was just absolutely convinced my supervisor was scrutinizing every single thing I did. So, yes, to answer your question, it wasn't just two weeks. It kept going for several weeks like that. Several weeks of just going about my normal routine, sleeping fine, feeling perfectly fine in my mood, but having my mind constantly bombarded by those voices and that deep, heavy fear that I was being monitored. It’s so strange, isn't it? You'd think if your body calms down and your mood goes back to normal, your mind would too, but no. For weeks and weeks, it was just me, my normal sleep schedule, and those relentless voices. It just makes you wonder how much a person is supposed to take.

Well, yes, actually. It's the strangest thing. You know how normally, if you only get a couple hours of sleep, you wake up feeling like you've been run over by a truck? Your eyes are heavy, your body aches, you just want to crawl back under the covers and hide from the world. But during those times... those buzzing, high-energy stretches... it wasn't like that at all. Not even a little bit.

I remember there were so many nights... I mean, just night after night where I would finally lay down around, oh, maybe two or three in the morning. And I wasn't even tired then, I just knew I was supposed to be in bed because that's what normal people do, right? They sleep at night. So I'd lay there, and my mind would still be racing, going over all the things I needed to do, all the projects I had started. I'd maybe drift off for two, maybe three hours tops. And then, boom. My eyes would snap open, and it was like someone had flipped a switch inside me. 

I wouldn't feel groggy or sluggish. I'd feel completely charged, like I'd just slept for a solid ten hours. It felt like electricity was just humming right beneath my skin. I'd get out of bed—and it wasn't a slow roll out of bed, I'd practically jump up—and I'd go straight back to whatever I was doing before I tried to sleep. Sometimes it was painting... I got really into painting these intricate patterns on the baseboards in my apartment, just spending hours on my hands and knees with these tiny little brushes. Or I'd start making calls. I know it sounds crazy, calling people at five in the morning, but I just had so much I needed to say, so many ideas I needed to share with people. 

And the thing is, I didn't feel tired later in the day, either. I'd go to work, do my whole shift with Mrs. Gable or whoever I was assigned to, and I'd still have that motor running inside me. It was like my body just completely forgot it needed rest. Two or three hours, and I was ready to take on the whole world. It was exhausting for everyone around me, I think, but for me? I felt like I could just keep going and going and going without ever stopping to take a breath. It's a very bizarre feeling, looking back on it, to be that awake on so little sleep. You just feel invincible, in a way. Like the normal rules of being a human being just don't apply to you anymore.

A week? Oh, goodness, if it were only a week... I mean, a week is nothing, right? You can power through a week. You just drink a little extra coffee and catch up on your sleep on Sunday. But no, it’s been much, much longer than that. 

If I really sit down and trace it back... it's been going on for about eleven months now. Eleven months of these... these stretches, I guess you'd call them. Stretches where I'm just completely charged up, sleeping very little like we talked about, and just constantly chasing after these big plans. And it's not just a one-time thing that happened and went away. It's been coming and going this whole time, for almost a year. 

I'll get into one of those modes where my brain is just firing on all cylinders, and I'll be up for weeks on end, working on a project or coming up with some massive plan to reorganize the entire scheduling system for the aides at work—which, let me tell you, the agency did not appreciate, even though my system was much more efficient. But I'll be doing all that, running on two hours of sleep and feeling invincible, and that stretch will last a good long while. And then it might fade out, and I'll think, okay, I'm back to regular old me. But sure enough, a little while later, boom, I'm right back in it. The switch flips, the motor starts running, and I'm back to sleeping three hours and mapping out these grand ideas for my clients or my apartment. 

So for nearly a year—eleven months, give or take—it's just been this constant back and forth. These stretches of being so revved up and chasing these huge plans just keep coming and going. It really takes over your whole life when it keeps returning like that, because you just never know when you're going to wake up at three in the morning ready to take on the world again, and it’s been happening over and over since late last year.

A head injury? Or a major medical illness? Well, let me think about that for a second... no, no, nothing like that. I mean, working as a personal care aide for as long as I have, you definitely get your fair share of bumps and bruises, that's for sure. You really have to be physically sturdy for this kind of work. You're lifting people, you're bending over bathtubs, you're on your feet all day long. 

I remember one time, oh, it must have been a few years ago now, I was helping this one client—he was a very heavy man, bless his heart—and he lost his balance while I was transferring him from his wheelchair. We both went tumbling right down onto the linoleum, and I banged my elbow pretty good on the doorframe. I think I might have bumped the back of my head a little bit on the wall on the way down, too, but it certainly wasn't a real head injury. I didn't black out or see stars or need to go to the emergency room or anything like that. I just put a frozen bag of peas on it and finished my shift, because you can't exactly just leave a client sitting there on the floor, you know? You just have to push through. 

But as far as something major? Like a real concussion, or a stroke, or a heart attack, or some terrible disease before all this started? No, absolutely not. I've always been very blessed with good health. I try to eat sensible meals, and I certainly get enough exercise just running around after my clients and doing all their light housekeeping and errands. My body has always held up just fine. I haven't been in the hospital for anything medical, haven't had any big surgeries. I get the usual sniffles or maybe a touch of a cough in the winter if I catch something from one of the folks I care for, but that's just life. Nothing serious at all. That's part of what makes all this so confusing, honestly, because physically, my health has always been my strong point. I've always prided myself on being dependable and healthy, so no, there was no sickness or injury that brought this on.

Alcohol or drugs? Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. I mean, I completely understand why you have to ask, being a doctor and all, you probably see all sorts of things come through your door, people trying to self-medicate or what have you. But for me? Absolutely not. I don't even like the taste of alcohol, to be perfectly honest with you. My ex-husband used to drink those cheap canned beers, and just the smell of them turns my stomach even now. Sometimes, maybe, oh... years and years ago, I might have had a little glass of sweet wine at a wedding or a Christmas party, but around the time all this started? Not a drop. 

And as for drugs, well, that's just entirely out of the question. I've never touched anything like that in my whole life. You have to understand, with the kind of work I do, you just can't be messing around with things that mess with your head. I'm a personal care aide, and my clients, they rely on me for absolutely everything. I'm sorting out their medications, I'm helping them bathe, I'm cooking their meals on the stove... if I were drinking or taking drugs, I could make a terrible mistake! I could give Mrs. Gable the wrong blood pressure pill, or leave a burner on, or someone could slip in the shower because my reflexes were slow. You have to be sharp in my line of work. You have to be completely present and on your toes. 

Plus, working the hours I do, and especially with my mind racing and buzzing the way it has been all year, I wouldn't even know when I'd have the time or the desire to go to a bar or wherever people go to do those kinds of things. I don't even like taking a Tylenol PM when I can't sleep, because I'm always so worried I'll be too groggy to hear the phone ring if the agency calls me in for an emergency shift early in the morning. So, no, definitely no alcohol and no drugs whatsoever. I just run on my own steam, I guess you could say, even if that steam has been running a little too hot and fast lately. But I keep my body clean of all that nonsense, I really do. I've just seen too many people in my neighborhood ruin their lives that way, and I have too many responsibilities to my clients to ever let myself go down that path.

Putting thoughts into my mind? Like... like making me do things like a puppet? Oh, no, no. My thoughts are my own, and my actions are my own. Nobody is controlling my hands or putting words in my brain. But... well, they were definitely interfering with my life in other ways, that's for sure. 

I don't know if you'd call it controlling, but I got it in my head—and honestly, I still know I was right about this—that the other home-care agency in town was watching me. Them, and some people from the local library, if you can believe it. 

See, I do these little paintings in my spare time. Just watercolors, mostly, flowers and things to brighten up the place, it helps me unwind. And I had all my client papers out, all those schedules and reorganization plans I was telling you about earlier, just spread all over my kitchen table. And I realized that they were watching my paintings and my client papers. The people from that other agency and the folks from the library, they were keeping tabs on everything I was doing, because they were trying to steal a chance that was meant for me. It was my opportunity, my special chance, and they wanted to take it for themselves. 

I tried to warn people about it. I told my supervisor, and I told my neighbor, but they just didn't want to hear it. Folks kept telling me it made no sense at all. They'd say, "Why on earth would the library care about your aide schedules?" or "What does another agency want with your little watercolor flowers?" They made me feel like I was talking gibberish. But

Caring less? Having less motivation? Well, it’s almost like... like a completely different person takes over, to be perfectly honest with you. Because I just told you how I get, right? Buzzing and rushing around and doing all those schedules and plans and keeping an eye on things. But then... when I’m not all wound up like that, when that engine finally runs out of gas, it’s the exact opposite. 

It’s like all the air just goes right out of the balloon. I get so... empty, I guess you could say. I can sit at my kitchen table for hours, literally hours, just staring at the wall. I’ll make myself a cup of coffee in the morning, set it down, and just sit there while it gets completely cold. I won't even care enough to stick it in the microwave to warm it up, I just let it sit there. 

And the phone will ring—and you know I said earlier how I always worry about missing a call from the agency for a shift, how I have to be dependable—but when I get in this state, I just listen to it ring. I don't answer calls. I don't even look to see who it is. Let it go to voicemail, I tell myself, but then I never check the voicemail either. 

I usually go to this walking club, too. Just a few ladies in the neighborhood who meet up at the park to get some fresh air and keep our joints moving, which is so important at my age, especially with the physical work I do. But I just stop going. I can't even find the will to put my sneakers on, let alone walk out the front door and make polite conversation. And my painting... I just told you about my watercolors, how much I love doing my little flowers to unwind. But when I'm like this, I don't even care to pick up my paintbrush. The brushes just sit there on the table gathering dust right next to my cold coffee, and I just look at them and feel absolutely nothing. It's like my whole body is made of lead, and nothing in the world matters enough to make me move.

Sad? Hopeless? You know, doctor, I wouldn't really say it's either of those things. I mean, I know what sad feels like. When my mother passed away, Lord rest her soul, back in—oh, it must have been '98 or maybe '99—I was sad. I cried every single day for a month straight. I felt hopeless then, just crying into my pillow, wondering how I was going to manage the house and pay the bills and do everything all on my own without her. That's what sadness is to me. You cry, your chest aches, you feel like the world is ending and you just want to curl up. 

But this... this thing that happens to me now when the engine runs out? It's not sad at all. It’s just... blank. You’d think I’d be sitting there crying at my kitchen table with my cold coffee, but I’m not shedding a single tear. I’m just staring at the wallpaper pattern, counting the little vines on it. If someone came in and told me the roof was caving in, I don’t even think I’d feel upset or scared about it, I’d probably just sit there and watch the plaster fall. 

It’s a very strange thing to try and explain to people, because they see you sitting in the quiet, not answering your phone, not going to the walking club, and they automatically think, "Oh, she’s so down in the dumps." My neighbor, she's a sweet lady, she'll knock on the door and ask what's wrong, wanting to bring over a casserole or give me a hug like somebody died. But nobody died, and I don't need a hug, because I don't feel bad. 

And I don't feel hopeless, either, because... well, to feel hopeless, you have to actually care about hoping for something in the first place, if that makes sense? You have to want something to happen to feel hopeless about it not happening. And in those periods, I just don't want anything. I don't care about the agency calling, or Mrs. Gable's blood pressure pills, or my little watercolor flowers, or anything at all. So no, I really wouldn't use the word sad. It's more like somebody just reached around back and pulled my plug right out of the wall. Just completely unplugged, like a TV that's been turned off.

Well, that is exactly what I was just trying to explain about my painting and the walking club. I am not sure if I would use the word pleasure, because that makes it sound like, I do not know, going to a fancy carnival or eating a big slice of rich chocolate cake. But interest? Enjoyment? Yes, all of that just dries right up. 

Like I was saying with my watercolors, I usually get such a kick out of doing my little flowers. I have this specific set of fine-tip brushes I had to take two buses to get at the big craft store over in the next county, because the local shop just does not carry the right ones for painting delicate stems and leaves. Um, no, not really. It seems to just be tied to my design work. I don't really find myself worrying excessively about other things... like, you know, everyday stuff, bills, or my health. Voices? Like... people who aren't there? No. No, definitely not. I mean, I hear voices all day, but they're real. They're on the radio. The voices I hear are the people at the depot who are coordinating all of this, and they are very, very real.

Less sleep? No, definitely not. I mean, full of energy? I wish. Honestly, if anything, I'm just completely exhausted all the time. You have to understand, driving a heavy transit bus takes a massive physical toll on you, your back, your shoulders, not to mention the mental part of it right now with everything going on with dispatch. 

I usually work the early shift, which means my alarm goes off at exactly 3:15 AM. I have this whole strict routine because I have to be at the depot by 4:00 AM to do my pre-trip inspections—you know, checking the air brakes, walking the perimeter of the bus, logging into the terminal system before I even pull out of the yard. And to do all that safely, and to keep my guard up, I absolutely have to get my seven or eight hours of sleep. I mean, I force myself to go to bed by 7:30 PM every night. I draw the blackout curtains, I make sure the room is completely quiet, I even make this specific chamomile tea to help me wind down, because if I don't get that sleep, my reaction times drop, and I just can't afford that. 

Not with downtown traffic, and definitely not with compliance watching my every move. I have to be sharp to catch those little discrepancies I was telling you about. So no, I'm not running on empty and feeling great about it or bouncing off the walls. It takes every ounce of energy I have just to stay one step ahead of them during the day. So, yeah, I definitely need my sleep, probably more now than I ever did before just to cope with how tiring the whole situation is.

Seizures? Head injuries? No. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know what a concussion feels like—when I was, gosh, maybe twelve, I fell off my bike going down this really steep hill near my parents' house and hit my head on the curb. I had to go to the hospital, and they did all these tests, shining the little light in my eyes, asking me what day it was, all that. I remember the headache lasted for like a week, and I couldn't look at bright lights. But recently? No. 

And as for neurological problems, I mean, if I had something wrong with my brain like that, I wouldn't be able to drive the bus. The Department of Transportation is incredibly strict about medical clearances for commercial drivers. We have to do these physicals, the DOT physicals, every two years, and they check everything. They check your vision, your hearing, your blood pressure, and they specifically ask about any history of seizures or fainting spells. If you even hint that you've had a dizzy spell, they can pull your medical card right then and there, and you're grounded. You can't even get behind the wheel of a shuttle van, let alone a forty-foot transit bus. 

So, I have to be completely healthy in that regard. My last physical was... let's see, it was about eight months ago, I think? Yeah, eight months ago, with Dr. Aris at the occupational health clinic downtown. He signed off on everything. My reflexes were perfect, my balance was fine. I mean, you need perfect coordination to maneuver those buses, especially when you're making those tight right turns at intersections where people park too close to the corner, or when you have to suddenly brake because a pedestrian steps out without looking. You can't have any kind of neurological delay or whatever you want to call it. 

So, physically, my brain is fine. It's just... it's the stress of what's happening at work that's getting to me, not some medical condition in my head. I haven't hit my head, I haven't passed out, no seizures, nothing like that. My brain works perfectly fine, which is exactly why I'm able to pick up on all these things that dispatch is doing. If there was something wrong with my head, I probably wouldn't even notice the GPS lags or the codes they use on the radio. But I do notice them, because I'm sharp. So, no, no head injuries or anything like that.

How long? Well, let me think... it hasn't been forever, but it feels like it's been a really long time because of how intense it is every single day. I'd say... it's been building for about eight months now. Yeah, exactly eight months. 

I know that for sure because that's when they put me in the temporary dispatch lead role. It was supposed to be a great opportunity, you know? They told me I had the seniority and the perfect safety record, so they brought me inside the depot to cover for Marcus when he went on paternity leave. I thought it was just going to be logging routes, managing the break schedules, and handling the two-way radio for the downtown grid. But the second I sat in that chair, in that little glass office overlooking the yard, I started noticing things. 

At first, it was just small stuff—like how the dispatch codes they were logging didn't match the actual GPS locations of the buses. I'd see a bus marked as being on 4th and Elm, but the live feed showed them sitting idle behind the old warehouse district. And when I tried to bring it up to Sarah in compliance, she just brushed it off, said it was a system glitch. But you don't get system glitches that specific, not every single day, and not always with the same three drivers. 

So, I started keeping my own log. I'd sit there during my breaks, cross-referencing the radio chatter with the transit maps. And that's when I realized they were using the radio static—the clipping I told you about—to coordinate whatever it is they're doing. When Marcus came back from leave and they put me back behind the wheel, I thought maybe it would stop, or maybe I just wouldn't be as exposed to it. But it actually got worse, because now I was out there on the routes, and I could hear them talking about me on the frequency. 

So yeah, eight months. Eight months of having to be constantly on high alert, checking my mirrors, listening to every single crackle on that radio, just waiting for them to slip up so I can finally prove what's going on. It's exhausting, it really is, but I can't let my guard down, not even for a second, not since I was in that dispatch office and saw how the whole thing actually works from the inside.

Trouble keeping up? I mean... I guess, if I'm being completely honest, yeah. It’s hard to admit because I’ve always been such an organized person, you know? But it’s just taking up so much of my mental space. 

At work, I’ve actually fallen really far behind on my route reports. We have to file these detailed end-of-shift logs—passenger counts, delay justifications, mileage—and lately, I just sit in the breakroom staring at the paperwork because my mind is just replaying everything I heard on the radio that day. And when I do have to use the radio to coordinate with the other buses at the downtown transfer hubs, my instructions have gotten confusing enough that the other drivers actually complain. They’ve complained to management! They say they don't know what I'm talking about, but that's just because I'm trying to factor in the weird codes dispatch is using, and they aren't paying attention to the big picture like I am. But still, it's causing problems.

And then at home... gosh, my poor husband. He's been an absolute saint through all of this, but I know it's not fair to him. I used to be the one who handled everything for us. I'd meal prep on Sundays, making sure we had healthy lunches for the week so we wouldn't waste money eating out, I'd keep the calendar... but now? I walk through the front door and I am just so depleted from tracking everything at the depot that I can't even think. My husband has had to completely take over all the meals. He's doing the cooking, the grocery shopping, everything. 

And it's not just the food, it's the phone calls, too. Like calling the landlord about the maintenance stuff, or paying the utility bills... I just can't bring myself to pick up the phone or look at a schedule because I'm so burnt out. He's basically had to take over all the basic planning for our lives right now because I’m just... I'm just not keeping up. I try, I really do, but there's only so much bandwidth a person has when they're dealing with what I'm dealing with all day.

Socializing? Yeah... yeah, I really have. Which is so strange for me, because I used to be the one who pulled everyone together, you know? Like, we have this recreational softball team at the depot—the Transit Titans, we call ourselves—and I used to be the one who hosted everyone after our Thursday night games. I’d set up the patio, have the cooler full of drinks, make these little barbecue sliders... I loved it. I loved having the team over and just laughing and unwinding. But lately? The thought of having the softball team over just makes me want to lock the door and hide. If anyone even hints at hanging out after a shift, I just make up an excuse. I don't want to talk to them, I don't want to entertain... I just don't want them around. 

And it's not just the people from work, either. I've been in a community choir for three years now. I sing alto. I used to look forward to our Tuesday night rehearsals all week long, just the feeling of all those voices coming together, you know? But I just... I don't feel like singing with the choir anymore. I haven't gone in weeks. The director actually texted me a couple of times to see if I was sick, and I couldn't even bring myself to text him back. I just look at the phone and feel nothing. The idea of standing on those risers and making small talk during the water breaks just feels completely impossible. 

It all just ties back into what I was saying before about home. It’s this heavy, empty feeling. Most days after my shift, I come through the front door, I drop my keys in the little ceramic bowl, and I just sit at the kitchen table. I still open my planner—out of habit, I guess, because I used to color-code everything in it—but I just sit there with the planner open in front of me. I stare at the blank pages. I know I need to do things. I know I should get up and start dinner, or make those calls to the landlord, or do the laundry, or literally anything else... but I just can't make myself start. I can't make myself care enough to move. I just sit there at the table, sometimes for an hour or more, just staring at the paper until my husband comes in and asks if I'm okay. I just don't want to do any of it anymore.

Before these past eight months? No... no, never. Honestly, if you had told me a year ago that I’d be sitting here talking to a doctor about radio clipping and GPS discrepancies, I would have thought you were joking. 

Before I took that dispatch cover for Marcus, my life was just... completely normal. I drove the Route 42 loop—that’s the one that goes past the community college and winds down through the arts district. It’s a really great route, actually. You get a lot of students, a lot of regulars who take the same bus at the exact same time every morning, so you really get to know people. I knew my passengers, I knew my schedule, and I never, ever felt like anyone was watching me or tracking me. I mean, sure, the transit supervisors do their routine checks, but that’s just standard procedure, you know? That’s just them standing on the corner with a clipboard making sure we’re hitting our time points at the major stops so the whole grid doesn't fall behind. 

I never had any reason to suspect anyone of anything malicious back then. I trusted the system completely. I trusted my coworkers! I used to think the static on the two-way radio was just... static. Just old, outdated equipment in a city with way too many tall buildings bouncing the signals around. It never even crossed my mind that people could be using the interference to coordinate, or that they’d use coded language right out in the open like that. I was just so naive. I was just driving my bus, waving at the other drivers at the red lights, totally oblivious to what was actually going on under the surface. 

So, no, absolutely nothing like this before eight months ago. It wasn't until I was sitting in that glass office, actually looking at the raw data and hearing the unfiltered feeds, that the veil kind of lifted. And I think that's why it's so incredibly exhausting now, because it’s like I woke up in a completely different reality eight months ago. I can't go back to being that person who just thought static was static, because now I know the truth, but before that? No, my mind was totally clear.

Yeah, I mean, that’s exactly what I was trying to explain just a little bit ago when I was talking about the choir and the softball team. I know I already brought them up, but it really is the best way I can describe it, because it's not just that I stopped going... it's that I feel completely hollow about it. Like, flat. That's a really good word for it, actually. Flat. Because I used to feel this... this rush of joy, you know? When the Transit Titans would play, or when I was harmonizing with the altos on a Tuesday night. I felt alive. I felt connected to things. And now? It's like someone took the volume dial on my emotions and just cranked it all the way down to zero. 

When I told you about ignoring the choir director's texts... a year ago, I would have felt terrible! I would have been agonizing over it, feeling so guilty, texting him back right away with a million apologies because I cared so much about letting people down. But now, I look at the glowing screen on my phone and there is just... nothing. No guilt. No sadness. No missing the music or the people. It’s just a blank wall. 

And it’s the exact same thing when I’m sitting at that kitchen table every day after my shift. I mentioned how I just sit there with my planner open, right? Well, the worst part isn't even that I can't make myself start dinner or make those calls to the landlord or do anything else. The worst part is that I don't feel anything while I'm failing to do it. I'm not sitting

Speech? Um... well, yeah, actually. A few of the drivers and the shift supervisor have made comments lately.
