I'm just trying to keep everything together. 

Like, at work, in the dispatch office, we have this massive board. It's half digital now, but we still use the physical board with all these little colored magnets and paper route slips for the secondary buses and the detours. And lately, I just... I’ll get completely stuck rearranging them. The magnets and the slips, I mean. They have to be in this very specific, precise pattern. I’ll just stand there sliding them around, lining up the edges of the slips with the little blue magnets, making sure the alignments are absolutely perfect. But people just don't get it. They get so impatient with me. The supervisor will come in and ask me to explain why I'm taking so long on the radio, or why I'm moving the magnets around again instead of just logging the raw data, and when I try to explain it to them... when I try to tell them that I'm just trying to keep the whole board from going wrong... they just stare at me. They look at me like I'm speaking a completely different language. They'll sigh and say they can't follow what I'm talking about, or that I'm just making things complicated for no reason. Hear my thoughts? Like... like they're playing over a loudspeaker or something? No. No, definitely not. Honestly, sometimes I wish they could, because if they could actually hear what was going on in my head, maybe they wouldn't look at me like I'm so difficult when I'm trying to explain the route alignments. If my thoughts were just broadcasting out into the dispatch office, then the shift supervisor—his name is Greg, he's been there for like fifteen years and thinks he knows absolutely everything—Greg would finally understand why the grid is so fragile right now. He'd hear my thoughts and say, "Oh, wow, she's actually right, we need to secure these time points." 

But no, they can't hear what I'm thinking. I know they can't because they're always so completely oblivious to it. When I'm sitting there in the glass office, watching the digital board and listening to the raw feeds, my mind is just racing, connecting all these dots about the tracking and the codes, and Greg will just walk by and ask if I want a stale donut from the breakroom. Just totally clueless. If he could hear my thoughts, he wouldn't be asking about pastries, you know? He'd be panicking right alongside me. 

So, no, my thoughts are... they're completely trapped in here. Which is honestly a relief, in a way, because with everything else going on, with the tracking and the radio static and feeling so exposed out in the open all the time... if they could get inside my head, too? I don't think I could handle that. The inside of my head is pretty much the only safe, private space I have left right now. Even if it is exhausting in there. So yeah, no, nothing like broadcasting. It's just the external stuff, the radios and the people watching, but my thoughts are just my own.

Neglecting self-care? Like not showering? No. No, I mean... I still shower every single day. Actually, showering is one of the only things that still makes sense to me right now, because it's a routine I can just follow without having to make any big decisions. My alarm goes off at 4:45 AM, and I am in the shower by 4:50. I just have to be. I use this eucalyptus body wash because the smell kind of... it kind of clears my head before I have to go in and put the dispatch headset on. And the transit center, especially back in the offices, it has this really specific, heavy smell to it anyway—like a mix of diesel exhaust from the bays, burnt breakroom coffee, and whatever that industrial floor cleaner is they use on the linoleum. So I have to be clean before I go into that, and then when I get home, I usually shower again just to wash the whole day off my skin. 

And as for my clothes, I definitely change them. We have a uniform policy, so I wear these navy blue polos with the transit authority logo embroidered on the pocket, and either khaki or black slacks. I actually have exactly five of the polos, one for every day of my shift week, and I wash them all on Sunday and line them up in my closet. I make sure they're perfectly pressed, too. It’s just... it's part of keeping everything orderly, you know? If I show up to the dispatch office looking like a complete mess, how am I supposed to manage the grid? Greg, the supervisor I mentioned, he’s always coming in wearing these terribly wrinkled button-down shirts, and I just don't understand how he can expect to run a tight ship when he looks like he literally slept in his clothes. It bothers me so much to look at it. 

But for me? No, I always make sure I'm clean and put

A month? Um, no, it has actually been longer than that. It has been... well, if I really look back at when it all started getting so undeniably obvious, it has been about two months now. Yeah, two solid months. Because I remember it started right around the time we did the quarterly route adjustments, which is always a massive headache anyway because they update the software on our dispatch terminals. And that is exactly when I started noticing the tracking through the computer system. 

At first, I thought maybe it was just a glitch with the new update, you know? Like maybe the GPS refresh rate was just lagging or the network was strained because everyone was logging in at once. But then it became an everyday thing. Literally every single day I sit down at my console, log into the transit grid, and I can just feel it. I can see the way the cursors move and the way the driver identification numbers blink on my screen, and it is not just raw data anymore. It is them tracking me. And

Unusual? Bizarre? I mean... I guess that depends entirely on who you ask, doesn't it? Because to me, it's not bizarre at all, it's completely necessary. But to other people—like Greg, or the drivers who just want to punch the clock and go home—yeah, I suppose they think I'm acting strange. 

Like, at work, in the dispatch office, we have this massive physical whiteboard that we use as a backup to the digital grid. It has all these little magnetic markers and route slips that correspond to the different bus lines and transit hubs. And lately... well, I have to arrange them. I'll get stuck there by the board, just rearranging the magnets and the slips in this very specific, very precise pattern. Because if they aren't lined up exactly right, the whole system feels off. It feels like the tracking is getting closer, like the grid is going to collapse. So I stand there, and I make sure the blue line magnets are perfectly parallel to the red line magnets, and the route slips are angled just so. And I know people are watching me. I can feel them staring at the back of my neck. I hear them whispering, wondering why I've been standing at the board for twenty minutes just adjusting pieces of plastic. 

And then there's the radio. When the drivers call in, they use these specific codes, right? And lately, before I can even key the mic to answer them, I find myself having to repeat their last few words back out loud. Just... echoing them. Like if a driver says, "Dispatch, this is 402, holding at the terminal," I have to say, out loud, to myself, "holding at the terminal," before I can press the button and say, "Copy that, 402." It's like I have to catch the words and process the code before I can respond, to make sure I'm not missing a hidden message or doing something that's going to trigger a route failure. 

And they hate it. The other dispatchers, the supervisors... they look at me like I'm just being difficult on purpose. Like I'm just trying to slow everything down or be an obstruction. Greg actually pulled me aside the other day and asked if I was "having trouble focusing." Focusing! I'm the only one who is actually focusing! They think it's just me being weird or bizarre, but they don't understand that I'm literally the only one trying to keep the whole board from going completely wrong. If I don't arrange the magnets, if I don't repeat the words to decipher the codes, the whole transit grid is going to fall apart, and they'll be the ones panicking. So, yeah, they think it's bizarre. But I'm just doing my job. I'm just trying to keep it all together.

Thoughts put into my mind? Like someone is forcing them in there? No. No, I haven't felt anything like that. I mean, my thoughts are definitely my own. They might be racing sometimes, especially when I'm at the console and trying to decipher all the codes coming over the radio, but they're still mine. I don't feel like someone is sitting in a control room somewhere beaming ideas into my head, if that's what you mean. 

It's actually the opposite, really. I feel like I'm the only one who is actually thinking clearly, the only one who sees what's really happening on the grid. Everyone else is just going through the motions, completely oblivious to the patterns. Like Greg, he just sits there drinking his burnt coffee and staring at the screen, and I know he's not really processing any of it. But my thoughts... they're sharp. They have to be, to keep up with the tracking and make sure the magnetic board is perfectly aligned. If I wasn't thinking my own thoughts, if I was just letting someone else dictate what I do, I'd probably be just as useless as the rest of them. So, no, nobody is putting thoughts into my mind. I'm just very, very focused on what I need to do.

Harm me? Well... yes and no. I mean, they aren't trying to, like, physically attack me in the breakroom or poison my lunch or anything out of a movie. It's much more... bureaucratic than that, but it's just as real, and honestly, it's just as damaging. It's all about my job, my livelihood. 

I'm actually here, sitting in this office talking to you, because dispatch and the compliance department have been actively tracking every single one of my route changes. They do it right through the computer system. And it's not just the digital tracking, it's the radio, too. I hear these little comments, these specific phrases they use when they key the mic. It's like a coordinated effort to build a case against me. And I know what you're probably thinking, or what anyone else would say—they tell me it's just "normal oversight," just routine quality assurance, making sure the transit grid is running efficiently. That's the company line. 

But I can tell. I can absolutely tell that certain drivers are reporting on me directly. Like driver 714, for example. Every time he comes through the main hub, he pauses just a little too long near the dispatch window, and then later I'll see a flag on his route data that correlates exactly with a shift I was managing. They're trying to set me up to take the fall for when the grid inevitably has a massive failure. They want to fire me, or maybe even bring me up on some kind of gross negligence charges, which would completely ruin my life. So, yeah, it's very real, everyday harm they're planning. It's not magic, it's just corporate sabotage, and they're using the drivers and the software to do it.

Depressed? Like, sad and crying all the time? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't think I've been depressed for two weeks straight, or really at all in the way you're probably meaning. It's not sadness that I'm feeling. It's more... well, it's just this intense, overwhelming pressure, you know? 

Because when you're the only one who actually sees the grid for what it is, when you're the only one keeping the route slips and the magnetic markers perfectly aligned so the whole system doesn't just collapse in on itself, there really isn't time to sit around and feel sad. I have to be on alert. I have to be watching the screens, listening to the radio codes, making sure driver 714 isn't lingering by the window again. If I were depressed, if I were just lying in bed all day with the curtains drawn, unable to get up, who would manage the board? Greg? Please. Greg can barely manage his own coffee order without messing it up. 

So, no, I haven't felt depressed most of the day. I'm exhausted, sure. I'm stressed out of my mind because of the tracking and the compliance department trying to build this ridiculous case against me. And it's incredibly frustrating, just deeply, deeply frustrating to be surrounded by people who think you're the problem when you're actually the solution. But that's not depression. That's just the reality of my situation at work right now. I'm just too focused on keeping everything from falling apart to be depressed.

Controlling my movements? Like a puppet on strings or something? No, no, definitely not. If anything, I have to have absolute, complete control over every single movement I make, down to the millimeter. 

When I'm standing at the magnetic board, you have to understand, it requires a very specific kind of physical precision. You can't just slap the route markers up there however you want. You have to slide them perfectly into the grid grooves, or the whole visual alignment gets thrown off for the next shift, and then you've got buses crossing paths in sector four. I mean, my hands are doing exactly what my brain tells them to do, and my brain is processing the grid. Sometimes my wrists actually ache by the end of a ten-hour shift from how tightly I have to grip the radio mic and how constantly I'm reaching and stretching to shift the heavy magnetic strips around on the upper tiers of the board. 

If some outside force was controlling my hands, I don't think I'd have these calluses on my fingers, you know? And honestly, if an outside force was controlling me, maybe they could do a better job of dealing with the compliance department, because I'm just exhausting myself trying to physically keep up with all the paperwork they keep generating. But no, every step I take across that dispatch floor, every time I reach up to adjust the frequency dial on the main console, every time I write down a timestamp... that's all me. It has to be me. Because if I let my guard down for even a second, if I wasn't in complete control of my own body and my own reactions, driver 714 would probably slip right past the window without me logging his exact entry time, and that's exactly what they want. So no, I'm the one moving my arms and legs. Nobody else is doing it for me.

Emotionally flat? Like I don't care about anything? Oh, definitely not. It's actually the exact opposite of that. I care so much, probably too much, honestly. Because if I didn't care, if I was just emotionally checked out, I wouldn't be paying such close attention to everything dispatch is doing. 

I mean, the whole tracking thing... it's happening right now, every day, and I am hyper-aware of it. It's not something that just pops up when I'm feeling numb. I am feeling everything, all the time. Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I... I guess I came in because I keep doing these odd things at church lately. 

Like, we have a potluck on Sundays. Sister Mary always brings her macaroni salad, though she puts way too much celery in it if you ask me. I used to grow celery when we had the house out on County Road 9, but the soil out there was always too sandy for a good garden. The tomatoes did alright, though. 

Anyway, I was standing by the potluck table, and I picked up the big serving spoon for the potatoes, and I just... held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and not moving at all. Just froze right there. 

And then later, I was at the end of the table with the napkins. They were those yellow paper ones. Yellow is such a happy color, it reminds me of the kitchen curtains I bought at Sears back when they still mailed out that big thick catalog... I really miss getting that catalog in the mail. But I was folding the same stack of napkins, just folding them over and over, smoothing them down and folding them again, and all those people were just standing there in line waiting on me to finish so they could get their silverware. I don't really know why I get stuck like that.

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just the regular sounds, you know? Like the wind chimes on my porch. I have these beautiful glass ones my sister got me when she went down to Florida. Clearwater, I think it was. Or maybe Daytona? She always loved the beach, but I could never stand the sand getting in my shoes. It just ruins a good pair of loafers. I used to have a pair of penny loafers that I wore until the soles practically fell off. They were so comfortable, like walking on clouds. But no... no voices. Just the wind chimes.

Energetic? Oh, heavens no. I don't think I've had that kind of energy since... well, since I was a girl. I remember one summer, I must have been about twelve, and we were staying at my aunt's farm. She had these big, beautiful draft horses. Clydesdales, they were. Such gentle giants, you know? They had those big feathery hooves. I used to brush their coats until they shone like copper pennies. Pennies used to buy you a whole handful of candy down at the mercantile. Peppermint sticks, licorice whips... I always liked the butterscotch discs the best. They came in those little shiny yellow wrappers. So pretty. But no, I wouldn't say I've felt unusually excited or anything like that lately. Just my normal self, I suppose.

Confusing? Oh, I don't know... I've always just been me, you know? I remember when I first started school, it was a little one-room schoolhouse out past the old mill. The teacher, Miss Gable, she had the most beautiful handwriting. Perfect cursive, all those loops and swirls. We used to practice on these little slate boards with chalk that always made my hands feel so dry. I hate that feeling, dry hands. I use this rosewater lotion now, comes in a pink bottle. Smells just like the roses my grandmother grew on her trellis. They were those big climbing roses, the kind that bloom all summer long... But no, I wouldn't say confusing. Just... normal, I guess.

A stroke or a head injury? Oh, goodness no. My head is perfectly fine. I haven't been sick or in a hospital since... well, since my Henry broke his collarbone. That was years and years ago. He was up fixing the roof on that old shed out back. It had those green shingles, you know? The kind that get all thick with moss if you don't scrape them down in the spring. I told him to hire someone to do it, but he was always so stubborn about fixing things himself. Just like his father. His father used to smoke this pipe that smelled just like sweet cherry wood. It would fill up the whole porch. Smelled a bit like cherry pie, actually. I love a good cherry pie, especially if you make the crust from scratch and do the lattice on top. You have to weave the dough strips just right or they sink right down into the fruit while it bakes... But no, no seizures or anything like that for me. Just healthy, I suppose.

Harm me? Oh, heavens no. Why would anyone want to do that? I keep to myself mostly, just me and my little garden out back. I've been trying to get the tomatoes to come in, but the squirrels keep getting to them before they turn red. They're such clever little things, squirrels. They have those bushy tails that twitch when they're excited. I used to watch them chase each other up and down the big oak tree we had in the front yard when I was a girl. That tree must have been a hundred years old. My brother built a treehouse up in the branches. We'd sit up there for hours and eat sandwiches... egg salad, usually. Mother always put a little bit of paprika in her egg salad, gave it such a nice color. I still have her old recipe box, it's made of tin with little painted daisies on the lid. But no, nobody's trying to control me or anything like that. I'm just fine.

Repeating words? No, I don't think I do that. It sounds a bit like an echo, doesn't it? Like when you stand at the edge of a canyon and shout down into it. We went to the Grand Canyon once, Henry and I, for our twenty-fifth anniversary. It was so hot that day, the sun just beating down on the rocks. The rocks were all these different shades of red and orange, like a painting. I bought a little postcard from the gift shop with a picture of a mule on it. They take people down into the canyon on mules, you know. I'd never ride one, though. Mules can be so stubborn. My uncle Arthur had a mule on his farm back when I was little. He called him Barnaby. Barnaby loved to eat carrots right out of your hand, but you had to keep your fingers flat or he'd nip you. I was always so careful with my hands around him... But no, I don't go around repeating what people say.

Over and over? No, I don't recall doing anything like that. I was just a regular little girl, mostly just running around outside. We did play jump rope a lot, I suppose, if that counts? You have to jump the exact same way every time or the rope catches your ankles. My friend Martha and I would jump rope for hours on the sidewalk until the streetlights came on. Martha had the most beautiful blonde hair, always tied up in two braids with little red ribbons. Her mother made those ribbons from scraps of velvet. Velvet is such a difficult fabric to sew, you know. It slips all over the machine if you aren't careful. I tried making a velvet dress for my baby doll once, but the needle kept jamming. It was a Singer sewing machine, one of those heavy black iron ones with the gold filigree painted on the side. My mother bought it second-hand from a lady down the street who was moving up to Chicago. Chicago always sounded so windy and cold to me, all those tall buildings blocking out the sun... I've never been, myself. But no, no strange routines or movements for me. Just regular playing.

Frozen? Oh, goodness, no. I don't freeze up like a statue or anything. And who would be trying to move my arms anyway? It's just me here. The only thing frozen around here is the ground beef I put in the icebox. I always buy the big family pack when it goes on sale at the market. You have to remember to separate it into little portions before you freeze it, though, or it takes absolutely forever to thaw out on the counter. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she just throws the whole big block right into her freezer, paper and all. Then she complains when she can't get her meatloaf made in time for supper. She makes a terribly dry meatloaf anyway, puts way too much onion in it. Onions give me such awful heartburn. I always have to drink a little glass of milk with a spoonful of baking soda stirred in if I have onions. My grandmother taught me that trick. She lived to be ninety-two, bless her heart, and she swore by baking soda for just about everything... But no, I move my own arms just fine. Nobody is posing me like a mannequin.

Stuck? Well, like I just said, I don't get frozen or stuck in the first place. And I certainly don't stop talking. My husband Henry, God rest his soul, he always used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey. He had all these funny little sayings like that. His father was in the Merchant Marines, you see, so Henry picked up all sorts of phrases from him. He had this beautiful old compass his father brought back from a trip... maybe it was Nova Scotia? It was solid brass and just so heavy. I used to have to polish it every Sunday before church with that stinky Brasso cream. It always left a terrible black smudge on my good dusting rags. I tried soaking them in bleach, but you have to be so careful with bleach or it eats right through the cotton. I ruined one of my favorite aprons that way, a lovely little yellow gingham one with pockets on the front. I used to keep my clothespins in those pockets when I hung the wash out on the line... But no, I don't stop talking or get stuck like you're saying.

Well, I suppose sometimes folks do look a bit confused when I'm talking. Like at the church, when the ladies ask me about the new blankets for the bazaar or what time choir practice is. I always mean to give them a straight answer, I really do. But then I start talking, and my words just sort of run off on their own... I'll start talking about the green beans I'm canning, and then that reminds me of a hymn we sang last Easter, and before I know it I'm going on about how my yellow roses are doing this year. And they just stare at me, like they can't quite find what I'm saying in all of that. My roses really are lovely this year, though. I put down some crushed eggshells around the roots, just like my mother used to do. She always saved her eggshells in a little tin cup on the windowsill. It was a blue tin cup, the kind that had those little white speckles all over it. We used to take those cups camping when I was a little girl... but yes, I suppose people do have a hard time following me sometimes.

Well, let me think... I'd say it's been about six months now that folks have been mentioning my talking being hard to follow, and noticing me acting a bit odd. Six months... that would mean it started right around the time of the big autumn bake sale at the church. I remember because I made three dozen of my special molasses cookies. You have to use the real dark molasses, none of that light stuff, or they just don't taste right. And a pinch of ginger, that's the secret. My sister Edna, she always tried to make them, but hers always came out flat as a pancake. She never did have the touch for baking, Edna. She was better with sewing. She made me the most beautiful quilt for my wedding, all done in the double wedding ring pattern. It had these lovely little scraps of calico fabric... I think some of them were from our old dresses when we were girls. I still have it folded up at the bottom of my cedar chest. Cedar smells so wonderful, doesn't it? It keeps the moths away, too. I always put a few cedar blocks in with my winter coats when I pack them up for the summer... but yes, it's been about six months since all this started.

So, it's either I'm a statue or I'm a wind-up toy, and people are starting to stare, and... yeah, that's why I'm here.

Yeah, I mean... yeah. It's pretty much all day, every day. It's like this heavy, gray blanket just sort of draped over everything. And it's been like that for... well, most of the time since all of this really started. I mean, sure, there are some weeks where it feels a little lighter, where maybe the blanket is just a sheet, you know? But it's always there in the background.

So yeah, even on the days where I can force myself to smile for a customer on the phone, all of that—the sadness, the guilt, the not caring, the terrible sleep—it's just always humming right there in the background, almost every single day.

Yeah. I was doing pretty normal before I moved into that place. Um, it all really started within the first couple weeks... right after I found all the water damage and realized the heat wasn't working right.

Not really. I mean, I work construction all day, so I'm pretty beat by the time I get home. Once I actually lay down, I pass out pretty fast. 

It's just... like I said, I don't usually get to bed until way late because I'm up messing with the pipes or trying to get the heater going. So I don't really have trouble falling asleep, I just don't get enough of it before my alarm goes off.
No, not really depressed. I mean, I'm stressed out and pissed off about the whole situation with the room, but I wouldn't say I feel down or sad. Just frustrated that I have to deal with it all.

Not really. I wouldn't call it anxiety. I'm not sitting around feeling nervous or worrying about what's gonna happen, you know? It's more just... I'm stressed because of the actual physical work I have to put into dealing with the place every single night. It's a massive headache, but no, I don't feel anxious.

Yeah, I really think they would. I mean, the whole housing mess hasn't ended yet. I'm still living in that room, and I'm still dealing with all the repairs and the landlord every day. 

So it's not like... this isn't something that just kept going long after the problem was over, you know? I'm still right in the middle of it. If that situation was actually fixed and I could just get a normal night's sleep, yeah, I'm pretty sure I'd be totally fine at work again.

No, it's not unsafe or anything. And the heat works fine. It's just... well, like I said, it's all the repairs and dealing with the landlord that's the problem. But as far as being dangerous or freezing, no, it's nothing like that.

Um... I guess I'm here because... my words aren't really staying in a straight line lately. Like, I'll try to talk about my overnight shift, and then... I don't know, suddenly I'm talking about soccer, or paint colors, or patient charts. People get lost. I can see it. So... yeah. That's why I'm here.
Um... no. Not really. I haven't... I don't think I've felt energetic.
No... I don't think so. I haven't heard anything like that. Just... regular noise.

Um... well... I don't know about harm. But... yeah. Watched. 

Just... at work. I know the supervisors watch me on the unit cameras. They, um... they changed my shifts around to see if I'm unsafe. People keep telling me it's just staffing shortages, but... I'm sure they're watching me.
No... I don't think so. I'm... I'm usually pretty tired, actually. I definitely need to sleep.

Yeah... I guess. I just... I stay in my apartment mostly. I usually just ignore messages when people reach out. I used to do stuff... play soccer on weekends, or cook for my friends... sketch murals... but... I don't know. It all just feels pointless now. I don't really want to be around anyone.
No... nothing like that. I haven't been sick or hurt my head.

Yeah... most days. I just... I feel really heavy. And empty, I guess, right from when I wake up. It's... well, after my shifts, I usually just sit in my car for a while. I end up... crying, mostly... before I can even get myself to drive home.

Yeah... I guess so. There was a stretch... maybe a few weeks, where I wasn't really in that... that dark place. But I still knew they were watching me. The cameras... the supervisors at work. I just... I had to be really careful. Guarded, I guess.
Yeah... like I just said. It was a few weeks. I wasn't... I wasn't depressed then. But I still knew they were monitoring me. The cameras and the supervisors. I just... kept acting guarded at work.
I don't know exactly. A while. Maybe... a little over a year? Like a year and a month, I think. That's when I started noticing it all.
No... I don't think it was a whole month. Just... what I said before. A few weeks, maybe. Not a full month.

Yeah... I guess so. Looking back on it... that heavy feeling, just being empty and not caring about anything... it's been there most of this whole time. Even when... even if the camera stuff or the scattered talking got a little quieter... the empty feeling was still there.

Well, it's nice to meet you too. I came in because... well, even on my better days lately, I just can't shake this feeling I've been having. It's the people at my church, and also the ladies in my walking club. I just know they're watching me. They keep putting these little messages about me in the Sunday bulletin, or they slip things into what they say when we're out walking. 

We usually walk around the reservoir, you know, the one over by the old highway? But last week it rained so much we had to walk at the indoor mall instead. I really don't care for the mall, the floors are too shiny and I always worry I'm going to slip in my sneakers. Plus, the smell from that soft pretzel stand is just overwhelming. My husband used to love those pretzels, though. He'd buy one every single time we went to Sears. It's such a shame Sears closed down, I used to get all my appliances there, and you just can't find that kind of customer service anymore. 

But... oh, anyway. The messages. They just keep slipping these little hints about me into their conversations at the club and at church, and I just don't know why they're doing it.

Well, yes, sometimes I do. It usually happens when the house is just... completely quiet. I'll be sitting there, maybe doing a crossword puzzle, and I'll hear my name. Or just a few words, clear as day, coming from the kitchen or out on the back porch. And it sounds exactly like my friend Shirley's voice. It's so clear that I'll actually answer back, like, "I'm in the living room, Shirley!" before I realize... oh, she's not here. Nobody's here. 

Shirley and I used to spend a lot of time on that porch. We'd sit out there with our iced tea—sweet tea, of course, the way she makes it with a pinch of baking soda so it doesn't get bitter. She swears by that trick, learned it from her grandmother who lived down in Georgia. Her grandmother had this beautiful old farmhouse with a wrap-around porch, the kind you just don't see being built anymore. They used real wood back then, not this composite stuff that looks like plastic. My son-in-law put a composite deck on his house, and I just think it gets far too hot on the feet in the summer... 

But yes, I hear her voice, or sometimes just my name, when it's quiet.

Well, depressed? I don't know if I'd say depressed most of the day, exactly. I mean, I've just been feeling... off, you know? Not quite myself. Sometimes I just sit in my recliner and don't feel like doing much of anything. It's that blue recliner I got at La-Z-Boy about five years ago. Oh, they had such a wonderful sale going on that weekend, it was Presidents' Day, I think. My daughter helped me pick it out because she said the floral pattern on my old one was just too outdated. But I loved that floral pattern, it matched the curtains my mother made for me when I first moved into the house. She was such a beautiful seamstress, my mother. She could look at a dress in a magazine and just make a pattern out of newspaper and sew it up perfectly. She made my wedding dress, actually. It had these delicate little seed pearls all over the bodice... it must have taken her weeks to sew them all on by hand. People just don't have that kind of patience for handiwork anymore, do they? Everyone's always in such a rush... But anyway, no, I haven't really noticed feeling terribly sad all day long, just sort of... drained.

Memory? Oh, no, I don't think so. My memory is sharp as a tack, usually. I never forget a birthday or an anniversary. I still send out cards for all my nieces and nephews, and let me tell you, there are a lot of them now. My sister Margaret had five children, and they all went on to have at least three of their own. It gets so expensive buying stamps these days. Have you seen how much a book of stamps costs now? It’s just ridiculous. I remember when you could mail a letter for just a few cents. And the designs on the stamps aren't nearly as pretty as they used to be. I used to save the really nice ones, you know, the commemorative ones with the flowers or the old presidents. I had a whole album of them at one point. I wonder where that album went... I think I might have put it in the attic when we had the roof redone back in 2008. The roofers made such a mess of the yard, trampled right over my hydrangeas. I was so upset, those hydrangeas took years to establish. You have to get the soil acidity just right if you want them to be blue instead of pink. I use coffee grounds, myself. But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, no, my memory is just fine.

Medical illness? Brain problem? No, goodness no, nothing like that. I haven't been in the hospital for anything serious since I had my gallbladder out, and that was... oh, it must have been the late nineties. Dr. Henderson did the surgery, such a nice man, though he always smelled a little bit like peppermint and cigar smoke. It's a funny combination, isn't it? He used to keep those little red and white peppermints in his pocket and hand them out, even to the adults. My husband, God rest his soul, used to love those mints. He'd always grab a handful from the bowl at the bank, too. The tellers knew him so well, they'd just slide the bowl right over to him when he walked in. That was back when they actually knew your name at the bank, before everything went to those machines and the internet. I still go inside to deposit my checks, I just don't trust those little slots on the ATM. You never know where the envelope is actually going, do you? It just gets sucked in and you just have to hope it gets to the right place. But anyway, no, my brain is fine, no medical problems like that.

Energetic? Revved up? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really get revved up about much these days. Well, except maybe when the neighborhood association decided to change the trash pickup day from Tuesday to Thursday. That certainly got me going. They just slipped a little note in the mailbox, no town hall meeting, no discussion. And Thursday is just terrible because that's the day the street sweeper comes, so if you put your cans out too early, they get in the way, and if you put them out too late, you miss the truck. My neighbor, Mr. Abernathy, he put his out early one week and the street sweeper knocked his recycling bin right over. Cans and papers everywhere! It took him an hour to clean it up, and he's got a bad hip, you know. He had it replaced twice. The first time, they used some sort of metal joint that got recalled. Can you imagine? A recall on a part inside your own body! It's not like a toaster you can just take back to Sears. Not that Sears is even around anymore. I used to buy all my appliances there. They had that wonderful Kenmore brand, lasted forever. My first washing machine was a Kenmore, and it ran for twenty-two years without a single repair. Now you buy a machine and it's got all these computer chips and screens, and it breaks down in three years. It's just planned obsolescence, that's what it is. But anyway, what was the question? Revved up? No, I don't get energetic like that, just my normal self, really.

How long? Oh, let me think... I suppose this has been going on since not long after my close friend died. That was about a year and five months ago now. It still feels like just yesterday, really. We used to do everything together. Every Tuesday we'd go down to the garden center just to look at the new arrivals. She absolutely loved orchids. I could never keep them alive myself, they're so finicky. You have to water them with just one ice cube a week, did you know that? Or at least, that's what the little plastic tag says. I always felt like an ice cube would freeze the poor roots. I prefer African violets, myself. I have three of them on my kitchen windowsill right now. They get just the right amount of morning sun there. The afternoon sun is too harsh, it scorches the leaves right off. I had to put up those sheer curtains to filter the light. I got them on sale at JCPenney before the one at the mall closed down. It's such a shame how all the good stores are closing. Now the mall is just phone repair kiosks and pretzel stands. I do like a soft pretzel every now and then, especially with that yellow mustard, but you can't exactly buy a decent pair of slacks at a pretzel stand, can you? You have to order everything online now, and you never know if it's going to fit. But... oh, what was I saying? Right, the timing. Yes, about a year and five months, right after she passed away.

Continuously? Oh, yes, definitely more than a month. The voices, you know, and those messages... and just having so much trouble keeping my thoughts straight. It's been happening for about eleven months now. It started right around the time I was trying to organize my recipe box. I have this beautiful wooden box my mother gave me, it's got little painted daisies on the lid. She bought it at a craft fair in Vermont back in 1978. We took a bus tour up there to see the fall foliage. It was just breathtaking, all those reds and golds. We stopped at this little diner that served the most wonderful maple syrup over buttermilk pancakes. Real maple syrup, not that high-fructose corn syrup nonsense they sell in the plastic bottles shaped like a lady. I always buy the glass bottles, even though they're heavier to carry home from the Piggly Wiggly. The bag boy, Tommy, he always offers to carry my groceries out, but I tell him I need the exercise. He's a sweet boy, going to community college for accounting. His mother must be so proud. But yes, eleven months of this... it's been quite a long time to deal with all that noise and confusion.

Hard to follow? Well, yes, people do get a funny look on their faces sometimes. Like when I try to explain things, I might start with a thought about the mail—because the mail carrier, Frank, he's always running late on Thursdays. He says it's because of the circulars, but I think he just likes to stop and chat with Mrs. Higgins down the street. She has that lovely rose bush, you know, the one with the yellow blooms that smell like lemon? I tried growing yellow roses once, but the Japanese beetles just skeletonized the leaves. Horrible little pests. I had to buy these special traps, the ones with the little bags that hang from a metal stand. You're supposed to place them far away from the plants you want to protect, which seems counterintuitive, doesn't it? But it works, they all fly over to the bag. Anyway, or I might start talking about church, and then somehow I end up talking about quilt patterns—I'm very partial to the Double Wedding Ring pattern, it's so classic—and then birds, like the cardinals at my feeder, and then the warnings I get... and then I can just see people don't know what I'm getting at. They just stare at me, blinking, like they've lost the thread entirely. It's very frustrating, because it all connects perfectly in my head.

Well, yes, I suppose it has been harder. I still live at home, you know, in the same house we bought in '85. It has that lovely wrap-around porch. But I just haven't been keeping up with my usual things. I used to go to my quilting gatherings every Wednesday. We'd sit around the big frame at the community center, all of us working on a different section. Helen always brought her famous lemon bars. She uses extra zest in the icing, that's her secret. I tried making them once, but I left them in the oven too long because the timer on my stove is broken. It just buzzes whenever it feels like it, completely unreliable. I really need to call the repairman, Mr. Henderson, but his truck is always parked outside the diner so I think he's mostly retired now. Anyway, I stopped going to quilting, and I haven't been to the walking club either. We used to walk the track at the high school, three miles every morning. The track is made of that bouncy rubber material, so it's easy on the knees. I bought a special pair of New Balance shoes just for it, the white ones with the blue N on the side. They have excellent arch support. But they're just gathering dust in the closet now. I haven't even been doing much of my gardening, which is a shame because the weeds are just taking over the hostas. My daughter, Sarah, she noticed. She's started coming over a lot more to check on my meals and make sure I'm getting to my appointments. She works at the bank downtown, the one with the big clock out front that chimes every hour. It's a very stressful job, so I feel bad that she has to worry about me on top of it all. But she insists on checking the fridge to see if I've eaten.

Controlling my thoughts? No, not controlling them... I don't feel like a puppet or anything. But I do feel... well, I came in today because even on my better days, when the sadness isn't so heavy, I just can't shake this awful feeling that people are watching me. Especially the people at church, and the ones from the walking club. I know I haven't been to the walking club in a while, but I still see them around town, you know? Like at the grocery store. I saw Brenda there last week in the produce section. She was thumping a cantaloupe, trying to see if it was ripe. You really have to smell the stem end to know for sure, thumping doesn't do much for melons. It works for watermelons, though. My father taught me that. He used to grow the biggest watermelons in our backyard, the Jubilee kind with the dark green stripes. We'd eat them out on the patio and spit the seeds into the grass. The grass was always so green back then... But anyway, Brenda gave me this look, and I just know they're talking about me. And the church bulletin! I've been finding these little messages in it. Just little phrases that seem directed right at me, or things people say during fellowship hour that have a hidden meaning. It's very unsettling. We always have coffee and those little powdered sugar donuts after the service. The donuts always leave white dust all over my good black wool coat. I have a lint roller, the kind with the sticky paper you peel off, but it never seems to get it all. I buy the replacement rolls in bulk at the warehouse club. Do you have a membership there? The savings on paper towels alone is worth the annual fee.

Well, yes, I suppose I have. When I was at my absolute lowest, just feeling so heavy and sad every single day... barely eating a thing and thinking I had just failed everyone in my life... that was exactly when I was hearing Shirley's voice the most, and believing all those church people were sending messages about me. It all happened right together. 

The not eating was very unusual for me, because normally I love a good bowl of oatmeal in the morning. I buy the steel-cut oats, not those quick rolled ones. They take much longer to cook, you have to simmer them on the stove for a good twenty minutes, but the chewy texture is so much better. I like to put a little brown sugar and a splash of half-and-half in mine. The half-and-half comes in those little cardboard cartons, but they always seem to leak around the spout, don't they? It leaves a sticky ring on the refrigerator shelf. I actually mentioned it to the manager at the grocery store, a nice young man who always wears a red tie. His name tag says 'Kevin', but I'm pretty sure his real name is Kenneth because his mother came in once and called him Kenny. She was buying an awful lot of canned cat food. I had a cat once, a Siamese named Cleo, but she completely ruined my good living room drapes... 

But yes, the deep sadness and the voices and the messages, they were all happening at the exact same time.

Well, yes, actually. I mean, the sadness isn't always there every single minute. There was a spell... oh, maybe for several weeks... where I was actually getting up and getting dressed in my proper clothes, not just my housecoat. I have this lovely blue floral housecoat I bought at Mervyn's years ago, before they closed all the stores. It has pearl snap buttons down the front, which are so much easier for my hands than regular buttons. My arthritis flares up when it rains, you see. But anyway, I was getting dressed, eating a bit better—I even made myself a nice tuna salad sandwich on toasted rye bread. I always use a little sweet relish in my tuna, just a spoonful. Some people use dill relish, but I think sweet relish gives it a much better flavor. 

But even during that time, when I wasn't feeling so weighed down by the sadness, I was still hearing my name being called in the house when no one was there. Just out of nowhere. And I still felt certain that the people at church were hinting about me in the bulletin and during fellowship. Even when I felt perfectly fine in my mood, that part didn't go away. It makes me think I should maybe switch to the Methodist church on Elm Street. They have a beautiful stained glass window of a dove, and I hear their choir director is very talented. He used to teach music at the junior high...

Yes, absolutely. Like I was just saying, there was a spell, oh, for several weeks at least. I wasn't feeling depressed at all. I was getting up, getting dressed, not feeling so weighed down by the sadness. I was even eating a bit better. But Shirley's voice... I was still hearing my name called out in the house, clear as a bell, even though I was completely alone. And I still felt absolutely certain that the people at church were hinting about me in the bulletin. 

It’s just so strange, isn't it? Hearing things when you're alone. The house is usually so quiet. Well, except for the refrigerator. It has this hum, a low sort of vibration. It’s an older model, a Frigidaire, almond-colored. You don't see appliances in almond much anymore, do you? Everything is stainless steel now. I don't care for stainless steel, it shows every single fingerprint. My neighbor, Helen, she remodeled her whole kitchen with stainless steel. She spent a fortune. Her husband left her a very comfortable pension when he passed. He worked for the railroad for forty years. They gave him a gold watch when he retired. I wonder what happened to that watch... maybe her son took it. He lives in Arizona now, works in real estate. But yes, for a good few weeks there, my mood was just fine, but the voices and the messages from the church people didn't stop at all.

I... well, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten to a point where I can't... I can't keep going like this. I do flooring for a living, you know, carpet, tile, lots of heavy installation work, and I have a crew who depend on me to keep the jobs lined up and keep things running smooth. I went to college for a couple of years before I got into the trades, so I've always prided myself on being the one holding it all together for them, and for my family at home. 

But lately, I just... I've messed everything up so badly. I've let everyone down. And I just lay there in bed at night, and I keep thinking it would be so much better if I just didn't wake up. I really do. I just stare at the ceiling and think about how I'm ruining my family's lives, how I'm failing my crew, and sometimes I honestly feel like dying would be the fair punishment for what I've done to all of them. It just plays on a loop in my head, over and over, how they'd be better off if I just paid the price for the damage I've caused. I just want to go to sleep and not have to face them in the morning, because the guilt of what I've done to my crew and my family is just... it's too much. I don't deserve to be here.

People say that, yeah. My husband, the guys on my crew... they try to tell me it's not true, that I'm just being too hard on myself or that I'm just going through a rough patch. But they're just being kind, or maybe they just don't want to admit the reality of it. Because I know exactly what I've done. 

I look at my husband, and I see how much worse he's gotten lately, how tired and just... drained he is all the time, and I know it's because of me. I'm the reason. I've dragged him down into this hole with me. And it's not just him. It's my crew, too. We had this great reputation, you know? Years of solid referrals for custom tile and carpet work. But I've caused them to lose work. I've ruined our chances on bids, or I couldn't get my head straight enough to organize the jobs right, and these guys—these guys who rely on me to put food on their families' tables—they are suffering because of my failures. 

And the jobs we actually did manage to do... I just keep thinking about the clients' homes. I know I messed them up. Even if the clients haven't called to complain yet, I know the work is tainted. It's like... it's honestly like I've poisoned everything I touched. Every person, every floor, every single house I stepped foot in. I just spread ruin everywhere I go. So when I say I should be punished, I'm not just saying it to be dramatic. I mean it. I deserve whatever happens to me. I deserve the absolute worst, because I'm the one who destroyed all of it, and no amount of them telling me otherwise is going to change the fact that I poisoned their lives.

I... yes. Yes, I have. It started a little while ago, and at first, I thought it was just the guys on the crew messing with me, or maybe just the noise of the tools, you know? Because when you're on a job site, there's always a saw running, or a compressor, or someone shouting over the radio. But then it kept happening when it was quiet. It's a man's voice. It's not my husband, it's not anyone on my crew... it's just this deep, clear voice. 

It happens when I'm working, like when I'm kneeling down trying to line up a seam on a carpet, or laying out a tile pattern. I'll hear it right behind me, just over my shoulder. It says things like, 'You missed it.' Just that. 'You missed it.' And I'll stop what I'm doing and spin around, thinking one of the guys is standing right there pointing out a mistake I made, because God knows I'm making enough of them lately. But there's never anyone there. The room is completely empty. 

And it's not just at the job sites, either. It happens at home now. I'll be in the kitchen, just standing by the sink, trying to wash a dish or something, and I'll hear it again. Right behind my ear. 'Everyone knows.' That's what it says. 'Everyone knows.' And it's so real, Doctor. It's as clear as if you were standing right behind me speaking into my ear. I'll turn around, expecting someone to be standing right there in my kitchen, but I'm completely alone. It just... it makes my heart pound out of my chest, because I know he's right. Everyone does know how badly I've failed, but the fact that I'm hearing someone say it when the room is empty... I just don't understand what's happening to me. It's terrifying, honestly, because I can't escape it. No matter where I go, work or home, that voice is just waiting to remind me of what I've done.

No, no, I've never... nothing like this. I mean, I've always been a worrier, sure, you know, making sure the bids are right, making sure the guys get paid on time, worrying about the house and the kids. But that was just normal stress, you know? Just the kind of stress anyone has when they're running a crew and trying to keep a family afloat. It was never like this. I've never felt this... this heavy, like I'm just dragging everyone down into the mud with me. And I certainly never heard a voice before. That's completely new. 

It really all started... well, I can tell you exactly when it started. It's been about a year and five months now. That's when my husband had his accident. He hurt his back, really badly. We thought it was just a strain at first, you know, the kind of thing you just sleep off or put some ice on, but it wasn't. It was a serious injury, and it just... it completely changed everything. He went from being this active guy who was always doing things around the house, to being mostly housebound. He can barely get up from the couch some days without wincing. 

And that's when it all started falling apart for me. Because suddenly, everything was on my shoulders. I had to be the strong one, I had to keep the business running, I had to take care of him, and I just... I couldn't do it. I started feeling like I was failing him because I couldn't fix his back, and I was failing the crew because my head was at home worrying about him, and then the guilt just started piling up. So, yeah, it's been about a year and five months of this... this nightmare. Before that, I was fine. I was holding it all together. But since his injury, it's just been a steady slide down, and now... now I'm just ruining everything I touch.

Nice to meet you too. Well, what brings me in is that I just can't keep my mind on one thing anymore. I work at a warehouse, and lately... it's like every little thing pulls me off my count. A beeper goes off, or a forklift alarm sounds, or even just someone moving a pallet nearby, and my attention is completely gone. Then I look down and realize I've put the wrong numbers into the inventory. It's getting really frustrating to deal with.

No, not really. I mean, I did fine in school, as far as I can remember. I wasn't the kind of kid who couldn't sit still or focus on homework. This... this feels different. It's just been happening lately at the warehouse, not something I've dealt with my whole life.

No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling depressed. I mean, I get frustrated with myself at work because of the mistakes I'm making, but I don't feel down or sad or anything like that. It's just the distraction that's really bothering me.

No, not really. I mean, I'm not a worrier. I'm just annoyed about messing up my inventory counts. But I'm not sitting at home stressing about things or anything like that. It's just the focusing part that's the problem.

Well, actually, yes. There are some days lately where I feel almost too upbeat. It's like I have so much energy I could fix up the whole house and sort out the whole warehouse all before dinner. But then... if my husband questions one of my plans or something, I just snap at him over something completely small.

No, not really. I mean... I haven't noticed any changes there. Even when I have all that extra energy during the day, I still feel like I need my regular amount of rest at night. I just go to bed at my normal time.
No, I don't use marijuana at all. Never have. So that definitely wouldn't have anything to do with it.
No, I don't drink. I mean, maybe a glass of wine at a wedding or something, but that's about it. So, no, alcohol isn't a factor when I get like that.

No, not really. I don't think I'm better than anyone else or anything like that. I just feel like I can get a lot more done than usual, but I don't feel overly confident or like I'm suddenly great at everything. Just... productive, I guess.

No, I wouldn't say they race. I mean, I'm thinking about what I need to do next, sure, but my mind doesn't feel out of control or anything. It's pretty clear, actually. I just stay focused on whatever I'm working on.

Yes, definitely. I get a lot more done. At work, I've been taking on all these extra safety-improvement projects at the warehouse. And outside of work, I've been signing up for way more art workshops than I normally would. I even started making all these lists and schedules to keep track of everything... it's almost like I'm running a whole operation by myself.

Yes, I definitely do. My husband and my coworkers actually tell me I talk so fast they can't even get a word in. I'll just be going on about new recipes, or my safety ideas for the warehouse, or those art classes... and I just, I honestly feel like I have to finish every thought right then and there, before it disappears on me.

Yeah, I do. Usually after my shifts at the warehouse, I'm pretty worn out, but on those days... I come home buzzing. I just have to keep doing things. I'll end up reorganizing the cabinets or, you know, sorting all the bins out in the garage. Just sitting down on the couch to relax feels completely impossible.

Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Well, I suppose I'm here because of what's been happening at work lately, and it's really starting to bother me. I'm a jeweler, I do a lot of custom metalwork and precious stone settings, repairs, things like that, which I've done for years. But I came in today because I've been having this awful trouble when talking to my customers. 

Someone will come in and ask me a really simple question, like, just asking when a ring repair will be ready for them to pick up. Just a basic, everyday question, right? But when I try to answer them, my answer just starts going all over the place. I'll start talking about the repair invoices, and then somehow that makes me start talking about the garden soil I need to pick up for my flower beds, and before I know it I'm going on about the mortgage papers I was sorting through on my kitchen table the night before. 

I just keep talking and I can actually see them losing me. I can see their expressions change, like they have no idea how we got from a broken clasp to my garden, and honestly, neither do I. It’s just so embarrassing because I know they just want a simple date and time, and I took some college classes in business years ago so I know how to be professional, but I just can't seem to stop my thoughts from stringing all these completely unrelated things together out loud. It just spills out of me before I can catch it.

High? Euphoric? Oh, heavens no. No, I don't think I've felt anything even close to euphoric in... well, I honestly can't even remember. 

I mean, when I hear the word euphoric, I picture someone just bouncing off the walls with joy, you know? Like... like when my sister won a little bit of money on a scratch-off ticket a few years back and she just couldn't stop talking about it. She was so thrilled she took our whole family out to this little Italian place downtown, the one with the really good garlic knots, and she was just glowing the entire night. But me? No, definitely not. I haven't had any sort of burst of happiness or extra energy like that at all. 

If anything, I just wake up, make my coffee—usually just a simple drip, nothing fancy, though sometimes I used to use the French press if I had the time on a Sunday morning... but lately, I just stick to the basic machine because I just want to get it over with. So, no, I'm definitely not feeling high or on top of the world or anything like that. I'm really just trying to get through my workday and figure out why my brain keeps jumbling up my words when I'm standing at the counter with my customers. There's certainly no euphoria in that, let me tell you, it's honestly just incredibly frustrating.

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's not like a whole crowd of people talking to me or anything like you see in the movies, but... yes. It usually happens when I'm at work and the shop is completely quiet. You know, those lulls in the afternoon, usually around 2:30 or 3:00, when everyone is still at their own jobs and the foot traffic just dies down completely. I'll be sitting there, maybe just sorting through some jump rings or organizing my files, and I'll hear this woman's voice. 

It's always a woman, and she just mutters my name. Just my name, but it sounds like it's coming right out of the polishing room in the back. The first few times it happened, I actually got up and walked back there, thinking maybe someone had slipped through the side door without the bell ringing, or maybe my sister had dropped by to bring me lunch and was trying to surprise me. But there's never anyone there. Just the polishing wheels and the dust collector sitting there turned off. 

And it's not just the voice, either. Sometimes, in that same quiet stretch, I'll suddenly smell burning metal. If you've ever worked with a jeweler's torch, you know exactly that smell—it's very distinct, sharp, almost acidic when the flame hits the flux. I'll smell it so strongly, so clearly, that I'll actually panic for a second. I'll drop whatever I'm doing and run over to the soldering station to make sure I didn't leave a torch on or that a valve isn't leaking. I'll check the dials, I'll check the hoses, I'll even touch the tips of the torches to see if they're warm. But they're always stone cold. Everything is off. But the smell is just so real, and the voice is so real, that I just have to go check every single time, even though part of me knows by now that I'm probably going to find an empty room. It's just so unsettling, you know? To experience something so vividly and then find out it's just... not there.

Seizures? Oh, no. No, I've never had a seizure. I mean, I know what they look like, of course. My neighbor, well, my old neighbor from about fifteen years ago, her name was Brenda, she had this little terrier mix that used to have seizures. Poor thing would just fall over in the yard and shake, and Brenda would get so upset, naturally. She'd have to sit there on the grass with him until it passed. But me? No, nothing like that. 

I've always been pretty healthy in that regard. I mean, working with my hands all day, doing such fine, detailed work with the stones and the metal, you really need a steady hand. If I were having seizures, or even just tremors, I don't think I could do my job at all. Setting a tiny diamond into a prong setting takes so much precision, you know? You have to hold the piece just right, apply just the right amount of pressure with the tools. So, no, definitely no seizures. My hands are steady... it's just my thoughts and my words that seem to be getting all tangled up lately. But physically, no, no seizures or anything like that.

Irritable? Well, I wouldn't say I've been unusually irritable, no. I mean, sure, everyone gets a little annoyed now and then, especially when things don't go according to plan. Like last Tuesday, I had this customer come in—a very nice lady, don't get me wrong, she's been coming to me for years—but she brought in this antique filigree ring that her grandmother had given her, and she wanted me to resize it. Now, resizing filigree is always tricky because the metal is so delicate, and if you aren't careful, you can completely ruin the pattern. So I explained all of this to her, very patiently, and told her it would take at least two weeks because I needed to order a specific type of gold solder to match the alloy perfectly. 

But then, not even three days later, she calls the shop wanting to know if it's ready! I had to explain the whole process to her all over again. And yes, in that moment, I suppose I felt a tiny bit of frustration, just because I had been so clear the first time. But I wasn't snapping at her or losing my temper. I kept my voice perfectly level and polite, just like I always do. 

And my sister, she's always telling me I have the patience of a saint, especially with the intricate work I do. You really can't be an irritable person and sit at a bench for six hours straight, peering through a loupe, trying to set a one-millimeter sapphire without scratching the surface. It requires a very calm, very centered disposition. So, no, I don't think I've been feeling unusually irritable. Just the normal, everyday little annoyances, but nothing out of the ordinary, and certainly nothing I can't handle with a deep breath and a cup of tea. It's really just the sadness and the... the confusion with my words and those strange moments in the quiet shop that are bothering me. But my temper? No, that's been perfectly fine.

Well, yes... yes, I have. It’s funny you phrase it like that, "most of the day, nearly every day," because that’s exactly what it feels like. It’s this constant, lingering thing. Most mornings I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness, like the color has just completely drained out of the house before I even get out of bed, let alone before I get to the shop. 

It’s hard to explain, really. You know how when you look at a beautiful piece of jewelry, maybe a really nice opal, and it has all that fire and play of color? That’s how life used to feel to me. There were bright spots, things to look forward to, even just small things like a good cup of coffee or a nice chat with a customer. But now, it’s like looking at a piece of rough, unpolished quartz. Just dull and gray. 

I’ll lie there in bed and look at the ceiling, and the thought of getting up and going through the motions just feels so... monumental. I still do it, of course, because I have the shop to run and my sister relies on me to keep things going, but the joy is just gone. I’ll sit at my bench, and even when I’m working on something I used to love, like a really intricate custom setting, I just feel this weight sitting right on my chest. It doesn't go away after lunch, it doesn't go away when I close up the shop for the evening. It’s just this quiet, heavy sadness that follows me around, day in and day out. So, yes, I would say I’ve been feeling depressed almost constantly lately. It’s exhausting, to be honest. Just exhausting to feel so empty all the time.

Well... yes, actually. Yes, they have. It’s strange to think back on it now, because the sadness feels like it’s been here forever, but there was a time before this heavy feeling really settled in. I was actually doing quite well, keeping very busy. I was still running my evening jewelry-making classes at the community center—which I loved doing, teaching people how to solder and work with silver clay, it’s so rewarding to see their faces when they finish their first piece. And I was gardening, too. I have these beautiful heirloom tomatoes I was tending to, and some lovely climbing roses along the trellis in the back. 

But even then, when I was feeling perfectly fine, not depressed at all, I was having these... experiences. It went on for several weeks, I think. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe just organizing my tools or sketching a new design, and I kept hearing these noises coming from the polishing room. It sounded like the tumbling machine was running, or like someone was moving the buffs around, but I was the only one there. And the smell of the burning metal would just waft in, so strong I’d have to check the torches even though I hadn't used them all day. 

And during that same time, I started getting so worried that customers were... watching the business. Not just looking in the windows, but really watching. I’d see someone pause outside the shop, maybe admiring a necklace in the display, but I’d get this overwhelming feeling that they were monitoring me, keeping track of my inventory or my hours. I even started keeping the blinds half-drawn during the day, which is terrible for a retail shop, I know, but I just couldn't shake the feeling. So, yes, all of that—the noises, the smells, the worrying—that was happening for weeks while I was still feeling quite energetic and involved with my classes and my garden, long before this terrible sadness took over.

Less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that. I've always been a fairly consistent sleeper, really. I mean, my sister always jokes that I run like clockwork, and it's true. Usually, I'm in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 if I've gotten caught up reading a good book—lately I've been reading this fascinating biography of René Lalique, his glasswork is just incredible, the way he incorporated those natural motifs into the Art Nouveau style, it really makes you think about how we approach design today. But anyway, yes, I'm usually asleep by 11:00 and up by 7:00, because the shop opens at 9:30 and I like to have a good hour and a half to myself in the morning to have my tea, read the paper, and just ease into the day before I have to start dealing with customers and vendors and all of that. 

Even back when I was feeling good, when I was teaching those evening classes and spending all my weekends out in the garden with the tomatoes and the roses, I still needed my full eight hours. I might have been busy and active, but I was definitely tired at the end of the day. In fact, teaching those classes takes a lot out of you, emotionally and physically, hovering over people's shoulders, making sure they don't burn themselves with the micro-torches... by the time I'd get home at 9:00 PM, I'd be ready to just collapse. So, no, I've never had a time where I was just buzzing along on three or four hours of sleep and feeling perfectly fine. If I don't get my rest, my hands get shaky, and you absolutely cannot have shaky hands when you're trying to set a tiny little diamond into a delicate prong setting. It's just not possible. So, no, I've always needed my sleep.

Well, yes, actually, just like I was saying earlier... it's funny how the mind works, isn't it? You kind of lose track of the timeline when you're in the thick of this heavy sadness, but yes, there was definitely a stretch of time before the depression really settled in. I was feeling quite myself, honestly. I was still running my evening classes at the community center, teaching the silver clay and the soldering, which I always found so fulfilling. And I was out in the garden every weekend, tying up those heirloom tomatoes—they get so heavy if you don't support them properly—and tending to the climbing roses. I felt perfectly fine, mood-wise. 

But even then, while I was feeling good, that's when those things started happening, and it went on for several weeks, easily. I would be in the shop, feeling completely normal, maybe sorting through a new batch of semi-precious stones that had just come in from my supplier in Jaipur—they do the most wonderful cuts on their amethysts, really top-notch work—and I'd just keep hearing these noises coming from the polishing room in the back. It was so distinct, like the tumbling machine was running or someone was shuffling the buffs around, but I was entirely alone in the store. 

And that was the exact same time I started getting so incredibly worried that people were watching the business. It wasn't just a fleeting thought, it was this persistent, gnawing worry for weeks. I'd see a customer outside, maybe just looking at the window display, and I'd be absolutely convinced they were monitoring my inventory or keeping track of when I opened and closed. I was so convinced of it that I started keeping the front blinds half-drawn during regular business hours, which my sister told me was ridiculous for a retail shop, but I just couldn't help it. So, yes, all of that—the noises from the back room, the intense worrying about being watched—that all went on for several weeks while I was still gardening and teaching, well before this awful, draining sadness took over my life.

Talking less? Well... I suppose it might seem like that to some people, but I don't really think so. I mean, my sister called the other day, and we were on the phone for a good forty-five minutes talking about our aunt's estate sale. It's such a complicated situation, trying to divide up all those antique furniture pieces without causing a family rift. Aunt Helen had this gorgeous Victorian settee, beautifully carved mahogany with the original horsehair stuffing, and my cousin Sarah thinks she should have it just because she has a larger living room, which is completely beside the point if you ask me. 

So, no, when I have something to say, or when I'm talking to my sister or my suppliers, I still talk just as much as I ever did. I was just on the phone with my metal supplier yesterday, actually, trying to sort out a mix-up with an order of sterling silver wire. They sent me half-round instead of dead-soft round, and you simply cannot use half-round when you're trying to do delicate wire-wrapping for pendants, it just doesn't sit right against the stones. I had to explain the whole process to the customer service representative, who clearly had no background in jewelry making whatsoever, bless his heart. I must have spent twenty minutes just trying to get him to understand the difference in the gauges and the temper of the metal. 

Now, I will say, because of this heavy, awful sadness I've been feeling, I haven't been going out to social events or chatting up the neighbors over the fence like I used to. When you feel this drained, this utterly exhausted down to your bones, the idea of making small talk about the weather or the local school board elections just feels impossible. It takes so much energy to put on a bright face and pretend everything is fine when inside you just feel like a lead weight. But as far as my actual ability to talk, or how much I speak when I do have a conversation... no, I haven't noticed any change there. I still have plenty to say, it's just that I don't always have the energy to find an audience for it right now.

Lost interest... oh, heavens, yes. That's actually been one of the hardest parts of all this, to be completely honest with you. It really is. 

I used to absolutely love—I mean, it was practically my favorite weekend activity—hunting for old clasps. You know, going to estate sales or those big antique fairs out in the county, sifting through boxes of broken vintage jewelry just to find a beautiful, intact Art Deco box clasp with the original paste stones, or maybe a really delicate Victorian barrel clasp. There's just something so thrilling about finding a piece of history like that, rescuing it from a dusty cardboard box, and thinking about how you can incorporate it into a modern design. I could spend hours doing that. And the classes, too. I used to get so much joy out of planning those little jewelry classes I mentioned earlier. I'd sit at my kitchen table with a pot of Earl Grey and draw up all the diagrams, figure out the exact amount of silver clay each student would need, make little sample pendants to show them what we were aiming for... I just loved doing that. 

But lately... I don't know, it's like a switch has been flipped inside me. I'll sit down at my workbench—I have this beautiful vintage oak jeweler's bench with the canvas catch tray underneath—and I'll pull out my organizers, but... I mostly just stare at the trays. I look at all those beautiful clasps I spent so much time hunting down, and the beads, and the wire, and I just feel like none of it is worth starting. It's this overwhelming, heavy feeling of 'why bother?' I'll sit there under the magnifier lamp for maybe twenty minutes, just looking at the little compartments, maybe I'll move a piece of turquoise from one slot to another, and then I just push the tray away. It just feels so utterly pointless right now. It breaks my heart, really, because my work has always been my passion, but the drive to actually create something, to put the pieces together... it's just completely gone.

Well, no, not that I can recall... it really didn’t happen like that. Actually, it was quite the opposite, if I'm being honest. When I think back to those worst months, you know, when that heavy, heavy sadness was just pressing down on me so hard that I couldn't even bring myself to care about my bench or my tools... that was exactly when all those other strange things were happening, too. They were all happening at the exact same time. 

I’d be sitting there in the shop, just completely drained, feeling that total loss of interest in everything I usually love, and out of nowhere, I would hear my name being called. Just clear as a bell, echoing right off the glass display cases. And there wouldn't be a soul around. It's such an unsettling feeling, being so low and then having your mind play tricks on you like that.

And the worry... oh, the worry was just eating me alive right alongside the sadness. I was absolutely, one hundred percent sure that the customers coming in weren't there to look at the jewelry at all. I’d see someone lingering by the front window, maybe looking at a display of turquoise pendants I’d put out, and I just knew—I was completely convinced—that they were checking up on our payments. It’s a tough business, retail, especially with precious metals because the overhead is so astronomical. You have to buy all your silver casting grain and your stones up front from the suppliers, so money is always on your mind anyway. 

But this was different. I’d be sitting there, too depressed to even pick up a pair of pliers, hearing my name in an empty room, and absolutely terrified that every person who walked through the door was secretly auditing my finances or making sure I was paying the bills.
