I'd just be staring out the window, watching the playground, or looking at the clock, completely lost in my own world instead of focusing on the lessons in front of me. 

And the schoolwork itself, man, it was a total disaster zone. I was constantly losing my worksheets. The teacher would hand them out, and by the time I got home, they were just gone, vanished into thin air. Or, even worse, I'd actually manage to force myself to do the homework, sitting at the kitchen table for hours just agonizing over it, and then the next day, I'd completely forget to turn it in. It would just sit crumpled at the bottom of my bag. It got to the point where my mother had to institute this whole strict nightly routine because she was so frustrated. She literally had to physically check my backpack every single night. She would pull everything out, smooth out the crumpled papers, pack it all back up, and remind me exactly what to turn in. If she didn't do that, if she missed even one night of checking my bag, absolutely nothing would make it to the teacher's desk. It was just this constant, heavy effort for her to keep me on track, and honestly, looking back, it feels like I'm still that exact same kid avoiding his worksheets, just with clinic budgets now instead. It never really stopped.

You know, it's funny you ask that, because people always assume that if you're not paying attention, it's because you're bored or you don't care about them, but honestly... no, I don't really have that problem. Like, if I'm sitting down with one of my clinic directors, or if I'm having a one-on-one with a staff member who's upset about their schedule, I'm actually really locked in. I can look right at them and hear exactly what they're saying. I don't find myself zoning out in the middle of a conversation or having to ask people to repeat themselves because my mind went somewhere else. 

I mean, sure, if it's a massive, two-hour all-staff meeting where someone is just droning on at the front of the room with a PowerPoint, my mind might wander a bit, but I feel like that's pretty normal for anyone, right? But if it's a direct conversation, just me and another person, face-to-face? No, I'm right there with them. I don't drift off. It's really just the paperwork and the solo, heavy-thinking tasks that completely derail me. When it comes to actually talking to people and listening to them, I feel like I'm completely present. I've never had a spouse or a boss get mad at me for spacing out while they were talking to my face, if that makes sense. So, yeah, I wouldn't say that's an issue for me at all.

Oh, man, all the time. It's actually incredibly embarrassing, especially given my job. I mean, I’ll be putting together a clinic staffing schedule, right? And I know how important it is. I've been doing this for years, I know the drill, I know the stakes. We have minimum coverage requirements, we have specific providers who need certain MAs on certain days... it's a whole puzzle. And I will sit there, and I will swear up and down that I have checked it, double-checked it, looked at every single row and column. I’ll finally hit send on the email to the whole staff, feeling like, okay, that's done, I can finally check that off my list. 

And then, without fail, within ten minutes, I'll get a ping from one of the lead nurses or a provider, and they'll be like, "Hey, you put Dr. Smith on Tuesday, but she's at the downtown clinic on Tuesdays," or "You completely left off a triage nurse for the morning shift." And I'll look back at it, and it's right there. The mistake is glaringly obvious. It's like my brain just skipped right over it when I was proofreading. 

And it's not just at work, either. I volunteer to coordinate this youth soccer league my nephew plays in—which, honestly, is a whole other headache, dealing with parents and field permits and all that—but I'll send out the weekly email to all the families, thinking I've got all my ducks in a row. And then I'll get five replies back asking where the game is because I completely left off the location, or I put the wrong date, like I'll write 'Saturday, October 12th' when Saturday is actually the 14th. Just these stupid, careless little details that I absolutely should have caught, that I *used* to catch, or at least I feel like I used to. It's just so frustrating because people look at that and they think you're sloppy or you don't care, and I *do* care, I just... I don't know how I miss these things when I'm staring right at them. It just slips right past me.

You know, it’s interesting you ask that, because you’d probably think with the scheduling mistakes and the emails I just mentioned, that reading would be a total nightmare for me, right? But actually... no. Not at all, really. If I have to sit down and read something long, I’m actually pretty good at it. I mean, in healthcare administration, you wouldn't believe the amount of reading we have to do. The state is constantly—and I mean constantly—sending down these enormous, dry, fifty-page compliance manuals or updated OSHA guidelines that you absolutely have to read cover to cover because the liability is just massive if you miss a new protocol. 

And when I get one of those, I just... I get a cup of coffee, I shut my office door so the staff isn't popping in every five minutes with a crisis, and I just read it. I don't find myself losing my place or staring at the same paragraph over and over without absorbing it. It’s almost like if it’s a continuous flow of text, you know, paragraphs and sentences rather than a grid or a spreadsheet, my brain can just lock right onto it and follow the path. 

It’s the same at home, too. I read a lot of history books in my downtime—mostly these massive, 800-page biographies about the Civil War or the Founding Fathers, that kind of thing. My wife jokes that they could double as doorstops. But I can just sit in my armchair and devour them for hours. I don't lose my spot, I don't forget what I just read on the previous page, I don't have to keep backtracking. I just keep going. So, yeah, it’s really just the fragmented stuff, the data entry and the little puzzle pieces like the schedules, that completely trip me up. But sitting down to actually read a long document or a book? No, I don't have any trouble with that at all. I could probably read all day if this job actually let me just sit in quiet, which, let's be honest, never happens in a clinic...

Yeah, that... that is actually becoming a real problem. Well, bills are mostly on autopay these days, thank god, because my wife set that up years ago after I missed the water bill twice in one summer. But other things? Absolutely. 

I mentioned that youth soccer league earlier, right? The one my nephew plays in? Well, since I’m supposed to be coordinating things, I get a lot of calls from the parent volunteers. And I have just been awful lately about returning those calls. I’ll be driving home from the clinic, I’ll listen to a voicemail from one of the dads asking about the referee schedule or field permits, and I’ll tell myself, 'Okay, I will call him back the exact second I walk through the front door and put my keys down.' But then I walk in, the dog needs to go out, or my wife asks me a question about dinner, and that phone call completely evaporates from my brain. I won't remember until three days later when the guy calls me again, and I have to do this whole song and dance apologizing for leaving him hanging. 

And it's not just the calls, it's the little errands for these events, too. Like, we had a fundraiser car wash for the league a couple of weeks ago, and my *one* job on the way there was to swing by the hardware store and pick up three extra packs of those microfiber sponges and some more soap. I drove right past the hardware store. Just completely missed it, showed up to the parking lot empty-handed, and had to turn right back around while they were waiting on me. It's so frustrating.

And meetings... man, the meetings. I’m on this community advisory board for our neighborhood, and it’s usually the first Thursday of the month. You’d think I’d know that by now, I've been doing it for a year. But once or twice recently, I’ve been sitting at home in my armchair, probably reading one of those Civil War books I told you about, totally relaxed, and my phone buzzes. I look down, and it’s a text from the board president saying, 'Hey, are you joining the meeting? We're waiting on you for quorum.' And my stomach just drops. The community meeting completely slipped my mind. Just vanished. I have to scramble to open my laptop and jump in, and I spend the first ten minutes profusely apologizing to everyone. 

It’s just... it's exhausting feeling like I constantly need a babysitter for my own schedule outside of work, you know? Because at the clinic, I have my calendar open on two different screens all day, but the second I step out of that environment, it's like all my everyday obligations just fall through a sieve.

You know, it’s funny you ask that, because you’d think with all the balls I’m dropping lately, I’d be a nervous wreck, but... no, not really. I mean, don't get me wrong, I get incredibly frustrated with myself *after* I mess up a schedule or completely miss a community meeting, like I was just saying. That bothers me a lot, and I beat myself up over it because I hate looking incompetent. But just sitting around worrying about things out of the blue? Anticipating disasters when everything is fine? No, that’s just not really how I'm wired. 

My wife, actually, she’s the worrier in the family. She’ll spend hours stressing over whether the roof is going to leak if the forecast calls for a heavy storm, or if the dog is acting slightly more tired than usual, or if our retirement accounts are allocated exactly right for our age bracket... all that stuff. She's always thinking five steps ahead to what *could* go wrong. But me? I just kind of take things as they come. 

Even at the clinic—and let me tell you, managing a healthcare facility is basically just putting out one fire after another all day long. A provider calls in sick at 7 AM, the EMR system goes down right when we have a full waiting room, the AC breaks in the middle of July... it's constant chaos. But I don't sit at home on a Sunday night sweating about what *might* break on Monday. I just... I don't know, I just deal with it when it actually happens. Honestly, if I worried about every little thing that could go wrong in a clinic, I'd probably have an ulcer by now. 

So, yeah, I definitely get mad at myself when I make those stupid, careless mistakes, but I don't really have that constantly spinning wheel of worry about life in general or hypothetical problems. I just kind of exist in the moment, for better or worse. Sometimes my wife actually gets annoyed and says I probably *should* worry a little more, especially when I forget to do things she asked me to do, but I just don't have that anxious gear in my brain. If there's no immediate fire to put out, I'm usually pretty relaxed.

No, honestly, no. I know I just spent all this time complaining about how mad I get at myself when I drop the ball on the soccer league stuff or miss a community meeting, but feeling actually depressed or hopeless? No, not at all. It's really more of an intense annoyance, you know? Like a... well, like a fly buzzing around your head that you just can't quite swat. But it doesn't drag my overall mood down into the gutter or anything like that. 

I'm actually a pretty upbeat guy by nature. Even with all the absolute chaos at the clinic—and believe me, there are days where the phones are ringing off the hook, three medical assistants call out sick, and I just want to lock myself in the sterile supply closet and hide—I don't go home feeling like the world is ending or that things are hopeless. I just leave it at the door. I still really enjoy my evenings, I still look forward to the weekends. Like, just this past weekend, my wife and I finally went to this little Italian place downtown that we've been trying to get a reservation at for literally three months, and we had a fantastic time. 

I feel like if I were depressed, I probably wouldn't care about stuff like that, right? I'd probably just want to lay in bed or sit in the dark. But I don't have that feeling whatsoever. I have plenty of energy, I still want to go out and do things, I still get totally excited to crack open a new 800-page biography and read for the evening. So, yeah, it's really just the frustration of not being able to keep my ducks in a row when it comes to the little details. Sometimes people at work will see me frantically digging through my desk and they'll ask, 'Oh, you look so overwhelmed, are you okay?' and I have to explain that I'm just trying to remember where I put the updated vacation request forms, not that I'm having some sort of existential crisis. So, no, definitely no hopelessness or feeling down. Just... a lot of scattered moments, I guess you could say.

You know, it is funny because people always seem to assume that if you have trouble focusing, you must have been one of those kids bouncing off the walls, but that was not me at all. Not even a little bit. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Higgins... or wait, was it Mrs. Gable? No, Mrs. Gable was fifth grade, Mrs. Higgins was fourth. Anyway, Mrs. Higgins used to tell my parents at parent-teacher conferences that I was a perfect angel because I was so quiet. I was never the kid jumping out of my seat to sharpen my pencil five times a minute or poking the kid in front of me. I was practically glued to my chair. 

But the thing is, I was just completely in my own world. I would be staring out the window at the playground, or I would have a book hidden inside my desk, usually something about history or airplanes, and I would just sit there for an hour without moving a single muscle. So physically, yeah, I was perfectly still. I never got in trouble for running around or being disruptive or not staying in my seat when I was supposed to. I was just... mentally miles and miles away. 

Even now, I am really not a big fidgeter. I can sit in those long, incredibly boring budget meetings at the clinic for two hours without tapping my foot or needing to get up and pace around. I mean, I might not hear a single word the finance director says because I am thinking about whether I need to rotate the tires on my truck or what chapter I am on in my book, but physically, I look like I am paying perfect attention. So, yeah, as a kid, staying seated was never the issue. It was what my brain was doing while I was seated that was the problem, if that makes sense. I was just a really quiet, spacey kid, definitely not a hyper one.

No, definitely not. Honestly, half the time I didn't even realize the teacher was asking a question in the first place, let alone what the question actually was, so I definitely wasn't the one blurting out the answer! Like I was just saying about Mrs. Higgins' class, or really any of my classes back then, I was so absorbed in whatever else was going on in my own head. 

I remember there was this one kid in my grade, Tommy... or maybe it was Timmy? No, Tommy, I'm pretty sure. Anyway, he was always the one shooting his hand up, just shouting out the answer before the teacher even got halfway through her sentence. He was always getting reprimanded for it, you know, 'Raise your hand, Tommy, wait to be called on.' But me? I was usually staring at the wall clock, trying to figure out the exact gear ratio of the second hand, or daydreaming about what I was going to build with my Erector set when I got home. You can't really blurt out an answer if you aren't tracking the conversation, right? 

And even if I did happen to be paying attention for a minute, which was pretty rare, I was way too reserved to just shout something across the room. I'd probably sit there second-guessing if I even had the right answer anyway, thinking, 'Well, maybe it's this, but what if she means something else?' By the time I'd even consider raising my hand, they had already moved on to the next subject entirely. So no, blurting things out, interrupting the teacher... that just wasn't me at all. I was practically the invisible kid in the back row.

I'm here because I'm having a really hard time at work lately. I do bookkeeping, and... well, I just can't stop going back over the same spreadsheets and calculations again and again. 

It's gotten so bad that I'm staying at the office for hours after everyone else leaves. Even when I know I've already checked the numbers, I just get this overwhelming feeling that if I don't do it one more time, something bad will happen and it'll be completely my fault. It's just getting to be too much.

Yeah, they definitely do. It's like... even after I know the numbers match, this thought just keeps jumping in that I missed one hidden mistake somewhere in the payroll or taxes. I start thinking that somebody's check won't go through, or the firm will get in huge trouble. I try really hard to push the thought away, but it just comes right back. It's like I can't even trust my own eyes anymore.

Yeah, I do. I know it's way too much. Like I was saying before, staying at work for hours after everyone else leaves just to look at the exact same spreadsheets... I know it doesn't make sense. 

I know I already checked the calculations. But I just can't stop going back over them again and again. Even when I tell myself it's excessive and I need to go home, I still have to do it. Because if I don't check it just one more time, I get that awful feeling that something bad is going to happen and it'll be entirely my fault.

I'm not really sure of the exact amount, to be honest. I haven't timed it or anything. I just know it's... it's a lot of hours. 

Once I start going back over everything, I kind of lose track of the clock. So I couldn't give you a specific number, just that it keeps me there way past when I'm supposed to clock out, and it basically takes up my whole evening.

Yeah, it really has. It's... it's causing some major problems. I actually missed a filing deadline recently because I couldn't stop checking, and I got called into a formal meeting with my boss about it. And outside of work, it's pretty much ruined my schedule. I've stopped going to my choir rehearsals, and I can't make it to my volunteer commitments at the youth center anymore. I just... I can never get out of the office on time to actually go to them.

Yeah, exactly. If I try to just close the laptop and walk away, the feeling is just... it's overwhelming. I get this intense thought that there's a mistake I missed, and if I don't go back and check it that one more time, the whole company's finances are going to be messed up, and it will be completely my fault. The urge is so strong that I can't ignore it. I just have to go back and look at the calculations again to try and make that feeling go away.

They definitely feel unwanted. I don't want to be doing it at all. Even after I've checked and I know the numbers match, this... this thought just keeps jumping into my head that I missed one hidden mistake somewhere in the payroll or the taxes. I'll start worrying that somebody's check won't go through or the firm will get in trouble. I try to push the thought away, I really do, but it just comes right back. It's honestly like I can't even trust my own eyes anymore.

No, not really. It's... it's pretty much just at work. I haven't really noticed that same urge to check things over and over when I'm at home or doing other stuff. It really just seems to be tied to the numbers and the accounts at the office.

Um, no, I don't think so. I mean, I'm not really sure, but nothing major really changed at the office. I didn't get a new position or a different boss or anything like that. Work is just the usual amount of busy. It just kind of... started happening on its own, I guess. I can't really point to one specific stressful thing that set it off.

No, I wouldn't say so. I mean, I try to do a good job, but I've never really been a perfectionist. Before all this started, I would just do my work, make sure it looked okay, and move on. I never really had this feeling that every little thing had to be exactly perfect. I was just kind of... normal about it, I guess.

Well, I’m only sitting in this chair because everybody keeps acting like I’m just imagining it. My wife, everybody... they look at me like I'm making it up. But I'm a fabricator, doc. I work with precision parts all day long for a living. I know exactly where things are supposed to be, down to the millimeter. And I know for an absolute fact that my wife’s relative has been coming into this house to get at me. 

It’s not a mistake, and I'm not seeing things. Tools don’t just move themselves. I have a very specific system in my garage. I'll put my torque wrench on the second shelf, facing left, right where it belongs. I come out the next morning, and it’s on the bottom shelf, facing right. Or my micrometers are taken out of their case and left on the workbench. He's coming in and messing with my stuff just to get under my skin, to make me doubt myself. 

And it’s not just the tools, either. Every single weekend, my fishing plans get completely spoiled, and it is never by accident. I'll have everything ready to go down to the lake—truck packed, bait sorted—and suddenly my good line is tangled to hell, or the latch on my boat trailer is mysteriously jammed with a piece of wire, or my tackle box has been dumped and reorganized all wrong. Every single weekend! 

It's been going on for months now, and nobody wants to listen to me. But I can see it plain as day. He’s been doing all this because he’s trying to take over my place. He wants to push me out of my own home, make me look like I'm losing my grip so he can just step in and take over my house and my life. And my wife just sighs and tells me I need to talk to a doctor, but if you saw the way he looks at my property, you'd know exactly what he's up to.

Look, if you're asking if I'm hearing voices whispering in the walls or seeing ghosts floating around the garage, no. Absolutely not. I'm not crazy, doc. I get my hearing checked every single year at the plant. It's a strict OSHA requirement, you know, because we work around heavy hydraulic presses and pneumatic riveters all day long, and you've got to wear your PPE, your earplugs, your muffs, so they test us annually. My hearing is perfectly fine for a fifty-four-year-old guy. 

And my eyes are fine too. I wear safety glasses on the floor, and I've got my reading glasses for the really fine micrometer work, but I don't see things that aren't there. That's the whole point I keep trying to get through my wife's head! I'm not imagining some phantom moving my stuff. I'm seeing real, solid, physical objects—heavy drop-forged steel tools—that have been picked up by a real human hand and moved to a completely different shelf. 

You can't hallucinate a jammed boat trailer latch. You can't just imagine a tangled spool of monofilament line. If you reach out and touch it, it's there. It's real, tangible evidence. So no, I'm not sitting here telling you I have magical visions or hear secret messages from the television. I'm telling you a flesh-and-blood guy is walking onto my property, breathing my air, and touching my things, plain as day.

Look, doc, I don't know what kind of people you usually sit and talk to in here, but no. Nobody is beaming thoughts into my head or steering me around like some kind of remote-control car. That is sci-fi stuff. That is late-night television. I deal in the physical world. I told you, I work with precision parts. If a piece of 6061 aluminum is out of tolerance by three thousandths of an inch, it doesn't fit the assembly. It is just a fact. It is not magic, it is not mind control, it is a physical reality. 

My thoughts are entirely my own. I wake up at 4:30 every single morning, I make my coffee—black, no sugar, the exact same way I have for thirty years—and I think about the production schedule for the day. I think about my wife, I think about my house, and yeah, lately, I spend a lot of time thinking about how to catch this guy in the act. But those are my thoughts. I generated them in my own brain. I am reacting to a real, physical situation that is happening right in front of me. 

If someone comes into your garage and touches your tools, you don't need someone putting thoughts into your brain to get mad about it. You just get mad because it is your property! I bought that torque wrench in 1998, okay? It is a heavy-duty piece of equipment. You don't just let people mess with a tool like that. If you came into your clinic and found your stethoscope or your patient files all rearranged on your desk, you would immediately think to yourself that someone was in your office. You wouldn't sit there and wonder if someone was controlling your mind to make you upset. You would know a physical person walked in and messed with your stuff. 

That is exactly what I am dealing with. So no, nothing impossible is happening to me. No mind-reading, no telepathy, no secret mind-control rays. Just a very real, very sneaky guy trying to play games with my life and my property, and I am apparently the only one thinking clearly enough to see it for exactly what it is.

No, doc, no. I haven't had any head injuries. I mean, you work on a factory floor for thirty-some years, you're going to get some bumps and scrapes, right? I've pinched my fingers in a press a few times, got a nice little scar on my left knuckle from a slip with a deburring tool back in '04, maybe '05. You get some metal shavings in your hands, you get a sore back from standing on concrete for ten hours a day. That's just the nature of the beast. But a head injury? Like a concussion or something? No, never. 

We wear hard hats in the designated zones, anyway. Safety first, right? They're always on us about safety. "Wear your PPE, watch your clearance, keep your area clean." So, no, nothing like that. No major medical stuff either. I've never had a heart attack, no strokes, no cancer, thank God. My blood pressure is a little high, maybe, but whose isn't these days? I take a pill for it, and it's fine. My cholesterol was up a bit a few years ago, so my wife got on this kick of making me eat oatmeal every morning instead of bacon and eggs. I hated it for a month, but I got used to it. Now I kind of like it. 

But no, I'm healthy as a horse. I haven't even had the flu in probably five years. I take my vitamins, I try to get enough sleep, even though I've been waking up a lot lately because I'm so worried about this guy coming around. But as far as some big medical problem or getting hit in the head with a wrench? No. My brain works perfectly fine, doc. Like I said, I'm not sick. I'm just dealing with a very real problem that nobody else seems to want to acknowledge.

Well, if you want to get down to brass tacks, it's been about nine months. Nine months of this absolute nonsense. And it is not a coincidence, doc, because that is exactly when my wife's relative moved into our home. 

You see, he had some sort of falling out with his landlord, or he couldn't make rent, or whatever the sob story was—my wife always has some excuse for him, always babying him. She comes to me and says, "Oh, he just needs a place to crash for a little bit, let's put him up in the spare room." I didn't want it. I told her right then and there, I said, look, I work ten, sometimes twelve-hour shifts on the factory floor. When I clock out and come back to my house, I want peace and quiet. I don't want a roommate at fifty-four years old. I've earned my space. But you know how it goes, you argue and argue, and eventually you just cave to keep the peace. So I let him move in. 

And I swear to you, almost the very first week he was living in our house, that's when the games started. That's when things started shifting around in the garage. Like I told you before, I keep a meticulous workspace. At the plant, we use the 5S system for organization—Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain. Every single tool has a shadow board, every part has a labeled bin. I do the exact same thing at home. So if my three-eighths drive ratchet is sitting on the second shelf instead of hanging on its specific peg, I know it.

Unusually energetic? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, look, I've always been a hard worker. You don't survive thirty-two years on a fabrication line by dragging your feet, right? You have to keep pace. The line doesn't stop because you're feeling sluggish. So I've always had a good motor on me, always been able to put in a solid day's work and then come home and mow the lawn or fix a leaky faucet or whatever needs doing. 

But as far as feeling, what did you call it, unusually energetic? No. If anything, I'm just running on pure adrenaline and frustration lately. And the sleep thing... well, like I mentioned a minute ago, my sleep hasn't been great, but it's not because I don't *need* sleep. Believe me, doc, at fifty-four, after standing on concrete all day, my body absolutely needs sleep. My back aches, my knees ache, my shoulders are tight. I want to sleep. I crave a solid eight hours. 

But I can't. Because how can you sleep when you know someone is creeping around your property, disrespecting your space, messing with the order of things? So I'll lay there in bed, staring at the ceiling fan, listening. Just listening to every little creak and groan the house makes. Is that the wind, or is that him out in the garage again? Did I hear the side door open? Did he leave a window unlatched? So I'll get up, put my slippers on, and go do a perimeter check. I check the locks, I check the garage, I make sure the motion sensor lights are working. 

By the time I get back to bed, I'm all wound up again. And then my alarm goes off at 4:30. So, no, I don't feel like I don't need sleep. I need it desperately. I'm exhausted, to be honest with you. I'm running on fumes some days. But I can't let my guard down, not even for a minute, because the second I do, that's when he'll strike. That's when he'll go in there and move my calipers or hide my socket set just to mess with my head. So, energetic? No. Just vigilant. Highly, highly vigilant.

No! No, he's not. And that's exactly the point, doc! That's what I've been trying to tell everyone, but nobody wants to listen to me! I’m here because everybody keeps acting like I’m imagining it, like I'm crazy or something. My wife, her sister, even the guys at the plant—they all look at me like I've got two heads when I bring it up. But I know what's going on. I know my wife’s relative came into this house to get at me. 

He moved out, what, three months ago? Said he finally got on his feet and found a place across town. But you think that stopped him? Not a chance. If anything, it's worse now because he's sneaking around instead of just living down the hall. My tools don’t move themselves, doc! I already told you about the shadow boards and the 5S system. A wrench doesn't just sprout legs and walk from the pegboard to the workbench. And it's not just the tools anymore. 

It's my whole life! Every weekend, I try to go out to the lake. I've got a little aluminum boat, a 14-footer with a 9.9 Evinrude on the back. Nothing fancy, but it's mine, and I like to go out early on Saturday mornings and just cast a line, get some peace and quiet. But my fishing plans don’t get spoiled by accident every single weekend. One week, the trailer lights are suddenly shorted out. The next week, the spark plugs on the outboard are fouled. Last week, I go out to hook up the trailer, and the hitch pin is gone. Just gone! You don't just lose a heavy-duty steel hitch pin! He's doing it. He's coming around when we're asleep or when I'm at the plant, and he's sabotaging me. 

And I know why, too. It took me a while to piece it all together, but after all these months I can see plain as day he’s been trying to take over my place and push me out. He sees what I have—a good job, a nice house, a stable life—and he wants it. He wants to drive me out of my own home so he can just slide right in and take over. Yes, I do. I feel like I’m constantly hunting for my work badge, my handwritten notes, or clinic folders. Sometimes it’s even the flash drive I literally just had in my hand right before a meeting. It’s really embarrassing, honestly, because I used to be the organized one.

No, not really. I don't have much trouble sitting still. I can sit at my desk or in long clinic meetings without feeling like I need to get up and move around. My mind might be somewhere else entirely, but physically... no, I wouldn't say I feel restless or fidgety.

Yes, definitely. I mean, I honestly believed I could fix the entire production workflow by myself, and do it faster than the whole consulting team we had brought in. No, I don't think so. I mean... people definitely told me my timelines were impossible, or that I was taking on way too much at once. But they never said the things I was talking about were actually untrue or completely out of touch with reality. It was all real work stuff for the plant, I just... I just thought I could execute it all perfectly and way faster than anyone else.

No, I wasn't. I mean... I was definitely intense and probably pretty difficult to work with during that time, but it never got to a point where I had to go to a hospital or anything like that. I was really just going back and forth between my house and the plant.

I'm not exactly sure how many days it was, to be honest. I didn't really keep track. It just felt like a continuous blur of working and going back and forth to the plant. I'd have to really think back to figure out the exact number of days.

No, not really. I wouldn't say it caused any serious problems. I mean, my coworkers were definitely annoyed with how intense I was being at the plant, and I was probably exhausting to be around. Yeah, it definitely lasted at least four days. Like I said, I'm not sure the exact number, but it was for sure longer than that. It was a solid stretch of just... going non-stop.

Yeah, I did. Actually, it's been going on for a while now. Lately, I wake up in my temporary apartment and just have this heavy, hollow feeling. No, not really. I mean, I don't think so. I still do the things I normally do, like watching TV after work or reading a bit. I wouldn't say I've stopped enjoying them, it's just... everything feels heavier right now. But the interest is still there.

Yeah, my eating is kind of all over the place right now. Um, some days I'll be at the plant and suddenly realize it's 4 p.m. and all I've had is coffee. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. Um, even though things feel really heavy and exhausting right now, I don't want to hurt myself. I definitely haven't thought about being better off dead or anything.

No, I wouldn't say I'm unusually tired. My energy levels are actually pretty normal. I know I said earlier that things feel heavy right now, but I still have the physical energy to get through my shifts at the plant and do what I need to do. I'm not, you know, physically drained or struggling to get out of bed or anything like that.

Well, it's nice to meet you too. Um, what brings me in... I guess my head just feels really foggy lately. Yeah, exactly, it's just like I was saying with that foggy feeling. I sit down to do my client notes and I just can't focus, so I end up making these little mistakes. My buddy Dave always says I should've been an accountant because I'm usually so good with details. But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, concentrating. Yeah, I just can't seem to keep my thoughts straight enough to get my work done right.

Well, it's funny you ask about sleep, because usually I'm out like a light by 10 PM. But lately... yeah, for several nights there I was only sleeping maybe three, four hours tops. And the weird thing is, I'd wake up feeling totally charged. Like, ready to go. I'd still make my morning coffee, but honestly, it was more just out of habit than actually needing it to wake up. 

I use this French press my sister got me for my birthday last year. She's really into all that artisanal coffee stuff, buys these beans from some little farm in Colombia. But yeah, I'd just sit there with my fancy coffee at 4 AM, not even tired, just... buzzing, I guess. It was strange.

Yeah, before this whole foggy, low feeling hit me, I did have a stretch where I felt... I don't know, almost too good? I'd get so sharp with my wife over the dumbest little things, or I'd bite my coworkers' heads off if they didn't do something exactly right. 

My wife, she's usually so patient with me. We actually just celebrated our 15th anniversary. We went to this little Italian place downtown, the one with the red checkered tablecloths? They make this incredible lasagna, supposedly an old family recipe from Naples or somewhere. The owner came out and talked to us for like twenty minutes about his grandmother who started the place. He was wearing this wild tie, bright yellow with little green turtles all over it. I remember thinking, who wears a tie like that to run a restaurant? But the food was great. 

Anyway, yeah, I was feeling fantastic, just really on fire, but then I'd just get so irritable and snap at people. It was a weird mix.

Yeah, I definitely was. I just couldn't sit still. It was like... if I stopped moving for even a second, all this grief and heavy stuff would just catch up to me, you know? So I just kept moving. I was making lists, running errands, calling people I haven't talked to in years, doing chores around the house. 

I actually decided to finally clean out the gutters, which I've been putting off forever. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he saw me up on the ladder and came over to give me advice. He's always doing that, thinks he's the neighborhood handyman just because he used to work in construction back in the eighties. He was telling me about this special type of sealant he uses on his roof, went on and on about the chemical composition of it. Honestly, I think he just gets lonely since his kids moved out. His daughter just had a baby, actually, a little girl. They named her something unique... Juniper, I think? Or maybe Willow. One of those nature names that are so popular right now. 

But yeah, I was just constantly finding things to do. If I wasn't doing something, I felt like I was going to explode.

Well, it definitely made things... messy. At work, I'm a personal care aide, so there's a lot of documentation for my clients. Lately, I've had to ask my coworkers to double-check my notes because I just keep missing things. Which reminds me, one of my clients, Mrs. Gable, she has this old grandfather clock in her hallway. Beautiful piece, dark mahogany, must be from the 1920s or something. It chimes every quarter hour, and she told me her late husband bought it at an antique auction in London. They used to travel everywhere before he passed. She showed me pictures of them in Egypt, riding camels right in front of the pyramids. The sky in the photos was this incredible, piercing blue... 

But anyway, yeah, at work I'm just not as reliable with the details right now. And at home, too. My wife has actually had to take over paying some of the bills and handling our schedule. She got this new planner, it's got these little stickers for different appointments. She's always been so organized, unlike me.

Well, let's see... it all started about two weeks ago. This whole shift really kicked in right after my uncle died. We were actually pretty close when I was a kid. He used to take me fishing out at this lake a couple hours from here. Lake... Oconee, I think? Yeah, Lake Oconee. We'd get up at the crack of dawn, pack these terrible bologna sandwiches on white bread with way too much mustard. He had this old aluminum boat that leaked just a little bit, so I always had to bail water out with a plastic Folgers coffee can while he handled the motor. The motor was this vintage Evinrude, smelled like gas and oil, but he swore by it. He said they didn't make them like that anymore. We caught a huge bass out there once, must have been five pounds. He had it mounted and put it in his den... 

But yeah, the not sleeping and all that energy, that started right after he passed, about two weeks ago.

Yeah, definitely. Like I said, this whole shift really started after my uncle died, which was about two weeks ago. And it's just been going ever since. Two weeks of just... zooming. It's funny, when my uncle died, they had this beautiful service for him. The floral arrangements were just incredible. There were these massive wreaths of white lilies and blue hydrangeas. My aunt, she insisted on hydrangeas because they were his mother's favorite flower. She grew them along the side of her house back in Ohio. The soil there must have been really acidic, because the flowers were always this deep, vibrant blue. I read once that you can change the color of hydrangeas by putting coffee grounds or pennies in the soil. I actually tried that in my own garden last spring, but the neighborhood stray cats kept digging it up. There's this one orange tabby that just won't leave my flowerbeds alone. He's got a nick in his left ear, looks like he's been in a few scraps... but yeah, it's been about two weeks straight of this.

Well, yeah, I did. I honestly believed I could just quit waiting around and start my own Spanish-speaking senior-care agency right away. Like, I had it all figured out in my head and I just couldn't fail. It made so much sense. I mean, my grandmother spoke Spanish, and she used to make these amazing tamales every Christmas. The whole family would get together in her tiny kitchen. It was always so hot in there, the windows would steam up completely. She had this old cast-iron pot she used for the masa, must have weighed twenty pounds. My cousin Hector dropped it on his toe once when we were kids, broke it right in two places. He had to wear this clunky black boot for six weeks, which really messed up his soccer season. He was the star goalie for our high school team. They actually went to the state championships that year, played against a team from up north that had these blindingly bright neon green jerseys. You could see them from a mile away... but yeah, I just felt like I had all the answers and could start that agency without a hitch.

Yeah, I guess maybe a little? I don't know, it's hard to tell when you're just going and going. But you know who did talk a lot? My high school speech teacher, Mr. Gable. That guy could talk for hours about absolutely nothing. He had this weird habit of jingling the change in his pocket while he lectured, and it drove everyone crazy. It was always pennies and quarters, just clinking away. I tried saving quarters once in this big plastic Coke bottle bank I won at the county fair. The fair was great back then, they had this ride called the Zipper that just flipped you upside down over and over. I threw up a funnel cake on that ride when I was twelve. Powdered sugar everywhere. My mom was so mad she made me ride home in the bed of my dad's pickup truck. It was an old Chevy C10, light blue, with a cracked windshield on the passenger side from a stray golf ball... but yeah, I'm not really sure if I was talking more than usual or not.

No, I didn't see anything that wasn't there, or think things that people said were crazy. I mean, my sister always tells me my ideas are crazy, but she's just like that. She's been super critical ever since we were kids. Like this one time, we were building a treehouse in the big oak out back, and she kept saying my knots weren't tied right. I learned how to tie knots in the Boy Scouts, actually. We had this scoutmaster, Mr. Henderson, who used to take us camping up near the lake. The mosquitoes there were just huge, like the size of small birds. I got bit so many times on my ankles that summer I had to wear these thick wool socks even though it was ninety degrees out. Wool socks are the worst when it's hot, they make your feet sweat so much and then they smell like wet dog. We had a dog, a golden retriever named Buster, who loved swimming in that lake... but no, I didn't have anything like what you're asking about.

No, I don't think so. I mean, not that I can remember before he passed. His funeral was really hard, actually. We had it at this little church off Route 9, the one with the white steeple that needs painting. The paint was peeling off in these big strips, looked like sunburned skin. I always peel my sunburns, even though you're not supposed to. I got a terrible burn in Florida back in '98. We drove all the way down there in a Honda Civic, four of us crammed in. The AC broke somewhere in Georgia, and we had to roll the windows down, which just blew all this hot, humid air in our faces. My buddy Dave was in the backseat, and he kept complaining about his knees being cramped. He's like six-foot-three, played basketball for a community college in Ohio. They actually made it to some regional tournament, but he sprained his ankle right before the first game. He was so bummed out, he just sat on the bench eating those little bags of pretzels they sell at the concession stand... but yeah, before my uncle, I don't remember ever feeling that revved up or skipping sleep like that.

I don't know, honestly. I mean, everybody handles grief differently, right? When my aunt passed, my cousin cried for like three weeks straight. She couldn't even go to work. She worked at this bakery downtown, the one that makes those amazing blueberry scones. I used to go there every Tuesday morning before my shift. I'm a personal care aide, so I have to be up pretty early to help my clients get out of bed and dressed. One of my guys, Mr. Higgins, he's got this old basset hound that just howls every time the toaster pops. It's the funniest thing. The dog is practically deaf, but he knows the exact sound of that toaster. He loves toast with a little bit of butter on it. Real butter, not the margarine stuff. Margarine is basically just oil and water anyway, I saw a documentary about how they make it in these massive vats... but yeah, I couldn't really tell you if the way I reacted was normal or not.

I don't really remember my wife or the guys at work saying anything about me acting different. My wife was pretty distracted anyway because we were dealing with this leak in the downstairs bathroom. The pipe under the sink kept dripping, just this constant tap-tap-tap all day. It really gets under your skin. We ended up having to call a plumber, this guy named Mike who drives a bright neon green van. You literally can't miss it. He told me he painted it green because his daughter's favorite color is emerald. She's in a high school marching band, plays the trombone, I think. I tried to play the trumpet back in middle school, but I could never get my lips to do the right thing on the mouthpiece. It just sounded like a dying elephant every time I blew into it. Our band teacher, Mr. Davies, had the worst comb-over I've ever seen in my life, he used to sweat so much during the concerts... but no, I don't think anyone told me I was acting out of the ordinary.

No, I don't think I did anything really risky. I mean, I'm usually a pretty careful guy. Like, I always check the tire pressure on my car before a long trip. You know, you can get better gas mileage if your tires are inflated right. I read this article once that said most people are driving around on under-inflated tires and wasting all this money on gas. Gas prices are just crazy right now, anyway. I remember when I first started driving, I could fill up my tank for like fifteen bucks. It was a '89 Ford Escort, manual transmission. I loved that car, but the clutch went out on me when I was stuck in traffic on the George Washington Bridge. That was a nightmare. Cars were honking, people were yelling, and I'm just sitting there sweating buckets trying to get it into gear. The tow truck took forever to get there because of the traffic, and the driver was this huge guy who looked like a professional wrestler... but yeah, I don't remember doing anything wild or impulsive.

Well, I guess before I crashed and started feeling this low, there was a stretch where I felt... I don't know, almost too good? Like really powerful, you know? But then the next minute I'd get real sharp with my wife over nothing, or snap at the guys at work. My wife actually said I was acting like a completely different person when we were trying to pick out a new rug for the living room. We went to this huge warehouse store, the kind where you have to have a membership card just to get in the door. I always lose those cards. I must have had them print me like five replacements in the last year. The lady at the customer service desk was giving me this look, you know, like I was the biggest idiot she'd ever seen. She had these bright pink acrylic nails with little rhinestones on them. I don't know how people type with nails like that, it seems like they'd get caught in the keyboard... but anyway, yeah, I'd feel on top of the world and then just snap at her out of nowhere.

Oh, definitely. I was pushing hard on all these plans at once, like it was nothing. I was sorting out memorial details, getting car repairs done, looking into CNA classes so I could move up at work, and coming up with all these new business ideas. I was calling up my relatives and coworkers way more than I normally would, too. I actually called my cousin Greg like three times in one day about this idea I had for a mobile dog grooming business. Greg has this golden retriever named Buster who sheds like crazy. I mean, there's just hair everywhere in his house. You sit on his couch and you stand up looking like you're wearing a fur coat. He tried buying one of those robot vacuums to keep up with it, but Buster hates the thing. He barks at it whenever it comes out of its little charging dock. It's one of those off-brand ones, not a real Roomba, so it always gets stuck under the coffee table anyway and just beeps until you rescue it... but yeah, I was just juggling a million things at once.

I mean, not really anything besides what I just told you about the CNA classes and the business stuff. I don't think I had like, a big master plan or anything. It's funny you mention goals, though, because my buddy Dave at the clinic—he's another aide there—he has this massive goal to visit every national park in the country before he turns fifty. He just took his RV out to Yellowstone last month. He was telling me all about how terrible the gas mileage is on those things. It's like driving a brick down the highway. Plus, he said the campsites are always completely booked up months in advance now. People just sit at their computers waiting for the reservations to open and boom, they're gone in two seconds. I could never plan a vacation like that. I like to just get in the car and see where the road takes me, you know? Like this one time I just drove up the coast for no reason and ended up at this diner that had the best cherry pie I've ever eaten... but yeah, I don't think I had any other big goals going on.

No, not really. I mean, I snapped at people, like I said, but nobody wrote me up or anything. I've been at that clinic for a while, so people kind of know me. Though, honestly, management there is so disorganized they probably wouldn't notice unless someone actually threw a punch. The HR lady, Brenda, she's always on leave. I swear she's taken three maternity leaves in the last four years. She brought the newest baby into the breakroom a few weeks ago, and it had this little knit hat with bear ears on it. Someone made it for her off Etsy, I think. Etsy's crazy, right? You can buy anything on there. My wife bought these custom wooden coasters with our initials burned into them, but they warp if you put a hot mug on them, which completely defeats the purpose of a coaster if you ask me. You're supposed to protect the table, not worry about ruining the coaster... but no, no big blowups at work or anything like that.

I don't think anyone really said anything to me about it. Maybe they noticed, but people usually keep to themselves, you know? Especially my neighbor, Tom. He's one of those guys who will just give you a little nod if you're both out getting the mail, but he never actually stops to talk. He's always out there working on his lawn, though. He's got this riding mower that looks like a small tractor, and he's out there every Saturday morning at exactly 8:00 AM. It's so loud it wakes up my wife, and she gets so mad because Saturday is her only day to sleep in. She works at the grocery store down the street, the one that just got bought out by that big chain. They completely rearranged the aisles, and now she says customers are constantly yelling at her because they can't find the bread. They moved it all the way to the back corner next to the frozen foods, which makes absolutely no sense. Why would you put bread next to the freezers? It's just going to get cold and stale... but yeah, nobody really pointed out that I was acting differently or anything.

Well, I'm here because I keep messing up little things. It's just... frustrating. Like, I'll write down the wrong time for a class at the senior center, or I'll be working on a project, measure a board, and still cut it a hair short because I just didn't pay attention to the small print on the tape. It's just these careless mistakes that keep happening.

Yeah, I have. Going all the way back to elementary school, actually. I remember my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was a bright kid, but I was constantly forgetting my books or losing my homework. They said I'd just sit there and stare out the window unless someone was right there to keep me on track. So, yeah, it's been happening for a long time.

Yeah, it does. It's not just one area. Those mix-ups have actually made me step back from helping lead a couple of DIY workshops recently. I just didn't want to mess things up for the other folks. 

And at home... well, my wife has had to start double-checking our plans. She has to step in and make sure I don't throw off our family visits or the different activities we're supposed to be doing at the center. So, yeah, it definitely spills over into both my home life and the things I do to keep busy.

Well, like I said, it's always been there in the background, but... it does seem like it's become more of an issue lately. Really, it's been noticeably interfering with things since we moved into the condo. That was about... a year and a month ago, I'd say.

No, my memory is actually pretty good. I don't really have trouble remembering conversations I just had or, you know, when my appointments are. It's more just getting distracted or losing focus, not forgetting things that just happened.

No, I haven't been feeling down or depressed. I mean, it's frustrating dealing with the distractions and the mix-ups, but I wouldn't say I feel hopeless or anything like that. My mood is generally fine.
No, not really. I mean, I worry about normal things here and there, but I don't just sit around worrying for no reason. It's not something that bothers me.

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Well... what brought me in is that I just keep getting up in meetings, or at dinner, when everyone else is perfectly fine just staying seated. Like, I’ll suddenly feel the need to refill my coffee, or check a handout, or just walk to the back of the room even though nothing is really urgent at all. 

And speaking of handouts, the new curriculum they just gave us for the 10th-grade history classes is an absolute nightmare. I mean, they expect us to cover the entire Industrial Revolution in two weeks! And the textbook they gave the kids is just... well, it’s practically falling apart. My husband says I shouldn't stress about it so much, but you know how it is when you've been teaching for 30-some years. You get attached to doing things right. We were actually having dinner at that new Italian place downtown last week to celebrate the end of the term—oh, what's it called, Giovanni's? The garlic bread there is incredible, you really have to try it. But anyway, I just couldn't sit still through the appetizers. I kept getting up to look at the dessert case or check on the coats. 

What was I saying? Oh, right, the meetings. Yes, it's just frustrating because I can't seem to stay in my chair.

Well, I don't know if it's an uncomfortable feeling exactly, but my legs are definitely always busy. Like when I'm sitting at my desk grading essays—and oh, don't even get me started on the essays this year. The grammar is just atrocious. I don't know what they teach them in middle school anymore, but it certainly isn't punctuation! I had one student, bless his heart, who wrote an entire page about the French Revolution as a single run-on sentence. 

But anyway, when I'm sitting there trying to get through the grading, or even when I'm in church on Sundays, I'll catch myself tapping my foot constantly. Or I'll be clicking my red pen, just click-click-click, and shifting around in my seat so much that I actually have to stop and remind myself to just settle down. The pews at our church are terribly hard, though. They haven't replaced the cushions since the late nineties, I swear. My husband always insists on sitting on the aisle because he likes the legroom, but I just end up squirming through the whole sermon.

Worried? Oh, no, I wouldn't say that. I don't feel nervous or anxious when I can't stay in my chair, it's just... well, I just feel like I need to be doing something. Though, speaking of being on edge, the only thing that really has me worried lately is the upcoming school board meeting. They’re talking about cutting funding for the music programs, which is just an absolute tragedy. I mean, my niece plays the cello, and she is phenomenal—just absolutely phenomenal. She’s actually looking at conservatories for next year. Juilliard, Peabody... we’re all so proud of her. 

My sister spent a small fortune on private lessons, of course, driving her all the way to Boston every single weekend. The traffic on I-90 is just dreadful, especially in the summer with all the tourists heading to the Cape. I told her she should just take the train, but she insists she needs the car for the instrument. 

But anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right. No, I don't feel worried or on edge in my own head when I'm getting up from my desk or the table. I just can't seem to stay put.

Worse in the evening? No, I haven't noticed it being worse then. It's pretty much the same no matter what time it is, just whenever I'm stuck sitting. 

Though, to be honest, by the time evening actually rolls around, I'm usually so exhausted from dealing with the teenagers all day that I just collapse in my favorite armchair. My husband and I have been watching that new British mystery series on PBS—oh, the one set in the Cotswolds? It is just delightful. You never design a structure to just barely hold the expected load; you design it to hold two, three, sometimes five times that amount, depending on the application. Like elevators. The cables on an elevator are usually designed with a safety factor of eleven. Eleven! That means a single cable could hold eleven times the weight of a fully loaded car, and most elevators have four to eight cables. It's incredibly redundant. But people still get terrified of getting in them. They watch too many movies where the cables snap and the car goes into freefall. But the truth is, even if all the cables snapped—which is statistically nearly impossible—Elisha Otis invented the safety hoist back in 1852. It's a mechanical braking system that engages automatically if the car falls too fast. It wedges into the guide rails in the shaft. It's a brilliant piece of engineering, really. So simple, but it completely changed the modern city. We wouldn't have skyscrapers without it.

Employee assistance programs are actually a relatively new concept in the corporate world. They really started gaining traction in the 1970s, mostly focusing on occupational alcoholism at first. But now they cover everything from financial counseling to mental health crises. It's a smart investment for companies, really, when you look at the cost-benefit analysis. The cost of replacing a specialized employee—especially in engineering, where you have to factor in recruitment, onboarding, and the loss of institutional knowledge—is astronomical. It can be up to 200% of their annual salary. So paying a third-party vendor a few dollars per employee per month for an EAP is just basic risk mitigation. It's like installing a pressure relief valve on a boiler. You hope you never need it, but if the pressure builds up too high, you absolutely want it there to prevent a catastrophic explosion. Boilers are terrifying if they aren't maintained properly. Water expands 1,600 times its volume when it turns to steam. If a boiler ruptures, it can level an entire building. Blankness is actually a huge problem in material science, though we usually call it voids. When you're pouring concrete, for example, if it's not vibrated properly, you get these air pockets or voids trapped inside the forms. We call it honeycombing. It looks exactly like it sounds, just this porous, brittle mess on the surface of the concrete. It completely compromises the structural integrity because those voids create stress concentrations. The compressive strength just plummets. And repairing it is a nightmare. You have to chip away all the defective concrete until you hit sound material, and then patch it with a high-strength grout, but the bond between the old concrete and the new patch is always a weak point. It's never as strong as a monolithic pour. That's why inspectors are so obsessive about slump tests and watching the vibration process during a pour. A single bad truckload of concrete can ruin a bridge pier. Well... okay, so earlier I said no about the numbers sending messages, and I know I sounded really sure about that. But... I mean, I guess it's more complicated than just "yes" or "no," right? Just data. But... sometimes... 

I know it sounds strange, really strange, especially coming from someone who literally does bookkeeping for a living, but sometimes I get absolutely convinced that certain numbers are... well, they're not just data. Like, specific invoice totals, or the account numbers for certain vendors, or even the net-30 due dates on the accounts payable aging report... I start feeling like they are messages. About me. Specifically meant for me to find. 

Like, last Tuesday, I was reconciling the bank statement against our general ledger, and I noticed this sequence of invoice totals—$412.50, $41.25, and then an account number ending in 4125. And I just stopped. I sat there at my L-shaped desk, staring at my dual monitors, and my heart started racing because I just knew, I *knew*, it was a message. It felt like the system was trying to tell me something, or maybe test me. So I spent, like, three hours digging through old archived files, pulling up vendor histories from like three years ago, trying to trace the origin of the 4125 pattern, completely ignoring the rest of the daily deposits I was supposed to be working on. 

My supervisor, Linda, she came over because she noticed I hadn't submitted the daily reconciliation report yet. She's usually really nice, she's been there for like fifteen years, and she sat down with me and looked at my screen. She pulled up the original invoices and the vendor contracts, and she walked me through it, step by step, showing me exactly why those totals were what they were. Like, one was just a standard order of printer toner with sales tax, and another was a prorated software license fee. She showed me all the documentation, proving they were just completely normal, everyday business entries. 

And logically, when she was explaining it, I could hear her words, and I could see the math on the screen. But even after she walked away, even after I finally submitted the report and went back to my turkey sandwich... I still felt it. Deep down. I still felt like those numbers were tracking me. Like whoever or whatever put them there was watching to see if I understood the pattern, to see if I was smart enough to figure out what the 4125 meant. And it's not just that one time, it happens with other numbers, too. It's like I can't shake the feeling that there's a hidden layer of meaning in the spreadsheets that only I am supposed to see, even when Linda proves to me that it's just regular accounting stuff. It's really hard to explain, but it just feels so real when it happens.

Watching me? Like, a person? No, no. I know I just said that thing about the numbers feeling like they were tracking me or testing me, which I guess sounds a little like being watched, but it's not a physical person spying on me or anything like that. And definitely no one is trying to harm me. 

My L-shaped desk is tucked way in the back corner of the accounting floor, and my back is technically to the main walkway, which I guess would make some people paranoid, but I never feel like someone is standing behind me staring at the back of my head. I mean, the only people who even walk by are Dave, who is way too busy stressing out and clicking his retractable pen to care about what I'm doing, and Linda, and she's practically the nicest person in the world. She brings in glazed donuts every other Friday from this little bakery near her house. She's definitely not out to get me or sabotage my work. Nobody is trying to poison my turkey sandwich in the breakroom fridge or anything crazy like that. 

And outside of work, it's the same thing. Like when I'm walking to my car after my night classes at the community college, it's usually pretty dark out by then, especially in the winter, but I don't get spooked. I just walk straight to my car, get in, and drive home. I don't ever look in my rearview mirror and feel like there's someone following my car, and I don't think anyone is hiding in the bushes waiting to jump out at me. I don't feel in danger at all. I'm just a twenty-two-year-old bookkeeping clerk, you know? I don't think I'm important enough for anyone to want to follow me around or hurt me. It's really just that weird hidden-message feeling I get with the spreadsheets sometimes, but not actual people out to get me.

Voices? Um... well, I mean... yes. But it's not like a whole crowd of people yelling or anything like that. It's usually just this one specific voice, and it only really happens when I'm completely by myself. 

Like, I'll be sitting at my desk—that L-shaped one I was telling you about, tucked away in the back corner of the accounting floor. It gets really quiet back there, especially around four-thirty when Dave is off getting his afternoon coffee and Linda is wrapping up her daily emails. I'll just be sitting there, staring at my dual monitors, maybe scrolling through a massive Excel spreadsheet for the month-end reconciliation, and out of nowhere, I'll hear this man's voice. And it sounds so incredibly real, like someone is leaning right over my shoulder. He'll say something really specific, like, "check line seven." 

And I mean, it's so clear and loud that I physically turn my office chair around. I'll spin around expecting to see Dave standing there holding his mug, or maybe a courier who wandered into the wrong department, but... there's literally no one. Just the empty carpeted walkway and the hum of the overhead air conditioner. I'll even stand up and look over the cubicle wall just to be absolutely sure, but I'm completely alone. 

And it's not just at work, either. It happens sometimes when I'm leaving my night classes at the community college, too. Like I said before, I usually just walk straight to my car, and it's pretty dark and empty out in that parking lot by the time my accounting ethics class gets out. Sometimes, when I'm halfway across the asphalt, just me and the orange streetlights, I'll hear that exact same man's voice. He'll say something like, "you missed the sign." 

I'll stop dead in my tracks right there in the cold. I'll look all around, checking behind the parked cars, looking back toward the brick wall of the science building, because I swear to you, it sounds like a real person is walking two steps behind me. But the lot is totally empty. And then I just stand there overthinking it, wondering, what sign? Did I miss a literal parking sign, or does he mean a sign like the weird number patterns at work? It really messes with my head because the voice doesn't feel like a thought inside my brain, you know? It sounds like it's traveling through the air, hitting my eardrums exactly the way your voice is right now. I've even pulled my phone out of my jacket pocket to see if maybe a YouTube video started playing by accident, or if I pocket-dialed a podcast, but my screen is always black. It's just... it's just this guy's voice speaking right to me, and I have absolutely no idea where it's coming from.
