I know they're all right there, and I know I should just put the spoon down or hand over the napkins. 

But it's like... like my body just won't listen to what my brain is telling it to do. I'm standing there, holding that spoon up, and inside my head I'm screaming, 'Martha, put the spoon in the dish! Serve the food!' but my arm just stays locked right up there in the air. And with the napkins, I can see the line of people, I can see little Timmy Jenkins practically bouncing on his toes waiting for a plate, but my hands just keep smoothing those creases. I'm there, I know I'm there, but I just can't seem to stop myself from doing it. It's the most helpless feeling in the world, doctor, just being stuck inside yourself while everyone watches.

Well, no, doctor, I don't think I do. I mean, I've thought about it, naturally, because you just want some sort of warning, don't you? Some little sign that tells you, 'Martha, it's about to happen again.' But there's just... nothing. No strange smells, thank goodness. My sister Agnes, rest her soul, she used to get these terrible migraines, and she'd always smell burnt toast right before one came on. I always thought that was the strangest thing, smelling something that isn't there, but she swore by it. She'd say, 'Martha, check the toaster,' and I'd know she needed to go lie down in a dark room with a cold washcloth over her eyes. 

But for me, with this... this freezing up business, there's no burnt toast. No funny tastes in my mouth either. I still have my morning coffee, just a half cup with a splash of milk, and maybe a piece of dry toast or half a grapefruit if they're on sale at the Piggly Wiggly, and it all tastes perfectly normal. And my stomach... well, my stomach gets a little fluttery sometimes, but that's just nerves, isn't it? Like when I have to read the announcements in front of the whole congregation because Mary Ellen is out sick with her sciatica again. But it's not a rising feeling or anything peculiar like that before I get stuck holding the spoon. 

It just... it just happens. One minute I'm scooping the casserole—and it's a heavy casserole, doctor, made with three cans of cream of mushroom soup and those crispy fried onions on top, just the way the pastor likes it—and the next minute, I'm just frozen. No warning, no funny feelings, just... stuck. I wish there was a warning, I really do. Maybe then I could at least put the spoon down first so I wouldn't look quite so ridiculous standing there like a statue. But no, nothing like that at all.

Well, yes and no, doctor. It's... it's a very strange thing to try and explain. I remember being there, like I said, I remember the sounds and the people waiting, but when it's over, it's almost like waking up from a daydream that you didn't know you were having. Like... like when you're watching television, maybe one of those nice Hallmark movies, and you just sort of drift off for a second, and then you blink and you're back, but you know you missed a piece of the story. 

I remember being frozen, holding that spoon up, and I remember little Timmy Jenkins bouncing around, but then... it's like a jump in time. Suddenly my arm is down, or I'm putting the napkins in the basket, and I have to sort of catch my breath and figure out how much time has passed. Did I stand there for ten seconds? A minute? Five minutes? I just don't know. 

Mrs. Higgins, she's a dear, she usually just pats my arm and says, 'Take your time, Martha, dear,' and that's usually what snaps me all the way back. But the actual time I spent frozen... it's just a blank space. A little hole in my memory right there in the middle of the fellowship hall. And it's so unsettling, doctor, to lose time like that, even if it's just a few moments. It makes me wonder what else I might be forgetting, you know? Like, did I leave the stove on at home? Did I lock the front door? If my brain can just switch off while I'm holding a serving spoon full of mushroom casserole, what else is it doing without my permission? It's just... it's just very worrying, that's what it is.

Well, see, that's just the thing, doctor, and it's what really finally made me make this appointment and come in to see you. Because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and it's getting so embarrassing. Like I said about standing by the potluck table, holding the serving spoon up and just... not moving. Or the napkins! Folding the same stack of napkins over and over again while people are just standing there, waiting on me. 

And to answer your question about moving my arm... well, yes. That's exactly what happened last Sunday, actually. I was frozen there with the spoon, holding it right up over the casserole dish, and Mary Ellen—she was feeling a bit better, her sciatica must have eased up because she was back at church—she came up beside me. She didn't make a fuss, bless her heart, she just gently took my elbow and sort of guided my arm down closer to the dish. And... it just stayed there. Exactly where she put it. 

It was the strangest feeling. I didn't resist her, my arm didn't feel stiff or heavy, it just... moved where she pushed it and then stopped again. Like I was a mannequin in one of those department store windows downtown, you know? The ones at Macy's where they dress them up for Christmas. She moved my arm, and I just stayed in that new position, still holding the spoon, still not scooping the casserole, just hovering an inch above the crispy onions instead of up in the air. I stayed like that until Mrs. Higgins finally patted my shoulder and I sort of snapped out of it. But yes, if someone moves me, I just stay right where they put me, like a doll. It's just not right, doctor, a grown woman acting like a statue while the whole congregation is waiting for their lunch.

Voices? Oh, no, doctor. No, I haven't heard anything like that. I mean, my hearing isn't quite what it used to be, of course. I had to ask Reverend Thomas to speak up just last week during the sermon because he gets to leaning on the pulpit and his voice just drops down to a mumble, and I couldn't hear a word he was saying about the Good Samaritan. But as for hearing people who aren't there... no. 

I live alone, you see, since my husband Henry passed—it'll be twelve years this November, God rest his soul—so the house is very quiet. Sometimes too quiet, if I'm being honest. That's why I like to keep the television on, or the radio in the kitchen when I'm doing my baking. Just for a little background noise, you know? But it's always Bob Barker on The Price is Right or the local news anchors, never... never strange voices just speaking to me out of thin air. 

I did have a neighbor once, Mrs. Gable, who lived two houses down, and she swore she could hear her late mother telling her how to prune the rose bushes, but I always just thought she was a bit eccentric. Or maybe just lonely, bless her heart. But no, for me, there's nothing like that. Just the usual creaks and groans of an old house settling, and the refrigerator humming, and sometimes the neighbor's dog barking at the mailman. But no voices, thank goodness. I think I'd be absolutely terrified if I started hearing someone talking in my living room when I knew the doors were all locked tight. That would just be the icing on the cake with all this freezing up nonsense, wouldn't it? But no, my mind might be playing tricks on my body, making me stand still like a statue, but it hasn't started making up voices yet.

Well, depressed? No, doctor, I wouldn't use that word at all. I mean, I have my moments, of course, just like anybody else who's getting up there in years and living all on their own. When my Henry first passed away, oh, I was in a terrible state for a long while. I'd just sit in the parlor and let the days go by without even opening the curtains, just watching the dust settle on his favorite armchair. But that was grief, you know, and the Good Lord and time do their work with that. 

Lately? No, I don't feel hopeless or sad in that heavy sort of way. I still get up every morning at six o'clock sharp, I make my pot of Folgers, I put on my face, and I make sure the bird feeders out back are full. The bluejays have been just ravenous this week, and if I were truly depressed, I don't suppose I'd care a lick about whether they got their black oil sunflower seeds, would I? I still love my garden, and I still love baking my casseroles. 

Now, I will say I've been feeling awfully frustrated. And embarrassed, too, like I was saying about the church potlucks. It's a heavy thing to carry, worrying about when my body is just going to decide to turn into a mannequin again, and it does make me a bit nervous to go out. Sometimes I think to myself, Martha, maybe you should just stay home today so you don't end up frozen over the ambrosia salad and making a scene. But I force myself to go because I love seeing Mary Ellen and Mrs. Higgins and the rest of the ladies. 

My sister Margaret, now she had real depression back in the nineties. She wouldn't wash her hair, wouldn't answer the telephone for days on end, she just pulled the covers right up over her head and shut the whole world out. It was a terrible worry for all of us, bringing her casseroles she wouldn't even touch. But I'm not doing anything like that. I want to be out and about, doctor, I really do. I have too much living left to do to be hiding under the bedsheets. I just want to figure out why I keep pausing like a broken television set so I can get back to enjoying my life properly without all the church ladies whispering about me. So no, I'm not depressed. Just... very bothered and worn out by all this freezing business, that's all.

Well, yes, actually. That goes right back to what I was telling you when I first sat down, doctor, and it's the whole reason I finally made this appointment in the first place. Because, like I said, I just keep doing these odd things at church, like standing by that potluck table holding the serving spoon up in the air and just... not moving at all. Or folding that exact same stack of napkins over and over again while folks are just standing there waiting on me to move along. 

Well, during that napkin business—they were the nice yellow ones we bought for the spring luncheon, with the little white lilies printed on the corners, very pretty but very thin paper—Mrs. Higgins told me later that she had been standing right across from me. She said she asked me, "Martha dear, could you hand me the salt shaker?" And apparently, I didn't say a peep. She said she asked me three separate times, doctor! Three times! And she told me I just kept right on creasing that same paper napkin, looking right through her like she wasn't even there. 

Mary Ellen said the exact same thing about the casserole incident with the spoon. Before she finally took my elbow and pushed my arm down, she said she had been saying my name. "Martha? Martha?" Just like that, in a loud whisper so as not to cause a scene. And I didn't answer her. I didn't even blink, according to her. 

It’s just so mortifying. I was raised to always answer when spoken to, it’s just common courtesy, you know? My mother would have tanned my hide if I ever ignored a grown woman looking right at me, let alone an elder in the congregation. But to hear them tell it, I was completely unresponsive, just off in my own world, doing those odd little repetitive things or standing like a statue while the whole buffet line is held up. It makes me sound so incredibly rude, but I promise you I don't mean to be! I just... I don't even realize they're talking to me until I finally snap out of it and see them all staring.

Confused? Well, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel confused at all. It's not like... well, you know how sometimes you fall asleep in your recliner in the middle of the afternoon, maybe with the television running, and you wake up and the room is all dim and for just a split second you don't know if it's Tuesday morning or Friday night? It is absolutely nothing like that. 

When I snap out of one of these little spells, I know exactly where I am and exactly what I'm doing. Like with the serving spoon at the potluck. When Mary Ellen finally pushed my arm down, my mind was clear as a bell. I knew I was in the fellowship hall, I knew we were serving the macaroni and cheese, and I knew all those ladies were waiting in line behind me. I didn't have to look around and wonder how I got there or who these people were. 

My brother-in-law, Arthur, God rest him, he used to get confused near the end of his life. He would wander out onto the porch in his slippers in the dead of winter and think he was waiting for the school bus. Now that is real confusion. But for me, it's just... well, it's just a terrible embarrassment, is what it is. I snap back to attention and the very first thing I feel is my face getting hot because I can see everybody staring at me. I realize I've been standing there like a statue, and I just try to smooth it over right away. 

I remember looking right at Mary Ellen and apologizing up and down, telling her I just drifted off for a second and handing her the spoon. If I was truly confused, I wouldn't have known to apologize, would I? I wouldn't have known she was waiting on me to move along the buffet line. So no, no confusion in my head, doctor. My brain is working just fine the very second I unfreeze. It's just my pride that takes a terrible beating, having to smile and pretend everything is perfectly normal when I know they're all going to be gossiping about it during choir practice.

Oh, heavens no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what folks might think when they see me just standing there frozen at the buffet line, they might think, "Oh, Martha's having some kind of a fit," but it is absolutely not a seizure. I've never been told I have epilepsy or any kind of nerve problem, not once in my seventy-one years. 

I actually know what a real seizure looks like, you see. My cousin Tommy, God rest his soul, he had the falling sickness back when we were growing up in the fifties. It was just awful to watch, bless his heart. He would drop right down to the linoleum, shaking all over, thrashing about, and his mother would have to run and get a wooden spoon or a rolled-up rag to put between his teeth so he wouldn't bite his own tongue clean off. It was a terrifying thing for a young girl to see, let me tell you. But I don't do anything even remotely like that! I don't shake, I don't fall to the floor, I don't lose control of my limbs or foam at the mouth. I just... well, I just get stuck. Like a statue. 

And as for my brain, well, Dr. Miller—he was my regular doctor for nearly thirty years before he went and retired down to Boca Raton, lovely man, always wore the most cheerful bowties—he always told me I had the constitution of a workhorse. Never had a single problem with my head. I didn't get much schooling, had to leave before the ninth grade to help my mother with the little ones, but my mind has always been perfectly sound. I don't take any nerve pills, I've never had to go for any of those fancy brain scans, nothing of the sort. 

So whoever is whispering about me having epilepsy at the church, well, they are just plain wrong, doctor. It's just this strange pausing thing I was telling you about. Aside from that, my brain and my nerves are just as healthy as they've ever been.

Smack my lips? Oh, my goodness, no. No, doctor, nobody has ever mentioned anything like that to me. If I was standing up there at the potluck table smacking my lips like a cow with the cud, well, Mary Ellen would have certainly told me. She doesn't miss a single trick, that woman, and she's not shy about pointing out a person's flaws, let me tell you. 

But no, when Mrs. Higgins was talking about the napkin incident, she just said I was staring blankly right through her. She didn't say a single word about my mouth moving. I actually make a point never to chew on anything unless I am properly seated at a dining table. My mother always said that chewing gum or smacking your mouth in public was just the absolute height of bad manners, especially in the house of the Lord! Can you imagine? 

I mean, I do have a partial lower plate—I got it about five years ago when my back teeth finally gave out on me, probably from too many of my Aunt Betty's peanut brittle squares at Christmastime over the years, she always made them entirely too hard—and I know sometimes folks with dentures might move their mouths around or smack their lips if the fit isn't quite right. You see it all the time with the older folks over at the care center. But my plate fits just beautifully. Dr. Evans made sure of it, took three separate molds just to get it perfect. 

So no, my mouth is just shut tight when these little spells happen. Just the freezing up and the staring, no chewing on thin air. If I was making odd faces or smacking my lips at Mrs. Higgins on top of ignoring her, I think I just would have died of embarrassment right then and there! It's bad enough just standing there like a bump on a log holding a serving spoon, don't you think?

Oh, a stroke or a tumor? Goodness gracious, no. No, doctor, nothing like that has ever happened to me. I've never had a stroke, and I've certainly never had a brain tumor or... what was the other one? Encephalitis? I don't even rightly know what that is, to tell you the truth, but I know I've never had it. 

My brain has always been perfectly fine, just like I was telling you before. Dr. Miller always said I was healthy as a horse, right up until he moved to Florida. And even my new doctor, Dr. Patel—she’s a very sweet young woman, very thorough, always asks about my diet and tells me I need to eat more leafy greens, which I do try, I really do, I put spinach in my salads now instead of just iceberg lettuce—she’s never found a single thing wrong with my head. 

I did bump my head once, though, now that I think about it. It was back in... oh, it must have been 1982, because it was the year of that terrible blizzard. I was out shoveling the front walk, just trying to clear a little path for the mailman, and I slipped on a patch of black ice right near the bottom step. Down I went, and I gave the back of my head a good whack on the concrete. I saw stars for a minute, I really did, and I had a lump the size of a goose egg for a week. My husband, bless his heart, he was so worried he made me lay on the couch with a bag of frozen peas on my head all afternoon. But I never went to the hospital for it, never passed out, and I certainly didn't have any lasting damage. It was just a silly slip on the ice. 

But as far as real illnesses go? Tumors or strokes? No, absolutely not. My friend Brenda, she had a mild stroke a few years back, and it was just awful. The whole left side of her face drooped, and she couldn't talk right for months. She had to do all that speech therapy and physical therapy, learning how to hold a fork again. It was a terrible ordeal for her family. But I don't have anything like that. I can talk just fine, obviously, and my face is perfectly even. It's just these spells where I freeze up like a statue, like I told you. Other than that, my brain is as healthy as can be.

An infection? Or a fever? Oh, goodness me, no. No, doctor, nothing like that at all. Like I was just saying, I have always had the constitution of a workhorse. I haven't even had so much as the sniffles in I don't know how long! 

Well... I suppose my youngest grandson, little Petey, he did have a terrible chest cold right around Thanksgiving. Just hacking and coughing all over the dinner table, bless his heart, he's only five and hasn't quite mastered covering his mouth yet. My daughter Susan was just beside herself, she kept trying to force me to take this awful elderberry syrup she buys at that expensive health food store. Tastes exactly like old shoes, if you ask me! But I told her, I said, "Susan, I do not need that snake oil," and wouldn't you know it, I didn't catch a single thing from him. Not a cough, not a sneeze, and certainly no fever. I haven't run a fever since... oh, it must be twenty years now. 

So no, these strange little pausing spells didn't come on after any sort of sickness or infection. They just started happening all on their own, right out of the clear blue sky. I was perfectly healthy, going about my business, making my potato salad, and then suddenly I'm just getting stuck like a statue for no rhyme or reason. There wasn't any bug or virus that brought it on, I can promise you that. I always make sure to get my flu shot down at the Walgreens every single October anyway, right when they put the little cardboard signs out on the sidewalk. The pharmacist there, Kevin, he has such a gentle hand, you barely even feel the needle go in, and he always asks after my hydrangeas. But no, no fevers or infections here, doctor. Just the freezing up.

Speak? Oh, heavens no. That's exactly why I finally decided I needed to come in and see you, doctor, because of these odd things I keep doing at church and how I can't even answer folks when they talk to me. 

Like I was saying before about the potluck table... when I get stuck just standing there, holding the serving spoon up in the air and not moving an inch, folks will come right up to me. Mary Ellen or somebody might ask, "Are you going to serve that?" or "Is there any of the macaroni salad left?" and I just... I don't say a single solitary word back to them. It's like my voice is just as frozen as my arm! 

And it was the exact same way with the napkins. I know I mentioned Mrs. Higgins earlier, but what happened was I just stood there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just creasing them, unfolding them, and folding them right back up, like I was in some sort of trance. And there was a whole line of people waiting on me to move so they could get to the silverware! They were standing right there waiting, saying, "Excuse me," and asking if I was feeling alright, and I just kept right on folding those napkins without making a peep. 

I can't tell you how rude it makes me feel, looking back on it. My mother, rest her soul, she would have tanned my hide if I ever just flat-out ignored someone who was speaking directly to me. It's the absolute height of bad manners! But during those little spells, I just can't seem to get a word out. I'm just stuck doing these odd things while everyone waits on me, and I can't even say "I'm sorry" or "Just a minute, please." It’s entirely out of my hands, I just can't speak at all until the spell passes.

Well... now that you ask it like that, yes. Yes, there was something just awful that happened. It breaks my heart to even talk about it, to be perfectly honest with you, doctor. 

You see, my dearest friend in the whole wide world... well, we sang in the church choir together. We were both altos, and we stood right next to each other on the second riser every single Sunday for, oh, it had to be near on thirty years. She was the only one in the whole congregation who could hit the low notes in our hymns without sounding like a bullfrog, bless her soul. We did just about everything together. We would carpool to practice on Thursday nights, and she would always bring those little hard butterscotch candies in her purse, the ones wrapped in the yellow cellophane, to keep our throats from getting dry during the long sermons. 

But she passed away. It was just a terrible, terrible shock to all of us. And that was... let me think, it was right before the spring jubilee, so it's been about 11 months ago now. Eleven long months without her. It was just the most upsetting thing I've ever been through in all my days, losing her like that. When she died, it felt like a piece of me just went right with her. I cried for days and days, I couldn't hardly eat my supper, and the church just felt so empty without her standing there next to me. 

And you know, you're exactly right. I hadn't really put two and two together until you just asked, but that is exactly when this whole change started. These spells, the freezing up like a statue and getting stuck at the potluck table... it’s been going on since my closest choir friend died, about 11 months ago. I was just so overcome with the grief of it all, and then suddenly I started having these pauses where I couldn't move or speak. It all started right after I lost her. I just haven't been the same since she passed.

Touch me or call my name? Well, no... no, that doesn't seem to break the spell at all, doctor. Like I was telling you just a minute ago about how I keep doing these odd things at church... it's just so embarrassing. I'll be right there by the potluck table, just standing there holding the serving spoon up in the air, not moving a single muscle. And folks will come right up to me, they'll say, "Martha, Martha, are you alright?" They'll say my name clear as day, and Mary Ellen even put her hand right on my shoulder last Sunday when I was stuck like that. She gave me a little shake, a gentle one, of course, because she's a sweet woman, but it didn't do a lick of good. I just stayed frozen there with the spoon.

And it's the exact same thing with those napkins. I told you about how I was folding that same stack of napkins over and over again, just creasing and unfolding and folding them back up while people were waiting. Well, Mrs. Higgins, she got so impatient—you know how she gets when she's hungry—she actually reached out and tapped my arm. She tapped me right on the elbow and said, "Martha, dear, we need to get to the silverware." But even with her tapping me and calling my name, I just kept right on folding. It didn't snap me out of it one bit. I just have to wait until the spell decides to pass on its own, no matter what anybody does to try and wake me up from it. It's like I'm locked inside myself until it's good and ready to let me go.

A seizure? Oh, heavens, no. No, nothing like that at all. I mean, I know what a seizure looks like, you see, because my cousin Earls youngest boy used to get them when he was just a little thing. He would fall right down on the floor and shake all over, and his mother would have to rush over and put a rolled-up towel under his head so he would not bang it on the kitchen linoleum. It was just a terrifying thing to watch, let me tell you, just a terrible fright for everyone in the room. But me? No, I have never had a single thing like that happen to me in all my seventy-one years. 

Before these freezing spells started up... the ones where I just get stuck holding the serving spoon or folding those napkins... well, I was always healthy as a horse, for the most part. I mean, my knees are not quite what they used to be, and I take a little pill in the mornings, but as far as my nerves and my brain went, I was perfectly fine. I never had any kind of fit or seizure or anything where I would shake or fall down. It is just these new spells where I freeze up like a statue that are the problem. I never had any trouble like that before my dear friend passed away. Never a seizure, no doctor, not once in my whole life.

Copying someone else? Oh, my word, no. No, I don't believe I've ever done anything quite like that. When I get stuck... well, like I was telling you about the potluck table, I'm just frozen in my own little world. I'm not paying a bit of attention to what Mary Ellen or Mrs. Higgins or anybody else is doing. 

I mean, if Mary Ellen was waving her hands around or saying a prayer, I certainly wouldn't start waving my hands or saying the prayer right along with her. I wouldn't even know she was doing it, to be perfectly honest. I'm just locked up tight as a drum, holding my spoon or folding my napkins. I've never caught myself repeating what folks say to me, either. When they ask if I'm alright, I don't say, "Are you alright?" right back at them like some sort of parrot. I just don't say anything at all. 

It's really just the freezing up, doctor. I'm not copying a soul. I'm just stuck exactly how I was when the spell decided to come over me. It's the strangest thing, it really is, but it's just me being frozen, not me trying to mimic anybody else in the room. I can promise you that much.

Confusion or memory problems? Oh, no, doctor, no... nothing like that at all. My mind is just as sharp as a tack, thank the Lord. I mean, well, I might forget where I put my reading glasses now and then, but that's just normal for a woman my age, isn't it? I'll set them down by the telephone when Mary Ellen calls, and then I'll spend ten minutes looking for them on the coffee table. But that's not what you mean, I know. 

As far as being confused or losing my memory... no, I remember everything clear as a bell. I remember exactly what happened at the church potluck, who was there, what Mrs. Higgins was wearing—she had on that awful floral print dress she bought at the rummage sale three years ago, the one with the big yellow sunflowers on it. I remember every single detail. I know what day it is, I know who the president is, I know exactly what I need to buy at the grocery store without even making a list. I just don't have any trouble with my memory or getting mixed up about things, not outside of those freezing spells, and not during them either, really. I just get stuck. But my mind? Oh, my mind is perfectly fine, doctor, perfectly fine. I've always prided myself on having a good memory, even when I was a little girl in school, before I had to leave to help my mother with the younger ones. I could recite whole poems by heart! And I still can, if you'd like to hear one, though I suppose we don't have time for that today. But no, no confusion, no memory problems at all. Just the freezing up, that's the only trouble I'm having.

Hi. Um... I guess I'm just having some trouble sitting through things. What finally pushed me to make an appointment is... well, I keep getting up during important things. Like sprint planning for work, or... I had these mortgage calls recently. 

I know I should just stay put, but I'll just... suddenly decide I need water, or I'll feel like I have to go check something in the other room. So... yeah. That's why I'm here.
Um... no. Not really. It's not about... preventing anything bad from happening. I just... I don't know, I just get up.
No, it's not panic. I just... I don't know, I just feel restless, I guess. It's not a panic attack or anything.
Um... no. I don't think so. I'm pretty much always just... like this. I haven't noticed any weird spikes in energy or anything.

Yeah, I guess so. Um... even if I'm just sitting there, looking calm on the outside... I still get this pressure inside. Like I just need to move, or... do something with my hands, or switch to a different task. It just... it feels like I'm going to crawl out of my skin if I don't.
Um... no, not really. I can usually follow a conversation fine. I haven't noticed any issues with that.
Um... no, not really. I don't think I'm worrying about anything when it happens. It's just... a physical feeling, I guess.

Yeah, I think so. Um... in elementary school, my teachers were always... moving my desk around. They had to remind me to stay in my seat a lot. I guess I was always getting up, or... blurting things out before it was my turn. And I'd rush through my work, even if I knew how to do it. So... yeah, it's been around for a while.

Well, I’m here because... honestly, it’s just been exhausting. For months now I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern. My sister’s appointments keep getting moved around, the bills show up wrong, and people just conveniently 'forget' to call me back. 

Which is completely unacceptable to me, because I actually supervise an entire team of administrative support workers. Like, when I'm working the night shift at the corporate park, I'll have my headphones on, listening to some classic rock or maybe a baseball game if it's the season, and I'm humming along, getting the floors done. I'm energized, sure, because of that engine feeling we talked about, but it's not like an unusual high or anything. It's just my normal, everyday level of... well, of being wound up. 

And irritable? I mean, sure, I get annoyed if the buffing machine breaks down or if somebody tracks mud right over the floor I just stripped and waxed. Who wouldn't get a little ticked off about that, right? You put in two hours of back-breaking work and some guy from accounting just waltzes right through it. But it's not like I'm walking around angry for days on end for no reason. It's just normal frustration. 

I don't have these big swings where I'm suddenly on top of the world or ready to bite everyone's head off for a week straight. It's more of a constant, steady stream of just... going. Always going. My wife sometimes says I can be a bit much when I'm trying to get a project done around the house on a Saturday, like if I decide I'm going to clean out the garage and I'm just tearing through boxes and talking a mile a minute, but that's just because I want to get it done and I've got the momentum going. It's not like my mood itself is somehow out of whack or anything. It's just the energy, you know? Just the engine always running. So, no, nothing like what you're describing. Just the usual me.

Well, it's nice to meet you too, doctor, though to be perfectly honest, my husband is the one who really pushed for this appointment. But I suppose I’m here because... well, it all goes back to our house. Specifically, the kitchen. We decided to do a remodel, just a simple update, you know, but for nearly two years now—almost twenty-four whole months of this absolute nightmare—I’ve been absolutely sure that the contractor we hired is doing something completely underhanded. 

And it’s not just him, which is the really upsetting part. It’s some of the people right on my block, too. I’ve seen them out the window, talking by the mailboxes, looking over at my house and then suddenly stopping when I open the front door. They’ve been quietly working together to cheat us, I just know it. They are deliberately trying to keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. The cabinet doors don't line up right, the grout is completely the wrong shade, the trim isn't finished... they leave it like that on purpose, just stringing the job along to mock me. 

And my husband, bless his heart, he just doesn't want to see the reality of it. He keeps pulling out this thick folder of receipts, sitting me down at the dining table and pointing at the line items and the dates, trying to show me that everything is accounted for. But no matter how many receipts my husband shows me, or how many ridiculous excuses the contractor gives him over the phone—blaming supply chains or weather or whatever new lie he comes up with—it doesn't change what's actually happening. I know what I see, and I know they're all in on it together.

Energetic? Oh, heavens, no. No, not at all. If anything, I am just completely exhausted by this whole ordeal. I mean, I’m sixty-seven years old, I haven't worked in quite some time, and I certainly don't have the energy of a teenager anymore, that's for sure. 

I always try to get my full eight hours of sleep every single night. Now, I will admit, sometimes I do wake up in the middle of the night—usually right around 3:00 or 3:30 in the morning, which is just the worst time to wake up—but that's absolutely not because I have extra energy. It's just because my mind won't shut off. I'm lying there worrying about what the contractor is going to mess up next, or I'm replaying what I saw out the window, wondering exactly what those neighbors were whispering about by the mailboxes. I just lie there in the dark, looking up at the ceiling, feeling my stomach tie itself in knots over that crooked cabinet hinge they refuse to fix. And my husband, he just sleeps right through it, snoring away, completely oblivious to it all. 

But I'm certainly not bouncing off the walls or getting up to scrub the floors at midnight or anything like that. I need my rest. By the time the 10 o'clock news is over, I am more than ready to turn in, maybe read a few pages of a book, and just close my eyes. So, no, I haven't felt unusually energetic in the slightest. This whole nightmare with the house has just completely drained whatever energy I do have, to be perfectly honest with you. It takes a lot out of you, having to be constantly on your guard in your own home.

Voices? Oh, no, no, nothing like that. I mean, I hear my husband snoring, like I said, and sometimes I hear the wind rattling that loose piece of siding the contractor promised to secure three months ago—which, of course, he hasn't done, and I'm sure he left it loose on purpose just so I'd have to listen to it every time there's a breeze. But actual voices? People talking when there's no one in the room? No, absolutely not. 

I know what I hear, just like I know what I see. When I hear those neighbors talking by the mailboxes, they are really there. I can see Mrs. Gable in her awful pink tracksuit, and Mr. Henderson with his little dog, and I can hear the murmur of their voices. I can't always make out the exact words, mind you, because they drop their voices on purpose when I open the door, but they are real people having a real conversation about me. 

But I certainly don't sit alone in my living room hearing phantom voices whispering in my ear. My hearing is perfectly fine, thank goodness. In fact, I had it tested just last year at Dr. Aris's office—my regular doctor, you know, over on Elm Street—and he said for a woman of sixty-seven, my hearing is quite sharp. Which is probably why I catch all the little sighs and muttered comments the contractor makes when he thinks I'm not paying attention. But no, doctor, I don't hear things that aren't there. I'm just very observant of the things that *are* there, even if my husband refuses to acknowledge them.

Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say so. Not at all. I mean, my husband and I have our little disagreements, certainly. Just last week we had a bit of a row over how to organize the pantry—which, frankly, is a mess right now because the contractor left the shelving half-finished, just bare wood with nails sticking out, if you can believe it. But that's just normal married life, isn't it? Disagreeing about where the soup cans go. 

But as for big, strong beliefs that people say aren't true? No, nothing like that. I've always been a very practical, down-to-earth sort of person. I don't go in for conspiracy theories or wild ideas or anything of that nature. I just pay attention to what's going on around me. I pay my bills, I keep a tidy house—or at least I try to, despite the dust that contractor tracks in on purpose—and I mind my own business. 

It’s really just this one specific situation. It’s so glaringly obvious, you see. Anyone with eyes in their head would see exactly what I see if they just spent a week in my house, watching how these people operate. But aside from this whole mess with the kitchen and the neighbors whispering by the mailboxes... no, there's absolutely nothing else. I’m just a normal woman trying to get her kitchen finished, and being thwarted at every turn. That’s the long and short of it, really.

Less interested? Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, yes, this whole remodeling fiasco takes up a tremendous amount of my mental energy—how could it not, when you have people deliberately leaving nails exposed just waiting for you to snag a sweater on them?—but I certainly haven't become a hermit. I still do all the things I've always done. 

Just this past Tuesday, for instance, I went to my regular book club meeting over at Shirley's house. We were discussing that new historical fiction novel—the one set in Paris during the war, though honestly, I found the protagonist a bit grating, but that's neither here nor there. The point is, I was there, I brought my famous lemon bars, and I stayed for the whole two hours. And I still go to church every Sunday morning, bright and early for the 8:30 service, just like I have for the last forty years. I sit in the third pew on the left, right next to the Johnsons, and I always stay for coffee hour afterward, even though the coffee they serve is dreadfully weak. 

And my household routines haven't changed one bit, aside from having to clean up after that contractor, of course. I still do the laundry on Mondays, I still go to the grocery store on Thursday mornings to beat the weekend rush, and I still talk to my daughter on the phone every Sunday evening. We're actually planning a little family get-together for my grandson's birthday next month, and I've been looking at recipes for a dinosaur-shaped cake. So, no, I haven't lost interest in my life or my friends or my family. It's just that right now, I have this one very large, very stressful situation happening right in the middle of my home, and it demands a lot of my attention. But outside of dealing with that awful remodel and keeping an eye on those whispering neighbors, my life is exactly as it has always been. I'm still very much involved in my day-to-day activities, I assure you.

Impossible? Oh, well... no, I wouldn't say impossible. I mean, what they're doing is certainly malicious, and highly coordinated, but it's not magic or science fiction or anything like that. It's just very, very sneaky. 

Like the contractor, for instance. There's nothing impossible about leaving a cabinet door slightly unhinged so it scrapes against the frame every single time I open it to get a tea bag. Anyone with a screwdriver and a mean streak could do that. And the neighbors, Mrs. Gable and Mr. Henderson—well, there's nothing impossible about standing by a mailbox and whispering. It's rude, certainly, and it's terribly upsetting to know they're coordinating their little stories about me, but it's just ordinary people doing awful things. 

I don't think they have special powers or hidden cameras in my walls or anything ridiculous like that. I mean, I did check behind the hallway mirror once, just to be absolutely certain, because the contractor spent an awfully long time hanging it, but there was nothing there. Just drywall and a rather sloppy patch job he tried to hide. So no, they aren't doing anything that defies the laws of physics. They're just using ordinary, everyday actions—like dropping off mail, or pretending to measure for tile, or walking that little yappy dog—to send me a message. To let me know they're watching, and that they're working together to drive me out of my own home. It's perfectly possible, doctor. It's just terribly, terribly cruel.

Trouble managing? Well, I wouldn't say I can't manage my usual chores—like I told you, I still do the laundry, I still cook our meals, although cooking is a nightmare with the kitchen in the state it's in. But... well, I suppose things have shifted a bit. Just in certain areas. 

It’s just that I’ve completely stopped trusting certain neighbors and the workers who come to the house. I mean, how could I? When you see the things I see, you can't just blindly hand over a cup of coffee to a man who you know is deliberately trying to ruin your baseboards. It used to be that I handled all the remodeling decisions. I was the one who picked out the backsplash—a lovely ceramic subway tile, very classic, not that trendy glass stuff that looks dated in five years—and I was the one who greeted the men when they arrived at 8:00 AM. 

But now? Now my husband has had to take over almost all of the remodeling decisions. I told him, I said, "Arthur, you are just going to have to be the one to speak to them from now on." Because if I do it, I just end up so frustrated. I keep questioning what these people are really doing. Every time the plumber asks where the main water shut-off valve is, I can't help but think, "Why do you want to know that? What exactly are you planning to turn off when we aren't looking?" 

So, Arthur does it now. He talks to the contractor, he handles the paperwork, and if Mrs. Gable or Mr. Henderson happen to wander over while the crew is here, Arthur goes out to the driveway to intercept them. It's just... it's too exhausting for me to constantly have to decipher everyone's true motives. I just can't be involved in the day-to-day of the kitchen project anymore, not when I know they're all coordinating behind my back. So yes, Arthur has had to step in and manage that whole side of things, just so I don't have to deal with the constant lying. But as for my own personal responsibilities, the house is still clean and dinner is still on the table at six o'clock sharp.

Oh, heavens, no. No, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own, thank you very much. I mean, I know some people talk about things like that—you see it in those science fiction movies my grandson likes to watch, where people wear tin foil hats or whatever nonsense it is, but no. I don't feel like anyone is putting thoughts into my head or stealing them away. 

Although, I will say, sometimes it feels like they know what I'm thinking, but not because of telepathy or mind reading! No, it's just because they're so terribly observant of my habits. Like Mrs. Gable. She knows exactly what time I usually go out to get the mail—10:15, right after I finish my second cup of tea—so of course she’s out there, pretending to deadhead her petunias, just waiting for me. And the contractor, he knows I hate a mess, so he deliberately leaves his muddy boots right on the edge of the drop cloth where he knows I'll see them and get upset. 

So, they can anticipate my reactions, certainly. Anyone could if they watched someone closely enough, and they are definitely watching me. But my actual thoughts? No, those are safe inside my own head. I don't feel like anyone is broadcasting them or putting foreign ideas in there. I know exactly what I think, and I know exactly what they're doing. It’s just old-fashioned snooping and manipulation, doctor, not mind control. I assure you, my mind is perfectly sound and completely my own, even if they are trying to drive me out of it with all this stress!

Disorganized? Hard to follow? Well... no, no one has said anything quite like that. I mean, Arthur sometimes says I get a bit... well, he calls it "wound up." He'll say, "Martha, you're getting wound up again, take a breath," but that's just because I have so much to explain to him! When you're dealing with a situation as complicated as this one, with the neighbors and the contractors all doing these little, tiny things—you can't just explain it in one sentence. It takes time to lay it all out. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to tell him about the incident with the plumber's wrench. I had to explain where the wrench was left, which was right on my good floral hand towel, and then I had to explain how Mr. Henderson had just walked his dog past the front window not ten minutes prior, and how the two things were obviously connected because the plumber had been looking out that exact window. Arthur got a little impatient, I suppose. He said I was jumping around too much. But I wasn't disorganized, I was just trying to give him the complete picture! You can't understand the malice of leaving a greasy wrench on a floral towel unless you understand the timing of Mr. Henderson's dog walk, you see? 

So, no, I wouldn't say my speech is hard to follow, not if someone is actually listening and paying attention to the details. My daughter, Susan, she called on Sunday—she calls every Sunday at 4:00, very predictable—and I was telling her about the cabinet door, the one the contractor ruined, and she said, "Mom, you're obsessing, I can't follow all this about hinges and screws." But again, that's not me being disorganized! That's just Susan not wanting to hear about the reality of what's happening to her mother. She's always been a bit dismissive, ever since she was a teenager. She used to roll her eyes when I'd ask her to explain where she'd been, and she does the exact same thing now when I try to explain what Mrs. Gable is up to. 

So, people might say I talk about it a lot, or that I give too many details, but my thoughts are perfectly clear. I know exactly what I'm saying from beginning to end. It's just that other people don't always have the patience to listen to the whole story, doctor. They want everything in a neat little summary, but life—especially when people are conspiring against you—just doesn't fit into a neat little summary. It takes time to explain.

Three months? Oh, heavens, I wish it had only been three months. If it were only three months, I might still have some of my patience left! No, no, it’s been... well, let’s see. It has been much, much longer than that. 

It all started—the real disruption, I mean—when we finally began the kitchen and garden remodeling. Arthur and I had talked about updating the house for years, and we finally took the plunge. That was... goodness, it’s been about a year and nine months now. Yes, exactly a year and nine months. I know the timeline perfectly because I keep all the original contracts and invoices in a blue binder in the den. 

The very first day they came to tear up the old garden beds and start knocking out the drywall in the kitchen, that's when the nightmare began. You open up your home, you know? You expect a mess, you expect some dust and noise, and you expect your routine to be disrupted. But you don't expect the people you've hired to start actively working against you. That’s when I first started noticing the looks they would give each other, and the way Mrs. Gable suddenly took such a keen interest in her side yard the exact same week we broke ground. 

So, to answer your question, yes, it has been continuously going on for a year and nine months. Every single day since that remodeling started disrupting my house. It never stops, not for a single week. Even on the weekends or holidays when the crew isn't supposed to be there, I can see the neighbors out there inspecting the progress, taking their little mental notes to report back. It’s just been a year and nine months of absolute exhaustion, doctor, just a continuous, never-ending campaign against me. You'd think a kitchen project would be finished by now, wouldn't you? But of course, they keep finding reasons to drag it out.

Well, I... my mom made the appointment, I think. I just, I don't really know how to explain it because there's not really anything happening, it's more like nothing is happening at all. Mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. I just sit in my room. And it's not like I'm doing anything in there, I just sit on the edge of the bed or in the chair by the window, usually with the exact same clothes on that I wore the day before, and the day before that, and probably the day before that too. 

I used to do things, you know? I had all this yarn, I used to knit these thick scarves, and I had this whole stack of notebooks where I would journal every single night, color-coded and everything. I even used to go walking around the neighborhood for hours just to get fresh air and look at the trees. But now... the yarn is just sitting in a plastic bin gathering dust, and I haven't opened a notebook in I don't even know how long. I look at them and it's like there's a huge, heavy wall between me and actually doing it. And my mom, she comes upstairs and knocks on the door and she keeps asking me what is wrong and why I am just sitting there and what is going on with me. And I hear her, I really do, but I barely even have the energy to open my mouth to answer her. It just takes way too much effort to push the words out of my throat, so I just stare at the wall instead. It's just... everything is just too heavy to move.

No... no, I don't think so. It's actually just really, really quiet in my room. Like, almost too quiet, you know? Because I'm just sitting there for hours and hours, so I end up hearing every little normal thing in the house. I hear the air conditioner kicking on through the vent right above my closet, and it makes this low rattling sound that never really stops. And I can hear the cars going by on the street outside, especially when it rains and the tires make that hissing noise on the wet pavement. 

And my mom, I hear her downstairs all the time. I can hear her slippers on the hardwood floor, just shuffling back and forth between the kitchen and the living room, and the TV murmuring in the background when she turns on her shows in the evening. But it's just regular stuff like that. There aren't any voices talking to me or anything out of the ordinary. It's mostly just... silence. Just this huge, empty silence that fills up the whole room and presses down on me while I'm looking at the wall. Sometimes the quiet is so thick it kind of makes my ears ring, just a high-pitched whine from absolutely nothing happening, but nobody is talking to me when they aren't there. It's just me in there. Just me and the quiet.

Well, I... I mean, my mom tells me I'm wrong about this, but she doesn't see what I see. She doesn't read the emails the way I do. It started back when I was still trying to take those college classes, before I just stopped going and started sitting in my room all day. I was trying to get into the healthcare program, doing the clinic practicum stuff, and... well, they didn't want me there. I know they didn't. 

It wasn't like they came out and said "we don't want you," because they can't do that, right? They have rules. So they did it through the school portal. Every time they sent an email or left a comment on one of my assignments, they would change the wording just a tiny bit. Like, they wouldn't use standard phrasing. They would use these specific, little altered words, and I realized it was a code. They were marking me. They were using those little wording changes to flag me in the system as someone who shouldn't be allowed to work in healthcare. 

I tried to show my mom. I printed out all the emails and the assignment rubrics and I highlighted the words—like how one professor said "ensure careful attention" instead of just "pay attention," or how the practicum coordinator kept using the word "monitor" in this really specific way. I laid them all out on the kitchen table to show her the pattern, how it was this whole coordinated thing between the professors and the clinic people to push me out. But she just sighed and told me they were just regular messages. She said I was reading too much into it and that professors just talk like that. But she doesn't get it. She doesn't understand that they have to do it that way so they don't get sued, but they still have to make sure the other people in the program know I'm marked. Even now that I'm not going to classes, I know the mark is still there in the portal. They made sure of it.

Well, I... I don't really think it works like that. It's not about being depressed. Because the emails were there before I stopped doing things, and they're still there now while I'm just sitting in my room. It's not like the mark in the portal goes away just because I'm sitting on the edge of my bed all day, you know? 

I remember when I first noticed it, I was actually doing okay. I was still knitting those scarves, I was still writing in my notebooks every night, using my different colored pens. I was going to my classes and getting my assignments done. I was just sitting at my desk, looking at my laptop, and I saw that first email from the practicum coordinator. The one where she used the word "monitor." And I just knew. I knew right then what they were doing. It didn't matter how I was feeling, it was just right there on the screen in black and white. And then the next week, the professor used that phrase, "ensure careful attention," and I started printing them all out. 

So it's not... it's not a mood thing. It's not because I'm heavy and tired now. The school did what they did, and they coordinated the whole thing, and that's just a fact of what happened. I could be out walking around the neighborhood looking at the trees like I used to, and it wouldn't change the fact that they coded those messages to flag me in the system. The mark is just there. It doesn't care if I'm happy or sad or just staring at the wall.

No, no one says that. I mean, my mom doesn't say that, and she's the only one I really talk to anymore. When I talk to her, I'm just telling her what I need, like if I want a glass of water or if I need her to pick up a different kind of soap from the store because the one she bought last time had a weird smell that made my head hurt. I explain it to her very clearly. I tell her exactly what I mean, from the beginning of the thought to the end. I don't jump around or get confused. 

Like yesterday, I was trying to explain to her why I couldn't eat the sandwich she made, because the bread was cut diagonally instead of straight across, and I explained the whole reason, step by step, about how the diagonal cut makes the corners too sharp and it changes the way the bread feels when you hold it. I went through the whole explanation, and she understood me perfectly. She just sighed and made another one. She never says my words are jumbled. She might not agree with me, like about the emails from the school and the way they marked me, but she never says she can't follow what I'm saying. I use all the right words. I make sure I do. I think about the words before I say them, and I put them in a line, like beads on a string, just one after the other so they make a perfect sentence. So, no, nobody tells me I'm hard to follow. They just... they just don't want to listen sometimes. But that's different. That's not because my words are wrong.

No, I... I don't think so. I don't get energized like that. It's actually the exact opposite, really. I don't have times where I feel "up" or like I don't need to sleep. Sleep is... well, I sleep a lot. Or I try to, anyway. I mean, I spend most of my time in my room now, like I said before. I'm usually just sitting on the edge of my bed, and my limbs feel so heavy, like they're filled with wet sand or lead or something. I don't have this... this bursting energy to go do things or run around. 

I usually go to bed at like 9:30 or 10 o'clock every night because there's just nothing else to do, and I turn off the main overhead light, but I always leave the little desk lamp on because it casts this softer shadow against the closet door, and I just pull the heavy quilt up and wait to fall asleep. I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get it, my head feels all fuzzy and thick. So I never feel like I can just skip it or like I only need a couple of hours. 

My mom actually gets frustrated with me because she thinks I sleep too much or that I'm just lying around all day, which I am, but it's not because I'm energized or awake. It's just... I'm just heavy. Even when I was still doing my notebooks and knitting the scarves, I still slept normal hours. I've never had a time where my body just didn't want to sleep. I don't even know what that would feel like, to be honest. I just feel tired.

No, I do not think sad is the right word. I mean, sad is when... when you drop something you really like or when a dog dies in a movie, right? That is sad. You cry when you are sad. I do not cry. I have not cried in... I do not even know how long it has been since I actually shed a tear. I just sit there. 

Like I was saying before about my bed, I just sit on the edge of the mattress. It has a blue fitted sheet, the one with the little white anchors on it that my mom bought at the store a few years ago because she thought it looked nautical and fresh. I just sit on those anchors and stare at the closet door. But I am not crying while I do it. I am not feeling heartbroken or miserable or anything like that. I think people always assume that if you are in your room all day you must be weeping into your pillow, but my pillow is completely dry. I make sure it is perfectly flat every morning against the headboard, right in the center. 

So, no, not depressed. Depressed sounds like a dark rain cloud, always sighing and feeling sorry for yourself. I do not feel sorry for myself. I just feel... well, I do not really feel much of anything emotionally. It is just that heaviness in my arms and my legs that I mentioned before. Like the wet sand. It is just a physical weight, pulling me down into the mattress, making it hard to even walk to the kitchen to get the water my mom leaves out for me on the counter next to the sink. But it is not a sad weight. It is just a completely empty weight. So I do not think depressed is right at all. I am just here. I am just existing in the room.

No, they don't. I mean, I don't even do them at all anymore, so I wouldn't know if they feel enjoyable, but just looking at them doesn't make me feel anything. I have this wicker basket in the corner of my room, right next to the closet door I was telling you about, and it's completely full of yarn. There's this really thick, chunky mustard-yellow yarn right on top that I bought specifically to make a winter scarf, and the knitting needles are just sticking right out of the center of the skein. They are size ten needles, the bamboo kind, because I always preferred those since they don't click as loud and sharp as the metal ones do. But I haven't touched them in... I don't even know. Months, probably. I just look at the basket from the bed. It doesn't look fun. It just looks like an impossible amount of work. 

And it is the exact same thing with my journaling. I have these black composition notebooks, the standard ones with the black and white marble pattern on the front cover, stacked perfectly on my desk. I used to write in them every single day, filling up the pages from the very top margin all the way to the bottom edge with blue ink. But now the pen is just sitting on top of the stack, and I don't write a single word. I don't knit, I don't journal, I don't even go for my walks around the neighborhood like I used to do in the late afternoons when the sun was starting to go down and it wasn't so bright. 

Mostly I just... I just can't make myself do anything anymore. Nothing at all. I just sit in my room on the anchors on my bed. And I don't even change my clothes. I've been wearing this same oversized gray t-shirt—the one with the faded college logo on it—and these soft black sweatpants with the frayed drawstring for... I think four days now? Maybe five. It just doesn't seem to matter if I change them, because putting on clean clothes takes a lot of steps, and I'm not going anywhere anyway. 

My mom will come in to bring me that water, and she sees me just sitting there, not knitting, not writing, wearing the exact same clothes as yesterday and the day before, and she gets this pinched, worried look around her mouth. She'll stand in the doorway and ask me, "What's wrong? Why aren't you doing your hobbies?" But I... I barely have the energy to answer her. It takes so much effort just to push the air out of my lungs to make a sound, let alone explain that I just don't care about the yarn or the notebooks anymore. I just stare at her, or I maybe mumble that I'm fine, because actually trying to form a real sentence about why I'm not doing anything is just too exhausting. It's just all too much effort.

I don't really know about two weeks, or keeping track of time like that. My mom has this big glossy calendar in the kitchen, the kind with a different picture of a bird for every month—I think this month is a blue jay, or maybe a cardinal, I can't remember—but I don't go out there to look at it anyway. So I don't know if it's been exactly two weeks or four weeks or what. The days just sort of blur together into one long, continuous thing. 

And like I was saying before, I really wouldn't use the word depressed. I know you're asking about that again, but it's just not the right word. Depressed people are sad. I'm not sad. I'm just empty. And as for losing interest... well, yes, I don't care about the yarn or the notebooks anymore, but it's not like it's some little two-week phase I'm going through. It's just how every day is now. 

The light comes through my window blinds—they're those cheap white plastic ones that get kind of brittle and yellowed from the sun—and it makes these long, thin stripes across the beige carpet. And I just sit on my bed on those blue anchors and watch those stripes slowly move across the floor, from the edge of the closet door over to the wicker basket, until the sun goes down and the room gets dark.
