You have to understand the prayer rug, because it's about patterns and kneeling, and finding a space that's yours when you're locked in or locked out. It's all connected, just like the chess pieces. The knights and the pawns, they all move in specific ways, just like how I have to move through the hallways with my mop bucket. But when I try to lay it all out for people, to show them how the keys and the jail and the rug and the chess pieces are all part of the same big picture, they just look at me blankly. They say I'm jumping around, that my words are a jumble. But I'm just trying to give them the whole story, every detail, because if you miss one part, the rest of it falls apart. So, yeah, I'm here because apparently, I can't explain things right, even though I'm trying as hard as I can to make them see it.

Well, harm me... plot against me... it's a strong word, plot, but yes, I do. I really do. It's the building people, the ones who work in the offices during the day while I'm mostly there at night, but sometimes our shifts overlap, you know? And it's not just a feeling, it's a knowing. I know they've marked me. They have this system, this whole intricate system of communicating about me. It's the hallway lights. Sometimes they flicker in this very specific rhythm when I walk past the third-floor conference room—tap, tap, pause, tap—and I know that's them signaling that I'm on the move. And it's the looks, too. These little, sharp glances they give each other when I'm emptying the shredder bins. They think I don't see, but I see everything. I see the way the accountant on the fourth floor adjusts his tie exactly when I walk in, and then the receptionist coughs twice. It's a warning system. They're warning each other about me. 

I even tried to prove it. I went to my supervisor, Mr. Henderson—he's been there fifteen years, always wears these scuffed brown shoes—and I told him, I said, "Mr. Henderson, you have to look at the security cameras. You have to see what they're doing with the lights and the looks." And he did. He brought me into his little office by the loading dock, and he played the tape back. He showed me the hallway, and he said, "Look, there's nothing there. The lights are fine. No one is looking at you." He pointed right at the screen, right at the timestamp. But... but even when he showed me that, even when the screen looked normal to him, I still felt it. I still felt absolutely sure that they had marked me. The camera just couldn't pick up the frequency of it, or maybe they altered the tape. Because I know what I see, and I know they're using the lights and those little looks to keep tabs on me, to plot whatever it is they're planning to do. It's all part of it.

Well, up... energetic... yes, yes, I suppose you could say that. There are these times, and it's not just a little bit of energy, it's like a whole current running through me, like the main power line to the industrial buffers we use on the lobby floors. When it hits me, I feel... I feel so high up, like I'm standing on the roof of the building looking down at everything, and I'm just so powerful. I get to laughing, just this loud, booming laugh that echoes all the way down the corridors, and I want to talk to everyone. I'll be pushing my cart and I'll see the night watchman, or maybe one of the late-night executives getting coffee, and I just start talking, loud and fast, telling them about the grand scheme of things, because suddenly I understand it all, right? I feel like I could clean the whole twenty-story building in an hour and still have time to reorganize the supply closets. 

But then... the thing is, if they don't get it, or if they look at me wrong—like if the watchman says, "Hey buddy, keep it down," or if someone questions why I'm talking so loud—it just flips. It flips so fast. It's like a circuit breaker tripping. One second I'm on top of the world, and the next, I just snap. I'll start shouting, really shouting, over the smallest little thing. Like if they ask why I haven't emptied a specific trash can yet, I'll just explode. I'll yell about how they don't understand the sequence, how they can't see the power I have in that moment. It's a very intense feeling, being that high up and then having someone try to pull you down. It's just... it's a lot of energy, a lot of power, and it has to go somewhere, you know?

Sleep? Oh, sleep is... well, during those times, sleep is just a waste. It's a complete waste of time. I mean, why would I lay there in the dark when my brain is firing on all cylinders, right? It's like... it's like the whole world is asleep, but I'm the only one awake, the only one who really sees what's going on. I'll lay down for maybe two, three hours tops. Two or three hours, that's it. And it's not even a deep sleep, it's just a resting of the eyes, really. 

And then, boom, I'm up. I'm up before the sun even thinks about coming up, before the first delivery trucks even hit the loading dock out back. And I don't feel tired. That's the crazy part, I don't feel tired at all. I feel completely fresh, like I just slept for a week. I'll get up, make a pot of coffee—strong, black, the way you need it when you're doing real work—and I just start planning. I start mapping out the whole shift in my head. I'll think, okay, I'll tackle the fourth floor first, get those shredder bins emptied before the accountant even gets his shoes tied, then I'll move down to the lobby, buff the floors till they shine like glass, and I still have time to reorganize the supply closet on the second floor, the one with the broken hinge on the door that no one ever fixes. 

I'll just be sitting there at my kitchen table, going over the schedules, the routes, the inventory of the cleaning supplies, figuring out how to make everything perfectly efficient. Because when I'm like that, I don't need sleep. Sleep is for the people who work in the offices during the day, the ones who need eight hours just to sit at a desk and stare at a computer. But me? I've got the energy, I've got the power. I don't need it. I can just keep going and going, like a machine that never needs to be plugged in. It's just two or three hours, and then I'm ready to take on the whole building, the whole world, really.

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It’s not just when my engine is running hot, you know, not just when I've got all that electricity in me. There are plenty of times... well, there was this one stretch, these calmer weeks, really. I wasn't feeling all high and mighty, and I wasn't feeling dragged down into the dirt either. I wasn't deeply depressed or anything, just... just regular. Punching in, doing my floors, punching out. 

But the thing is, doctor, even when I'm feeling perfectly steady like that, the signaling doesn't stop. It never really stops. I remember this one period, it went on for more than two weeks straight during that calm spell, where I still knew exactly what they were doing. The office people, they were still doing the taps, the looks, the coughs. And... well, it’s not just them, actually. It’s the vents, too. During that whole time, that whole two-week period when I was feeling totally level, I still heard him. The man in the vents. 

It’s the big HVAC ducts, the square aluminum ones that run right over the dropped acoustic tiles in the main corridors. You can hear the air rushing, sure, but underneath the air,

Yes, yes, exactly. The man in the vents. It doesn't matter if I'm feeling level or not, he's still there. I'll be in the mop closet, you know, the one on the third floor near the freight elevator, mixing the floor cleaner—just the right ratio, you can't use too much or it leaves a sticky film—and I'll hear him. Clear as day. It's not a mumble, it's not the wind. It's a man's voice. 

He'll say my name. Just... call out my name, echoing down through the aluminum ductwork. Or sometimes, and this is the part that really gets to me, he'll tell me I ruined everything. "You ruined everything," he says. Over and over. And I'm just standing there with my hand on the mop handle, looking around, because it sounds... Doctor, it sounds exactly like there is a man standing right beside me, right over my shoulder in that tiny closet. 

I'll even turn around, I'll drop the mop and look behind the utility sink, thinking maybe one of the maintenance guys snuck in there to mess with me. But there's never anyone there. Just the cinderblock walls and the smell of industrial pine cleaner. But the voice, it's so real. It's got a deep pitch to it, kind of gravelly, like someone who's been smoking for forty years. And he just keeps telling me I ruined it all, even when I'm just trying to do my job, even when I'm feeling perfectly fine and just trying to get the scuff marks off the linoleum. It's just... it's impossible to ignore when it sounds that real, you know? Like he's right there in the room with me.

A month? Oh, doctor, a month would be a vacation. A month would be nothing. No, no, it's been... well, let me think. It started way before the winter holidays last year, because I remember the salt on the sidewalks and how the lobby floors were constantly a mess, and I was already hearing him then. And the people in the offices, the signaling, that started right around the same time. 

So, it's been... it's been about a year and a half. A solid year and a half of this. Every day, every single shift. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday or a Friday, if I'm on the day shift filling in or doing my regular night rotation. For eighteen months, I've had to walk into that building knowing they're watching me, knowing they've got some kind of system figured out to keep tabs on me. The coughs, the way they shift their chairs when I walk by with the trash cart... all of it. And the voice in the vents, that gravelly voice telling me I ruined everything, that's been there the whole time, too. A year and a half of looking over my shoulder, of checking the grates, of trying to figure out what I'm supposed to have ruined. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is. You try buffing a thousand square feet of marble while a man in the ceiling is whispering at you for a year and a half straight. It changes how you do your job, it changes how you walk down a hallway. You start stepping quieter, you know? Trying not to trigger whatever it is they're signaling about. So, yes, much longer than a month. A year and a half, at least.

Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I appreciate you taking the time. I've been retired for a little while now, and, well, my wife actually suggested I come in. We've been married thirty-two years, and she's a saint, really, but lately we've been having these... well, I guess you'd call them miscommunications, but it's really on my end. 

What really brought me in is that, for example, she’ll be telling me about my cousin’s appointments or, you know, coordinating rides for him—he’s been having some health issues lately, poor guy, and we try to help out where we can since he doesn't drive anymore. So she'll be standing right there in the kitchen, going over the schedule, and I’m looking right at her. I'm nodding, I'm making eye contact, I'm fully intending to listen. But then, maybe a minute or two later, she'll ask me to confirm what time I need to pick him up, and I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said. It's like the words just washed right over me. I hear the sound of her voice, but the meaning just doesn't stick. And it frustrates her, understandably, because she thinks I'm ignoring her, but I'm really not trying to. It just sort of... slips away.

No, no, it's not my hearing at all. Actually, when this first started becoming a real point of contention between us, I thought, well, maybe I'm just getting older and my ears are going. My dad had terrible hearing by the time he was my age—he worked around heavy machinery, you know, the old metal stamping presses back in the day, and he never wore ear protection because they just didn't really push safety standards back then like they do now. 

So, just to be safe, I actually went down to the clinic and had my hearing checked a little while back. I sat in that tiny soundproof booth with the heavy headphones on, pressing the little button every time I heard a beep. And the audiologist came out and told me my hearing was practically perfect for a man my age. Honestly, I can hear a pin drop. I can hear the refrigerator humming all the way from the living room, which actually drives me a bit crazy sometimes when I'm just trying to sit quietly and read the morning paper. 

So, no, when my wife speaks, the volume is fine, the clarity of the sound hitting my eardrum is perfectly fine. I hear the syllables, the tone of her voice, the pitch, everything. It's just... it's like the bridge between my ears and my brain is temporarily out of service. The words go in, but they don't get unpacked, if that makes sense? I'm not deaf to the sound of her voice at all, I'm just... absent for the meaning of it.

Well, you'd think so, wouldn't you? That's what I thought, too. I figured, if I can just look at it, if it's written down right there in black and white, it'll stay put. But honestly, it's not much better. 

Like, for example, I help out with the parish council down at St. Jude's. Have for years. And occasionally I'll help coordinate the catering for some of the bigger events, like the spring fish fry or the fall festival. So, I'll sit down at the kitchen table with the catering menus and the order sheets, and I'll have my reading glasses on, a fresh cup of coffee, completely ready to tackle it. I'll start reading through the options—how many pounds of coleslaw we need, the pricing for the tartar sauce packets, all that. And I start off fine. I'm reading the words, I'm understanding the prices. 

But then, I don't know, maybe five minutes in, my eyes are still moving across the page, line by line, but my mind is... it's just gone. I'll be thinking about the gutters that need cleaning, or wondering if I remembered to put the recycling bin out, or just thinking about absolutely nothing at all. And then I'll look down and realize I've "read" three whole paragraphs about potato salad, but I have no earthly idea what any of it said. I have to go back to the top of the page and start all over again, reading the exact same notes like I never even looked at them the first time. 

It happens on the planning calls, too, when we do those conference calls. I'll be taking notes, trying to write things down so they stick, but my mind just drifts off right in the middle of someone explaining the volunteer schedule. So, whether it's spoken or written down, if I have to focus on it for more than a few minutes, it just slips right through my fingers.

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask about that, because I actually got to thinking about this very thing the other day. I was digging through some old boxes in the attic—my wife has been on me to clear out some of the clutter up there, and I found a box of my old report cards and keepsakes my mother had saved from when I was a boy. And looking at those report cards from, gosh, third grade, fourth grade, right up through sixth grade, so well before I was twelve... it was like reading a script of exactly what I just described to you. 

My teachers—Mrs. Gable in fourth grade, I remember her specifically, she was a wonderful woman, very patient, but she used to write these long notes to my parents. She’d say, you know, "He’s a very bright boy, he has so much potential," but then there would always be the "but." "But he spends half the day staring out the window daydreaming." Or, "He forgot his spelling homework in his desk again for the third time this week." 

And it wasn't just the homework. Even when I was sitting right there in the classroom, with the assignment right in front of me, Mrs. Gable or Mr. Henderson in fifth grade, they were constantly having to tap my desk or call my name to remind me to actually finish the classwork. I’d start it, do the first two math problems, and then my mind would just wander off to what I was going to do at recess, or watching a bird outside, or just getting lost in my own thoughts. So, yes, looking back on it, that same sort of drift, that inability to just stay locked onto what I was supposed to be doing... it’s been there pretty much my whole life, even way back then. I guess I just always thought of it as a personality quirk, you know? Just being a bit of a space cadet. But those old report cards, they really laid it out in black and white.

Well, you know, it's interesting you ask about work, because honestly, I retired a few years ago, mostly because I just felt like I was slowing down, but looking back, I think a lot of it was this... this exact same thing. But where it's really showing up now, where it's actually becoming a real problem, isn't so much a traditional job, but the responsibilities I have now. 

You see, my cousin, Arthur, he's been having some health issues lately, quite severe actually, and my wife and I have been helping out with his care. We take turns going over there, making sure he's taken his medications, getting his meals sorted, that sort of thing. And it has started causing some real tension at home between me and my wife, because she feels like she just can't count on me to handle it. Like, last Tuesday, she asked me to make sure Arthur took his afternoon pills and to write down his blood pressure reading. And I went over there, we had a nice chat, I made him a sandwich, and I came home. And my wife asked, "What was his blood pressure?" And I just drew a complete blank. I hadn't even thought about the pills, either. I was there, I was doing things, but the actual important tasks just completely evaporated from my mind. She was so frustrated with me, and I don't blame her, I really don't, because it's a serious matter, Arthur's health. 

And it's not just with Arthur, either. Like I mentioned earlier with the parish council and the catering—I've had to double-check or completely redo so many of those tasks lately. I'll be in charge of ordering the napkins and the plastic cutlery for the fall festival, a tiny, simple job, right? But I'll forget if I placed the order, or I'll order the wrong amount because I wasn't paying attention when I read the inventory sheet, and then I have to spend an hour on the phone with the supplier trying to fix it so these small jobs don't get completely mixed up and ruin the event. 

So, I guess to answer your question, it's not a nine-to-five job anymore, but the "work" I am doing now, the things people are relying on me for... it's definitely creating problems. My wife is just at her wit's end with it, feeling like she has to manage me on top of managing Arthur's care and the household, and I hate making her feel that way, I really do. It's just so frustrating to know you're capable of doing a task, but your brain just won't stay on the tracks long enough to get to the station.

No, no, I wouldn't say so. You know, it's funny you ask that, because if anything, I might be the exact opposite. My wife, she’s always telling me I’m like a bump on a log once I sit down. I have this old leather recliner in the den—had it for, oh, must be fifteen years now, comfortable as anything, perfectly broken in right at the lower back—and once I settle into that chair after lunch to watch a bit of the news or maybe one of those historical documentaries, I am perfectly content to just sit there for hours without moving a muscle. 

I really don't get that urge to get up and pace around, and I'm certainly not bouncing my leg up and down or tapping my fingers on the armrest. I have a nephew, Jimmy, my sister's boy, and he does that—he just cannot sit still for two minutes without jiggling his knee or drumming his fingers on the table. It drives his mother absolutely up the wall, especially at Thanksgiving dinner when we're all trying to sit and have a nice, quiet meal. But no, that's never been my problem. 

My body stays put just fine. I can sit perfectly still at the kitchen table when I'm trying to look at those catering menus, or in the pew at church, or in my chair at home. It's just my mind that's wandering off to Timbuktu. Physically, though? No, I wouldn't say I'm restless or fidgety at all. I'm actually quite relaxed, physically speaking. Maybe almost too relaxed sometimes, if you ask my wife when she’s trying to get me out the door to go run errands!

Well, it’s interesting you phrase it that way, comparing it to earlier in adulthood. Because, like I said, I’ve always been a bit of a space cadet, always had that tendency to drift off. Throughout my thirties and forties, you know, I managed it. I had my routines, my wife kept the house organized, and I got by just fine. But has it gotten worse? Yes. Absolutely. 

But it wasn't just some slow, creeping thing over the last few years. It really spiked quite recently. I'd say... well, it's been noticeably harder for about eleven months now. Exactly eleven months, actually, because we just passed the anniversary of the whole ordeal. You see, that cousin I mentioned earlier, Arthur? Well, about eleven months ago, he had to have a pretty major surgery. It was supposed to be a standard procedure, but there were complications, and the recovery was just grueling for him. He was living in this older split-level house over in the Heights, stairs everywhere, just completely impractical for someone trying to get around on a walker after an operation like that. 

So, my wife and I, we sat down and talked it over, and we decided the only sensible thing to do was to have him move in with us while he recovered. We have a nice guest room on the first floor, right next to a full bath, so it made perfect sense on paper. But let me tell you, ever since he moved in with us after that surgery, my ability to keep my thoughts straight has just gone completely out the window. 

It's like the extra layer of things to remember—the physical therapists coming and going on Tuesdays and Thursdays, the new dietary restrictions my wife has us all on for Arthur's sake, all the little disruptions to the quiet routine we used to have—it just completely overloaded my circuits. Before he moved in, if my mind wandered while I was reading the paper or fixing a hinge on a cabinet, it wasn't the end of the world. I'd just circle back to it eventually. But these past eleven months, with him living right there in the house with us and needing so much coordination, it’s been so much more difficult to just stay focused. The stakes are higher, and my brain just feels like it's scattering in a dozen different directions every time I try to sit down and focus on a task for him. So, yes, it's definitely gotten worse, but it really traces right back to when he moved in with us eleven months ago.

Depressed? No, no, I really wouldn’t use that word. I mean, don't get me wrong, it’s been stressful, like I was just saying, with Arthur being here and all the extra commotion in the house. And it is incredibly frustrating when I forget things, and I do feel terrible when my wife gets upset with me because I’ve dropped the ball on something important. It weighs on you, sure, feeling like you're letting people down. 

But actually feeling depressed? Down in the dumps, sad, hopeless? No, not at all. If anything, my mood is generally pretty good. I still really enjoy my days when I'm not tripping over my own forgetfulness. Just the other afternoon, for example, I was out in the garage—I like to tinker a bit, mostly just light woodworking, birdhouses, fixing up old chairs, that sort of thing—and I was perfectly happy out there. The weather was beautiful, we finally got a break from that humidity we were having all last week, I had the radio tuned to the classic rock station, and I felt just fine. I still have a good appetite, I still look forward to my morning coffee out on the back porch with the newspaper, even if I can't always get through a full article without my mind wandering off to think about the gutters or the lawn. 

So, no, it's definitely not a mood thing. I'm not sitting around crying or feeling like life is bleak. It's really just the pure frustration of my brain not cooperating with the tasks I need to do. My wife actually asked me that exact same thing a few months ago. She said, "Are you depressed?" because I was sighing so much around the house, but I told her, "I'm not sad, honey, I'm just annoyed that I forgot why I walked into the kitchen for the third time today." So, no, definitely not depressed. Just... scattered. Very, very scattered.

Anxious? Worried? Well... hmm. I suppose it depends on how you define it. Am I sitting around wringing my hands, terrified that the sky is falling or that something terrible is going to happen to my family? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm not a nervous wreck in that sense. I don't get panic attacks or feel my heart racing out of my chest for no reason. 

But... am I worried? Yes, I suppose I am, but it's a very specific kind of worry. It's not a general anxiety about the world, it's a constant, nagging worry about *myself*. About my own brain. Ever since Arthur moved in and things got so chaotic, I just have this underlying hum of anxiety about what I'm going to forget next. It's like I'm always waiting for the other shoe to drop. I'll be sitting there, watching a baseball game—say, the Astros are playing, and it's the bottom of the seventh, a really tense moment—and instead of just enjoying the game, this thought will just pop into my head: "Did I remember to call the pharmacy to refill Arthur's blood pressure medication?" And then my heart will sink a little bit, and I'll have to get up and check, and usually, I haven't forgotten, but sometimes I have. 

And it's that *sometimes* that really gets to me. It makes you second-guess yourself constantly. I used to trust my own mind, you know? If I said I was going to do something, I did it. But now, I'm just so worried that I'm going to let my wife down, or worse, that I'm going to mess up something important for Arthur's recovery. The other day, my wife asked me to pick up some specific low-sodium chicken broth from the grocery store—the one in the blue carton, not the yellow one—and I was so anxious about forgetting it that I repeated "blue carton, blue carton" the entire drive there. And you know what? I still ended up standing in the soup aisle for ten minutes staring at the shelves because I started second-guessing whether she said blue carton or blue label. 

So, yes, I am worried, but it's a worry born out of frustration. It's the anxiety of not being able to rely on your own memory to just get through a normal day without causing a problem for everyone else. It's exhausting, honestly. Just constantly being on guard against my own forgetfulness. But it's not like a clinical anxiety disorder, I don't think. It's just the natural reaction to feeling like your brain is a sieve.

Well, now, that’s a very interesting distinction to make, and I’m glad you asked it exactly that way. Because my wife, bless her heart, she sometimes gets it into her head that my memory is just completely failing me, like I'm getting senile early or something. But I always have to stop her and say, "Hold on, it’s not that the file got deleted from the hard drive, it’s that it was never saved in the first place!" 

If I am actually dialed in—if I'm looking right at you, and I’m actively engaged in what we’re doing—my memory is honestly like a steel trap. I don't forget things that I've actually absorbed. Just this past Tuesday, for instance. Or wait, was it Wednesday? No, it was Tuesday, because that’s one of the days Arthur’s physical therapist comes to the house. This young guy, Mark, very polite kid, went to Texas A&M. Anyway, Mark was explaining this entirely new stretching routine for Arthur's knee. And because I knew it was absolutely critical that we get it right so we don't set back his recovery, I made a very conscious effort. I put down my coffee mug on the side table, I turned my chair to face Mark directly, and I just locked in. 

And you know what? I can tell you right now, days later, exactly what he said word for word. He said we need to elevate Arthur's leg to exactly a forty-five-degree angle, hold it for fifteen seconds—not twenty, fifteen—and make absolutely sure his heel is flexed toward the ceiling the entire time. I remembered every single detail of that conversation perfectly, without writing it down, because I was truly paying attention. 

The trouble only rears its head when my mind starts drifting. If my wife is telling me about her sister's new patio furniture while I’m standing there trying to calculate if it’s been three months since I last changed the air filter in the HVAC system... well, then, sure, ten minutes later I won't have a clue what color cushions her sister bought. But that’s simply because I wasn't really listening to her in the first place, you see? I was miles away, thinking about fiberglass filters and dust buildup. So, no, to answer your question, if I am truly paying attention and focused on the moment, I don't forget conversations or events at all. The machinery up there still works fine, it’s just... it's just getting my brain to stay tuned to the right channel long enough to record the program, if that makes any sense.

No, no, not at all. Like I was trying to explain just a minute ago, it’s really just that one specific thing. I’m honestly not a worrier by nature. Never have been, really. I mean, my wife, she’s the one who can fret about the electric bill going up a few dollars in the summer, or whether the neighbor's big oak tree is leaning a little too close to our property line after a bad thunderstorm. But me? I’ve always been the type to just take things as they come. Especially since I stopped working, I really don't have those big, looming, everyday stresses hanging over my head. 

Just last month, for example, the check engine light came on in my truck. Now, a lot of guys would lose sleep over that, right? They'd be lying awake thinking about the transmission failing, or how much the dealership is going to charge for parts, because you know you can't just get under the hood with a basic wrench anymore. Everything is all computerized and sealed up with plastic covers, so they charge you an arm and a leg just to plug it into their machine. But I just looked at the dashboard and thought, well, I'll take it down to the shop on Tuesday and whatever it is, it is. I didn't lose a single wink of sleep over it. I just don't have that kind of... generalized panic about life, you know? 

So, no, my worries are very, very localized. If Arthur wasn't staying with us right now, and if I wasn't constantly dropping the ball on my daily tasks because my focus keeps drifting off into the clouds, I'd probably be the most relaxed guy on the block. It's really just the frustration of my own brain letting me down that gets my heart rate up. The rest of the world? The economy, the house maintenance, the news? Nah. I just let all that stuff roll right off my back.

I... well, I came because of church. I guess I've been doing some things that aren't quite right. Like... standing by the food with the serving spoon just up in the air. Not moving. Or... folding the same stack of napkins over and over when people are waiting. I don't know why.
No... no, it's not like that. I don't feel like anything bad is going to happen. I just... I don't know. I'm just folding them.
No... I don't hear anything like that. Just regular people talking.
No... I don't think so. I understand folks just fine. I haven't really had any trouble with that.
I... no. I don't think so. Nobody's moving my arm around. I just... I don't know about that.
I don't... no. I ain't fighting nobody. Mostly folks just let me be. I don't really pay much mind to it.
I... I don't rightly know. I ain't really one to get all worked up. It just... happens when it happens, I guess. I don't really keep track of all that.
I... I don't know. I reckon I talk as much as I need to. Ain't got much to say most days anyway.

Like those sci-fi movies my ex-boyfriend used to watch. He was obsessed with them. He had this huge collection of DVDs, which took up a whole shelf in the living room. DVDs are so obsolete now, you know? Everything is streaming. I have a subscription to this one service, mostly just to watch this baking competition show. It's so relaxing. They make these incredible cakes that look like real objects, like a purse or a shoe. I don't know how they get the fondant so smooth. I tried using fondant once for my niece's birthday cake. It was supposed to be a unicorn, but the horn kept drooping and the fondant tasted like sweet plastic. The kids didn't care, though, they just ate the frosting. Frosting is the best part anyway. I like the kind that comes in a can, the chocolate fudge one. Sometimes I just eat a spoonful of it right out of the fridge when I need a quick sugar fix. The fridge in my apartment is always making this weird rattling noise, though. I think the ice maker is broken, but I don't even use ice that much. It waters down your drink too fast. Especially iced coffee. If I get iced coffee, I always ask for light ice, otherwise it's just brown water by the time I get to work. The coffee shop near the clinic has the best cold brew, though. They put this little splash of oat milk in it...

Wait, sorry. Controlling my thoughts? No, definitely not. Nobody is doing that.

Mixed up? No, I don't think my ideas are mixed up. I mean, I explain things exactly how they happen. If people don't understand, maybe they just aren't listening closely enough. People don't really listen anymore, you know? They just wait for their turn to talk. 

Like, I was trying to tell Brenda about this new patient at the clinic—well, not a new patient, but someone who hadn't been in for a while. He had these incredible veins, just right there on the surface, perfect for a blood draw. I love when that happens. Sometimes you get people who are so dehydrated you have to poke them twice, which I hate doing. It makes me feel terrible. I always tell them to drink plenty of water before they come in, but they never do. They always say they forgot or they drank coffee instead. Coffee actually dehydrates you, though. It's a diuretic. I learned that in my anatomy class back in college. I only took a few classes before I decided to do the phlebotomy certification instead. College was just so expensive, and I didn't want to take out all those loans. My cousin took out loans for a degree in art history, and now she works at a shoe store. She gets a great discount on shoes, though. She got me these really comfortable sneakers for work. They have memory foam insoles. Standing all day really does a number on your lower back. I tried doing yoga to help with it, but I just end up falling asleep during the relaxing part at the end. The instructor plays this soft flute music and turns the lights down...

But yeah, no. Nobody has told me they can't understand what I mean. I make perfect sense.

A head injury? No, not that I can remember. I haven't hit my head or anything. I mean, I'm pretty careful. 

Although, I did bump my elbow really hard on the edge of the centrifuge at work last week. It bruised up immediately. It was one of those really ugly, dark purple bruises that turns green and yellow after a few days. It's right on the funny bone, too, so it tingled all the way down to my pinky finger. I hate that feeling. It's like when your foot falls asleep because you've been sitting on it wrong. I do that all the time when I watch TV. I sit cross-legged on the couch, and then when I try to stand up, I have to hobble around for a minute until the pins and needles go away. My couch is really deep, though, so it's easy to just sink into it. It's this dark grey microfiber, which is supposed to be easy to clean, but it shows every single piece of lint. I have to use one of those sticky rollers on it constantly. I go through so many of those rolls. You can buy them in bulk at that big warehouse club. My mom has a membership there, and she always takes me with her so I can stock up on paper towels and stuff. They sell these massive muffins in the bakery section there. Like, they're the size of a grapefruit. I got the blueberry ones last time, but they put way too much sugar on top. It gets all crunchy and makes a mess everywhere when you take a bite. I ended up having to vacuum my car because I ate one on the way home. My car vacuum is just this little handheld thing that plugs into the cigarette lighter... well, they don't call it a cigarette lighter anymore, do they? It's a power outlet now. Nobody really smokes in their cars anymore. The smell just gets trapped in the upholstery...

But no, a head injury? Definitely not. I haven't had anything like that.

Words not fitting together? No, I don't think so. I mean, I speak English perfectly fine. Sometimes I talk a little fast if I'm excited, but people can understand me. I've never had anyone tell me I sounded mixed up. 

Although, there was this one time at the grocery store last week where the cashier couldn't understand me, but she had her headphones in. She was listening to something, maybe a podcast. I listen to a lot of podcasts when I'm cleaning the apartment. Mostly true crime ones. It's fascinating how they solve those cold cases using DNA now. It makes me think about all the blood samples I take at the clinic. Like, what if one of those people is secretly a criminal and their DNA gets put into a database? Not that we run DNA tests, we just do basic panels, cholesterol, A1C, that kind of thing. But it's crazy how much information is just floating around in your blood. My aunt got one of those ancestry kits for Christmas a few years ago, the ones where you spit in a tube. She found out she's like, two percent Scandinavian, which she thought was so exotic. She started buying all this lingonberry jam from IKEA. IKEA is so overwhelming, though. It's like a maze. You go in for a lamp and you end up leaving with three house plants and a bag of meatballs. The meatballs aren't even that good, they're kind of spongy. I prefer making my own with ground turkey. It's healthier, you know? Ground beef is so heavy, it always gives me heartburn if I eat it too late at night. I have to sleep propped up on two pillows if I eat red meat after 7 PM. My pillows are getting kind of flat, actually. I need to get new ones. Maybe bamboo ones? I heard those stay cool...

But no, nobody has ever told me my words don't fit together. I'm very clear when I speak.

Personality changed? No, I don't think so. I'm exactly the same person I've always been. I mean, my mom says I'm working too much, but that's just because we've been short-staffed at the clinic. We had two girls quit in the same week. One of them moved to Texas because her husband got a job out there in the oil fields or something. I can't imagine living in Texas, it's way too hot. I sweat so much just walking from my car to the grocery store in the summer here. I have to carry one of those little travel deodorants in my purse. I buy the clinical strength kind, the one that clicks when you turn the dial at the bottom. It smells like baby powder, which I actually really like. It reminds me of my grandmother's house. She used to have this huge powder puff on her vanity that she'd use after her bath. Her vanity had this beautiful trifold mirror, the kind where you can see the back of your head if you angle it right. I've always wanted one of those so I could try doing French braids on myself. I can never get the back to look right, it always gets bumpy. I tried watching tutorials on YouTube, but they do it so fast. YouTube has a tutorial for literally everything now, though. I watched one last week on how to fix a leaky faucet because my kitchen sink was dripping and driving me crazy. It was just a worn-out washer, super easy to replace. You just need an Allen wrench. I have this little toolkit I keep under the sink that has a bunch of different sizes...

But yeah, my personality hasn't changed. I'm still just me.

Seizures? Oh, no, definitely not. I've never had a seizure or anything like that. I've never even fainted, actually. 

Although, I did get really dizzy once when I stood up too fast after donating blood. It was during that big community blood drive they do every summer at the high school gym. The gym always smells so strongly of floor wax and old sweat, it's just a very distinct smell. It reminds me of pep rallies when I was a teenager. I was in the marching band, I played the clarinet. We had these awful, heavy wool uniforms that were so itchy, especially during the August parades. We had to wear these tall hats with plumes on them, and they'd always blow off if it was windy. My friend Sarah lost her hat right in the middle of a routine once, and it rolled all the way down Main Street. Sarah's a real estate agent now, she sells these huge houses out in the suburbs. She showed me pictures of this one place that had a double oven in the kitchen. I would love a double oven. I tried to bake two sheets of cookies at once in my little oven last Christmas, and the bottom ones got completely burnt while the top ones were still raw in the middle. I had to throw the whole bottom batch out for the birds. The crows in my neighborhood are huge, they'll eat anything. They sit on the power lines and just watch you when you take the trash out. It's a little creepy, honestly. They're so smart, though. I read somewhere that crows can recognize human faces and remember if you were mean to them. So I always try to be nice and just leave them alone...

But anyway, no, I haven't had any seizures. I'm totally fine in that department.

I feel like you asked me something really similar a few minutes ago. But no, nobody has ever told me my sentences are disorganized. I make perfect sense. I have to be really clear at work, especially when I'm talking to the older patients at the clinic. Sometimes they can't hear very well, so I have to enunciate. And you have to write everything down clearly, too. We use these specific fine-tip markers for the blood tubes so the lab can read the patient names. I actually hide my favorite marker in my scrub pocket so the other girls don't take it. 

Scrubs are so comfortable, honestly. It's like wearing pajamas to work. I buy the ones with the extra cargo pockets on the side because I always need a place to keep my lip balm. I'm obsessed with this peppermint lip balm I found at a farmer's market last fall. The farmer's market is so nice, there's this one guy who sells the most amazing heirloom tomatoes. They're so ugly, like all lumpy and purple, but they taste incredible with just a little bit of salt and olive oil. Olive oil has gotten so expensive lately, though. I saw a tiny bottle at the store for like fifteen dollars the other day. It's ridiculous. I ended up just buying canola oil, even though they say it's not as good for you. You read so many different things about what's good for you and what isn't, it changes every week. One day coffee is bad, the next day it prevents heart disease. I try to just stick to one cup in the morning, otherwise I get the jitters. 

But anyway, no, my sentences don't get disorganized. People understand me perfectly.

New prescription medicine? No, I haven't started anything new. I don't really take any prescriptions. I just go to the pharmacy for my vitamins, mostly. 

The drive-thru line at the pharmacy near my apartment is always so backed up, though. It spills right out onto the main road, so I usually just park and go inside because it's actually faster. Plus, then I can look at the greeting cards while I wait. I had to get a birthday card for my niece last week, she just turned seven. Greeting cards are getting so expensive now, it's honestly crazy. I paid almost eight dollars for one that played a little song when you open it. It played that "Walking on Sunshine" song. It's a catchy song, but it gets stuck in your head all day. I actually heard it playing on the radio at the dentist's office a few months ago. I hate going to the dentist. The sound of that little metal scraper tool just goes right through me, it makes my teeth ache just thinking about it. My hygienist is really nice, though, her name is Brenda and she always gives me a free travel toothpaste and a toothbrush. I only use soft-bristle brushes because the medium ones hurt my gums. I read an article that said you're actually supposed to brush really gently, like you're polishing a tomato, which is a weird comparison but I guess it makes sense. Tomatoes bruise so easily. I tried growing them in a pot on my balcony last summer, but the squirrels kept taking exactly one bite out of the red ones and just leaving them on the railing. They are such menaces. 

But no, I'm not taking any new medicines. Just my regular vitamins.

Hi, yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, well, what really pushed me to finally make this appointment is... I just keep starting these follow-up items at work. I'm an auditor, so there's always a ton of follow-up after audits, or even after these mentorship events I run. I'll sit down with every intention of finishing them. I even bought this new planner—it's got these little color-coded stickers, which I thought would help because my sister uses them and swears by them. She's a teacher, so she's always organizing something. But anyway, I'll start the task, and then days later, I find out that the final email, or the review note, or the form never actually got done. It's just sitting there, half-finished. Like, last week I was supposed to send out this summary email, and I got distracted because my cat knocked over a plant, and by the time I cleaned up the dirt, I totally forgot what I was doing. So yeah, the follow-ups just aren't getting finished.

Oh, absolutely. Even back in elementary school... I remember my report cards always said the exact same thing. They'd say I was bright, but I constantly lost my assignments, or I'd just rush past all the small details. And I talked out of turn a lot. Actually, my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she had this huge collection of ceramic frogs on her desk. Like, dozens of them. I always wondered where she bought them all, or if students just kept giving them to her as gifts, you know? Because what do you even buy a teacher? I usually just give Starbucks gift cards now. 

But anyway, she was always having to remind me to finish my classwork. My mother still jokes about it to this day. She always says I could completely ace a test, but then I'd totally forget the big project just sitting right there in my backpack. It was this bright pink Lisa Frank backpack, too, with the neon dolphins. God, I loved that thing. I took it everywhere until the zipper finally broke on a family trip to Florida...

Unwanted thoughts? Um, no, not really. I mean, my mind is always going a mile a minute, but it's not like I'm having bad thoughts I can't get rid of. It's more just... thinking about a million things at once. Like yesterday, I was trying to reconcile this account, and suddenly I was wondering if I ever paid my water bill, which reminded me that I need to buy a new filter for the Brita pitcher. I got the pitcher on sale at Target, actually. Target's dangerous for me, I always go in for one thing and come out with a cart full of stuff I don't need. Last time I bought this throw pillow shaped like a taco. It's hilarious, but it doesn't match my couch at all. My couch is this dark grey microfiber—super easy to clean, which is great because of the cat. But yeah, no, not like scary or weird thoughts that I can't shake. Just regular thoughts, but a lot of them.

Worrying excessively? Um... I don't think so. I mean, I worry about normal stuff, I guess. Like getting my audits done on time, or if I remembered to lock the front door. Oh, actually, speaking of the front door, I just got this new smart lock installed last week. It's supposed to connect to my phone so I can check it from anywhere, which is super convenient, but the app keeps crashing. I spent like forty-five minutes on hold with customer service on Tuesday. The hold music was that one classical song—what is it, Vivaldi? Spring? Anyway, it was so loud and staticky. I ended up just hanging up because my cat started scratching at the screen door. He loves trying to get out onto the balcony, even though he's strictly an indoor cat. I bought him this elaborate cat tree to distract him, it's got three different levels and a little hammock... but yeah, I wouldn't say I worry excessively. Just normal worrying, really.

Well, I’m here because... I mean, honestly, it’s about my house, but everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just, you know, standard paperwork and missed payments. Like it's just some normal financial mistake or a clerical thing. But it’s not. I supervise the sales floor at my retail job, so I know how to track things, I know how to spot when things don't add up, and I have been watching this happen for almost two years now. Two whole years. 

And I know for an absolute fact that the bank, the loan servicer, and even people at my job—which I know sounds strange to people who aren't paying attention, but I am—they have all been quietly working together to push me out of my house. They coordinate it behind my back. People just look at the mail and say, 'Oh, it's just a late notice,' but they don't see the whole picture. They don't see how the dates on the bank letters line up exactly with when my coworkers start acting weird around me or whispering when I come into the breakroom. 

It's a whole orchestrated thing to force me out of my home, and no amount of papers they show me, no matter how official they make these foreclosure documents look with their stamps and their legal jargon, changes what I’ve been seeing with my own two eyes for the last twenty-something months. They just want me out, and they're all in on it together, and no one will just sit down and look at what is actually happening to me.

Energized? Like... high? No, I mean, I don't know why you'd ask that. I certainly don't feel great about any of this. If I'm not sleeping, it's definitely not because I have some kind of boundless energy or feel unusually good. It's because I'm exhausted, but I have to stay vigilant. You try sleeping when you know there's a coordinated effort to steal your house. 

I mean, I'm up at 2 AM sometimes, sure, but I'm sitting at my kitchen table, going through the mail with a yellow highlighter, trying to cross-reference the postmarks on the bank envelopes with the exact days my manager schedules me for closing shifts. Because I noticed a pattern—they always seem to time the delivery of these so-called 'default notices' for the nights I'm too tired from closing the sales floor to properly analyze them. It's completely calculated. 

So, no, I don't feel high. I feel drained. I want to sleep. I really do. I bought blackout curtains, I drink chamomile tea, I do all the things you're supposed to do to wind down, but how can you actually rest when you know the minute you close your eyes, the people who are supposed to be ringing up customers at your job are probably texting the loan servicer to give them updates on my schedule? If I'm awake and getting less sleep, it's purely out of necessity. It's survival. I'm just trying to keep a roof over my head while everyone else is playing these games, so no, no extra energy here. Just a lot of stress.

Depressed? Well... no. I wouldn't use that word. I mean, people throw that word around a lot, don't they? Like, 'oh, I had a bad day at work, I'm so depressed.' But no, I'm not sitting around crying or, you know, staring at the wall feeling hopeless or empty. I honestly don't have the time to feel empty. I have a house to save.

Voices? Like, hearing things that aren't there? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I know why you're asking that, I've seen the movies, but no. My hearing is perfectly fine, and I only hear what people are actually saying. 

The problem isn't that I'm hearing imaginary voices, the problem is what I'm hearing real people say when they think I'm not listening. Like, just last Tuesday, I was in the stockroom—I'm the supervisor, so I do the inventory checks, right?—and I heard two of the cashiers whispering on the other side of the shelving unit. They didn't know I was there. And they were talking about 'the timeline.' That's the exact phrase they used: 'the timeline.' Now, why would two part-time cashiers be talking about a timeline unless they were referring to the bank's timeline for my house? They were whispering, but I heard them clear as day. 

And then, when I walked around the corner, they completely stopped talking. Just dead silence. And one of them—Sarah, who just started three months ago—she looked at her phone and then looked at me with this really specific expression. So, no, I don't hear voices in my head. I hear the very real conversations that my coworkers are having about me and my property. I hear the loan servicer on the phone when I call them, talking in circles, using all this jargon to confuse me, but their tone of voice tells me everything I need to know. They get this smug, condescending tone, like they know something I don't, like they know the trap is already set. 

So, no, no hallucinations. No voices from the walls or anything crazy like that. I'm completely grounded in reality. I just have very good ears, and I pay attention to the things people say when they think I'm out of earshot. That's how I know they're all working together. You don't need to hear imaginary voices when the real ones are conspiring against you right out in the open, if you just know how to listen.

Jumbled? No, I mean, no one has ever said that to me. If anything, I think I'm probably too clear for them. That's the issue, isn't it? When you start putting the pieces together and you can articulate exactly how the bank is coordinating with the scheduling manager to exhaust you so you miss the fine print on the default notices... people don't like that. They don't want you to be clear. 

So no, nobody says I'm hard to follow. Sometimes my sister will say, 'You're overthinking this,' or 'You're talking too fast,' but that's just because she doesn't want to hear it. She doesn't want to admit that the situation is as bad as it is. It's much easier for her to just pretend everything is fine and that I'm just stressed about work. But my thoughts aren't jumbled at all. I have them all written out, actually. I have a whole notebook where I track the shifts, the mail deliveries, the phone calls. It's incredibly organized. It has to be. If my thoughts were jumbled, I would have lost the house months ago. 

I mean, just look at how I manage the store. You can't be a supervisor and have jumbled thoughts. I handle the inventory, I handle the cash drops, I manage a team of six people—even if two of them are clearly feeding information to the loan servicer. I still manage them effectively. You have to be sharp. You have to be ten steps ahead. So if someone were to say my thoughts were hard to follow, it would just be a tactic. It would just be another way to discredit me so that when I finally take all this evidence to a lawyer, they'll say, 'Oh, don't listen to her, she's confused.' But I'm not confused. I know exactly what's happening.

Control my thoughts? Put thoughts in my mind? No, no, of course not. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My thoughts are completely my own, and honestly, my mind is the one thing I have absolute control over right now. If the bank or the loan servicer could just magically put thoughts into my head, don't you think they would have done it by now? They would have just planted a thought like, 'Oh, this is all too hard, I should just let them foreclose,' or 'I should just sign this modification paperwork without reading the addendum.' 

But they can't do that. They can't get inside my head like that. What they do try to do, though, is influence my thinking through exhaustion and stress. Like the scheduling manager at work? He’s been giving me these back-to-back closing and opening shifts—we call them 'clopens' in retail—and I know exactly why he's doing it. He's doing it to wear me down physically so that my resolve weakens. They figure if I'm tired enough, I'll make a mistake, or I'll just get so overwhelmed that I'll surrender the property. They leave the inventory logs a complete mess on purpose so I have to stay an hour past my shift fixing them, which cuts into the time I have at home to review my case files and track the discrepancies in my escrow account. 

So they use psychological pressure, absolutely. They use manipulation, they use surveillance—like Sarah and the others watching me—but they do not control my actual thoughts. I am incredibly protective of my mental space. I don't even listen to the radio on my commute anymore. I drive in total silence for twenty-five minutes just so I can review my strategy for the day, step by step, without any distractions. I know exactly what I think and why I think it. My mind is my armor in all of this. It's the one thing they can't touch, and frankly, I think that's why they are escalating things at the store. They're frustrated because I'm still thinking for myself and I'm still ten steps ahead of them. So no, nobody is putting thoughts in my mind. I wouldn't let them even if it were possible.

Less interested? No, not at all. I mean, I still want to do the things I love, I just literally do not have the luxury of free time right now. There's a huge difference. 

Like, I used to go out with my friends Melissa and Jen every other Friday. We’d go get margaritas and do the trivia night down at this pub near the mall. I love trivia. I’m usually the one who carries the team on the history and geography questions. I haven't lost interest in that, I still really want to go! But, I mean, how can I sit there and try to remember the capital of North Dakota when I know for a fact that the bank is actively trying to push through a fraudulent default notice on my house? I can't just turn my brain off and drink a margarita when I have deadlines to meet and documents to review. Plus, they don't really get it. Melissa just tells me to 'take a breath' and 'let the lawyers handle it,' which just shows how naive she is about how these servicers operate. So I haven't lost interest in my friends, it's just hard to relate to them when they refuse to see what's right in front of them.

And it's the exact same thing with my hobbies. I have this garden out back, and I planted these incredible heirloom tomatoes in the spring—Cherokee Purples, they're my absolute favorite, they get this amazing dark color and they taste incredible. I love being out there in the dirt, it's usually so relaxing. I really miss it. But by the time I get home from one of those exhausting 'clopen' shifts I told you about, and then I have to spend three hours cross-referencing my certified mail receipts with the postal service tracking database to prove they're withholding my correspondence... it's pitch black outside. And I can't exactly go out into the yard with a flashlight at midnight. That just draws attention to the house, and I know for a fact they have people driving by to check on my occupancy status to try and claim the property is abandoned. 

So, no, my interests haven't changed. I'm not sitting around depressed or apathetic, if that's what you're getting at. I have zero lack of interest in my life. It's strictly a matter of prioritization. When your entire livelihood and your property are under a coordinated attack, you have to put the fun stuff on the back burner. It's just survival. If I had my way, I'd be out in the garden every single evening, but they've made absolutely sure I don't have that option right now.

Intensely sad? Hopeless? No. No, not at all. I mean, I'm angry, sure. I'm incredibly frustrated, absolutely. But hopeless? If I were hopeless, I would have just handed over the keys to the bank months ago. You only feel hopeless when you don't know what's going on or when you've given up, and I am so far from giving up. 

Actually, it's funny you use that word, "hopeless," because I think that's exactly the state of mind they are actively trying to push me into. That's the whole point of the 'clopen' shifts I was telling you about, the messing with my inventory logs, the delayed mail. They want me to sit down on my living room couch, look at the stack of fraudulent default notices, and just cry. They want me to feel like there's no way out, like the machine is just too big to fight. But I don't feel that way. I feel... energized, in a way. I mean, it's an exhausting, stressful energy, but I am in a fight, and you don't fight if you don't have hope that you're going to win.

Like, just last Tuesday, I got this letter from the servicer—certified mail, of course, but they deliberately smudged the tracking barcode on the envelope. They do that so it won't scan properly in the system and I can't prove exactly when it was delivered. So I had to go all the way down to the main post office branch on my thirty-minute lunch break to get the delivery manager to manually pull the route data from their internal server. Did I sit in my car and cry about it? Did I feel sad? No! I marched right in there, got the printout, had them time-stamp it, and put it straight into Binder Number 4. That’s my correspondence binder. I have five of them now, all color-coded. You don't build five binders of meticulously cross-referenced evidence if you're feeling hopeless. 

So, no, no two weeks of intense sadness. I literally do not have the luxury of being sad. Sadness requires downtime. Sadness means you're sitting around wallowing, and I am way too busy defending my property and my livelihood to sit around feeling sorry for myself. I have to be the strong one here. If I let myself get sad or mopey, my sister would just use it as an excuse to say, 'See, you're just depressed, you need to let the house go, you're not thinking straight.' And I am absolutely not giving her, or the bank, or my manager the satisfaction of seeing me break. So, no. Not sad, not hopeless. Just highly, highly motivated to expose all of this.

More than a month? Oh, doctor, I wish it had only been a month. A month would be an absolute vacation compared to what I've been dealing with. No, this has been going on continuously, without a single day of rest, for about a year and nine months now. 

It all really started... well, I mean, they were probably laying the groundwork long before that, doing their little surveillance and messing with the accounts, but the actual, overt attacks? That was a year and nine months ago. That's exactly when the first so-called foreclosure notices started showing up in the mail. And I say 'so-called' because I've already proved the signatures on those initial filings were robo-signed by a third-party vendor, which is a whole other layer of fraud I've documented. But that's when it really started taking over our home life completely. 

And the bank calls... it wasn't just one or two polite calls during normal business hours. It was relentless. They would call at 7:15 in the morning, they would call at 8:45 at night, trying to catch me off guard, trying to create this atmosphere of constant panic in my own home. You couldn't even sit down to eat dinner or try to relax for five minutes without the phone ringing. And if you didn't answer, they'd just call back three minutes later from a slightly different local area code to trick you into picking up. They use these VoIP spoofing programs, you know. 

It just completely hijacked my entire life. Before that year and nine month mark, I was just a normal person going to work, managing the floor at the store, coming home, maybe working in the garden like I told you. But ever since those notices started flooding in and the phone started ringing off the hook, it's been a second full-time job just defending myself from them. I've had to completely restructure my entire existence around protecting this house. So yes, way, way more than a month. It’s been twenty-one months of absolute, coordinated harassment, and they haven't let up for a single second.

Other beliefs? Like, what, like the government is reading my thoughts or something? No. No, not at all. I'm a very practical person. I supervise a retail floor for a living, you know? I deal with concrete things—inventory counts, employee schedules, profit margins, point-of-sale systems. I deal in facts. I don't just go around making things up. 

So, aside from the house? There is nothing else, because the house is the entire issue. The only thing that people seem to have a hard time believing is the actual, documented reality of what they are doing to me. I mean, honestly, I think that’s exactly why I’m here talking to you right now, isn't it? Because everyone keeps acting like this foreclosure is just... just some standard administrative paperwork, or some simple issue of missed payments. They act like I just misplaced a bill or forgot to balance my checkbook and now the bank is just following standard procedure.
