Well, hello, doctor. It's nice to meet you, too. I... well, I came in today because I just can’t seem to get anything in order anymore. It's really gotten completely out of hand. Just to give you an example, if you were to walk into my house right now and look at my kitchen table, you wouldn't even be able to see the wood underneath. It is just completely covered in piles. 

I mean, there are my husband’s appointment papers—he's had quite a few lately, and they always hand you those thick printouts with the instructions and the dates, and I bring them home and just set them down. And then right on top of those are all the church flyers. I try to keep up with the Sunday social hour, so I have all these bulletins and announcements. Oh, and the senior-center notes! They send out these newsletters and activity calendars, and I keep meaning to go through them, but they just pile up right alongside all these half-finished lists I make. I'm always starting lists on the backs of envelopes to try and remember what to do, but I never finish them. 

And the worst part, the absolute most frustrating part, is that I will pull out a chair and sit there at that table, looking at this mountain of paper, and I just... I don't know which thing to do first. I sit there trying to figure out where to start, and I get so overwhelmed that I just stare at it, or I shuffle a few things around, and before I know it, the sun is going down and the whole day is just gone. Completely gone. And I just sit there feeling terrible about it, but I don't know how to fix it.

Oh, goodness, no. No, it's not just the last few years at all. It feels like it’s been my entire life, really. I mean, my husband thinks it’s just me getting older, you know, because when you reach seventy you expect some things to slip a little bit. But if I’m being completely honest with myself—and with you—it’s always been exactly like this. 

I was actually just thinking about this the other day. I was going through an old cedar chest in the spare bedroom, trying to find a specific photo album, and I happened to come across a stack of my old report cards from elementary school. My mother had saved every single one of them in this little tied-up bundle. And I sat on the edge of the bed reading them, and it was just... well, it brought tears to my eyes, honestly, because it was exactly the same struggle. Even as a little girl, my teachers would write these notes to my parents, and they always said the exact same things. They wrote that I was a bright girl, very capable, but just so careless. That was the word they always used: "careless." 

I was constantly forgetting my reading books, or I would actually do my homework and then leave it sitting right on the counter at home, which used to drive my mother up the wall. And the seatwork... oh, my goodness. We would have these little worksheets to do at our desks, and I would just sit there looking out the window, watching the other children or just daydreaming, and the teacher would always have to come over and tap on my desk. I needed constant reminders to just finish my seatwork, because if I didn't finish it, I wasn't allowed to go outside for recess. I would just sit there at that little wooden desk with the inkwell hole, feeling so frustrated because I desperately wanted to go outside and play, but I just couldn't seem to get my brain to focus on finishing the paper in front of me. 

So, no, doctor, it’s definitely not a new thing. It’s just... I suppose the piles are just different now. Instead of schoolwork, it's church bulletins. But the feeling of sitting there and not knowing how to start is exactly the same.

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I think people always assume that little girls are perfectly still and quiet, but I... well, I was never really the type to be jumping off the furniture or running around the classroom, if that's what you mean. I wasn't getting up out of my seat and causing a ruckus like some of the little boys did. But still? Oh, I don't think I've ever been truly still a day in my life. 

Even now, at my age, I just cannot seem to sit quietly. I go to these committee meetings at the church—I'm on the altar guild, and we have these long meetings to discuss the flower arrangements and the linens, and they can go on for an hour or more. And I try, I really do try to just sit politely with my hands folded in my lap like a proper lady. But before I even realize I'm doing it, I'll catch myself rubbing my hands together over and over, or I'll be tapping my foot against the leg of the chair. Tap, tap, tap. And if I have a pen in my hand to take notes? Forget it. I'll be clicking the top of it, or rolling it between my fingers, or taking the cap off and putting it back on. 

And I shift in my chair constantly. I'll cross my legs, and then uncross them, and then lean to one side, and then adjust my skirt, and then lean forward. I just get this... this restless feeling in my body, like my muscles just can't settle down. And I know it's noticeable, because sometimes the other ladies will stop talking and look over at me, and I'll realize I've been jiggling my foot so hard that the whole table is shaking. It's terribly embarrassing, really. You'd think a seventy-year-old woman would know how to sit still through a meeting, but I just can't seem to manage it. I try to stop, I'll tell myself, "Just be still," but then five minutes later, my foot is going again. It's like I have a little motor inside me that just never shuts off, even when I'm supposed to be perfectly still.

Oh, yes. Oh, it really has. It breaks my heart, it truly does, because I’ve always tried to be so involved and useful, but it feels like it's just ruining everything lately. 

I mean... just to give you an example, just last month, I was supposed to be in charge of this big event at the senior center. It was their annual Spring Jubilee luncheon, which is a lovely gathering, we do a silent auction and a big catered meal to raise money for the community pantry. I was so honored when they asked me to chair the committee. But... well, I had all the vendor contacts, and the volunteer sign-up sheets, and the donation forms, and I just couldn't organize any of it. The papers were scattered all over the house, just like my kitchen table. I missed the deadline to order the centerpieces, and I kept forgetting to call the caterer back to confirm the final headcount because I couldn't find the list of who had RSVP'd. It got so chaotic, and I was so paralyzed by all the details, that I actually had to step down. I had to call the director and give up leading the whole event completely. It was just humiliating to admit I couldn't handle it. I felt like I let all those lovely people down.

And it’s taking a toll on my family, too. Especially with my daughter, Sarah. She’s such a sweetheart, she really is, and she works so hard at her own job, but she's had to start stepping in to manage me, basically. It started a little while ago when a couple of important notices got buried under those church bulletins I mentioned, and now... well, now she comes over every single Sunday afternoon. She says she's just coming to visit and have tea, but I know exactly what she's really doing. She sits down at that messy table and she double-checks all of our bills and goes through every single one of my husband's and my appointments. She literally takes my calendar and cross-references it to make sure I haven't messed up the dates or forgotten to mail a check. 

She does it because she just doesn’t trust that I can keep everything straight on my own anymore. And I can't even be angry with her for interfering, because she's right! I *can't* keep it straight. But it just feels awful, you know? To be seventy years old and have your own child double-checking your mail because you're too scatterbrained to run your own household. I used to manage everything when she was a little girl, and now I can't even be trusted to pay the water bill on time without supervision. It just feels like this... this inability to organize anything is just bleeding into absolutely every part of my life.

Oh, no, no. I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I get frustrated, certainly. Like I was just saying about Sarah having to check my mail and stepping down from the Spring Jubilee... those things make me feel terribly foolish and upset in the moment. I might even have a little cry about it in the bathroom, just out of pure frustration with myself. But depressed? No, I really don't think so. 

I still wake up looking forward to the day, you know? I still love going out to my garden in the mornings. I have these absolutely beautiful hydrangea bushes that my husband and I planted when we first moved into this house—oh, goodness, it must have been thirty-five years ago now, back when the neighborhood was still mostly empty lots and young families. And I go out there with my coffee every morning and I just love looking at the blooms, deciding which ones to cut to bring inside. And I still enjoy my friends! I meet the girls for lunch every Tuesday at the little bistro downtown, the one that makes that lovely spinach quiche, and we just talk and laugh for hours about everything under the sun. 

So, no, I don't have that dark cloud hanging over me that people talk about when they have real depression. I'm not lying in bed unable to face the day. I *want* to face the day! I want to do all these things and be involved! It's just that when I try to actually do them, I get so terribly tangled up in the details and the paperwork and the organizing. It’s more of a... well, a deep exasperation with my own brain, if that makes sense, rather than a true sadness. I just wish I could be as capable as I feel on the inside, instead of constantly letting things slip through the cracks. But no, doctor, not depressed. Just... very, very annoyed with myself.

Oh, goodness, no. No, my memory is actually sharp as a tack, thank heavens. I know people sometimes assume that because I'm seventy and my house is a bit of a disaster area with all the papers, that I must be losing my mind or getting dementia or something awful like that. But it's really not my memory at all! 

Like, if I have a conversation with someone, I remember every single detail. Just this past Tuesday, at that lunch I was telling you about with the girls? Susan was telling us about her grandson, David—he just moved out to Seattle for a new job, and I remembered to ask her how his drive across the country went, because I knew he was taking his golden retriever with him and stopping at Mount Rushmore. And I remembered that his new job is with some big aerospace firm, working on the navigation systems. I remember all of that perfectly! 

And it's the same with my own life. I don't forget that an event is happening, or that I had a conversation with my husband about fixing the leaky faucet in the downstairs half-bath. I remember exactly what we talked about. The problem is just... well, like with the bills that Sarah comes over to check. It’s not that I *forget* we have a water bill. I know exactly when it’s due, it's always the fifteenth of the month. But I’ll take the mail out of the box, and I’ll set it on the kitchen counter to go make a cup of tea, and then I’ll see a gardening catalog, and then the bill just gets buried under a stack of magazines and those church bulletins I mentioned. So I don't forget the bill exists, I just... I lose the physical envelope, or I get entirely sidetracked before I can sit down and write the check. 

So, no, I'm not forgetting recent events or what people say to me. If anything, my head is entirely too full of all the things I *know* I'm supposed to be doing, and I remember every single one of my failures to do them! It's just getting the actual tasks organized and executed that completely trips me up. But my memory itself? Oh, it's perfectly fine. I could tell you exactly what I wore to my high school graduation, and I could tell you exactly what the ladies and I discussed over our quiche two days ago. It's just the organizing that's the problem.

Well, I... I'm here because of things at the warehouse. The routing system, specifically. It isn't just a computer to me anymore. I know it's been marking my moves, sending these messages through the hand scanners to push me out because I'm one of the old hands. 

I've been operating the trucks and tractors there for years. We used to drive these big propane ones, you know? Now they're all electric. Much quieter. Sometimes too quiet, honestly, you can't even hear them coming around the blind corners near the loading docks. My buddy Carl almost got clipped by one last week. Carl's got a bad knee, so he can't move out of the way like he used to. He tore his meniscus playing softball back in '98. We had a really great company team back then, won the regional league and everything. They gave us these cheap plastic trophies, but we were proud of them. I think my wife threw mine out when we moved to the new house. The basement there flooded twice in the first year, completely ruined the drywall... 

But anyway, the system. It knows I'm older, so the scanner keeps targeting me.

Well, the voices and the whole thing with the scanners... it's been about a year and eight months now. Started right around the time they brought in those new electric pallet jacks. I remember because the warehouse manager, Tom, made a big speech about efficiency and going green. Tom's a nice enough guy, I guess, but he wears these awful patterned ties. I mean, who wears a tie in a warehouse anyway? It's a safety hazard. If that thing gets caught in the conveyor belt by the packaging station, he's a goner. I saw a guy get his sleeve caught once back in the 80s. Ripped his shirt right off his back, lucky it wasn't his arm. They didn't have the same safety guards back then. We used to just eat our lunch sitting right on the pallets of dog food. The smell was terrible, especially in the summer when the AC broke... but yeah, about a year and eight months since the system started on me.

High? Energetic? No, no, I haven't felt like that at all. Honestly, it's been the opposite most days. It's hard to find the energy to even drag myself out of bed, let alone feel high or wired. I used to have a lot of energy, though. Back when I was working the night shift, I could go on four hours of sleep, no problem. We'd finish up around 6 AM, and me and a few of the guys would head over to this diner on 4th Street. It's not there anymore, they tore it down to build a bank, which is a shame because they had the best hash browns. Crispy on the outside, soft on the inside. You can't find hash browns like that anymore. Now everywhere you go, it's just those frozen patties they deep fry. It's just not the same. My wife used to try and make them from scratch on Sunday mornings, but she'd always burn the onions. I never told her, though, because she'd get so upset. She's sensitive about her cooking ever since her mother criticized her pot roast at Thanksgiving back in '05... but no, I haven't had any of those energetic periods you're talking about. Just tired. Very tired.

No, no major illnesses. And no head injuries, thank god. I've always been pretty careful about my head. You have to be, working around heavy machinery. Hard hats are mandatory now, of course, but it wasn't always like that. I remember when they first introduced the hard hat rule, oh, must have been '86 or '87. Half the guys complained it messed up their hair or gave them a headache. My buddy Phil refused to wear his for a week until the foreman threatened to dock his pay. Phil was stubborn like that. He drove a forklift like a maniac, always taking the corners too fast. He actually knocked over a whole pallet of canned peaches once. Took us three hours to clean up the syrup. The smell of peaches makes me sick to my stomach to this day. My wife bought some peach preserves last month and I had to ask her to throw them out. She bought them at that farmer's market downtown, the one they set up by the old courthouse on Saturdays. Parking down there is a nightmare, though. The city really needs to build another garage... but no, my head is fine. No injuries.

Drugs? No, no drugs. I don't touch any of that stuff, never have. And no new medications either, just the same blood pressure pill I've been taking for years. The one with the little score mark down the middle. I have to break it in half because the full dose makes me dizzy when I stand up too fast. I learned that the hard way when I was fixing the gutter on the back porch last spring. Almost took a tumble right into the rose bushes. My wife planted those bushes when we first bought the house. They're these beautiful yellow roses, 'Peace' roses, I think she called them. They take a lot of upkeep, though. You have to prune them just right or they get all leggy and don't bloom. The neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she has these climbing roses that just take over everything. They're growing right up the side of her garage and into the power lines. I told her she ought to call the city to come trim them back before a storm knocks the power out for the whole block. We lost power for three days back during the ice storm of '98. Had to sleep in our winter coats and eat cold soup straight out of the can... but yeah, no drugs or new pills or anything like that. Just the regular one.

Hard to follow? Me? No, nobody's ever said that. I mean, my wife says I don't listen, but that's different. That's just marriage, right? You tune things out after thirty years. Like when she starts talking about her sister's dog. That dog is a menace, a little yappy terrier thing that bites at your ankles. They brought it over for the Fourth of July barbecue last year, and it chased a squirrel right through my wife's prized petunias. She was furious. Said the dog ruined the whole aesthetic of the patio. We spent a fortune on those patio pavers, too. Had a guy come out from over in Shelbyville to lay them. He did a good job, but he left his thermos behind. A big green Stanley thermos, the kind that keeps coffee hot all day. I tried calling the company to return it, but they went out of business a few months later. Shame, really, they did good work. Hard to find reliable contractors these days. Everyone's just looking to make a quick buck and cut corners. Like the guy who fixed my cousin's roof—used the wrong nails and the whole thing leaked the next time it rained... but no, nobody says my speech is hard to follow. I think I make perfect sense.

Yeah, yeah exactly. Like... I'll just be sitting out in my garage, right? Everything is completely shut off, dead quiet. But I hear the dispatch voices, clear as day. They're calling out my operator number, telling me I'm dangerous, saying security is on the way to come get me. It's just like the old two-way radios we used to have on the forklifts before they upgraded to the new digital system. Those old radios had terrible static. You'd be trying to hear if you needed to pull a pallet from aisle four, and all you'd get is this awful crackling noise. My buddy Phil, the one I told you about, he used to tape a piece of wire to the antenna thinking it would boost the signal. Didn't do a damn thing, of course. Phil was always coming up with these crazy fixes. He tried to fix a leaky radiator in his Chevy with an egg once. Read it in some magazine. The car smelled like sulfur for a month, and it still leaked. He ended up having to sell it for scrap. It was a shame, too, it was a classic, a '72 Chevelle. They don't make cars like that anymore. Heavy steel, you felt safe in them. Now everything is plastic and crumples if you look at it wrong. I saw a fender bender at the grocery store parking lot last week, and the whole front bumper just popped off like a Lego piece... but yeah, the voices. They just keep calling my number and saying security is coming. Even when I'm alone.

Yeah, I... I guess I have. It's just... I used to love fishing. Used to go down to the lake every Sunday morning, early, before the sun was even fully up. Choir practice, too, on Wednesday nights. And I'd spend hours out in the garage tinkering with wood, making little birdhouses or fixing up old chairs. It used to really settle me, you know? Keep my hands busy. But now... I can walk right out there, look right at my fishing rods or my tools, and I just feel... nothing. No pull to touch them at all. It's like looking at someone else's stuff. I bought this beautiful piece of cherry wood a few months ago, thinking I'd make a new coffee table. Cherry is a real nice wood to work with, but you have to be careful when you stain it because it can get blotchy if you don't condition it first. My uncle Arthur, he was a master carpenter. Built his whole house from the ground up, just him and his two boys. They used oak for the floors, solid oak. That house is still standing today, solid as a rock. Arthur was a tough guy, fought in Korea. He brought back this old brass lighter from the war, used to let me play with it when I was a kid. You had to strike it just right or it wouldn't catch. They don't make things with that kind of quality anymore. Everything is disposable now. You buy a toaster, it breaks in a year, and you just throw it away instead of fixing it. It's a real shame, the amount of waste we produce. Landfills just filling up with cheap plastic junk... but anyway, no, I just don't care about the fishing or the woodworking anymore. I just sit there.

No, no, they don't say that. Nothing about dying or... or being punished. Just that I'm dangerous and security is coming to get me. Getting in trouble at the warehouse was a big deal, though, if you actually messed up. We had this safety inspector, an OSHA guy, who used to come around twice a year. You could always tell he didn't actually work on the floor because his hard hat was spotless. Not a single scuff on it. He always carried this heavy aluminum clipboard, clicking his pen. I actually had a clipboard just like that for a while. Used it to keep track of the scores for my bowling league. We bowled every Thursday night over at Pinewood Lanes. Man, that place had a very specific smell... a mix of stale beer, floor wax, and that spray they put in the rental shoes. But they had the absolute best french fries. Crinkle cut. You really don't see crinkle cut fries much anymore, do you? Everywhere you go now it's those seasoned curly fries, or the shoestring ones that get cold in two minutes. Fast food just isn't the same. The portions are smaller, and they charge you an arm and a leg just for a combo meal. I went to a burger joint down the street last month and it was almost fifteen bucks just for myself. Used to be you could get a whole meal for a five-dollar bill and still have change for the jukebox... but, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, the voices. No, they never say I should die or anything like that. Just the dispatch calling my number.

Well, yeah, it did. After that whole incident with the forklift, they actually took me off operating duties completely. Put me on leave. They said I just wasn't safe around the equipment anymore. Which is crazy, because I've driven those things for thirty years. Thirty years! You get to know a machine after that long. You know the exact sound the hydraulics make when they need fluid. It's this high-pitched whine, almost like a mosquito right in your ear. My neighbor's kid, little Tommy, he got this electric scooter for Christmas, and it makes that exact same whining noise. Zips up and down the sidewalk all afternoon. I don't know how his parents stand it. Kids these days, they don't play outside like we used to, though, right? Unless it's got a motor or a screen. We used to play kick the can until the streetlights came on. You had to be fast, too, because old Mrs. Higgins down the block would call the cops if you stepped on her prize-winning petunias. She was serious about those flowers. Won a ribbon at the county fair three years running. The fair used to be such a big deal. They had this funnel cake stand that made them fresh, piping hot, covered in powdered sugar. You'd get sugar all down your shirt, but it was worth it. Now the fair is just overpriced rides that look like they're going to fall apart... but yeah, I'm on leave now. And even at home, I just can't keep up. My wife has had to take over paying all the bills, keeping track of my appointments, even most of the chores around the house. I just... I can't seem to manage it reliably anymore.

Yeah, my wife... she actually brought that up just the other day. She says my face has gone flat, like a board. Says I hardly answer her when she talks to me. Most days I just sit at the kitchen table, just staring at my coffee instead of starting anything that needs doing. It's funny, I used to drink my coffee black, just straight black. But then a few years ago, my stomach started acting up, giving me this awful heartburn. The doctor told me to cut back on the acid, so I started putting a little splash of whole milk in it. Not cream, cream is too heavy. Just milk. We used to get milk delivered to the house when I was a boy. The milkman, Mr. Peterson, he drove this white truck with a picture of a cow on the side. He'd leave the glass bottles right on the porch in a little metal wire carrier. You had to bring the empty bottles back out the next morning so he could take them back to the dairy to be washed and reused. It made a lot of sense, really. Good for the environment, not like all these plastic jugs we use now that just end up floating in the ocean somewhere. I saw a documentary on TV about the ocean, about how there's this giant patch of garbage just swirling around out there in the Pacific. It's the size of Texas, they said. Can you imagine that? Just miles and miles of plastic bags and soda rings and old fishing nets. It makes you wonder what kind of world we're leaving for the next generation. My grandson, he's only four, and he loves those little juice boxes, you know the ones with the tiny straws wrapped in plastic? We buy them by the case. It's convenient, sure, but... what was I saying? Oh, right, my wife. Yeah, she says I just look blank now. And I just sit there with my coffee.

Dangerous? I... I don't know if I'd say dangerous, but I know I'm a burden. I just sit there and I keep going over every single mistake I ever made at that warehouse, and all the ones at home, too. Like this one time, I clipped a pallet of canned peaches with the forks. Dented about forty cans. They had to sell them at a discount down at the surplus store. My wife loves that surplus store. She actually used to make this incredible peach cobbler on Sundays. Real thick crust, you know? You have to use ice-cold butter for a good pie crust. If the butter gets too warm, the pastry gets tough. My mother taught her that trick. My mother was a baker, actually. Worked at this little bakery on 4th Street that made the absolute best sourdough bread. People would line up around the block on Saturday mornings just to get a warm loaf. There was this one guy, wore a yellow raincoat no matter the weather, always bought three loaves and a dozen oatmeal cookies. Oatmeal raisin, not chocolate chip. I never understood that. Chocolate chip is clearly superior, especially if they're soft-baked. The crunchy ones just crumble all over your shirt and make a mess on the couch... but, anyway, I just feel like my family would have been so much better off if I hadn't let everyone down. I just ruined everything for them.

Yeah, they do. I mean, when I was at my absolute lowest... I was barely eating a thing, I stopped going to choir practice entirely, and I just felt like I had failed everybody. And those messages from the scanners and the dispatch voices, they were happening right along with all of that, just piling on. 

I did miss choir, though. I sing baritone. We were practicing for the spring service, and our director, Martha, she had just ordered us these brand new robes. Burgundy with gold sashes. They looked real sharp, but I'll tell you, they were made of this heavy polyester. You start sweating the second you zip it up, especially since the church's air conditioning has been on the fritz since last summer. The building committee keeps dragging their feet on hiring a repair guy. They have to have a meeting just to schedule another meeting, you know? My buddy Phil is on the committee, and he says half the time they just argue about who's bringing the donuts. I always tell him to get apple fritters. None of that custard-filled nonsense. Custard goes bad so fast if you leave it sitting out in a warm room. You have to be real careful with dairy, it'll give you awful food poisoning if you aren't paying attention... 

But, uh... what was I saying? Oh. Yeah, the voices and the scanner messages were definitely happening right at the same time I was feeling so down on myself.

Well, yeah... there was a stretch, I guess. My mood had eased up some, you know? I was actually eating decent meals again, talking a little more to my wife instead of just staring at the table. We even had chicken parmesan one night. She makes a really good chicken parmesan, pounds the cutlets real thin so they get crispy on the edges. You have to use the seasoned breadcrumbs, though, not the plain ones, or it just tastes like cardboard. And lots of mozzarella. We usually get the block of cheese and shred it ourselves. Those pre-shredded bags have some kind of powder on them to keep the cheese from clumping together, and it just doesn't melt right. It gets all greasy and separates. I saw a video online about how they make that anti-caking powder out of wood pulp. Cellulose, they call it. Can you believe they put wood in our food? It's just like those fast-food places using pink slime in the burgers. You really have to read the labels on everything these days, or you don't know what you're putting in your body. My neighbor, Gary, he started growing all his own vegetables in the backyard because he doesn't trust the grocery stores anymore. He's got these huge tomato plants, must be six feet tall, tied up to wooden stakes. He uses this special organic fertilizer that smells absolutely awful when it rains, just like... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, the voices. Right. Yeah, even when I was feeling a bit better and eating the chicken parmesan, for several weeks I still heard dispatch calling my number. I still believed that routing system was tracking me, even when the depression wasn't so heavy.

No, no doctor has ever said anything like that to me. No Parkinson's or dementia or anything. I mean, my memory isn't what it used to be, but whose is at sixty-two? I misplace my keys sometimes, but that's just because my wife bought this new bowl for the entryway table. It's this ugly ceramic thing, painted bright orange with little green frogs on it. She got it at a craft fair down at the community center. They have those fairs every spring, right around the time the cherry blossoms bloom. The cherry trees down by the river are really something else. People come from all over just to take pictures with them. They have this whole festival with food trucks and live music. Last year, they had a bluegrass band that was actually pretty good. The banjo player was missing half his index finger, but you wouldn't know it from how fast he was picking. He said he lost it in a table saw accident when he was building a deck for his brother-in-law. You've got to be so careful with power tools. Always use the safety guard. My uncle didn't use the guard on his circular saw and it kicked back on him, took a chunk right out of his thigh. He had to get thirty stitches. The scar looked like a giant centipede... 

But, uh, anyway, no, my brain is fine, far as any doctor has ever told me. No nerve illnesses or anything like that.

Yeah, it's been every day for... gosh, way more than a month now. Even when I'm just sitting out in my garage, you know? I'll have the door down, everything shut off, dead quiet, and I still hear those dispatch voices clear as day. They'll call out my operator number and say I'm dangerous, or that security is on their way to come get me. It's real loud, too. 

I spend a lot of time in that garage. I've got a whole setup in there. Workbench, pegboard for all my tools. I spent a whole weekend last fall just organizing my sockets. You know how it is, you always lose the 10-millimeter one. I swear there's a black hole somewhere that just swallows up 10-millimeter sockets and guitar picks. I don't even play guitar, but I found three picks under the passenger seat of my truck when I was vacuuming it out last week. I take it down to that car wash on Elm Street, the one with the free vacuums. They say they're free, but the suction is terrible. You're better off just using a Shop-Vac at home. I bought a really nice Shop-Vac at a yard sale a few years back. Five bucks. The guy selling it was moving to Florida. Everybody moves to Florida eventually, it seems like. My sister went down to Tampa two years ago. She says the humidity is awful, makes her hair frizz up like a poodle. She sent me a picture of this alligator that was just sunning itself on her front lawn. Can you imagine? You walk out to get the morning paper and there's a dinosaur sitting in your grass. You'd have to call animal control, but I bet down there they get so many calls they don't even hurry. They probably just tell you to wait for it to leave. 

But, uh... what was the question? Oh, the voices. Yeah, every single day for months, telling me security is coming for me, even when I'm just sitting in the quiet garage.

Well, yeah, my wife mentions that a lot. She says my face has gone completely flat, like I'm wearing a mask or something. And I hardly answer her when she talks to me. Most days I just sit at the kitchen table, staring into my coffee mug instead of starting any of the projects that need doing around the house. 

I drink a lot of coffee, though. Usually that French roast, the dark one. We used to get the breakfast blend, but it just tastes like hot water to me now. You really need a good, strong cup to wake up, you know? I use a French press. It makes a huge difference compared to those drip machines. The oils from the beans stay in the coffee instead of getting trapped in a paper filter. You have to make sure the water isn't boiling, though, or it burns the grounds and gets all bitter. I learned that from this barista at a little cafe downtown. We went there for our anniversary a couple of years ago. They had these incredible almond croissants. Flaky, with powdered sugar all over the top. I ended up getting powdered sugar all down the front of my good navy blazer. It's a real pain to get out, too. You can't just brush it off, it smears. I had to take it to the dry cleaner on 4th Street. The guy who runs it, Mr. Kim, he's been there forever. He always has these butterscotch candies in a little glass dish on the counter. The ones with the yellow wrappers that look like gold cellophane. My grandfather used to carry those in his pocket. They'd always get covered in lint, but we ate them anyway...

But, um, what were you asking? Oh, right. The withdrawn thing. Yeah, I just sit there staring at the coffee, not doing much of anything, and my wife says I don't show any expression anymore.

Well, yeah, there was a time... I guess it was a few months back. My mood had actually eased up a bit, you know? I wasn't feeling so down in the dumps, and I was eating a little more, talking a bit more with my wife. We even went out to dinner once, to this little Italian place over on Main Street. Luigi's, I think it's called. They have this garlic bread that is just out of this world. They bake it with real butter, not that cheap margarine stuff, and they load it up with parmesan cheese. You can smell it before they even bring it to the table. The waiter we had, he was a young kid, maybe early twenties, going to the community college. He said he was studying criminal justice, wanted to be a state trooper. I told him he'd better get used to drinking bad coffee on the night shift. My buddy Dave was a cop for thirty years, and he always complained about the coffee at the station. He said it tasted like battery acid. Dave actually retired down to Arizona a few years ago. He bought this RV, one of those huge Class A motorhomes, and he just drives around the desert. He sends me pictures sometimes. The sunsets out there are incredible, all purple and orange. But I don't think I could handle the heat. I mean, dry heat or not, 110 degrees is just too hot. You can't even go outside without feeling like you're in an oven. I prefer having four seasons, even if the winters get a little rough. Last winter we had that ice storm that knocked out the power for three days. We had to huddle around the fireplace...

But, uh, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the voices. Yeah, so even during that stretch when my mood was better and I was eating and talking more, for several weeks I was still hearing the dispatch calling my number. Clear as a bell. And I still knew the routing system was tracking me, even when I wasn't feeling depressed.

Hi. Well, I guess I'm here because the clinic doctor got on me about my eating. I mean, most days I just keep it simple. I usually just have coffee in the morning, maybe a few bites of something between painting jobs, and... a small dinner, if I'm not too busy with my class paperwork. It's just my normal routine, but they wanted me to come talk to you.

Yeah, I suppose I am. It's just... if I eat something heavy, like pizza or a big sandwich, I get this really panicky feeling. I start worrying that I'll wake up bigger and slower. My work is physical, so I have to be up and down ladders and moving around rooms all day. I just get scared that if I put on weight, I won't be able to move around the way I need to for my job.

Um, no, I wouldn't say I feel overweight. When I look in the mirror, I just... I see my normal body. I don't think I'm too big right now, I just want to make sure it stays that way. I guess I just check to make sure I haven't gained anything so I can keep working the way I do.

Yeah, the doctor at the clinic did tell me it was below what's healthy. I mean, my work pants hang pretty loose on me now, and... well, people on the job sites keep saying I look too thin. But honestly, I don't really see it that way. I see it more like I've just leaned out from staying on my feet all day for work.

No, not really. I mean... I don't think my weight is some kind of emergency, even though everyone keeps acting like it is. To me, it just feels like they're making a really big deal out of me being disciplined and staying busy with my work. I just don't see it as a problem.

Yeah, I am. If I eat something heavy, like pizza or a big sandwich, I just... I get this panicky feeling. I start worrying that I'll wake up bigger and slower. I have to be able to move around ladders and rooms the way I need to for my jobs, so... yeah, I definitely eat less on purpose to make sure I don't gain weight and lose my edge.

Well, I suppose I'm here because things got a little out of hand lately. I took on the historical society project, and I just felt like I could run the entire fundraiser myself, honestly. I started drawing up all these new quilt designs for it. Which reminds me, my grandmother used to make the most beautiful quilts. She had one of those old cast-iron pedal sewing machines. I actually saw one exactly like it at the antique mall last Tuesday when I was in there looking for a brass teapot. They wanted way too much for it, though. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, the fundraiser. Right. So I was calling all the volunteers and making these incredibly detailed schedules, just promising all these deadlines I couldn't possibly meet. And getting people to commit on the phone is just impossible these days. I called Susan to help, and she just went on and on about her daughter's wedding in Ohio. Can you imagine having a February wedding in Ohio? The snow must be an absolute nightmare for the guests driving in. But yes, the historical society... I guess I just bit off more than I could chew.

Well, yes, for a while there I was hardly sleeping at all. Maybe two or three hours a night? And I'd pop right out of bed, completely ready to start sewing or making my phone calls. I actually called my sister Martha at 4:30 in the morning once because I had this brilliant idea for the quilt backing. She was furious, of course. Martha has always been so particular about her sleep, especially since she bought one of those fancy memory foam mattresses. You know, I read that those things off-gas terrible chemicals. I saw an article about it in a magazine at the dentist's office. Dr. Evans, he just retired last month, which is a real shame because he was so gentle with the novocaine... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, my sleep. Yes, I had all that energy then. But lately it's completely different. Now I either just lie awake in the dark worrying about every little thing, or I end up sleeping way too late and I still feel completely worn out when I finally drag myself up.

No, no, nothing like that. I've always had a very vivid imagination, but I wasn't seeing things that weren't there. Although, speaking of seeing things, the other day I was looking out my kitchen window and I saw the strangest bird at my feeder. It had this bright blue patch on its wing, and I've been trying to figure out what it was. I have this wonderful old bird-watching book that belonged to my uncle Arthur. He was an avid bird watcher, you know. He used to take me out to the state park when I was a little girl with his big heavy binoculars. They had leather straps that smelled just like saddle soap. I love the smell of saddle soap, it reminds me of the tack room at the stable where my daughter used to take riding lessons... 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, seeing things. No, I wasn't hallucinating or anything like that. Just regular things, like that bird.

Hospitalized? Oh heavens, no. I've never had to go to the hospital for anything like that. I mean, the last time I was in a hospital was when my husband had his gallbladder out a few years back. That was over at Mercy General, and let me tell you, the cafeteria food there is just abysmal. They gave him this green Jell-O that looked like it had been sitting out since the Reagan administration. I actually tried to bring him some homemade chicken soup in a thermos to make up for it. 

It was my mother's recipe—she always swore by adding a little parsnip to the broth. Parsnips give it this wonderful earthy sweetness, you know? You can't really find good parsnips at the regular grocery store anymore, though. You have to go to the farmer's market on Saturday mornings, and parking down there is just an absolute nightmare ever since they started letting that local bluegrass band set up right next to the tomato stands. I love music, but the banjo is just so loud when you're trying to count your change... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, the hospital. Right. No, I wasn't in the hospital during all that fundraiser business. I was just at home, running myself ragged.

Well, yes, I suppose it did cause some problems. I mean, my husband has had to take over all the household routines lately. And he's had to deal with the historical society for me because I just completely stopped keeping my commitments there. I couldn't even face the people waiting on me. Which is a shame, really, because we were right in the middle of planning the annual bake sale. 

I usually make my famous lemon pound cake for it. It's an old recipe, uses real butter and a whole cup of sour cream. The sour cream is the secret, it makes it so moist. I buy my sour cream from that little dairy farm out on Route 9. The couple who runs it, the Millers, they've been there for forty years. Mrs. Miller has the most beautiful garden, just overflowing with hydrangeas. I tried to grow hydrangeas once, but the soil here is too alkaline, so they always turned out pink instead of that lovely deep blue. I read somewhere that you can put coffee grounds in the soil to change the acidity. My husband drinks so much coffee, I don't know how he sleeps. He likes that dark French roast, the kind that smells almost burnt...

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, right, problems. Yes, I just couldn't face anyone, so he had to step in and handle everything with the house and the society.

A week? Oh, goodness, it was much longer than a week. That whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months before everything finally fell apart. 

Five whole months. It started right around the time I was putting in my spring bulbs. I always plant the King Alfred daffodils, you know, the ones with the really big, bright yellow trumpets? I order them from this wonderful catalog that comes all the way from Holland. Though, getting packages delivered here has been such a headache lately. Our regular mail carrier retired—Bill was his name, such a sweet man, always had a milk bone in his pocket for the neighborhood dogs—and the new fellow just can't seem to read the house numbers right. 

Just last Tuesday he left my neighbor's electric bill in my box. I had to walk it over to Mrs. Gable, and she kept me on her porch for nearly an hour talking about her grandson's new braces. Those metal wires look so terribly painful, don't they? I remember when my daughter had braces, she could only eat mashed potatoes for days after getting them tightened. I used to make them from scratch with a little bit of roasted garlic and cream cheese. The cream cheese makes them so fluffy... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what were you asking me? Oh, the time. Yes, it wasn't a week. It was about five months of running on that high energy before the bottom just dropped out.

Activity? Oh, my, yes. I was constantly moving. I had so much energy I couldn't even sit through a single television show with my husband. We usually watch those British murder mysteries together on PBS, you know the ones? The scenery is always so lovely, all those thatched-roof cottages and rolling green hills. One second I'm looking at the line of cars, trying to gauge if I need to flip my paddle to "Stop" so the paving crew can move the roller across the lane, and the next second... it's just gone. The thought is gone. But my stomach feels completely normal. Well, as normal as it can feel when I'm dealing with all of this. But I don't get any kind of physical warning sign like that, no sudden dropping or rising feeling in my belly. I really wish I did get some kind of physical warning, honestly. If my stomach did a flip right before my brain shut off, at least I could maybe step back onto the grass shoulder or warn the foreman that I was about to check out. But no, it just happens, with no warning from my stomach at all.

Unable to move? Like, completely paralyzed? I... I really don't know for sure, because like I said, it's just a total void for me. I don't remember being in my body during those moments. 

But, well, if I had to guess based on what happens when I come out of it, I don't think I'm frozen stiff or anything. Because usually when the fog lifts and I snap back, I'm still standing right there on the asphalt. I haven't collapsed, I haven't dropped my stop-slow paddle. My hands are still gripping the pole, my feet are still planted on the ground, usually right on the white line where I was standing before. So I must be maintaining some kind of muscle tone or posture, right? I'm not just crumpling into a heap. 

And nobody on the crew has ever come running up to me screaming, asking why I'm standing there like a statue. The foreman, Dave, he's a good guy, but he's got a short temper when we're trying to lay down hot mix before a storm rolls in. If I was just standing there completely rigid, totally unable to move a muscle while cars were backing up, he would definitely be yelling on the radio, "Hey, what's wrong with you, move your arms!" But he doesn't. 

So maybe I'm still doing the basic motions? Maybe I'm still slowly turning the sign or shifting my weight? I honestly have no idea. It's so frustrating not knowing what my own body is doing. It's like my brain just unplugs, but my body is just left there on autopilot, or maybe just standing still enough that nobody notices I'm completely checked out. I wish I could give you a better answer, I really do. It's just so terrifying to think about what I might be doing—or not doing—when I'm supposed to be protecting the crew and I have absolutely no memory of it. But as far as being completely, totally unable to move? I really don't think that's what's happening, even though I can't say for absolute certain.

In bed? No, no, they don't happen then. When I'm falling asleep or waking up, my mind is usually just racing with all the normal anxieties, you know? Did I set my alarm, what's the weather going to be like for the shift tomorrow, that sort of thing. The blank spells... they don't happen when I'm relaxed or just lying there. 

They happen when I'm right in the middle of things. That's actually why I finally came in to see someone. It's not just a momentary lapse when I'm dozing off; it's happening at the absolute worst possible times. I'll be out there on the job, and I'll look down at the road-closure forms I need to fill out, or I'll be holding the stop-slow paddle, and suddenly... my mind just completely empties out. 

It's terrifying, honestly. I've been doing this job for years. I know the procedures backwards and forwards. I know exactly how to set up the cone taper, I know the distance we need for the advance warning signs based on the speed limit. It's second nature to me. But then, right in the middle of a shift, with cars lining up and the paving crew waiting on my signal, I'll look at the paddle in my hand and I just... I cannot remember the steps. I can't remember what I'm supposed to do next. It's like someone just took an eraser to my brain for a few minutes. I'm standing there, supposed to be directing traffic and keeping everyone safe, and my mind is just a total, terrifying blank. So, no, it's not in bed. It's right out there in the middle of the road when I need my brain the most.

Déjà vu? Like feeling like I've been somewhere before or lived a moment already? No, I don't... I don't think I get that at all. It's really hard to explain, but the moments right before the blankness hits, it's not like a movie playing in my head or some weird feeling of repeating history. It's just... it's just this heavy, dark feeling. 

I mean, I stand on the same stretches of highway for hours, days, sometimes weeks at a time when we're doing a big milling and paving project. So, in a way, everything looks exactly the same every single day. The same orange barrels, the same flashing arrow boards, the same angry drivers glaring at me through their windshields because I'm making them five minutes late. You'd think I'd have déjà vu all the time just because the job is so incredibly repetitive. You stand there, you flip the sign to "Stop," you wait for the pilot car to come back around, you flip it to "Slow." Over and over and over. 

But right before my brain just shuts off? No, there's no sudden mystical feeling of "Oh, I've lived this exact second before." It's more just... a total collapse of everything. The sadness just kind of pools up in me, this horrible, heavy emptiness, and then the fog rolls in and wipes the slate clean. It's not a memory playing tricks on me. It's just my mind giving up. I wish it was something as simple as déjà vu, honestly. People talk about déjà vu like it's this quirky, interesting little glitch in the matrix, you know? Like, "Oh wow, how weird, I feel like I've had this conversation before." But what happens to me isn't quirky. It's devastating. It's like I cease to exist for a few minutes, right there on the hot asphalt, with cars whizzing past me. So, no, no déjà vu. Just the dread, and then the blankness.

Well, occupational health sent me here. They're saying I'm not eating enough. But honestly, most days I just have black coffee, maybe a plain yogurt, or just a few bites of chicken at night. Eating a full meal just... it feels like I'm letting my standards slip, you know?

Yeah, I am. If I step on the scale and it's up even half a pound, I get this... this jolt, like I've completely lost control. When that happens, I'll spend the rest of the day cutting back even harder. I just really can't stand the idea of putting weight back on.

Yeah, I do. When I look in the mirror, I just... I don't see what everyone else says they see. They might tell me I'm too thin, but I immediately focus on my stomach and my waist. Honestly, I judge my entire day by what I see right there. If I don't look lean enough, it's hard to even respect myself.

Yeah, they told me that at the clinic. I know my uniform hangs off me now, and I've had to tighten my belt past the old notches just to keep it up. But honestly, even when the nurse told me my weight was dangerously low, I just... I still thought to myself, I could stand to be a little sharper.

I hope I'm giving you the right kind of information. Does that answer what you were asking?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Basically, what brings me in is that I feel like I’m just constantly running on a motor lately. No, I wouldn't say I'm much of a worrier. I mean, sure, my job can be stressful sometimes—teaching special ed definitely has its moments—but I don't find myself getting anxious or worrying when there isn't a clear reason for it. So, no, that's not really an issue for me.

Yes, absolutely. My mother actually used to joke that even back in elementary school, I basically taught the class from my seat. Um... well. I guess I just haven't been doing much lately. The things that usually make me feel like myself... like my photography walks, or mentoring the kids... even just keeping a clean calendar. I guess my mom made me come. I mostly just... I can't really make myself do anything anymore. I just sit in my room. I think I've had these same clothes on for a few days, I don't even know. I used to knit a lot, actually. I made this really long scarf once, it was like, mustard yellow, and I wore it all the time until I left it on the bus. The bus driver was this guy who always wore a Mets hat, and he told me he'd look for it, but he never found it. I liked taking the bus, looking out the window, but I don't go walking or anything like I used to either. I don't even journal anymore. And when my mom asks what's wrong, I just... I barely have the energy to even answer her. It's like, what's the point of talking, you know? My throat just feels tired.

Voices? Um... no, not really. I mean, sometimes I hear people talking, but it's just the TV from downstairs. My mom watches a lot of game shows. The one with the big wheel, you know? I used to watch it with her, but I always thought the wheel was rigged. Like it always stops on bankrupt right when the person really needs the money. I won ten dollars on a scratch-off ticket once, though. I bought it at the corner store when I was getting... they have those little powdered donuts there. The ones in the crinkly bags. I haven't had one of those in forever. I don't really go out to the store anymore, so...

Another time? Um... no, I don't think so. I mean, in high school I went to classes and did stuff. I wasn't like this. I took this biology class and we had to dissect a frog once. The smell was... it was really bad, that chemical smell. It just gets stuck in your hair and your clothes for the rest of the day. My lab partner, Chloe, she always chewed this really strong wintergreen gum to block it out. She gave me a piece once, but it just made my eyes water. I don't really like mint anyway. It tastes too cold, you know? I prefer fruit flavors, like those watermelon ones that come in the little plastic squares. But they always lose their flavor in like, five minutes, and then you're just chewing on nothing. It just turns into rubber. So I just stopped buying gum altogether.

Harm me? I mean... they're trying to ruin things for me, if that counts. Since I was taking those college classes, I've just known that the school portal and the clinic practicum people are doing it. They use these little wording changes in all their emails and in the assignment comments just to mark me as someone they don't want in healthcare. My mom says they're just regular messages, but she doesn't get it. She doesn't even know how to log into the portal anyway. She always forgets her passwords. She has this little green notebook where she writes them all down, but she can never read her own handwriting. Her handwriting is really loopy, like cursive, but messy. We had to learn cursive in the third grade. Our teacher was Mrs. Gable, and she smelled like baby powder all the time. She had this huge collection of ceramic owls on her desk. One time, a kid named Tommy knocked one over and it shattered into a million pieces. It was a brown one with big yellow eyes. I liked owls for a while after that, but then I watched a video about how they swallow mice whole and throw up the bones. It's called a pellet. We dissected those in science class, too, actually. Kind of like the frog. But they don't smell as bad as the frogs did. They're just dry and dusty.

High or full of energy? Um... no, not really. I don't think so. Sometimes I'll drink an energy drink if I'm feeling really draggy, though. The ones in the tall cans with the textured grip on them. There's this pink one that tastes exactly like cotton candy. I used to get them at the gas station right down the street from my old high school. The guy who worked behind the counter there always wore these really weird bucket hats. Like, neon green or bright orange, indoors. He told me once it was because the fluorescent lights in the store gave him headaches. My mom gets headaches sometimes, well, migraines really. She just lies in her bedroom with the curtains drawn and puts a cold washcloth over her eyes. We have these blue washcloths, but they're getting all frayed at the edges. The threads just pull right out if you catch them on a fingernail. I actually need to cut my nails, they're getting kind of long and they keep tapping on my phone screen when I type. It makes this annoying little clicking sound. But um... yeah, no, I don't really get super energetic or anything like that.

Even when I wasn't depressed? Um... I don't really know. I don't think I keep track of it like that. They just do it whenever they want, because the portal is always up. You just log in and it's this really bright blue screen. It's actually the exact same shade of blue as my old winter coat. The puffy one I had in middle school. It had this fake fur around the hood, but the fur got all matted and weird when I left it out in the rain one time. My mom tried to brush it out with a dog brush, but it just pulled all the little hairs out and left these ugly bald patches on the hood. We didn't even have a dog, so I don't know why we had the brush. We had a hamster named Barnaby, but he escaped his cage and chewed a hole straight through the drywall in the laundry room. My dad was so mad because he had to patch it, and he hates doing house projects. He always gets that white spackle stuff all over his jeans, and it never washes out in the machine. It just leaves these chalky white streaks. But um... what did you ask? About the school people? Yeah, I'm not really sure about the timing of it all.

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? About the timing and the depression stuff? I really don't keep a calendar of it or anything. It's just... the portal is always there. It doesn't care how I'm feeling. It's just a website. Websites don't have feelings, you know? They just sit there on servers. I saw a documentary once about these massive server farms out in the desert. Just rows and rows of blinking lights in these huge, freezing cold warehouses. They have to keep them super cold so the computers don't overheat. Kind of like how grocery stores keep the meat aisle freezing. I always have to wear a sweater when my mom makes me go to the store with her, even in the middle of summer. Summer here is just so humid anyway. The air gets all thick, like you're breathing soup. My hair always frizzes up when it's humid. It gets this halo of little flyaways that just won't lay flat, no matter how much of that smoothing serum I use. The serum comes in this little glass bottle with a pump, but the pump always gets clogged halfway through. Then you have to unscrew the top and bang it on your hand to get anything out, and it makes a huge mess. It smells like coconuts, though, which is nice. I used to love coconut water, but then I got a bad batch once that tasted metallic, like pennies. So I stopped drinking it. But yeah... I don't know what else to tell you about the school people. I just don't really track it like that.

Why do you keep asking me the same thing over and over? I just told you I don't track it. Two weeks, three weeks, I don't know. I don't mark things down on a calendar. My grandma has this giant calendar in her kitchen, though, with pictures of lighthouses on it. Every single month is a different lighthouse. I don't really get the point of lighthouses anymore, honestly, because don't boats just have GPS now? My dad has a GPS on his dashboard, but it has this really bossy British lady's voice. She always tells him to make a U-turn whenever we pull into the drive-thru at Wendy's. I always get the spicy chicken nuggets there, but you have to specifically ask for fresh ones, or they give you the ones that have been sitting under the heat lamp for hours. They get all rubbery when they sit out. Kind of like pencil erasers. I used to chew on my pencil erasers in math class until the little metal part got totally flattened out and sharp. It tasted like metal and dust. I had this math teacher who always smelled like old coffee and peppermint, and he used to eat those little red and white mints right out of his pants pocket. They were always covered in pocket lint, which is super gross if you actually think about it. Pocket lint is basically just dead skin and fabric fibers. But um... yeah, no. I don't know if it was two weeks. I just don't know.

Um, no? I don't think people say that to me. I mean, I talk just fine. I actually had to take this public speaking class in high school, and I passed it. Mr. Henderson made us stand up at this big wooden podium that had a massive scratch down the front of it, like someone took a car key to it. We had to write our speeches on those little lined index cards, but I always hated them because they give you the absolute worst paper cuts. Paper cuts are so weird, right? Because they barely even bleed, but they sting so much worse than a normal cut. Especially if you get hand sanitizer in them. The hand sanitizer they put in the dispensers at my high school smelled exactly like cheap tequila. My friend Jessica told me that, anyway. She actually got suspended for drinking behind the bleachers during a pep rally. Pep rallies were always so loud, the marching band would play the snare drums so hard you could literally feel it vibrating in your teeth. It always gave me a headache right behind my eyes, kind of like when you eat ice cream too fast and get brain freeze. I love mint chocolate chip ice cream, but only if the chips are those really tiny flakes, not the big chunks. The big chunks get stuck in your molars. But um... wait, what did you ask me? If people say my speech is hard to follow? No, I don't think anyone has ever told me that.

Punished? No, I don't think I've done anything that bad to deserve punishment. I mean, my mom used to ground me when I was little, like if I stayed out past the streetlights coming on. Our streetlights were those weird orange ones that buzzed really loud when it rained. It sounded like a giant angry bee trapped in a jar. I caught a bee in a jar once when I was seven, but I poked holes in the lid so it could breathe. You have to use a nail and a hammer to poke the holes, but you have to be careful not to bend the lid or it won't screw back on right. My dad had this huge toolbox in the garage that smelled like oil and sawdust. He was always building birdhouses, but the birds never actually lived in them. They just built their nests in the gutters instead, which was super annoying because then the gutters would overflow every time it stormed, and the water would wash out all the mulch in the front flowerbeds. Mulch always smells like wet dirt and vinegar to me, I don't know why people put it everywhere. But um... no, I don't think I deserve to be punished. I haven't done anything wrong.

I don't really know when the depression started versus the portal stuff. It all just kind of blends together, you know? Like when you mix too many paint colors together and it just turns into that ugly muddy brown color. We had to do that in art class in tenth grade. Mrs. Gable made us paint these still-life bowls of fruit, but the fruit was totally fake. It was made of that hollow plastic, and someone had actually bitten into the plastic apple and left deep teeth marks in it. I don't know why anyone would bite a fake apple, it probably tasted like chemicals and dust. Dust always collects on the edges of the ceiling fan in my bedroom. I try to wipe it off with an old pillowcase, but then the dust just falls all over my bed and I have to wash the sheets anyway. I hate doing laundry because the dryer in our building takes like three full cycles to actually dry anything, and you have to use quarters. Quarters get so heavy if you have a lot of them in your pocket. My grandpa used to collect those quarters with the different states on the back, and he had this big cardboard map where you pop them into the little slots. He was missing Rhode Island for the longest time. Rhode Island isn't even an island, which is basically false advertising if you think about it. It's just a regular state. But um... wait, what were you asking? Before I was depressed? I don't know. I can't really remember the exact order of how it all happened.

Like I was just saying, I really can't remember the timeline. Time is just super blurry to me. Blurry like when you go to the eye doctor and they put those yellow drops in your eyes that make your pupils huge and sensitive to the light. I had to get that done when I was twelve because I couldn't read the whiteboard in math class. Math was the absolute worst, especially geometry. Who even cares about the hypotenuse of a triangle? Triangles are a really strong shape though, I think that's what they use to build bridges. There's this huge metal bridge near my aunt's house that's painted bright blue, but the paint is peeling off in these big long strips. It looks like a giant blue snake shedding its skin. Snakes are totally misunderstood, you know? Everyone thinks they're slimy, but they're actually really smooth and dry. My cousin had a pet corn snake named Noodle, but it escaped its glass tank and we found it three days later curled up inside a winter boot in the hall closet. Closets always smell kind of weird, like old shoes and mothballs. Mothballs are so toxic, they look exactly like little mints but you definitely shouldn't eat them. But yeah, um... I really don't know which came first. The portal people or feeling down. It's just all mixed up together.

Unusual beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, my beliefs are just normal. Normal is such a weird word though, right? Like, what even is normal? My mom always said it was a setting on the washing machine. We had this really old washing machine when we lived in our first apartment, it was this horrible avocado green color from the seventies. The seventies had the worst colors, everything was mustard yellow or brown or that weird green. My grandma still has a mustard yellow refrigerator in her basement. She keeps all her extra Diet Cokes in there. She drinks like six cans a day, which is probably terrible for her teeth. Teeth are so weird if you think about it, just these little bones sticking out of our gums. I had to get my wisdom teeth out last year and my face swelled up so big I looked like a chipmunk hoarding acorns. Chipmunks are pretty cute, but they dig holes all over the yard and ruin the grass. Grass is so annoying to take care of, you have to mow it constantly in the summer. The smell of fresh cut grass makes me sneeze really bad. I think I'm allergic to it, or maybe it's just the pollen. But um... no, I don't have any other beliefs like that. Just the portal stuff.

I don't think so, I mean, I really just can't remember a time like that. It's like I said before, my memory of it is all just... smushed together. Smushed like a peanut butter and jelly sandwich at the bottom of a backpack. I used to always carry my lunch in my backpack in middle school, and my mom would put the sandwich in a Ziploc bag, but by lunchtime it was completely flattened. Ziploc bags are actually really bad for the environment, all that single-use plastic just ends up in the ocean. The ocean is terrifying, honestly. It's so deep and dark, and there are all those weird fish with the glowing lights on their heads down at the very bottom. They look like aliens. I watched a documentary about them once on a Tuesday night when I couldn't sleep. Tuesday is the most boring day of the week, it's not the beginning and it's not the end, it's just stuck right there. But yeah, I don't remember there being a time when I wasn't feeling depressed but the portal people were still there. I just don't know.

I mean... I don't think my mood ever felt normal when the portal stuff was going on. But like I was saying before, normal is just really hard to pin down. Like, normal body temperature is 98.6, right? I remember learning that in health class. The school nurse's office had this giant plastic thermometer hanging on the wall, but it had red liquid painted inside, not the silver stuff. The silver stuff is mercury, and that's super poisonous if the glass breaks. Mercury is a planet, too. It's the closest one to the sun, so it must be literally burning up all the time. I get sunburned so easily, I have to wear SPF 50 even if I'm just sitting inside by a window. People don't realize windows still let the UV rays through. My mom actually bought these heavy blackout curtains because the sun was totally fading the living room rug. It's this big rug with a crazy complicated pattern, it almost looks like a maze. I used to try and trace the path to the center with my finger when I was little. But um... yeah, no, I don't remember ever feeling normal with the portal people. It was all just bad.

Sad? I mean, I guess. I'm not really sure if it's most of the day, every day... days kind of blur together, you know? Like when you look out the window of a car on the highway and all the trees just turn into this big green smear. I used to love road trips when I was little. We drove all the way to Florida once, and it took two whole days. My dad refused to stop for anything except gas. Gas stations always smell so strongly of coffee and those little rotating hot dogs. I don't understand how anyone can eat those, they look like they've been spinning there since the dawn of time. Time is such a weird concept anyway. I read somewhere that astronauts in space actually age slightly slower than people on Earth because of gravity or relativity or something. Anyway, I don't really know about feeling worthless. I just feel... not much of anything.
