And... well, I've also been turning down my neighbors and friends a lot more than usual lately when they ask for help or want to get together. It's just taking a bit too much out of me right now.

No, not really. I mean, it's definitely worse when I think of her, but... the sadness is just kind of there all the time. It doesn't really matter what I'm doing or if I'm thinking about her or not. It's just this constant heaviness.

Yes, I have. Food just... it doesn't really call to me much anymore. I'll usually just fix a little toast or maybe some soup, and then I'll realize by the evening that I've barely eaten anything all day. I'm definitely not trying to lose weight or anything like that, I just don't have much of a desire to eat right now.

Yes, I have. It's... well, I kind of just fall asleep in bits and pieces. And then I end up waking up way before dawn, with my mind already turning. Once I'm awake like that, I usually just can't get settled again before the day even starts.

Well, maybe not worthless exactly, but... I do feel a lot of guilt. I just keep going over those last few weeks with my sister. I keep telling myself that I should have called her more, or listened better... just done something more useful for her. Even though part of me logically knows I couldn't have changed what happened, I just can't shake the feeling that I should have done better by her.

No, I don't. I know I didn't cause it... her passing wasn't my fault. It's just, well, like I was saying, it's more about wishing I had been a better sister to her at the end. But no, I don't actually feel responsible for the fact that she died.
No, I don't think so. I mean, I have moments where I miss her terribly, of course, but I wouldn't say I feel sad or empty most of the day, every day. It comes and goes.
Like I mentioned just a moment ago, no, not really. I don't feel sad all day, every day. It just comes in waves when I miss her, but it isn't a constant thing.

No, I wouldn't say that. I think... well, losing a sister is just a hard thing to go through. My reaction feels pretty normal to me. I expected to grieve and to miss her, and that's exactly what's happening. So, no, it really hasn't been more intense than I would have thought.

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, I move around at my normal pace... well, normal for me, anyway. And my speaking hasn't changed at all. I'm pretty much exactly the same in that regard.

I mean, I miss her, certainly. But... I wouldn't really use the words longing or yearning, not constantly anyway. It's just the normal amount of missing someone after they pass away. I'm not consumed by it or anything like that.

Yes, actually, I have noticed that. I'll sit down to look at my budgeting spreadsheet, or try to read something for a workshop I'm taking, and... I'll just stare at it. I can reread the same paragraph three or four times and still not really take in what it says. It's just hard to focus.

No, not really. I still make myself show up for things, like my book club or the community dance night, but... lately I just sit there feeling like I'm behind a pane of glass. Even the things I used to really enjoy, like working in my garden or cooking for the neighbors, they just don't give me that little lift they used to. I just feel kind of flat, no matter what's going on.

Yes, I really have. It's... well, even doing simple errands takes it out of me lately. Or just trying to get my papers together for the Cultural Center, which shouldn't be hard at all, but it just leaves me feeling completely worn out. It honestly feels like my body is moving through thick mud most of the time.

Hi, it's nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what brings me in is this constant restless feeling I’ve been having. It’s like I’m wound just way too tight and I can’t fully settle down, even when I’m supposed to be doing something really calm. Like sitting through a planning meeting for work—I'm a retail buyer, so we have these endless seasonal planning meetings—or even when I'm just painting at home. 

Or yoga! I actually started taking this yoga class on Tuesday nights at that new studio downtown, the one next to the really good Italian bakery? They have the absolute best cannolis there, by the way. I usually grab one after class, which probably completely defeats the purpose of the yoga, but anyway, the instructor plays this really specific flute music that reminds me of a vendor trip I took to New Mexico a few years ago. Beautiful pottery out there, just stunning colors. But yeah, even during the quiet parts of class when everyone else is perfectly still on their mats, I just... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the restlessness. I just can't seem to sit calmly through any of it.

Not really for several days in a row, no. I'm just kind of always at this baseline level of fidgety, I guess. Well, unless I drink way too much espresso. My husband actually bought me one of those incredibly fancy espresso machines for my 50th birthday last year. You know, the ones with the built-in bean grinder and the milk frother? It's gorgeous, all stainless steel, but it takes up half the kitchen counter, honestly. We had to completely relocate the toaster oven just to fit it, and I use that toaster oven all the time for these little flatbread pizzas I like to make on Friday nights. Friday is usually our easy dinner night. We watched this really fascinating documentary last week while we were eating, all about the history of department stores—which is obviously right up my alley with the retail buying, seeing how they used to merchandise everything in the 1920s—and... wait, I'm sorry, what was the question? 

Oh! Right, being wired for days. No, nothing like that. Just my everyday normal amount of not being able to sit still.

Yeah, actually, I really did. I remember back in elementary school, my teachers were always sending notes home to my parents because I just could not stay in my seat. I was always popping up to go look at something or talk to someone. And I was terrible about talking over my classmates, or blurting out the answer before the teacher even finished asking the question. 

I was just always in a rush, you know? Like I had to get the words out right that second. My third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—oh my gosh, she wore these incredibly bright floral dresses every single day. Like, large-scale Hawaiian prints, but we lived in Ohio, so it was a very specific look, especially in the dead of winter. She actually gave me this little squishy ball to hold under my desk to try and keep my hands busy, which was nice of her, I guess. But then one day it rolled away and went all the way to the back of the room where the reading nook was. We had this amazing beanbag chair back there, bright orange corduroy. I loved that chair. I used to try to read Nancy Drew mysteries in it, but I usually just ended up staring at the dust motes in the sunlight... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being a kid. Yeah, I've pretty much always been like this.

Not really. I mean, I don't think I worry any more than the average person does. I definitely don't have that kind of constant anxiety or anything. I just get frustrated because I feel so restless. 

But worrying? No. I mean, sure, I worry about normal things, like whether a big shipment is going to clear customs in time for the spring floor set. We had this huge issue last year with a container of patio cushions that got stuck at the port in Long Beach for like three weeks. It was a total nightmare because the colors were specifically matched to this line of ceramic planters we'd already put out, and the planters were selling out fast. They were these gorgeous glazed pots, kind of a seafoam green with a crackle finish? Really heavy, though. The shipping costs on those alone were astronomical. I actually went to the factory in Vietnam where they make them, and it was fascinating to see the kilns. They had these huge wood-fired kilns, and the heat coming off them was just intense. We ate the most incredible pho from a street vendor right outside the factory gates... wait, sorry. What did you ask me? 

Oh, worrying. Right. No, I don't really sit around worrying about a bunch of different things. I'm usually moving too fast to stop and worry, to be honest.

Well, I'm here because... it's about driving. Specifically, driving over bridges. What finally made me come in is that the moment my car reaches one of those long bridges toward Miami, my chest just tightens up. My hands clamp down on the steering wheel, and I get this sudden, overwhelming certainty that I have to get off right away... even though there's nowhere to go once you're on it.
No, not really. If I'm just driving on regular roads or... running errands around town, I feel perfectly fine. It's really just the bridges. I don't get that feeling anywhere else.

I'm not really sure if it's the height, to be honest. I haven't really thought about it quite like that. It's more just... the bridge itself, I think. Just being out there and knowing I can't pull over or get off. So, no, I wouldn't say how high up I am is the main thing I'm focusing on.

I'm not entirely sure if that's it. I mean... I haven't really tried to pinpoint what the absolute scariest part is. It all just sort of hits me at once, and I just know I don't want to be there. So I really couldn't say for sure if feeling trapped is the main thing.
No, I don't think so. If it's just a regular road on the ground, I'm fine. It's really just the fact that it's a bridge that bothers me.

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's that either. I don't really think about what's underneath the bridge, whether it's water or a valley or whatever. It's just... being on the structure itself that gets to me. I don't really look down and worry about what's below.

No, I can't say that's it either. I know they're built well enough, so I don't sit there thinking the whole thing is going to break apart. And I'm usually just sitting inside a car, so I'm not worried about tumbling over the edge. It's just... well, it's just a terrible feeling of being on it, without any specific thought like that.

No, I don't think it makes a difference. Water or land... it's really all the same to me. Like I was saying a minute ago, I don't pay much attention to what's underneath. A bridge is a bridge, and just being on one is what causes that terrible feeling, no matter what it happens to be crossing over.

Well, like I just mentioned a moment ago, no, the water doesn't really have anything to do with it. It doesn't matter to me if there's a river down there or just dry land. It's purely the bridge itself that I can't handle.
No, I really don't. Being on a balcony or looking out a window from a high floor doesn't bother me at all. I don't have a general fear of heights. It's... it's just bridges. Only bridges.

Yes, I'm sure it would. Like I said, a bridge is a bridge. Whether I'm in a car or... well, walking across one on foot, the feeling is exactly the same. I just wouldn't do it. The fear is just as strong because I'm still on a bridge, and that's the part I can't handle.

Well, doctor... I came in because... well, it's about the domino table. I play down at the center, you know. Been going there since my brother passed back in '98. He was a real good player, my brother. Always held onto his double six too long, though. I tell the fellas now, you can't hold onto it like that, but they don't listen. 

But anyway, the men at the table... lately they've been giving me these little messages. Just little things meant for me. And it's not just them, sometimes the radio announcer does it too. I always listen to the AM station in the mornings while I have my coffee. Used to be a fellow on there who talked about the weather, sounded just like my Uncle Joe. Joe had a farm out east, grew the biggest tomatoes you ever saw... 

But the messages, my wife, she says it's just talk. She tells me to just play my tiles and ignore it. But I know they are warning me to be careful. You just have to be careful these days. Especially with how they changed the bus schedule... I almost missed my ride here because they moved the stop down a whole block, didn't even put up a sign...

Oh, I know it for certain. Yes, sir. Even when my wife says it's just talk... she always says, "Just play your tiles." She's been brushing me off like that since we bought our first house. Cost us eight thousand dollars back then. Eight thousand! And it had a real nice front porch. I used to sit out there in the evenings and whittle. Made a little wooden bird for my grandson once. He’s in college now, studying... well, I don't know what he's studying, something with the computers. Everything is computers now, nobody works with their hands. 

But I know what I hear, doctor. Those men at the table, and the radio announcer too, they give little messages meant just for me. I know they are warning me to be careful. You just have to be careful. Like with the groceries... the prices they charge for a carton of eggs now, it's highway robbery. I went to the store on Tuesday and the girl at the register, she didn't even look up from her phone to give me my change. Just handed it right over without a word...

Memory? No, doctor, my memory is sharp as a tack. I haven't noticed any trouble with it at all. Why, I can remember things from way back better than these young folks remember yesterday. Like my first car... it was a '54 Ford. Blue, with a white roof. I bought it off a fellow named Miller who lived down by the old creek. 

That creek used to flood every spring, washed out the wooden bridge twice in one decade. They finally put in a concrete one, but it took the county three whole years to get around to it. Three years we had to drive the long way around past the Miller place just to get to town. He had these two big hound dogs, always howling at the moon... kept the whole neighborhood awake. Course, there wasn't much of a neighborhood back then, just dirt roads and pine trees. They cut all those trees down in the seventies to build that strip mall. The one with the hardware store that closed last year. Shame, really, they always had the best prices on nails...

Confused? No, no, my head's as clear as a bell. I don't get confused. Well, maybe just about how they run things down at city hall these days. You know, I went down there last month to pay my water bill. Used to be you could just hand it to Mary at the front desk. She's been there since... oh, must be 1985. We went to the same church, Saint Jude's, over on Elm Street. 

They got a new priest there now, Father Thomas. Nice fellow, but he talks too fast. You can barely understand the homily. Not like Father O'Malley, he used to project his voice so even the folks in the back pew could hear every word. He had this big booming voice, like a foghorn. Speaking of fog, we used to get the thickest fog coming off the river in November. You couldn't even see your hand in front of your face. I remember one time, my buddy Frank and I were trying to walk home from the bowling alley in it... Frank, he bowled a 300 game once. Got his picture in the local paper and everything. They gave him a little trophy with a gold bowler on top...

Lost? Oh, no, sir. I know my way around this town like the back of my hand. I've walked these streets since they were dirt. Never get lost. Although, you know, they did go and change the name of Main Street to Martin Luther King Boulevard a few years back. Caused a whole lot of fuss at the time. My neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, she was furious because she had to get all new return address labels printed. 

She used to order those labels from a catalog... Harriet Carter, I think it was. They sold all sorts of little knick-knacks. I bought a set of those magnetic screwdrivers from them once. Best thing I ever bought. You drop a screw in the engine block, you just fish it right out. I was working on my son's lawnmower when I first used 'em. It was one of those old Snapper riding mowers, the red ones. He left it out in the rain all winter and the carburetor got all gummed up. Kids today, they don't take care of their things. Just throw it away and buy a new one, that's their motto. Like those paper plates... my wife bought a whole stack of them for the Fourth of July barbecue. We always had ribs, slow-cooked over hickory wood...

Nobody's told me that. My daughter Betty comes by every Sunday and she's never said a peep about my memory. She usually brings a pot roast. Now, she makes a fair roast, but she puts way too much salt in the gravy. I always tell her she's gonna rust her pipes with all that salt, but she don't listen. Just like my brother Arthur, he used to salt his ham. Can you imagine that, salting a cured ham. He worked down at the railyard for forty years, loading freight. Hard work, that was. He had these big thick leather gloves he wore right through the fingers. Bought them at the old mercantile. You just can't find good leather gloves like that anymore. Everything now is made of plastic or nylon or whatever they call it. Makes your hands sweat something awful when the summer heat sets in...

Trouble with bills? No, no, I pay 'em just fine. Every month, right on time. I keep 'em all in this old cigar box on the kitchen table. It's a wooden box, real sturdy... Dutch Masters, I think. My uncle Charlie used to smoke those. He'd sit on the porch all evening, puffing away, telling stories about the Navy. He was stationed out in Hawaii before the war. Brought back this little ukulele for my sister. She tried to learn how to play it, but she didn't have much of an ear for music. Not like my cousin Sarah, she could play the piano by ear. Just hear a song on the radio once and sit down and play it perfect. We used to listen to the Grand Ole Opry on Saturday nights. Had this big wooden console radio, took up half the living room. The tubes in the back would glow orange when it warmed up...

Voices? Well, you know, sometimes in the afternoons when the house gets real quiet... I'll hear my old friend Jimmy call my name from out on the porch. Or sometimes he's humming one of those old choir songs, clear as day, like he's standing right there next to me. Jimmy had a beautiful baritone voice. We used to sing in the church choir together back in... oh, must have been the fifties. The choir director was a fellow named Mr. Henderson, wore these thick horn-rimmed glasses that always slid down his nose when he got worked up waving his arms around. He drove a Nash Ambassador, one of those big heavy cars that looked like an upside-down bathtub. Smooth ride, though. We took it all the way to the state fair one year, packed five of us in there with a picnic basket my mother made. She fried up a whole chicken in a cast iron skillet. You can't get chicken that tastes like that anymore, all the birds today are pumped full of water and raised in those big metal sheds...

No, Jimmy... no, he passed away. It's been about a year and five months now since we lost him. That's right around when this all started, hearing him and all, right after he died. We laid him to rest out at Oak Hill Cemetery. They got him a real nice spot, right under this massive weeping willow tree. I always did like willow trees, the way they just sort of sway when the breeze catches them. My grandfather had a big old willow in his front yard back in Ohio. We used to swing from the branches when we were little. You gotta be careful, though, the wood on those branches is mighty soft. It snaps real easy if you put too much weight on it. I fell out of it once, oh, I must have been seven or eight, and scraped my knee up so bad my mother had to paint it with iodine. Boy, did that sting. It was bright orange, left a terrible stain on my good trousers. Getting stains out of clothes back then was a real chore, we didn't have these fancy washing machines with all the buttons and dials. Just a washboard and a big tin tub of hot soapy water...

Forgetful? No, Martha hasn't said anything to me about that. I remember things just fine. Now, Martha, she's the one who writes everything down on those little yellow pads. Leaves 'em stuck to the icebox door so she doesn't forget to buy milk or butter. We just got a new icebox last year, one of those shiny silver ones. Terrible thing to keep clean, shows every single fingerprint the second you touch it. I told her we should have kept the old white one, it ran just fine. It was a Whirlpool, bought it over at Sears Roebuck back when they had the big store downtown. You could buy anything at Sears back then, tools, clothes, even a whole house out of a catalog. My old neighbor, Mr. Higgins, his father built one of those catalog houses. Came on a train in a hundred different boxes, every piece of lumber stamped with a number. Took him and his brothers a whole summer to put it together. They used real solid oak for the floors, not like the cheap stuff they build with today. You walk into a new house now and the floors just squeak and bounce right under your boots...

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I feel alright, mostly. Just... you know, regular. Though the weather hasn't been helping much lately, has it? All this rain we've been getting, it just turns the yard into a muddy mess. Martha's been after me to reseed the back lawn, but you can't put down seed when the ground is soaking wet like a sponge. It just rots right there in the dirt. I used to keep a beautiful lawn, back when I had my old push mower. The heavy kind, with the spinning blades that you had to sharpen with a file. You don't see those much anymore. Now everyone's got these loud gas-powered things that sound like airplanes taking off on a Sunday morning. Wakes up the whole neighborhood. My neighbor two doors down, he starts his up right at seven o'clock. Guy works at the hardware store, sells paint, I think. Paint is so expensive nowadays, too. I went in there last month just looking for a little quart of white for the porch railing, and they wanted an arm and a leg for it...

It's, uh... 2023, isn't it? Yes, 2023. I remember because Martha bought one of those big wall calendars with the pictures of the lighthouses on it for this year. She loves lighthouses. We took a trip up to Maine once, oh, it must have been thirty years ago now, just to drive up the coast and look at 'em. The water up there is so cold, though, even in the middle of summer. I dipped my toe in at a beach near Portland and thought my foot was going to freeze right off. We had some wonderful lobster on that trip, though. Bought it right off the boat from this fella in yellow overalls. You can't get seafood like that around here, it's all frozen and shipped in on trucks. By the time it gets to the grocery store, it doesn't even taste like fish anymore, just tastes like ice and cardboard. I tried to tell the butcher down at the Piggly Wiggly that once, but he just looked at me like I was crazy. Young kid, probably no older than nineteen, had his hat on backwards. I don't understand why kids today wear their hats backwards, the brim is supposed to keep the sun out of your eyes...

Well, Martha hasn't exactly had to take over my chores, but I suppose I haven't been keeping up with my own things too well. I've let parts of my garden go lately, just weeds everywhere out by the back fence. I used to grow the biggest beefsteak tomatoes you ever saw. You slice one of those thick, put a little salt and some mayonnaise on white bread... oh, that's a meal right there. You can't get good white bread at the store anymore, it's all that expensive stuff with the hard seeds that get stuck under your dentures. My dentist, Dr. Evans, he's a nice enough fella but his hands are just too big for my mouth, always stretching my cheeks out. 

Anyway, I've also missed my choir rehearsals down at the church. Just haven't been going. We sing out of those old red hymnals, you know, the ones where the gold lettering is all rubbed off the covers from people holding them. I love the old hymns. My mother used to play them on the piano in our parlor when I was a boy. It was a big upright piano, heavy as a tractor. Took four men and a mule to move it into the house when my daddy bought it. 

And, well, I guess I made the domino games down at the lodge a bit uncomfortable for the fellas lately, too, so I just do not join like I used to. We always played on this green folding card table, but one of the legs was short, so somebody had to fold up a matchbook to stick under it so the tiles wouldn't slide. You don't see matchbooks much anymore. Every diner and gas station used to have a glass bowl of them right by the cash register, free for the taking, with their little pictures printed on the front. I used to keep a whole shoebox full of them in the garage...

Seeing things? No, no, my eyes aren't what they used to be, but I don't see anything that isn't there. Though... some afternoons, when the house is real quiet and Martha's out at the store, I do hear things. I hear my old friend Charlie calling my name right from the front porch. Sometimes he's humming one of those old choir songs we used to sing, clear as a bell, like he's standing right there next to the screen door. Charlie had a beautiful baritone voice, you know. Deep and rich, like molasses. We used to sit on that porch for hours, drinking iced tea out of those heavy glass mason jars. You don't see people using mason jars for drinking much anymore, mostly just for canning peaches or tomatoes. My grandmother used to can the best peaches, put 'em up in a sugary syrup that would stick to your fingers. We'd keep them down in the root cellar where it was nice and cool. Root cellars always smelled like damp earth and potatoes... potatoes are getting awfully small at the grocery store lately, have you noticed that? They used to be the size of softballs, and now they're just these little things, hardly worth peeling. Peeling potatoes is a young man's game anyway, my arthritis acts up if I hold the peeler too long...

Physically ill? No, I don't think so. I haven't had any big medical problems before all this started, just the usual aches and pains a fella my age gets. My knees click like a pair of castanets when I walk up the stairs, but that's just getting old, I suppose. Castanets... my sister Mary had a pair of those when she took up Spanish dancing back in the fifties. She wore this bright red dress with ruffles all down the skirt, twirling around in the living room until she knocked over Mother's good lamp. The one with the hand-painted roses on the shade. Mother was furious, of course. Sent Mary to her room without supper. Supper back then was always meat and potatoes, none of this fancy food you see on the television nowadays. People put avocado on toast now, can you believe that? Avocado is supposed to go in a salad, maybe with a little squeeze of lemon. Lemons used to be so cheap, you could buy a whole bag for a quarter down at the fruit stand on Elm Street... I wonder whatever happened to the man who ran that stand. He always wore a straw hat with a green ribbon...

Confused? Well, Martha hasn't said anything like that, no. I don't think I've been confused. I mean, sometimes I misplace my glasses, but who doesn't? I usually leave them on the little table by the armchair. That armchair has been in the house since 1968. We bought it from Sears Roebuck. You used to be able to order just about anything from that Sears catalog... even a whole house! Can you imagine? Just ordering a house out of a book and having it delivered on a train. Trains used to run right through the center of town here, blew the whistle at noon every day. You could set your watch by it. My pocket watch belonged to my grandfather, actually. Silver case, heavy chain. He worked on the railroad, laid track all the way out to Omaha... Omaha's supposed to have good steaks, but I've never been. I don't travel much anymore, not since gas got so expensive. Used to be you could fill your tank for a few dollars and drive all Sunday afternoon just to look at the changing leaves...

Harm me? Well... I don't know about harm exactly, but I do know I have to be careful. That's why I came in, really. The men down at the domino table at the senior center, they slip little messages into their talk. And the fellow on the radio, the one who does the evening news, he does it too. Little warnings, meant just for me. Martha tells me it's just regular talk, that I'm making a mountain out of a molehill, but I know what I hear. Dominoes is a funny game, you know. You have to match the dots... we used to play with these beautiful ivory tiles my uncle brought back from the war. He was in the Navy, stationed out in the Pacific. Sent home all sorts of things... a silk kimono for my mother, and those dominoes. They don't make them out of ivory anymore, of course. Banned it, I think. Probably for the best, you shouldn't go shooting elephants just for a board game. Elephants are smart animals, they say they never forget a thing. I saw an elephant at the circus when I was a boy, must have been 1948 or so. The whole tent smelled like roasted peanuts and sawdust. You could buy a bag of peanuts for a nickel back then... nickels used to have a buffalo on them, did you know that? I used to collect them in an old cigar box...

My memory? No, Martha hasn't said anything about my memory getting worse. She always jokes that I only remember what I want to, anyway. Like I remembered to pick up her favorite peppermints at the pharmacy yesterday. They have those soft ones, you know, the ones that just sort of melt in your mouth. Peppermint is good for the stomach, my grandmother always used to say. She grew it right in her backyard, next to the tomatoes. You just can't get a good tomato from the grocery store these days. They look red, but they taste like water. Back when we had the house on Maple Street, I had a big garden out back. Grew tomatoes as big as softballs. We used to can them at the end of the summer... the whole kitchen would steam up and smell like vinegar and basil. We had Mason jars lined up all across the counter. You have to boil the jars to seal them right, otherwise the food spoils. People don't know how to preserve things anymore, they just buy everything in plastic bags or boxes. Plastic is everywhere now... I heard on the television there's a whole island of it floating out in the ocean somewhere. Makes you wonder about the fish. I used to love going fishing down at the creek with my brother when we were little. We'd use a cane pole and a bobber...

Well, a specific group? I don't rightly know if they're all in cahoots together, but it's like I said, it's the men down at the domino table at the senior center, and that fellow on the evening news on the radio. They're the ones giving me those little messages, warning me to be careful. Martha, my wife, she just shakes her head and tells me it's just regular talk and I'm imagining things, but I know what I hear. I know they're warning me. The radio is an old Zenith, you know. Beautiful wooden cabinet, got it at a rummage sale back in '75. The tubes take a minute to warm up, not like these new digital things that turn on instantly. We used to gather 'round the radio when I was a boy, listen to The Lone Ranger and The Shadow. "Who knows what evil lurks in the hearts of men?" That's what they used to say. It was a whole different world back then, people had more respect. You'd hold the door open for a lady, tip your hat... hats used to be a real staple of a man's wardrobe. A good fedora, maybe a straw boater in the summer. I had a gray felt fedora I wore to church every Sunday. Church was a big part of the week, everyone in their Sunday best. My mother made my suits by hand, out of wool... wool gets mighty itchy in the summer heat, though...

Hard to follow? Well, no... nobody's said anything like that to me. I speak just as plain as I always have. Martha never has any trouble understanding me, 'course sometimes she says I mumble if I'm talking to her from the other room while she's watching her programs. She loves those game shows, you know. The ones where they spin the big wheel. We used to watch a lot of television back when there were only three channels. You had to get up and turn the dial by hand, and sometimes you had to fiddle with the rabbit ears just right to get the static out. We had a piece of tin foil on ours for the longest time. If the wind blew too hard, you'd lose the picture completely. Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's not every single day, but I definitely go through these... these stretches where everything just feels so heavy. Well, that's... I mean, that's a really interesting way to put it. I guess I wouldn't say I feel like I *can't* stop, exactly. I'll be standing there, and the house is so quiet, you know? Just the hum of the refrigerator. Well, yes. Yes, I'd say so. It’s... it’s not just a fleeting thing, you know? It’s not like I wake up feeling a little down because it’s raining and then by lunchtime I’m fine. It really settles in. I go through these stretches—and they definitely last for weeks at a time, sometimes longer—where the whole house just feels... gray. And heavy. I’ll just sit there at the kitchen table, the one by the window where I usually like to have my morning tea, and I’ll just feel so incredibly empty. The mail came, the birds are at the feeder, everything is perfectly normal, but inside I just feel this profound, hollow sadness. I’ll sit there staring at the grain of the wood on the table—it’s this lovely old oak table we got at an estate sale years ago, and it has all these interesting knots and swirls in it—and I’ll just trace them with my finger and feel completely drained of any joy or energy. 

It’s almost like someone turned the color dial all the way down on my life. And it’s not just for an hour or two; it’s most of the day, pretty much every single day during those periods. I’ll try to get up and do something, maybe sort through the mail or water the spider plant in the living room, but the heaviness just follows me from room to room. So, yes, when those periods hit, they really take hold and linger for quite a while.

Well, yes, absolutely. You mentioned art, and it’s so true. I used to love going down to the galleries in the arts district—there's this one little cooperative on 4th Street that always has the most wonderful local watercolors, and I used to make a whole afternoon of it. I'd get a coffee, stroll through, talk to the owners. But during those heavy weeks, the thought of going just feels so exhausting. 

And it’s not just the art, really, it's everything. Things I used to look forward to just completely lose their spark. Take my book club, for instance. We meet every other Tuesday, usually at my friend Sarah's house because she has this gorgeous, bright sunroom with all these wicker chairs, and I used to be the first one to finish the monthly book. I'd even bake something to bring, like my lemon blueberry scones, which everyone always asks for. But when that grayness settles in, I just stare at the book sitting on my nightstand. I don't even want to open the cover. It just feels like a massive chore that I keep putting off, week after week, until I'm making up excuses not to go.

It's the same with cooking. I usually love being in the kitchen, chopping vegetables, trying out new recipes I found in magazines, simmering sauces... but then it just becomes this monumental task. Standing at the stove just feels like work. 

Even my rose beds! I have these beautiful apricot-colored roses out back, and they need regular pruning and deadheading, which I usually find so incredibly therapeutic. You know, getting my hands in the dirt, feeling the sunshine on my back, listening to the neighborhood wake up. But when I'm in that gray place, I look out the kitchen window at them and I just think, 'Ugh, another thing I have to do.' I just keep putting it off and putting it off until the petals are all browning and dropping onto the soil. It's like all the joy is just siphoned right out of the things that make me *me*, and everything just turns into this endless list of obligations I want to hide from.

Well, that's the thing, yes. I do. It doesn't really seem to matter if the house is perfectly quiet and everything is fine. But then, out of nowhere, that heavy, gray feeling just rolled in like a fog. And I just couldn't move. There was no reason for it. No arguments, no bad news, no stress. Just... quiet. But the sadness was so overwhelming. I sat there for hours, just watching the dust motes float in the air, feeling completely hollowed out. 

It's almost more frustrating when it happens during the calm times, you know? Because when things are chaotic or stressful, at least you can point to something and say, 'Oh, that's why I feel this way.' But when everything is fine, when there's no reason to be sad, and you still feel like you're dragging a boulder behind you... it just makes you feel so broken. So, yes, even when things are perfectly calm, those gray periods still find me. They just invite themselves right in and unpack their bags.

Well... yes. Yes, I suppose I have. Especially at night. The nights are the hardest. My husband will be asleep, breathing so steadily next to me, and the house is perfectly quiet—just the hum of the refrigerator or maybe the wind rattling that one loose pane in the bedroom window, the one we’ve been meaning to fix since last autumn. And I’ll just lie there, staring at the ceiling, watching the shadows from the streetlamp outside shift across the plaster. And in those moments, when I’m just so incredibly tired of feeling so empty and heavy, I do think... I think it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up the next morning. 

It’s not that I want to die, exactly, it’s just that being alive feels like such a monumental effort. Like dragging that boulder, you know? And the thought of just... slipping away in my sleep, of not having to face another day of that hollow feeling, of not having to force myself to get out of bed and pretend everything is fine... it just seems peaceful. 

But I want to be clear—I haven’t actually made a plan to hurt myself. I haven't done anything like that. I wouldn't do that to my husband, or my sister, who relies on me to help her with her garden in the spring. I know it would devastate them. I don't have pills hidden away or anything like that. It's just... a thought that creeps in. A wish, almost, on the very worst nights, that the universe would just quietly take the decision out of my hands so I could finally just rest.

But the thing is, and this is what's really confusing about it, is that it can turn so quickly. I'll be flying high, feeling so wonderful and productive, and then something tiny will happen and I just... I

Well, yes, actually. It’s incredible, really, because normally I love my sleep, especially when I’m in one of those gray slumps where I feel like I could stay under the covers for a week. But when I’m feeling bright and energetic, it’s like my body just entirely forgets how to be tired. 

I mean, I’ll finally force myself to go to bed at maybe one or two in the morning because I’ve been so busy with my painting or whatever else I've gotten myself into, but then... I can sleep just three or four hours, tops, and I'll just pop right awake. And I don't wake up groggy or dragging my feet at all. I wake up feeling completely charged. It’s like electricity is running through my veins. 

It’ll be 4:30 in the morning, pitch black outside, the whole neighborhood is dead silent, and I’m already out of bed, making a pot of coffee, and I'm just ready to go. I'll sit down at the computer and start writing these incredibly long blog posts—I have this little blog about upcycling furniture and gardening that I usually completely neglect—but suddenly I have so much to say, and I'm drafting three or four posts before the sun is even up. Or I’ll be planning out all these massive new projects, sitting at the kitchen table drawing diagrams for a completely new landscaping design for the backyard, making lists of seeds and soil I need to order. 

My husband will come downstairs at seven, rubbing his eyes, barely awake, and I’ve already been up for hours, feeling like I’ve accomplished a whole day's worth of work. You’d think I’d crash, you know? You’d think anyone would be exhausted by noon after only getting three hours of sleep, but I just don't feel it. I just keep going and going. I actually kind of love those early mornings because no one is awake to interrupt me, but my mind is just racing with all these brilliant ideas...

Oh, yes, absolutely. It's... well, it's actually a wonderful feeling, to be honest. It's like all the self-doubt just completely evaporates. Normally, I second-guess everything, you know? But when I'm in one of those bright phases, I feel like I have this incredible clarity and purpose. 

Like, for example, I've been taking these online courses for art therapy—just a few classes here and there, nothing official yet, I haven't even finished the basic certification—but when I get like that, I become absolutely convinced that I'm ready to launch this massive program. I'll sit there, at the dining room table with all my paints, and I'll start drafting these elaborate business plans and curriculum guides. I become completely sure that my art-therapy workshop is going to change people's lives in a major, profound way. 

I mean, I can just see it so clearly in my head. I imagine renting out this beautiful studio space downtown with exposed brick and big windows, and I can picture the people coming in, and I just know, without a shadow of a doubt, that I have the exact insight and talent to heal them through art. I'll start telling my husband about it, explaining how we need to take out a loan because this is going to be a huge success, a total breakthrough. I feel so powerful, like I have this unique gift that no one else has, and it's my absolute duty to share it with the world right that very second. I don't even worry about the fact that I'm not technically qualified yet, because in those moments, I feel like my natural intuition is far superior to any piece of paper or training program. It's just this overwhelming sense of... destiny, I guess you could call it.

No, no, I've never been in the hospital for being too energetic. I mean, I've never had to pack a bag and go stay in a ward or anything like that. My husband—he gets very stressed when I'm buzzing around like that.
