And sometimes I'll argue with him, you know, telling him he's stifling my creativity and that he just doesn't understand my vision. We had this huge argument about the landscaping thing because he said we absolutely could not afford the three pallets of river rock I was trying to order at five in the morning. 

But even when it gets really heated, and I'm just practically vibrating with all these plans and ideas, it's never gotten to the point where anyone had to call an ambulance or a doctor said I needed to be admitted somewhere. I just sort of... stay home. I burn through it at home. Eventually, the energy just sort of fizzles out, or the irritability takes over like I mentioned before, and then the wave crashes, but I've always managed to just stay in my own house while it happens. So, no, no hospitals. I don't think I could handle a hospital anyway, to be perfectly honest. The fluorescent lights, the strict schedules, people telling you when to eat and sleep... it would drive me absolutely up the wall when I'm feeling that inspired and need to be doing things on my own time.

Well, I suppose... I mean, you're asking about major trouble, and I wouldn't call it a total catastrophe where we're losing the house or anything, but yes, it does cause a fair amount of friction. Especially with my husband. Like I was saying about that argument over the river rock, that kind of thing happens a lot when I'm in that state. The tension just builds and builds between us because he just wants things to be normal, you know? He wants to have dinner at six, he wants to sit on the couch and watch his shows, he wants to go to bed at ten, and I am just completely out of sync with all of that. It makes it so hard to just keep our normal routines going. The whole household rhythm gets entirely thrown out the window, and we end up snapping at each other because I feel like he's holding me back, and he feels like I'm spinning out of control. 

And then, ironically, even though I feel like I'm accomplishing so much with all that energy, I actually end up falling behind on the things I really should be focusing on. Like my art therapy facilitator training. I told you about how I get these grand plans for the studio and the business, right? But the actual coursework I'm supposed to be doing for the certification? I completely drop the ball on it. 

It’s because my mind is going a million miles an hour, and my projects just become so incredibly hard to organize. I'll sit down to do an assignment for the class, or even just try to do some work on my private blog—the gardening one I mentioned earlier, where I'm drafting all those posts before the sun comes up—but when I actually look at what I'm doing, my explanations are just all over the place. I can't keep my thoughts in a straight line to save my life. I'll start writing a blog post about planting hydrangeas, and suddenly I'm writing four pages about the spiritual meaning of the color blue and how it relates to childhood trauma, and I just can't rein it in. 

So I end up with all these half-finished, messy projects that don't make sense to anyone but me in that exact moment. I'm not getting fired from a job since I don't work outside the house right now, but my personal work, my training, my blog... it all gets completely derailed. I just can't organize any of it. And then, of course, my husband is upset because the dining room table is a disaster zone of papers and paint and business plans that don't make sense, and the tension at home just makes it even harder to get back on track...

Well... I mean, my husband definitely thinks I do. He calls it my overactive imagination, but to me, in the moment, it feels incredibly real and, honestly, quite overwhelming. It really only happens when I’m in those extremely charged, unstoppable stretches—you know, the ones I was just telling you about where I'm planning the art therapy workshops and drafting all those curriculums and sleeping very, very little, maybe just an hour or two a night. My brain is just firing on all cylinders, but that’s also when things start to get a bit... strange. 

For instance, I'll be sitting at the computer in the dark, checking my gardening blog or reading through different online forums, and the comments people leave stop looking like normal comments. They start to feel like coded warnings. Someone will write something completely mundane, like "Make sure to watch out for the frost this weekend," or "I wouldn't plant those too close together," and suddenly I am absolutely convinced that they aren't talking about plants at all. I feel this deep, intense certainty that it's a secret message meant specifically for me, like someone is trying to warn me that I'm in danger or that someone is watching the house. I will sit there for hours, analyzing the timestamps, looking at the spacing of the words, trying to decipher the true meaning behind what they typed. My husband will come out at four in the morning, rub his eyes, and tell me that a comment about mulch is just a comment about mulch, but I just cannot believe him. It feels too real. 

And it's not just the internet, either. During those exact same periods, when the house is completely dead silent and I'm the only one awake, I'll hear things. Well, mostly, I may hear my name when no one is there. It's as clear as day. I'll be hunched over my business plans at the dining room table, and I'll hear someone say my name right over my shoulder. It's so distinct that I'll physically jump out of my chair, sending my papers and pens flying everywhere, and I'll go creeping down the hallway to check the bedroom. But my husband is always fast asleep, snoring away. There's no one else in the house. But I know what I heard. It's so unnerving, but it really only ever seems to happen when I'm in that high-gear, no-sleep mode, spinning all these massive projects. So, yes, I suppose I do believe and experience things then that my husband says are completely unrealistic.

I guess I'm here because... well, mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I stopped doing all the things I used to do. Like hiking, or coaching... I used to coach a youth league. We had this one kid who could throw a curveball that would just drop right at the plate. His dad bought him these expensive cleats, the kind with the metal spikes, even though they weren't allowed in our division. I had to tell the umpire about it before a playoff game because the other coach was getting real worked up. People get so angry over little things, you know? 

But anyway... I just stopped going to the games. I stopped playing my guitar, too. I don't even call people back when they leave a message. Most days I just sit in my small rental for hours. I know there are things I need to do, but I just can't make myself start. The landlord was supposed to fix the blinds in that place three months ago, but he never did. They just hang there crooked, letting the streetlights in. Did I... what did you ask me originally?

Memory? No, I don't think so. My memory is fine. I can still remember all the ten-codes from when I was on patrol. And the badge numbers, too. Like Miller was 4922. He always drove the cruiser with the squeaky fan belt. We wrote it up for the motor pool like a dozen times, but those guys in the garage never fixed anything. They just sat around on folding chairs listening to sports radio all day. AM radio, you know? It always has that fuzzy static sound in the background. My grandfather used to listen to AM radio on this little silver transistor he carried in his front shirt pocket. He worked at a canning factory for thirty years. Canned peaches, mostly. I can't even look at canned peaches anymore, they're just too sweet, sitting in all that heavy syrup. They get mushy if they sit in the can too long... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask me about my diet?

Stressful? Yeah... yeah, I guess you could say that. Things have really been unraveling since I moved into the smaller rental after my divorce. That was about a year and two months ago. Having to pack up everything... I had to do the whole garage by myself. I had all these tools, you know? Snap-on wrenches. Really good quality. You can't buy tools like that at the regular hardware store anymore, they're all made of cheap metal now. They strip the bolts the second you put any real torque on them. I tried to fix a lawnmower with one of those cheap socket sets once and the thing just snapped right in half. Cut my knuckle wide open. Bled all over the driveway. The driveway at the old house was asphalt, but it got so hot in the summer it would get soft. You could press a quarter right into it if you pushed hard enough. The neighborhood kids used to leave their bikes out and the kickstands would sink right into the blacktop... Wait. Why am I talking about the driveway? What did you ask me? Did you ask if I owned a home?

Depressed? I don't know... maybe? I just feel so flat. Like there's no energy left in the battery, you know? Like when the battery in your flashlight dies when you're on a night shift. I had this heavy Maglite, the big metal ones that take the D batteries. You could use it as a baton if you really had to, but mostly it was just heavy to carry on your belt all night. The belt itself was heavy, with the radio and the cuffs and everything. My lower back used to ache so bad after a twelve-hour shift. I went to a chiropractor for a while, Dr. Henderson. He had this office above a bakery, so the whole place always smelled like sourdough bread. I love sourdough bread, especially when it's toasted with just a little bit of butter. Real butter, not that margarine stuff. Margarine is basically just plastic, I saw a documentary about it once. They said if you leave a tub of it outside, even the flies won't touch it. It's unnatural. Like those fake plants people put in their offices... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask me what I eat for breakfast?

Jumping? No, I don't think they jump. My thoughts are pretty steady, actually. Steady like... like when you're walking the beat, you know? Heel, toe, heel, toe. You have to keep a steady rhythm when you're walking a long perimeter, like down by the old railyards. We used to have to check the chain-link fences down there every night. The freight trains would roll through at 2:00 AM and the whole ground would just vibrate. You could feel it right up through the soles of your boots. I always wore those heavy steel-toed boots, the black leather ones you have to polish yourself. You use a lighter to melt the shoe polish just a little bit before you rub it in, makes it shine way better. My dad taught me that. He was in the Navy. He had this old silver Zippo lighter with an anchor engraved on it. It made this really distinct metallic clink sound when you flipped the lid open. You don't see people carrying Zippos much anymore, everyone just uses those cheap plastic lighters from the gas station checkout counter. The gas station near my old apartment used to sell these little cherry pies in wax paper wrappers, the kind that are glazed all over with sugar... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask me if I wanted a snack?

Before the divorce? No, I... I don't think so. Things were okay before that. At least, I think they were. I was working a lot, pulling a lot of overtime at the precinct. You know how it is when you're trying to save up for something big. We were going to remodel the kitchen. She wanted those granite countertops, the really heavy ones with the little specks of silver in them. They look nice, but you have to seal them every year or they get stained. My buddy Dave had granite in his place and he spilled red wine on it once. Just a few drops, but it soaked right in. He tried everything to get it out—baking soda, peroxide, even some industrial cleaner he got from the janitor at the station. That janitor, old man Higgins, he had a key ring the size of a dinner plate. He jingled everywhere he went. You could hear him coming down the hall from a mile away. It sounded like sleigh bells, kind of. Like Christmas... wait. Why am I talking about Christmas? What did you ask me? Did you ask if I bought her a present?

Trouble with bills? No, I don't... I don't think so. I mean, they just come in the mail, right? You open them and write a check. Or do it online now, I guess. Everything's online. They want you to go paperless for everything, to save the trees. Which is good, I like trees. We had this huge oak tree in the front yard of the house I grew up in. Massive thing. In the autumn, the leaves would turn this deep, rusty red color, and they'd cover the whole lawn. My brother and I used to rake them into these giant piles and jump in them. You had to be careful, though, because sometimes there'd be sticks or dog poop hidden in the pile. We had a Golden Retriever named Buster back then. He was the smartest dog. You could throw a tennis ball into the woods, and he would always find it. Always. He had this one ball that was his absolute favorite, it was completely worn down, no fuzz left on it at all. It looked more like a gray rock than a tennis ball... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask if I have a dog?

Head injury? No, no, I've never had anything like that. My head is fine. Hard headed, actually, that's what my training officer used to say. He said I had a skull like a concrete block. Concrete is funny stuff, you know? It takes forever to cure properly. You pour it and it looks dry on top, but underneath it's still wet for days, sometimes weeks if the weather is humid. We poured a new driveway at the precinct a few years back, and this stray cat walked right across it while it was still wet. Left these perfect little paw prints all the way up to the front doors. They tried to smooth them out with a trowel, but you could still see the faint outline of them. I always liked looking at those prints when I came in for the night shift. Made me wonder where the cat went. Probably hunting mice near the dumpsters out back. We had a real problem with raccoons in those dumpsters for a while. Big, fat ones. They figure out how to open the lids with their little hands. They have hands almost like people, with the little fingers... wait. What did you ask me? Did you ask if I got scratched by a cat?

What day is it? Um... I think it's... well, it's a weekday, I know that. The traffic was pretty heavy on the way over here. Stop and go the whole way down 4th street. They've been doing construction on that road for what feels like five years now. They dig a hole, fill it up, and then dig it up again two weeks later. The guys out there in those bright orange vests, they must get so hot in the summer. Orange is a weird color to wear, anyway. It's supposed to be for safety, like hunting vests. My uncle used to take me deer hunting when I was a kid. We'd sit up in this blind for hours, freezing our toes off, drinking out of this old plaid thermos. It smelled like stale coffee and metal. I never actually wanted to shoot anything, I just liked sitting out there in the quiet. The woods get so still right before the sun comes up. You can hear every twig snap, every little rustle in the brush. Sometimes it was just a squirrel, but it sounded like a bear crashing through the trees. Bears are actually really fast, you know. People think they're lumbering and slow, but they can outrun a horse over a short distance. You're supposed to play dead if a grizzly attacks you, but make noise if it's a black bear. Or is it the other way around? Wait... why are we talking about bears? Did you ask me if I went to the zoo?

Where we are? Uh... we're in a room. An office, I guess. It's got walls and... a ceiling. The ceiling tiles are those white ones with the little holes poked in them. Have you ever noticed that? They look like someone took a tiny needle and just went to town on them. I wonder how they make those. Probably a machine that stamps them out by the thousands. Assembly lines are fascinating. I watched a documentary once on how they make cars. Just a giant conveyor belt, and these robotic arms welding sparks everywhere. It takes a lot of electricity to run a factory like that. My electric bill was so high last month. I think I left the porch light on for three days straight. It's one of those yellow bug lights, supposed to keep the mosquitoes away. Mosquitoes are terrible this year. They breed in standing water, you know. Even just a little puddle in an old tire is enough for them to lay hundreds of eggs. You have to be careful about tires, too, because if they get too bald, you can hydroplane on the highway. I had a blowout on the interstate once, right in the middle lane. Scared me half to death. The rubber was flying everywhere, and I had to wrestle the steering wheel just to get over to the shoulder. The tow truck guy took two hours to show up. He had a really cool tattoo of an anchor on his forearm... wait. What did you ask me? Did you ask if I drove here today?

Who you are? Well, you're the doctor, right? You're sitting in the big chair with the notepad. My regular doctor has a notepad just like that, with the little spiral wire at the top. I always end up bending that wire when I have notebooks like that. Once it gets bent, you can't ever turn the pages right again, they just catch and tear. Paper cuts are the worst, aren't they? They don't bleed much, but they sting like crazy. I got a bad one once opening a letter from the IRS. It was just a standard notice, nothing bad, but I saw that return address and my heart just dropped. Taxes are so complicated now. I used to do them myself, just fill out the 1040EZ and mail it in, but now you need software for everything. Computers make things easier, I guess, but they also crash all the time. My partner at the precinct, his computer froze right in the middle of typing up an incident report. He lost two hours of work. He was so mad, he almost threw his coffee mug at the screen. It was one of those insulated mugs, the kind that keeps coffee hot all day. I prefer my coffee lukewarm, honestly. If it's too hot, it burns your tongue and then you can't taste anything for the rest of the day. Taste buds are funny little things, aren't they? They say you lose them as you get older... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask me if I brought you coffee?

Dementia? No, I don't think anyone's ever told me that. No brain problems like that. Dementia is when you forget stuff, right? My grandmother used to forget things all the time. She'd leave the stove on. Gas stoves are really dangerous if you aren't careful. You have to make sure the pilot light is actually lit. If it goes out, the whole house just fills up with gas, and one little spark could blow the roof right off. We responded to a house fire once, back when I was on regular patrol. The heat from a fire like that is just unbelievable. It gets so hot it actually melts the siding right off the houses next door. Vinyl siding is cheap anyway, though. People really should just use brick. Brick houses last forever. Look at those old Roman buildings, still standing after thousands of years. The Romans really knew how to build things. They even had indoor heating under the floors. I learned about that in college. I took this Roman history elective my sophomore year, and the professor had this massive, bushy white beard. He looked exactly like Santa Claus. Do kids even believe in Santa Claus anymore? With the internet, they can just look everything up instantly. The internet really ruined the magic of things, if you ask me. You can't even have a good argument with the guys at the station anymore, because someone just pulls out their phone and Googles the answer. Smartphones are basically just little tracking devices anyway, they listen to everything you say... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask me if I have my phone on me?

Medical cause? No, no doctor ever found anything like that. I mean, they do tests sometimes, but they never find a reason. The worst part about going to get those tests is just the waiting rooms. You just sit there for hours in those uncomfortable chairs, and all they have to read are those magazines from like three years ago. I was flipping through a National Geographic in one of those rooms once, and it had this huge article on wolves. Wolves are incredible, the way they hunt in packs. It's all about communication and hierarchy. Kind of like the K9 unit down at the precinct. Those German Shepherds are so smart, they practically understand English. But man, they eat so much. The main handler, Dave, he told me he goes through a fifty-pound bag of dog food every couple of weeks. Have you seen the price of dog food lately? Actually, the price of everything at the grocery store is just out of control. A carton of eggs is ridiculous now. It's because of the supply chain issues, I guess. The truck drivers are all quitting because the hours are terrible. Driving a big rig cross-country sounds really lonely anyway. Just you and the open road, listening to AM radio late at night to stay awake. The static on AM radio always gives me a headache after a while... wait. What were you asking me? Did you ask if I listen to the radio?

What month? Well, it's... um, I'm not exactly sure right now. Honestly, the days just kind of blur together lately. Speaking of blurring, my vision was doing that the other day when I was driving. I had to pull over near that old diner on Route 9. You know the one? They have the best cherry pie there. They serve it warm with a huge scoop of vanilla ice cream right on top. Ice cream melts so fast in the summer, though. You have to eat it quickly before it just turns into soup in the bowl. I dropped a bowl in the kitchen once and it shattered into a million pieces. Sweeping up glass is the worst because you always miss that one tiny sliver, and then someone steps on it barefoot a week later. My buddy Mike stepped on a nail once at a construction site before he joined the force. Went right through his boot. They had to give him a tetanus shot, and his arm was sore for days. Shots always make my arm sore. The flu shot is the worst for that. They tell you to move your arm around to help, but it never really does. I wonder if they'll ever invent a shot that doesn't hurt... wait. What did you just ask me? Did you ask if I like pie?

Depressed for two weeks? Before this year? No, I don't think so. I haven't really felt like that before. I mean, everyone has bad days, but not for two whole weeks. Two weeks is a long time. It's the standard length for a vacation, though. Most guys at the department take their two weeks in the summer to go down to the shore. The boardwalk down there gets so crowded, you can barely walk. And the seagulls, they're aggressive. I saw one swoop down and steal a whole slice of pizza right out of a kid's hand once. Pizza isn't even that good down there, honestly. The best pizza is always in those tiny, hole-in-the-wall places in the city. The ones with the brick ovens. The crust gets that perfect char on it. It's all about the temperature of the oven, it has to be incredibly hot. Fire is fascinating, really. The way it moves and consumes things. We had this arson case a few years back, this guy was setting dumpsters on fire just to watch them burn. Dumpsters always smell terrible anyway, especially in the heat. The garbage juice leaks out and bakes on the asphalt. Asphalt gets so soft in the summer you can almost leave footprints in it. Like those footprints in the cement outside the Chinese theater in Hollywood. I've never been to California, but I've always wanted to see the redwoods. Trees that big, it's hard to even imagine. They've been there for hundreds of years, just growing... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask if I've been to California?

Every day for two weeks? Yeah, I guess so. Mostly I just don't feel like myself anymore. I used to do a lot, you know? I stopped hiking, stopped coaching the youth league, haven't picked up my guitar in... I don't even know how long. I don't even call people back anymore. Some days I just sit in that small rental for hours. I know there are things to do, but I just can't make myself start. Starting things is always the hardest part, isn't it? Like when you have to start a new report at work. The blank page just stares at you. We use this old software at the precinct for reports, it's from like the nineties. It crashes all the time if you type too fast. I used to type really fast, took a keyboarding class in high school. They had those covers over the keys so you couldn't look down at your hands. You just had to memorize where the letters were. Muscle memory is a crazy thing. Like riding a bike, they say you never forget. I had this red Schwinn when I was a kid, with the banana seat. Man, I rode that thing everywhere until the chain finally snapped. Bike chains are so greasy, you can never get that black grease off your hands no matter how much soap you use. You need that special pumice soap mechanics use. Mechanics always have such rough hands from working on engines all day. Car engines are so complicated now, everything is computerized. You can't even change your own oil anymore without a special tool... wait. What were you asking me? Did you ask if I play guitar?

Felt like this before? No, I don't... I don't think so. I've never been this down or just empty before this past year. Everything before this was just normal, you know? Time just feels completely different lately. It's like my internal clock is broken or something. Speaking of clocks, I used to have this heavy silver watch when I first started at the academy. My dad gave it to me when I got my bachelor's degree. It was waterproof up to like fifty meters. Not that I ever went diving. The deepest water I ever get in is the municipal pool, and even then, the chlorine is just way too strong. Chlorine always makes my eyes sting for hours afterward. It actually reminds me of the industrial bleach they use to clean the holding cells at the precinct. That smell just gets right into your uniform and you can never really wash it out. My dry cleaner, Mr. Henderson, he tried everything to get it out of my good shirts. He's been running that shop on 4th street for thirty years. Thirty years is a long time to just stand there and steam press shirts all day. The steam press always makes that loud hissing sound, kind of like a radiator about to burst. The radiators in those old city buildings are always clanking and banging in the winter. It keeps you awake at night if you're not used to it. I'm a pretty light sleeper anyway, the slightest noise wakes me up. Even just a branch tapping on the window glass. We have this massive oak tree in the front yard... wait. What were we talking about? Did you ask if I wear a watch?

Worthless? Guilty? I don't know... I guess I haven't really thought about it like that. I don't think I feel guilty about anything. I just feel... empty. Like I'm just taking up space. Space is a funny concept, though, isn't it? Like outer space. I used to watch all those documentaries on PBS about black holes and supernovas. The scale of the universe is just terrifying if you really think about it. We're just these tiny specks on a rock spinning around a giant ball of gas. Gas prices have been ridiculous lately, by the way. I went to fill up my tank the other day and it was almost four dollars a gallon. Four dollars! I remember when I was a teenager, you could fill up a whole tank for twenty bucks. I drove this beat-up old Chevy Nova. It was rust-colored, mostly because of actual rust. The heater didn't work, so in the winter you had to drive with a blanket over your lap. Blankets are never long enough, though, your feet always stick out the end and get cold. My grandmother used to knit these huge afghans that were actually long enough. She'd sit in her rocking chair for hours just knitting and watching Jeopardy. Alex Trebek was always so calm, no matter what happened. He just had this soothing voice... wait. What did you ask me? Did you ask if I watch Jeopardy?

Apple, table, penny. Yeah, I can say those. Apple, table, penny. Pennies are practically useless now, aren't they? They cost more to make than they're actually worth. It's all zinc anyway, not even real copper like they used to be. Real copper turns green when it oxidizes, like the Statue of Liberty. I've never actually been to New York to see it, though. The city just seems too crowded, too loud. The sirens there must be constant. We get enough sirens in my line of work, the wail just cuts right through you, especially at night when the streets are empty. The yellow streetlights make everything look kind of washed out and sick. Streetlights used to be that bright white, but they changed them all to those energy-efficient LED ones. They're supposed to last for years without needing a bulb change. Changing lightbulbs is such a hassle, especially the ones in the high ceilings. You have to drag the stepladder out of the garage. My garage is a complete mess right now, just boxes of stuff I haven't unpacked since I moved into this rental. Cardboard boxes attract spiders, you know. Brown recluses like dark, dry places... wait. Did you ask me to spell something?

The three words? Uh... I don't... I can't remember them. I know you just said them, but they're gone. My memory has just been slipping lately. It's like water through a sieve. Sieves are great for making powdered sugar frosting, though. My ex-wife used to bake these incredible lemon cakes from scratch. She'd use a real zester for the lemon peel. Zesters are so sharp, you have to be really careful not to scrape your knuckles. I cut my hand pretty bad once trying to fix the lawnmower blade. Lawnmowers always seem to break right at the beginning of summer, when the grass is growing the fastest. The smell of cut grass is supposed to be a distress signal from the plants, did you know that? It's like they're screaming because they're being chopped down. I read that in a magazine at the dentist's office. The dentist always has those old, crinkled magazines from like three years ago. The waiting room chairs are always that weird vinyl material that sticks to the back of your legs if you wear shorts. I never wear shorts anymore, not since I had to get those stitches on my knee from when I tripped on the curb outside the station... wait. What did you want me to remember again? Was it about a cake?

Nice to meet you too, Doc. Well, I guess what brings me in is... I just keep messing up these little things lately. Careless stuff, really. Like, I was working on this wood project in the garage—my neighbor asked me to build a birdhouse for his grandkids. Good kids, they visit him every July from Ohio. I think it's Ohio. Anyway, I measured the board, just the once, and still ended up cutting it a hair short because I just skipped right over the small print on the plans. It’s frustrating. 

And then the other day at the senior center, I ended up writing the completely wrong time on the sign-up sheet for a class. Martha at the front desk—she's a sweetheart, makes this incredible pecan pie, though she uses way too much corn syrup if you ask me—she had to track everybody down to fix my mess. I felt awful about it. So, yeah... wait, what did you ask me again? Oh, right, why I'm here. Just... making those kinds of little mistakes a lot.

Memory? No, not really. My memory is actually pretty sharp. I can remember conversations just fine. Like, just yesterday I was talking to my brother-in-law, Gary, and I remember every word. He called to tell me he bought this old Chevy truck—a '78, I think. Beautiful baby blue color. Though he was saying the transmission slips a little when you get it into third gear. He thinks he can fix it himself, but let me tell you, Gary is not exactly a mechanic. I mean, this is the same guy who tried to fix his own kitchen sink a few years back and ended up flooding his entire basement. Ruined his wife's favorite rug. Cost him an absolute fortune to get the water damage sorted out, and she didn't let him hear the end of it for months. 

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my memory. Yeah, no, I don't forget appointments or what people tell me. It's not a memory thing. Just... you know, missing the details when I'm actually doing things.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I was just looking through some old boxes in the attic the other day. My wife wanted me to find the Christmas ornaments—she insists on putting up the tree the day after Thanksgiving, which I think is a bit much, but you know how it is. Happy wife, happy life. Anyway, I found this old box of my report cards from when I was a kid. Elementary school stuff. 

And looking at them... boy, it brought back memories. The teachers always wrote the same kind of things. They'd say I was a bright kid, but I was always forgetting my books or losing my homework. Mrs. Gable in third grade—she was a tough old bird, wore these thick glasses on a chain around her neck—she wrote that I'd just sit there staring out the window at the playground unless she came over and tapped on my desk to keep me on track. I remember they had this big oak tree outside the window, and I'd watch the squirrels chasing each other for hours. So, yeah... I guess it's not really a new thing. It's been happening since I was just a little guy.

Well, I guess the main thing is that I just stopped caring about everything I used to look forward to. My fishing gear is still sitting untouched out in the garage, and going out to the woodshop just feels like a chore now. Even when my kids try to get me to play chess with them, I’m really just going through the motions. I don't get anything out of it anymore. So, I figured I needed to come in.

It's been a while now. I'd say... about a year and seven months. That's when my wife started having health problems, and it really just changed everything at home. Ever since then, I just haven't been able to get into anything.

I'm not really sure. I mean, it was definitely a stressful time, obviously, but I don't know if that's what actually caused it. I just know that's right around the time everything kind of went flat for me.

Yeah, I'd say so. Pretty much every day. I mean, I guess there might have been a day here or there where I was just too busy at work to notice, but... no, it's been pretty constant. I just wake up and it's that same flat feeling, every single day.

Not really. I mean... I wouldn't say I feel sad or down, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting around crying or anything like that. It's mostly just that flat feeling I was talking about. I just don't really feel much of anything.

I really couldn't say for sure. Like I mentioned a minute ago, the timing definitely lines up with when she got sick, so maybe it played a part. But I don't know if that stress is the main reason I don't care about things anymore. It's just... I just don't have any interest in much of anything these days, and I honestly don't know exactly why.

No, I wouldn't say hopeless. I don't really sit around thinking things are doomed or that the future is bleak or anything like that. It's really just that flat feeling I mentioned. I just feel empty, not hopeless.

Yeah, it definitely is. At work, I've started missing things. I manage construction sites, so you can't really afford to do that—it affects deadlines and, more importantly, safety. We actually had a near-miss recently, and after that happened, I realized I couldn't just pretend it was only stress anymore. 

And it's affecting things at home, too. I mean, I'm there physically, but that's about it. My wife and kids are basically having to work around me now, instead of being able to count on me the way they used to.

No, I haven't really felt down or sad like that. I know people usually think of being depressed as crying all the time or feeling miserable, but that's not it for me. It's just that emptiness. I haven't had any stretches where I felt specifically sad or depressed, just... flat.

Yeah, I have. A lot, actually. I just keep thinking that I've completely failed my wife, my kids... and the guys at work, too. It's like, if anything goes wrong—if there's a missed appointment at home, or a cost overrun on a project, or especially a safety issue on site—I just take it as proof that I'm completely useless. I really feel like everyone would just be better off without me in charge of things.

Yeah, I have. I mean... on those early drives to the sites, before anyone else is even awake, I catch myself thinking that it would just be easier if I didn't make it there. And sometimes, the thought of just steering off the road crosses my mind. It actually scares me when that happens, because it feels a little too close.

No, I'm not. I don't... I don't actually have a plan to do it or anything like that. Like I said, the thought just kind of flashes through my mind and it really scares me when it does. I wouldn't actually go through with it. I think I just... I just want the pressure to stop.

Yeah, my sleep has been pretty bad for a while now. I mean, I can get into bed completely exhausted from the day, but then I just lie there. My mind keeps running through bills, schedules, everything going on at work. And even if I do fall asleep, I end up waking up around three or four in the morning. Then I just stare at the ceiling until it's time to get up and drive to the site. It's been happening pretty much every night for weeks.

No, I don't think so. It hasn't really let up at all. I mean... maybe there's a day here or there where I'm just too busy on a site to dwell on it, but definitely not a stretch of two whole months. It's been pretty constant this whole time.

No, I wouldn't say that. I don't really... I don't feel bad about myself as a person, if that's what you mean. I know I'm good at my job, and I know what I'm doing when I'm managing a site. So, no, it's not really an issue with my self-esteem.

I don't know. People just tell me they can't follow what I'm saying. My talking gets... mixed up, I guess. I try to explain things to them... like about the keys, and then the jail... the prayer rug... the chess pieces... I don't know. They just say they can't understand me. So I'm here.

I don't know... sometimes, I guess. Sometimes I feel... real good. Like, high up. Powerful. I end up laughing and... talking real loud to everybody. 

But... if they start asking me things, questioning what I'm doing... I don't like that. I snap. Might just shout at 'em over some little thing. I just... yeah.

I guess... maybe. Sometimes. When I feel like that... I just know I could fix the whole building. Every floor. Better than anyone. I could probably... teach the bosses how to actually run the place. 

I don't know. I just think... maybe people all over town would know me. For... how I see things. My special way. That's all.

...Yeah. Sometimes. Just... when I'm working, I guess. By the vents... or the mop closet. 

I hear a man. He... he says my name. Tells me I ruined everything. It sounds real. Like... like he's standing right next to me. But nobody's there. That's it.

...Yeah. I do. 

Even when I'm... just normal. Not feeling high up, not feeling low. Just... regular. There was a stretch, maybe... a few weeks, a month back. I was fine. But I still heard him. In the vents. 

And... I still knew the people working in the offices were doing things. Moving their pens a certain way. Coughing when I walked by. Signaling each other about me. Even when I was calm. It didn't stop.

...Yeah. I guess so. 

Some days... bad days... I just sit there. On the edge of the bed. After my morning prayer. I just... I feel heavy. Empty. Like... what's the point? No point in getting cleaned up. No point going outside. Just... sit there.

...Yeah. I suppose. 

I used to... do things. Take pictures. Play chess. Go to the mosque. 

Just... don't care to anymore. The camera just stays in the drawer. And... when people call, neighbors I used to cook for... I just don't answer.

...Yeah. 

I just... I think about things. Things I've done. I feel like... I brought shame. On my family. On the mosque. 

Every time I lose a job... every time the neighbors look at me that way... it's just... it's my fault. I deserve it. Whatever happens. I just... I deserve it.

...I don't know. 

I mean... sometimes. When things get real dark. 

I just... I catch myself hoping I won't wake up. Just go to sleep and... that's it. Sometimes I just think it'd be easier if I... disappeared for good.

...I don't know. 

I guess... maybe? I mean, the voice is just... it's there a lot. And the heavy feeling... that comes and goes. 

I don't really keep track of the days like that. It's just... a lot of days.

...I guess so.

They use it to fill the forklift tires, and it has this huge gauge on it with a little red needle. Red needles always remind me of compasses. My dad gave me a compass when we went camping upstate once. We slept in this green tent, but it leaked when it rained. It rained so much that weekend. The mud got absolutely everywhere, all over my sneakers. They were those white ones with the blue stripe. I tried to wash them in the sink when we got back, but the mud just stained the porcelain. The landlord was so mad about the sink. He always wore these tiny little glasses that sat right on the very end of his nose.

Making friends? No, I don't think it was hard. I had friends when I was little, I understood them fine. Like my friend Tyler in elementary school. We used to trade those little plastic alien figures at recess. They came in these round plastic capsules from the vending machines at the grocery store. You had to put in two quarters and turn the heavy metal knob, and it made this loud clacking sound. Clack, clack. The grocery store always smelled like bleach and old cardboard near the front doors. My mom used to get so many cardboard boxes from them when we moved. We packed everything in them, even the good plates. She wrapped the plates in newspaper so they wouldn't break, and the newspaper ink got all over my hands. It was black, but when you washed it in the sink it turned kind of grayish-purple. Purple is a weird color. You don't see a lot of purple cars on the highway.

Yeah, I guess... I guess that's why they brought me in. At the warehouse, I keep doing things like freezing with my arms up by the forklift. Or I'll copy the beeping sounds it makes when it backs up, or I'll do the hand signals, or I just move the boxes in these strange little patterns. Even when everyone is yelling for me to stop, I just... keep doing it. Yelling is so loud in that warehouse because of the high ceilings. They have these huge metal rafters up there, and sometimes pigeons get inside and sit on them. Pigeons always bob their heads when they walk, it's so funny. I tried to feed one a piece of a hotdog bun once when I was sitting on a park bench. The bench had all this chipped green paint on it. Green paint always flakes off in these little curly pieces. My uncle had a green truck that did that. He drove it all the way to Florida once to see the ocean. The ocean is so salty, it makes your skin feel all tight when it dries.

No, um... I don't think anyone really moves my arms around for me. People don't usually touch me like that. Except maybe my supervisor when he grabs my shoulder to get my attention at the loading dock. He always wears these really thick leather work gloves. Leather gets so stiff when it's cold out, you know? Like if you leave it in your car overnight. I left my jacket in my car once during a snowstorm and it was basically frozen solid the next morning. My car's heater is totally busted anyway, it just blows out this freezing air and all this gray dust from the vents. Dust is actually mostly dead skin cells, which is pretty gross when you really think about it. I saw this whole documentary about dust mites on the TV in the breakroom once. The volume on that TV doesn't work, so it's just silent video of microscopic bugs and stuff crawling around. Bugs always have way too many legs. Centipedes are the worst ones.

No, nobody really says that to me. I don't think my face looks blank, I mean, I smile and stuff. I see my face in the mirror every morning before work. The mirror in our bathroom has this weird smudge in the corner that won't come off, no matter how much glass cleaner I spray on it. Glass cleaner always smells so strongly of ammonia, you know? It smells exactly like the heavy-duty stuff we use at the warehouse to mop the breakroom floors. The mop bucket we have is bright yellow and one of the little plastic wheels is totally busted, so it just squeaks and drags across the linoleum. Squeak, scrape. Linoleum gets so dangerously slippery when it's wet. My roommate slipped on some wet leaves outside our apartment stairs last week and completely ruined his favorite shoes. They were these canvas sneakers with red laces. Red is the color of stop signs, but people in my neighborhood just roll right through them anyway. It's really dangerous to just ignore traffic signs like that.

I... I don't know, I mean, you haven't tried to do that. I don't really think my arm would just stay there, but I guess I don't know for sure. I don't really like people touching my arms though. I got this really bad sunburn on my arms once when I fell asleep at the beach. The sand gets everywhere when you lay down on a towel. It's so hard to get sand out of your car floor mats once it's in there. I tried using those big vacuums at the car wash, the ones that take quarters? But they never have enough suction. Quarters are so heavy if you have a lot of them in your pocket. My grandpa used to collect state quarters in this big blue binder. He had almost all of them before he lost the binder when he moved to a new apartment. Moving is such a hassle, you have to pack everything into those cardboard boxes. Cardboard gives you the worst paper cuts if you're not careful. I got a paper cut on my thumb yesterday and it stung every time I washed my hands. The soap in the warehouse bathroom is that cheap pink stuff that smells like fake cherries. Cherries always have pits in them, which is annoying when you're trying to eat them. You have to spit the pits out into a napkin or something. Napkins at fast food places are always so thin, you need like ten of them just to wipe your hands.

No, um... I don't hear any voices telling me to do stuff like that. I mean, it's really loud at the warehouse anyway, so it's hard to hear people even when they're standing right next to you. The forklifts are always driving around, and they have that really high-pitched backup alarm. Beep, beep, beep. It echoes all the way up to the ceilings. The ceilings in there are just exposed corrugated metal. Metal gets so incredibly hot in the summer when the sun beats down on the roof. You could probably fry an egg on the hood of a car in that parking lot in July. I tried frying an egg on the sidewalk when I was a kid because I saw it on a cartoon, but it just made a gross, sticky mess. Eggs are so weird if you really think about it, just liquid inside a fragile little shell. I dropped a whole carton of eggs at the grocery store once and felt so bad. The floor was covered in this yellow slime. Yellow is a really intense color, like those high-visibility vests they make us wear at work. The reflective tape on mine is starting to peel off at the edges. Tape never sticks right once it gets dusty.

Yeah, people say that a lot, actually. Like at work, when the supervisor asks me which pallets are going on the truck, I start trying to explain the load sheet, but then my words just kind of jump... like, I'll start talking about the load sheet, and then suddenly I'm talking about my old house, and then fishing, and then these boxes from church. And by the time I'm done talking, nobody has any idea what I meant. Church always smells like old wood and those little wax candles. They have those tiny little cups for communion, they look like little shot glasses but they're made of flimsy plastic. Plastic is so bad for the ocean, you know? I saw this documentary where a sea turtle had a plastic straw stuck in its nose, and the guys on the boat had to pull it out with pliers. Pliers are really handy to have around. I keep a pair in the glovebox of my car just in case. My glovebox is mostly full of old registration papers and ketchup packets from the drive-thru. Fast food ketchup always tastes sweeter than the kind you buy in the bottle at the store. Glass bottles are so heavy to carry in grocery bags, especially if the handles on the bags start stretching out.

I don't think so... I mean, people don't usually say my beliefs are strange. Sometimes they just don't listen to me anyway. Like the other guys at the warehouse, they just talk about sports or whatever they watched on TV. I don't really watch TV much anymore, the screen gives me a headache if I stare at it too long. My TV is one of those older flat screens, the kind with the really thick plastic border around the edge. Dust always settles right on that bottom edge, no matter how much you wipe it. I tried using those microfiber cloths, but they just sort of push the dust around instead of picking it up. You have to wash those cloths separate from your regular clothes, or else they get all these little lint balls stuck to them. Lint traps in dryers are so satisfying to clean out, you just peel it off in one big fuzzy layer. But if you forget to clean it, it's a huge fire hazard. Firefighters have to wear all that heavy gear, even in the summer. It must be so exhausting carrying all that weight around. I used to carry my backpack full of textbooks in college, and my shoulders would ache by the end of the day. Textbooks are ridiculously expensive, they make you buy a new edition every year just because they changed a couple of pictures. Pictures never look as good printed on paper as they do on a screen anyway.

Yeah, it's been going on for a while. The confusing talking and, you know, the weird stuff I do at the warehouse... it's been happening for about six months now. Six months is a long time, half a year. That's how long it takes to get a car's oil changed, if you drive a lot. I always forget to change my oil until the little sticker on the windshield gets all faded and curled at the edges. Windshields get so dirty in the spring with all the pollen. The yellow dust just coats everything, it looks like someone dumped mustard powder all over the cars. Mustard is okay, but I prefer mayo on sandwiches. Mayo goes bad really fast if you leave it out of the fridge. Refrigerators hum so loud at night when the house is quiet. It's like this low buzzing noise that just drills into your head. Drills are super loud too, especially the heavy-duty ones they use for concrete. Concrete takes forever to dry, and if you step in it, you leave a footprint forever. I saw a dog footprint in the sidewalk once, just this perfect little paw shape right in the middle of the square. Dogs are always sniffing everything, they have such a strong sense of smell. I wonder if they can smell the pollen before it even falls from the trees. Trees look so bare in the winter without their leaves.

Yeah, it's... it's definitely been worse. They actually took me off forklift duties at the warehouse because they said they can't trust me to keep things safe around me anymore. And I've fallen way behind in my community college classes, too. I even stopped showing up for my shifts at the church food bank because people kept saying they couldn't count on me. Canned food is really heavy when you have to carry a whole box of it. Some of those cans don't even have the pull-tabs on top, you have to use a manual can opener. Manual can openers always get rusty if you wash them and don't dry them right away. Rust is so hard to get off metal, you have to scrub it with steel wool or something. Steel wool feels so scratchy, it's like touching a Brillo pad. Brillo pads always have that weird blue soap dried inside them. Soap smells nice, but if you get it in your eyes, it burns so bad. I got shampoo in my eye once and it was red for the rest of the day. Red is a warning color, like stop signs and fire trucks. Fire trucks are huge, I don't know how they turn those tight corners on city streets without hitting the parked cars. Parked cars get so hot inside during the summer, it's like an oven when you first open the door.

Hi, thank you so much for seeing me. Um, I hope I'm explaining this right, but... well, honestly, what made me finally make an appointment is just some little things at work. I'm in advertising sales, and we have these really, really long strategy meetings. 

And I just... I keep getting up when I know I’m supposed to stay seated. Like, I’ll make up little reasons to leave my chair, even if it’s just to go refill my water for the third time, or I'll kind

Um, well, I guess so? I mean, I was a good kid, I promise. But I do remember this starting way back, like, way before high school. In elementary school, my teachers would always write on my report cards that I was... well, they always made sure to say I was a bright student! Which was really nice of them. 

But, um, they'd also say I rushed through my work a little bit. And maybe talked out of turn sometimes? I feel a little silly admitting this, but they also mentioned I'd forget my homework, and my desk was always just kind of... stuffed with half-finished papers. I think I was just really eager and enthusiastic to move on to the next thing, you know? Is that the kind of thing you mean?

Um, worrying? Not really, no. I mean, I care about my job and doing well, of course, but I wouldn't say I sit around worrying about things that aren't happening. I try to stay pretty positive! I'm more of an upbeat person, I think. I don't really get stuck in my head with anxious thoughts or anything like that. I hope that's okay? I just... I don't think worrying is really one of my struggles.

Hello. Well... I guess what really scared me enough to finally come in today is... I just keep thinking that it would be a relief if I didn't wake up. You know, if I just went to sleep and that was it. I haven't tried to hurt myself or do anything like that, but... having those thoughts just really frightened me.

No, like I was just saying... I don't have any real intention or plan to do it. I haven't tried to hurt myself at all. It's really just that feeling I mentioned, where I keep thinking it would be such a relief to just not wake up. I don't actually want to kill myself, but having those thoughts sitting there in my head is what scared me enough to come get help.
Yes, I have. Most mornings I just wake up with this heavy sadness in my chest. It's like... like I've already failed the day before it even starts.
No, I don't think so. I mean, I've had sad days before, like anyone else, but... never anything like this. This is the first time it's been this bad, where it just doesn't go away.
Well, I suppose it started about four months ago. That's when my aunt moved in to live with us. It's been going on ever since then.

Yes, I have. I used to really look forward to my watercolors, and going to dance class, or just walking with the ladies. But lately... I just leave my painting things sitting there. I just can't seem to make myself care about any of it anymore.
I'm not really sure. I mean, it started right around the time she got here, but... I don't know if it's actually because of her. It's hard to say. I just know they happened at the same time.
No, I haven't really noticed any change there. I still eat my regular meals, so... my appetite seems about the same as it always is.
No, my sleep has been fine, really. I still go to bed around the same time and wake up when I usually do. So, no trouble there.
No, not really. I haven't noticed any problems with that. I can still pay attention to things just fine, like if I'm watching TV or just doing things around the house. So my focus seems okay.

Yeah, actually, I have. Even after a full night in bed, my body just feels worn out. It seems like just doing normal things around the house, like carrying a basket of laundry or making breakfast... it takes a lot more out of me than it should.

Yeah, I do. Sometimes when I feel tired or get annoyed with my aunt, I just... I start thinking I'm a bad woman. I get it in my head that I'm bringing shame on my family because I should be more grateful.

Well, my husband says I do. He tells me I move like everything takes extra effort now. And I guess I do notice it when I go to the market... I'll just stand there way too long before I actually pick up what I came for.

Yeah, I have. I just... I've stopped going to my dance class and my walking group. I even stopped doing my shifts at the food pantry. And since I get stuck and just fall behind on everything, my husband has had to take over a lot more of the errands for me.

Well, I came in because... I just feel completely flat inside. It doesn't matter what's going on around me. Even when my children come over to sit with me, or when the sun is shining right on my garden—things that usually make me happy—I just don't feel anything good. It's like the part of me that could feel glad or comforted just shut off completely.

No, I haven't. I mean, at my age, you certainly go through your share of hard times and sad days, but... no. I've never had a time where I just felt absolutely nothing at all like this. This is the first time.
No, nothing like that. I haven't seen or heard anything that isn't really there. My mind is clear in that way, just... empty.

No, I haven't. I don't want to die or anything like that. I know I said I feel empty, but... well, I haven't had any thoughts about life not being worth living. I just wish I could feel the good parts of it again.
No, I don't think so. I mean, at my age, I don't exactly rush around anyway, but... no, I haven't noticed myself moving or talking any slower than my usual.
No, my appetite has been fine. I still eat my regular meals every day, just like always. I haven't noticed any changes with that.
No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad or down. I'm not sitting around crying or anything like that. Like I mentioned earlier, it's more just... an empty feeling. But no, I haven't really felt sad.

No, not unusually tired. I have about the same amount of energy I normally do. I mean, at my age I get a bit worn out by the end of the day, but it hasn't been any worse than usual. I don't feel drained or anything out of the ordinary.
No, I still like doing my usual things. I still tend to my garden a bit in the mornings, and I watch my programs in the evening. I haven't lost interest in any of that.

Yes, actually, I have. I used to... well, I used to plan all my own meals and keep my calendar straight without any trouble. But lately, I just stare at a grocery list or the schedule for the senior center, and my mind just goes completely blank. My daughter has had to start helping me decide on even the most simple things because I just can't seem to focus on it.

No, I haven't felt that way. I mean, it's a little frustrating having to rely on my daughter so much lately for things I used to do myself, but... I don't feel worthless. I know I still matter to my family, so no, I wouldn't say I've been feeling like that.
No, my sleep hasn't really changed. I still go to bed around the same time and wake up when I usually do. I haven't noticed sleeping any more or less than I normally would.
Well, this has been going on for about two weeks now. It started right after my husband collapsed... ever since the paramedics were in our kitchen working on him, I've just felt this way.

Hi. Nice to meet you too. Um, I decided to come in because... well, lately, especially after some really long days out on the site, or if I've had a late neighborhood meeting, I’ll come home and just eat way more than I meant to. 

I'll just kind of go through whatever's there—leftover takeout, cereal, chips, just whatever is around—and I don't really stop until I’m just uncomfortably full. It's been bothering me enough that I figured I should probably talk to someone about it.

Yeah, that's exactly what it feels like. Once I start on those evenings, it's like I'm just on autopilot. I'll be standing there, telling myself I need to stop because I have an early start with the crew the next morning, but... I just keep going back to the kitchen for more anyway. I know I shouldn't, but I just can't seem to make myself stop once I get going.

Yeah, um... I do sometimes. Not every time, but maybe a few times a month after those bad nights, I'll go into the bathroom and make myself throw up. I just... I start to panic, honestly. I get really worked up about undoing all the effort I’ve put into staying in shape and looking put-together, especially since I need to maintain a certain presence on the job site. So, yeah, I do make myself sick to try and fix it.

Well, looking back over the last few months... I guess the whole pattern of overeating and then making myself sick averages out to about once a week. It varies, though. Like, some weeks it might happen twice, and then other weeks it won't happen at all. But yeah, if I really average it out, it's probably about weekly.

It affects me a lot, honestly. Since I started wearing more fitted work clothes and being the one up front running the site meetings... I don't know, I just catch myself judging my whole day based on how I look. Like, if my pants feel even a little tight, or if I think people can see my stomach, it just ruins my mood. It's pretty much always on my mind.

Well, it's nice to meet you too. I, uh, I guess what brings me in is just... I cannot keep my mind on one thing anymore. Not for the life of me. It's getting so bad at work, and I've been a carpenter for, gosh, almost forty years now, so you'd think I'd have a handle on things, right? But lately, it's just impossible. I'll be right in the middle of measuring out a cut, or trying to review an invoice in the trailer, and the second something else happens—like, if someone starts up a table saw on the other side of the site, or even if one of the guys just walks past the window—bam. My focus is gone. I'm looking at them, wondering what they're working on, or I'll suddenly remember this completely different job we're supposed to bid on next week, and I'll start thinking about the lumber costs for that. And then, before I know it, twenty minutes have gone by, I haven't made my cut, I haven't finished the invoice, and I'm off doing something else entirely. It's like the whole day just completely gets away from me, piece by piece, and I get to the end of my shift and realize I've barely finished a single thing I set out to do in the morning. It's just exhausting, you know? I didn't used to be this scattered.

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've been thinking about the timeline a lot lately, just trying to make sense of it all. I mean, I've always been a little distractible, sure, but nothing like this. This... this specific level of trouble, where I feel like my brain is just a sieve, that's been going on for about a year and a month now. I know the exact timing because it all started right after I broke my wrist. It was a stupid accident, really—just slipped on some ice loading up the truck—but it meant I couldn't swing a hammer or handle the heavy materials for a good long while. So, the boss, he's a good guy, he shifted me into the shop, doing all the paperwork, the ordering, the invoicing, and just sort of supervising the younger guys instead of doing the hands-on carpentry I've been doing my whole life. 

And I thought, okay, this'll be fine, it's a nice break for my body, right? But sitting at that desk... oh my gosh. When I'm working with my hands, building something, it's like my body keeps my brain anchored. But sitting there looking at spreadsheets and supplier emails? It's like my mind just detaches and floats away. I'll be trying to reconcile a lumber bill, and then I'll hear the guys laughing outside, and suddenly I'm out there in my head, or I'm reorganizing the filing cabinet, or I'm just staring at the screen thinking about a completely different project. So, yeah, it's been about thirteen months of this absolute chaos since they moved me off the tools and into the office. It's just been a completely different world, and honestly, I don't think my brain was built for it.

No, no, I didn't hit my head. I know that's probably what you're thinking, like maybe I got a concussion or something, right? Because I know that can mess with your memory and your focus. My brother-in-law got a bad concussion a few years back playing softball, of all things, and he was in a fog for months. But no, nothing like that for me. 

When I slipped, it was one of those really sudden things where your feet just go completely out from under you. You know how black ice is, you don't even see it until you're already going down. I was carrying this heavy bundle of trim, and I think my instinct was just to drop it and put my hand out to catch myself, which, you know, they always tell you not to do, but it's just a reflex! So all my weight, plus the momentum, just went right into my right wrist. Heard a horrible crunching sound, which I'll never forget. But my head? No, my head never touched the ground. I ended up kind of twisting as I fell, so I landed hard on my side and my arm, but my head was perfectly safe. 

I even went to the emergency room right after—well, one of the guys drove me, I obviously couldn't drive with my wrist swelling up like a balloon—and they checked me over pretty thoroughly. Did the x-rays on the arm, obviously, but the doctor there, he asked me the same thing, if I hit my head, if I felt dizzy or sick, and I told him no. And I haven't had any headaches or anything since then, either. Just the wrist. And then, of course, the whole nightmare of being stuck at that desk trying to do paperwork when my brain just absolutely refuses to cooperate. So, yeah, no head injury, just a really, really busted wrist and a whole lot of frustration.

Down? Depressed? No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, frustrated? Absolutely. I am so frustrated I could spit nails most days, just because I can't seem to get my brain to do what it's supposed to do. But depressed... no. It's not like a sadness or a dark cloud or anything like that. I know what that looks like. My older sister went through a really rough patch with depression a few years back, and she couldn't even bring herself to get out of bed or make a cup of tea. It was just heartbreaking to watch her go through that. 

But for me, it's nothing like that. I still have plenty of energy. I'm up at 5:00 AM every morning, bright and early, I make my coffee, I pack my lunch, I'm ready to tackle the day. I still love my life, you know? I love my husband, I love spending time with my grandkids on the weekends—we just built a little birdhouse together last Sunday, actually, which was wonderful because I finally got to use my hands again and just show them how to sand down the edges properly. So the joy is still there, and the motivation to do things is definitely still there. 

It's just... it's just this invisible wall I hit the second I sit down at that desk in the trailer. It's exasperating, and sure, I come home complaining about it to my husband, probably talking his ear off about how I stared at a purchase order for an hour without reading a single word. He's even asked me a couple of times, "Honey, are you getting depressed about being off the tools?" And I tell him the exact same thing I'm telling you: I'm not sad, and I'm not down in the dumps. I'm just completely and utterly fed up with my own brain for not cooperating with this office work. So, no, definitely not depressed. Just... annoyed. Very, very annoyed with myself.

Well, you know, it’s funny you ask about school, because I was actually just talking to my husband about this the other day when we were cleaning out the attic and found some of my old report cards. My mom kept everything, bless her heart, every single little piece of paper. And looking back at those... oh boy. Even way back then, like, grade school, definitely before I was even twelve years old, it was the same story over and over. 

I mean, I wasn't a bad kid. I wasn't running around the classroom causing trouble or anything like that. But every single teacher, from Mrs. Higgins in second grade to Mr. Abernathy in fifth, they all wrote the exact same things in the margins. "Bright but careless." That was the phrase. "She’s a bright girl, but she’s so careless." 

I was always, always losing my homework. I’d do it at the kitchen table, I know I did it, but by the time I got to school, it was just... gone. Vanished. Or the teacher would stand at the front of the room and give us three simple instructions, like, "Get out your math book, turn to page forty, and do the odd numbers." And by the time she finished the sentence, I was already lost. I’d have my spelling book out and be wondering what we were having for lunch. 

I spent half my childhood just staring out the window. I remember in fourth grade, my desk was right next to this big window that looked out over the playground and the street, and I would just watch the cars go by, or watch the janitor sweeping the sidewalk, instead of finishing whatever worksheet we were supposed to be doing. My mom would get so frustrated at parent-teacher conferences, because they’d tell her I just wasn't applying myself. But it wasn't that I didn't want to! It was just like my brain had a mind of its own, even back then. So, yeah, the trouble paying attention? It’s definitely not a new thing, even if it feels a hundred times worse now that I'm stuck behind a desk all day. It’s always been there, just kind of humming in the background, making me lose my math homework.

Nice to meet you too. Well, I'm here because... people just keep telling me I'm not listening. 

My supervisor at the plant, or my wife, they'll be talking straight to me, and a minute later I realize I only caught about half of what they said. Then I'm stuck asking them to say it all over again. It's causing a lot of frustration, so I figured I needed to come in and see what's going on.
No, my hearing is fine. I passed the hearing test at work not too long ago. It's not that I can't hear them talking, it's just... the words don't always stick.

Yeah, I was like this even as a kid. I remember teachers were always moving my seat around because I just couldn't stay put. I'd call out answers in class, and... well, I got into trouble a lot for butting into other kids' work. That was all happening way back before middle school, even.

Yeah, it definitely happens at home. My wife and kids... they get pretty frustrated with me. Instead of helping keep things running smoothly around the house, I just end up disrupting whatever routine we have going. 

And honestly, it's getting really bad at the plant, too. It’s serious enough now that I’ve actually had formal warnings. I'm really worried I could lose my job over this, or... or even cause a safety problem on the line. That's really why I had to come in.

No, I wouldn't say I'm an anxious person. I mean, sure, I'm worried about my job right now, but that's not what's causing the problem. It's not like I'm sitting there panicking and that's why I can't listen. It's just... I just can't seem to stay tuned in, no matter how calm I am.

Yeah, all the time. If I'm sitting in a safety huddle at the plant or just at the dinner table at home, my leg is always bouncing. My hands are always messing with something, like a pen or my keys. People even tell me I'm shaking the whole bench sometimes. It's just really hard to sit still.

Well, I guess what brings me in is... I've just stopped wanting to do the things that usually keep me going. 

I don't really know how else to say it, but I just don't have it in me lately. Usually, I'm out doing things—going to salsa nights, church gatherings, or cooking for the neighbors. But I've stopped doing all of that. I don't even want to walk out into my shop just to enjoy the smell of the wood anymore. And I'm a carpenter, so... that's usually my favorite place to be. I just don't have any interest in any of it right now.

Yeah, I have. Most mornings I wake up with this... this heavy, empty feeling right in my chest. It's hard to explain, but it just feels like all the color has completely gone out of the house. I honestly have to force myself not to break down in front of my wife.

Yeah, it did. It started about two months ago. My wife's health suddenly declined, and... well, our whole daily routine just changed overnight. That's really when this whole change in my mood and how I've been acting started. It's been going on for about two months now.
My sleep? Um... I haven't really noticed any changes there, to be honest. I guess I'm sleeping about the same as I always do.
No, not really. I mean, I guess I'm still eating my regular meals. I haven't noticed any real change with my appetite.
