Yeah, I do. Mostly it's... well, I just feel a lot of guilt. I keep replaying every single appointment and every little change in my wife's health in my head. I just keep telling myself that a better husband would have caught it sooner. Like I should have been able to protect her somehow, and I didn't. So, yeah... I feel pretty worthless when I think about that.

Yeah, I have. It's actually been a real problem at work. I'm a carpenter, and... well, lately I'll just stare at blueprints that I've been reading my whole life, and the lines just kind of blur together in my head. I can't seem to process it. I end up having to ask the younger guys on the crew to repeat things that I should understand right away. It's just really hard to keep my mind on what I'm doing.

Yeah, the guys at work have actually pointed that out. Sometimes I feel like... like my boots are full of wet cement. It takes me forever just to walk across the shop or bend down to pick up a board. Everything just feels so heavy. But then other times, I get stuck doing the opposite. I'll just be pacing around the shop, rubbing my hands together, not actually getting any work done. It's like I can't settle down, but I'm not moving with any purpose either.

I... I honestly don't know. I mean, I've never been through something like this before, with her being so sick, so I don't really have anything to compare it to. It's just... it's all pretty overwhelming right now. I couldn't tell you if it's stronger than it should be, or what's normal to expect. I just know I feel awful.

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I’m here because... honestly, work has just become completely unmanageable lately. I’m a registered nurse, and I work on a really busy floor—which I used to love, you know, the fast pace and everything, I’ve got my graduate degree and I’ve always pushed myself to be on top of things—but lately, the main reason I’m here is that I just lose my train of thought constantly on the floor. Like, constantly. It’s actually getting kind of scary. 

I’ll be in the middle of figuring out a really complex patient flow issue, like trying to coordinate discharges and admissions or sorting out who needs to go where, and all it takes is one little thing to completely derail me. An IV pump starts beeping down the hall, or, you know, someone at the nurses' station asks another nurse a totally unrelated question about a chart or something, or a call light goes off three doors down. And it's like... poof. My brain just wipes completely blank. Suddenly I’m standing there and I have absolutely zero idea what I was just working on or what I was about to do. And in nursing, you really can't afford to just forget what you're doing, so I spend half my shift just trying to retrace my own steps because every single noise or interruption just completely pulls my attention away and I can't get it back.

Yeah, actually, I really did. It’s funny you ask that because I was just talking to my mom about this recently when I was trying to figure out why I'm struggling so much now. I mean, if you look all the way back to elementary school, like second or third grade, it was always the exact same story. Every single parent-teacher conference, every report card, the teachers would always write these long notes saying that I was a really bright girl, that I had so much potential, but that I was just so... careless. That was the word they always used. Careless. 

Because I was just constantly losing things. I'd do a worksheet—like those spelling or math worksheets we always had—and I would actually do the work, or at least most of it, but then it would just vanish into the black hole of my desk or get completely crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack. Or I'd just completely forget to turn it in. I'd walk right past the homework tray in the morning. It was like there was a total disconnect between doing the assignment and actually finishing the process of handing it over. 

And it got to the point where my mom... bless her heart, she was working too, but she literally had to sit with me at the kitchen table every single night. Just to keep me on track. If she got up for even a second to stir a pot on the stove or answer the landline, I'd instantly be staring at the wall or peeling the paper off my crayons or just completely off in my own world. She had to sit right there, hovering over my shoulder, basically micromanaging my entire evening just so I could get through a basic half-hour assignment. It was exhausting for her, and honestly, it was frustrating for me because I wanted to just do it and go play, but I couldn't seem to stay focused unless she was right there acting like my... I don't know, my external brain. And even then, after all that effort of her sitting with me, I'd still somehow manage to lose the paper on the bus the next morning, which would just start the whole cycle over again...

Oh, absolutely. It’s not just work at all. It’s... honestly, it’s everything. It bleeds into every single part of my life, which is just so exhausting. Like, I’ll have these totally routine things that I need to do, things that a normal adult should just be able to handle without a second thought, and they just completely slip my mind. 

For instance, paying bills. You’d think that would be easy, right? You get a bill, you pay it. But I’ll get the electric bill in the mail, I’ll open it, I’ll look at it, and I’ll think, "Okay, I need to log in and pay this." And then maybe the dog barks, or I notice a spot on the counter that needs wiping, and... it’s gone. Completely gone from my brain. I’ve had my electricity shut off before, not because I didn’t have the money, but literally just because I forgot to click the button to pay it. And I’ll even try to outsmart myself, you know? I’ll set a reminder on my phone. "Pay electric bill at 6 PM." The alarm goes off at 6 PM, I look at it, I swipe it away thinking, "Okay, I’ll do that in exactly two minutes when I finish making this sandwich," and then... poof. Two weeks later, I’m sitting in the dark.

And it’s not just chores, it’s my relationships, too. My sister will call me and leave a voicemail, or text me to ask a quick question, and I’ll read it and think, "Oh, I need to call her back as soon as I finish this shift or as soon as I get home." And I genuinely mean to. I want to talk to her! But the thought just evaporates. Days will go by, and then she’ll text me again, clearly annoyed, asking if I’m ignoring her. And I feel so terrible because I’m not ignoring her, I just literally forgot she existed in that context for three days. 

Even appointments. I’ll schedule a dentist appointment six months in advance, write it on the calendar on the fridge, put it in my phone calendar, set a reminder for the day before... and I will still somehow manage to miss it. Because on the actual day, I’ll get distracted by something else in the morning, and suddenly it’s 3 PM and I was supposed to be in the chair at 1 PM. It’s like my brain just cannot hold onto these basic, everyday tasks, no matter how many safety nets I try to set up for myself. It’s just so incredibly frustrating to feel like I can’t even manage my own life outside of the hospital, let alone inside it.

Well, I mean, like I was just saying about the childhood stuff with my mom having to sit with me, that underlying scattered feeling has always kind of been there, humming in the background of my life. But it was never, ever this severe. I mean, I managed to get through nursing school, I got my graduate degree, I had all these little workarounds that kept me afloat. 

But this current situation? Where I feel like I'm completely losing my grip on reality? This has been a major problem since I took on the expanded charge-nurse responsibilities almost two years ago. It’ll be exactly two years this fall, actually. Because before that, I was just a regular floor nurse. I had my specific patients for the shift, usually just three or four, and I could just zero in on them. I had my checklist, I had my routine, and I could handle it. 

But then our unit manager pulled me into her office and gave me this whole speech about how I had my master's now and I was such a strong clinician, and they really needed someone to step up and take over the charge role for the day shift. And of course, I was flattered, so I said yes. But I had no idea what I was actually agreeing to. Suddenly, I’m not just managing my own assignment, I’m managing the entire floor. I'm doing the staffing matrix for the next shift, I'm fielding back-to-back calls from the ER about incoming admissions, I'm tracking which of our thirty-two beds is being cleaned by environmental services, I'm dealing with pharmacy delays, I'm stepping in when family members are upset... all at the exact same time. 

It’s just... it's like someone opened a hundred tabs in my brain and then froze the computer. Ever since I took that on, almost two years ago, it's just been this massive, snowballing disaster. I kept telling myself, "Oh, you just need a few months to adjust to the new role, everyone gets overwhelmed at first," but it's been two years. Two years of just constantly dropping the ball. And because my brain is so completely fried by the end of my shift from trying to juggle all those expanded duties, I have absolutely nothing left for my actual life when I clock out, which is why the bills and the appointments and my sister are all just falling through the cracks now...

Worrying? Um... no, not really. I mean, not in the sense of just sitting around agonizing over things when everything is actually fine. I know some people do that, like they just spin out over the "what ifs" or borrow trouble from the future, worrying about things that haven't even happened yet or might never happen at all. 

But for me, it's... well, I don't really have the luxury of worrying about things that aren't immediate problems, because I feel like I am constantly drowning in actual, tangible, immediate problems. The things I get stressed out about are the very real, very concrete things that I am currently messing up or forgetting right in that moment. Like, I'm not sitting at home worrying "oh, what if something bad happens next week." I'm stressing because I know I forgot to update the staffing matrix at work, or I'm stressing because I know I was supposed to call my sister back three days ago and I still haven't done it and now she's mad at me. It's always tied directly to a ball I've actually dropped. 

My brain is just so incredibly consumed with trying to keep up with the sheer chaos of my actual, current reality that there's just no room left to invent things to worry about, if that makes sense? I'm basically just trying to survive the next ten minutes of my shift, or trying to remember what I walked into the kitchen for, so sitting around worrying about random possibilities or abstract things just isn't really something I do. It's just the overwhelming weight of the things I'm actively failing to manage that gets to me, not really... generalized worry.

Down or depressed? Um... no. Not really. I mean, I know what depression looks like, right? Being a nurse, I see it all the time. You see patients who just can't get out of bed, who have that flat affect, who just feel this heavy, pervasive sadness or emptiness that colors every single thing they do. And that’s... that's really not me at all. 

I don't wake up feeling hopeless or sad. Actually, it's almost the exact opposite? I wake up almost every single morning feeling like, "Okay, today is the day! Today I'm going to be organized, today I'm going to get my shift assignments done early, today I'm going to remember to pay that bill!" I have all this motivation and good intention when I start my day. I really do want to do things and I look forward to things. 

It's just that by, like, 2 PM, when I've lost my clipboard for the third time and I realize I never sent that email to the pharmacy that I drafted at 8 AM... *then* I feel bad. But it's not depression, it's just... profound frustration. I get so mad at myself. I feel defeated because I keep trying so incredibly hard and I just keep failing at these basic things. So, sure, I have moments where I want to go cry in the clean supply closet because I'm just so completely overwhelmed by everything I'm dropping, but it's always a direct reaction to me messing up, you know? It's not this dark cloud that follows me around for no reason. 

If I actually have a good day where I manage to keep my head above water, or if I'm just at home on a day off and I don't have a million demands being thrown at me, my mood is totally fine. I can laugh, I can enjoy things. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed most days. I'm just... really, really tired of feeling incompetent. But the sadness is just frustration, really.

Restless? Like, physically can't sit still? No, not really. I mean, I'm a nurse, so I'm on my feet for twelve hours a day anyway, constantly walking from room to room, going to the Pyxis machine, running to the supply closet, walking down to the ER to get a report... so I don't really have the opportunity to just sit and realize I can't sit still, if that makes sense? 

But even when I am home, like on my days off, I don't feel that physical urge to move. Like, I don't tap my foot, I don't bounce my leg, I don't feel like I have a motor running inside me. I see that sometimes in my pediatric patients, you know, the ones who literally cannot stay in the chair, they're climbing the exam table, they're touching everything. That's not me. 

Actually, when I finally do get to sit down at the end of the day, I just kind of... crash. I'll sit on the couch and just completely zone out because I'm so physically and mentally exhausted from the shift. I can definitely sit still for hours if I'm watching a movie or something, assuming I don't get distracted by my phone or remember a chore I forgot to do. So it's more like my *brain* is restless, constantly jumping from one thought to the next, but my body is perfectly fine staying put. I don't have that physical hyperactivity at all. I'm just tired, mostly. Really tired.

Well, I suppose what brings me in is this memorial I'm putting together for my brother. It's, well, it's gotten a lot bigger than I originally meant it to. 

I’ve been spending most of my days just chasing down the right songs, calling folks up, planning out these displays and even some trips. It takes a lot of focus. But my wife... she says I’ve completely pushed aside the garden, my walking group, and just about everything else I usually do. She's the one who thought I should come talk to you about it.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I still go to bed around my usual time. I haven't really noticed needing any less sleep... I just wake up and get right back to working on the plans for my brother. But my sleep seems about the same as it always is, as far as I know.

Well, I suppose I do have a lot of energy right now. Sometimes I just feel... lit up, you know? Full of purpose. Like I finally have this clear vision and the whole town is going to see this memorial and finally understand our family. It feels really good when I'm in that zone. But... then someone will slow me down. Like my wife, or one of the folks down at the senior center, if they question how big the display is getting. And then I just snap at them. I get real irritable if they get in the way of what I'm trying to do.

Yes, they have actually. It happened just the other day at the senior center meetings. I was trying to explain the whole vision for the memorial—you know, the songs I picked out, the quilts we're going to display, all the old photos—and I guess I just got going. Before I even realized it, I had talked right over three different people. My pastor actually had to step in and gently say, 'Aaron, let’s let someone else speak.' So, yes, I suppose I have been talking a lot more than usual when I get on the subject.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean... I'm just a regular person. I don't think I have any special gifts or anything like that. I'm just doing what needs to be done to honor my brother, you know? I don't feel more important than anybody else, I just have a job to do with this memorial, that's all.

Yes, they have. My mind just keeps jumping from one idea right to the next. Like, one minute I'm thinking about how to set up a display case for the memorial, and then... well, then I'm suddenly planning a road trip to track down a cousin of ours. And right after that, I'm focused on a verse from an old ballad I want to include. 

It just goes so fast. I try to get it all down on paper so I don't forget, but I honestly can't slow my head down enough to write any of it out in order.

Yes, I have been. I just... I can't seem to sit down in my chair like I used to. I'm constantly up and moving around. I've been hauling boxes, making phone calls, rearranging all these papers for the memorial. I just keep walking from room to room. It honestly feels like my body has more steam in it right now than a man my age ought to have. I just can't stop moving and getting things done.
Yes, they did. It's been going on for about two months now. Right after he passed away, I started working on his tribute... and well, that's exactly when all this started.

Yes, they really have. I've... well, I've completely missed my walking group and the book club I usually go to. I've just let the garden go to weeds, too. And I guess I've upset some friends down at the senior center, because... well, everything I say or do has just become about this memorial display. 

And my wife... she says our whole day just revolves around her trying to calm me down. She tells me she constantly has to step in and redirect me to stop me from making another phone call, or leaving on another trip, or getting into an argument with somebody. So, yes, it's definitely taking a toll on things.

No, I haven't done anything like that. I mean... I'm not spending money I don't have or doing anything dangerous. All my focus is just on getting this memorial right for my brother. I haven't been buying things I don't need or making any reckless choices. So, no, nothing like that.

Well, yes, actually. Sometimes when I'm sitting at the kitchen table, you know, sorting through his old song sheets for the display... I'll hear him. 

I hear his voice, clear as day, just humming right behind me. Or sometimes he's telling me which tune is supposed to come next. My wife says it's just the grief playing tricks on me, because she doesn't hear a thing when she's in the room. But to me... it sounds real.

Well, yes, I do. I mean... I know it sounds odd when I say it out loud. But I’m certain those old ballads my brother kept, they aren’t just songs. They’ve got warnings tucked inside them, specifically for me. My wife keeps saying I’m just reading too much into it, but... well, I still know what I heard in those words. I really believe he's trying to tell me something through them.

No, I hadn't. Before I got swept up in all this memorial work after he passed... I never heard his voice in the house. And I never felt like those songs were sending me personal warnings, either. All of that—the humming, the messages in the ballads—it all started at the exact same time as this burst of energy and the nonstop planning I've been doing.

No, I can't say that I have. I mean... before he passed, I was just living a pretty quiet life, you know? Taking it easy. I never had a time where I felt so wired or felt like I had to get so much done all at once. This whole thing... this energy I have right now... it's really the first time I've ever felt anything like this.

No, they've only happened together. Like I said before, I never heard his voice or got those warnings from the songs before all this energy and memorial planning started. It all came on at the exact same time. There hasn't been a time where I felt normal or tired but still heard him... it's all tied up with this nonstop drive I've got right now.

Well, it's a mix. I wouldn't just call it cheerful. It's more like... I'll feel completely lit up and full of purpose one minute. I get this feeling like the whole town is finally going to understand our family once this memorial is done. 

But then... well, if my wife or somebody down at the senior center slows me down, or if they question the display I'm working on, I just snap at them. So I do feel great and driven most of the day, but I get pretty short-tempered if people get in my way.
No, I haven't. I mean, I've had sad days like anyone else, especially when my brother got sick, but I've never been down in the dumps for weeks at a time. I've never had a depression like that.

Well, yes, I do. I know it sounds odd to some people, but I'm absolutely certain about it. You see, my brother kept these old ballads, and I know they aren't just songs. They've got specific warnings tucked into them, meant just for me to find and understand. My wife tells me I'm reading too much into it, that I'm making things up, but I know what I heard in those words. It's a message for me to carry out this work.

Yes, I do. Um... I keep telling myself that if I had just picked a different route for us that day, or... or if I had pushed harder about avoiding that crossing, she might still be alive. Hard to follow? Um, no, I don't think so. Nobody's ever said that to me. Usually, it's the clients who talk a mile a minute, honestly. Like my client Mrs. Gable, she comes in every three weeks for a root touch-up. We use this really specific auburn color on her, and she just talks the entire time about her grandson's baseball games. He plays in this travel league, and they have to drive all over the state for tournaments every single weekend. I don't know how people do that, driving hours and hours on the highway. I hate driving long distances. My car, like I was saying earlier, the AC is totally busted, and the radio antenna is bent so it only picks up country stations for some reason. I don't even like country music. I prefer pop, or maybe some indie bands. I went to this indie concert last year at that little venue downtown, and it was so incredibly crowded. The whole place smelled like stale beer and cheap perfume. I really can't stand strong perfumes, they always give me a headache right behind my eyes... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, jumping from topics. No, no one has mentioned anything like that about me.

Um, a period without feeling depressed? Yeah, actually. Before the depression really took over and I just felt completely drained, there was a stretch of several weeks where I wasn't feeling down at all. I was still getting up, going to work, and functioning pretty normally, but I was already hearing that voice and feeling absolutely sure that someone at the salon was messing with my schedule. I remember because I was still trying to keep up with my regular morning routine back then. I used to make myself a smoothie every single morning. I had this really nice blender that I got on sale at Target. It was one of those Ninja ones, you know, with the multiple blades stacked up the middle? It blended ice so perfectly. I used to put frozen strawberries, a banana, and a handful of spinach in there. You can't even taste the spinach, which is crazy because it turns the whole thing this murky green color. Kind of like that "Seafoam Whisper" paint Brenda used on the salon walls, actually. It's funny how colors can remind you of things. My favorite color used to be yellow, like sunshine yellow, but I don't really wear it anymore because it clashes with the all-black dress code at work. Black is supposed to be slimming, but it just shows every single piece of lint and stray hair. I have this lint roller in my station drawer that I must use ten times a day. The sticky sheets always tear weirdly when you try to peel them off, though... But yeah, there were definitely a few weeks where I wasn't depressed yet, but the voice and the schedule stuff were already happening.

Yeah, it does say things like that. Sometimes when I'm sweeping up hair around the chairs or rinsing out the color bowls in the back, I hear this woman's voice over near the shampoo stations. She just keeps telling me that I'm ruining everything. And it happens even when the salon is totally empty or when nobody is anywhere near me. The shampoo stations are actually my least favorite part of the salon to clean. The bowls are black, so you'd think they wouldn't show stains, but the hard water leaves this weird chalky residue around the drain. We have really hard water in this town. My apartment has it too, and it completely ruins my shower head. I have to soak it in white vinegar every couple of months just to get the water to spray straight. The smell of vinegar always makes me crave salt and vinegar potato chips. I used to eat a whole bag of those while watching reality TV shows on my couch. I love the shows where people buy houses and renovate them, but they always knock down perfectly good walls to make an "open concept." I don't get why everyone wants an open concept, sometimes it's nice to have walls so you don't have to see the messy kitchen from the living room. My kitchen is so tiny, I barely have counter space for my microwave and my toaster. The toaster is one of those cheap plastic ones, and the dial is broken so it either barely warms the bread or completely burns it to a crisp... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, the voice. Yeah, she tells me I'm ruining everything while I'm cleaning.

Um, emotionally flat? Yeah, I guess so. Even when I wasn't feeling totally bogged down by the depression, I still wasn't really... me, you know? Like, I used to chat with all my clients, help the newer stylists mix their colors, and on weekends I'd go hiking with my friends. We used to go up to this state park about an hour from here. The trails there are gorgeous, especially in the fall when the leaves change. I love autumn, it's my favorite season. The air just smells so crisp, and you can finally wear sweaters again. I have this huge collection of oversized knit sweaters that I keep in a cedar chest at the end of my bed. The cedar smells so good, it reminds me of my grandfather's workshop. He used to build birdhouses out of cedar and pine. He had this massive table saw in his garage that always terrified me when I was little. It was so loud, and there was sawdust everywhere. I hate sawdust, it gets in your eyes and makes you sneeze. Kind of like the hairspray we use at the salon. Brenda buys this industrial-strength aerosol stuff that literally leaves a sticky cloud in the air. If you walk through it, you can feel it coating your eyelashes. I have to use waterproof mascara just so it doesn't run when I try to wipe the hairspray off my face. Waterproof mascara is a nightmare to take off at night, though. You need that special oil-based makeup remover, and it always gets in my eyes and makes my vision blurry for like ten minutes... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, not talking much. Yeah, now I mostly just keep my head down and avoid people. I just don't have that spark in me anymore, even when I'm not feeling super depressed.

Um, slowed down? Yeah, actually, a few people have mentioned it. It's weird because my hands feel like they're moving through glue at work. Like, even just sectioning hair or mixing color takes me forever now, and people have started noticing that I'm just way slower than I used to be. Mixing color is usually my favorite part of the job, honestly. You have to be so precise with the ratios, like a little chemist. We use these little digital scales that measure in grams. Mine has a crack across the screen from when I dropped a bottle of developer on it. Developer is so annoying to clean up, it's thick and creamy and it kind of bleaches whatever it sits on for too long. I ruined my favorite pair of jeans that way. They were these perfectly distressed Levi's that I found at a thrift store for like ten bucks. I love thrifting, you can find the best stuff if you have the patience to dig through the racks. The thrift store near my apartment always smells like old books and mothballs, but in a comforting way. My grandma's house used to smell like mothballs. She had this huge attic full of old clothes and weird antique furniture. She had this one velvet chair that was bright pink, like, aggressively pink. I always wanted to take it for my apartment, but it wouldn't fit in my tiny car. I drive a Honda Civic, and the trunk is practically nonexistent. Plus, the AC is broken, so in the summer I just have to roll all the windows down and let the wind mess up my hair... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, moving slow. Yeah, my hands just feel like they're stuck in glue, and it takes me forever to do anything at the salon now.

Um, enjoying things? No, not really. Like I was saying before, I used to love chatting with all my clients and helping the newer stylists mix their colors, and going hiking with my friends on the weekends. But now I mostly just keep my head down and avoid people because I just don't have that spark in me anymore. Even when I'm not feeling super depressed, I just don't care about doing those things. Like the hiking... we used to go to that state park, the one with the gorgeous trails. I actually bought these really expensive hiking boots for those trips. They're leather and they took forever to break in. I got so many blisters the first few times I wore them. Blisters are the worst, especially when you have to stand on your feet all day at the salon. Brenda makes us wear closed-toe shoes, which makes sense because of all the sharp scissors and hot tools dropping, but my feet get so sweaty in the summer. I tried buying those little charcoal inserts for my shoes to absorb the moisture, but they just made the inside of my socks turn gray. I had to throw away like three pairs of my favorite fuzzy socks. I love fuzzy socks, especially the ones with the little grippy things on the bottom so you don't slide on hardwood floors. My apartment has hardwood floors, well, fake hardwood, but it's still really slippery. I almost fell the other day carrying a bowl of cereal to the couch. It was Cinnamon Toast Crunch, which is definitely the best cereal. The milk at the bottom gets so sweet and cinnamony... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, enjoying things. Yeah, I just don't have the spark to do the things I used to like, even when the depression isn't as bad.

Um, balance? No, I haven't really noticed any trouble with my balance or walking or anything. I mean, I almost slipped that one time in my apartment with the cereal, but that was just because of the fake hardwood floors and my socks. Those floors are so annoying to keep clean, by the way. Dust bunnies just collect in the corners like crazy. I bought this Swiffer thing with the wet pads, but the pads dry out so fast. You do like two swipes and suddenly you're just pushing dry dirt around. I think I need to get an actual mop, like one of those string ones with the bucket that wrings it out for you. My mom used to have one of those when I was growing up. The bucket was bright yellow and had this pedal you stepped on to spin the mop head. It was actually kind of fun to use when I was a kid, like a little ride for the mop. I used to pretend the mop was a lady with wild, wet hair getting on a carousel. I was always playing with hair, even back then. I used to cut the hair off all my Barbie dolls, which made my mom so mad because they don't grow back. I gave my favorite Barbie this awful, choppy bob. I tried to use kitchen scissors, the ones we used to cut open those plastic freeze pops in the summer. The blue ones were the best, they turned your tongue completely blue for hours. We used to have contests to see whose tongue was the darkest... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my balance. No, I walk fine, my balance is totally normal.

Um, depressed nearly every day? Yeah, definitely. It's been way longer than two weeks, honestly. Most days I just wake up with this heavy, flat sadness right in my chest, like... like there’s just no point in trying to build the life I was planning, you know? I used to have this whole vision board in my bedroom for my career. I cut out all these pictures from Vogue and Harper's Bazaar. Magazines are so expensive now, though, have you noticed? Like, seven or eight dollars for one issue. I usually just read them at the dentist's office. My dentist has this really nice waiting room with a huge saltwater fish tank. Watching the fish is supposed to be calming, I guess, but I always just feel bad for them being stuck in that little glass box. There was this one bright yellow tang fish that just swam in circles all day. It kind of reminded me of finding Dory, which is such a cute movie, but I cried so hard when I watched it. I cry at almost every movie now, even the happy ones. I sobbed at the end of a rom-com last week, and I was just eating popcorn by myself on the couch. I accidentally burnt the first bag of popcorn because my microwave is so old and the numbers on the buttons are all rubbed off. You have to just guess where the '2' and the '0' are. I really need to buy a new microwave, maybe a stainless steel one to match the fridge... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, feeling depressed. Yeah, it's just this heavy sadness most days, like I said. It's been pretty constant.

Um, unusually sensitive to cold? No, not really. I usually just wear a cardigan over my smock. I have this really soft black one I got from Target. Target has the best cardigans in the fall, they're so cozy. I went there last week just to buy toothpaste and walked out with like fifty dollars worth of candles. They had this one that smelled like pumpkin spice and cedar, it was amazing. I love lighting candles when I take a bath. I use those bath bombs from Lush, the ones that turn the water all sparkly and pink. But then you have to scrub the tub afterward because it leaves this weird glitter ring around the porcelain. Scrubbing the tub is literally my least favorite chore. I hate the smell of bleach, it gives me such a headache. My mom used to clean our whole house with bleach every Sunday, and the smell would just linger for days. We had this white linoleum floor in the kitchen that she was obsessed with keeping spotless. It had these little gray flecks in it that looked like dirt, so she was always scrubbing it for no reason... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, being cold. No, I haven't noticed being extra cold or anything like that. Just normal.

Um, I'm actually not sure. I didn't really... keep track of the exact timeline like that. So I couldn't say for certain if it started specifically within that three-month window.

No, never. I mean, I've always been a little particular about my art, just wanting it to look right, but... nothing like this. This whole thing with the unwanted thoughts and the constant checking, it's completely new. It only started with this portrait.

I'm not really sure, to be honest. I haven't... I haven't actually put it away long enough to find out. I couldn't tell you if the thoughts would completely stop if I just stopped working on the portrait altogether.

I don't think so, no. I mean, I am grieving, of course, but the thoughts aren't really about missing her or feeling sad. It's just... this intense focus on getting the portrait exactly right, and the fear that if I don't, something bad will happen. It doesn't feel like it's about the grief itself.

Hi, yeah, it's nice to meet you too. So, I guess... well, it's a bit of a long story, but what really made me finally make the appointment and come in today is that I've just been noticing this really unsettling shift in myself. 

You see, I've always been a very engaged, organized person. I'm an executive assistant, so keeping a pristine, perfectly managed calendar is basically my whole life, and usually, I get a real sense of satisfaction and pride from doing it well. But lately, even just looking at my schedule or trying to organize my week feels... I don't know, just completely flat. The whole thing just feels incredibly heavy. 

And it's not just work, which is the most concerning part to me, because it's spilling over into everything that usually makes me feel like myself. Like, I normally do these photography walks on the weekends—mostly urban architecture, I've been doing it for years, it's my main creative outlet and it usually clears my head—and I also mentor some kids at the local youth center on Tuesday evenings. Usually, I'm the one rallying everyone, setting the dates, getting things going. But recently, I just... I stopped initiating any of it. The camera is just sitting on my desk gathering dust, and I haven't reached out to the youth center in weeks. The idea of going out, or even just making the effort to start an activity, it just feels like wading through wet cement. It's this heavy, flat emptiness, and I just can't seem to muster the spark to start doing the things I actually care about anymore. It's just not like me at all to stop engaging with my own life like this, so I figured I really needed to come in and figure out what's going on.

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it didn't happen overnight, like a light switch flipping, but if I trace it back... it really started about a year and three months ago. Give or take a couple of weeks, but right around then. And it was definitely tied to a big change, a really stressful one. 

My brother, he... well, his health took a really sudden turn. And it wasn't just physical, his whole behavior started changing, becoming really unpredictable and difficult to manage. And because of the nature of my job, you know, being an executive assistant, I'm the organized one in the family. I'm the one who handles the logistics, the schedules, the crisis management. So, naturally, it all fell on me to coordinate everything for him. The doctors' appointments, the specialists, figuring out his insurance, managing his daily care needs, trying to keep the rest of the family updated without causing a panic... it was like taking on a second, incredibly demanding, full-time job. 

And at first, I was just running on adrenaline, just powering through it, making the spreadsheets, making the calls. But then, as the months dragged on—and like I said, it's been about a year and three months now of this constant, low-grade (and sometimes high-grade) crisis mode—that's when I started to feel this... this draining of my own energy. It was like I was pouring so much of my executive function into managing his life that there was just absolutely nothing left for mine. And that's when the photography stopped, and the youth center, and just... everything else. So yes, it definitely started after that whole situation with my brother began, and I just haven't been able to bounce back since.

Oh, yes, absolutely. Like I was just mentioning a moment ago, it’s been about a year and three months now. And when you ask if it's been continuous, I mean... yes, painfully continuous. It's not like I have a good week where I suddenly feel like myself again and then a bad week. 

Ever since my brother's health and his whole behavior took that dive and I had to step in to coordinate everything for him... it's just been this constant, unending stretch. Being someone who practically lives inside a calendar for a living, I track time very, very closely, so I know exactly how long it's been. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, you know? Like, maybe a Tuesday will roll around and I'll wake up and think, "Hey, I want to grab my camera today and go shoot those new buildings downtown," but... no. It's been every single day, week after week, month after month, for well over a year now. Fifteen months, give or take, of just... this. I haven't had a single reprieve since I took on all that extra weight with his care. It's just a straight, unbroken line on the calendar of feeling completely drained.

You know, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that, because... well, I’ve actually spent a lot of time analyzing that precise distinction in my own head. Being an assistant, I'm very particular about words and what they mean. And when I hear the word 'depressed' or 'down,' I immediately picture, you know, someone crying all the time, or feeling this profound, crushing sadness, or maybe feeling worthless or guilty about things. And honestly? I don't really have that. 

I'm not sitting at my desk weeping over my boss's travel itinerary, you know? I don't feel sad in that deep, dark way. I mean, obviously, I feel a normal amount of sadness about my brother's health, because it's a tragic situation, but it's not this overwhelming black cloud of despair that follows me around all day. It’s actually... it's more like someone just unplugged my power cord from the wall. It’s an absence of feeling rather than a negative feeling, if that makes any sense at all? 

Like, I'll be sitting there, looking at an email from the youth center, and I don't feel down about it, I just feel... nothing. It's just a void. A heavy, blank void. I've had friends ask me if I'm depressed lately, and I always have to explain this whole exact thing to them, too, because they see me not taking my architecture photos and they just assume I'm sitting in a dark room crying. But I'm really not. I'm just... existing, I guess. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel down or depressed most of the day. It's just that total, flat emptiness I was talking about.

No, not at all. And it's interesting you ask that right after the depression question, because it really reinforces what I was just trying to explain about this whole... void I've been stuck in. 

If anything, I'm crying less than I normally would. Or maybe not less, but just... not at all. You know, I'm a guy who usually gets a little misty-eyed at a good movie, or even a particularly touching long-distance commercial, you know? I'm not afraid to admit that. I've always been relatively in touch with my emotions. But lately? Nothing. Absolutely nothing. 

Even with everything going on with my brother—and there have been some objectively heartbreaking moments there, times where I've had to sit in these awful, sterile hospital waiting rooms for hours on end, just me and my laptop, coordinating his care while he's going through some really rough, unpredictable patches—I haven't shed a single tear. It’s like the mechanism for it is just broken or, I don't know, turned off entirely. 

I remember sitting there just last month, staring at this incredibly complex insurance denial form for one of his specialists. It was the kind of bureaucratic nightmare that, a year and a half ago, would normally have had me either furious or in tears from the sheer, overwhelming frustration of it all. And I just... stared at it. Dry eyes. Just completely flat. I didn't feel the urge to cry, I didn't feel a lump in my throat, nothing. So no, no extra crying. If anything, I'm almost a little disturbed by how dry my eyes have been through this whole ordeal, because you'd think I'd be weeping into my spreadsheets on a weekly basis with the amount of stress I'm under, but I'm just... not. The tears just aren't there.

Hopeless... no, no I wouldn't use that word either. It’s funny, because when you say 'hopeless,' I think of someone who has just completely thrown in the towel, you know? Someone who looks at the future and sees absolutely nothing, or thinks there's no point in even trying to move forward. And that’s really not me. 

I mean, just look at my day-to-day life. As an executive assistant, my entire career is literally built on the future—planning it, anticipating it, making sure everything is lined up for next week, next month, next quarter. I'm currently booking flights and hotels for a conference my boss is attending eight months from now. If I were truly hopeless, I don't think I could do that. I'd probably look at that calendar and think, "What's the point? None of this matters." But I don't. I still know the future is coming, and I still believe things will happen. 

And with my brother, too. I mean, I was just talking about those insurance denials a second ago. If I felt hopeless, I would have just crumpled up that denial letter and tossed it in the recycling bin under my desk, right? I would have just accepted that they weren't going to pay for his specialist and given up on the whole system. But I didn't. I filed an appeal. I drafted a very thorough three-page letter, I gathered all his medical records, I highlighted the relevant policy clauses... I did all of that because I still have hope that the appeal will go through. I still expect things to function, eventually, if I just put the right pieces in the right places. 

So, it's not a lack of hope. I know things can get better, or at least that time will keep moving forward and situations will resolve. It’s just... like I said before, I just don't have any emotional reaction to any of it while it's happening. I'm going through the motions of hoping, I'm doing all the administrative tasks a hopeful person does, I'm just doing them with a completely empty tank. So no, definitely not hopeless. Just... flat. Does that make sense? Because I really think there's a huge, fundamental difference between having no hope and just having no... no spark, I guess you could call it.

Thoughts don't just radiate out into the ether for anyone to pick up on a whim. 

And again, just logically speaking—which is how I approach everything—if I were broadcasting my thoughts, why on earth would the property manager need to rifle through my recycling bin? Why would his people need to press acoustic sensors against the drywall to hear when I walk from the kitchen to the bedroom? If they could just tune in to my brainwaves, all of that physical, highly risky surveillance would be entirely redundant. It would be a massive waste of time and manpower. And as a management analyst, I can tell you that people running these sorts of coordinated harassment campaigns do not waste resources. They are ruthlessly efficient. 

So, no. My thoughts are not being broadcast. They are entirely contained within my own skull, just like anyone else's. And frankly, I would appreciate it if we could move away from these... these fantastical hypotheticals and get back to the actual, documented evidence I brought with me. Because every minute we spend discussing imaginary mind-broadcasting is a minute we aren't discussing the very real, very physical campaign of constructive eviction that I am currently enduring.

Three months? Doctor, if this had only been going on for three months, I might still be in the phase of trying to rationalize it as a string of bizarre coincidences. No, no, this... this highly orchestrated campaign against me has been continuously active for about eleven months now. 

It started almost immediately—well, shortly after I signed the lease and moved my things into the new apartment. I remember the timeline perfectly because I had just finished unpacking the last of my reference books—the organizational behavior texts, specifically—when the first "misdirected" piece of mail occurred. And from that exact moment, eleven months ago, it has been a relentless, daily, continuous presence in my life. 

There hasn't been a single day—not a weekend, not a holiday—where they have let up. I wake up, the floorboards are tracked. I check my mail, it's been tampered with. I walk through the lobby, the neighbors make their calculated remarks. It is a constant, grinding pressure. Eleven months of it, Doctor. Eleven months of meticulously logging every incident, cross-referencing every anomaly, and building the case that you see in the binders I brought today. So yes, to answer your question, it has been continuously present, but for far, far longer than a mere three months. It has been nearly a year of my life consumed by their efforts to force me out.

Well, nice to meet you too. I guess I’m here because... well, for almost two years now, I haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty that ever since my big commission, a few people in the ensemble have been quietly undermining my work. It’s always subtle things, you know? Sudden schedule changes, weird seating choices, these little pointed comments during rehearsals. And they’ll show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, but I know what's really happening. 

Which is funny, actually, because emails have been a total mess for the group lately anyway. Our server migrated last month and I lost half my inbox. Do you use Outlook? I swear, every time they do an update, they move the search bar and it takes me ten minutes just to find a message from the brass section. I actually missed a dentist appointment last week because the reminder went straight to my spam folder, and my dentist was so annoyed. He collects vintage metronomes, actually, which is a weird coincidence for me, but he has this one from the 1800s sitting right by the chair. 

But, um, anyway... yeah, the ensemble situation. It's just been really stressful dealing with them, so I figured I should probably talk to someone about it.

Confirmed it? Well... no, not exactly in so many words. Because, like I was saying, it’s been almost two years since the commission, and I just have this absolute certainty that they are quietly undermining my work. They’re smart about it, you know? They use the sudden schedule changes and the weird seating choices, and whenever I try to point it out to someone else in the group, the people doing it just pull out those same emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away. So everyone else just looks at the notes and believes them. 

Speaking of notes, actually, we switched to using iPads for our sheet music this season. It's supposed to save paper, which is great, but the glare from the stage lights is just terrible. We played at this historic theater downtown last weekend—beautiful acoustics, built in like 1924, I think—and the lighting guy absolutely refused to dim the overheads. I had to order one of those matte screen protectors online, but I could not get the air bubbles out of the corners. Have you ever tried putting one of those on a large tablet? It is literally impossible to keep the dust out. I spent like twenty minutes in my bathroom with the shower running just to get the steam to settle the dust, and it still didn't work perfectly. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking me? Oh, right, if anyone else sees them doing it. Yeah, no, they just look at the schedule emails and tell me it's just normal administrative stuff.

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. No voices or anything. Although, speaking of hearing things, my neighbor just bought this wind chime. It's one of those massive, heavy metal ones, you know? The tubes are like two feet long. And they hung it right outside my bedroom window. Every time the wind picks up, it sounds like a cathedral bell going off. I mean, I appreciate good resonance as much as the next guy, but at 3:00 AM, it's a bit much. 

I actually tried to buy them a smaller, wooden one as a sort of passive-aggressive gift, but the hardware store down the street was closed for renovation. They’re putting in this new coffee shop attached to it, which is weird, right? Coffee and power tools. Seems like a liability waiting to happen. I used an angle grinder once for a sound art installation I was working on in grad school, and even with the safety goggles, I was terrified. The sparks flew everywhere, and I ended up singing the sleeve of my favorite sweater. It was this really nice merino wool one my sister got me in Ireland. 

But, uh... no, to answer your question, I don't hear any voices. Just the wind chimes. And the occasional siren, since I live pretty close to the hospital.

Energized or euphoric? Um, no. I don't think so. I mean, I get excited when a piece comes together, but not for days at a time. I usually just feel tired, honestly. 

Especially with this new espresso machine I got. It’s one of those manual lever ones, you know? Beautiful piece of machinery, Italian made, lots of chrome. But pulling a shot takes so much physical effort, and half the time I don't grind the beans fine enough, so it just gushes out and tastes sour. I’ve been buying beans from this local roaster who supposedly sources directly from farms in Colombia, but honestly, I think they roast them too light. The bags have these really intricate illustrations on them, though—like, line drawings of toucans and jaguars. 

My cousin used to draw like that. She went to art school in Chicago and then ended up doing graphic design for a dog food company. It’s funny how that happens, right? You study fine art and then you’re designing kibble bags. She has a golden retriever that sheds constantly. I visited her last Thanksgiving and I swear I was picking blonde hairs off my black slacks for a week. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no unusual energy or euphoria or anything like that. Just regular tired.

Strange beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, outside of what's happening with the ensemble, everything else is just... normal. 

Although, speaking of strange things, I did see the weirdest documentary the other night. It was about these deep-sea tube worms that live near hydrothermal vents. They don't even have a digestive system, they just rely on this symbiotic bacteria to turn the toxic chemicals into food. It’s absolutely fascinating how life adapts to such extreme pressure and darkness. It made me want to write a piece based on that environment, you know? Something really low and rumbling, maybe using a contrabassoon and some heavy synth drones. 

I actually looked up the price of a decent analog synthesizer, and they are ridiculously expensive. Even the used ones on Reverb are going for thousands. I guess there’s this huge vintage revival happening right now, kind of like how everyone is buying vinyl records again. My dad still has his original pressing of Abbey Road, but he keeps it in the basement where it’s totally damp. I keep telling him he needs a dehumidifier down there, or the sleeve is going to get completely ruined by mildew. He just brushes me off, though. He’s always been stubborn like that, especially when it comes to his old stuff. 

But, wait... what did you ask? Oh, right, other strange beliefs. No, definitely not. Just the ensemble stuff. That's the only thing.

Hard to follow? Off track? I don't think people say that. I mean, I think I communicate pretty clearly. I'm used to directing musicians, right? You have to be precise when you're explaining how you want a phrase articulated. If you want it detached but not quite staccato, you have to find the right words. 

Like this cellist I worked with last month. He was incredibly talented, technically flawless, but he played everything so aggressively. I had to spend like twenty minutes explaining the concept of a 'whispered' tone to him. We ended up using this special rosin on his bow—it was this dark amber stuff from France, supposedly made using a recipe from the 1800s. It smelled amazing, kind of like pine needles and old books. I actually bought a candle that was supposed to smell like old books once, but it just smelled like vanilla and dust. I got it at this little boutique downtown that sells all these imported soaps and artisanal honey. The honey was good, though. I put it in my tea when I get a sore throat, especially during the winter when the heating in my apartment dries out the air. The radiators are ancient and they clank so loudly. 

But, uh, no... people don't usually say I'm hard to follow. I think I make sense.

Worse? I mean, not drastically. The main thing is that rehearsals and, you know, professional emails just take a lot more energy now. I find myself rereading my decisions or asking for extra clarification from the musicians just to be absolutely sure. But I haven't lost any work, and I'm still taking care of myself. 

Speaking of taking care of myself, I actually started trying to make my own sourdough bread last week. Everyone says it’s so relaxing, but keeping the starter alive is like having a pet. You have to feed it at the exact right time or it gets this weird liquid on top called 'hooch.' I used this organic rye flour I found at the farmers market. The market was packed, by the way. I ended up buying these heirloom tomatoes that were purple and green. They looked amazing, but when I sliced them up for a sandwich, they were completely mealy inside. There's nothing worse than a mealy tomato, right? It ruins the whole texture. I had to throw the whole sandwich out and just eat a bowl of cereal instead. I buy that brand with the little dried strawberries in it, but they always sink to the bottom of the bag so the last bowl is just overwhelmingly fruity. 

But, um... yeah, to answer your question, my day-to-day is mostly fine. Just a bit more exhausting with the extra checking.

Medical issues? Like before all this? No, I've always been pretty healthy. Never had anything major like that. 

I did break my wrist once when I was a kid, though. I was trying to ride my bike down this steep hill near my house, and I completely wiped out on some loose gravel. The cast was so itchy, especially during the summer. We went to the beach that year, and I couldn't even go in the water. I just sat on the sand under an umbrella reading these old sci-fi paperbacks my uncle gave me. He had this massive collection of Isaac Asimov and Arthur C. Clarke. The covers always had those amazing, retro-futuristic paintings on them, you know? The ones with the giant geometric spaceships and the weirdly colored planets. I actually tried to find some of those specific editions online a while back, just for nostalgia. Turns out they're actually worth a bit of money now if they're in good condition. Most of the ones I found had completely yellowed pages, though. Old paper gets that distinct smell, kind of sweet and musty. 

But, uh, anyway... no, no major medical or neurological stuff. Just the broken wrist when I was little.

Mistaken? I... I don't see how I could be. I mean, that's why I'm here, right? Because for almost two years now, I haven't been able to shake this absolute certainty about it. Ever since that big commission, a few of them have been doing it. Just quietly undermining my work. It's the schedule changes, the seating choices, the little comments during rehearsals. And I know they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it all away, but it doesn't change what I know is happening. 

It's like when you're tuning an orchestra, you know? The oboe plays the A, and everyone else is supposed to match it. But sometimes the strings will be just a fraction of a cent flat. Not enough for a casual listener to notice, but if you have a trained ear, it drives you absolutely crazy. It creates this subtle dissonance that just hangs in the air. I actually bought a new digital tuner last month because I thought my old one was losing its calibration. It's one of those strobe tuners, really precise. I ordered it from this specialty music shop in Chicago. I went to Chicago once for a conference, right in the middle of winter. The wind coming off Lake Michigan is no joke. I had to buy a new coat while I was there because the one I brought was completely useless. It was this heavy wool peacoat, navy blue. I still have it in my closet, actually, but I never wear it because it weighs like ten pounds and the buttons are loose. I tried to sew one back on, but I used the wrong color thread, so now it looks a bit ridiculous. 

But, um, anyway... no, I'm not mistaken. I know what they're doing, even if they try to cover it up with their little explanations.

Impossible by ordinary means? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, they're just musicians, right? They're not doing anything supernatural or... or reading my mind. It's just normal, everyday sabotage. Missing cues, changing schedules, that kind of thing. 

Speaking of schedules, I actually bought a new planner recently to try and keep everything straight. It's one of those really nice leather-bound ones, you know? With the thick paper that doesn't bleed through when you use a fountain pen. I love fountain pens. I have this vintage Parker 51 that I found at an estate sale a few years ago. It took me forever to figure out how to clean the old dried ink out of the aerometric filler. I ended up watching like, three hours of YouTube tutorials on pen restoration. There's this whole community of people who just restore old pens. One guy had this amazing video where he fixed a cracked celluloid barrel using some kind of solvent welding technique. It was fascinating. I actually tried to buy some of the solvent he used, but you can't get it shipped to residential addresses anymore because it's apparently highly flammable. Probably for the best, honestly. I'd probably end up melting the pen entirely or setting my desk on fire. My desk is this old oak roll-top that I got from my grandfather, so I'd hate to ruin it. It has all these tiny little cubby holes that are completely useless for modern things, but they look great. 

But, uh, no... to answer your question, they aren't doing anything impossible. Just normal, frustrating things to undermine me.

Less interested? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still love music, obviously. I'm still composing, still trying to get my work out there despite... well, despite everything. I still enjoy reading, too. I just finished this incredible biography of Mahler. 

It's actually a really heavy book, physically, I mean. Hardcover, almost a thousand pages. I usually prefer reading on my tablet because it's easier to hold when I'm lying in bed, but the screen glare was starting to give me headaches. I went to the optometrist a few weeks ago to see if I needed a new prescription, but he said my eyes are fine. He suggested I try those blue-light blocking glasses. I bought a pair online, but they have these really thick, tortoiseshell frames that make me look like a 1950s librarian. I wore them to the grocery store once and the cashier kept giving me these weird looks. Or maybe it was because I bought like, six jars of artichoke hearts. They were on sale, and I was going to make this Mediterranean pasta salad I saw on a cooking show. The host of the show was this really energetic Italian guy who kept shouting at the camera. He made it look so easy, but when I tried it, the dressing split and it just looked like an oily mess. I ended up eating it anyway because I didn't want to waste the artichokes. They're surprisingly expensive when they're not on sale. 

But, um, anyway... no, I haven't lost interest in things. I still enjoy my usual hobbies and everything.

Depressed? No, no, I haven't had anything like that. I mean, I get frustrated with the ensemble, obviously, but not depressed. I don't really get down like that. Well, maybe a little gloomy when it rains for days on end, but that's just the weather. 

Actually, the last time it rained really heavily, my ceiling started leaking right over my piano. It's just a Yamaha upright, but I love the action on the keys. I had to scramble to put this orange plastic bucket on top of it to catch the water. The funny thing is, the sound of the water hitting the bottom of the bucket was pitching a perfect B-flat. Just... drip, drip, B-flat, B-flat. I actually pulled out my phone and recorded it to see if I could sample it for a piece I was working on. I use Logic Pro for my mixing, mostly. A lot of my friends swear by Ableton, but I just can't get used to the interface. It feels too blocky to me. I watched this masterclass by Hans Zimmer recently where he showed off his studio, and it is just wall-to-wall modular synthesizers. It looks like the bridge of a spaceship. I'd love to have a setup like that, but my apartment barely has enough room for a decent dining table. I usually end up eating dinner on my couch while watching nature documentaries. I saw this amazing one about cephalopods the other night. Did you know octopuses have three hearts? It's wild. They pump blue blood, too, because it's copper-based instead of iron. 

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Oh, right, feeling depressed. No, no periods of depression for me.

Jumbled? No, I don't think anyone has ever told me that. I mean, my musicians complain about a lot of things, but usually it's about my tempos or the rehearsal schedule, not that I'm hard to follow. 

Speaking of rehearsal schedules, I was trying to coordinate a string quartet practice last week, and trying to get four musicians in the same room at the same time is like herding cats. I had to use this online scheduling poll thing, Doodle, I think it's called? But the cellist, David, he completely ignored it and just texted me a list of times he *couldn't* do, which is entirely unhelpful. David is a great player, don't get me wrong. He has this beautiful 19th-century French cello that just sings in the upper register. He bought it at an auction in Paris a few years ago. I've always wanted to go to Paris. I had a layover at Charles de Gaulle once, but I don't think that counts. The airport there is huge and confusing, honestly. I almost missed my connection to Berlin because I couldn't figure out which terminal I was supposed to be in. The signage was terrible, or maybe I was just sleep-deprived. I always get terrible jet lag when I fly east. I read somewhere that taking melatonin can help, but last time I tried it, I just had these incredibly vivid dreams about being trapped in a giant hourglass. Sand getting everywhere. It was awful. I ended up waking up at 3 AM and just eating cold pizza in my hotel room. 

But, uh, no, nobody's ever said my thoughts are jumbled. I think I'm pretty clear when I speak.

Go off on tangents? Lose track of the question? No, I don't think anyone's ever said that. I mean, I'm a director, I have to be pretty focused to keep everyone on the same page. 

Although, keeping people on the same page is literally impossible with sheet music these days. Half the ensemble uses iPads now, and they all have these Bluetooth page-turning pedals. It's supposed to be seamless, but during our last run-through, the second violinist's pedal disconnected right in the middle of a tricky allegro section. He had to stop playing to swipe the screen, and it totally ruined the momentum. I told him he should just go back to paper, but he says paper is bad for the environment. Which I get, I try to recycle as much as I can. I actually started composting recently, too. I got this little bin for my kitchen counter. It's supposed to be odor-free, but I put some onion skins in there last week and the whole apartment smelled like a deli for two days. I ended up having to buy this expensive citrus room spray to cover it up. The bottle said it was made with essential oils from the Amalfi coast. I love the smell of citrus, especially grapefruit. Have you ever tried a grapefruit brûlée? You cut it in half, sprinkle some sugar on top, and use a blowtorch to caramelize it. It's incredible. I got a kitchen torch for Christmas last year from my sister. She's a pastry chef in Chicago. Chicago is great, but the winters are just brutal. The wind off the lake goes right through your coat. 

But, um... wait, what were you asking about? Oh, tangents. No, no one's ever told me I do that. I usually get right to the point.

Avoiding people? No, not really. I mean, I have to be around people all the time for work. Rehearsals, meetings with venue managers, all that stuff. It's actually exhausting sometimes. 

Like yesterday, I had to meet with the lighting director for our upcoming performance at this old theater downtown. The place is gorgeous, all this ornate gold leafing and red velvet everywhere. It feels like stepping back into the 1920s. But the lighting rig is an absolute nightmare. It's half digital, half analog, and the guy running it kept complaining about the power draw. He was wearing this vintage leather jacket that squeaked every time he moved his arms. It was so distracting. I used to have a leather jacket like that in college, but I accidentally left it at a diner in Boston. We had gone there after a concert, and I ordered this massive plate of blueberry pancakes. Best pancakes I've ever had. I think the secret is they put a little bit of lemon zest in the batter. I tried making them at home once, but I totally messed up the ratio of baking powder and they came out flat as crepes. Crepes are good too, though, especially with Nutella and strawberries. I went to a crepe stand in Montreal once, and the guy making them was juggling the spatulas. It was like dinner and a show. 

But, uh, avoiding people? No, I'm pretty social. I don't really hide away or anything.

Well, you see, I'm here because for almost two years I've been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it. 

Which reminds me of this one email chain we had about the seating arrangement for the cellos. It was a complete disaster. The first chair cellist, Sarah, she insisted on being closer to the violas, saying it helped her hear the inner harmonies better. But I know she just wanted to be further away from the air conditioning vent. Those vents in the rehearsal hall are so loud, they sound like a jet engine taking off. Speaking of jet engines, I was watching this documentary the other day about how they test those things. They literally shoot frozen chickens into the turbines to simulate bird strikes. It's wild. I can't imagine being the person whose job it is to buy frozen chickens for that. Do they just go to a regular grocery store? I went to the store yesterday to get some chicken, actually, but they were completely out of thighs, which are the best part for roasting. I ended up getting breasts instead, but they always dry out so fast unless you brine them first. I have this great brine recipe with peppercorns and bay leaves. Bay leaves are funny, aren't they? You put them in, but you're not supposed to eat them. It feels like a trick. 

But anyway, yeah, that's why I think they're undermining me.

Controlled by someone else? Like mind control? No, I've never felt anything like that. My thoughts are my own. 

Though, sometimes I wish someone else could take over my thoughts just so I could get a break, you know? Especially when I'm trying to figure out the pacing for a new piece. I'll just lie in bed staring at the ceiling, trying to hear the transition from the woodwinds to the brass, and my brain just won't shut off. Speaking of brass, I had to take my French horn in for a cleaning last month. It's a vintage Conn 8D, beautiful instrument, but the valves get sticky if you don't oil them religiously. The repair guy I go to is this older gentleman who works out of his garage. His garage is amazing, it's packed floor to ceiling with instrument parts and old radios. He actually fixes antique radios as a hobby. He showed me this one from the 1930s that he restored, it had this gorgeous wooden cabinet with a glowing dial. It made me want to start listening to those old radio dramas, like The Shadow or something. I tried listening to a podcast once that was styled like an old radio show, but the voice acting was just so over the top I couldn't get into it. I mostly just listen to audiobooks now when I'm driving. I'm on this huge sci-fi kick right now. I just finished this book about a colony on Mars where they have to farm potatoes in their own... well, you know. It's fascinating how much science goes into making those stories believable. 

But no, my thoughts are definitely my own. No one's controlling them.

Meant specifically for me? Like hidden messages? No, I don't really think like that. I mean, I read reviews of our performances, and sometimes it feels like a critic is taking a personal swipe at my tempo choices, but that's just normal criticism, right? 

Speaking of reviews, there's this one local arts blogger who always has something to say about the percussion section. He's obsessed with the timpani. I actually ran into him at a coffee shop a few weeks ago. He was ordering this incredibly complicated matcha latte with oat milk and two pumps of vanilla. I don't get the whole matcha craze, honestly. It tastes like grass clippings to me. I prefer just a straight black coffee, maybe an espresso if I'm really dragging. I bought an espresso machine for my apartment last year, one of those shiny Italian ones. It took me a solid month to figure out how to pull a decent shot without burning the beans. You have to get the grind size exactly right, and the tamp pressure... it's practically a science experiment every morning. My neighbor actually complained about the noise of the grinder once. She's this sweet older lady who knits these tiny sweaters for her Chihuahua. The dog's name is Barnaby, and he barks at literally everything. A leaf blows across the sidewalk? Barnaby loses his mind. It's kind of hilarious, but also a little annoying when I'm trying to write a score. 

But yeah, no, I don't think random things are secretly meant for me. Just normal stuff.

Stop in the middle? Like going completely blank? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My brain is usually going a mile a minute, honestly. 

Though, I do get writer's block sometimes when I'm staring at a blank score. It's the absolute worst feeling, just looking at the empty staff paper. I actually have to use a very specific type of staff paper, it has to be this slightly off-white, almost cream color, because the bright white glares way too much under my desk lamp. My desk lamp is one of those vintage architect lamps with the adjustable spring arms. I found it at a thrift store for like ten bucks. It was a total steal, but I had to rewire the whole thing myself because the original cord was completely frayed and I really didn't want to start a fire. Speaking of fires, the fire alarm in my apartment building went off at 3 AM on Tuesday. Turns out someone on the fourth floor fell asleep while boiling eggs. Who boils eggs at 3 AM? And how do you even burn boiled eggs? All the water has to evaporate first. I usually soft-boil mine for exactly six and a half minutes, then drop them straight into an ice bath. It makes the shells peel off so easily. 

But anyway, what were we... oh, right. No, my thoughts don't just stop or go blank.

Seen things? You mean like hallucinations or something? No, definitely not. I've got pretty good eyesight, actually. 

Though I did have to get new glasses a couple of months ago. My prescription barely changed, but I sat on my old frames by accident. I was in a rush to get to rehearsal and just flopped down on the couch without looking. They were these great tortoiseshell frames, too. I ended up getting wire-rimmed ones this time, kind of a retro look. The optometrist was this guy who wouldn't stop talking about his trip to Iceland. He spent like twenty minutes telling me about the hot springs and the puffins while he was shining that bright light in my eyes. I'd love to go to Iceland someday, maybe record some ambient soundscapes near the glaciers. I've been experimenting a lot with field recordings lately. I bought this portable Zoom recorder, and I just take it on walks and record random stuff—traffic, birds, the subway doors closing. I actually used a sample of a subway train braking in this experimental piece I wrote for a string quartet. The cellist hated it, she said it was too jarring, but that was exactly the point. I'm trying to push boundaries, you know? The classical music scene can be so rigid sometimes. If you don't write exactly like Mahler or Shostakovich, people look at you funny. I went to this concert last week where they played a piece entirely composed of silence and occasional coughing. It was... an experience. 

But no, I don't see things that aren't there. My vision is perfectly normal.

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I guess what finally made me ask for help is that I just keep forgetting little things that I normally handle fine. Like, you know, returning calls at work or turning in a registration form, or even just stopping for an errand on the way home. Which is funny because there's this little grocery store right on my route home, the one with the really good local honey? I love their honey. I usually get the clover one, but last week they had this wildflower batch that was just amazing. I meant to pick up more, but I drove right past it three days in a row. My husband was like, "Didn't you say you were getting honey?" and I just completely blanked. But yeah, I'm just dropping the ball on these little everyday tasks and it's getting frustrating.

Oh, yeah, definitely. Even back in elementary school... I was always that kid who forgot permission slips, or I'd somehow lose my finished homework right in my own backpack. I had this huge purple backpack, I think it was from L.L. Bean? You know how those things last forever? My mom actually still uses it to store her knitting supplies. She knits these amazing little baby blankets, she just made a really cute yellow one for my cousin's new baby. 

But yeah, my backpack was just a total black hole for papers. And school projects were the worst. I always needed my mom or my teacher to literally sit there and remind me, like, step by step to actually finish them. Otherwise I'd just get caught up in picking out the right markers for the cover page and completely forget to do the actual work.

Yeah, it's pretty much everywhere. I mean, I’m still getting by, you know? But it is happening at work and at home. I've missed enough small work follow-ups and, like, my kids' school deadlines lately that I'm really starting to worry it's going to affect my reputation. Which is a big deal right now because I really want to move into this Office Manager role at my company. 

The current Office Manager, Linda, is actually retiring in the spring. She and her husband bought this massive RV and they're just going to drive around the country. I think they're starting in Arizona because she absolutely hates the cold. I don't blame her, honestly, the winters here are getting brutal. My own heater at home has been making this weird clanking noise for a week and I keep meaning to call the repair guy, but... well, there's another thing I forgot to do. 

But, um, anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the promotion. Yeah, I just worry that if I keep dropping the ball on these little things, the bosses are gonna notice and completely pass me over for Linda's job.

Um, yeah, I'd say so. It's not really about how I'm feeling, you know? Like, even on a really good day, when everything's fine and I'm not stressed at all, I'll still walk into the kitchen and completely forget why I went in there. Or I'll leave my coffee in the microwave for three hours. I actually got this new coffee blend recently, it's a hazelnut roast from that little cafe downtown? The one with the green awning?
