Well, I came in because... my family and friends made me. They keep waving these bank papers at me, saying it proves nothing was taken. But paper doesn't mean anything. Like, the other day I found a receipt in my pocket and all the ink was just rubbed off. Completely blank. I found it in my heavy winter coat, the one I got from the thrift store.

High? No, I don't... I don't feel high. I'm just normal, you know? But speaking of high, I used to live on the fourth floor of this apartment building. The elevator was always broken, so I had to walk up all those stairs. It was a real workout. I'd carry my groceries up, and by the time I got to my door, I was sweating so much. I'd have to sit down for a good ten minutes before I could even put the milk away. And the neighbors, they were always playing this loud music, like, thump, thump, thump, all night long. It drove me crazy. I tried knocking on their door once, but they just ignored me. I don't know how people can be so inconsiderate, especially when the walls are so thin. You could hear everything. I could even hear the lady next door talking on the phone to her sister about her cat's stomach problems.

Stole it? Well, yeah. I mean, my family and friends keep saying those bank papers prove nothing was taken, but they're lying. It's been over a year, and I know for a fact they’re hiding my money. They use all these... these fake bills, and fundraisers, and trip plans to cover it up. So I just have to keep confronting them until they tell the truth. 

You know, speaking of trips, my cousin was planning a trip to the lake. The lake is always so full of mosquitoes this time of year. I went a few summers ago and got bit up all over my ankles. I had to use this pink lotion... calamine, I think it's called? It smells real chalky. My grandma used to keep a bottle of it in her medicine cabinet right next to the bandages with the little stars on them. I always liked the star ones better than the plain brown ones, they just looked nicer. But anyway, yeah, they use all those trip plans and fundraisers and stuff to hide what they took from me.

Voices? No, I don't hear voices. Just the regular sounds, you know? Like the wind, or the cars outside. Speaking of cars, I used to have this old blue sedan. The muffler was completely shot, so it sounded like a tractor every time I started it up. It was so embarrassing, especially when I had to go to the grocery store. The grocery store near my old place always had the best apples, though. Honeycrisp, they were called. So sweet and crunchy. I'd buy a whole bag and just eat them on the porch. My porch had this wooden swing that squeaked every time you moved. I tried putting oil on it once, but it just made a mess on the floorboards and then the dog tracked it into the kitchen. He was a good dog, though. A golden retriever mix. He loved chasing those little green tennis balls.

Well, it started right around the time my income dropped... so, about a year and two months ago, I'd say. I remember because I was trying to figure out how to pay my light bill. The electric company, they send those envelopes with the little plastic windows, you know? And the paper is always that weird recycled gray color. I used to save those envelopes to write grocery lists on the back of them. My mom taught me that. She was always saving things, like butter tubs and glass jars. We had a whole cabinet just full of old jelly jars. The strawberry jelly was my favorite, the kind with the seeds still in it. You spread it on toast and the butter melts all into it... I used to eat that every morning before I stopped working. But yeah, it's been about a year and two months since they started hiding my money.

Less sleep? No, I don't think so. I sleep pretty regular, mostly. I mean, unless it's too hot in the room. I can't sleep if it's hot. I used to have this little box fan, you know, the square ones? I kept it right by the bed, pointing right at my face. It had three speeds, but the button for the highest speed got stuck, so I had to use a butter knife to pry it back up if I wanted to turn it down. I don't know why I kept that knife in the bedroom. Oh, I used to eat peanut butter crackers in bed sometimes. Just the cheap kind in the orange wrapper. They always leave crumbs everywhere, though. You wake up and it feels like you're sleeping in sand. I went to the beach once when I was a kid and got sand all in my swimsuit, it was awful. It took days to wash it all out of my hair. But yeah, no, I just sleep normal, I guess. Nothing special about it.

Special powers? No, no, they don't have powers or... or technology. They're just regular people. My brother works at a hardware store, actually. He's always wearing those heavy work boots, the tan ones that scuff up the linoleum. He came over once and tracked mud all the way from the front door to the kitchen sink. I had just mopped, too. I use that pine-scented cleaner, it comes in a big green jug. You only need a little capful, but it makes the whole house smell like a forest. I went camping in a forest once, up near the mountains. We slept in this tent that smelled like old canvas and mildew. It rained the whole weekend, so we just sat inside playing card games. Go Fish, mostly. The cards got all damp and stuck together. I hate when things get sticky like that. Like when you spill syrup on the table and don't wipe it up fast enough. But no, they aren't using anything special like that, just... regular ways, I guess.

Hard to follow? I... I don't think so. Nobody's ever said that to me. I mean, my mom used to tell me to slow down when I was little, but that was just because I'd get so excited about things. Like when the ice cream truck would come down our street. It played this song, I think it was "Turkey in the Straw," but it sounded all tinny and warped, you know? Like a music box that was running out of steam. I always got the kind shaped like a baseball glove with a gumball right in the middle for a baseball. The gumball was always rock hard, though. You could break a tooth on it if you weren't careful. My cousin actually chipped his front tooth on a piece of hard candy once at a parade. We used to sit on the curb and wait for them to throw the candy, but you had to be fast because the bigger kids would just scoop it all up. He had to go to the dentist, the one over by the old strip mall that shut down. They put a big plywood board over the window where the shoe store used to be. But no, nobody says I'm hard to understand or anything. I just talk normal.

Lost interest? I don't... no, I wouldn't say that. I still like the things I like. I watch my shows, you know. Mostly in the afternoons. The one with the judge, she has that wooden hammer... a gavel, right? She always bangs it so hard on the desk. I had a desk once, when I was in school, before I stopped going. It had all these carvings in the wood from the kids who sat there before me. Somebody carved a heart with an arrow through it, but the arrow was crooked. It looked more like a bent nail. My dad had a whole jar of rusty nails in the garage. He kept them in an old mayonnaise jar, the glass kind. You don't see glass jars for mayonnaise anymore, it's all plastic now. The plastic gets all greasy on the outside if you don't wipe it off. I hate when my hands get greasy. Like when you eat fried chicken at a picnic. We went to a picnic at the park by the lake, and the ducks kept trying to steal our bread. One of them actually bit my shoe. It didn't hurt, just felt weird. But no, I still enjoy things fine, I guess. Same as always.

All of a sudden? I... I don't really know if it was sudden. I don't keep track of the days very good. My grandma used to have this big calendar on her fridge, right next to the ice maker. It had pictures of kittens in baskets for every month. The August one was a little orange kitten tangled up in green yarn. My cat got into my yarn once. I was trying to make a scarf, just a plain blue one, because it gets so cold in the winter. The draft comes right under the front door. We tried putting one of those heavy snake things, you know, the fabric tubes filled with beans or whatever, to stop the wind. But a mouse chewed a hole in it. Tiny little dry beans spilled everywhere on the rug. The vacuum couldn't even pick them all up. It's one of those old vacuums with the big cloth bag that puffs up like a balloon when you turn it on. It sounds like an airplane taking off, it's so loud. My ears ring if I use it too long. So... no, I don't know exactly when it started with the money. I just know they're doing it.

Supernatural? I... no, I don't think it's magic or ghosts or anything like that. That's just silly. People don't do magic. They just... they hide things. Like how squirrels hide their acorns before the snow comes. I saw a squirrel bury a whole peanut in its shell right in the middle of Mrs. Gable's flower bed once. She had these big, bright yellow tulips. They only bloomed for a couple of weeks in the spring, and then the petals would just fall off, all over the sidewalk. They looked like little yellow boats when it rained and the water rushed down the gutter. I made a paper boat once out of a newspaper, the Sunday edition with the color comics. I liked the one with the big orange cat who loved lasagna. We had lasagna for dinner last week, but the edges got all burnt and crispy because the oven gets too hot on the left side. You have to turn the pan halfway through if you want it to bake even. The timer on the stove doesn't buzz anymore, it just makes this weak little clicking sound. So you really have to watch the clock on the wall. The clock with the big red second hand that sweeps around... but no, it's not impossible what they're doing with my money. They're just doing it.

My way of talking? I don't... I mean, this is just how I talk. I've always talked like this, I think. My mom used to say I could talk the ears off a brass monkey. We had a little brass monkey statue on the bookshelf in the hallway. It was supposed to be one of those "hear no evil, see no evil" things, but it was just the one monkey covering his eyes. His little brass fingers were all tarnished and green from people touching him. I tried to polish him once with that silver cream in the pink plastic tub, but it smelled so bad, like rotten eggs and chemicals. It made my eyes water. I had to open the window in the hall, the one with the screen that had a hole in it where a grasshopper got stuck. It was a huge green grasshopper, with those long, spiky legs. They make that weird clicking noise when they fly, like a tiny little motor. My brother caught one in a jar and fed it blades of grass, but it died anyway. He buried it in the backyard under the old oak tree. That tree dropped so many leaves in the fall, we'd rake them into massive piles and jump in them. They smelled so dusty and earthy. But yeah, I don't know, my talking hasn't changed. Just always been me.

Put thoughts in my mind? No, nobody can do that. That's... that's like science fiction or something. Like those movies with the aliens that have the big giant heads and the silver suits. We watched one of those on a Friday night once. My dad used to make popcorn in this big metal pot on the stove, not the microwave kind. You had to shake the pot back and forth, back and forth, so the kernels wouldn't burn on the bottom. It sounded like a maraca. Shake, shake, pop, pop. We'd pour real melted butter over it, and it would make the popcorn shrink a little bit and get all soggy, but it tasted so good. I got a kernel stuck in my teeth once, way in the back, and it hurt for three days. I tried using a toothpick, but it just pushed it in deeper. Toothpicks always splinter anyway if you bite on them too hard. My uncle used to chew on toothpicks all the time after dinner. He had this plaid shirt he wore every single Sunday, red and black squares. It was flannel, and it was so soft from being washed a million times. The elbows were practically worn through. So, no, nobody's putting thoughts in my head. My thoughts are just mine.

Less than two weeks? I... I don't really know how fast it started. Time is kind of funny like that. Sometimes a week feels like a whole year, you know? Like when it rains every single day. We had a week like that last April. Just gray and pouring, non-stop. The gutters overflowed and made this huge puddle at the bottom of the driveway. It looked like a little lake. The mushrooms get all wrinkly and black when they bake them, they don't even look like mushrooms anymore. My cousin grows mushrooms in her basement. It's so dark and damp down there, it smells like wet dirt. She has these big plastic bags filled with sawdust and spores, and they just sprout right out of the plastic. It's kind of creepy, honestly. Like little alien fingers pushing out. She gave me some to cook once, but I threw them away because I was scared they were poisonous. You hear stories about people eating the wrong mushroom and just dropping dead in the woods. So, yeah, no, my face is fine, my voice is fine.

Harm me? No, nobody is trying to hurt me or anything like that. It's just the money they're after. People get so crazy about money, you know? Like my aunt, she used to buy those scratch-off lottery tickets every single Tuesday. She said Tuesday was her lucky day because she was born on a Tuesday. She'd buy five of the shiny gold ones, the ones that cost five dollars each, and sit at her kitchen table scratching them with a special silver coin. It was a quarter from 1976, the Bicentennial one with the drummer boy on the back. She said the regular eagle quarters didn't work. One time she actually won fifty bucks, and she went right out and bought a huge ham for Sunday dinner. It was one of those spiral-cut hams with the sweet glaze on the outside, and it came with a little packet of extra sugar to melt over it. We ate ham sandwiches for a week after that. White bread, yellow mustard, and a slice of American cheese. The cheese always sticks to the roof of your mouth if you don't drink enough water with it. I prefer Swiss cheese, honestly. Um... no. Not really. I don't think I do that.

Well, I guess... I mean, I didn't really decide to come here on my own, they kind of made me. It’s all because of work, down at the freight warehouse. No, no, I... I don't think so. I mean, my mom always said I was a pretty normal kid, you know? I don't know why it's happening now, with the boxes and the sounds. It's just... it's just the warehouse, I guess. It's the warehouse that makes it happen. But no, not when I was little. Not at all.

No, I... I haven't had anything like that. No seizures or anything. I try to eat okay, you know, not too much fast food, though sometimes the guys at work want to grab burgers on the lunch break and it's hard to say no. But yeah, physically, my body is fine. It's just... it's just the stuff at the loading dock, the way I get stuck and the patterns with the boxes. But nothing is actually wrong with my health, like a disease or a brain injury or anything like that. I'm sure of it.

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't had any days where I felt like I was on top of the world or full of energy, or where I was just snapping at everyone. I'm pretty even, I guess. I just wake up, have my bowl of cereal—usually the frosted flakes, I like how the milk gets sweet at the end—and I go to work. I don't get these big bursts of energy where I feel like I could run a marathon or stay up all night painting the house or whatever it is people do when they feel like that. I don't feel high or energized, I just feel like I have to do what I'm doing. So, no, no days like you're talking about. Just regular days, mostly.

No, I... I don't think depressed is the right word at all. I mean, I don't feel sad or heavy or anything like that. You know how when people are depressed, they just want to lay in bed all day and they cry or they don't want to eat? Like when I was taking a few classes at the community college before I dropped out and started working full-time at the warehouse, my roommate got really depressed because his girlfriend broke up with him, and he wouldn't even get up to go to the dining hall for pizza on Fridays, which was his absolute favorite. He just laid there staring at the ceiling fan. 

But I'm not like that. I get up every morning the second my alarm goes off at 5:30. I take a shower, I have my cereal, and I walk down to catch the 42 bus right on the corner. It drops me off a couple of blocks from the loading dock, and I just walk the rest of the way, usually just looking at the cars going by. I'm not walking along feeling down or hopeless or like life is terrible. I just... I just go to work. 

And even when things get stressful there, like when the foreman gets on my case and starts shouting about me being too slow because I'm making sure the boxes are in the right shapes, I don't go home and cry about it. It doesn't hurt my feelings. I just go home, maybe microwave some macaroni and cheese—the kind with the white cheddar, it tastes a little better than the orange kind—and sit on the couch and watch whatever is on TV. I don't feel sad. It's really just that my mind is so busy with the boxes and the sounds and making sure the patterns on the pallets are exactly right. It takes up all my focus, you know? So there isn't really any room to feel depressed or anything like that. I'm just doing what I have to do at the warehouse.

Well, I mean, my mood is always pretty normal, I think. Like I was just saying, I don't get super high or super low. I'm just... I'm just me. Just regular. So, yeah, all the time, basically. When I'm at the warehouse and I get stuck, like when I'm standing by the conveyor belt and my body just won't move, or when I have to arrange the boxes so the barcodes are facing a specific way—like, they have to form a square, and if it's not a perfect square, I have to start over, even if the foreman is yelling at me to hurry up and get the pallet wrapped—my mood is totally fine. I'm not sad or angry or anything when that happens. 

And the sounds, too. When I hear the forklift backing up, that *beep beep beep*, and I just have to make the exact same sound back, right out loud, *beep beep beep*, at the same pitch and the same speed... I'm not feeling weird emotionally when I do it. I just feel normal. It's just that I *have* to do it. It's like my brain is telling me the pattern has to be completed, the sound has to be matched, but my mood is just... flat, I guess. Or not flat, just regular. Like how you feel when you're just standing in line at the grocery store waiting to pay for your milk. You're not happy, you're not sad, you're just there. That's how I feel when all this stuff is happening. It's been happening a lot, actually, the freezing and the sounds, pretty much every shift now, but my mood hasn't changed at all. It's just my body and the boxes and the noises that are doing all this stuff. I feel completely normal inside, like mood-wise.

Well, it's been... let's see. It's been going on for a while now. I'd say about six months, maybe a little more, but definitely around six months. I remember because it started right around the time the weather started getting really cold, back in late October or early November. I had just bought this new heavy winter coat from the surplus store downtown—the one with the deep pockets and the thick lining, because the warehouse gets freezing in the winter since the loading dock doors are open all the time. And I was standing there, wearing the new coat, and that was the first time I got stuck. I was trying to reach for a box of automotive parts, and my arm just stopped mid-air, and I stood there for what felt like ten minutes, just staring at my own hand. The foreman thought I was messing around. 

And then the sounds started a few weeks after that, right around Thanksgiving. I remember because the guys in the breakroom were talking about turkey and stuffing, and someone dropped a metal thermos on the concrete floor, and it made this loud *clack-ping* sound, and I just repeated it, *clack-ping*, right out loud, completely automatically. And since then, it's just been happening more and more. The box patterning really picked up after Christmas, when we had all those returns coming in and there were so many different sizes of boxes. I just couldn't put them on the pallets normally anymore. They had to be in the right shapes. So yeah, it's been about six months of all this... this confusing talking and the freezing and the sounds and the boxes. Six months of it happening almost every day at the warehouse. It's really taken over my whole shift, honestly, ever since I bought that winter coat.

Voices? No, no, I don't hear any voices. Just the regular sounds, you know? The warehouse sounds. Like the forklift backing up, or the pallets dropping, or the conveyor belt squeaking. I mean, there's always noise at the warehouse, but it's not voices talking to me when nobody is there. It's just... well, sometimes the guys talk, obviously, like when they're yelling across the dock to get someone's attention, or when they're complaining about the schedule in the breakroom. Usually they're complaining about the new supervisor, Dave, who always schedules people for closing and then opening the next day. It's called a "clopen," they say. I don't mind it so much because I just get up at 5:30 anyway, but they really hate it.

But when I'm alone? Like when I walk home or when I'm just sitting in my apartment eating my white cheddar macaroni and cheese? No, it's just quiet. Well, except for the TV, or maybe the hum of the refrigerator. My refrigerator has this really specific hum, it goes *mmm-hmmm-mmm*, and sometimes I catch myself making that sound back, just like I do with the forklift. But it's not a voice. It's not someone talking to me or telling me things or anything like that. I just hear the normal things that are actually there, and then my brain just... makes me copy them. But definitely no voices. I think I'd be really scared if I started hearing people talking when my apartment was empty. It's just me and the refrigerator hum.

Controlling my actions? Like, like someone else is making me do things? No, no, I don't think so. It's not like there's a guy with a remote control or some kind of microchip in my brain, you know? I've seen movies like that, where the government or aliens are steering people around like video game characters, but that's not what this is. It's just... it's just my own brain, I think. It's my brain getting stuck. Like a record player that hits a scratch and just keeps skipping on the same note over and over. 

When I freeze up at the conveyor belt, it's not because someone is holding me there. It's just that I... I can't find the next movement. Like the signal from my brain to my arm just gets lost somewhere in the wires. And with the boxes, the patterning, it's me doing it. I know I'm doing it. I'm the one looking at the barcodes and making sure they line up into a perfect square. It's just that I feel this intense pressure that it *has* to be done that way, otherwise it's wrong. It's like an itch you have to scratch, but it's in my head. 

And the copying sounds, too. When I hear the forklift and I go *beep beep beep*, it's my mouth making the sound. It's not someone else talking through me. It's just... automatic. Like when a doctor hits your knee with that little rubber hammer and your leg kicks out. You didn't decide to kick, but it's still your leg doing it, right? Nobody is forcing your leg, it's just a reflex. That's what it feels like. A really complicated reflex that makes me arrange boxes and repeat the refrigerator hum. But it's all me. Just a very stuck, very glitchy version of me. So no, I don't think anyone is controlling me. It's just my own body doing these weird things on its own.

Well, continuously? Like, every single day without stopping? I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by continuously. If you mean, has there been a whole month where this stuff happens every day, then yes, definitely. Like I said, it's been going on for about six months total, since I bought that winter coat, and it's definitely been happening every single day for way more than a month. 

I mean, I go to work at the warehouse five days a week, Monday through Friday, usually the 6:00 AM to 2:30 PM shift, unless Dave makes me do a clopen, which like I said, I don't really mind, but the other guys hate. And every single shift, without fail, I freeze up at least once. Usually it's by the conveyor belt when the smaller packages come down, the ones from the online retailers that are all wrapped in that gray plastic instead of cardboard. I'll just be standing there, and my hand goes out to grab one, and then... nothing. I just stop. And it's not just a quick pause, it's a real freeze. The other day, I think it was Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday—no, it was Tuesday because they were serving meatloaf in the cafeteria—I froze for so long that a whole line of packages backed up and fell off the end of the belt. The supervisor was yelling, but I couldn't move. 

And the sounds, too. That happens every day. Like the forklift backing up, the *beep beep beep*, or the scanner going *boop*. I do it all the time. Even on the weekends when I'm not at work, I'm doing it at home with the refrigerator, the *mmm-hmmm-mmm*. Or if a car drives by my apartment and honks, I'll honk back, out loud. So yeah, it's not like it takes a break. It's not like I have a week where I'm totally fine and then a week where it comes back. It's every day. It's been every day for months now. 

And the boxes... well, that's every time I have to load a pallet, which is constantly. I can't just throw them on there anymore. I have to find the corners, I have to match the barcodes, I have to make the shapes. And if I don't, if someone else tries to help me and puts a box in the wrong spot, I have to take it off and do it again. So it's definitely continuous. It's a constant, everyday thing that just... it just doesn't stop. It's like my brain is stuck in this loop, every single day, for way more than just one month. It's been a solid block of this since the weather got cold.

Before? Oh, no, before all this started I was doing fine. I mean, I was busy, but I was handling it all. It was only after this whole stuck-brain thing started that everything went downhill. Because now... well, now it is just a mess. 

Like at the warehouse, I actually used to drive the forklift. Dave, the supervisor I told you about, he pulled me aside and said I was a liability. He told me people were saying they could not keep things safe around me anymore because I would just stop moving in the middle of the loading dock, or I would be making the backup beeps with my mouth instead of actually paying attention to where I was driving. So they took the keys away and put me back on the floor, which is why I am always standing at the conveyor belt now.

And it is not just work. I was taking classes at the community college, just trying to get my general education credits done so I could maybe get a degree later on. I had this history class on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the professor always wore these really thick wool sweaters

Suddenly? Like, I just woke up one morning and couldn't move my arms? No, no, it wasn't like that at all. It wasn't just a few days where everything went crazy all at once. If I really think about it, the whole thing... it's actually been a really long time coming. Things have really been going downhill for about 11 months now. 

Yeah, 11 months. That was right around the time I moved into this shared apartment. I was trying to be smart about things, you know? I wanted to be closer to work at the warehouse and closer to the community college, because before that, I was taking the bus from way across town. It was like a forty-five-minute ride each way, sometimes an hour if the traffic was bad, which it always is on Thursdays for some reason. So I found this place, it's a four-bedroom apartment, and I moved in with these three other guys I didn't really know, just to cut down on the commute. I thought it was going to make my life so much easier and give me more time to study and sleep. 

But almost as soon as I unpacked my stuff in that new room—it's the one at the very end of the hall, right next to the bathroom, so I hear the pipes rattling all the time—that's when the downhill slide really started. It wasn't the full-on freezing at the conveyor belt right away, but it was just... things slipping. The pressure in my head starting to build up. I'd be trying to organize my new closet or set up my desk for school, and it would just take forever because things didn't feel right, or my thoughts would just start getting tangled up. 

So it definitely wasn't a sudden, over-the-weekend kind of

Yeah, they do. They actually do say that. A lot, actually, especially lately. Dave, the supervisor I was just telling you about? He gets really frustrated with me about it now. 

Because, okay, so part of my job, even when I'm just on the floor by the conveyor belt and not driving the forklift anymore, is helping check the staging lanes. And Dave will come up to me with his clipboard—he always has this heavy metal clipboard with the big clip at the top that snaps really loud—and he'll ask me which pallets are going on the outbound truck. The 3:00 PM truck, usually. Which should be a really simple question, right? It's just pointing to a lane. But when I open my mouth to answer him, to just tell him what's going on, it's like my words just completely slip off the track. 

I start trying to explain it to him, but then my words just jump. I'll be talking about the load sheet, the yellow carbon copy one we use for outbound freight, but then something about it just jumps my brain over to my old house. The one I lived in before I moved into this new apartment with those three guys. And suddenly I'm telling Dave about the old house, and the garage out back, which makes me think about packing up the truck for fishing. Because we used to go fishing all the time, early in the morning, and you have to organize all the tackle boxes perfectly so the hooks don't get tangled. And then just talking about the tackle boxes... it jumps me over to the church boxes. Like, the big wooden donation boxes

Depressed? Or high? Like... like really happy or energetic? No, no, I haven't really had anything like that. Not for a whole week, definitely not. I mean, I'm not exactly thrilled about losing my forklift privileges, obviously. It's a huge bummer being stuck at the conveyor belt all day because it really does a number on your lower back. You're just standing there on that hard concrete floor, and they have these anti-fatigue mats, but honestly, they don't do anything. They're just these thin pieces of rubber with holes in them, and by the end of an eight-hour shift, my knees are just killing me. So yeah, I get down about that sometimes, because who wouldn't? 

But it's not like a deep, dark depression where I can't get out of bed or anything. I still get up. I still go to the apartment kitchen and make my oatmeal—I have the instant kind, the maple brown sugar one, because it's fast and you just need hot water from the kettle, which is good because one of my roommates, Greg, he always leaves his dirty dishes in the sink, so I can't even use a real pot to cook anything. 

And as for feeling unusually high or super energetic... no, definitely not that either. I don't get these big bursts of energy where I feel like I can conquer the world or stay up for three days straight. If anything, I'm just trying to keep my head above water with the warehouse and the community college classes. Well, the classes I was taking, anyway. The history one with the professor in the thick wool sweaters. He actually wears them even when the heater in the building is cranked all the way up, which I never understood. It's got to be at least eighty degrees in that lecture hall, and he's up there in this heavy, scratchy-looking maroon sweater, just talking about the Industrial Revolution. 

But no, to answer your question, my mood hasn't been stuck way up high or way down low for a week or anything like that. It's just... I'm just trying to get through the days with everything else going on, you know? The stuck-brain feeling and the words jumping tracks. That's the main thing. My mood is just... normal, I guess. Normal for someone dealing with all this.

Caring less? Losing motivation? I mean... I wouldn't say I've lost interest or stopped caring about things, not really. It's not like I just don't care anymore. It's more like... well, take the warehouse, for example. Like I said, I'm stuck at the conveyor belt now, right? And I still go, I still show up for my shifts, even though it's super repetitive and my back hurts. I still care about doing the job, it's just harder to do it now with my brain getting stuck and the words jumping around when Dave asks me questions. But I still want to do a good job, you know? I want to get my forklift privileges back eventually. I haven't just thrown in the towel on that. 

And with school... well, the community college classes. I haven't stopped caring about them either. I mean, I was talking about that history professor, the one with the maroon wool sweater? I actually really liked that class. I thought the Industrial Revolution stuff was pretty interesting, especially how it changed all the factories and the way people worked, which kind of made me think about the warehouse and how we use the conveyor belts now instead of just carrying everything by hand like they probably had to do back then. I still care about learning all that. It's just that it got so hard to concentrate with the pressure in my head, and my thoughts getting all tangled up when I tried to read the textbook. The textbook was this massive, heavy thing, too—like, literally heavy, it must have weighed five pounds, and the pages were that really thin, glossy paper that reflects the light from my desk lamp right into my eyes. 

But I didn't lose interest in it. I didn't just wake up and say, 'I don't care about history anymore.' It's just that the other stuff, the slipping and the freezing, got in the way. 

And as for seeing other people... I mean, I live with three other guys now. I see them every day. Well, mostly I just see Greg leaving his dirty dishes in the sink, or I hear the other two playing video games through the wall. They play these first-person shooter games, and they have the bass turned way up on their TV, so I can feel the explosions vibrating through the floorboards when I'm trying to study or sleep. But I don't avoid them because I don't care about them. I'm just... I'm just dealing with a lot right now. So I might stay in my room a bit more, the one at the end of the hall by the rattling pipes, just to try and keep my head straight. But it's not because I've lost motivation to have friends or anything. I just... I haven't really noticed a drop in how much I care. It's just harder to do the things I care about.

Well, if someone tries to move me... I mean, I guess that's actually the whole reason they brought me in here in the first place, to be honest. Because at the warehouse, I keep doing these things where I just... I get stuck. Like, I'll be standing right by the forklift—not driving it, like I said, just near it on the floor—and I'll just freeze with my arms up in the air. Just stuck like that. And I don't even know if they try to push my arms down or move my body because mostly they just start yelling at me right away. 

But while I'm frozen there with my arms up, I start copying the sounds the forklift makes. You know that really loud, piercing backup alarm? That OSHA safety thing? The *beep, beep, beep*? I just start making that exact sound out loud, over and over, and I'll start copying the hand signals the spotters use for the drivers when they're backing into the tight staging lanes in aisle four. I just keep doing the signals and the beeping while I'm frozen.

And it's not just the freezing and the beeping, either. When I'm back at the conveyor belt, I'll start taking the boxes—the heavy corrugated cardboard ones with the yellow shipping labels—and instead of pushing them down the line, I keep moving them into these strange little patterns. Like, arranging them so the corners touch in a specific way, making these little geometric shapes on the concrete floor, over and over. And Dave and the other guys will be standing right there, literally yelling at me, just screaming for me to stop and get back to work, but I just... I just keep doing it. The patterns and the freezing and the beeping, even with everyone yelling. So I guess that's why they made me come talk to you.

Speaking much less? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, you can probably tell I'm talking plenty right now, right? I definitely haven't lost my words or stopped talking to people. If anything, I feel like I'm constantly having to explain myself to everyone, probably more than I used to. 

Like with Dave at the warehouse... I'm always trying to tell him why the boxes have to go in those specific shapes, those geometric patterns on the floor that I was just telling you about. I'll stand there and explain the whole system to him, how the yellow shipping labels need to face a certain direction so the barcodes catch the overhead scanners properly. Because the scanners on line four have been acting up since last Tuesday when maintenance tried to fix the belt motor, and they just left this big grease stain on the concrete that nobody bothered to mop up. So I talk to him about it, I try to explain my reasoning and how the corners of the boxes have to align, even if he is just yelling at me to get back to the conveyor belt. 

And with my roommates, too. I definitely haven't stopped talking to them. Just yesterday, I had a really long conversation with Greg about the sink situation. I explicitly told him that I just need enough space to put my ceramic mug under the faucet to get hot water for my oatmeal. Because, like I said, I eat the maple brown sugar instant kind, and if his crusty plates from his late-night pizza rolls are piled all the way up to the spout, I can't even get the water in the mug without the bottom of it touching the gross, dried-up tomato sauce and the cheese crusts. So I explained all that to him, in a lot of detail, probably for like ten or fifteen minutes straight while he was just sitting there on the couch trying to play his shooter games with the bass turned all the way up. 

So no, I'm definitely still talking. My voice works fine, the words come out... well, sometimes they jump tracks in my head, like I said before

Harm me? Plotting against me? No, no, I don't think anything like that. I mean, I know I said Dave and the other guys yell at me a lot, but they aren't trying to hurt me or secretly conspiring against me or anything. It's not a plot. It's just... well, it's a warehouse, you know? They have these really strict daily quotas they have to meet. If the corrugated boxes don't get down the conveyor belt and loaded into the freight trucks by 4:00 PM, the whole supply chain gets backed up, and then the regional manager comes down from the upstairs office and gets on Dave's case. 

So when Dave is standing there screaming at me to stop making the geometric patterns on the floor and get back to work, his face gets all red—like, right up to the rim of his plastic safety glasses, the ones with the little scratch on the left lens that he's always rubbing at with his shirt—but he's just stressed out about the shipping metrics. He's not trying to harm me. 

Actually, the whole place is very strictly regulated for safety anyway. We all have to wear steel-toed boots and those bright neon orange high-visibility vests with the reflective silver strips, and there are OSHA posters everywhere in the breakroom, right next to the vending machine that's always out of the peanut butter crackers I like. So nobody is going to physically hurt me there. The only thing that hurts is my lower back from standing on that hard concrete all day, and maybe my eyes from the overhead fluorescent lights that have that constant, low buzzing sound. But as far as the other guys go, no, they definitely don't have the time or the energy to plot against me. They're just trying to get their hours in. They just want me to stop doing the backup alarm noises and push the boxes down the line so everybody can clock out and go home.

Well, see, that's the thing, I don't really know if they move my arm or not, because like I was trying to say before, when I get stuck like that, freezing by the forklift, they don't usually come up and physically touch me. Well, yes... actually, I have. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about it the other day, trying to figure out if I was just overtired or what. I just stand there holding the mop handle, feeling like I'm losing my grip on things, because how can you hear something so clearly when there's absolutely nothing there to make the sound?

Well, you know, it's interesting you ask that, because I was trying to figure that out myself. It was all still right there with me, every single night.

Six months? Oh, well... actually, it's been quite a bit longer than that. If I sit and really trace it back—and I do, I spend a lot of time trying to make sense of all this when I'm just pushing the mop around—it’s been... gosh, it’s been about 11 months now.

Yes, actually. There was this one stretch... it must have been a few weeks, maybe a month or so ago. I wasn't feeling radiant or grand at all. Aunt Clara, she lived in this beautiful brownstone. She used to send me these delicate little porcelain teacups for my birthday every year. I had quite the collection by the time I was twelve. No, no seizures. I've never had anything like that happen to me. I did know someone who had them, though. It was my high school biology teacher, Mr. Henderson. I always used a green pen for biology, I felt like it matched the subject matter, you know? Plants and chlorophyll and all that. Anyway, he just collapsed. The ambulance came and everything. They had these incredibly bright flashing lights on the ambulance, red and white, just bouncing off the brick walls of the school building. It reminded me of a carnival I went to when I was a little girl. They had this Ferris wheel with the most vibrant lights, and you could see the whole town from the very top. I remember eating a candy apple that was so sticky I thought I'd lose a filling. Do you like candy apples? I think they look much better than they taste, honestly. The red coating is always so hard to bite into. I prefer caramel apples, especially if they have crushed peanuts on the outside.

Depressed? No, I don't think I've had weeks where I'm just sad all day like that. I haven't really noticed feeling down. My sister used to get that way, though. She would just sit in her armchair for days—this awful, scratchy floral armchair from the 1970s. It had these huge orange and brown daisies all over it. I always told her she should reupholster it, maybe in a nice velvet. A deep emerald green velvet would have been so elegant. 

I actually saw a winter coat exactly that color in a shop window downtown just last Tuesday. It had these beautiful, heavy brass buttons down the front, shaped like little anchors. It made me think of the ocean. I haven't been to the beach in absolute years. The sand always gets everywhere, doesn't it? You bring it home in your shoes and then it's buried in the carpets for months. I have a terrible time getting my vacuum cleaner to pick it all up. The vacuum has been making this strange, high-pitched whining noise lately anyway. I think the rubber belt inside might be slipping, or maybe it's just getting too old. Things just aren't built to last anymore, are they? You buy an appliance and five years later it's completely useless.

Suddenly? Hmm, let me think... I don't really know if it was sudden or not. It's hard to pin down exactly when things begin, isn't it? Time just sort of blends together. 

Like when my husband and I bought our first house. I remember packing all those cardboard boxes. We got them from the grocery store down the street. They smelled faintly of overripe bananas and cardboard dust. The produce manager, a lovely man named Arthur, saved them for us out back. Arthur had this magnificent mustache, thick and gray, like a walrus. He used to wax the ends of it, twirling them up into little points. It must have taken him ages every morning. I could never spend that much time in front of a mirror. I just wash my face, brush my hair, and that's that. My grandmother used to say that brushing your hair one hundred strokes before bed made it shine, but who has the energy for that? I tried it once when I was a teenager, sitting on the edge of my bed with this silver-backed brush she gave me. It had a little dent on the handle from where she dropped it on a tile floor in 1952. Tile floors are so unforgiving. Drop a glass, and it shatters into a million invisible pieces. You're finding shards for weeks, usually with your bare feet. I stepped on a piece of a broken wine glass once, right on the heel. It bled terribly. I had to wrap my foot in a tea towel until my husband could find the bandages.

No, I've never been told I have a brain condition or anything like that. My thinking is just fine, as far as I know. My doctor back in Ohio—Dr. Miller, his name was—he always said I was perfectly healthy. He had this little office right on Main Street, next to a bakery that made the most incredible cinnamon rolls. You could smell them baking all morning. It was absolute torture sitting in the waiting room, smelling that cinnamon and sugar, especially if you hadn't had breakfast. They used this really thick cream cheese frosting, the kind that just melts into the dough when it's warm. I tried making them at home once, but the yeast didn't rise right. Baking with yeast is so temperamental, isn't it? If the water is too hot, it kills it, and if it's too cold, it just sits there doing nothing. I ended up with these dense little pucks instead of fluffy rolls. My husband ate them anyway, bless his heart. He would eat just about anything I put in front of him, even that time I accidentally used salt instead of sugar in the peach cobbler. Oh, that was a disaster. We had to throw the whole thing out for the birds, but even the crows wouldn't touch it. Crows are so smart, though. I read once that they can remember faces for years. Imagine that, a bird holding a grudge because you didn't share your sandwich with it at the park...

Robins are such cheerful birds, but they can be quite aggressive when they're nesting, you know. I saw one chase a squirrel right up the big oak tree in my front yard last spring. I spend hours on my knees in the dirt, packing the soil just right, and the very next morning, there's a hole and the bulb is just sitting there, half-eaten on the grass. I tried sprinkling cayenne pepper on the dirt to keep them away, but then the wind blew and it got right in my eyes... it burned for hours, even after I flushed it with cold water from the garden hose. Garden hoses always have that metallic, rubbery taste if you drink from them, don't they? My brother and I used to drink from the hose all summer long when we were kids...

I think I just told you that, didn't I? Yes, the voices and that absolute certainty that people are watching my archive, it's been about eight months now. Eight months. The professor was this incredibly tall man, he must have been six foot six, with this wild gray hair that stuck up everywhere. Humphrey Bogart had such a distinctive voice, a little bit raspy, like he'd smoked too many cigarettes. Which he probably had, everyone smoked back then. You could even smoke on airplanes! Can you imagine? The whole cabin just filled with a cloud of gray smoke. It would be terrible for your lungs, but there's something sort of glamorous about it in retrospect. Glamour is something we've really lost in modern society, I think. People just wear sweatpants everywhere now. I always make sure to put on a nice blouse and a string of pearls before I leave the house. My grandmother gave me these pearls when I graduated. I feel like we're going in circles, Doctor. But yes, like I said earlier, there was definitely a period of several weeks where my mood was just completely normal. It needs good drainage, you know, or the roots just rot right in the ground...

If a friend canceled dinner plans because they claimed they were sick, but I saw them out getting coffee the next morning, I'd file that away. But I didn't assume malicious intent. I just... So, no, I wasn't walking around paranoid or suspicious of everyone I met. I didn't think the barista was out to get me or my neighbors were spying on me. I had a very normal, stable baseline of trust in my relationships. That's what makes this current situation so profoundly disturbing, doctor. It's not that I'm suddenly projecting a lifelong trust issue onto my wife. It's that the person I trusted most in the world has systematically dismantled that trust through these highly specific, deliberate structural changes in her communication. The trust was there. It's the data—the undeniable, empirical data of her behavior—that forced me to re-evaluate it.

Euphoric? Unusually high? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, I'm a forty-eight-year-old teaching assistant grading freshman composition papers, doctor. There is very little room for euphoria in my line of work, I assure you. The closest I get to feeling energized is when I find an essay that actually uses a semicolon correctly, and even then, it's more of a quiet, fleeting satisfaction than anything approaching a state of being "high." 

I've never had a period like that, where I'm just buzzing with energy for days on end. I know the kind of thing you're talking about—the manic episodes you see described in abnormal psychology texts, where people stay up for three days straight painting a mural or starting a tech company because they feel invincible. That is entirely foreign to my experience. My energy levels are, and always have been, exceedingly steady. Plodding, even. I wake up at 6:15, I have my coffee, I go to campus, I hold my office hours, I grade, I come home. It's a very metered, predictable existence. 

Even now, with everything going on with my wife, I wouldn't say I'm energized in that euphoric sense. Am I focused? Yes. Am I spending late nights cross-referencing her emails against her credit card statements? Yes, I am. But it's not born out of some grand, sweeping high. It's born out of necessity. It's a meticulous, exhausting process, frankly. I don't feel good doing it. I don't feel on top of the world. I feel like a man who is trying to solve a very complex, very painful puzzle that someone else has deliberately constructed to confuse him. 

So if you're looking for mania, or whatever the clinical term is for running around feeling like a superhero, you won't find it here. I'm just a tired academic trying to make sense of the inconsistencies right in front of me. There's no euphoria in that, doctor. Only a very heavy, very grounded reality.

Work? No, no, absolutely not. I mean, as I mentioned, my schedule is highly structured. If anything, the discipline required to maintain my teaching duties has been a... a grounding force, really. I haven't missed a single seminar, my grading is entirely up to date, and my office hours are conducted exactly as they always have been. And as for my personal responsibilities, I still iron my shirts every Sunday evening, I still prepare my meals... my self-care and daily routines are completely pristine. I am not falling apart, doctor. I am functioning perfectly well. 

Where this situation *has* taken a toll, and I suppose this is unavoidable given the circumstances, is within the marriage itself. It has mostly affected my home life. You can imagine the atmosphere. It's... well, it's incredibly fraught. We have these repeated, highly tense conversations at the house. I try to present my findings to her—calmly, rationally, just laying out the timeline of her sudden shifts in schedule and the discrepancies in her text messages—and she becomes immediately defensive. She completely refuses to engage with the empirical evidence, which leads to these protracted, exhausting arguments in the living room that go round and round. 

It actually reached a point where we started seeing a couples therapist a little while ago. I thought having a neutral, objective third party in the room would help mediate, perhaps finally get my wife to acknowledge the inconsistencies I’ve been documenting. But instead of focusing on the structural anomalies in her behavior, the therapist... well, she took a rather unexpected tack. After a few sessions of me simply explaining my methodology and showing her the data, the couples therapist essentially stopped focusing on our dynamic and suggested that *I* get an individual assessment. 

Which is, frankly, why I am sitting here talking to you right now. I agreed to come just to demonstrate, definitively, that my faculties are perfectly intact and that my work and routines are entirely undisturbed. The issue is the tension at home, doctor, not with my ability to function in the world.

Well, if we are pinpointing the exact timeline of when the certainty solidified... I'd say this has been going on for about a year now. Yes, roughly twelve months. And the timeline is highly significant, doctor, because it correlates perfectly—and I mean without a margin of error—with when my wife started working outside the home again. 

She had been doing some freelance editing from the house for a few years prior to that, which was a very transparent arrangement. Her schedule was visible, her communications were standard, literal, and entirely decipherable. But then, about a year ago, she accepted an administrative position at a mid-sized logistics firm across town. Now, I initially supported this. I thought the change of scenery would be beneficial. But almost immediately upon her re-entering the traditional workforce, the linguistic anomalies in her text messages and emails began.

At first, you know, I tried to brush it off. I thought perhaps she was just adopting the corporate jargon of her new environment. People do that, they absorb the vernacular of their colleagues. So when she started sending these oddly phrased texts—things like, "The primary shipment is delayed, proceed without me," or "Recalibrating the afternoon itinerary"—I didn't immediately assume she was encoding information. I gave it a few weeks. I tried to view it through a lens of mundane professional influence. But as someone who spends his life analyzing texts, I couldn't help but notice that the syntactical structures she was using were entirely disproportionate to the nature of her actual job. She's an admin, doctor. Why would an admin need to use such heavily guarded syntax just to tell me she's picking up dry cleaning? 

So, I started documenting it. I cross-referenced the phrasing of her messages with her actual arrival times, her stated locations, and the structural inconsistencies became glaringly obvious. It took maybe a month of this rigorous cataloging before the pattern was undeniable. So, yes, for a solid year now, ever since she took that external job, I have been absolutely certain that she is communicating through these deliberate, coded subtexts. It's the only variable that changed in our lives, and the data from the past twelve months speaks for itself. I even mapped out the frequency of the codes against her office hours, which I'd be more than happy to walk you through if you want to see how the progression... well, how it escalated once she was out of the house.

Socializing? Less interested? No, I wouldn't say that at all. In fact, I'd argue that my engagement with the outside world is exactly as it has always been. I am not isolating myself, if that’s the implication. 

I still show up for all my teaching sections, of course, which inherently involves a great deal of interpersonal interaction with the undergraduates and the department faculty. And outside of the university setting, my personal routines and social engagements remain entirely intact. I still keep up with my data analysis—both for my academic research and the, well, the personal documentation I mentioned earlier. I still get out and ride my bike on my usual routes through the city, which I find clears the mind quite effectively. And socially, I still meet my friends for our regular chess games. We play at a little café near the square, usually on Sunday afternoons. My focus during those games is as sharp as ever, and I enjoy the company just as much as I did five years ago. I haven't withdrawn from the world in the slightest, doctor. 

As I was trying to explain just a moment ago, the friction in my life is entirely localized. The main place this causes trouble—really the *only* place it causes any significant disruption—is when my wife and I get stuck arguing about what her work schedule really means. That is the epicenter of the issue. I’ll come home from a perfectly pleasant, intellectually stimulating afternoon of chess with my friends, completely relaxed, and she’ll present me with an itinerary for her upcoming week that is just... well, it's full of glaring logistical impossibilities. 

And then we get stuck in this terrible loop. I try to break down the timeline for her, showing her how a so-called "vendor meeting" at 2:00 PM on the east side cannot possibly align with a sudden "late lunch" at 2:45 on the west side, especially considering the current transit schedules, and she just digs her heels in. We argue in circles about what she is actually doing during those missing forty-five minutes, and what her coded texts about "delayed shipments" are actually meant to convey. 

So, no, my interest in other people hasn't waned at all. My friends, my students, my colleagues—those relationships are perfectly fine. It's just those exhausting, cyclical debates at home about her schedule that drain my energy. Outside of that specific dynamic, my social life is exactly as it should be.

Hi. Thanks. Well, what finally made me come in is that I just keep making these small, but really embarrassing mistakes. Like, I'll turn in applications or research notes, and I'll find out later that I mislabeled an artwork date or completely skipped a question. And the thing is... I honestly thought I had checked them over before submitting them. It's just getting pretty frustrating.

I don't think so, no. When I sit down to work on something, I feel like I'm paying attention. I don't really notice myself zoning out or losing focus when I'm trying to get a task done. It's more just... making those small mistakes I mentioned, even though I feel like I'm focused on it the whole time.

No, not really. I usually just look it over once, maybe twice, and think it's fine. I don't sit there checking it over and over again. I just... I assume I caught everything when I looked at it the first time, so I submit it and move on. It's only later that I realize I missed something.

No, not really. I mean, I get frustrated when I realize I messed up on an application or something, but I don't just feel worried out of nowhere. I'm usually pretty relaxed unless there's an actual reason to be stressed out.

No, not really. If I sit down and start something, I usually finish it. I mean, I might make those careless mistakes along the way, like I mentioned, but getting to the end isn't really the issue. I don't usually leave things half-done. Once I start a task, I just push through until I submit it.

Yeah, definitely. If I'm sitting at my desk trying to read or write, almost anything can pull my focus. Like, if a siren goes by outside, or I hear someone talking out in the hallway... I just lose my place. Even just a random thought, like an idea for an exhibit or something, will pop into my head, and I'll get completely sidetracked. Sometimes twenty minutes will go by before I even realize I stopped working.

Yeah, I think so. Even back in elementary school, my teachers would write notes saying that I had good ideas, but I'd always forget to turn in my worksheets or I'd somehow lose the instructions. I was always missing little details like that. Honestly, nothing really got turned in unless my parents checked my backpack every single night to make sure I had everything.

Well, I came in because... at work, you know, I manage the retail floor, and when I try to explain the inventory numbers or the weekend schedule to the team, my words just start jumping. I'll be talking about the delivery trucks, and then suddenly it's about Thursdays, and then I'm thinking about the church grill we used last summer, which reminds me of my boss's tone of voice when he's annoyed. Speaking of my boss, he always wears these terrible ties, like the ones from the 90s with the little geometric shapes. I think he gets them at thrift stores, which is fine, I like thrift stores too, found a great lamp at one last week... but anyway, people just look at me like they can't follow what I'm saying. They get this blank stare.

High? No, no, I don't feel high or euphoric or anything like that. I just feel regular, you know, just trying to get my point across to the team. It's just normal work stuff. Like dealing with the new seasonal displays they just sent us. They shipped these massive cardboard cutouts this year, and they're taking up half the stockroom right now. Which actually reminds me, my own garage is looking exactly like that stockroom lately. I've been meaning to clean it out, maybe have a yard sale this weekend. Yard sales are funny, aren't they? People will stand there and haggle over fifty cents for a used coffee mug. I have this one mug I got on a trip to Seattle back in '98, it has a little chip on the handle, but I still use it every single morning. The coffee just tastes better out of it, you know? My sister lives near Seattle, actually, in this little house with a green roof...

Voices? No, no, I don't hear anybody talking when they aren't there. Just the regular sounds, you know? Like at work, it's mostly just the store radio. They play the exact same forty songs on a loop every single day. I swear, if I hear that one Phil Collins song again... I actually used to love Phil Collins, though. Saw him live back in, oh, must have been '85? Or '86? We drove my buddy's old Ford Bronco all the way to Chicago for the show. Man, that truck was an absolute beast, drank gas like you wouldn't believe. Gas was so much cheaper back then, too. Now you pull up to the pump and it's like taking out a second mortgage just to get to work. My commute isn't even that bad, maybe twenty minutes, but there's this one traffic light on 4th street that stays red for a solid five minutes. I sit there every morning just staring at the bakery on the corner. They make these blueberry scones...

Sleep? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm sleeping my usual amount, maybe six or seven hours. I usually try to get to bed right after the late news. The anchors on the local station, they just changed the guy who does the weather. The old guy, Bob, he was there for like twenty years. He always had these terrible puns. The new guy seems a little stiff, you know? He wears these suits that look just a bit too tight in the shoulders. I used to buy suits like that when I first started in retail, thought it made me look sharp. Ended up splitting the seam on a jacket while reaching for a box of winter coats on the top shelf. That was embarrassing. My manager at the time, Brenda, she just laughed and handed me a stapler. Stapled my jacket together for the rest of the shift. Brenda was great, she moved to Florida a few years ago. Somewhere near Tampa, I think. Or maybe it was Orlando? I've never been to Orlando, but I hear the humidity is just brutal down there...

Plot against me? No, I don't think anyone's out to get me or anything like that. People are mostly just focused on themselves, you know? Like at the store, everyone's just rushing to get their shopping done and get home. Though we did have this one guy last Tuesday who tried to walk right out the front doors with a whole cart full of power drills. The new security sensors went off, and let me tell you, those things are incredibly loud now. Almost gives you a heart attack when they trigger. It actually sounds exactly like the fire alarms at my old college dorm. I lived in this massive brick building, third floor, and they'd run these drills at two in the morning in the dead of winter. We'd all be standing out there in the freezing snow in our pajamas. I had these great flannel pajama pants back then, red and black plaid. You really can't find good quality flannel like that anymore. Everything you buy nowadays just shrinks the second you put it in the dryer. I bought a nice button-down shirt just last month, washed it exactly how the tag said, and now the sleeves don't even reach my wrists...

Distracted in school? I don't really remember them saying that, no. I mean, school was a long time ago. I went to this little elementary school, Lincoln Elementary. The building was so old, it had those huge windows that rattled whenever the wind blew hard. And they had these radiators that would hiss and clank all winter long. It was always either freezing cold or boiling hot in those classrooms. My fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she used to keep a fan on her desk even in December. She was a real character, Mrs. Gable. She had this massive collection of porcelain frogs. They were everywhere—on her desk, on the bookshelves, even lining the windowsills. I always wondered where she got them all. You know, my aunt had a collection like that, but hers was thimbles. She had thimbles from all over the world. She went on this big cruise to Alaska once and brought back a thimble with a little moose painted on it. I've always wanted to go to Alaska. I saw a documentary about the salmon run up there, and the bears just standing in the river catching them right out of the water. It's amazing how nature works like that...

More energy? No, I wouldn't say so. Just my normal, everyday energy, I guess. It takes a lot to keep up at the store, especially when they schedule me for the morning shift right after a closing shift. We call those "clopens" in the business. They really take it out of you. Especially lately, because corporate decided to send us all the spring patio furniture early this year. It's still freezing out, and we've got boxes of wicker chairs stacked up to the ceiling in the back room. Wicker is so fragile, too. My grandmother had a whole sunroom full of wicker furniture when I was growing up. It was painted white, and the paint would always chip off if you sat on it wrong. We used to sit out there and drink iced tea in the afternoons. She made the absolute best iced tea, always put a little sprig of fresh mint in it from her garden. She had this massive garden out back, grew tomatoes the size of softballs. You really just can't buy tomatoes like that at the grocery store anymore. They always look perfect and red on the shelf, but you bite into them and they just taste like water. I bought a pack of those hothouse tomatoes last week for a sandwich, and it completely ruined the BLT I was making. The bacon was good, though. Thick cut, applewood smoked. I get it from the butcher down on 4th street, the guy with the big handlebar mustache...

Emotionally flat? Less motivation? I don't... I don't really think so. I mean, I still get up and go to work every day. It's just that the mornings are so dark right now, you know? The sun doesn't even come up until I'm already halfway through my commute. I take the bus, the 42 line. It's usually pretty empty that early, just me and this one lady who always knits. She knits these incredibly intricate sweaters, all cables and different colored yarns. I tried knitting once, back in my twenties. I thought it would be a relaxing hobby, but I could never get the tension right. My stitches were either way too tight or so loose they'd fall right off the needles. Needles are funny things, aren't they? They make those bamboo ones now, which seem nice, but I had the metal ones. They clacked together so loudly. It sounded exactly like my neighbor's wind chimes. He has these huge metal pipes hanging on his front porch, and whenever there's a storm, it's just this constant clanging noise. Last week, we had a storm that knocked out the power for three whole blocks. I had to use a flashlight to find my way around the kitchen. It was one of those heavy, industrial flashlights, the kind that take the big D batteries. They weigh an absolute ton...

Irritable? No, I wouldn't say unusually irritable. I mean, things get on my nerves at work sometimes, but that's just retail. Like yesterday, someone left a half-empty coffee cup right on top of a stack of the new spring sweaters we just put out. It left a ring on the display table. Those tables are made of this cheap particle board, you know, with the fake wood veneer on top. If water gets under the veneer, it bubbles up and looks terrible. I tried to fix a coffee table like that once in my old apartment. I bought all this wood glue and clamps from the hardware store. The guy at the hardware store was so helpful, he showed me exactly what to get. He was wearing this bright orange apron with all these pockets. I always thought it would be handy to have an apron like that for gardening. My neighbor has one, actually. He grows the most incredible zucchini. He brought me over a loaf of zucchini bread last week. It was still warm from the oven. Baking bread from scratch seems like such a lot of work, all that kneading and waiting for the dough to rise. You have to get the water temperature just right for the yeast, or it won't activate. I remember doing a science experiment with yeast in middle school... we put balloons over these glass bottles to see them inflate. Balloons always remind me of the county fair. They used to have this guy making balloon animals, but he could only ever figure out how to make a dog or a sword.

Depressed? No, I haven't really had anything like that. I mean, sure, you get a little down when the weather is miserable, but not depressed. It's been raining so much lately, just this constant, freezing drizzle. There are puddles everywhere downtown. I completely ruined a good pair of loafers stepping off the curb yesterday. They're these brown leather slip-ons, really comfortable for standing on the sales floor all day, but leather and water just do not mix. You have to let them dry out naturally, you know. You can't put them near a radiator or the leather cracks. I learned that the hard way with a baseball glove when I was a kid. I left it right on top of the heating grate in the hallway to dry out. My dad was so mad, he had spent a good chunk of change on that glove. It was a Rawlings, smelled amazing when it was brand new. There's nothing quite like the smell of new leather, is there? Kind of like that new car smell. I haven't bought a new car in... gosh, must be fifteen years now. It's a Honda, runs like a top, but the upholstery is starting to fray on the driver's side seat. I tried putting one of those wooden beaded seat covers over it, the ones cab drivers use, but they just end up pinching your back when you take a sharp turn...

Episodes? No, I wouldn't say it's like that. It's just... it's been building for a while, you know? Like, maybe 11 months or so. It really started when the new district manager came in. He started pushing us so hard on all these forecasts and the weekly schedules. Schedules are such a nightmare to write anyway, especially around the holidays when everyone wants time off. Last year, I had three cashiers all request the same weekend off in December to go to this music festival down in the city. I don't understand the appeal of those festivals, to be honest. It's just thousands of people crammed into a muddy field, paying fifty dollars for a bottle of water. I went to a concert once in the seventies, saw Fleetwood Mac. We had lawn seats, and it rained the entire time. We had to use these cheap plastic ponchos we bought at a gas station on the way there. They were bright yellow, the kind that rip the second you try to put your arms through the holes. Gas stations used to sell the weirdest stuff, didn't they? Now it's all just energy drinks and those little phone chargers that break after two days. I bought one of those chargers for my son last Christmas, and the wire frayed right at the base...

Well, yeah, I guess my mood has been fine mostly. Normal, you know. But... the jumbled explanations and all those odd stops I make on the sales floor, that's been pretty noticeable for about six months now. The district manager actually pulled me aside about it. We were standing right next to the clearance rack, the one with the red stickers. Red stickers always mean final sale, no returns. People get so angry when they try to return something with a red sticker. They bring it up to the register, and you have to point out the policy printed right there on the receipt. Receipts are so long these days, aren't they? You buy one pack of gum and they hand you a foot of paper with all these surveys and coupons on the back. I used to clip coupons with my grandmother on Sunday mornings. She had this special pair of scissors, really heavy metal ones, that were only for coupons. She kept them in an old cigar box on the kitchen counter. The box smelled like dried tobacco and peppermints. I love the smell of peppermint, especially around the holidays. We used to hang candy canes on the Christmas tree...

Energetic? No, I've never really been the revved-up type. If anything, by the time my shift is over, my feet are killing me and I'm just looking forward to sitting down. You stand on that hard commercial tile all day and it just drains the energy right out of you. The younger kids on the floor, though, they are always revved up. They drink those giant cans of energy drinks in the breakroom. I don't know how their hearts don't just explode out of their chests with all that caffeine and sugar. I stick to regular black coffee, myself. We have this old drip machine in the back office, the kind with the glass carafe that always gets that burnt brown ring at the bottom because someone leaves it on the hot plate all afternoon. I tried bringing in a nice French press once, but nobody wanted to take the time to clean it out. Cleaning out coffee grounds is a mess anyway, they get stuck in the sponge and then you're just smearing grounds all over the next mug you wash. I have this favorite mug at home, it's got a picture of a moose on it from when we went up to Maine years ago. Maine is just beautiful in the fall, the leaves turn these incredible shades of orange and red. We stayed in this little bed and breakfast right on the coast, and every morning you could hear the foghorns from the harbor...

Powerful? No, I wouldn't say that. I'm just a floor supervisor, you know? There's nothing grand about making sure the endcaps are stocked and the registers have enough change. Although, getting change has been a real hassle lately. The bank down the street changed their hours, so now I have to go on my lunch break if we need rolls of quarters. I hate going to that bank. The tellers are always so slow, and they have these velvet ropes set up like it's a movie premiere or something. I remember when going to the movies was an event. You'd dress up a little, get a bucket of popcorn that actually tasted like real butter. Now it's all fake butter flavoring, just yellow oil they pump out of a jug. It leaves this weird film on the roof of your mouth. I tried making popcorn on the stove at home the other night, the old-fashioned way with oil in a pot. I must have had the heat too high because I burnt the whole batch. The smoke detector went off, and my dog, Buster, he absolutely hates that sound. He went hiding under the guest bed and wouldn't come out for two hours. I had to bribe him with a piece of deli turkey. Turkey is getting so expensive at the grocery store...

Well, it's nice to meet you too, Doctor. I suppose what brings me in today is... well, it’s this whole situation with the local historical society. You see, I’ve been a member for years, mostly just attending the meetings and bringing a pie now and then, but recently they mentioned needing to raise funds for the old courthouse roof. And I just—I don't know, it was like a lightbulb went off, and suddenly I was taking on the entire fundraiser myself. I mean, I genuinely believed I could run the whole thing single-handedly. 

I started drawing up all these intricate quilt designs—because a raffle is always a good moneymaker, you know?—and I had fabric swatches spread out all over my dining room table, the living room floor, everywhere. Then I started calling all the volunteers, and I mean *all* of them, even people who hadn't been active in the society since the nineties. I was making these massive, color-coded schedules for everyone, assigning them tasks, and... and I was promising the board all these deadlines that, looking back now, I couldn't possibly meet. I told them we’d have three quilts done in a week and a fully catered gala planned by the end of the month. It was just... I was doing so much, and I felt like I had to do it all right that very second, and now it’s all just sort of crashed down on me.

Well, yes, I suppose euphoric is a good word for it. At first, anyway. I felt... oh, I felt almost glowing, really. It was like every single idea that popped into my head was just absolutely wonderful, pure gold. I remember standing in the living room looking at all those fabrics—the calicos and the little floral prints I'd pulled out of the attic—and just feeling this incredible warm rush, thinking, 'I am going to save the courthouse, and it's going to be magnificent.' I felt so capable, so alive, like I was finally doing exactly what I was meant to do for the town and everything was just clicking into place perfectly. 

But then... well, you see, the trouble started when people didn't quite see the vision. If anyone questioned me—like Martha, she's the treasurer of the society, and she had the nerve to call and ask if maybe three quilts in a week was a bit too ambitious for our volunteer base—I just got incredibly snappish. I mean, unusually short-tempered for me. I snapped right back at her on the phone. I acted like she was deliberately standing in the way of progress, just dragging her feet to ruin my plans. I think I even told her that if she didn't want to help, she should just step aside because we had history to save and no time for doubters. I was just so intensely irritated that they couldn't keep up with how wonderful everything was, and it felt like they were all just intentionally trying to block me from getting this glorious project done.

Well, let me think back, because it all blends together when you're moving that fast, you know?
