I remember the leaves were just starting to turn when I first got the idea for the quilts, right around the time they put the pumpkins out at the grocery store. And then it just... it kept going. I was running on that high, just pushing and pushing through the holidays, through the new year, even into the early spring. So, goodness, that whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project went on for about five months, give or take. 

Five whole months of me just buzzing around like a bee trapped in a jar, making phone calls at all hours, reorganizing the fabric piles, arguing with Martha about the budget for the gala catering... I mean, I can hardly believe it went on that long when I sit here and say it out loud. But it did. Day in, day out, just this constant, humming energy and that terrible, prickly irritability every time someone couldn't match my pace. It wasn't until late March, maybe early April, that the bottom just completely fell out and everything fell apart. But for those five months, I was just... I was an absolute whirlwind, and I couldn't stop if I tried.

Oh, no, no, I was never in the hospital for any of it. Goodness, the thought never even crossed my mind, and I don't think it crossed anyone else's either, at least not that they said to my face. I mean, where would I have even found the time to be hospitalized? I was much too busy! I had all those schedules, the fabric swatches, the caterers to wrangle... I suppose, looking back, people probably thought I was just being incredibly eccentric or maybe just a bit too passionate about local history. 

You know, my neighbor, Susan—she lives right across the street, lovely woman, always keeps her petunias looking so nice—she did come over one afternoon when I was dragging a massive roll of batting out of my trunk. She asked if I was feeling quite alright because I was talking a mile a minute about the courthouse roof and how we were going to have a silent auction with a Victorian theme. But even she didn't suggest a doctor or a hospital or anything like that. She just brought me a casserole a few days later and told me to remember to breathe. 

So, no, no hospital visits. I was just out there in the world, running around town, arguing with Martha at the bank, buying out the entire craft store's supply of rotary cutters... just living my life at a hundred miles an hour, completely unsupervised, if you can believe it. It's almost frightening to think about now, how I was just out there, spinning like a top for all those months, and nobody stepped in to stop me or take me to a clinic. But no, I managed to stay out of the hospital through the whole ordeal.

Well, let me think about that... depressed or lost interest. You know, it's funny you ask it just like that, because after all that rushing around with the quilts and the historical society—after that whole five-month whirlwind I was just telling you about—I did crash, like I said. The bottom just fell out. But... was it two weeks? Was it depression? 

I don't really know if I'd call it being depressed, exactly. Or maybe I would? It's so hard to put a label on these things when you're the one living inside them. I mean, I remember sitting in my armchair in the living room—the blue floral one, right by the window where the afternoon sun comes in—and just looking at all those leftover fabric scraps in the corner. Piles and piles of calico and gingham that I had been so obsessed with just days before. And I just... I didn't care about them anymore. The thought of sewing another stitch made me feel almost physically heavy. 

But as for it being a whole period of two weeks where I felt down or lost interest in everything... I'm really not sure. I mean, my daughter came to visit right around Easter, and we did go out to brunch at that little bistro on Main Street, and I think I enjoyed the mimosa and the eggs benedict. I don't remember feeling completely hopeless or anything like that. I was just so exhausted, you know? Like a balloon that had all the air let out of it. 

I stopped returning Martha's calls, of course, but that was mostly because I was too embarrassed about how I'd spoken to her before. And I stopped going to the society meetings. I just wanted to sit in my quiet house and watch the dust motes in the sunlight and not have to make any decisions about centerpieces or fundraising goals. But was it a true, deep depression that lasted for weeks on end? I really couldn't say for certain. It felt more like a terrible, lingering hangover from all that energy, just this profound tiredness where nothing seemed as shiny or important as it had before. So, I don't know if that counts as what you're asking about.

Well, before that five-month period? No, no, not before. The timeline is... well, it’s all very specific in my mind because of how things played out with the historical society and the quilts. See, the really bad part—the part where I felt just completely awful every single day—that didn’t happen *before* the whirlwind. It happened *after*. 

It started right around the time I realized what a mess I’d made of everything. The orders for the quilts had fallen completely behind because I’d promised far too many to far too many people, and the volunteer conflicts... oh, they just blew up spectacularly. Martha and I had that terrible row over the catering budget, and then Susan got involved, and before I knew it, half the committee wasn't speaking to me. And when I finally stopped moving fast enough to see the wreckage, that’s when it hit me. 

And it didn't just last two weeks. Heavens, no. I’ve been stuck in this incredibly low, heavy, guilty place ever since. It’s been... goodness, it’s been about nine months now of just feeling utterly weighed down by it all. Nine whole months of waking up and feeling this pit in my stomach about the quilts I never finished and the people I snapped at. I just sit in that blue armchair and think about how I ruined the gala, and the days just bleed into one another. So, no, not before the high energy. But after? Yes, for nine long months, just feeling completely stuck in the mud.

Um... just really stressed out, I guess. 

It’s... mostly about my dad. Well, his lab results. I draw blood for a living, so I know what I'm looking at. And for the past year, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is... changing his numbers. Or holding parts of the results back. 

My family and the doctors keep telling me everything is fine, but... I know the chart doesn’t match what I actually saw. It’s just... it's wearing me down.

I mean... yes. I know what I saw. I do this for a living, so... I know when something's missing. They can say whatever they want, but the numbers in the chart aren't the whole picture. I just... I know it.
No. I don't... I don't have anything like that going on. I just look at the charts. That's all.
I mean... I check them when I need to. Just to see if anything changed. But it's not... I'm not doing it all the time. Just when I have to.

I... I don't know what you mean by proof. For the last year, everyone—my family, the doctors here—they all keep telling me the numbers are fine. 

But... the chart doesn't match what I saw. I've been trying to prove it for a year, and... it's just wearing me down. So... I don't know. I just know what I saw.

I mean... maybe. I feel like... at work, they aren't really considering me for lab supervision anymore. I guess some people think I make record issues too confrontational. And... it's not just work. My family has started leaving me out when they plan his appointments. So... yeah. I guess it has.
No. Not really. I mean... I still go to my shifts at the clinic. I pay my rent. I... I take care of my own stuff. Everything else is just... normal. It's just this one thing with his records.

I... no. I'm not mistaken. 

I know what I saw. I've spent a year trying to prove it. Someone in the clinic system is changing them, or... holding parts of it back. It doesn't matter how many times my family or the doctors tell me the numbers are fine. The chart doesn't match. I just... I know I'm not wrong about this.

Hi, yeah, nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I came in because... well, I'm a high school teacher. And I'll sit down with a stack of essays or like, a new curriculum document, fully intending to just power through and work. 

Like, this past weekend I had this huge pile of papers on the Industrial Revolution. Which, honestly, the kids actually did a pretty good job on this year. Usually it's like pulling teeth to get 10th graders to care about the spinning jenny or textile mills, you know? One kid even made this little 3D model out of popsicle sticks for extra credit, which was wild because he usually never turns in his regular homework, so I was actually pretty impressed... 

But, um, anyway, sorry. What was I saying? Right, the grading. I'll sit down to grade them, and within ten minutes I'll realize I’ve just been staring at the exact same page the whole time. Like, my eyes are on the paper, but I'm thinking about three completely different things—like if I need to get my car's oil changed, or a podcast I listened to yesterday—and I'm barely taking in a single word of what's actually in front of me.

Yeah, actually, I did. I mean, even way back in primary school. I remember my parents used to get so frustrated with me. My mom had this whole filing system for my brother's schoolwork, like these color-coded binders, which is funny because my brother is an accountant now, so I guess the organization really rubbed off on him. He lives in Chicago, actually, just bought a place out there near the lake. 

But anyway, my stuff? Not organized at all. My parents were constantly finding old worksheets just completely crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack. Like, I would actually do the homework sometimes and then just totally forget to turn it in. I had this blue JanSport bag that was basically a black hole for paper. And my report cards always said the exact same thing every single year. The teachers would write that I was bright but careless, or they would complain that I wouldn't finish my work unless I was being closely supervised by them. So yeah, it definitely goes pretty far back.

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel down. Mostly I just feel... frustrated? Like, annoyed with myself for not getting things done. But not sad. Honestly, the weather's been so nice lately, it's hard to be too bummed out. I actually went for a hike this past weekend up at State Park. The leaves are just starting to change, which is my absolute favorite time of year. I usually try to get up there at least twice in October. My buddy Dave was supposed to come with me, but his dog had this weird stomach thing, so he had to stay home. It's a Golden Retriever, super cute, but man, that dog eats everything. He ate an entire sock once. 

But yeah, anyway, no, I don't think I'm depressed. Just... scattered, I guess.

No, I wouldn't say I'm a big worrier. I mean, I stress about the grading piling up, but that's a pretty obvious reason, right? It's not like I'm just sitting around anxious about nothing. Actually, my mom is the worrier in the family. She watches the news constantly, like, 24/7. I keep telling her she needs to turn off the TV and maybe read a book or something, but she says she likes to stay informed. She called me the other day panicking because she heard about some new scam going around where people steal your information through text messages. I had to spend like twenty minutes explaining to her how two-factor authentication works. Which, honestly, is such a pain to set up, but I guess it's worth it. I had to redo all my passwords last month because I got locked out of my school email... but yeah, no, I don't really worry about stuff for no reason. Just the normal stuff.

Well, I'm here because... everyone keeps acting like I'm just imagining things. But I know I'm not. I know for a fact that the hospital people, and some folks from the agency, have been watching our house. They even watch my cleaning routes when I'm out working. They're trying to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. I just... I know they're doing it, even if people say I'm making it up.

Yes, I have. Um, even when the house is completely quiet, I hear this woman's voice. It usually comes from right near the kitchen window. She tells me to check the locks, or... or to move my husband's pills. It's not a whisper or anything, it's as clear as if she's standing right there in the room with me.
No, I haven't. Um... I've never been told I have any kind of brain disease or nerve problems. Nothing like that.

No, I haven't ever felt like that. My thoughts are just my own. I mean, I hear that woman telling me things, like I said, but she's talking to me from the outside. Nobody is forcing thoughts inside my head or anything like that.
Well, the voices, and... also this feeling I get that people are watching us... it's all been going on for about 11 months now.
No, it's just the one woman's voice. I've never heard anyone else, and she's just talking to me, not to anybody else.
No, she doesn't do that. She doesn't... describe what I'm doing. Like if I'm at work cleaning or something, she's not giving a play-by-play of it. She just says things directly to me.
No, I haven't ever felt like that. My thoughts are just... they're just in my own head. Nobody else can hear what I'm thinking.

Yeah, they have. Sometimes when I try to explain what is happening, the words just kind of run all over the place. I'll go from talking about my husband's heart pills, straight into the church schedule, and then onto the numbers on my client list for my cleaning jobs. People tell me they just can't follow me when I get like that.

Hi. Yeah, um... well, I came in because I'm just having a really hard time lately. I drive a cab, and even when I know for a fact I did my safety check on the car, this thought just keeps hitting me that I missed something. Like, I keep thinking somebody could get hurt because of me, or my boss is gonna say I lied about checking it. And I just... I can't make the thought shut up. It doesn't matter if I'm driving or just trying to sit down and study, it just won't stop.

Yeah, I do. Um... before I can even take a ride, I keep going around the car checking everything. The tires, the lights, the doors, the meter, my paperwork... I just check them over and over again. Sometimes I even take pictures of everything just to prove to myself I did it. And if the routine doesn't feel exactly right, I have to restart the whole check from the very beginning. It gets so bad that I'm doing it even when passengers are literally standing there waiting for me and I'm already late. I just have to be sure.

Yeah, for sure. I mean... I know it's way over the top. Logically, I know the car is fine after the first time I look at it. It's definitely excessive. But... even knowing that doesn't help at all. I still have to do it. Like, I know I probably look crazy making people wait while I stare at a tire I just checked two minutes ago, but the feeling that I missed something is just so strong I can't ignore it.

I don't really know exactly how much time it takes up. I mean, I've never actually timed it or anything. It's just... it feels like it takes up a lot of my day, honestly. Especially before I start a shift, but I couldn't give you an exact number of hours or minutes.

Yeah, they really have. Um... at work, I've actually lost rides and gotten warnings because I just can't get on the road on time. And I'm trying to study for my CDL, but that keeps getting pushed back because so much of my day just gets eaten up by all this. 

It affects my personal life, too. I barely see my friends anymore. I'm always either behind on my shifts or trying to catch up after all the delays from checking everything. So, yeah, it's causing a lot of problems.

Yeah, exactly. That's actually why I came in. Like, I'll do my safety check on the cab, and I know I did it. But then this thought just hits me out of nowhere that I missed something. It just pops into my head that a tire is going to blow or the brakes will fail, and somebody's going to get hurt, or my boss is going to think I lied about doing the check. I definitely don't want those thoughts, but I just can't make them shut up. It happens all the time while I'm driving, or even when I'm just sitting there trying to study for my CDL.

I'm not really sure. Um... I mean, I guess I know nobody else is putting the thoughts in my head, but... they don't really feel unreasonable to me. Not when it's happening, anyway. 

It feels like a real warning, like something terrible is actually about to happen with the cab if I don't go back and check. So, I don't know. It's hard for me to just say it's all in my own mind when it feels that real.

Um... no, not really. It's pretty much just the cab. I mean, I guess I think about normal stuff, like passing my CDL test or paying my bills, but it's not like a constant worry or anything. 

The safety checks are what really take up all my time and energy. I don't really stress about other parts of my life the way I do about that.

Nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I'm here because... well, I just keep feeling like I ruined things for everybody lately. Like I'm a total fake in my apprenticeship. I'm training to be a pipefitter, and I just feel like I let my family down, and even the younger apprentices, over stuff I know other people would probably just fix and move on from. 

Like cutting a piece of pipe a quarter-inch too short, you know? Which, actually, reminds me, I lost my favorite pipe cutter the other day. It was this really nice Milwaukee one, bright red. I think I left it on the bumper of my truck when I stopped at this gas station on Route 9. The guy who works the counter there, Gary, he always has these crazy stories about his dogs. He's got three golden retrievers and they just completely destroy his yard. I mean, dogs are great, I grew up with a beagle myself, but three big ones? That's a lot of dog hair. I don't know how his wife deals with it, honestly. 

But um... what was I saying? Oh, right. Yeah, I just feel like a fraud at work and like I'm letting everyone down.

Um, I don't really think so? Like, I wouldn't say I'm depressed most days. I'm just... I don't know, maybe just drained. I've actually been staying up way too late watching this documentary series about deep-sea welders. It is wild what those guys do underwater. I actually thought about getting into underwater welding when I first started my associate's degree, but honestly, deep water kind of freaks me out. My uncle used to have this little aluminum fishing boat, and we took it out on the lake once, and he caught this massive catfish. It was like half my size when I was seven. Those whiskers were just thrashing everywhere on the deck, it was completely terrifying. I wouldn't even go near the cooler for the rest of the weekend. But... wait, sorry, what did you just ask me? Something about being sad?

Um, not really? I mean, I lost that pipe cutter, but I usually keep pretty good track of my stuff. My phone's basically glued to my hand anyway because I've been texting my sister a lot. She just got engaged last weekend, actually. It was this whole surprise thing at a vineyard, which is crazy because she doesn't even really drink wine. She's more of a hard cider person. We used to go apple picking every fall when we were kids, and my mom would make these huge batches of homemade cider on the stove. It made the whole house smell like cinnamon and cloves for days. I tried making it myself last year in my crockpot, but I definitely messed up the spices because it tasted like straight-up potpourri. I ended up pouring the whole batch down the sink, which was a bummer because I bought all these expensive honeycrisp apples for it. But yeah, no, I don't really lose my keys or anything like that. Just the pipe cutter.

Um, easily distracted? I don't... I don't think they said that. I mean, I got decent grades in school, mostly. I really liked history class, especially when we learned about the Industrial Revolution. All those massive steam engines and factories being built, it's just fascinating how quickly everything changed. My teacher for that class, Mr. Henderson, he had this incredible collection of antique pocket watches. He'd bring them in sometimes to show us how the gears worked. I actually bought a cheap replica pocket watch at a flea market a couple of years ago because of him. The flea market was huge, out in this big dusty field near the county line. They had everything there—old furniture, weird taxidermy, even a guy selling homemade hot sauce out of the trunk of his Buick. I tried a sample of the hottest one, and I swear I couldn't feel my tongue for an hour. I had to buy a giant lemon slushie just to cool my mouth down. The slushie was so cold it gave me a brain freeze, you know that sharp pain right behind your eyes? It was brutal. But um... yeah, I don't remember anyone saying I was distracted in school.

Trouble focusing? Um, no, not really. I'm usually pretty good at listening. Like on the job, you have to listen really closely when you're roughing in pipes or you'll mess up the whole layout. My journeyman, Greg, he's always giving me these super detailed instructions. He has this really deep, rumbly voice, kind of like a radio announcer? Actually, he told me he used to do voiceovers for local car dealership commercials back in the day. You know those ones where they just yell about Sunday blowout sales? My dad used to absolutely hate those commercials. He'd mute the TV every single time one came on. We had this old boxy TV in the living room that weighed like two hundred pounds, and the remote was completely held together by black electrical tape. We used that TV until the screen literally just went bright green one day, right in the middle of a hockey game. The Bruins were tied in the third period, too. My dad was so mad he actually threw a couch pillow at it and knocked over his coffee on the rug. It left this huge stain that never came out. But um... yeah, no, I don't really zone out when people are talking to me. I pay attention.

Um, a stressful event? I mean, I guess it started about five months ago, right after I took on this sustainable plumbing certification course. I was already doing my apprenticeship, so adding the classes on top of that was a lot. The classes are actually really interesting, though. We're learning all about greywater systems and how to reuse water from sinks and showers to flush toilets and water gardens. It's wild how much clean water we just flush down the drain every single day. My instructor for the course, she's really passionate about it. She actually lives in this tiny house she built herself, completely off the grid. She has solar panels and a composting toilet, which, honestly, I don't know if I could ever get used to. I watched this whole documentary on tiny houses last week because of her. Some of them are built on trailers so you can just hook them up to a truck and drive away whenever you want. That sounds kind of nice, just being able to pack up your whole house and move to the mountains or something. I've always wanted to visit the Rockies. I saw a picture of Banff National Park once and the water in the lakes there is this insane, bright turquoise color because of the rock flour from the glaciers. It doesn't even look real. But um, yeah, so I guess the whole thing with my mood and energy, it's been going on for about five months now, since I started that extra certification.

Um, if I stopped the course? I don't know, maybe? I mean, I can't really just drop it now, I've already paid the tuition and bought all the textbooks. Have you seen how expensive textbooks are lately? It's ridiculous. I had to buy this one massive manual on advanced pipefitting techniques, and it cost like two hundred dollars. It's so heavy, I actually use it to prop open the door to my apartment when I'm bringing in groceries. My apartment building is so old, the doors are solid wood and they swing shut so fast if you don't wedge something in there. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she got her hand caught in the lobby door once because she wasn't paying attention. She's this really sweet older lady who always smells like lavender and bakes these amazing snickerdoodle cookies. She brings me a plate of them every Christmas. Last year she put them in this really pretty vintage tin that had a picture of a snowy village on it. I actually kept the tin, I use it to store all my extra drill bits and screws now. It's perfectly sized for that. But um... yeah, I'm not sure if quitting the class would make a difference. I haven't really thought about stopping.

Um, yeah, actually. It's getting kind of bad. My instructors and my foreman, Greg—the guy with the radio voice I mentioned?—they've both had to chase me down lately because I'm leaving sketches unfinished and my work is just... slower than it should be. I'm really scared I'm going to mess up this apprenticeship and the certification, and I worked so hard to get here. It took me forever just to find a company that would take on a female apprentice, honestly. A lot of the older guys in the union are still pretty old-school about that stuff. My uncle is in the union, actually, he's an electrician, and he told me I'd have to work twice as hard to prove myself. He's a really great guy, though. He helped me rewire my entire kitchen when I moved into my apartment because the outlets were completely fried. We found these old newspapers stuffed in the walls for insulation from like, 1952. It was crazy, there was this huge ad for a brand new refrigerator that only cost like a hundred bucks. Can you imagine buying a fridge for a hundred dollars now? You can barely get a toaster for that. I bought a toaster last week and it has this weird setting just for bagels, but it always burns the edges anyway. I love everything bagels, though, especially with that jalapeño cream cheese from the deli down the street. But um... yeah, so my foreman and instructors are definitely noticing that I'm falling behind, and it's really stressing me out.

Um, worrying about other things? I don't know, I guess I worry a normal amount? Like, I wouldn't say I'm constantly stressing about everything. Mostly just the apprenticeship right now. Though, I did spend like an hour yesterday worrying about whether I left my straightener plugged in. I have this really bad habit of doing my hair and just running out the door. My straightener gets so hot, too, it's one of those ceramic ones. I bought it at the mall last year from one of those kiosks where they practically chase you down to curl a piece of your hair. The girl who sold it to me had the most amazing pink hair, though. It was like a really bright, neon magenta. I asked her what dye she used, and she said it was this brand you can only buy online. I thought about dyeing my hair pink once, but I figured it would look weird with my hard hat. Plus, the dye stains everything. My friend Sarah dyed her hair blue in high school and her bathtub was permanently Smurf-colored for like three years. Her mom was so mad. They ended up having to re-glaze the whole tub before they sold the house. But um... yeah, no, I don't think I worry about too many other things besides work and school.

Um, yeah, I guess I have. It's weird because I used to love drawing and stuff. But lately I can just walk right past my sketchbook and not even care. Same with my volleyball league, I've skipped the last few games. I even ignore the group texts for this volunteer thing I do. It's like I don't feel much of anything about them anymore, even though those were the things that made me feel like myself, you know? The volunteer group is actually really cool, we help build community gardens in empty lots around the city. Last month we planted this huge row of heirloom tomatoes in this lot over by the old textile factory. The factory is totally abandoned now, but the brickwork on the outside is amazing. It has these huge arched windows that are all boarded up. Some guy spray-painted this really intricate mural of a dragon on one of the boards. It's actually really good, way better than the usual tagging you see around there. I tried to take a picture of it, but my phone camera is completely scratched up because I dropped it in my toolbox last week right onto a pile of loose screws. I really need to get a new phone case, maybe one of those heavy-duty ones that construction workers use. The guy at the phone store tried to sell me one that looked like a tire tread, but it was so bulky it wouldn't even fit in my pocket. Women's pockets are useless anyway, they barely hold a tube of chapstick. I buy this cherry chapstick that comes in a three-pack, but I always lose two of them within a week. It's a mystery where they go. But um... yeah, I just don't have the energy or interest for my usual stuff right now.

Um, sad or down? I don't think so. I mean, I'm stressed about the apprenticeship and all, but I wouldn't say I feel sad most days. Just kind of... blank, maybe? Like with the volleyball and the drawing. But not really sad. My mom is always telling me I need to smile more, though. She's got this whole theory that if you just force yourself to smile, your brain gets tricked into being happy. She read it in this magazine she gets at the hair salon. She goes to the same salon every three weeks to get her roots touched up because she's terrified of anyone knowing she's going gray. The stylist there, her name is Brenda, she has these tiny little dogs that just run around the salon all day. They're Chihuahuas, I think, but they look like little rats. One of them actually chewed on my shoelace once when I went in there to drop off my mom's keys. I was wearing my good work boots, too, the steel-toed ones. They take forever to break in, so you really don't want a dog chewing on them. You have to rub mink oil on the leather to soften it up, which smells kind of weird, honestly. It smells like... I don't know, old basement? But um... yeah, no, I don't think I've been feeling sad for five months or anything. Just mostly stressed and tired.

Um, before these last five months? Well, honestly, this whole stretch of just... not caring about anything has been going on for like nine months now. It's just that I could kind of fake it better before, but then school and work started slipping, so it became way harder to hide. It's like when you have a leak behind a wall, you know? You don't see it for a long time until the drywall gets all mushy and the paint starts bubbling. I had to fix a pipe like that last week in this really old apartment building downtown. The walls were plaster and lath, which is such a nightmare to cut through. You need a special saw blade or it just ruins the plaster. The lady who lived there was so nice, though. She kept offering me these little hard candies from a crystal dish on her coffee table. They were those strawberry ones with the wrapper that looks like a strawberry? I haven't seen those since I was a kid. My grandma used to keep them in her purse. Her purse was this massive leather bag that weighed like ten pounds, and she had everything in there. Mints, tissues, old receipts, a tiny sewing kit. Once, she pulled out a whole stapler to fix my cousin's hem at a wedding. It was a beach wedding, too, which was a terrible idea because everyone's heels kept sinking into the sand. But um... yeah, so it's been about nine months of feeling like this, not just five.

Um, before this? No, I don't think so. I've always been a pretty busy person, you know? Like in high school, I was always doing something. I took all these vocational classes because I absolutely hated sitting still at a desk. We had this one shop teacher, Mr. Henderson, who let us build pretty much whatever we wanted for our final project. Me and my friend Sarah built this crazy go-kart out of scrap metal and an old lawnmower engine. It was super loud, like deafeningly loud. My dad has a riding mower that sounds exactly like it, actually. It's this vintage John Deere that he refuses to get rid of, even though the carburetor gets flooded literally every other time he tries to cut the grass. He spends way more time fixing it than actually mowing. He keeps all the spare parts in these old Folgers coffee cans on his workbench. Do you remember when coffee used to come in those heavy metal cans? Now everything is just cheap plastic. I guess it's cheaper for the companies to make, but plastic just cracks so easily in the cold. I bought a plastic toolbox a few months ago for my apprenticeship and the main latch snapped off the second day I had it. It's just so frustrating when things aren't built to last anymore. But um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling like this before. Yeah, no, this is definitely the first time I've ever felt this way.

Well, I’m here because... honestly, for months now I’ve been trying to get people to understand what my husband’s family is doing. They're quietly messing with our money and our good name. Like, I work as a billing clerk, and lately these little billing errors just keep showing up out of nowhere. It's funny, actually, because it reminds me of when we switched our computer system back in 2018, and my old supervisor Brenda—she retired and moved down to Florida, somewhere near Tampa, I think, or maybe Clearwater—she always hated that new software. She said it was too sensitive. 

But this isn't a computer glitch. And it's not just at work, it's church too. People there are suddenly acting funny toward me. Just last Sunday I was talking about the upcoming bake sale, and I always make my grandmother's lemon pound cake for it. She used to grow her own lemons, right in her backyard, the absolute biggest lemons you've ever seen... but anyway, what I'm saying is, no matter what records anyone pulls up or what they try to tell me, I know it all ties back to his family. They're the ones behind it.

Voices? No, I don't hear anything like that. I mean, my hearing is really sharp, though. I can hear the hum of the refrigerator from all the way in the living room. It’s a Whirlpool, actually. We bought it on sale at Sears right before they closed the one over at the Westside mall. That mall used to be so nice back in the day, you know? They had this amazing soft pretzel stand right by the food court, and at Christmas, they’d put up a tree that went all the way up to the skylight. I took my niece there to see Santa once when she was maybe four or five. She had on this little red velvet dress with white tights that got a chocolate stain on them before we even made it to the line... but, anyway, no, I don't hear people talking when nobody is there. Just regular house noises.

Unusually high or energetic? No, I don't think so. I've always been pretty steady. I mean, I have to be, with my job. Working as a billing clerk, you sit a lot. You really have to make sure you get up and stretch, otherwise your lower back just completely locks up. My sister-in-law, the one who married my brother David, she bought me one of those ergonomic cushions for my desk chair last Christmas. It’s got this memory foam in it that's supposed to mold to your shape. She got it off one of those home shopping channels, I think. She watches QVC all day long, buying the most ridiculous things. Last month she bought this set of copper pots that she swore were non-stick, but the very first time she tried to make scrambled eggs, they stuck right to the bottom. It took her three days of soaking just to get it clean. But anyway, no, I haven't had any days where I felt like I was full of energy or anything like that. Just my normal routine.

Clear proof? Well... what kind of proof are we talking about? Because I've seen the records they pull up, and I know how easy it is to doctor a spreadsheet or a bank statement. People think computers are foolproof, but they aren't. My nephew, the one who just started his freshman year at State—he's studying computer science, actually. He built his own computer in his bedroom from parts he ordered online. It took up his whole desk, and it had these glowing blue lights inside the case. His mother was furious because he spent his entire summer job savings on it instead of saving for a car. She drives this old Honda Civic that’s been making a terrible rattling noise under the hood, but she refuses to take it to the mechanic because she says they always try to upsell her on air filters and wiper blades... 

But anyway, what I'm saying is, I wouldn't believe their "proof." I know what I know. For months I've been trying to get people to understand that his family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. The billing errors at work, the way the ladies at church are suddenly acting so funny toward me... no matter what piece of paper someone tries to show me, I know it all ties back to them. They're doing it, and I'm not going to just pretend they aren't because someone hands me a fake printout.

Jump around? No, nobody's ever said that to me. I think I'm pretty clear when I speak. You have to be clear when you work in billing. If you get one number wrong, or explain a code poorly, the whole insurance claim gets kicked back. And you know how insurance companies are. They'll use any excuse to deny a claim. My cousin Brenda, she had this terrible time with her insurance last year when she needed that knee surgery. She tore her meniscus slipping on the ice in her driveway. It was one of those freak ice storms we got in February, remember? The whole city basically shut down for two days. The salt trucks didn't even make it to her neighborhood until the second afternoon. She was trying to walk down to get the mail because she was waiting for a birthday card from her son who lives out in Arizona. He moved out there for the dry heat, says it helps his allergies. But anyway, no, people don't tell me I'm hard to follow. I just tell things exactly how they happen.

Losing interest? No, I don't think so. I mean, I still like doing the things I usually do. Like my garden, I try to keep up with the flower beds out front. Mostly marigolds and some petunias. Though I will say, the slugs have been absolutely terrible this year. Have you noticed that? It's because we had such a wet spring. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he's lived next door for thirty years, he told me to put out little shallow dishes of beer to catch them. He says they're attracted to the yeast or something and they just crawl right in and drown. He buys the cheapest beer he can find at the discount liquor store over on 4th Street. The one next to that old dry cleaner that closed down? I used to take my winter coats there, but the last time I did, they lost the belt to my navy trench coat and refused to pay for it. The owner was this very stubborn man who insisted I brought it in without a belt. Why would I bring a trench coat in without a belt? It completely ruins the silhouette. But anyway, I still enjoy my garden and things like that. I just haven't been as social lately, but that's only because of everything going on with his family, you know? You have to be careful who you spend time with.

Read my thoughts? No, I don't think anyone can do that. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My husband loves those kinds of movies, the ones with aliens and mind readers and spaceships. He used to make me watch them with him when we first got married. We had this huge, heavy tube TV back then, the kind that took two people just to lift it onto the stand. The picture quality was terrible compared to what we have now, but we didn't know any better. We'd rent VHS tapes from Blockbuster on Friday nights. Remember Blockbuster? It's such a shame they all closed down. I used to love walking down the aisles, looking at all the covers. The smell of the popcorn they sold by the register... I bought a box of microwave popcorn last week, the extra butter kind, but it just doesn't taste the same. I think they changed the oil they use or something. The bag says "new and improved flavor," but whenever a company says that, it usually just means they found a cheaper way to make it. It's like the brand of coffee I used to buy for the office breakroom. One day the packaging changed, and suddenly it tasted like burnt toast. I had to switch us to a different brand, which caused a whole fuss with the accounting department because it cost fifty cents more a can. But anyway, no, nobody can read my thoughts. I just keep them to myself, especially with everything his family is doing. You have to keep your thoughts private these days.

Special powers? No, no, they don't have magic powers or anything like that. That's ridiculous. They're just very... manipulative. They know how to pull strings. Speaking of pulling strings, did you know I used to knit? I made this beautiful cable-knit sweater for my husband for our fifth anniversary. It took me months. I had to special order the yarn from a little shop up in Maine because I wanted this specific heather gray color. The woman who ran the shop, Mrs. Higgins, she was so sweet. She used to send a little handwritten note with every order and a complimentary stitch marker. They were always shaped like little sheep. I had quite a collection of them by the time she retired and closed the shop. It's so hard to find good quality wool these days without spending a fortune. Everything in the craft stores now is acrylic. It just doesn't breathe the same way, you know? You put on an acrylic sweater and five minutes later you're sweating, but you're still cold. It makes no sense. I tried to explain that to my sister when she started making baby blankets, but she just wanted something you could throw in the washer. But no, his family doesn't have special powers. They're just very good at getting people to do what they want, normal things, just... twisted.

Distrust people? Oh, no, not at all. I've always been a very trusting person. Too trusting, maybe. I used to be the one at the office who would leave my purse right out on my desk when I went to the restroom. I mean, we're all adults, right? We had this one woman, Brenda, who started in the billing department a few years ago. She was always borrowing things. A pen here, a stapler there. One time she borrowed my favorite mug—it was this ceramic one I got on a trip to Sedona, painted with these beautiful little desert flowers. The glaze was so vibrant. Anyway, she borrowed it for her tea and then left it in the sink for three days. I finally had to wash it myself. The water in our breakroom sink was always lukewarm, never hot enough to really get things clean, which I always thought was a health hazard. I brought it up to the building manager, this guy named Tom, who always wore these terrible clip-on ties. He said he'd look into the water heater, but he never did. He was always making excuses, saying the pipes were too old. But anyway, no, I've never been the suspicious type. I always try to see the good in people, until they give me a reason not to. It's just that now, with his family, they've given me plenty of reasons. But before that? No, I never thought people were out to get me.

Oh, definitely more than a month. It's been going on for about nine months now. It all started right around the time we had that big blow-up over money and the holiday expectations. Holidays used to be so nice, you know? I used to bake these incredible gingerbread cookies from scratch. My grandmother gave me the recipe. She always insisted on using dark molasses, not the light kind, and you have to chill the dough overnight or it spreads too much in the oven. I had these antique copper cookie cutters shaped like little stars and reindeer. They were so hard to keep clean, though. Copper tarnishes so fast if you don't polish it. I used to buy this special cream polish from a hardware store downtown, but they closed last year to make room for another one of those fancy coffee shops. You can't even get a regular cup of drip coffee there anymore, it's all lattes and macchiatos and things you can't pronounce. And they charge six dollars for it! It's highway robbery. My husband used to drink his coffee black, just like his father did. His father was a very stern man, never smiled in pictures. We have this one photo of him from our wedding... but anyway, yes, it's been about nine months since they started all this nonsense with me.

Controlling my actions? Putting thoughts in my head? No, no, I'm fully in control of myself. My thoughts are my own. I've always had a very strong mind, actually. My mother used to say I was too stubborn for my own good. She was always trying to get me to wear dresses when I was little, but I hated them. I only wanted to wear these corduroy overalls. They were navy blue with little brass buttons on the straps. I wore them until the knees completely wore out. You just can't find good corduroy anymore. Everything now is that thin, stretchy material that loses its shape after one wash. I bought a pair of pants last month from that department store at the mall—the one that used to be a Sears before they remodeled the whole wing. They put in a huge food court with this terrible lighting that gives you a headache if you sit there too long. I went there to get a pretzel, you know, the soft ones with the big grains of salt? But the line was a mile long, so I just left. Anyway, no, nobody is putting thoughts in my head. I know exactly what I'm doing and thinking. It's just his family that's the problem, not my own mind.

Hear my thoughts? Oh, goodness, no. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. Like that one with the aliens that came down in those big silver saucers—what was it called? The Day the Earth Stood Still? My husband loved those old black-and-white movies. We used to stay up late on Friday nights watching them on this tiny little Zenith television we had in our first apartment. It had the rabbit ear antennas, and you had to wrap aluminum foil around the tips just to get a clear picture of channel 4. We lived right near the airport back then, so every time a plane flew over, the screen would get all fuzzy and the sound would buzz. It was so annoying, especially during the summer when we had the windows open. We didn't have air conditioning, just this big box fan that rattled and shook the whole window frame. I tried wedging a piece of cardboard in the side to stop the rattling, but it never really worked. The cardboard came from a box of oranges my uncle sent us from Florida. He had a grove down there, Valencia oranges, I think. They were the sweetest oranges I've ever tasted, so much juice you had to eat them over the sink. But anyway, no, nobody can hear what I'm thinking. That's just silly. My thoughts are perfectly private.

Depressed? No, I wouldn't say I've been depressed. I mean, it's stressful dealing with his family, obviously, but I haven't been sitting around crying all day or anything like that. I still go to work every day. I do billing at a dental office, you know. It keeps me busy. Too busy, sometimes. The new software they installed last month is just a nightmare. It's supposed to be "cloud-based," whatever that means, but it crashes every time I try to run the end-of-day reports. I told Dr. Henderson we should have just stuck with the old system. It was slow, sure, but at least I knew how to fix it when it froze. You just had to hit Control, Alt, Delete, and wait for the little hourglass icon to go away. Do you remember when computers used to have that hourglass? Now it's just that spinning blue circle. It makes me dizzy if I look at it too long. I actually had to get new glasses last year because I was getting such bad headaches from staring at the screen. I went to that optometrist over on Elm Street, the one with the green awning. He told me I have a slight astigmatism in my left eye. My sister has that too, but hers is much worse. She can't even drive at night because the headlights look like big starbursts to her. She used to drive this old Volvo station wagon, the kind that looked like a tank... but no, I haven't been depressed. Just frustrated with his family, that's all.

Trouble keeping up? No, no, I manage just fine. I still get up every morning, make my coffee, and go in to handle all my billing clerk duties at the dental office. I keep the house going, too. I even find time for my gardening and painting. I was just out in the garden yesterday evening, actually, trying to save my hydrangeas. The Japanese beetles have been absolutely terrible this year. They just skeletonize the leaves, you know? It's heartbreaking after you put so much work into them. I tried spraying them with that neem oil mixture my neighbor recommended. She swears by it, says it kept all the bugs off her prize-winning tomatoes last summer. She grows those big heirloom ones, the Cherokee Purples, I think they're called. They make the best BLT sandwiches if you toast the sourdough bread just right and use a really thick-cut bacon. My husband used to get this applewood smoked bacon from a butcher shop two towns over, but they closed down during the pandemic. Such a shame, it was a family-owned place, been there for three generations. The grandson was running it, but I guess he just couldn't keep the lights on... But anyway, my daily responsibilities are fine. The only real trouble I have is when I try to warn people about what my in-laws are doing. That's what takes up my energy, trying to make people understand what's going on with them. But the house and work? I'm completely on top of all that.

Hard to follow? Me? No, nobody's ever said that. I mean, I speak perfectly clearly. I was in the debate club in high school, you know. We went all the way to the state championships my senior year. Our topic was whether or not the voting age should be lowered, and I had to argue the affirmative side. I wore this awful navy blue suit my mother bought me from JCPenney. It had these huge shoulder pads that made me look like a linebacker. That was back when everyone was wearing those big shoulder pads, like on Dynasty or Dallas. My mom never missed an episode of Dallas. She had this huge crush on Patrick Duffy. She even bought a mug with his face on it at a garage sale once. It was a really nice garage sale, actually, over in the nice part of town by the golf course. I bought a set of vintage Pyrex mixing bowls there for practically nothing. The primary colors ones—red, yellow, green, and blue. The blue one is my favorite, I use it every time I make my grandmother's potato salad. The secret is to add a little bit of sweet pickle relish and a dash of paprika on top. It looks so pretty when you serve it at a picnic. We used to have picnics all the time down by the lake before they built those ugly new condos... But no, no one has ever told me I'm hard to follow. I think I'm very easy to understand.

Controlling my actions? Like, making me move my arms or something? No, I'm the only one in control of what I do. I mean, my in-laws try to control my life with all their scheming, but they aren't physically controlling my body like a puppet. That sounds like something out of a science fiction movie. My husband loves those movies, the ones with the aliens and the spaceships. We went to see that new one last month, the one with the really loud sound effects. The theater was freezing, too. They always keep the air conditioning blasting in those places. I had to wear my heavy wool sweater, the gray one I knitted myself. It took me three months to finish that sweater because I kept messing up the cable stitch on the sleeves. Knitting is supposed to be relaxing, but sometimes it just makes me more tense. My aunt Martha taught me how to knit when I was ten. She lived in this tiny little house that always smelled like peppermint and mothballs. She had a cat named Barnaby who was missing half his left ear. He got into a fight with a raccoon, she said. Raccoons can be so vicious, you know. They get into the garbage cans and just make a huge mess. I had to buy those special bungee cords to keep the lids on our cans because the raccoons were having a feast every Tuesday night before trash day... But no, nobody is controlling my actions. I do what I want to do.

Lose track of the main point? No, I don't think anyone has ever said that to me. I'm actually very good at keeping track of things. You really have to be in my line of work, you know? Doing all the billing at the dental office, if you lose track of even one little decimal point, it's a complete disaster. 

Just last Tuesday, I caught a huge error on an insurance claim for Mrs. Higgins' new crown. She got a gold crown on her back molar. You really don't see gold crowns as much anymore, do you? Everyone wants the porcelain ones now so they blend in with their real teeth. My uncle Arthur had a whole mouthful of gold teeth, though. He used to chew on ice cubes all the time, which is just terrible for your enamel. Dr. Evans is always telling our patients not to do that. He’s the senior partner at the practice. Well, he’s retiring next year, actually. He and his wife bought a condo down in Florida. Sarasota, I think. Or maybe it was Naples. 

My sister went to Sarasota for her honeymoon back in... oh, it must have been 1998. They stayed at this gorgeous resort right on the water, but it rained for four days straight. She was so furious. She spent almost the whole trip just sitting in the hotel lobby drinking overpriced coffee and reading paperback romance novels. She loves those Nora Roberts books. She has a whole big oak bookshelf dedicated to them in her guest room, the room with the yellow floral wallpaper. She put that wallpaper up herself, which is really hard to do without getting air bubbles in it... but anyway, no, nobody has ever told me I go off on tangents. I always get right to the point.

Special messages? From the TV or the newspaper? No, I don't think so. I mean, the news is just the news, right? Though honestly, I barely watch the news anymore. It's just so depressing lately. Always about the economy or some terrible accident on the highway. 

We had a really bad accident near my house last winter. A semi-truck jackknifed on the overpass right when it started snowing. It was that really wet, heavy snow that just sticks to everything and brings down the power lines. We lost power for three whole days. I had to empty out my entire chest freezer because everything started to thaw. All that meat, just ruined. My husband had just bought a quarter of a cow from a local farmer, too. It was grass-fed beef, which is supposed to be so much better for you, but it's terribly expensive. We had to throw out at least thirty pounds of ground beef and these beautiful ribeye steaks. 

I tried to save some of it by cooking it on the little camping stove we have in the garage, but you can only eat so many hamburgers in one day, you know? That camping stove is older than my kids. We bought it at a sporting goods store that went out of business years ago. They had a huge liquidation sale, and we got it for half price. My husband loves a good bargain. He’ll drive twenty miles out of his way just to save five cents a gallon on gas. I keep telling him he's probably burning more gas just driving there, but he won't listen. He’s stubborn like that. His whole family is stubborn. His sister once refused to speak to him for a year because of an argument over a game of Monopoly... but anyway, no, I don't get any special messages from the TV or anything. Just the regular programs.

Well, yes, absolutely. I'm here because for months now I’ve been trying to get people to understand that my husband’s family is quietly messing with our money and our good name. It's been going on for a long time. I see it in these little billing errors that show up at work. And it's not just at work, either. Someone at church will suddenly act funny toward me, like they've heard some rumor, and no matter what records anyone pulls up, I know it ties back to his family. 

They go to a different church, though. A big Methodist one over on the east side of town. It has these enormous stained glass windows that must have cost a fortune. I’ve always loved stained glass. I tried to take a class on making it once at the community center, but the instructor was this awful man who kept breathing down my neck. He smelled like stale coffee and cheap cigars. I can't stand the smell of cigars. My grandfather used to smoke them on the back porch, and the smell would just seep right through the screen door. He had this old rocking chair out there, the wood was completely worn smooth on the armrests. He’d sit there for hours listening to baseball games on a little transistor radio. He was a huge Cubs fan. They never won anything back then, but he was so loyal. He had this lucky baseball cap that was practically falling apart... but yes, I've been convinced for months that his family is trying to ruin me. I just know they're behind it all.

Well, honestly, I'm just... I've been struggling a lot lately with this overwhelming sense that I'm just messing everything up. What made me come in is that I keep feeling like I ruined things for everybody. I'm a pipefitter apprentice right now, and I just can't shake this feeling that I'm a total fake in the program. Like, I'll make a mistake on a job—maybe I didn't measure a pipe cut exactly right, or I took too long threading something—and instead of just learning from it, it just eats at me. I feel like I'm letting my whole family down because they were so proud of me getting into the union, and I feel like I'm letting the younger apprentices down too, because I'm supposed to be setting a good example and I'm just... not. I know, logically, that other people make mistakes on the job site all the time. I see the journeymen mess up and they just fix it, patch it, and move on like it's nothing. But for me, it just lingers. It feels so heavy, like this massive guilt that I can't wash off at the end of the day, no matter how hard I scrub my hands. It's just exhausting carrying that around all the time, you know?

Oh! No, no, I'm sorry, I think I made that sound way more literal than I meant it. I don't—I don't have a thing about germs or feeling like my skin is actually dirty, not like that. 

I mean, obviously, working as a pipefitter, you get incredibly dirty. We’re dealing with pipe dope, flux, threading oil, old rust, just all this thick black sludge that gets right down deep into your cuticles and under your nails, so I *do* scrub my hands pretty hard at the end of the shift. We have this gritty orange pumice soap at the shop, and you really have to work it in to get the grease off so you don't ruin your steering wheel on the drive home. But once the grease is gone, I'm done. I don't keep going back to the sink or anything. 

What I meant was more... it's like a metaphor, I guess? Like, I'll be standing there at the wash station, scrubbing the actual physical dirt off my hands, and the water is running brown down the drain, but my mind is just replaying whatever stupid mistake I made that day. Like maybe I didn't tighten a fitting enough and it wept during a pressure test, and I'm just standing there scrubbing, wishing I could just wash away the fact that I messed up. The physical dirt washes off fine, it really does, but that heavy, sinking feeling in my chest just... stays. So, yeah, no literal obsessive washing, just... just a lot of emotional baggage that won't rinse off, no matter what I do.

Well, it's funny you ask that, because I've actually spent a lot of time trying to pinpoint exactly when this all started. I keep going back over it in my head, trying to figure out if there was one specific job or one specific mistake that triggered it, you know? But it really goes back about five months ago. That's when I decided to take on this sustainable plumbing certification course. 

I thought it was a great idea at the time, because, you know, everything is going green now, and I wanted to be ahead of the curve. My union hall was offering it, and I figured, 'Hey, I'm already in the apprenticeship, I might as well add this on and make myself more valuable.' But honestly, it's just been so much. It's not just the extra hours, which are a lot—I'm working my regular shifts, and then I have these evening classes and all this extra coursework about greywater systems and high-efficiency fixtures and all these new codes that are totally different from the standard stuff I'm just barely getting the hang of. 

So, yeah, about five months ago, right when I started that certification on top of my regular apprenticeship duties, that's when this whole pattern really kicked in. I think the added pressure just sort of broke the dam. Suddenly I wasn't just worrying about getting my regular pipefitting right; I was worrying about all these new sustainable systems, and if I messed up a regular job, my brain would immediately jump to, 'Well, how are you ever going to handle the advanced green tech if you can't even sweat a basic copper joint perfectly?' It just snowballed from there, and for the last five months, it's just been this constant, heavy feeling that I'm failing at both things instead of succeeding at one.

Honestly, no, not really. It's funny, actually, because you'd think if someone was this stressed out, it would just bleed into everything, right? Like, I've got friends who worry about everything—the news, the economy, whether they offended the barista, just... everything. But for me, outside of work and this certification, my brain is actually pretty quiet. 

Like, take my family, for instance. I still live at home, and things are pretty chill there. My mom handles her stuff, my dad handles his, and I don't really sit around stressing about their health or if the house is going to fall apart or anything like that. And my social life, well, I don't really have a ton of time for one right now with the apprenticeship and the classes, but when I do hang out with my friends, I'm not obsessing over whether they secretly hate me or if I wore the wrong shirt. I just kind of exist. 

Even with money—like, apprentices don't make a ton, obviously, and gas prices are what they are, but I just budget it out and I don't lay awake at night staring at the ceiling, panicking about my bank account. It really is just this one specific lane. It's like my brain has this giant magnifying glass, and it's only focused on the pipefitting and the green tech course. If I'm not actively doing something related to the union or my classes, I'm actually pretty okay. I mean, I might be exhausted, but I'm not worried. It's just... as soon as I put on my steel-toe boots, or open that textbook on greywater systems, that's when the dread just drops like an anvil. But outside of that? No, I wouldn't say I worry about much else at all.

Well, I mean... no, not really depressed. I know I just talked a lot about that heavy, sinking feeling and the dread when I put on my boots, but it's not like a sadness, if that makes sense? It's not like I'm crying all the time or feeling hopeless about life in general. 

I actually had a buddy in high school who went through a really bad depression, and it was like he couldn't even get out of bed. He just stopped caring about everything—his car, his guitar, hanging out. He just kind of went blank. And I'm definitely not like that. I still get up every morning at 4:30 AM, make my coffee, pack my lunch—usually a turkey sandwich and an apple, nothing crazy—and I drive to the site or the shop. I still have energy to do the physical work, to lift the pipes and run the threader. I'm still engaged with the guys on the crew, joking around at break time, things like that. 

And when I get home, even though I'm tired from the physical labor and then having to study all that greywater system stuff, I don't feel... dark. I don't feel like life is pointless or anything. It's really just the anxiety about messing up the work. It's the stress of the job and the certification that weighs on me, not a general feeling of being down. Like, if you took the apprenticeship and the classes away tomorrow, I think I'd feel completely light as a feather. I'd probably just sleep for two days straight, but I'd be perfectly happy. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm depressed. Just really, really stressed out about my performance and keeping up with everything I've taken on.

Well, that's the thing, isn't it? That's kind of why I'm here, honestly. I mean, I try to keep it all together, I really do. I show up early, I bring my tools, I try to stay focused, but... yeah, it's definitely bleeding into the work now. And that's what terrifies me. 

Like, just last week, my foreman—his name's Dave, he's this older guy who's been in the union for like thirty years, total hard-ass but a good guy—he actually pulled me aside. We were roughing in the plumbing for this new commercial build, a mid-rise office building, and he had to point out that I was taking way, way too long measuring and cutting my cast iron. And he wasn't wrong. I was just standing there, double, triple, quadruple checking the measurements because I was so paralyzed by the thought of cutting it too short and wasting material. He told me I need to pick up the pace or I'm going to throw the whole crew behind schedule. 

And it's not just the site work, either. It's the classes. The certification course requires us to submit these detailed isometric sketches for different greywater routing scenarios, right? And I used to be pretty good at the drafting part, but lately, I just... I can't finish them. I sit down at my desk at home, I get my T-square and my pencils out, and I just stare at the paper. I'll draw a line, erase it, draw it again, and then I just get so overwhelmed that I put it away. My instructor has had to email me twice now, chasing me down for these assignments that are past due. 

So, yeah, it's definitely interfering. I mean, I worked so hard to get into this apprenticeship. You have to pass an aptitude test, do a massive interview, wait on a list... it's a huge deal to get a spot. And then taking on the green tech certification was supposed to be this amazing career move. But now, with my foreman getting on my case about being slow, and my instructors hounding me for unfinished sketches... I'm just so scared I'm on the verge of totally wrecking both of them. I feel like I'm watching myself sabotage everything I've built, and I just can't seem to make my brain move fast enough or confidently enough to stop it.

Well... yeah, I guess so. I mean, I know it's a stressful program. Everyone says the first year of an apprenticeship is a grind, and adding the extra certification on top of it, I mean, everyone told me I was crazy to do it. But... I look around at the other first-years, like this guy Tommy on my crew. He's taking extra classes too, not the green tech one, but some advanced welding stuff at the community college. And he's just... fine. He comes in, he cuts his pipe, he makes jokes, he eats his lunch, and he goes home. He doesn't look like he's going to throw up every time Dave walks by. 

And I remember when I was studying for the aptitude test to even get into the union, I was stressed, sure, but it was a productive stress. It made me study harder. This is different. This is like... paralyzing. It's like my brain is screaming at me that if I cut this one piece of cast iron a quarter-inch too short, I'm going to get kicked out of the union, fail my classes, and end up living in my car. And logically, I know that's not true. Dave isn't going to fire me over one bad cut, he's just going to yell at me and make me do it again. But my body feels like it's a life-or-death situation every single time I pick up the tape measure. 

So, yeah, I think it's definitely out of proportion. I mean, I've always been a bit of a perfectionist, like back when I was getting my associate's degree, I always wanted A's, but it never stopped me from actually doing the work. Now, it's like the fear of not being perfect is actually making me worse at my job. And I just... I don't see anyone else in my cohort struggling like this. They just do the work and move on. I feel like I'm stuck in mud while everyone else is just walking on dry land, you know? It's just so frustrating because I know I'm smart enough to do this, I know I have the mechanical aptitude, but my brain is just making it impossible.

Quitting? No... I mean, I know logically that would be the easiest way to fix the stress, just drop the class and focus on the apprenticeship, but... no, I haven't actually considered quitting. It's just not in my DNA, I guess. 

My dad—he's an electrician, actually, been doing it for like twenty-five years—he always drilled it into me that you don't walk away from something just because it gets heavy. Plus, this green tech certification, it's really the future of the whole industry. With all the new water conservation codes coming down the pipeline—no pun intended—having this on my resume as a first-year apprentice is huge. It puts me so far ahead of the curve. 

And honestly, I fought so hard just to get a seat in that class. There was a waitlist of like thirty people, and I literally sat at my laptop until midnight the day registration opened, just refreshing the page over and over so I could snag one of the last spots. I already paid for the materials, too. Overwhelming? I was doing all the work! Just like at the lab. People just can't handle it when someone actually has vision and tries to elevate things beyond the bare minimum. They just want to drag you down to their level of mediocrity.

Impossible? I mean, I don't know. I haven't really noticed anyone saying that to me. I'm not sure what they actually think behind closed doors, to be honest. People don't really say things to your face anymore, they just... they just smile and nod. 

Which is exactly what happened with the contractor who was supposed to renovate my kitchen last month. He stood right there in my house, looked at the blueprints I drew up—which were perfectly scaled, by the way, down to the millimeter—and said, "Sure, no problem." Next thing I know, he's leaving me a voicemail saying the custom cabinets are delayed because of some supply chain issue in Italy. Italy! I called him back and asked why we're sourcing wood from Italy when there's a perfectly good commercial lumber yard two towns over. But he started giving me this whole lecture about European craftsmanship and the moisture content of the wood. Moisture content! I'm a physical scientist, I think I understand how humidity affects porous materials better than a guy who drives a pickup truck with a cracked windshield. 

And speaking of windshields, the parking situation on campus has gotten completely out of hand. They repainted the lines in the North lot over the weekend and somehow managed to eliminate fifteen spaces. Fifteen! Where are the adjuncts supposed to park? I had to circle for twenty minutes on Tuesday. It's just... it's a complete mess.

Impossible for an ordinary person? I mean, what even is an ordinary person? I guess I don't really think about it like that. I don't think I've ever believed I could do something literally impossible, like... like flying or something. I just do what I know I can do. 

Which is why I still don't understand why they wouldn't let me install the new centrifuge myself. I mean, it's just a matter of calibrating the rotor balance and securing the mounting bolts. I've read the entire technical manual, twice. But they insisted on calling the manufacturer's technician, who didn't even show up until three days later. Three days! And when he finally got there, he didn't even use a torque wrench on the base plate. I watched him just hand-tighten it. I actually had to go back in after he left and do it properly myself because I'm not going to have a piece of equipment spinning at 15,000 RPMs secured by some guy who looked like he was hungover. 

And honestly, the coffee in the breakroom isn't helping anyone's productivity either. They switched to this new generic brand last month to save money, and it tastes like burnt cardboard. I actually brought in my own French press and a bag of Ethiopian Yirgacheffe, but then someone—I'm pretty sure it was Dave from the next lab over—broke the glass beaker and didn't even leave a note. Just threw it in the trash. The lack of basic respect for shared spaces is just... it's astounding. But no, I don't think I've tried to do anything impossible. Just things that need to be done right.

Watching me? I mean... no, I don't think so. I don't think there's some big conspiracy or anything like that. People are way too self-absorbed to spend their time secretly watching me or plotting against me. I mean, they interfere, sure, but just out of sheer incompetence, not because it's some organized campaign. 

Like Brenda down in the department office. She's supposed to sort the incoming lab packages, right? But last week, a shipment of specialized thermal paste I needed for the heat sinks just sat on her desk for four days. Four days! And when I finally went down there to find it myself, she didn't even apologize. She just started rambling about her daughter's wedding. Which she has been talking about non-stop since January, by the way. I don't even know why they're insisting on an outdoor reception in late October. Do you know how unstable the barometric pressure is around here that time of year? It's almost guaranteed to rain. And the tent rental company she hired—I looked them up—they have terrible reviews for not anchoring their tie-downs properly in saturated soil. If they get a wind gust over thirty miles an hour, that whole canopy is going to become a giant sail. I actually tried to explain the physics of it to her, just to be helpful, you know? Just drawing out a basic vector diagram on a sticky note. But she just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. People just do not appreciate basic meteorology.

Special messages? No, I don't think so. I mean, events are just events, right? They happen because of cause and effect, basic physics. There's no magical meaning behind a traffic light turning green or... or a bird landing on a windowsill. It's just probability and environmental factors. 

Speaking of environmental factors, the HVAC system in my lab has been an absolute nightmare lately. The temperature fluctuates by almost three degrees throughout the day, which completely throws off my calibration curves. I've put in six work orders since Tuesday. Six! And the maintenance guy—Gary, I think his name is—finally shows up yesterday and tells me the system is "working within normal parameters." Normal parameters! I had to pull up the sensor logs on my laptop and show him the exact timestamps of the thermal spikes. I even color-coded the graph so it would be impossible to miss. But he just kept wiping his forehead with this greasy rag and talking about how the compressor on the roof is twenty years old. 

Well, if it's twenty years old, replace it! It's not like the university doesn't have the endowment for it. Did you see the new bronze statue they just put up in front of the library? It must have cost at least eighty thousand dollars. And it's not even structurally sound! The center of gravity is completely off. I give it two harsh winters before the frost heave tilts the pedestal and the whole thing comes crashing down. I actually wrote an email to the dean of facilities about the tensile strength of the mounting brackets they used, but of course, no one ever replies to me. So no, I don't get any special messages from the universe. I just wish people would read the messages I actually send them.

Impossible? I mean, maybe someone said that, but they just don't see the big picture. They told me I was taking on too much, but I genuinely believed I could rescue the entire multi-site project by myself. It was failing, obviously failing, because the other PIs were dragging their feet. I knew I could redesign the whole spectroscopy approach, mentor every single grad student better than their actual advisors were doing, and still beat the grant deadline. It was totally doable if people would just stop getting in my way. 

Which, speaking of getting in the way, you wouldn't believe the traffic on I-95 this morning. It's like people forget how to use their turn signals the second they get on the highway. There was this one guy in a silver sedan who merged across three lanes without even looking. Just drifted right over. It's basic spatial awareness, really. If you're traveling at sixty-five miles per hour, your stopping distance is roughly three hundred feet. You can't just cut into someone's following distance and expect physics to magically suspend itself for you. 

And then, of course, the toll booth lanes were completely backed up because half the automated scanners were down. I don't understand why the state doesn't upgrade the RFID readers. The technology has been around for decades. I actually read a white paper last month about a new high-frequency transponder system they're using in Europe that has a 99.9% read accuracy even at high speeds. I mean, I could probably draft a proposal for the Department of Transportation in a weekend if I really sat down and did it. It's just a matter of optimizing the signal processing algorithms. But anyway, yeah, I could have saved that project if they had just let me handle it.

False or impossible? No, I don't think so. I mean, my ideas are grounded in reality, in data. I don't just make things up. If I say I can do something, it's because I've run the numbers and I know it's feasible. People might not understand the math, but that doesn't make it false. 

Like the math on my grocery bill the other day. I swear, inflation is just out of control. I went to get coffee beans—just the regular medium roast I always get, nothing fancy—and the price had jumped by almost three dollars. Three dollars! And the bag is smaller now, too. It used to be a full sixteen ounces, and now it's twelve. They think people won't notice, but I notice. It's called shrinkflation, and it's incredibly deceptive. I actually stood in the aisle and calculated the price per ounce difference on my phone. It's a twenty-five percent increase in cost for twenty-five percent less product. 

And don't even get me started on the produce section. The avocados were rock hard, and they were charging two-fifty each. Who pays two-fifty for an avocado that won't even be ripe for a week? By the time it softens up, the inside is usually all stringy and brown anyway. It's a complete gamble. I actually read an article about how they're trying to genetically modify avocados to stay ripe longer without oxidizing, which is fascinating from a biochemical standpoint. They're trying to suppress the polyphenol oxidase enzyme. If they could actually perfect that, it would revolutionize the supply chain. But no, I don't have any false beliefs. Just a very clear understanding of how things actually work.

Hi, yeah, it’s nice to meet you too. Thanks for fitting me in. I, uh... well, I guess I’m here because things have just gotten to a point where I can't really ignore them anymore.
