Yeah, you know, it’s funny you ask that because for the longest time, I didn't really think so. I mean, I made it through grad school, right? So I always just assumed I was fine back then, that I was just a normal kid. But lately, since things have gotten so overwhelming at work, I’ve actually been looking back and thinking about it, and... yeah. It was absolutely there, long before I was even a teenager. 

My mom actually kept all my old report cards from grade school in this big plastic storage bin, and if you look at them, every single year, almost like clockwork, the teachers would write the exact same thing in the comments section. They’d say I was a bright kid, very capable, but that I spent half the day daydreaming. I was always just staring out the window or getting completely lost in my own head instead of paying attention to whatever the lesson was. 

And the organization... oh man, it was a total disaster. I would actually do the homework, which is the crazy part. I’d sit at the kitchen table, do all the math problems, finish the whole worksheet, put my pencil down, and then I would just completely forget to turn it in the next day. It would just sit crumpled up in my desk. Or worse, I’d lose the entire homework folder. I remember having these specific, brightly colored folders that we were supposed to use, and they would just vanish into the abyss of my locker or the bottom of my backpack, and my parents were constantly having to replace them. So, yeah, it wasn't just a college or an adult thing, it was definitely happening way back in elementary school. It's just so frustrating to think about how much extra effort I had to put in just to keep track of a simple piece of paper, you know? Like, why couldn't I just put it in the tray like everyone else did? It just feels like I've been fighting this exact same battle with my brain for forty years.

No, I don't think so. That doesn't really sound like me. 

If anything, my mood is pretty tied to whatever is going wrong with my schedule at that exact moment. Like, if I'm trying to figure out those patent notes I mentioned, and my brain just feels like it's wading through wet concrete, I get frustrated with myself. I'll sit there and think, "Come on, you know this stuff, just focus," and when I can't, yeah, I get annoyed. And maybe if someone interrupts me right then, I might sigh a little too loudly or give a short answer, but it's not a mood that takes over my whole life for days. It's just a reaction to the immediate frustration of not being able to make my brain do what I want it to do. 

And as for feeling unusually high or energetic... no, definitely not. Honestly, I'm usually just tired. Mental fatigue is kind of my baseline these days because I'm spending so much energy just trying to keep all the plates spinning. I don't really have these bursts of feeling on top of the world or having boundless energy. It's more of a constant, low-level exhaustion from trying to manage the chaos. So, no, I haven't really experienced anything like that. Just the regular, everyday frustration of feeling like I'm always two steps behind where I should be.

Well, yeah, actually. It’s not like it happened overnight, but there was definitely a turning point. So, about a year and a month ago—give or take a few weeks, but right around then—I won this industry award for a piece of software architecture I designed. Which, you know, was great. I was incredibly honored, and it felt like a real validation of all the hard work I’d put in over the years. But the thing about getting recognized like that is it completely shifts how people see you at the company, and suddenly, they want you doing different things. 

So, right after the award, management decided to promote me, or at least shift my role, into something way more coordination-heavy. Instead of just putting my head down and coding—which I’m good at, I can just hyper-focus on the screen and make things work—they wanted me leading multiple teams, setting the strategic vision, running these cross-departmental workshops, and basically being the point person for all these different moving parts. 

And that’s when the wheels completely fell off. I mean, the inattentive stuff, the daydreaming, the losing track of things—that was always there, like I said about my report cards. But I had managed to build a career where I could mostly hide it, or at least compensate for it by just being really good at the technical side. But this new role... it’s all the things I’m terrible at, dialed up to eleven. It’s constant context switching. I’ll be trying to review a junior dev’s code, and then I have to jump into a meeting about budget allocation, and then I have to go back to writing those patent notes, and my brain just... it just blue-screens. It’s been about thirteen months of this now, and it’s just gotten progressively worse because the demands keep piling up and my old coping mechanisms just absolutely do not work for this level of coordination. So, yeah, the award was great for my resume, but it basically threw me into the deep end of exactly the kind of work I’m least equipped to handle, and that’s really when this all became completely unmanageable.

No, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I sit around and just... worry about things that aren't happening. It's not like I'm lying in bed at night, staring at the ceiling, agonizing over whether the house is going to catch fire or if I'm going to get some terrible disease, or, you know, worrying about the economy or something abstract like that. That's never really been my thing. 

If I'm stressed, it's almost always tied directly to something very tangible and immediate that I'm dropping the ball on. Like, I'll stress about the fact that I have three unread emails from the VP of Engineering that I know I need to respond to, but I can't bring myself to open them because I know I haven't finished the project timeline she asked for on Tuesday. And then I'll stress about the timeline because I can't find the notes I took during the kickoff meeting, which I'm pretty sure I wrote on a legal pad that is now buried somewhere under a mountain of coffee cups and printouts on my desk. So, it's a very specific, practical kind of stress. It's the stress of knowing I'm behind, knowing I'm forgetting things, and knowing that people are waiting on me. 

But it's not this free-floating anxiety, if that makes sense? It's not like my brain is just looking for things to be afraid of. It's more like my brain is acutely aware that it's failing to manage the actual, real-world tasks in front of it, and the stress is just the natural byproduct of that failure. If I actually managed to get my inbox to zero and finish all my reports—which, let's be honest, is a complete fantasy at this point—but if I did, I don't think I'd be worrying about anything at all. I'd probably just take a nap. So, no, I don't think I have that kind of excessive, unprompted worrying you're talking about. It's really just the immediate chaos that gets to me.

Well, they brought me in because... well, it was down at the fair. I was giving my talk, and I just climbed right up onto the tractor. I kept jerking the controls all around to show the crowd the 'new pattern.' 

Speaking of patterns, my granddaddy used to plant his sorghum in these tight little rows. He had this old red Farmall, rusted out on the sides, but it ran like a top if you knew how to choke it right. He always said a good farmer knows his dirt by the taste. I never did try eating it myself, always seemed like a good way to ruin your teeth, but... what was I saying? 

Oh, right, the tractor at the fair. I was yanking the controls, showing them the pattern, and I just couldn't make myself stop. Even with people yelling and hollering at me to get down, I couldn't stop doing it. My brother was one of the ones yelling, actually. He still owes me fifty bucks from last Thanksgiving for a bet on the Cowboys game. Never pays up, that guy. Always has an excuse about his truck needing tires.

Voices? Well, sure. Mostly out by the north pasture. Right around dusk, when the light gets all long and orange, I hear these clear voices coming straight out of the irrigation lines. They tell me exactly which rows are poisoned and which ones are blessed. 

You know, setting up those irrigation lines is back-breaking work. I always preferred the heavy aluminum pipes, none of that cheap plastic they push on you down at the co-op nowadays. That plastic cracks if it gets a hard freeze, and a hard freeze will cost you your whole morning just patching leaks. Last winter, my blue heeler, Buster, he actually found a leak before I did. Just stood there barking at the ice. Smart dog, really smart. 

But yeah, the voices in the pipes... they tell me about the poison and the blessings. And the thing is, I hear them even on the weeks when I'm not all fired up. Even when I'm just feeling regular and quiet, not like at the fair, they're still out there talking to me. Buster doesn't seem to hear them, though. He mostly just listens for the jackrabbits. Have you ever tried to cook a jackrabbit? It's awful tough meat. You really gotta stew it all day with some carrots and onions, otherwise it's just like chewing on an old work boot...

Head injury? Medical illness? No, no, nothing like that. I've been healthy as a horse. Speaking of horses, I used to have this beautiful quarter horse named Rusty. Got him at an auction down in Abilene. He had this white blaze right down his face, looked almost like a lightning bolt. 

Boy, he was stubborn though. If he didn't want to cross a creek, you weren't crossing that creek. We were out riding the fence line one spring—must have been right after that big storm washed out the county road—and he just stopped dead at this little puddle. Wouldn't budge. I had to get off and lead him through it. Ruined a perfectly good pair of boots in the mud. You know how hard it is to get mud out of good leather? You gotta brush it, then saddle soap it, and even then, it never really looks the same. 

Anyway, no, I haven't been sick or hit my head or anything. Just the usual aches and pains from working the land, you know? But my neighbor, Earl, he actually fell off his barn roof last month trying to fix some tin. Broke his arm in two places. Had to have pins put in and everything. He's got his nephew helping him out now, but that kid doesn't know a wrench from a screwdriver. I saw him trying to fix a fence post with duct tape the other day...

Depressed? Well... no, I wouldn't say that. I don't really get down in the dumps like that for weeks on end. You know, speaking of feeling down, my Aunt Martha used to get terribly low every winter. We called it the winter blues, but she swore it was because she couldn't get out and tend her rose bushes. 

She had these incredible tea roses, big yellow ones that smelled like peaches. Won a blue ribbon at the county fair three years running. The judges always loved them. One year, the judge was this fella from over in Lubbock, wore a seersucker suit in the middle of August. Can you imagine? Seersucker in August. You sweat right through it before you even make it to the livestock barns. 

The livestock barns always smell so strong, don't they? It's that mix of sawdust and manure and sweet feed. I actually like the smell of sweet feed. It's got molasses in it. I tried putting molasses on my oatmeal once, thinking it would be like the feed, but it was just too sticky. Stuck right to the roof of my mouth. Took me half an hour to get it off with a cup of hot black coffee. I take my coffee black, none of that cream or sugar nonsense. My wife, God rest her soul, she used to put so much milk in her coffee it looked like dirty water... but no, I haven't really felt depressed for weeks at a time. Just busy, mostly.

Well, yeah, actually. I think I mentioned that earlier, didn't I? There were several of those quieter weeks, you know, when I wasn't feeling all fired up and grand like I do when the fair's coming to town. Just regular, everyday kind of weeks. But I still heard the irrigation lines talking to me, clear as a bell. And I still knew that all the farm data coming in was carrying those hidden warnings about the poison. 

It's funny how things can carry warnings if you just know how to look at them. Like the Farmer's Almanac. My granddaddy swore by the Almanac. He wouldn't plant a single seed of corn unless the Almanac said the moon was right for it. He used to keep a copy in the back pocket of his overalls until the cover completely wore off. Those overalls were Liberty brand, the ones with the green stitching on the bib. You can't find that kind of quality anymore. Now everything's made overseas and the seams bust out if you bend over too fast. I bought a pair of jeans last year, bent over to check the oil in the tractor, and rip! Right down the middle. Had to walk all the way back to the house holding my jacket around my waist. Good thing the only one out there was Buster, and he doesn't judge... but yeah, even when I'm feeling completely normal, the voices are still out there in the pipes.

Yeah, I'd say so. Like I was just saying, there were those quieter weeks, you know? I wasn't feeling all energized or grand or anything like that. Just... normal. But I still heard the irrigation lines talking to me, and I still knew the farm data had those hidden warnings in it. 

You know, speaking of the farm data, the new computer system my son set up for me is supposed to be top of the line. It tracks everything—soil moisture, fertilizer rates, yield maps. It's got this big screen, curved like a movie theater. We used to go to the drive-in theater over in Plainview when I was a kid. My dad had this big old Ford Galaxie, and we'd pile in the back with a bunch of blankets. They always played a double feature. I remember falling asleep during the second movie once, must have been some John Wayne picture, and waking up when they were playing the national anthem at the end of the night. The speaker hanging on the window was crackling so loud... but yeah, even during those couple of weeks when my mood was just fine, not high or low, I still heard the voices and knew about the warnings.

Well, yeah, it's been going on for a while now, definitely most days for the last month or so. Especially out by the north pasture, right around dusk. I'll be out there checking the lines, and I hear them clear as day, coming right out of the irrigation pipes. They tell me exactly which rows are poisoned and which ones are blessed. And like I said, it happens even on those weeks when I'm not feeling all fired up and energized. 

Dusk is a funny time of day, isn't it? The light gets all golden and long. My dog Buster, he always gets a little restless right around dusk. He's a blue heeler mix, smart as a whip. I swear he understands English sometimes. The other day, I told him to go find his rope toy, and he went right to the porch and dug it out from under the rocking chair. That rocking chair belonged to my grandmother. It's got a squeak in the left runner that I've tried fixing a dozen times. WD-40, graphite powder, nothing works. It just keeps squeaking. Kind of a comforting sound, though, if you're used to it. Like crickets in the summer. We used to catch crickets in mason jars when we were kids, punch holes in the lid so they could breathe... but yeah, the voices from the pipes, they've been there most days for at least a month now, telling me about the poisoned rows.

Well, gosh, how many days in a row? I couldn't rightly give you an exact number on that. Time gets a little slippery when I'm feeling all revved up and grand like that. 

I used to try and keep track of my days on this big calendar out in the tack room. It's one of those promotional ones they hand out at the feed store, you know the kind? This year's got pictures of vintage tractors on every month. April was a beautiful old Massey Ferguson. I actually tried restoring a Massey once, back in... oh, must've been '98. Had to drive three counties over just to find a carburetor that would fit. The fella running the salvage yard had a glass eye. Told me he lost his real one to a snapped piece of high-tensile wire fencing when he was just a boy. Fencing is dangerous work if you aren't paying attention, I tell you what. You gotta wear thick leather gloves, the heavy-duty kind. I always buy mine at the co-op in town, usually get a size large so I can wear wool liners when it gets cold out... but anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, the days. Yeah, I'm really just not sure how many days straight it was.

Well, the longest stretch... if I look back at this past year or so, those charged-up, nonstop stretches where I barely sleep, they've taken up about ten months of it. Just going and going, ten months out of the year. 

Ten months is a long time, you know, almost a full cycle of the seasons. Speaking of the seasons, the winter we had this past year was a lot milder than usual. We barely got any snow pack up on the ridge, which really had me worried about the spring runoff. If you don't get a good snow pack up in the hills, the reservoirs don't fill, and then the county water district starts putting restrictions on the irrigation allotments. It happened back in 2012, I think it was. We had to let a whole forty-acre field of alfalfa just burn up in the sun because we couldn't get the water down to it. Broke my heart to see it all turn brown and brittle. Alfalfa is a real thirsty crop, you know. My neighbor, Tom, he actually switched over to drought-resistant sorghum after that bad year. He's always trying out the new hybrids. He buys his seed from a fella out of Nebraska who drives this massive red dually truck with custom mud flaps... but yeah, out of the last year or so, it's been about ten months of just being completely wired and going nonstop like that.

Well, yeah, sleep just kind of goes out the window during those times. Most nights I'll just doze for maybe two, three hours right there in my recliner, or sometimes I don't sleep a wink. But then I'm up before the sun, feeling completely charged up and ready to work the whole place like I just slept ten hours. 

That recliner, though, it's getting a bit worn out. It's one of those big overstuffed ones, brown corduroy. My wife bought it for me back when we celebrated our twentieth anniversary. She always said corduroy holds up better than leather if you've got dogs in the house, and she was right about that. Buster loves sleeping at the foot of that chair. Though, the lever on the side is getting real stiff. You have to yank it real hard to get the footrest to pop up, and when it does, it makes a sound like a shotgun going off. Scared the mailman half to death one time when he came to the door with a package and I was just kicking back. He dropped the box right on the porch. It was just some replacement filters for the tractor, but still. You can get those filters a lot cheaper online these days than at the dealership, but I always worry about shipping delays. The post office out here is only open three days a week now, ever since they cut the budget... but anyway, yeah, two or three hours in that chair, and I'm up and roaring to go before dawn.

Well, yeah, it definitely lasts a full week, sometimes longer. It's a funny thing, really. Some mornings I'll wake up and I feel like the whole valley is just opening up for me, you know? I'm standing on the porch grinning at absolutely nothing, just feeling on top of the world. But then, if one of the hired hands questions how I want a fence line run, or if my wife tells me I need to slow down and eat something, I just snap. I get so mad, like they've insulted the family name or something. 

Speaking of the family name, my grandfather was the one who originally homesteaded this place back in the twenties. He came out here with nothing but a team of mules and a wagon. Those mules were tough as nails, let me tell you. My dad used to tell stories about how one of them, a big gray named Samson, kicked the barn door clean off its hinges because a barn owl spooked him. Barn owls are great for keeping the mice down, though. We've got a pair nesting up in the rafters of the main hay barn right now. You can hear them screeching at night if you're out checking on a calving heifer. Calving season is always stressful, especially when it's cold. You gotta have the heat lamps ready in the barn, and sometimes you end up bringing a shivering calf right into the mudroom to warm up by the wood stove. My wife hates when I do that, says it tracks muck everywhere, but you can't just let a calf freeze... but yeah, to answer your question, it's a full week of feeling on top of the world, and then getting mad enough to spit fire if anyone gets in my way.

Well, depressed... I mean, I don't know about two whole weeks of feeling down like that. I don't think so. I've always been a pretty busy guy, you know, not much time for sitting around feeling sorry for myself. There's always chores to do. 

Like just yesterday, I had to fix the float valve in the main water trough out in the east pasture. The darn thing kept sticking open, and water was just flooding everywhere, making a huge mud bog. The cows were loving it, of course, just standing in the muck, but it's a real waste of water. And water is precious out here, I tell you. We've got a well that goes down about four hundred feet, but the pump is starting to make this awful grinding noise when it kicks on. I called the well guy, Steve, he's been servicing our pumps for twenty years. Good guy, Steve. He's got a son who just went off to college on a baseball scholarship. Pitcher, I think. Throws a mean fastball, or so Steve says. He's always bragging about that kid. I don't blame him, though. My own kids, they moved off to the city years ago. Neither of them wanted anything to do with the farm. It's hard work, I get it, but it's a good life. You're your own boss, mostly, except for the weather and the markets... but no, I can't say I've had two weeks of just feeling depressed like you're saying, with the voices and all.

Well, I'm here because... I've been having this issue with eating lately. Some evenings after work, especially on days where I've been really strict about what I eat all day, I just... I end up eating way more than I meant to. It's like I'll have dinner, and then I'll have a bowl of cereal, and then crackers, and then whatever leftovers are in the fridge, and then sweets... all just packed into a couple of hours. It's just getting to be a bit much.

Yeah, exactly. Once I get started on those nights, it's like... I just keep going back to the kitchen. Even while I'm actively telling myself to stop, I just can't seem to listen. I don't really feel back in charge of myself until I'm uncomfortably full.
No, I don't do that. I've never tried to make myself throw up or anything like that. I just... I mostly just deal with feeling overly full and guilty about it, but no, I don't make myself sick.

Yeah, I do. The next day after one of those nights, I'll tell myself I'm making up for it. I'll usually skip breakfast and lunch... or I'll go take an extra-long hike. Sometimes I'll just push myself a lot harder at my softball conditioning, even when I'm really tired. I just feel like I have to do something to balance it out.
No, I wouldn't say so. My weight is... it's pretty normal for my height, really. I'm definitely not underweight or anything like that.

No, not really. I mean, I'd prefer not to gain weight, obviously, but I wouldn't say I'm terrified of it. I don't really obsess over the scale or anything like that. It's more just about how uncomfortable and guilty I feel after I eat too much, rather than a huge fear of gaining weight.

Well, just like I mentioned a minute ago, yeah. I'll usually skip breakfast and lunch the next day, or I'll push myself to go on a really long hike. I just do those things I brought up earlier to try and balance it out. But I don't really do anything else besides that, if that's what you mean.

Well, for the past few months, it's been happening most weeks. Usually, there's one or two nights a week where I end up eating way more than I planned to. And then, like I said, the next day I try to make up for it by skipping my meals or going on a longer hike to exercise it off.

Yeah, I guess it's pretty much exactly what I just mentioned, since it goes right along with the eating. So, for the past few months, it's been most weeks. Whenever I have one of those one or two nights where I eat far more than I planned, the very next day is when I try to make up for it by skipping my meals or exercising longer. So, on average, I'd say about once or twice a week.

Yeah, I do. It's actually a big part of what brought me in to see you. Some evenings after work, especially when I've been really strict with my eating all day, I just end up eating way more than I ever meant to. I'll sit down and have my dinner, but then... I'll just keep going. I'll have a bowl of cereal, some crackers, whatever leftovers are in the fridge, and then sweets on top of that. And it's all just within a couple of hours.

Hello, doctor. It's very nice to meet you too. I, uh, I hope I'm not taking up too much of your time today. 

Well, I suppose what brings me in is... I've just been a little, I don't know, scatterbrained lately. Nothing too terrible, I don't think! But... well, I keep forgetting things that I really shouldn’t. It's a bit embarrassing to admit, honestly. Like, um, slipping up on my heart follow-up appointments, or forgetting to call the clinic back when I'm supposed to. And I like to do little repair jobs just to keep busy, but lately I keep showing up to do them and realizing I didn't even bring the right tools. 

It's just a bit silly of me, I suppose. Does that make sense? I just wanted to make sure I'm doing the right thing by coming in to talk to you about it.

Oh, no, no, I wouldn't say I need a caretaker or anything drastic like that! I can still manage the house and feed myself just fine, I promise. I hope I didn't make it sound worse than it is. 

But, um... well, I suppose I do rely on others a bit more to catch my mistakes lately. It's just... well, it’s gotten to where the senior-center repair group can’t really count on me the way they used to, which I feel just awful about. I hate letting them down when I'm supposed to be helping. And my regular doctor’s office, they've had to chase me around a bit about those missed heart follow-ups. I really hate being a nuisance to the nurses there, having them call to remind me. 

So, I guess I am dropping the ball a little bit when I'm left entirely to my own devices... is that the sort of thing you were asking about?

Oh, goodness, no. I really wouldn't say it's clearly gotten worse. I hope I didn't give you the impression that my mind is going! 

I feel like my thinking is still perfectly fine, honestly. I've sort of always been someone who... well, who jumps into things a bit fast, you know? Always on the go, always moving, maybe not pausing to double-check my pockets before I run out the door. So being a little scattered and rushing into things isn't exactly a brand-new trait for me. 

I don't think my memory is actually failing or anything scary like that. Just a few silly slip-ups here and there. That's fairly normal, don't you think? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right picture here and not making a mountain out of a molehill.

Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. I haven't had any strokes or... or Parkinson's, or anything serious with my brain. My doctor has never mentioned anything along those lines, thank heavens. 

I'm perfectly healthy in that department, I promise! Just a bit of a scattered fellow sometimes, like I said. I hope you don't think I'm wasting your time by coming in when it's nothing major like a stroke. I just wanted to be thorough, you know? Did I answer that right for you?

Yeah, nice to meet you too. Um... I guess I'm just having a hard time staying put. 

Like, whenever I'm supposed to sit still in the radiology suite at work, or in class... I just get this feeling like I'm crawling out of my skin. I've been trying to just tough it out for months, but... I don't know. I still just end up pacing or shifting around, or finding some excuse to get up and move. So... yeah. That's why I'm here.
No. Um... I don't take any medications. So... it's not that.

Yeah... I guess so. Um... my parents still bring up my elementary school conferences. Teachers would always say I was out of my seat, or... calling out. Rushing ahead before they even finished giving directions. So... yeah. It was happening way before middle school. It's not just something that started with my radiology training.
No. Um... I don't do that.
No. Um... not really. I don't... I don't think I worry more than anyone else. So... no.

Hi, yeah, good to meet you too. Um... well, what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. I mean, at work, it's just... it's a lot. Patent notes, workshop prep, gallery deadlines for my wife—oh, she’s an artist, mostly mixed media, really incredible stuff. We actually just went to this gallery opening last weekend downtown, the one near that old Italian place? They have the best garlic knots, honestly, I could eat them for every meal. But anyway, yeah, the deadlines, the team decisions... I just end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. Like, I’ll be trying to focus on a piece of code, and then an email pings, and suddenly I’m down a rabbit hole about, I don't know, mechanical keyboards. Did you know there's a whole subculture for those? I spent three hours last Tuesday just watching videos on different switch types... but yeah, the organization thing is just falling apart.

Yeah, actually... looking back, it was definitely there in grade school, long before I was a teenager. I remember my parents kept all my old report cards in this big plastic bin in our basement. The basement always smelled like cedar because my dad built this huge storage closet down there... he was really into woodworking. Actually, I tried getting into woodworking a few years ago, bought a lathe and everything, but I just never set it up. It’s still sitting in the garage taking up space. 

But anyway, the report cards! Yeah, my teachers would always write the exact same thing. They’d say I was a bright kid, but that I daydreamed constantly. And the frustrating part is I’d actually do the work. Like, I’d finish the worksheets or whatever, but then I’d just... forget to turn them in. Or I'd completely lose my homework folders. I had this one folder, it had the Thundercats on it—man, that was such a great show. Did you ever watch the reboot they did a while back? The animation style was totally different, kind of anime-influenced, which some people hated, but I thought the line work was pretty crisp... wait, what was I... right, childhood focus. Yeah, losing folders, daydreaming, forgetting to hand in finished assignments. It’s been happening since I was little.

Unusually energized? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'll get excited about things, sure. Like when I first started learning about espresso extraction. Oh man, I went down such a rabbit hole with that. I bought this fancy burr grinder, the kind they use in actual cafes, and I spent an entire weekend just calibrating the grind size to get the perfect crema. Did you know that humidity actually affects how the coffee beans grind? It’s wild. If it’s raining outside, you literally have to adjust your settings. My wife thought I was losing my mind because I was pulling like, twenty shots a day just to test the variables. I didn't even drink them all, obviously, I'd be vibrating through the walls if I did. But no, I wouldn't say I feel unusually high or anything for days on end. Just... really interested in things sometimes.

Worrying excessively? Um... I don't really think so. I mean, I stress about normal things, like deadlines or... or making sure the cars are inspected on time. Actually, speaking of cars, I just took my Subaru in last week because it was making this weird rattling noise near the heat shield. The mechanic said it was just a loose clamp, but it got me looking into how exhaust systems are put together. I ended up watching this documentary on the history of the catalytic converter. It’s actually fascinating how they use precious metals like platinum and palladium to filter out the toxic gases. I guess palladium prices have been all over the place lately because of supply chain issues. My brother-in-law is really into investing in commodities like that, he’s always talking about silver and gold at family dinners. It gets a little exhausting, to be honest. He’s got this whole theory about the gold standard... but anyway, what was the question? Oh, worrying. Yeah, no, I don't think I'm an overly anxious person or anything like that. Just the normal stuff.

Well, I figured it was time to come in because... well, I volunteer at the local art museum. Have you been there? They just put up this new exhibit on post-war abstract expressionism, and the colors are just incredible. I actually tried painting a little bit myself a few years ago, mostly watercolors, but I could never get the paper to stay flat. Anyway, what brings me in is that, lately, people at the museum will be talking right to me about, say, the next art walk or scheduling, and I’ll be looking right at them... but then I realize I completely missed the middle part of what they said. I have to ask them to run it by me again, which is getting a bit embarrassing. It’s like my brain just takes a little vacation. I think it started happening more around the time I retired, which was... gosh, was it five years ago? No, six. Time really flies when you're not punching a clock, doesn't it?

My hearing? No, I don't think so. I mean, I can hear the birds outside just fine. Actually, I’ve been getting really into birdwatching lately since I have the time. I set up this beautiful cedar feeder out on the back porch... I bought it at the farmer's market from this fellow who makes them by hand out of reclaimed barn wood. It’s got this wonderful rustic look to it. I always admired woodworking, though I never really had the patience for all the exact measuring myself. Anyway, the squirrels figured out how to jump onto the feeder from the oak tree, so I had to buy one of those plastic dome things to keep them off. They're clever little guys, aren't they? 

But... wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, my hearing. No, no, my ears work perfectly fine. I can hear a squirrel scratching at that wood from clear across the house.

Forgetting recent things? Um, no, not really. I mean, my memory is pretty sharp. I can remember the names of all the different birds that come to the feeder, like the tufted titmouse and the Carolina chickadee. Speaking of chickadees, I read the most fascinating article the other day about how they can lower their body temperature at night to survive the winter. It’s called regulated hypothermia, I think. Nature is just amazing, isn't it? I’ve started keeping a little journal of all the birds I see. I bought this beautiful leather-bound notebook at a little stationery shop downtown. The owner there is such a nice lady, she actually imports the paper from Italy. It has this wonderful texture, almost like fabric. I love writing on it with my fountain pen. I’ve had that pen for... oh, must be twenty years now. 

But, um, anyway, no, I don't think I'm forgetting things. Just the listening part, really.

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about when I was younger. I was actually just looking through some old boxes in the attic last week. I was trying to find this old model train set I had as a boy—an O-gauge Lionel, beautiful piece of machinery. The locomotive was die-cast metal, not like the cheap plastic they use today. I used to spend hours setting up the tracks around the Christmas tree. We had this huge Douglas fir one year, must have touched the ceiling... 

But anyway, in one of those boxes, I found a stack of my old report cards from grade school. My mother kept everything, bless her heart. She had this big cedar chest at the foot of her bed where she stored all our keepsakes. It smelled so wonderful when you opened it. And looking at those report cards, I noticed my teachers were always writing things like, "daydreams in class" or "needs reminders to finish work." I guess I've always been a bit like that. In fact, before I was twelve, my mother used to have to pull up a chair and sit right beside me at the kitchen table just to make sure I actually got my homework done instead of staring out the window at the neighbor's dog. It was a Golden Retriever named Buster, sweetest dog you ever met, used to chase his own tail for hours... 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, right, losing track of conversations. Yeah, I suppose the daydreaming thing has been with me for a long, long time.

Anxious? No, not really. I've always been a pretty relaxed sort of fellow. My wife, now, she's the worrier in the family. She'll get anxious about everything, especially when we used to take the camper out. We had this old Coleman pop-up camper... bought it secondhand from a neighbor down the street. It had that distinct canvas smell, you know? Like a mix of old campfire smoke and just a little bit of mildew, but in a good way, if that makes sense. We took it all the way out to Yellowstone back in... oh, must have been the late nineties. The drive out there was just spectacular. I remember we stopped at this little diner in South Dakota that had the absolute best cherry pie I've ever tasted in my life. The crust was so flaky, it just melted right there in your mouth. I tried asking the waitress for the recipe, but she said the cook guarded it like state secrets. Funny how people get so protective over a pie, isn't it? I mean, it's just butter and flour when you get right down to it. 

Anyway, I'm rambling again, aren't I? What was it you asked? Oh, right, if I get worried. No, I don't really get anxious about much of anything these days. Life's too short to fret over the small stuff.

Well, I suppose it has caused a few bumps here and there. I volunteer down at the local history museum a few days a week. We have this wonderful exhibit right now on the old textile mills that used to be the lifeblood of this town. It's fascinating, really. They have these actual looms from the 1920s, and the intricate gear work on them is just a marvel of engineering. I spent a whole afternoon last month just talking to the curator about how they used to source the cotton. He's a brilliant young man, went to school up in Boston, I think. Or maybe it was Providence. Anyway, he knows everything there is to know about industrial history. We were supposed to be organizing a new display case for some old ledger books, which, by the way, have the most beautiful penmanship you've ever seen. People just don't write in cursive like that anymore. 

But, um, where was I? Oh, right, problems. Well, I've noticed the museum group has had to quietly shift some of the planning pieces away from me. I think I was missing some of the details during our committee meetings. And... well, I’ve stopped feeling confident leading the art walks the way I used to. I’d get to talking with someone in the group about a painting, and then I'd completely lose the thread of the tour schedule or forget what the other folks had just asked me. So, I mostly just help out in the archives now. It's quieter back there anyway.

Hearing the sounds but not the words? No, no, my hearing is perfectly fine. I actually had it checked just a couple of years ago when I went in for a physical. My mom would have to practically yell at me to come into the kitchen to eat dinner because I was just so completely absorbed in it. I wouldn't even hear her the first three times she called. 

And school was the same way, really. I mean, I wasn’t some academic genius—I just got my high school diploma and went straight into an apprenticeship to learn metalworking—but I never had teachers calling home saying I was daydreaming or bouncing off the walls or anything like that. I’d just sit quietly, usually sketching designs in the margins of my notebooks or just doing the work. So this whole... brain jumping around thing? It’s completely new. It’s not like I was one of those kids who couldn't sit still or needed extra help paying attention. It’s just happening *now*, which is why it’s so incredibly frustrating for me. Because I *know* what it feels like to focus. I used to be the most focused person in the room, and now it's like that part of my brain just suddenly forgot how to do the one thing I've always been best at.

Worrying? No, not really. I mean, obviously if a client is mad about a custom piece being late, I’ll stress about that specific thing, but just sitting around worrying about nothing? No, that’s never really been my personality. 

My mom, now, she’s a huge worrier. She’ll call me up on a Tuesday morning and ask if I’ve checked the air pressure in my tires because she read some article on Facebook about blowouts on the highway, and I’m just like, "Mom, I drive two miles to the shop at thirty miles an hour, I think I'm fine." But me? I don’t do that. I actually think working with metal for so long kind of trains you out of worrying about things that haven't happened yet. Because when you're soldering a joint on a gold ring, right? You have the torch in your hand, the flame is right there, and if you worry about melting the gold, your hand shakes. And if your hand shakes, you move the heat to the wrong spot and you actually *do* melt the gold and ruin hours of work. So you just have to be completely in the moment. If a problem happens—like a stone chips or a bezel tears—you just fix it right then and there. You don't sit around beforehand agonizing over whether the stone *might* chip. 

So, yeah, no, I don't really have that floating worry or whatever you want to call it. My brain is definitely jumping all over the place right now, like I was saying before with the ticket orders and the window and all that, but it's not because I'm scared or stressed about some imaginary problem. You know, you hear about people getting older and suddenly they only sleep four hours a night and wake up at the crack of dawn to just stare at the ceiling—like my neighbor, Martha, she tells me she’s up at 3 AM every single morning just listening to the house settle and waiting for the sun to come up. But me? Oh, no. 

By the time evening rolls around, after all that puttering and organizing and volunteering I was telling you about, I am just plum tuckered out. I usually have my cup of decaf tea, maybe watch a little Jeopardy or Wheel of Fortune, and I am in bed by 10 o'clock sharp. And I sleep right through until about 6 or 6:30 in the morning. So that's a good eight solid hours, which I think is pretty normal for anyone, let alone someone my age. 

I really do need my full night's rest to keep up with myself the next day! If I didn't get my sleep, I don't know how I'd manage all the projects I end up starting. So, no, I definitely haven't noticed needing less sleep. Once my head hits that pillow, I am out like a light, just like I was twenty years ago. It’s really just the daytime where my engine is running high and I can’t seem to stop moving. But at night, oh yes, I absolutely need my full rest. I've always been a good sleeper, ever since I was a little girl, really.

Oh, well, no... I wouldn't say unusually cheerful. I mean, I'm a fairly positive person, generally speaking, always have been. My mother used to say I was born with a smile on my face, but I certainly don't feel like I'm walking on air or anything like that. I'm just... normal cheerful, I suppose? Like, if the sun is shining or if I see a nice cardinal at the bird feeder out the kitchen window, I'll feel happy about it. But it's not like I'm bursting with joy for no reason while I'm cleaning out that front hall closet or organizing the church bake sale. 

In fact, sometimes when I'm so busy, I actually feel a little bit frustrated with myself! Like, I'll be scrubbing the baseboards in the guest room—and nobody has even stayed in the guest room since my nephew visited three years ago—and I'll think to myself, "Why on earth am I doing this right now? I should be resting." So it's definitely not a feeling of being high in spirits or overjoyed. It's more of a restless energy, like a motor running inside me that just won't shut off, rather than a feeling of being overly happy. 

I mean, sure, it feels nice to get things done, and I like checking things off a list, but it's not an unusual kind of happiness. I'm not running around singing show tunes or feeling like I won the lottery. I'm just... busy. Just constantly, constantly busy, and maybe a little tired of being so busy, if I'm being perfectly honest. I just wish I could sit down and enjoy a cup of tea without feeling like I need to go wipe down the counters while the water is boiling, you know? So, no, not unusually cheerful at all. Just my regular self, but with far too much energy for an 87-year-old woman!

Oh, heavens no, I wouldn't say I'm a worrier. I mean, everyone has their little concerns, don't they? Like, if there's a big storm coming, I might wonder if the sump pump in the basement is going to hold up, because back in '98—or was it '99?—we had that awful flooding and it was just a mess. But I don't sit around wringing my hands over it. I just go down and check the pump, and maybe move a few boxes off the floor just in case, and then I'm on to the next thing. 

I'm really not one of those people who sits in their chair fretting about the bills or what the neighbors think or if the roast is going to be dry for Sunday dinner. My friend Gladys, bless her heart, she worries about everything under the sun. She'll call me up and talk for an hour about whether she offended the mailman by not saying good morning quickly enough, and I just think, "Gladys, the mailman has already forgotten about it!" 

But me? No, I don't have the time to sit and worry! Like I said, I'm always up and doing something. If a thought about something everyday pops into my head, like, "Oh, did I remember to buy stamps?", I don't sit and stew about it. I just pop up right then and there, go check my desk drawer, and if I don't have stamps, well, I might just grab my purse and head to the post office right that minute, even if I was in the middle of folding laundry. I just do it. So, I don't really spend time *worrying*, no. I just take action, probably faster than I should sometimes! But no, I wouldn't call myself a worrier at all.

Oh, goodness, no. No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, I'm just me! I'm just Margaret. I don't feel like I'm suddenly the Queen of England or the CEO of some big company just because I have the energy to clean the gutters out. 

I know some people get like that, you know, they get a little burst of energy and suddenly they think they know everything about everything. Like my brother-in-law, Arthur, rest his soul. Whenever he'd get a new hobby, whether it was woodworking or investing in the stock market—which he knew absolutely nothing about, let me tell you—he'd talk to you like he was the world's foremost expert. He'd stand there at the Thanksgiving table, carving the turkey, and lecturing us all about mutual funds as if he'd invented them. It was exhausting, really. 

But I'm not like that. I don't feel any more important or capable than I did yesterday or the day before. I know exactly what I can and can't do. I know I'm an 87-year-old woman who shouldn't be climbing up on a stepstool to dust the top of the china cabinet, but sometimes I just can't help myself because my body just wants to move. But it's not because I feel invincible or unusually confident! I actually know it's a bit foolish while I'm doing it. I'll be up there thinking, "Margaret, if you fall and break a hip, your daughter is going to be furious," but the urge to just get it done is so strong. 

So, no, there's no grand feeling of importance. I don't feel like I could go run for mayor or solve all the world's problems. I just feel like I need to keep busy, keep my hands moving, keep doing things around the house. It's just my normal self, just... sped up, I suppose you could say. But definitely not feeling more important or anything grand like that. Just regular old me, with a motor that won't quit.

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've always been a doer, as I said. Always on the go, always keeping a tidy house and making sure everything is just so. But... yes, I suppose there has been a change. A very distinct change, actually, if I really stop and think about it. 

It hasn't always been this... relentless. This feeling like I simply cannot sit still. I'd say it really started getting noticeably worse, where it felt like a real shift from my usual self, about a year and five months ago. I remember the timing quite well because it was right around the time all those awful insurance bills started piling up, and then, wouldn't you know it, the roof started leaking in the sunroom. It never rains but it pours, right? Literally, in the case of the sunroom! 

Anyway, dealing with the insurance people on the phone—which is a full-time job in itself, let me tell you, pressing one for this and two for that and waiting on hold for forty-five minutes just to speak to a person who doesn't even know what a sunroom is—and then trying to coordinate with the roofers... it was just so much. And to cope with it all, I started taking on more responsibilities down at the senior center. I thought, "Well, Margaret, if you're going to be stressed, you might as well be useful." 

So I started organizing the Tuesday morning bingo, and then I took over the hospitality committee, which means baking two dozen muffins every Thursday, and before I knew it, I was practically running the place. And ever since then, ever since that period about a year and five months ago, this restless energy just hasn't let up. It’s like I shifted into high gear to get through the roof and the bills and the bingo, and I just never found the brakes again. Even now that the roof is fixed—thank goodness, they did a wonderful job, though the shingles are a slightly different shade of gray than the old ones, but you can only tell in a certain light—I still feel like I'm running at top speed. So, yes, that would be the clear period when it really changed from just being an active person to being this... constantly humming motor.

Oh, heavens no. No, no, no. The hospital? Goodness, at my age, you try to stay as far away from the hospital as you possibly can, because you go in for a stubbed toe and you come out with pneumonia! So, no, nothing like that. And serious trouble? Well, I suppose the only trouble I get into is with my daughter. She’s always scolding me, saying, "Mom, you’re going to hurt yourself, you need to just sit down and watch television like a normal person." 

But I haven't done anything that required a doctor or the police, if that's what you mean! I mean, I did have a little mishap... oh, when was it? Last Tuesday, I think. Yes, Tuesday, because it was the day the garbage gets collected. I was rushing to get the bins out, and I realized I hadn't emptied the little wastebasket in the guest bathroom, so I was practically running through the hall with this trash bag, and I tripped over the cord of the vacuum cleaner—which I had left out because I was planning to do the rugs right after the trash. I took a bit of a tumble, I won't lie. Scraped my shin right on the leg of the hall table. 

But did I go to the hospital? Absolutely not. I just marched myself into the kitchen, got a bag of frozen peas—the petite peas, mind you, they mold to the leg much better than the regular ones—and sat with it for exactly ten minutes before I realized I still needed to get that bin out before the truck came. I didn't even tell my daughter about it because she would have made a huge fuss and tried to take my vacuum away or something ridiculous.

So, no, no serious trouble. Just a few bruises here and there from moving a bit too fast and bumping into the corners of the coffee table. But certainly nothing that would put me in the emergency room or get me into any real trouble. I'm energetic, yes, and maybe a bit too hasty for my own good sometimes, but I'm not reckless! I still have my wits about me, thank goodness.

Talking more than usual? Well, I suppose you might have to ask my daughter about that, because she always says I talk a mile a minute, but if you ask me, I'd have to say no. No, I don't think I'm talking any more than I usually do. I've just always been a conversationalist, you see. 

Ever since I was a little girl, my mother used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. But I really haven't noticed any change in how much I speak since this whole restless period began. I still have my regular weekly phone calls with my sister, Beatrice—she lives out in Scottsdale now, you know, she moved there for the dry air because of her arthritis, which she absolutely swears by, though honestly I couldn't stand the heat myself, baking in the sun like a lizard on a rock. Anyway, we talk for exactly one hour every Sunday afternoon, just like we always have. 

And down at the senior center, well, yes, I talk to people when I'm handing out the bingo cards or serving the muffins, but that's just being polite, isn't it? You can't just shove a blueberry muffin at someone and walk away in dead silence. You have to ask about their grandchildren, or how their hydrangeas are doing. Take Mrs. Higgins, for instance—she has the most beautiful hydrangeas, though she uses entirely too much coffee grounds in the soil if you ask me, which makes them a bit too acidic, but I digress. 

The point is, I'm just making normal conversation. I'm not suddenly babbling at people or cornering them in the grocery store aisle to talk their ear off about nothing. I might be moving faster, and I might be doing three things at once—like dusting the baseboards while I'm on the cordless phone with Beatrice—but the talking itself hasn't sped up or gotten out of hand. I'm certainly not talking to myself, thank goodness! Well, except to say, "Margaret, where on earth did you put your reading glasses," but everyone at my age does that. So, no, my talking is just the same as it's always been. I'm just a sociable person, but I haven't turned into a chatterbox just because I have all this extra energy.

Depressed? Oh, goodness, no. No, I really don't have the time for that, to be perfectly honest with you. I mean, I know some people my age get very down, and I suppose it's understandable if you just sit around all day, but that's simply not my way. 

Take my neighbor, Doris, for example. Now, Doris is a lovely woman, she really is, but she sits in that beige recliner of hers from dawn until dusk, just watching those terrible twenty-four-hour news channels. And I always tell her that if I watched the news all day, I would be depressed too! It is nothing but doom and gloom, and who needs that at our age? But me? No, I have never had a period like that, not for a couple of weeks, not even for a couple of days, really. 

Even when my late husband passed away—oh, goodness, it must be going on fifteen years ago now, time just flies, doesn't it?—I was terribly sad, of course I was. We were married for a very long time. But I didn't just sit around feeling depressed all day for weeks on end. I threw myself into organizing his affairs, and I repainted the guest room, and I made sure the garden was weeded, because he always loved his tomatoes and I couldn't bear to see them overgrow. You just have to keep moving, don't you? 

So, no, I haven't ever

Well, no, like I was saying, I really haven't. Not for two weeks, not every day, nothing like that. I just don't have it in me to be down in the dumps for that long. There's always something that needs doing! 

I mean, just think about it—if I were depressed for two whole weeks, the house would fall to pieces. Who would polish the silver? My daughter certainly wouldn't, she puts everything in the dishwasher, which just ruins the finish, absolutely ruins it. And the garden! The weeds don't care if you're feeling sad, they just keep growing. I remember one time, I think I had a bad cold, or maybe it was the flu—this was back in, oh, 1998 maybe? I had to stay in bed for three days, and when I finally got up, the dust on the mantelpiece was thick enough to write my name in. I couldn't stand it. 

So, no, I just don't let myself get that way. If I ever feel a little bit blue, I just find a project. I'll reorganize the pantry, or I'll go through the old photo albums and put them in chronological order—which is a huge task, let me tell you, because nobody ever wrote dates on the back of the pictures in the seventies. You have to guess based on how wide my husband's lapels were! But it keeps the mind busy, you see. You can't be depressed if your mind is busy and your hands are moving. So, no, never a two-week period of that. I simply wouldn't allow it.

Lost interest in things? Oh, absolutely not. Good heavens, I have too many interests to keep up with as it is! If I lost interest in things, I honestly don't know what I'd do with myself all day. 

I mean, take my knitting, for example. I've been knitting since I was, oh, maybe eight years old? My grandmother taught me. She used to make these incredibly intricate cable-knit sweaters, the kind that weigh about ten pounds and keep you warm in a blizzard. I don't make those anymore, my hands get a bit stiff if I try anything too complicated, but I still knit baby blankets for the hospital. I must have made at least fifty of them this year alone. Yellow and mint green are my favorites to use, because you never know if it's going to be a boy or a girl, and I think those colors are just so cheerful. I haven't lost a bit of interest in that. I'm actually working on a lovely lemon-yellow one right now with a scalloped edge, which is a new pattern I found in a magazine at the dentist's office. 

And then there's my baking. Oh, I could never lose interest in baking! Just last week, I made three dozen snickerdoodles for the church bake sale. I always use a pinch of cream of tartar, that's the secret, you see, it makes them perfectly chewy in the middle. Some people just use baking powder, but it's not the same, it really isn't. And my garden, well, I already mentioned my garden, didn't I? The weeds certainly don't let you lose interest. 

So, no, I've never had a time where I didn't want to do the things I enjoy. If anything, my problem is that there aren't enough hours in the day to do everything I want to do! I'm always finding new little projects. Just yesterday I decided I was going to learn how to make my own preserves. I bought a flat of strawberries from the farmer's market—though they were terribly overpriced, if you ask me, four dollars for a little pint!—and I'm going to try canning them this afternoon. So you see, I'm just as interested in my hobbies as I've always been, maybe even more so lately with all this energy I have!

Before a year and five months ago? Oh, heavens, yes! Goodness me, you make it sound like it just appeared out of thin air. No, no, if you ask anyone who has known me for any length of time, they will tell you I have always been a bit like a motor that simply won't switch off. 

I mean, going all the way back! I remember very clearly being in grade school—this would have been, oh, the early nineteen-forties, I suppose. We had those heavy wooden desks, you know the ones with the little inkwells built right into the top right corner? Well, I simply could not stay in mine to save my life. I was always getting scolded for popping out of my seat. I'd rush up to the chalkboard, or I'd run over to the window because I saw a robin, or I'd just stand up because my legs felt like they had springs in them and sitting felt almost painful. 

And the talking! Oh, my mother used to say I was vaccinated with a phonograph needle. I was constantly talking over my classmates, just blurting things out because I couldn't hold the thought in my head for another second. The teachers were always writing notes home or pulling me aside. I remember one teacher in particular, Mrs. Gable—she wore these terribly strict wool skirts—she told my parents that I was just 'too lively.' That was the exact phrase she used, 'too lively.' And this was long, long before I was a teenager! 

So this feeling, this restless sort of drive to keep moving and doing... oh, it's not new at all. It’s just how I’m built. Even when I was a young woman, before I met my husband, I would walk miles and miles every single day just to burn it off. I simply can't sit still for long, I never have been able to. I always have to be doing something with my hands or my feet, which I suppose is why I get so much knitting done, like I was telling you earlier. If I just sat there like my neighbor Doris, I think I would burst out of my own skin!

Hi, it's really nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for fitting me in. 

Um, I hope I'm explaining this right, but... I guess what really brought me in is just that my mind kind of won’t stay on one thing anymore. It's probably normal to get a little scattered sometimes, but lately at the bench—I'm a jeweler—I'll just jump from reading a customer email, to looking at a saw mark on a piece of metal, to some random noise outside... and then I realize I’ve completely lost track of the whole work order I was supposed to be doing. 

I just don't want to mess up at work or let anyone down, you know? Does that... is that the kind of thing I should be coming here for?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I was pretty average, I think. I didn't really have trouble paying attention in school or anything like that. I actually liked focusing on the little details, which is probably why I ended up making jewelry. 

I was a pretty good kid, always tried to do my homework and follow the rules. I didn't want to cause any trouble for my teachers or my parents. So, yeah, this feeling of being so easily distracted... it's kind of new for me. I hope that makes sense? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.

Well, um... I guess I wouldn't say I'm, like, severely depressed or anything. I'm still getting up and going to work every day. But... I don't know, maybe a little down? 

These past couple weeks, I've just been waking up with this... heavy, kind of hollow feeling. It's almost like the shine has just gone out of everything, even the pieces I usually love working on. I mean, it's embarrassing to admit, and I hope you don't think less of me, but... I've actually cried in my truck a few times before opening the shop. 

I just wipe my face and go in because I don't want the customers to see, but... yeah, it's been a little tough. Is that... does that sound like depression to you, or just a normal slump? I really want to give you the right answer here.

Well, um... I guess maybe a little bit? Like I mentioned, the jewelry making hasn't been as exciting lately, but... I don't want it to sound like I've just given up on everything. I'm still trying my best to stay engaged, you know? 

I still like seeing my friends sometimes, and I try to keep up with my hobbies... it's just that the feeling I get from them isn't quite as strong right now. It's probably just a phase, right? I mean, everyone gets a little bored sometimes. I hope I'm not making too big a deal out of it. Am I answering your question okay?

Well, um... I've been racking my brain trying to figure that out myself, to be honest. But... no, not really. Work at the shop has been fine, no big fights with anyone, nothing like that. 

I actually feel a little guilty about it, because I know people go through some really terrible things, and here I am, just... feeling this way for no good reason. I almost wish I had a better excuse for you so it would make more sense. I hope it's okay that I don't really have a specific trigger to point to? I just want to be completely honest with you and not make something up just to justify how I've been acting. Is it normal for this to just happen out of nowhere?

Well, um... I wouldn't say I've been worrying *a lot* more, no. I mean, I have the usual stuff on my mind, like keeping the shop running and making sure the customers are happy with their pieces. But... nothing out of the ordinary, I don't think. 

I try really hard not to let things get to me too much. I don't want to be a burden on anyone by constantly stressing out, you know? So, I think I'm doing okay in that department. I hope that's the kind of answer you were looking for? I just want to make sure I'm giving you an accurate picture of what's going on.

Well, um... no, nothing like that. I've been pretty healthy, honestly. No hospital visits or major injuries or anything. 

I try to take good care of myself, you know? Eat right, get enough sleep when I can... I don't want to cause any extra trouble for anyone by getting sick. So physically, I think I'm doing just fine. I hope that helps rule out anything complicated? I'm really trying to be as helpful as I can with all your questions.

Well, um... I guess maybe a little bit? I don't want to make it sound worse than it is, because I'm still getting my work done. But... I have noticed that sometimes I'll stare at a repair ticket, or like, a tray of sapphires, and I just... I can't seem to hold the measurements in my head long enough to decide what to do next. 

It's a little embarrassing to admit, honestly. I usually pride myself on being really sharp with those details. I just sort of lose my train of thought for a second. It's nothing too terrible, I promise, and I always double-check my work so I don't mess anything up for the customers. Is it okay that I'm struggling with that a little? I hope it doesn't make me sound incompetent or anything.

Well, um... no, I don't think anyone has really noticed. I mean, I work pretty independently at the bench most of the day, so it's mostly just me and the stones. 

If I do have a little slip-up or need to reread a ticket, I just handle it quietly. I really try not to let it show, you know? I wouldn't want my boss or the customers to think I'm not paying attention or that I don't care about their pieces. I always make sure the final product is perfect before anyone sees it. So... I think I've done a good job of keeping it under wraps. I hope it's alright that I haven't told anyone at work about it? I just want to keep things running smoothly for everyone.

Well, um... no, I haven't started anything new. No medications or supplements or anything like that. I really try to just keep things simple, you know? 

I wouldn't want to take something over-the-counter that might mess up whatever you're trying to figure out, or make your job harder. So I just stay away from all those extra pills and powders and just try to drink enough water. I hope that's okay? I mean, if there's a vitamin or something you think I really should be taking, I'd definitely be open to it. I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing here and giving you a clean slate to work with.

Well, um... no, I don't think so. I mean, maybe every once in a while I'll pause for a second, but nothing out of the ordinary, I promise. 

I feel like I can still explain things clearly to the customers when they come in to ask about a repair or a custom setting. I really try to be careful with how I talk to people, because I want them to feel confident leaving their jewelry with me. So, I make sure to speak clearly and use the right terms. I haven't noticed any real issues with finding my words, thankfully. I hope that's a good sign? I'm trying my best to stay on top of everything.

Well, um... yeah, I guess it's been a little while now. I really didn't want to admit it to myself, but... this whole feeling down and, I don't know, just feeling guilty all the time... it's been hanging over me for about a month, I think. 

I've tried so hard to just push through it and keep smiling for the customers, you know? I really didn't want to be a burden or seem like I was complaining. I kept hoping it would just pass if I worked harder. I'm sorry if I should have come in sooner. I hope it's not too late to figure this out? I just want to get back to being myself and doing a good job.

Well, um... no, my appetite has been pretty normal, I'd say. I mean, I still try to make sure I eat my meals and keep my strength up for work. 

I don't want to get weak or shaky when I'm working with the tiny tools, you know? So I make a point to eat lunch, even if it's just a sandwich or something small. I haven't noticed any big changes, like eating way too much or totally skipping meals. I really try to take care of myself that way. I hope that's helpful to know? I'm doing my best to keep a good routine going.

Well, um... I guess my sleep hasn't been perfect lately, if I'm being completely honest. I always try to get into bed at a normal hour, because I know how important it is to be sharp for work, but... I just kind of toss and turn for a while. 

And then, yeah, I have been waking up pretty early, like before dawn. My mind just starts racing about work, like this one missed delivery we had, and I just can't seem to turn it off and go back to sleep. When I finally drag myself out of bed, I really don't feel rested at all. I'm sorry, I know I should be managing my stress better so I can sleep. I'm trying to fix it, I promise. Is it normal to get stuck on things like that when you're trying to sleep?

Hi, nice to meet you too. I'm a barber, and... well, I'm here because I've gotten to the point where I'll do almost anything to avoid using the straight razor at work. I'll switch clients with someone else, tell them the blade's missing, or just hide it in my drawer. And if I absolutely can't get out of it, I'm just shaking through the whole shave. It's become a real problem for me.

Yeah, exactly. I mean... I know it’s just a tool, and it's what I trained with. I can use clippers all day long without any issue at all. But when that straight razor is just sitting open at my station, it really feels like I’m about to hurt somebody, or cut myself badly.

No, it's not really like that. I don't get, like, pictures in my head of doing something terrible on purpose or anything. It's just this intense fear that an accident is going to happen, that the blade is going to slip and someone is going to get hurt.

No, not really. I mean, I worry about normal stuff sometimes, like paying bills or if my car needs work, but it's nothing major. The only thing that really gets to me and makes me panic is that straight razor. Everything else is pretty much fine.

No, I wouldn't say I've been depressed. I'm not sad or down, really. I mean, it's stressful, dealing with the project and feeling like I have to watch my back all the time. But it's not depression. I'm just focused on getting the work done and proving what they're doing.

I used to talk a lot more, especially when I was mentoring the younger analysts at work or chatting with people at those astronomy nights. But now, I just don't have the urge to hold a conversation with anyone.

I suppose so. It really just ties back into what I was just telling you. When I'm sitting there for hours at my desk, or out in the garage with the telescope still covered up, I'm just... blank. I don't really feel much inside, so I guess it makes sense that my face and voice wouldn't show much either. Even if I think about the things that used to get me excited, like hiking, or mentoring the younger analysts, or going to those astronomy nights... there's just no reaction. I just don't feel that pull to express anything anymore.

Yeah, it definitely has. I've... well, I've fallen pretty far behind on my modeling deliverables at work.
