Yes, exactly! That's just it. It's like everything I put in my mouth is just... well, it's just bland. Like cardboard, or dust, like I said. I used to love making this chicken salad, with the little bits of celery and the grapes—oh, it was so lovely, especially in the summer—but I tried making it last week, and I took one bite and it was just... nothing. No sweetness from the grapes, no savory flavor from the chicken. It's just chewing for the sake of chewing. And it's not just the chicken salad, it's everything. My morning tea, the little shortbread cookies I get from the bakery down the street... nothing has that spark anymore. I just don't understand it, because my sense of smell seems fine, I think, but the taste is just completely gone. It makes eating feel like such a chore, you know? Just going through the motions without any of the joy it used to bring me.

Well, I... I wouldn't say I've completely lost it, no. It's not like when you get a terrible head cold and you literally can't taste a single thing, not even a strong peppermint. It's not like that. If I put something very salty on my tongue, I suppose I can tell it's salty, and if I eat a lemon, I know it's sour. So the mechanics of it, I suppose, the actual taste buds, they must still be working on some level. 

But it's just... the enjoyment of it, the richness of the flavor, that's what's gone. It's like the volume has been turned way, way down on everything. So no, I haven't gone completely numb in the mouth or anything like that. It's more of a... a dullness. A terrible, persistent dullness that just won't go away, no matter what I try to eat. I even tried putting extra pepper on my eggs the other morning, thinking maybe I just needed to spice things up, but it just tasted like hot dust. So I haven't lost the ability to taste, exactly, it's just that the tastes themselves don't mean anything to me anymore.

Oh, yes. Yes, I have. It's funny you ask that, because my daughter was just saying the exact same thing to me on the phone the other day. You see, I have always been a very active person, very involved with my friends and my little community here. I used to look forward to my watercolor class on Tuesday mornings—we've been painting landscapes lately, and I just loved mixing the greens and blues to get the trees just right. And then there's the quilting circle on Thursdays, which I've been a part of for, oh, it must be fifteen years now. We're working on a beautiful star pattern for the church bazaar. And my Sunday book club, too! I used to just love all of it, every single bit of it. 

I'd get my little canvas tote bag ready the night before, make sure I had my brushes or my thimbles or whatever book we were reading—we were supposed to read a lovely historical novel this month, though I haven't even opened it. Because lately... well, I'll pack my bag the night before, just like always, mostly out of habit, I suppose. I'll set it right there by the front door so I don't forget it. And then the morning comes, and it's time to put my coat on and walk down to the community center, and I just... I look at the bag, and I look at the door, and I just can't make myself care enough to go. 

I often just leave the bag sitting right there by the door. It's the strangest thing, just this complete lack of interest in the things that used to be the absolute highlights of my week. I'll just sit back down in my armchair instead and watch the cars go by out the living room window, and I'll think about how I should be at quilting, how the ladies are probably wondering where I am, but I just don't have the heart for it anymore. It's just like the food, really. It feels like all the color and the joy have just been washed right out of my routine, and I just can't seem to muster up the energy to care about any of my hobbies at all...

Well, yes. Yes, I really have. It's... it's hard to explain without sounding silly, but most mornings I wake up with this terrible, heavy, low feeling. It settles right over me the moment I open my eyes. I've always been an early riser, you know, up at six-thirty every morning to get the coffee going and pull the curtains open, but lately... well, I just lie there. It's like the color has completely gone out of the day before I even manage to get dressed. 

I'll look over at my closet, at the nice blouses I have hung up in there, and I just feel so weighed down by it all. The sun could be shining right through the window, but everything just feels gray and dreary to me. And it just stays with me, that heavy feeling, following me from the bedroom to the kitchen, right to that armchair I mentioned. Day in and day out, it's just this constant, low cloud hovering right over my head. I just can't seem to shake it, no matter how hard I try to put on a brave face for the neighbors or when my daughter calls. So, yes, I'd say I feel very down almost every single day now, from the very minute I wake up.

Oh, well... that's a difficult question, isn't it? It's not the sort of thing you want to admit to, especially when you've always prided yourself on being strong for your family. I don't want to worry my daughter, you know. She has her own life, her own family, her job at the bank—she's a loan officer, very busy, always running here and there. I wouldn't want to add to her plate. 

But... well, to be completely honest with you, doctor, I have had some dark thoughts lately. I want to be very clear, though—I haven't made any sort of plan. I wouldn't do that. I don't have pills hidden away or anything terrible like that. I wouldn't take my own life, I really wouldn't. It's against my beliefs, and it would just leave such a mess for everyone else to clean up. I've always been very tidy, very organized, and I couldn't bear the thought of leaving my daughter to sort through that kind of tragedy.

It's just that... well, with this heavy feeling every day, sitting in that armchair and looking at the canvas tote bag by the door, knowing I'm not going to quilting or book club... I just catch myself thinking sometimes. I think about how tired I am, how gray everything is, and I think... well, if I just went to sleep one night and simply didn't wake up the next morning... it might not be the worst thing. It might actually be a bit of a relief. A relief for me, to be free of this awful dullness, and a relief for my family, so they wouldn't have to worry about their poor old mother sitting alone in her house all day. It's just a passing thought, usually when I'm lying in bed before the sun comes up, but it's there. Just this quiet little wish that maybe I could just slip away peacefully and not have to face another heavy day.

Well, yes, actually. It's funny you should ask about the timing, because I've thought about that quite a bit while sitting in my armchair. It hasn't always been like this, you know. I used to have so much energy, like I said about my watercolor class and the quilting circle. But this whole change, this awful heaviness and losing interest in everything... it's been going on for about a year and five months now. 

I know the exact timeline because it started right around the time my sister's health took a very serious turn. My sister, Martha—she's two years older than me, lives over in the next county, in a lovely little ranch house she and her husband bought back in the seventies. We've always been so close, talking on the phone every Sunday evening without fail. But then, about a year and a half ago—well, a year and five months, to be precise—she had this terrible fall in her kitchen. She was just reaching for a can of soup on the top shelf, lost her balance, and down she went. Broke her hip, and at our age, well, you know how devastating that can be. 

It was just so stressful. I was driving back and forth to the hospital, then to the rehabilitation center, trying to make sure she was getting the right care, dealing with her doctors, trying to help her husband, who was just beside himself with worry. He's a sweet man, but he doesn't handle medical things well at all. I was trying to be strong for everyone, packing overnight bags, making casseroles so they'd have something to eat... and it just took so much out of me. It was terrifying seeing her so frail, and I think the worry just seeped right into my bones. That's when I first started noticing that I didn't want to go to my book club, and then the heavy feeling in the mornings started creeping in, and it just hasn't lifted since. So yes, it's been about a year and five months since all of this started, right when Martha had her accident.

Oh, goodness, no. No, I really haven't. I was actually just thinking about that the other day when I was sitting in my chair, looking over at the bookshelf where I keep all the old family photo albums. My daughter had brought them down from the attic for me last Christmas... or was it Thanksgiving? No, it must have been Christmas, because I remember we had the red poinsettia tablecloth out on the dining table. Anyway, I was thinking about all those years, looking at pictures from my twenties and thirties, and I realized I've always been such a busy, cheerful person. 

Even when my late husband passed away—God rest his soul, that was back in ninety-eight, a sudden heart attack, just terrible—I was heartbroken, of course. Completely devastated. We had a beautiful service for him at the First Methodist church, flowers everywhere. But even with all that grief, it was a... well, a normal kind of sadness, if that makes sense. I still got out of bed every morning. I still made sure the house was spotless, I still went down to the Piggly Wiggly for my groceries, and I kept up with my garden. I never had this... this awful, paralyzing heaviness that I have now. 

I've always been a doer, doctor. When the girls were little, I was PTA president for three years running, organizing bake sales and holiday pageants, always running the carpool. I always had a smile on my face and a casserole in the oven. Even when things were tough, like when the local plant closed down in the eighties and money was terribly tight for a while, I just rolled up my sleeves and found ways to make do. I've never, ever had a time in my life where I just sat around for weeks on end, feeling gray and empty like this. This whole terrible cloud is completely new to me. It's just so unlike me, which is why my daughter finally insisted I come talk to someone. So, no, before Martha's fall a year and five months ago, I had never experienced anything even remotely like this. I was always right as rain.

Pleasure? Oh, doctor, I... I really don't think I do. And that's perhaps the strangest part of all this, it truly is. 

Like I was saying earlier about my watercolor class, and the quilting circle... oh, I used to just live for those afternoons. Tuesdays were watercolors down at the community center—we have this wonderful instructor, a retired art teacher who always brings in the most beautiful fresh flowers for us to paint, peonies and daffodils and what have you. And Thursdays were the quilting circle at the church. I was working on a lovely double wedding ring pattern for my grandniece, picking out all these cheerful yellow and blue fabrics. I used to look forward to those groups so much, and my book club on the first Wednesday of the month, too. We'd take turns hosting, making little cucumber sandwiches and brewing a nice pot of Earl Grey tea, just chatting for hours...

But now? Now, I just... I can't seem to muster up even a drop of enthusiasm for any of it. It's the saddest thing. I have that canvas tote bag I mentioned, the one sitting by the front door. It has my good brushes and my little paint palette in it, and sometimes on a Tuesday morning I even get as far as putting my spectacles in the front pocket, thinking, 'Alright, today is the day, I'm going to go.' 

But then I just stand there and look at it. I look at the bag, and I look at the door, and I just... I leave the bag sitting right there. I turn around and go back to my armchair. I just can't make myself care enough to go. I don't care about the painting, I don't care about the book we're reading—it was a historical fiction novel this month, which is usually my absolute favorite—but I just feel completely blank about it all. Nothing seems to bring me that spark of joy anymore, not even the things I used to love so dearly.

Nice to meet you too. Well, I guess what finally scared me into coming in is that... after I eat too much, I’ve been making myself throw up in the bathroom. I just do it so I won't gain weight. But it’s gotten to the point where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore, and I knew I needed to talk to someone about it.

Yes. Once I start during those times, it just feels like I’m on automatic. I'll be thinking to myself that I really should stop before my husband notices, but I'm still reaching for one more thing anyway. I just can't seem to stop myself once I get going.
No, I wouldn't say that. I'm pretty average for my height, I think. I haven't lost a significant amount of weight or anything like that. I just... I try to keep it where it is.

Well, for at least the past several months, it's been happening most weeks. I'll have one of those secret eating spells and then go make myself sick afterward. I can't honestly call it occasional anymore. It's a pretty regular thing now.

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, it's a bit of a long story, but I'll try to explain. I'm an auditor—I've been in accounting for years, got my bachelor's ages ago, and you'd think in my line of work that I'd have everything completely buttoned up. And I really try to. But what finally pushed me to make this appointment, what really made me realize I need to talk to someone, is that I keep starting these follow-up items at work and just... not finishing them. 

Like, after a massive audit wraps up, or even after these mentorship events I help run for the junior staff at the firm, there's always a list of wrap-up tasks. I will sit down at my desk with every intention of finishing them right then and there. I'll open the files, I'll start typing, I am fully engaged in getting it off my plate. But then, somehow, I find out days later that the task never actually got done. 

Someone will message me asking for a document, and I'll realize that the final email just sat in my drafts and I never hit send. Or a review note I swore I completed is just sitting there half-typed in the system. Or a compliance form never actually got submitted. And it is incredibly frustrating, and honestly so embarrassing, because I *know* I started it. I remember sitting there doing it! But the actual follow-through just sort of evaporates. I can't keep dropping the ball like this, especially not at my level, so... yeah, that's really why I'm here. It's just driving me crazy.

Oh, gosh, yes. Honestly, it goes all the way back to elementary school. It’s funny you ask that, because I was just talking to my mother about this the other day, and we were laughing—well, I was laughing, but also kind of wincing—about my old report cards. I mean, my parents kept everything, so I’ve actually seen them recently. Every single year, the teachers would write practically the same paragraph. They’d say I was bright, that I had so much potential, but then there would be this whole list of... well, issues. 

They’d say I was constantly losing my assignments, or I’d rush through things and make all these careless mistakes on the small details because I just wanted to be done with it. And I was always talking out of turn, interrupting people—which, frankly, I still have to stop myself from doing in meetings now. But the finishing tasks thing, absolutely. The teachers always noted that I needed constant reminders to actually finish my work. My mother still jokes about it to this day. She always says, "You could ace a test in five minutes, but you’d completely forget to hand in the big project that was literally sitting right there in your backpack." And it was true! I’d do the work, or at least start it, and then it would just live in my backpack until it was crumpled and three weeks late. So, yes, it’s definitely not a new problem, it’s just... it feels like it has higher stakes now, you know? When you're a kid, it's a zero on a diorama, but now it's a compliance form for a major client, and I just... I can't keep doing it.

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I worry about things, sure, but it's usually very specific things. Like, if I know I have a massive audit coming up and the client is notorious for having their files in complete disarray, yes, I will stress about that. I'll lay in bed thinking about how long it's going to take to untangle their mess, and I'll worry about missing a deadline because of it. Or I'll worry about whether I remembered to send that email we were just talking about. But it's always tied to something real, something tangible that's actually happening in my life or at work. 

I don't just sit around agonizing over random things or having this vague sense of doom for no reason. My husband, actually, he's a bit of a worrier. He'll read the news and spend the whole evening stressing about the economy or something happening halfway across the world, and I just... I don't really operate like that. My brain is usually too busy bouncing between the ten things I'm supposed to be doing right now to invent things to worry about, if that makes sense. So, no, I don't think I have that kind of excessive, free-floating worry. It's more just the practical, immediate stress of trying to keep my head above water with all my tasks and making sure I don't drop the ball on something important.

No, not really. I mean, I still love the things I love. It’s just... finding the time or the focus for them, you know? Like, I love gardening. Absolutely love it. My backyard is usually my sanctuary, and I have these raised beds that I built a few years ago—well, my husband helped, but I planned them all out—and I usually grow tomatoes, peppers, some herbs. And I still really enjoy the *idea* of it, and when I'm out there, I like it. But lately, it's more like I just can't get myself organized enough to actually go out and do the weeding or the pruning. 

I'll look out the window and think, "Oh, I really need to get out there, I want to get out there," but then I remember I have to put my gardening shoes on, and find my gloves, and where did I leave the pruning shears? Probably in the garage somewhere from last weekend when I meant to put them away but got distracted by the recycling bin... and by the time I think through all the steps, I just feel exhausted by the process and end up doing something else instead. But it's not that I don't *enjoy* gardening anymore. If someone handed me my gloves and shears and put me in front of the tomato plants, I'd be perfectly happy. It's the same with reading. I love a good mystery novel, but sitting down and actually focusing on a book when my brain feels like a pinball machine? It's tough. But the enjoyment is still there, definitely. I haven't lost that spark for the things I care about, it's just the execution that gets in the way.

I'm here because... well, I just can't stop thinking about my appearance. It's mainly my hairline and my face. My coworkers tell me they don't see what I'm talking about, but I just can't shake it. It's really starting to get to me.

Yeah, I do. Especially right before a shift. I'll just keep checking the bathroom mirror over and over. I even take pictures on my phone from different angles to see how bad it looks. I'll stand there combing my hair forward, trying to fix it, just... replaying in my head exactly how the guests might see me when I greet them. It gets to the point where I end up running late, or I get so worked up that I can barely bring myself to go out to the front.

Yes, I do. It's actually gotten me into trouble at work. I’ve been written up at the restaurant because I end up being late, or sometimes I just miss my shifts completely when I can't get past it. 

And outside of work... yeah, I've stopped doing a lot of things. I refuse to be in any staff photos now, and I've stopped going to gallery events and hikes with people. I just... I can’t handle being seen that way.

Yeah, I do. I know they say they don't see it, but... well, I figure they're just being polite, or maybe they just aren't looking as closely as I am. But I know what I see in the mirror. It's definitely there, no matter what anyone else tells me.
No, not really. It's... it's just my appearance. I don't really have unwanted thoughts about anything else, just the way I look. That's the only thing that gets stuck in my head like that.

No, I don't think I'm mistaken. I mean, I look in the mirror every day, and it's right there. I know what I see. It's not something I'm just imagining. My hairline is receding in this really uneven way, and my face just... it looks wrong. I know people say it's fine, but they aren't the ones who have to live with it. I'm absolutely certain about how bad it looks.

No, not really. I mean, I definitely get frustrated with myself when I fall behind on my grading, but I wouldn't say I feel depressed. My mood is generally fine. It's really just the focus thing that's bothering me.

No, not really. I mean, I get a normal amount of tired if I stay up too late trying to catch up on grading, but I wouldn't say I'm unusually sleepy. I don't have trouble staying awake during the day or anything like that.

No, I wouldn't say it's because I'm worrying. I mean, I have normal stress with teaching and all, but my lack of focus isn't really driven by anxiety or stressing over things. It's more like my brain just... sort of drifts off to completely random thoughts, rather than getting stuck on something I'm worried about.

Yeah, it's definitely been more than two weeks. Like I was saying, it's pretty much every day. That heavy, gray feeling just stays with me, you know? It doesn't really matter if I'm at work, driving, or at home... it's just this constant hollow feeling that doesn't go away.

Yeah, definitely. It's... it's really messed things up for me lately. Ever since I lost the structure of my old job, my reputation has just taken a massive hit. I've been trying to do some freelance stuff, but I keep losing clients because I just can't seem to stay on top of things. And I even missed out on this senior service-manager role I was up for. People just don't trust me to follow through anymore, and it's putting a lot of stress on my wife and me because now we're worrying about money. 

Which is awful, because my wife, she's usually the one who handles the finances. She's got this whole system with color-coded spreadsheets. She actually learned how to do all that Excel programming—macros and pivot tables and whatever—from this online course she took during the pandemic. We were stuck in the house for months, and she just decided to learn spreadsheets. I tried to learn how to bake sourdough bread like everyone else was doing, but I kept forgetting to feed the starter. You have to feed it every day, like a pet, and it just got moldy and I had to throw the whole jar away. It was a nice jar, too, one of those thick glass ones with the wire clamp lid. We used to keep coffee beans in it. But yeah, the money stuff is really stressing us out right now.

Down or depressed? No, not really. I mean, I'm stressed about the money and the job stuff, obviously, but not depressed. I actually felt pretty good yesterday because I finally got around to cleaning out the garage. Well, part of the garage. I started with this old workbench that belonged to my grandfather. He was a carpenter, built these beautiful wooden boats up in Maine. Real craftsmanship, you know? Not like the cheap plywood stuff you buy at the big box stores today. I still have some of his old hand planes. They're heavy, solid iron, but they're covered in rust now. I watched this whole series of videos on YouTube about how to restore antique hand tools using electrolysis. It's fascinating, really, how you can just use a car battery charger and some washing soda to reverse the rust. I bought the washing soda—had to go to three different grocery stores to find it, actually. The first two only had baking soda, which isn't the same thing. But anyway, yeah, I'm not depressed, just... stressed, I guess.

Worrying? No, not really. I mean, I worry about the bills and stuff, like I said, but not just... out of nowhere. If there's no problem, I don't really sit around worrying about one. Actually, I usually try to keep busy. Like with the garage thing. Or... oh, last week I decided I was going to fix the leaky faucet in the downstairs bathroom. It’s been dripping for months. Drip, drip, drip. Drives my wife crazy. So I went to the hardware store—the big one out on Route 9, not the local one, because the local one never has the right size O-rings. And while I was there, I saw they had this massive sale on outdoor lighting. Solar-powered pathway lights. We don't even have a pathway in the backyard, just grass, but they looked so nice, like little copper lanterns. I ended up buying a dozen of them. Spent like two hours trying to figure out the best pattern to put them in the grass. I still haven't fixed the faucet, actually. I should probably do that. But no, I don't really worry about things unless there's a reason to.

Well, nice to meet you too. I came in because... well, it's the people at my apartment. I know they're watching my comings and goings. It's a big brick building, you know, built back in the 70s. My uncle actually used to do bricklaying on places like that. He helped build the old library downtown before they tore it down. Real shame they knocked it down, they had this whole section on old cars I used to look at. 

But anyway... yeah, they're watching me, and they keep slipping notes about me to the front office. I know they are. Everybody keeps telling me, oh, it's just regular notices on the doors, like for the water getting shut off or whatever, but I know what they're really doing. Like this one guy I saw on Tuesday... Tuesday is usually when I go get my groceries because the bus is less crowded, and I like to get those frozen meatloaf dinners, but... yeah, they're definitely slipping notes about me to the office.

Well, I wouldn't say high or energized. I don't really get like that. But depressed... yeah. Most mornings I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling, like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor. It's just this weight. My mattress doesn't help either, it's one of those old spring ones. I bought it at a discount place over on 4th Street, you know the one with the big yellow sign? The guy there told me it was firm, but I think he just wanted to make a sale. He had this little dog behind the counter, a terrier mix, I think. Reminded me of a dog I had when I was a kid, Buster. Buster used to chase the mail truck every single day... but yeah, I just feel so down and empty most days.

Yeah, actually... there was a spell a little while back. It lasted for several weeks, I think. I wasn't waking up feeling so hopeless, and I was actually eating a bit better. I had started making those big pots of chili again. My sister taught me how to make it—she puts just a little bit of cocoa powder in the pot. Sounds strange, I know, but it really deepens the flavor. She moved out to Ohio back in '08, right near Cleveland. I took a Greyhound bus out there once to visit, and let me tell you, those buses are not built for comfort. My knees were aching for days. The driver was this older fella who kept playing old Willie Nelson tapes the whole way... 

But, uh, what was I saying? Oh, right. Even during those weeks when my mood lifted and I was doing okay, I still knew the neighbors were watching my door. I still knew they were reporting on me. Feeling better didn't change the fact that they were out there doing that.

No, no major medical stuff, and I haven't bumped my head or anything like that. Well, I mean, I did scrape my elbow pretty bad last winter when I slipped on the ice outside the corner store. They never shovel that sidewalk right. The guy who runs it, Mr. Patel, he's always inside drinking tea out of this little thermos. It's one of those old plaid thermoses, the kind my dad used to take to the factory. Dad worked at the bottling plant for thirty years, stamping caps. He used to bring home these glass bottles that had misprints on the labels... but no, my head is fine. No medical problems like that.

Voices? No, I don't... I don't hear anything like that. Just the usual sounds around the apartment, you know? The radiator clanking. That thing makes a racket every time the heat kicks on. Sounds like somebody hitting a pipe with a wrench. My landlord, Gary, he keeps saying he's gonna bring a guy in to bleed the valves, but he never does. Gary's always too busy fixing up that old Chevy Nova he's got parked in the back alley. It's a '72, I think. Painted this awful mustard yellow color. He says he's gonna take it to car shows when it's done, but it's been sitting on blocks since before the pandemic. I told him he ought to just sell it for scrap, but he got real defensive about it. He's a sensitive guy, Gary. But no, no voices. Just the radiator and Gary's car radio when he's out there tinkering.

Well, let's see... it's been a while now. I'd say it's been about a year and a month since I really noticed them watching me and slipping those notes around the office and the apartment. A year and a month. That would mean it started right around the time the old bakery on the corner closed down. You know, they used to make these incredible bear claws. Huge things, bigger than your hand, with all this sliced almond on top and just drowning in glaze. The lady who ran it, Mrs. Gable, she was a sweetheart. Always gave me an extra one if I came in right before closing. She had this little poodle that used to sit behind the counter, wearing a little red sweater in the winter. The dog's name was Barnaby. But then her rent went up, and she had to pack it all in. Now it's one of those fancy coffee shops where they charge you five dollars for a cup of black coffee, and the chairs are all made of metal so you can't even sit comfortably. I went in there once and asked for a bear claw, and the kid behind the counter looked at me like I had two heads. He had this little mustache, you know, one of those ones that twirls up at the ends... but yeah, about a year and a month since I started noticing the neighbors doing all that.

Well, yeah, sometimes people do say that. Like, when I try to explain things, I'll start off talking about the rent, and then somehow I'm talking about the marina, and then the choir robes, and the wires in the walls, and people just look at me like I skipped half the story. It's like they can't keep up. The marina down by the lake, though, that place is really going downhill. Used to be you could rent a little aluminum rowboat for ten bucks for the whole afternoon. My buddy Dale and I used to go out there and fish for crappie. Dale had this tackle box that was older than I am, rusty green metal, and it always smelled like old bait and motor oil. He lost half his index finger in a table saw accident back in the eighties, but he could still tie a fishing knot faster than anyone I ever met. He moved down to Florida a few years back, lives in one of those retirement parks with the manufactured homes. Says the humidity is terrible for his arthritis, but he likes being near his grandkids. His oldest grandson plays the tuba in the high school marching band. Those uniforms they wear look so heavy, especially in the heat... but yeah, people do say I get off track and they can't follow what I'm saying sometimes.

Putting thoughts in? Taking them out? No, no, nobody's doing that. That sounds like something out of one of those old science fiction movies. You know, the ones they used to show on channel 11 on Saturday afternoons? "Creature Double Feature," they called it. The host was this guy in a cheap vampire cape who always held a rubber bat. I used to watch those with my brother, Tommy. Tommy was crazy about monsters. He had this whole collection of those plastic models you had to glue together and paint yourself. The Wolfman, Frankenstein, the Mummy. He spent hours getting the paint just right on the Mummy's bandages. Used a little toothpick to get the dirt in the cracks so it looked real. He kept them all on this shelf above his bed, and my mother hated dusting in there because she was afraid she'd knock one over and break it. Tommy ended up working at a hardware store out in Ohio. Sells lawnmowers and snowblowers now. He says the winters out there are brutal, not like here. They get lake-effect snow that buries the cars overnight. He had to buy a special heavy-duty shovel just to get to his driveway... but no, I don't have anybody messing with my thoughts like that. Just my own thoughts in there.

No, nobody's really said anything like that to me. My voice is just my voice, I guess. It's not like I'm trying to be an announcer or anything. I used to love listening to those old radio announcers, though. Late at night, you'd get those AM stations coming in from hundreds of miles away, guys with those really deep, smooth voices. I had this silver Panasonic radio with a telescoping antenna that got bent when my buddy Phil sat on it. Phil was a big guy, worked down at the freight yards. He used to bring home these heavy wooden pallets and break them down for firewood. We'd sit out back and have a fire, maybe roast some hot dogs. You can't beat a hot dog cooked over real wood, gets that nice char on the outside. We used those cheap buns, though, the ones that fall apart the second you put mustard on them. I always liked the spicy brown mustard, not that bright yellow stuff. The yellow stuff stains your shirts, and I ruined a perfectly good flannel that way once. Had a tear in the elbow anyway, but still... what were we talking about? Oh, right, my face and voice. No, no one's told me I'm less expressive or anything like that.

Well, they don't have special devices or anything crazy like that, but I know they're watching me. The people at my apartment building, I mean. I came in because I know they're keeping track of my comings and goings, always peeking out when I walk down the hall. And they're slipping notes about me to the front office. Everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices they tape to the doors, like for water shut-offs or pest control. They had the exterminator come out last month because the lady in 4B said she saw a roach. Big water bugs, really, not the German kind. The German ones are the ones that really infest a place, get into the appliances and everything. My uncle Ray had an apartment in Chicago back in the seventies that got so bad he had to throw out his toaster. He said you'd turn it on and it would smell like burnt hair. He ended up moving out to the suburbs after that, bought a little brick ranch house. Had a nice yard, too, planted a bunch of tomato plants along the fence. Beefsteaks, I think they were. You slice one of those thick, put a little salt and pepper on it, maybe some mayonnaise on white bread... best sandwich in the world. But yeah, those notes on the doors, I know they're really about me, no matter what anyone says.

Energetic? No, not really. I'm usually pretty tired, honestly. Never had a time where I didn't need sleep. Sleep's important, you know? My grandfather always used to say that an hour of sleep before midnight is worth two after. He worked the third shift at the bottling plant for thirty years, so he knew all about messing up his sleep schedule. He'd come home right when the sun was coming up, and my grandmother would have to pull these heavy, dark green curtains shut so he could get some rest. They were made of this really thick velvet material. She bought them at a discount store that used to be downtown, right next to the old movie theater. The theater got torn down back in the eighties to make room for a parking garage. It was a shame, too, because it had this beautiful marquee with all these flashing lightbulbs. They don't make signs like that anymore. Everything's digital now, just big screens everywhere you look. I saw a billboard the other day that changed pictures every ten seconds. It was advertising a car dealership, then a lawyer, then some kind of new energy drink. Those energy drinks can't be good for your heart, all that caffeine and sugar. I stick to coffee, mostly. Just black coffee. But anyway, no, I've never felt like I had too much energy or didn't need to sleep. I just feel worn out most of the time.

Six months? No, it's been longer than that. It's been about a year and a month now, dealing with them watching me and the notes and everything. I know exactly how long because it started right around the time the transmission went out on my old Buick. Just clunked out right in the middle of the intersection over by the hardware store. 

That hardware store's been there since I was a kid, you know. You go in there and it has that specific smell... like sawdust and fertilizer mixed together. They used to have this old golden retriever that just slept by the front door. You'd have to step right over him to get to the paint aisle. Paint's gotten so expensive lately, too. I was looking at a can of white semi-gloss a while back just to touch up the baseboards, and I couldn't believe the price. Used to be you could get a gallon for a few bucks. My dad was a house painter for a little while, back in the seventies. He always wore these white overalls that were just covered in every color imaginable. He looked like a modern art painting himself by the time he got home. He'd leave his boots on the porch so he wouldn't track it in... 

But, uh, yeah. To answer your question, it's been a year and a month since all this stuff with the neighbors started.

Well, yeah, I guess I have. I used to look forward to a lot of things, really. Choir practice on Wednesdays, playing bridge with the guys, even just cooking up a big pot of beans on Sunday... I used to do little repair jobs for folks around the building, too, fixing leaky faucets or patching drywall. But now, I just mostly let the phone ring. I tell myself there's no point in going or doing any of it. 

I used to be real handy, you know. I had this big red toolbox my brother gave me for my birthday one year. It had all these little compartments on top for screws and nails, kept everything sorted. Sorting things used to be real calming for me. I'd sit at the kitchen table and organize all my hardware by size. My brother, he moved out to Arizona about ten years ago. Said he couldn't take the winters here anymore. He bought a house out in the desert, said he doesn't even have to mow the lawn because it's all rocks and cactus. Sounds kind of nice, not having to worry about yard work. Mowers can be a real hassle when the carburetor gets gunked up. You gotta take the whole thing apart and soak it in carburetor cleaner... smells awful, that stuff. Gives you a headache if you don't do it in a well-ventilated area. But yeah, I just don't have the energy or the care for any of my old hobbies anymore. Just seems pointless.

Yeah, there was. There was a spell of several weeks, maybe a month or so ago, where I was actually eating a bit better. Woke up not feeling quite so... heavy and hopeless, you know? But I still knew they were watching my door. Still knew they were reporting on me. 

Speaking of doors, my front door has this squeak that just won't quit. It's the bottom hinge. I've tried WD-40, I've tried rubbing a bar of soap on it—my mom used to swear by that trick for squeaky floorboards. She had this old house with these original hardwood floors that groaned every time you took a step. It was impossible to sneak down to the kitchen for a midnight snack when I was a kid. She'd always catch me. She'd be sitting there in the dark, drinking a glass of warm milk. Said it helped her sleep. I never understood how people could drink warm milk, it just coats your throat in this weird way. But she liked it. She always had it in this chipped blue mug with a little white sailboat painted on it. I wonder whatever happened to that mug... probably got lost in the shuffle when we cleaned out her house. It's funny the things you hold onto and the things that just slip away. But yeah, even when I was feeling a bit more normal, eating alright and not so down, I still knew they had their eyes on me and were sending those notes.

Outside forces? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm the one moving my own arms and legs, you know? I do what I decide to do. 

Speaking of legs, though, my left knee has been acting up lately whenever it rains. Just aches right down to the bone. Reminds me of when I fell off the roof of my buddy Al's garage back in '88. We were trying to fix the shingles before a big storm rolled in. Black clouds just sitting over the whole neighborhood, looked like the end of the world. Al had this old Ford pickup truck parked in the driveway, a real beauty, cherry red. He used to spend every Saturday polishing that thing until you could see your reflection in the bumper. Chrome bumpers... they don't make 'em like that anymore. Now everything's just plastic and fiberglass on cars. If you get into a fender bender nowadays, the whole front end just crumbles like a soda can. Used to be you could just take a rubber mallet and pound a dent right out yourself. I had a really good rubber mallet, actually... heavy wooden handle. Left it in the trunk of that Buick I was telling you about earlier. Shame to lose a good tool.

Well, no, not really other things. It's just... I came in here because I know the people at my apartment are watching my comings and goings. They're slipping notes about me to the office. Everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices on the doors, like for pest control or whatever, but I know what they're really doing. 

Pest control, though... they came by a few months ago spraying for roaches. Used this stuff that smelled like burnt tires. Reminded me of when I worked at the junkyard for a bit, back in my twenties. We'd have these huge piles of tires, mountains of them. Sometimes in the summer, the heat would just bake the rubber and the smell would hang over the whole lot. We had this big guard dog there, a Rottweiler mix named Buster. Meanest looking dog you ever saw, but he was a total softie if you had a piece of beef jerky. I used to buy those long sticks of jerky from the gas station on the corner. The guy who ran the place, Sal, he always gave me a discount because I helped him fix his cash register once. It was one of those old mechanical ones with the heavy keys that make a real loud *cha-ching* sound. You don't hear that sound anymore. Now it's all just beeps and touchscreens. You can't even feel the buttons. I like to feel a button when I press it, you know? Makes you feel like you've actually done something. But yeah, everybody says it's just notices on the doors, but I know they're keeping track of me.

Well, yeah, sometimes I guess they do. Like, I'll be trying to explain something to somebody, and I start off talking about the rent being due, and then somehow I'm talking about the marina down by the lake, and then the old choir robes from church, and then the wires they put in the walls... and people just look at me like I skipped half the story. 

Speaking of the marina, I used to go down there and just watch the boats come in. There was this one guy, Captain Dan they called him, he had a pontoon boat that he rigged up with a grill right on the deck. He'd be out there flipping burgers while he was steering. Smelled so good, especially on a Tuesday afternoon when it wasn't too crowded. Tuesdays are always the best day to go to the grocery store, too. They restock the shelves on Monday nights, so everything is fresh. I always get the iceberg lettuce because it stays crunchy longer than that leafy green stuff. You ever try to make a sandwich with soggy lettuce? Ruins the whole thing. A good sandwich needs a firm foundation. My grandma used to make the best sandwiches, always on rye bread with a thick slice of tomato from her garden. She had these huge tomato plants, practically trees. She used to tie them up with old strips of pantyhose to keep them from falling over. Pantyhose are surprisingly strong, you know. But yeah, people look at me like I'm not making sense when I try to explain things.

Hear my thoughts? No, I don't think anyone can do that. I mean, they're inside my head, behind the bone, you know? Unless they've got some kind of machine, but I haven't seen anything like that. 

Machines are getting pretty crazy these days, though. I saw this thing on the TV the other day, a commercial for a refrigerator that tells you when you're out of milk. Now, why do I need a refrigerator to tell me that? I just open the door and look. It's got a whole screen on the front of it, like a computer. Computers are everywhere now. I remember when they first started putting them in the library downtown. Big clunky things with green letters on the screen. The librarian, Mrs. Gable, she hated them. She said they ruined the quiet. She was a real stickler for quiet. If you even coughed too loud, she'd give you this look over her glasses that would freeze you right in your tracks. She wore those glasses on a little chain around her neck, pearl chain. My aunt had a chain like that for her glasses, but hers was gold. Real gold, she said, but I think it was just plated because it started turning green after a few years. Turned her neck green, too, right where it rested. She used to scrub it with a washcloth and some of that harsh orange soap they use in garages. Smells like citrus, but it's got grit in it. Good for getting grease off your hands if you've been working on an engine. I haven't worked on an engine in years, though. But no, nobody's listening to what's in my head.

Stop in the middle? No, I don't think my mind just stops like that. I usually just keep going until I'm done saying what I need to say. 

Speaking of stopping, though, the brakes on my old Ford used to do that. Just lock right up if you hit 'em too hard. I had this '82 pickup, powder blue, rust around the wheel wells. I used to drive it down to the hardware store on Saturday mornings. The guy there, Earl, he always had a pot of coffee going in the back room. Strong stuff, tasted like it had been sitting there since Tuesday. But he'd pour you a cup in one of those styrofoam cups if you bought something. Styrofoam is terrible for the environment, you know. They say it takes a million years to break down in a landfill. Just sits there, taking up space. Kind of like those old encyclopedias I have in my closet. A whole set, A to Z, from 1995. Bought them from a door-to-door salesman. You don't see door-to-door salesmen anymore. Used to be guys selling vacuums, brushes, encyclopedias. He had this nice suit on, but his shoes were scuffed up real bad. You can always tell a lot about a man by his shoes. My dad always said, "Keep your shoes shined and your watch wound." He had this old pocket watch, silver, with a train engraved on the front. It ticked so loud you could hear it across the room. Tick, tick, tick... very steady. But no, my mind doesn't just stop in the middle of a sentence.

Well, yeah, it’s gotten pretty bad. I’ve fallen way behind on my bills, and I keep missing my appointments. I even stopped showing up for church and the volunteering I used to do because I just can't keep my days organized anymore, and I don't really trust talking to people right now. 

Speaking of bills, the electric company sent me a letter on this pink paper last week. Why pink? It used to be white with a little red stamp, but now it’s this bright pink. Reminds me of the cotton candy they used to sell at the county fair. We used to go every August when the weather was so hot you could fry an egg on the sidewalk. They had this guy who would spin the sugar right in front of you, huge clouds of it on a paper cone. I always got the blue kind, tastes like blue raspberry. Raspberries are hard to grow, though. The bushes get all thorny and tangled if you don't prune them back in the late winter. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he tried growing them along the fence line, but the birds got to them before they ever ripened. He put up this fake owl to scare them away, plastic thing with big yellow eyes. It worked for a week, and then the crows just started sitting right on its head. Crows are smart birds, they figure things out quick. They like shiny things, too. I read once they collect bottle caps and bits of foil for their nests. Foil is getting thinner these days, you notice that? You try to wrap a baked potato and it just tears right down the middle. But yeah, I can't really manage my days or the bills or any of that stuff lately.

Well, I came in because things have been pretty stressful lately. Ever since my father-in-law moved in with us, I just haven't quite been myself. 

I mean, I’m holding it together at work fine, but at home and with my coursework, I’m just... I'm a lot more wound up and short-tempered than I’m used to being. And I've noticed I've started skipping the things that usually keep my head clear. I haven't been fishing, haven't touched my woodworking, and I even stopped going to the first-aid workshops I usually like. I just figured I should probably talk to someone to get a handle on it.

Yeah, it really did. He moved in about four months ago, and I'd say I started noticing the strain within the first couple of months. It just took a little bit of time for the new home routines and the caregiving demands to really settle in, and once they did, that's when the stress started catching up with me.

No, not really. I wouldn't say I feel depressed or down. It's more just... feeling tense and on edge all the time, you know? Like my patience is just wearing thin, but I don't feel sad or anything like that.

No, not really. It's pretty much just focused on the situation at home. I mean, I don't sit around worrying about my job or bills or anything like that more than I usually would. It's really just the new routine and the extra demands with my father-in-law that are keeping me so on edge.

Well, my regular EMT work is going fine, I'm still doing all my shifts. But... yeah, I have fallen behind on some of my paramedic coursework. It's just hard to find the time and focus right now. And I've also stopped showing up consistently for the community first-aid workshops I usually help out with. I've just kind of had to drop the ball on that extra stuff to keep my head above water at home.

I mean, I don't know if it's stronger than normal. It's a lot to deal with, having him move in and need so much help. I think anyone would be stressed out by it. I don't really have a baseline for what's normal to feel right now, it's just... it's just hard.

I wouldn't say it's caused serious problems with my marriage or anything like that. We're both just really tired. Like I mentioned a minute ago, the main issue is really just how it's affecting my extra responsibilities. I'm still getting to my regular EMT shifts fine, but... yeah, I've fallen behind on my paramedic classes and had to stop going to those community first-aid workshops. I just don't have the bandwidth for much else outside of work and helping out at home right now.

I mean, I think I just answered that, but... no, I don't think it's out of proportion. Like I said, it's a lot to take on, having him move in and need all this care. I think most people would be pretty stressed out trying to juggle all of this. It just makes sense that I'm feeling this way.

Hi. It's nice to meet you too. 

Well, I'm here because I've realized I keep arranging my own house around not seeing spiders. It's getting to be too much. I put off doing laundry because the machines are in the basement, and I completely avoid the garden shed. I'm even paying people to do small jobs around the house that I know perfectly well how to do myself, simply because I can't make myself go into those spaces.

Yes, exactly. I mean, logically, I know a spider hanging out in the corner of an old house probably isn’t going to actually hurt me. But... the moment I even just picture one dropping out of a storage box, or sitting there near the washer, it just feels enormous. It becomes this incredibly threatening thing in a way that I’m honestly pretty embarrassed to admit.

Yes, absolutely. If I actually spot one, my chest tightens up right away. My hands start shaking, and I just... I either completely freeze in the doorway or I back out of the room so fast. It's almost like my body has decided to run away before my brain even has time to process what's happening.

Hi. Well, I guess what brings me in is that my head just feels kind of foggy lately. I've been making these little mistakes in my client notes at work, or, uh, just forgetting what I was about to do right in the middle of doing it. It really isn't like me to be this scattered, so I figured I should come see someone.
Yeah, actually. My uncle died about two weeks ago, and that's really when I noticed this whole shift starting.

Yeah, I have. Lately I just wake up with this... heavy, empty feeling right in my chest. I mean, I can still get through my shift and talk to my clients and everything, but inside, I'm just feeling really sad and... flat, I guess.

Not really, no. I still like doing my usual stuff when I get off work. I still watch my shows and, you know, tinker around the house. It's just... I guess I just have that sad feeling in the background while I'm doing it. But I wouldn't say I've lost interest in them.
No, not really. I mean, I'm sad about my uncle, obviously, but I'm not feeling extra anxious or worried about anything in particular. Just... just the sadness, mostly.

Yeah, actually, I have. My head just feels kind of... foggy lately. I've been making these little mistakes in my client notes at work, or I'll just completely forget what I was about to do right after I thought of it. It's really not like me to do that.

Drinking? No, no, I don't... I mean, I have a couple beers on the weekend, maybe, but I'm not some kind of drunk. I don't get the shakes or anything like that. Sick? No. Hit my head? No, nothing like that. I've got a thick skull anyway, but I always wear my hard hat on the floor. You have to. OSHA is always breathing down our necks about PPE these days. We had this one inspector come through a while back, guy with a clipboard who probably never held an angle grinder in his life, trying to tell us our welding curtains were two inches too high off the floor. I mean, come on. 

You ever do any TIG welding? It's an art. It's all about puddle control. Especially with aluminum. Aluminum is tricky because it doesn't change color before it melts, it just drops right out on you if you aren't paying attention. You gotta really watch it. My buddy Dave, he was a master at it. Best welder I ever saw. He retired down to Florida a couple years ago, actually. Bought himself a little pontoon boat, just fishes for snapper all day... 

But anyway, no, my brain is fine. No medical problems at all. I'm perfectly healthy. That's why I know I'm not making this up. My head is clear, and I know for a fact he's coming in here messing with my stuff.

Voices? Like, hearing things? No, no, I don't hear anything like that. Just the normal sounds of the house, you know? The pipes clanking, the fridge humming.
