They built things to last back then, not like the junk they sell now with all the computer chips in them. My neighbor, Frank, he bought one of those smart fridges last year, and the screen on the front went out after three months. Three months! You can't even get a glass of water out of the door without the thing freezing up on you. I told him he should have just bought a basic model, but he's always got to have the newest gadget. He's got this riding mower, too, zero-turn radius, cost him a fortune... 

But no, no voices. Just him sneaking around when I'm not looking. He's quiet about it, I'll give him that, but he's definitely coming in here.

It's been about nine months. Yeah, going on nine months now, ever since my wife's relative moved into our home. He had some money trouble or something, so she told him he could take the spare room. Brought so much junk with him, too. Just boxes and boxes. I had to help him carry this heavy oak dresser up the stairs. Real solid wood, not that cheap particle board crap you get at IKEA. I can't stand that stuff. You drive one screw into it and the whole thing just crumbles like a stale cookie. 

If you're gonna build furniture, you should use real fasteners, maybe some dowels and wood glue, or at least a decent cam lock system. I actually built our kitchen table myself out of reclaimed maple. Welded the base out of two-inch square steel tubing, powder-coated it flat black. It's a beautiful piece of work. Weighs an absolute ton, though. You aren't sliding that thing across the linoleum without a buddy. My wife wanted to put a tablecloth over it, but I told her, why cover up the wood? Maple has such a nice, tight grain, it's a shame to hide it. We had to go to three different lumber yards just to find boards that weren't warped. 

But yeah, nine months. Right when he moved into the house, that's exactly when all this started.

Hard to follow? No, nobody says that. I mean, my wife says I talk too much sometimes, but she's always saying stuff like that. She's got this habit of half-listening when she's watching her shows. You know those renovation shows on TV? Where they take a perfectly good house and just gut it for no reason? They always tear down load-bearing walls without even putting up proper temporary supports. It drives me crazy. I saw one episode where this guy, some designer with a scarf indoors, wanted to remove a whole structural column just to make the kitchen "flow" better into the living room. You can't just do that! The roof load has to go somewhere. You need a massive steel I-beam if you're gonna span that kind of distance, and even then, you gotta make sure the footings in the foundation can handle the point load. 

I actually helped pour a foundation for my brother-in-law's garage a few years back. Not the relative living with us, different guy. We ordered two trucks of ready-mix, 4000 PSI, and it was a hot day, so we had to work fast before it set up on us. We were screeding that concrete for hours. My back was killing me for a week. But we got it perfectly level. You drop a marble in the corner of that garage, it doesn't roll an inch. That's how you do a job right. 

So, no, I don't go off track. I just explain things thoroughly. People just don't have the attention span for details anymore.

Caring less? No, I still care about things just fine. I care about my job, I care about doing things right. Like at the shop, I'm the only one who actually checks the tolerances on the sheet metal before we start bending it. You get a batch of 14-gauge steel from the supplier, and sometimes it's rolling in at, like, .083 inches instead of .074. If you don't adjust the brake press for that, your angles are gonna be all out of whack. I tried telling the new kid that last week. He just started, straight out of high school, nice enough kid, but he's got his face in his phone half the day. I told him, you gotta measure twice, bend once. It's not like woodworking where you can just sand it down if you mess up. Metal is unforgiving. 

I remember when I first started fabricating, back in the nineties. We didn't have these fancy CNC machines doing all the work for us. You had to lay everything out by hand with a scribe and a combination square. It took real skill. I made this custom exhaust manifold for my old Chevy truck using just a manual tube bender and a TIG welder. Took me three weekends, but the welds were like a stack of dimes, just beautiful. I sold that truck to a guy two towns over, and I still see it driving around sometimes. Sounds incredible. 

But yeah, no, I still care about things. I just want people to leave me alone, mostly. That relative of hers, though, he definitely doesn't care about personal boundaries, I'll tell you that.

No, it's just him. Just her relative. Nobody else is bothering me. I mean, I don't really talk to a lot of people outside of work anyway, so who would even bother? Most people just mind their own business. Like my neighbor, Dave. Dave's a good guy. Keeps his lawn immaculate. He's got one of those zero-turn mowers, a Toro, I think. Real nice machine. Dual hydrostatic transmission, so you can spin on a dime. I was looking into getting one myself, but my yard isn't really big enough to justify the cost. Plus, I kind of like walking behind my old Honda mower. It's got that twin-blade system, cuts the grass into tiny little pieces so it mulches right back into the soil. You don't even have to bag it. 

I actually rebuilt the carburetor on that Honda last spring. Ethanol gas just destroys those small engines if you let it sit over the winter. Gums up the jets something awful. You gotta pull the bowl off, soak the whole thing in carb cleaner, and blow out the passages with compressed air. I've got a 30-gallon air compressor in the garage, a two-stage upright. Runs on 220 volts. I had to wire a dedicated circuit for it myself. Ran 10-gauge wire all the way from the main breaker panel through conduit. You don't want to mess around with electrical work, you gotta make sure your connections are tight and you're using the right size breaker, otherwise you're just asking for an electrical fire. 

But yeah, nobody else is spying on me or anything. It's just him sneaking around.

Impossible? Like, magic or something? No, no, nothing like that. He's just a regular guy, just... sneaky. Sneaky and disrespectful. It's all real-world stuff, you know? Like going through my things or moving my tools. Speaking of tools, I was looking for my 10-millimeter socket the other day. It's always the 10-millimeter that goes missing, isn't it? Every mechanic I know says the same thing. You buy a whole set, and within a week, the 10-millimeter is gone. I think I left it under the hood of my wife's sedan when I was changing the battery terminals. 

Those factory terminals are garbage, just stamped steel. They corrode so fast. I cut them off and crimped on some solid brass marine-grade terminals. Much better connection. You gotta use a proper hydraulic crimper for that, though. You can't just smash it with a hammer or use those cheap wire strippers. A bad crimp means high resistance, and high resistance means heat. Next thing you know, your alternator is working overtime trying to charge the battery, and you're stranded in a parking lot. 

I helped a guy jump his car at the grocery store last month. He had these cheap jumper cables, like 10-gauge wire at best. The insulation was melting right off them before the car even turned over. I told him, you need at least 4-gauge copper for a proper jump, especially on a V8. I keep a set of custom-made 2-gauge cables in my trunk. Made them myself with welding lead. They'll start a diesel tractor in the dead of winter. 

But no, he hasn't done anything impossible. He's just a nuisance, a very real nuisance.

Flat? No, nobody's ever told me that. I mean, my face is just my face, you know? I talk normal. 

But you know what actually *is* flat? A Grade AA granite surface plate. We have this massive one at the shop, weighs about eight hundred pounds. Sits on a special heavy-duty steel stand with leveling feet. It's calibrated to within, like, fifty millionths of an inch. You take a precision gauge block and slide it on there, and the two surfaces are so perfectly flat they just wring together. It feels like they're magnetized, but it's really just the air getting pushed out and atmospheric pressure holding them tight. It's incredible. 

I was trying to explain that to the new kid last week, how you use it to check if a machined part is warped. But like I said, he doesn't really appreciate the science of it. You really need a good dial test indicator to measure runout on a plate like that anyway. I've got a Starrett indicator in my toolbox, ruby tip, made right here in America. Cost me a pretty penny, but you absolutely cannot trust those cheap imported knockoffs. They'll lose calibration if you just look at them funny, and then your measurements are garbage for the rest of the day. You drop one of those cheap ones, you might as well throw it in the scrap bin. 

But yeah, no, my voice isn't flat. I just talk how I talk. Nobody's complained about it.

Hard to follow? No, I don't think so. I mean, my wife says I talk too much about work, but nobody else says I'm hard to follow. I explain things pretty clearly, I think. You just have to pay attention to the details. 

Details are everything, especially in fabrication. Like when you're TIG welding aluminum. A lot of guys can't do it because they don't pay attention to the details. They don't prep the metal right. You can't just take a wire brush to it and start welding. Aluminum has an oxide layer that melts at a way higher temperature than the base metal, so if you don't clean it with acetone and use a dedicated stainless steel brush—one you've *never* used on carbon steel, mind you—you're just going to push contaminants right into the weld pool. 

And you gotta use alternating current on the machine. AC is what actually breaks up that oxide layer while you're welding. The positive half of the cycle cleans the metal, and the negative half penetrates. Most modern inverter machines let you adjust the AC balance, so you can dial in exactly how much cleaning action versus penetration you want. I usually run mine at about 70 percent EN—electrode negative—but it depends on how thick the material is. 

I was welding up a custom intake manifold for a buddy's drag car a few years back. Beautiful piece of work. Used 6061-T6 aluminum tubing, mandrel bent. You gotta back-purge the tubes with argon when you weld them, otherwise you get this nasty sugaring on the inside of the weld, and that disrupts the airflow. And in a drag car, airflow is horsepower. He ended up shaving two-tenths off his quarter-mile time with that manifold. 

But yeah, nobody says I'm hard to follow. I just like to make sure people understand how things actually work.

Hi, yes, nice to meet you too. Thank you so much for fitting me in. 

Well, as to what brings me in... it's a bit embarrassing to admit at my age, honestly. I'm sixty, and I've been a high school teacher for decades—mostly history, some government classes—so you would really think I'd have mastered the art of sitting through a long meeting by now. But I just... I keep getting up. That's the main thing. I keep getting up in situations where everyone else is perfectly content being seated, and it's starting to become a real issue for me. 

Like, if I'm in a faculty meeting, everyone else is just sitting there, listening to the principal or taking notes, but I will suddenly feel like I absolutely have to stand. I'll make up little excuses to myself, you know? I'll think, "Oh, I need to refill my coffee right now," even if my cup is still half full, or I'll get up to check a stack of handouts on the back table, or I'll just walk to the back of the room and stand by the door, even though nothing is really urgent at all. 

And it’s not just at school, it’s in my personal life too. At dinner! My husband and I will be eating, maybe we even have friends over for a nice meal, and everyone is sitting and chatting, but I'll just pop up out of my chair. I'll go check the oven, or look for a different serving spoon, or just stand by the kitchen island for a few minutes. My husband actually joked the other night that I’m like a jack-in-the-box, which, well, it made me laugh at first, but then it made me realize how much I'm actually doing it. It makes other people feel rushed or distracted, I think. I just can't seem to stay planted in my seat when I'm supposed to, and I really don't understand why I can't just sit through a meal or a meeting like a normal adult. So, that's why I'm here.

No, no, it's not like that. I don't have any sort of physical ache or tingling or anything creepy-crawly like that. My legs themselves feel completely fine. There's no pain, no discomfort in the muscles or the joints or anything of that nature. It's more just... well, it's this overwhelming sense that I shouldn't be sitting anymore. Like the chair is suddenly just the wrong place to be. 

I'll just be sitting there, and my legs are perfectly comfortable, but my brain is just saying, "Okay, time to get up now, let's go." It's almost like a spring uncoiling, but not in a physical or painful way, if that makes sense? Just a sudden, absolute necessity to be vertical. Like yesterday, I was grading papers at the kitchen table—just AP History essays, which take forever, honestly, because the kids write these sprawling paragraphs and you really have to focus to follow their arguments—and my legs were totally fine, just resting on the rung of the stool. But I just had to stand up. I ended up taking the whole stack of rubrics and papers over to the island to grade standing up for the next twenty minutes. 

I didn't feel any physical relief in my legs when I stood, because they didn't hurt or feel restless to begin with, but I just felt... better, overall, being up. Like I was finally doing what I was supposed to be doing. So, no, definitely no uncomfortable feeling in my legs specifically. It's not a physical ache at all.

Well, no, I wouldn't say it's about refocusing, exactly. It's not like I'm sitting there and my mind is drifting off to, oh, I don't know, what I'm going to make for dinner or my grocery list or wondering if I left the porch light on. I mean, sure, everyone's mind wanders a bit, especially during those long professional development days where they bring in some consultant who hasn't been in a classroom since 1995 to tell us how to engage teenagers. But it's not that I'm losing my train of thought and standing up brings it back. 

It's actually almost the opposite? Like, I can be completely focused on what's happening. I could be totally engrossed in a student's presentation on the Industrial Revolution, or right in the middle of a really good conversation with my husband about our weekend plans, and I still just have to get up. My brain is right there in the moment, fully engaged, but my body just... rebels against the chair. 

I remember last week, we had a faculty meeting about the new grading software, which, let me tell you, is a nightmare to navigate, but I was actually really trying to pay attention because I needed to know how to input my midterm grades. I was taking notes, I was following along on my laptop, I was completely dialed in. And yet, I still found myself standing up and migrating to the back of the library. I didn't stand up to concentrate better on the software demonstration; I just stood up because I couldn't sit anymore. And honestly, sometimes getting up actually distracts me more because then I have to think of a reason why I'm standing, like pretending to look at the bulletin board, instead of just focusing on the meeting. So, no, I don't think it's a matter of my mind wandering and needing to reset my focus. It's just... the sitting itself that I can't seem to tolerate for very long.

Well, an inner restlessness... I suppose that's one way to put it, though I'm not entirely sure if "restlessness" captures the whole picture, or maybe it captures it too perfectly? It's hard to explain without sounding a bit dramatic. But yes, I suppose there is this... this buzzing feeling inside. It’s not physical, like I said about my legs, but it's like my engine is just idling too high. 

I remember trying to explain this to my sister once—she’s a retired librarian, very calm, very sedate, could sit in a wingback chair with a cup of tea for six hours straight and not twitch once. I told her it feels like I have a motor running inside me that I can’t quite shut off. Even when I’m sitting, even when I’m perfectly comfortable, there’s this low-level hum of energy that just builds and builds. It’s like when you’re waiting for water to boil, and you see those little bubbles starting at the bottom of the pot, and you know it’s about to roil over. That’s what it feels like inside my chest or my head, just this constant, low-grade need for motion. 

It’s exhausting sometimes, to be honest. Like last weekend, I was sitting on the patio, beautiful weather, a lovely breeze, reading a biography of Eleanor Roosevelt—fascinating woman, really, the amount of energy she had was astounding—and I should have been perfectly relaxed. But inside, I just felt this... this tightness. This urge to do something, anything, other than just sit there. I ended up getting up to deadhead the petunias, then I swept the porch, then I went inside to reorganize the Tupperware drawer, all because I couldn't just sit with that feeling. So, yes, I suppose "inner restlessness" is a good way to describe it, though it feels more like an internal pressure that just demands I get moving.

No, no, definitely not. It's not a happy feeling at all. I wouldn't call it euphoric or upbeat in the slightest. It's actually quite the opposite, really. It's more of an annoyance, a frustration that I can't just be still like everyone else seems to be able to do. 

I mean, when I'm up and moving because of that internal pressure, I'm not doing it with a spring in my step or a song in my heart. I'm not whistling while I work, like some cheerful cartoon character. Take that time I was reorganizing the Tupperware drawer—I wasn't thrilled to be doing it. I was actually quite irritated because I *wanted* to be sitting on the patio reading about Eleanor Roosevelt. I *wanted* to be relaxing. But I was practically throwing the plastic lids around because I was just so aggravated by this need to be doing something. 

My husband, bless him, sometimes he’ll see me pacing around the living room during a movie—we were trying to watch that new historical drama on PBS last night, beautifully costumed, really quite stunning, but I couldn't stay on the sofa for more than twenty minutes—and he'll ask if I'm excited about something. And I have to tell him, no, I'm not excited, I'm just... compelled. It's not a joyful energy. It's just a relentless one. So, no, there's no euphoria involved at all. Just a lot of sighing and wishing I could just sit still and enjoy a quiet moment without my body deciding it's time to run a marathon.

Anxious? Well... I suppose it depends on how you define anxious, doesn't it? I mean, I'm not sitting there worrying about, oh, whether I left the stove on, or if my students are going to fail their state exams—though, frankly, with the way the curriculum is structured these days, that's a valid concern for any teacher. But it's not a fearful anxiety. It's not like my heart is pounding because I'm scared of something or because I'm having a panic attack. I've had colleagues who get panic attacks, and it sounds just awful, but this isn't that.

But, on the other hand, if you mean anxious as in... keyed up, or agitated? Then maybe yes. Because when I can't get up, when I'm forced to just sit there and endure that buzzing feeling I told you about, I do start to feel a bit frantic. Like, I remember being at my niece's graduation ceremony last spring. Oh, it was lovely, she looked beautiful, valedictorian and everything, but the ceremony was *three hours long*. Three hours! Sitting on those hard metal folding chairs in a stuffy gymnasium. And by the second hour, when they were only halfway through the M's, I was practically crawling out of my skin. I wasn't worried or scared, but I was so incredibly tense and agitated that I felt like I was going to scream if I couldn't stand up and stretch my legs. I kept crossing and uncrossing my ankles, shifting my weight, checking my watch every two minutes. 

My sister kept giving me these side-eyes, you know the look, the "stop fidgeting, you're embarrassing me" look. And that made me feel a little stressed, I suppose, because I knew I was being disruptive, but I just couldn't help it. The longer I had to suppress the urge to move, the more unbearable it became. So, it's not a psychological anxiety, where my mind is racing with worries. It's more of a physical distress, a desperate need for release. I don't know if that's what you mean by anxious, but that's the closest I can get to describing it. It's just this overwhelming, physical imperative to move, and when I can't, it's sheer torture.

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't started any new medications recently, nor have I changed the dose of anything I'm currently taking. I mean, I take a daily multivitamin, and calcium for my bones—you know, at my age, you really have to start thinking about osteoporosis, especially since my mother had it quite terribly in her later years, shrinking down to practically nothing, poor thing. And I take a little something for my blood pressure, just a very low dose that Dr. Evans prescribed about five years ago, but that's been perfectly stable. 

I haven't tweaked a thing. I'm very particular about following instructions when it comes to medications. I have one of those little pill organizers, the ones with the days of the week printed on them in big letters? Sunday through Saturday. I keep it right next to the coffee maker so I don't forget. So, no, it's definitely not a medication issue. This feeling, this... constant motor running, it's not a new development tied to a pill. It's just... well, it's just how I've been. It's not a side effect of anything I'm swallowing in the morning with my orange juice, I can assure you of that.

Less sleep? Oh, no, not at all. I mean, I certainly wouldn't say I *need* less sleep. If anything, I wish I could get more of it! I still aim for my solid eight hours every single night. I'm quite disciplined about it, really. I try to be in bed by 10:00 PM, lights out by 10:30 PM after I've read a chapter or two of whatever biography I'm currently absorbed in—right now it's a fascinating one on Abigail Adams, she really was quite ahead of her time, you know. 

But my sleep hasn't changed. I still feel tired at the end of the day, just like anyone else. Teaching teenagers all day takes it out of you, let me tell you! By the time I've graded the last essay and prepped the lesson plan for the next morning, I am more than ready to put my head on the pillow. It's not like I'm staying up until three in the morning scrubbing the baseboards or feeling like I could run a marathon. I don't have that kind of... limitless energy where I just don't feel the need to rest. 

Now, actually *falling* asleep, well, sometimes that takes a minute because my mind might still be going over the events of the day, or I might be tossing and turning a bit because my legs feel restless—like they haven't gotten the memo that it's time to power down. But the *need* for sleep? Oh, yes, that is very much still there. If I don't get my eight hours, I am absolutely dragging the next day in the classroom, and you simply cannot be sluggish when you're trying to explain the intricacies of the American Revolution to thirty 11th graders. They will eat you alive! So, no, my sleep requirements haven't decreased in the slightest. I need every minute of rest I can get.

Disorganized? Hard to follow? Well... I don't think so. I mean, certainly not in a way that anyone has ever felt the need to point out to me as a problem. As a teacher, you have to be organized in your speech, don't you? You have to be able to lay out a lesson plan clearly—first we discuss the causes, then the major battles, then the aftermath. If you're disorganized, the students just check out immediately. They'll start looking at their phones under the desks, or staring out the window, and you've lost them entirely. 

Now, do I sometimes go off on a tangent? Oh, absolutely. I'll be talking about the Boston Tea Party, and then suddenly I'm reminded of this fascinating article I read about the history of tea smuggling in the 18th century, and how it impacted the East India Company, and before I know it, I've spent five minutes talking about maritime trade routes instead of the Sons of Liberty. But I always bring it back around! It's just... I get enthusiastic, you know? There's so much interesting context, and I want them to see the whole picture, not just memorize a list of dates. 

My husband, Arthur—bless him—he sometimes jokes that I take the scenic route when I'm telling a story. Like the other day, I was trying to tell him about a disagreement two of my colleagues were having in the staff room over the new grading policy, and I started explaining the background of the policy, and then how the principal introduced it at the last faculty meeting, and what she was wearing—she had this awful mustard yellow scarf on, I don't know who told her that was her color—and Arthur just sort of chuckled and said, "Darling, I think we've lost the plot." But he was just teasing. It wasn't that I wasn't making sense, I was just giving him all the details! 

So, no, no one has ever told me my speech is actually disorganized or impossible to follow. I might talk a lot, and I might weave a few different threads together, but it all makes sense in the end. I'm not speaking gibberish or jumping from one completely unrelated thought to another without any connection. It's just a very... detailed way of communicating, I suppose.

An outside force? Oh, heavens, no. Nothing like that. It's not as though I'm being puppeted on strings or... or possessed by some sort of spirit, if that's what you're asking! It's entirely me. It's completely internal. 

It's just this... this build-up of energy, I suppose you could say. It comes from right inside my own bones. Like just last week, we had this dreadful professional development seminar—two solid hours on the new standardized testing protocols, and they had us sitting in those awful, rigid plastic folding chairs in the gymnasium. You know the ones, they absolutely murder your lower back. And about forty-five minutes in, my legs just started to feel... fizzy. That's really the best word for it. Fizzy, like there was carbonation right under my skin. 

And my own brain was just telling me, "You need to stand up, you need to stretch your calves right this very second or you are going to simply burst." It's my own body demanding it. There's no mysterious entity pulling the levers or forcing me out of the chair, it's just my own absolute inability to stay glued to a seat for hours on end without getting terribly uncomfortable. 

I mean, even at home, Arthur and I were watching a documentary on the Apollo missions the other night—fascinating stuff, really, the engineering involved is just staggering when you think about the technology they had in the sixties—and even in my own perfectly comfortable recliner in my own living room, I eventually had to get up and pace behind the sofa for a bit while we watched. Arthur didn't mind, he's used to it by now, but it was just me wanting to move. Not some invisible hand pushing me up. So, no, definitely no outside forces at work here. Just my own restless self.

I came in because... well, I've been having this issue with eating. When I'm alone at night, once I start, it just feels like something takes over. I can't stop. Even when I'm literally telling myself in my head to put the food away, I just keep going.

Yeah, I do. Especially on nights after I work a late shift. I'll eat... well, things like a whole frozen pizza, then cereal straight out of the box, whatever leftovers are in the fridge, and just any snacks I can find in the cabinet. It all happens within maybe an hour or two. It's definitely way more food than I'd ever eat in front of anyone else.

Yeah, I do. After I eat like that, I usually end up in the bathroom making myself throw up. It just... it feels like the only way to undo it, you know? Like I have to get it out before the calories actually settle in.

I'd say... for at least the last four months, it's been happening about once a week. There is usually at least one night each week where I'm alone, I end up eating way more than I ever meant to, and then I make myself throw up afterward.

So, yes, every single day since the school job ended, it's just been this steady building of... well, of nothing. Just the same empty flat feeling, from the minute I open my eyes till the minute I close them.

No, no breaks. Not a single one, doctor. Not a week, not a month, certainly not a couple of months. Like I was saying, it just started and it stayed. I keep thinking back to last spring, when the daffodils came up. I planted those bulbs myself, oh, must have been ten years ago now, the yellow ones with the orange centers, right along the front walkway where the sun hits them in the afternoon. And usually, when they pop up, I get a little thrill, you know? I'd go out with my shears and cut a few for a vase on the kitchen table. But last spring, they bloomed, and they looked just as pretty as ever, but I just looked at them through the glass and didn't feel a thing. I didn't even go outside to smell them. And then the summer came, and the heat set in, the kind of heat that makes the tar on the street soft, and I still just sat there in the air conditioning. And then autumn... well, you get the picture. There hasn't been a time where I woke up and thought, "Oh, I feel like myself again today! I think I'll bake a pie or call my friend Shirley." It's just been one long, unbroken stretch of this... this flatness, ever since the retirement. It's like a gray blanket got thrown over everything and nobody ever came to pull it off.

Sleep? Oh, no, doctor, no trouble with that at all. In fact, sleeping is about the only thing I do seem to have any real talent for these days. It's funny you ask, because my neighbor, Mrs. Gable—she lives in the blue house next door, the one with the overgrown rhododendrons that keep scraping against my gutters—she's always complaining about her insomnia. She tells me she's up at two, three in the morning, pacing the floor, drinking warm milk, watching those infomercials where they try to sell you a blender that can chop up a whole pineapple. She says her mind just races. 

But me? I don't have that problem. Like I said, my mind doesn't race, it just sort of... sits there. So when it gets dark, usually right after the evening news with David Muir—I've always liked him, he has such a kind face, though I miss Peter Jennings, he had that wonderful voice—anyway, right after the news, I just turn off the television and go to bed. And I fall asleep right away. My head hits the pillow, that goose-down pillow I've had for years, probably should replace it but it's just got the right squish to it, you know? And I'm out. 

I sleep all through the night. I don't wake up to use the restroom, I don't wake up because I'm hot or cold, I just sleep a solid eight, sometimes nine hours. And then I wake up, and there's that flat feeling again, waiting for me like an old dog at the foot of the bed. So, no, my sleep is perfectly fine. I just wish I had something to do with myself once I actually woke up.

Appetite? Well... no, I haven't really noticed any change there. I mean, I still eat my three meals a day, just like I always have. It's funny, you'd think with everything feeling so flat and gray, I wouldn't want to eat, but my stomach still rumbles right on schedule. 

I usually start with a piece of toast in the morning—just plain white bread, usually Wonder Bread, because it toasts up so nice and crisp, you know? And I put a little pat of butter on it, the salted kind, because the unsalted just tastes like wax to me. I used to make eggs, sunny-side up, with a little sprinkle of black pepper, but the pan is just so heavy to wash these days, so toast it is. And for lunch, I usually have a bowl of soup. Campbell's, mostly. The Chicken Noodle is classic, of course, but sometimes I go for the Cream of Mushroom, especially if it's chilly out. I heat it up on the stove—never the microwave, it always heats unevenly in there, leaves cold spots in the middle—and I have a few saltines with it. 

And dinner is just whatever is easy. A frozen dinner, maybe a Salisbury steak or a piece of baked chicken. I don't really taste it much, to be honest. It's not like I sit there and think, "Oh, this is delicious," the way I used to when I'd make my pot roast with the little pearl onions and the carrots that get so soft they melt in your mouth. Now, eating is just something I do because the clock says it's time to do it. It's noon, so I eat soup. It's six o'clock, so I heat up a dinner. But the amount I'm eating, the actual appetite itself? No, that hasn't changed. I'm not eating any more or any less than I did before I retired. It's just... routine, I suppose. Just going through the motions of chewing and swallowing without any of the joy that used to come with a good meal.

Worthless? Oh, no, I wouldn't use that word. No, I don't feel worthless. I know I have value, doctor. I worked hard my whole life, you know? Started when I was just a girl, helping out, and I've always paid my own way, always kept a clean house. Even now, with everything feeling so gray and heavy, I still make sure the trash goes out on Tuesdays. The garbage men come so early, usually around 5:30 in the morning, and you can hear the big truck grinding its gears all the way down Elm Street. If you don't have the bins out the night before, they just drive right past, and then you're stuck with it for a whole week. And you know how melon rinds get in the summer if they sit too long. 

So no, I don't feel worthless. I just feel... empty. Like a pitcher that somebody poured all the water out of and just left sitting on the counter. It's still a perfectly good pitcher, it's not broken, it's not trash... it's just not doing anything. My sister, Brenda, she used to say that when people retire, they lose their purpose, and maybe that's what this is. But worthless? No. I still have my dignity, I still have my home. I just don't have any... any spark left to do anything with them. But I don't sit around thinking I'm a bad person or a waste of space, nothing like that. It's just this awful flatness.

Lost interest? Well... yes, doctor, I suppose I have. That's actually what brings me in, really. I just don't have the push I used to have for the things I used to do. It's like the starter motor is broken, you know? Like, take my quilting. I used to quilt all the time. I'd sit by the big window in the front room, the one that gets the good afternoon light, and I'd piece together these intricate patterns—Log Cabin, Flying Geese, Double Wedding Ring. I'd spend hours picking out the right calico fabrics at JoAnn's, matching the colors just so. But now... my sewing machine is just sitting there under its plastic cover. It's a Singer, a good heavy one from the seventies, not those plastic things they make now, but I haven't turned it on in months. 

And choir, too. I've been singing alto in the First Methodist choir for, oh, it has to be thirty years. We rehearse on Thursday nights, 7:00 PM sharp, and Pastor Miller is always so particular about us being on time. I used to love the harmonies, the way all our voices would blend together, especially on the old hymns like 'How Great Thou Art' or 'In the Garden.' But lately, I just... I don't go. I know they're expecting me, I know they're probably wondering where I am, maybe even a little short on altos, but I just can't bring myself to put my coat on and walk out the door. 

Same with visiting folks. I used to bake a nice lemon pound cake—the secret is a little bit of sour cream in the batter, makes it so moist—and go over to Brenda's or Mrs. Gable's just to chat and have coffee. But now, most days, I just sit at home in my recliner. It's a La-Z-Boy, the kind that rocks, in a sort of tan microfiber that doesn't show stains. I just sit there with the TV on low. Not even watching it, really. Just having it on so the house isn't so quiet. The Price is Right will be on, and I'll see the colors moving on the screen, but I don't care if they win the showcase showdown or not. I just sit there, knowing I should be doing something, knowing people are expecting me, but that push... it's just gone. Completely gone.

Enjoy things? Well... I suppose I try to think back on that, and it's hard to say. I mean, you say two years, but really, this whole thing, this... this heavy, gray feeling where the starter motor is just broken, like I said, it hasn't just been two years exactly. It’s been building, you see. It’s been building up ever since I retired from the school office, and that was a little over two years ago. 

I was the attendance secretary at Lincoln Elementary, you know. Oh, I knew every child’s name, and their parents’ names, and who was out with the chickenpox and who was just trying to skip a spelling test. I had my desk organized just so, with the pink slips for tardiness in the top left drawer and the blue slips for early dismissal right next to them. I had a whole system. And when I retired, they threw me a lovely party in the staff lounge. They had a sheet cake from Costco—half vanilla, half chocolate, with the buttercream frosting, not that whipped stuff that melts if the room gets too warm. They gave me a beautiful glass vase, too, heavy crystal, the kind that catches the light if you put it on the windowsill. 

But after that... after the cake was eaten and the vase was put on the shelf, that’s when it started building. At first, I thought I was just tired, you know? Just catching my breath after working all those years. I thought, "Oh, I’ll just rest a bit." But the resting never stopped. The quiet just got louder. So, to answer your question about enjoying things during this time... it’s just been a slow fade. Like a photograph left out in the sun too long, where the colors just sort of bleach out day by day. Since I left that school office, it’s just been creeping up on me, this... this nothingness. So, enjoy things? I don't know. Maybe right at the beginning, a little, before the gray really settled in, but it's been building for a while now.

Like I was just saying, doctor, it really has been building right since I walked out of that school office, which was a little over two years ago now. You ask if I felt like my usual self right after, and... well, maybe for just a handful of days? I remember waking up that very first Monday after my party—the one with the nice cake I told you about—and I didn't have to set my alarm clock. It’s a little wind-up one, brass on the top, loud enough to wake the dead. Usually I’d be up at 5:15 AM, brewing my coffee and making a little egg salad sandwich for my lunch, always with a dash of paprika in the mayonnaise. 

That first week, I thought, well, this is just a nice vacation. I felt okay then, I suppose. I even cleaned out the hall closet and folded all my bath towels so the blue ones were on the bottom and the white ones on top, making sure the tags were all tucked inside so it looked neat. But that didn't last. Once the closet was clean, there was nothing else to do. So there wasn't some long stretch of time where I was my old self, no. Like I said, it’s been building up ever since that retirement started two years ago. It just started quiet, you know, like dust settling in a room nobody uses anymore, and then it just kept piling up until the flat feeling took over completely.

Concentrating? Well... I don't know if I'd say I've had trouble concentrating, exactly. I mean, it's hard to say what trouble concentrating really looks like when you're just sitting in the recliner all day, isn't it? It's not like when I was at the school, where I had to keep track of Mrs. Higgins' third-grade class going on a field trip to the dairy farm, and make sure all twenty-two permission slips were signed and filed in the manila folder with the green label. That took concentration, making sure little Timmy didn't get on the bus without his inhaler. 

But now... I don't really have anything to concentrate *on*. Like I said, I'll have the TV on, maybe The Price is Right or sometimes Let's Make a Deal—though I never did care for Wayne Brady as much as Monty Hall, rest his soul, Monty just had such a nice way with the contestants, didn't he? Always so polite. Anyway, I'll have the TV on, and I'm not really paying attention to it, but it's not because I *can't* concentrate. It's just because I don't care to. I don't care if they guess the price of the Rice-A-Roni or the jet ski. 

And I suppose I still read my Bible sometimes, usually just a Psalm or two before I go to sleep. I keep it on the nightstand next to my little lamp with the fringed shade. I can read a Psalm just fine, read the words right off the page, so my mind isn't wandering off or anything like that. It's just that there's not much I'm trying to focus my mind on these days. So, no, I haven't really noticed any trouble with my concentration, doctor. Just... just the lack of wanting to do anything that needs it.

Well, taking care of things... I suppose it has, yes. I mean, it's not like I'm not eating or bathing—I still manage to make my little egg salad sandwich, and I always make sure to shower in the mornings, using that lavender soap my niece bought me for Christmas two years ago. It comes in a purple box with a little ribbon tied around it, so pretty you almost don't want to open it. But as for the other things, the things outside the house... yes, it's been getting in the way. 

You see, I used to be very involved at my church, St. Jude's on Elm Street. I was the choir director for... oh, it must have been twelve years. We had practice every Wednesday evening at 7:00 PM sharp, and I was always there early to set out the sheet music and make sure the piano was dusted. We sang all the traditional hymns, you know, "How Great Thou Art" and "Amazing Grace," none of that modern guitar nonsense they do at some of the other parishes now. But lately... lately I just haven't had the energy for it. I had to step back from leading the choir. I just couldn't bring myself to go, and I'd sit in my recliner thinking about how they were all waiting for me, and I just couldn't move. 

And it's not just the choir. I used to help out a lot with the projects down at the senior center, too. We were knitting little caps for the premature babies at the hospital—I was using a soft yellow yarn, very gentle on the skin. But I stopped going to that, too. I’d promise to bring in a batch of hats by Tuesday, and then Tuesday would come and go, and the yarn would just sit in the basket next to my chair, untouched. I just couldn't keep up with what I promised. It got to the point where I felt so guilty, but even the guilt wasn't enough to make me pick up the knitting needles. 

Now, my friends from church, like Martha and Susan—Susan is the one who always brings those wonderful lemon bars to the potlucks, with the powdered sugar on top—they've started calling me more often. They come by to check on me, bringing casseroles and asking if I need anything from the grocery store. They never used to do that. They know something's not right, even if I try to tell them I'm just resting. So, yes, doctor, I suppose this heavy feeling has been interfering with the things I used to do, quite a bit.

Tired? Low on energy? Well, I suppose you could say that, but it's not tired like I used to get tired. You know, when I was working at the school, by Friday afternoon I'd be absolutely exhausted. My feet would ache from standing on that hard linoleum floor all day, and my head would be spinning from all the phone calls and the children running in and out. That was a good tired, though. You'd come home, take your shoes off—I had these sensible navy blue pumps, Dr. Scholl's, very good for the arches—and you'd sit down with a cup of tea, maybe Earl Grey with just a splash of milk, and you'd feel like you earned your rest. 

But this... this isn't like that. I'm not doing anything to *be* tired, am I? Like I said, I'm just sitting in my recliner. It's a La-Z-Boy, a nice sage green color, very comfortable, but you shouldn't get tired just sitting in it all day. I sleep alright, I think. I put my head on the pillow—I use a down alternative because the real feathers always poke through the casing and scratch my cheek—and I sleep through the night. But when I wake up, I don't feel refreshed. I don't feel that spring in my step like I used to. 

It's more like... like my limbs are made of lead. Just getting up to make that egg salad sandwich feels like I'm dragging weights behind me. So I wouldn't say it's exactly that I'm tired, doctor, not in the normal sense of the word. It's just that the energy... well, it's just not there anymore. It's like a car that's run completely out of gas, just sitting in the driveway, and no matter how much you turn the key, the engine just won't catch.

Two weeks? Well... I couldn't rightly point to any specific two weeks on the calendar, doctor. You see, when you're just sitting in the house all day, the days just sort of blend into one another. I have this calendar hanging on the refrigerator—it’s one of those free ones they give you down at the pharmacy on Main Street, the one with the pictures of the national parks. October has a beautiful picture of the Grand Canyon, all those red and orange rocks, just lovely. I used to take a little red marker and put an 'X' through every day before I went to bed, just to keep track of things. But lately, I haven't even been doing that. The red marker is just sitting there in the little ceramic mug I keep my pens in. 

So I don't really keep track of the weeks anymore. But as for it getting noticeably worse... no, I wouldn't say it ever dipped down worse than usual. It hasn't been like a rollercoaster, you know, going up and down and making your stomach drop. It’s just been one long, flat stretch. It actually reminds me of when my late husband Arthur and I drove out through the Midwest in our old Ford station wagon—it was powder blue with that fake wood paneling on the side, a real boat of a car. We drove through Nebraska, and it was just flat, flat, flat, as far as the eye could see, for hours on end. You'd look out the window and nothing ever changed. 

That’s exactly how this feeling is. It’s just the same heavy, flat feeling every single day, from the time I wake up until I turn off my little fringed lamp at night. It doesn't get heavier, but it doesn't lift, either. So, no, I haven't had any particular two weeks where it took a sudden turn for the worse. Just the same steady flatness, day in and day out.

Oh, yes, doctor. Very much so. It hasn't gone away at all, even though the retirement is well in the past now. Honestly... well, this whole thing, this heavy, flat feeling, it's been building since I retired from the school office. That was a little over two years ago now. 

I remember my last day so clearly. It was a Friday in late spring, and the principal, Mr. Henderson—such a tall man, he always wore those sweater vests with the little argyle patterns on the front—he brought in a sheet cake from the bakery down on 4th Street. It was vanilla with that whipped frosting, not the heavy buttercream, because he knew my stomach can't handle too much rich butter. They gave me a lovely little plaque, brass with my name engraved on it, thanking me for all my years keeping that front desk running and answering those ringing phones. I packed up my things, including that little ceramic mug I keep my pens in, put it all in a cardboard box, and I thought... well, I thought, now I’m going to have all this time to do my knitting and my church work and tend to my hydrangeas. I have the blue ones out front, you know, and you have to put coffee grounds in the soil to keep them that pretty color, otherwise they turn pink. 

But... instead of doing all those things, I just sort of came home, set that cardboard box on the kitchen counter, and sat down in my chair. And it’s just been building ever since that very afternoon. A little over two years of just... sinking deeper into it. At first, I told myself I was just taking a few days to rest after all those years of working, but then the resting just never stopped, did it? The days turned into weeks, and the weeks into months, and here we are, two whole years later, and I’m still just feeling so terribly flat. It didn't happen all at once, like a light switch turning off. It just sort of crept up on me, building and building, day by day, since the moment I walked out of that school office for the last time.

Stresses? From the retirement? Well, no, not really. I mean, the retirement itself was quite straightforward. As I was saying, Mr. Henderson gave me that lovely plaque, and my pension paperwork was all sorted out by the district office weeks in advance. I had a very nice lady named Brenda help me with it—she had these beautiful, thick glasses with little rhinestones in the corners, very stylish for her age. She made sure all my forms were signed in triplicate, so the checks just started coming in the mail right on schedule, the first of every month, like clockwork. 

So, financially, there hasn't been any stress. Arthur—bless his soul—he left me the house free and clear, so I don't have a mortgage to worry about. It’s a sturdy little brick ranch, built in the fifties, very solid bones. The only thing that ever gives me trouble is the gutters getting clogged with leaves from the big oak tree in the front yard, but the neighbor boy, Timmy, he comes over and cleans them out for a few dollars. He’s a good boy, always polite, always says 'Yes, ma'am' and 'No, ma'am.' 

So, no, there hasn't been any stress about money or losing the house or anything like that. And I don't have to worry about getting up and fighting the traffic on Route 9 anymore, which used to be a terrible headache, especially when it rained and people forgot how to drive. It's just... quiet. The house is quiet, the street is quiet. There's no stress, doctor. There's just... nothing. Just me and the recliner and the clock ticking on the mantelpiece. It's an anniversary clock, the kind with the little gold balls that spin around at the bottom. Arthur bought it for our 25th wedding anniversary. It's very pretty, but when the house is this quiet, you can hear every single tick. Tick, tick, tick. But no, no stress. Just... just the quiet.

Yeah, pretty much every day. Most mornings I just... I wake up with this heavy, hollow feeling. It's like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor. And it just kind of stays with me.

No, I... I don't think I did anything wrong. I mean, I'm not a bad person or anything. I don't feel like I'm being punished. It's just... I just feel low all the time, but it's not because I feel guilty about something I did.
Well, I guess... those thoughts about the neighbors and the office people watching me, sending those notes... it's been going on for about a year and a month now.

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, the depression has been there a lot, but... there was a spell of several weeks where I was actually eating a bit better. That part never stopped.
No, I haven't really noticed that. I mean, I don't go out of my way to talk to people much anyway, but I don't think I'm talking any less than normal when I do.
No, I haven't. Um... I've never had a doctor tell me I have any kind of brain problem or nerve condition. Nothing like that.
No, not really. I mean, I still get up and do what I need to do around the house. I wouldn't say I've lost the drive to do everyday things, no.
No, I can't say I've ever felt like that. My thoughts are my own. I don't feel like anybody or anything else is pulling the strings up there, if that's what you mean.
No, I don't think so. I mean, I still feel things pretty much the way I always have. I haven't noticed my emotions feeling flat or anything like that.
No, nothing like that. Like I was saying a minute ago, my thoughts are just my own. I don't have any outside forces or anyone trying to put things in my head.

Yeah, I'd say so. It's been going on for a lot longer than two weeks, really. Most mornings I just wake up with this... this heavy, hollow feeling inside. It's like the day already went bad before I even get my feet on the floor. And that feeling just kind of stays with me pretty much the whole day.

Yeah, I have. I used to really look forward to things. Like choir practice, playing bridge, cooking a pot of beans on Sundays... even just doing little repair jobs for folks. But now, I mostly just let the phone ring. I just tell myself there's no point in going or doing any of it anymore.

Yeah, that's actually the main reason I came in. I just know the people at my apartment are watching my comings and goings. They keep slipping notes about me to the front office. Everybody keeps telling me it's just standard notices taped to the doors, but I know what they're really doing.

Yeah, there was. A while back, there was a spell of several weeks where... well, I was actually eating a bit better, and I wasn't waking up feeling so hopeless every single morning. The heavy feeling kind of lifted for a bit. But even then, I still knew the neighbors were watching my door. I still knew they were reporting on me to the office. That never stopped, even when my mood was better.
No, I can't say I have. I've never seen anything that wasn't really there, or anything like that. It's just the stuff with the neighbors I told you about.

Yeah, it definitely has. I've... well, I've fallen behind on my bills, and I keep missing appointments. I actually stopped showing up for church and the volunteer work I used to do, too. It's just getting too hard to keep my days organized. And honestly, I just don't trust ordinary interactions with people anymore, not with everything going on. So, yeah, my day-to-day life has definitely taken a hit.

Yeah, I've heard that a few times. People say they can't follow what I'm saying. Like, I'll try to explain something... I'll start talking about the rent, and then I'll mention the marina, and then the choir robes, and the wires in the walls. And they just look at me like I skipped half the story. I guess it all connects in my head, but it doesn't come out right for them.

Well... I suppose it's my sleep. It's become completely unmoored lately. 

At first, I was waking up after just two or three hours... drafting plans, feeling ready to go. But now... I don't know. I just lie awake before dawn. My stomach gets tight. There's just... no sense of rest anymore.

I... suppose you could say that. Yes. I just felt very capable. 

I... well, I truly believed I was going to single-handedly repair my retirement accounts. I thought I could advise three different start-ups, and... I had this whole plan to turn the local arts council into some sort of regional powerhouse. 

It's uncomfortable to admit now, but... at the time, it just seemed like my judgment was suddenly superior to everyone else's. That's all.

Well, doctor, it's... it's a long story, but I suppose the main reason I'm sitting here today is because of the things I've been noticing lately. My wife, Mary, she gets so frustrated with me. She tells me, "Arthur, it's just talk, they're just talking about the weather or the game," but she doesn't hear it the way I do. Alcohol? Oh, no, no, doctor. I haven't been a drinking man for... oh, it's got to be decades now. She runs a tight ship, my Mary. If she even smelled a drop of spirits on my breath, she'd have me sleeping on the davenport, stiff knees and all. So, no, doctor, no heavy drinking here. Memory? Well... I suppose that depends on what you mean, doctor. If you mean, do I forget where I put my reading glasses? Sure, I do that. But who doesn't at my age? Mary always finds them right where I left them and gives me that look she has. You know the one. 

But my real memory? The important things? No, that's sharp as a tack. I can tell you the starting lineup for the '55 Dodgers, clear as a bell. I can tell you exactly what the weather was like the day Mary and I got married—it was unseasonably warm for October, and the leaves were just starting to turn that bright orange down by the creek. Sometimes Mary will say, "Arthur, I told you to take the trash out," and I'll tell her she never said any such thing. But that's not me forgetting, doctor. A head injury? Or a stroke? Oh, goodness, no, doctor. The Good Lord has spared me from all that, thankfully. The ladder slipped right out from under me in the mud. I came down hard and whacked my head on the stone birdbath. Mary came running out the screen door with a dish towel and a bag of frozen peas, hollering that I was going to be the death of her. 

But I haven't done anything foolish like that in a long, long time. When you get to be eighty-four, doctor, you learn to take things slow. You have to, really. You rush around, you trip on a throw rug, and the next thing you know you've broken a hip and you're lying in a hospital bed catching who-knows-what from the other patients. So I hold onto the banister when I take the stairs, I watch exactly where I step, and I just stay out of harm's way. So no, no recent illnesses or injuries or any of those terrible things you just mentioned. Just an old man trying to keep his footing, that's all.

Hard to follow? Making sense? Well, doctor, I wouldn't say that at all. Not at all. I mean, sure, sometimes Mary will give me that look—the one I told you about, where her eyebrows go all the way up to her hairline—and she'll say, "Arthur, what on earth are you going on about now?" But that's just Mary. She's got her mind on her knitting patterns or the price of ground chuck at the A&P, and she just isn't paying attention to the bigger picture. 

I speak perfectly clearly, if you ask me. I take my time, I lay out all the facts, just like I'm doing with you right now. You have to explain things properly, don't you think? If you just give a yes or no, people miss all the important details. Like the other day, I was down at the hardware store—the one on Elm Street, not the big new one out by the highway, I don't care for that one, it's too bright and the aisles are too wide, it doesn't smell like a hardware store should—anyway, I was talking to young Jimmy behind the counter about the right kind of nails for fixing a loose board on the back porch, and I was explaining to him how the wood swells in the humidity we've been having. I told him all about how the weather patterns have been changing, and how it ties into those messages I've been picking up on, the ones the government is sending through the television static. Jimmy just stared at me with his mouth half open, like a fish out of water, and then he said, "Mr. Higgins, I just need to know if you want galvanized or not." 

But that's not me being hard to follow, doctor. That's just young people today. They don't have the patience to listen to a full thought. They want everything in a hurry, zip-zip-zip, on those little phones they're always staring at. If they'd just slow down and listen to how all the pieces connect—the weather, the wood, the static, the warnings—they'd see it makes perfect sense. So no, I don't think I'm hard to understand. Lost interest? Well... I suppose it's not so much losing interest as it is... just not having the energy for it all anymore. I still love my family, doctor, don't get me wrong. Used to be, I'd be out in the garden at the crack of dawn. I used to enjoy that so much, feeling the dirt on my hands. And choir practice! Every Thursday evening down at the First Methodist, rain or shine, I was there. I've sung bass in that choir for forty-two years. 

But now... I don't know. Many days I just... I get up, I put my robe on, and I just sit at the kitchen table. Mary will pour me a cup of coffee, and I'll just sit there looking out the window at the bird feeder. The squirrels get into it, you know, they're terrible pests, but I don't even go out to chase them away anymore. I just sit there and say very little. Mary will ask me if I want to go to choir, or if I'm going to finally pull those dandelions that are taking over the front walk, and I just... I let it go by. I don't feel like moving. How long? Well, now, let me think on that a minute, doctor. Time has a funny way of slipping by when you're not punching a time clock anymore, and the days sort of bleed into one another when you're just sitting around the house. But if I really sit down and trace it back... yes, it's been about nine months now. 

I remember specifically because it was right around the time Mary decided we absolutely had to have the living room carpets steam-cleaned. We had to sit out on the back porch for practically the whole afternoon while the rugs dried out, just staying out of the way. That was the very first time I really noticed the voices out there. Just murmuring, you know, right underneath the sound of Mary's wind chimes. 

And the messages on the television, those started right around the same time, maybe a few days later when we finally moved our chairs back into the living room and turned the set on. Now, it hasn't been every single day, mind you. It's not like a radio that's left on all the time. It's been happening on and off. Sometimes I'll go a week, maybe two, and the television static is just regular old static, and the porch is perfectly quiet except for the crickets and the neighborhood dogs. But then, sure enough, the patterns come back and the voices start up again, trying to tell me things. So yes, I'd say it's been going on just like that, on and off, for a solid nine months now. Mary thinks I'm just losing my hearing and getting confused by the neighbors' conversations, but I know what I'm picking up on. Nine months is a long time to be paying attention to something, doctor, you don't just imagine that.

Seeing things? No, no, doctor, I wouldn't say that. But as for seeing people or things that aren't really there? No, nothing like that. The Good Lord gave me enough trouble with my joints, I suppose He decided to spare my eyes for the most part. 

But... well, since we're talking about things that maybe other folks aren't picking up on... it's not so much the seeing, it's the hearing. I know I mentioned those murmurs on the porch earlier, but there's something else, too. 

Some afternoons, when the house gets completely quiet—you know, when Mary goes off to her sister's house to play cards and the television is switched off—the house just settles. It gets so still you can hear the refrigerator humming all the way from the front room. And on those quiet afternoons, I hear my old friend. 

It's the strangest thing, but it's as real as you sitting there in that chair. I'll hear him call my name, "Arthur," right from the back porch. Or sometimes he doesn't say my name at all, he'll just be out there humming a choir song. We sang together in the First Methodist choir for decades, you see, so I know his voice anywhere. He always had this rich, steady baritone, and I'll hear him humming "The Old Rugged Cross" or maybe "Rock of Ages." And it is so clear, doctor. Confused about where I am? Oh, no, no. No, doctor, I know exactly where I am. I've lived in the same house on Elm Street for, oh, it must be fifty-two years now. Mary and I bought that place right after the youngest was born. It's a sturdy house, you know, built back when they actually cared about the framing. And as for what day it is... well, now, that's a slightly different story, but not because I'm confused, mind you. I know it's the present day, I know who the president is—though sometimes I wish I didn't, if you catch my drift—and I know I'm sitting right here in this office with you. 

I suppose the only time I ever get a little turned around is... well, maybe when I'm listening to my friend humming out on the porch.
